en: Preface to the Explanatory Glossary of Terms and Meanings in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
As for the teaching of the Vinaya, it is the precious raft for the three vehicles and the cloud-stairway for the four pairs of noble ones.
All Buddhas have attained Bodhi by means of it; all sages have ascended to Nirvāṇa through it. It is like a bright pearl, and may be compared to—
It is pure and snow-white. The outer assembly is not permitted to participate in its transmission; it is bestowed in secret by the inner disciples.

The Triple Gem relies upon it to manifest its glory, and the five classes of followers depend upon it to be established. How weighty is this Dharma! Long ago, at the Golden River, the final instructions were given once more.

Upāli succeeded in proclaiming [the teachings]. The sages of the Western Regions, teacher and disciple, received them with solemn reverence and divided the *kaṭhina* (woolen cloth) to transmit and uphold them for over a thousand years.

Upon reaching the Eastern Lands, they were first heard of during the Han and Wei dynasties; they gradually became complete during the Qi and Liang; and they flourished greatly during the Sui and Tang.

From the Song dynasty down to the present day, everyone has taken these as their primary studies, all emerging from the cage of worldly existence. Monks alike follow these rules, and all transcend to the further shore. In recent times...

Erroneous points were raised against one another, and Chan and Vinaya practitioners vied with each other in their divisions. Since their views differed, there was inevitably error in how they received and transmitted the teachings.

This resulted in later generations having no gateway for entry and beginners losing the proper order of practice. When opening a scroll, they did not recognize its name; following the text, how could they possibly understand its meaning?

I, Zan, have come to preside over this altar; my endeavor is akin to that of a bird returning to its dark nest. It is I who, with wings outstretched, have sought through the Three Piṭakas and eyes wide open, have hunted through the multitude of texts.
Examining the Sanskrit language of the Western Heaven to interpret the phonetic discussions of this Eastern Flower [China], I have specifically adopted the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya.

Regarding all passages therein that are difficult to penetrate, I have merely noted their names and then composed a commentary to explain their meaning, drawing extensively from the arguments of various schools to establish the correct interpretation.

In expounding upon the profound mysteries of the sūtras and śāstras, although I have cited essential passages from the four classes of scriptures, I have not intermingled them with their respective sectarian lineages.
This is for fear that such confusion would disrupt the rules of observance and transgression, making it difficult to maintain proper protection and restraint.

What has been related herein consists entirely of general practices and a brief elucidation of what is permitted and what is prohibited, so that one may understand the similarities and differences between observance and transgression. It is not intended to substitute minor articles for major sections, nor to diminish the great.
Transgressions are easily committed as minor offenses; this is because the Sage’s intention fundamentally did not permit them, and the purport of the Vinaya completely prohibits them.

If the thieving mind is not severed, it is difficult to speak of faith and precepts. For this reason, I have singled out one section to provide explanations according to specific matters, so as not to conflict with other schools.

This is intended for beginners so that they may read through the volume without obstruction, and for those who review it so that they need not look elsewhere, ensuring they do not become confused by the text or lose its essential meaning. My intent is...

Having departed from that place, he raised his hand toward the high pavilion and never looked back again for the rest of his life. From this point on, the study of the Vinaya was abruptly halted, and the Jewel of the Sangha gradually declined.

Reflecting upon these matters, I venture to present this brief report, compiled into sections and chapters, which systematically explains the phenomena of the teachings and briefly clarifies their essential principles.

As for the rules of opening and closing, maintaining and violating, these are fully detailed in the Vinaya commentaries; likewise, regarding the nature of the precepts, their prohibitions, and their gravity— [The remainder of the text follows as provided in the source.]
By studying this, one will immediately attain [realization]. To counteract afflictions and delusions, the essential requirement is profound investigation; this has not been elaborated upon here.

Furthermore, how could someone of shallow understanding like myself exhaustively fathom its deep treasury? I await the time when my learning is sufficient and the light of the precepts shines forth naturally of itself.

As for all other minute and subtle esoteric tracks, they shall be presented in the commentary on the Vinaya (*Śīlaskandha-vibhāṣā*). What is indicated here first will not be repeated later, as the intent of that commentary makes the principles easily manifest.
Having obtained the threads, the binding has now been completed. Yet, I am ashamed of my mediocre talent, fearing it cannot avoid the deception of selling diluted milk.

As for what is missing, doubtful, or incomplete, I entrust it all to future sages to together illuminate the Southern Pole, to make the jewel of the precepts shine through the long night, and to brighten the sun of wisdom in the midst of heaven.
May the True Dharma endure forever and the holy stages remain firm and eternal—this is my joyous aspiration.
The wise discern all things.
Written on a summer day in the gengwu year of the Chongzhen era by the śramaṇa Hongzan, who cherishes the Great Bodhicitta. Foreword.

Tracing back to the silent proclamation of Śāriputra, followed by the continued exposition of Upāli, reciting the words of the Tathāgata, the text fills eighty fascicles. Entitled:
It is said that there is the Vinaya of the Eighty Recitations (*Aśīti-saṃgīti*). First, it was received upon the crown of the head by Kāśyapa; next, it was upheld by Ānanda;
third, by Madhyāntika; fourth, by Śāṇavāsa; and fifth, by Upagupta. These are the five masters.
The essence of expedient means opens the Way, transmitted and upheld in succession for over one hundred and ten years, with the lineage of transmission remaining unchanged.
Later, King Aśoka reigned over the world; he venerated the Triple Gem and convened a great assembly of the monastic community to recompile the Tripiṭaka.

At that time, the bhikṣus each held their own views and experiences, excerpting and editing the Sūtras and Vinaya, each citing the teachings of their own masters to compose formal records and documents. These were cited...

Holding different views, they eventually split into two schools. Accusing one another of being right or wrong, they sought a royal adjudication. They cast white and black voting sticks to represent their respective factions—the new and the old.
At that time, those who took the old [view] were numerous; because they were the majority, they became known as such, and thus the school was named Mahāsāṃghika (the Great Assembly).
This is the Mahāsāṃghika school. Those who adopted the new [teachings] were few; they were the Sthaviras, so named from "Sthavira" (Elder).
They are called Tāmraśāṭīya, which is the Sthavira school. Thus, these two schools produced eighteen sub-sects over the course of two hundred years.
Among these eighteen schools, five served as the primary pillars; therefore, the present sūtras and vinayas...

The treatise was thus established in five schools. The first is called the Dharmaguptaka (alternatively *Dharmagupta*; this is translated as "Mirror of the Dharma," "Treasury of the Dharma," or "Secret of the Dharma"). The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples shall receive, uphold, transcribe, read, and recite the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures, yet they shall explain them erroneously; therefore, they shall conceal the Treasury of the Dharma. To say "conceal" (*yin fu*) carries the meaning of "secret" (*mi*).

As for the person's name, it is Dharmagupta; as for the name of the dharma, it is the *Caturvarga-vinaya*. The second is the Sarvāstivāda (the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-ki* states: "This means 'Proponents of All That Exists. It is so named because...")

As for the "Existents" (Sarvāstivāda): the doctrinal tenets of the other schools differ. The Sarvāstivādins maintain that the past, future, present, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) each possess their own intrinsic nature; therefore, they are called "All-Existents. The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, he studies, recites, and transcribes non-Buddhist scriptures;

he understands the three times as well as the internal and external; he refutes non-Buddhists and is skilled in debate; he explains all natures and is fully qualified to receive the precepts; whatever questions or challenges are posed, he is able to answer them all. For this reason, he is named Sarvāstivāda.

The name of the Dharma is the *Daśabhāṇavāra*. The *Lidai Sanbao Ji* states: "In the past, Mahākāśyapa fully upheld the Dharma-piṭaka, transmitting it down to the fifth patriarch, Upagupta. The original text consisted of eighty recitations (*bhāṇavāra*). Upagupta, by..."

Those of dull faculties in later generations were unable to receive [the teachings] in their entirety; therefore, they were abridged into the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), which takes "recitation" (*bhaṇa*) as its name, signifying that the Dharma should be recited and upheld. Regarding the differences in their doctrinal tenets: the Sarvāstivāda school maintains that all three time periods exist—what has been, what is currently being, and what will be.

"What will be" refers to the future. The Dharmaguptaka school maintains that the past and future are non-existent, while only the present exists. (Other matters need not be discussed at length). Third, the Kāśyapīya (translated as "The View of Repeated Emptiness").

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states: "It is taught that there is no self nor any experiencer; one turns away from all afflictions as if they were a corpse. Therefore, it is named Kāśyapīya. The Dharma is called liberation (*vimukti*). It ceases...

The *Vinayamokṣa-sūtra* (解脫戒本經), one fascicle, has arrived here; it is identical to the [Mahīśāsaka] *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. Some say that the Sanskrit original has already arrived but has not yet been translated.

Fourth is the Mahīśāsaka (meaning "contemplation that does not cling to existence or non-existence"). The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states: "One does not form the notion of earth, nor the notions of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; for this reason, it is called Mahīśāsaka. Its Dharma is named the *Pañcavargika*.

Fifth is the Vātsīputrīya (meaning "Calf"). In ancient times there was a rishi who begot a son by a cow; since then, those of this lineage have all been named "Calf" (*Vatsa*). This school maintains that the self is neither identical to the aggregates (*skandha*) nor separate from them, yet there exists a real self.

The Vinaya-mūla does not arrive [here]. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* says: "They all claim there is a self and do not speak of the characteristic of emptiness; they are like small children. For this reason, they are called Vatsaputra.
Thus, regarding the regulations established by the five schools—whether light or heavy, permitted or prohibited—the major points are no different, yet the minor details are not without variation.

This is also because in the past, the Dharma King skillfully responded to the various capacities of sentient beings, transforming them according to their faculties, or establishing teachings in accordance with the time and place.

Some regulations are established according to the suitability of one's disposition; some are prohibited in this region but permitted in another, while others are permitted for one person but prohibited for another.
Because their fundamental bases differ, the transmission of the Dharma is not uniform. This is the origin of what the five schools maintain.

All were spoken personally by the Tathāgata; it was only because [the teachings] were not heard extensively and were recited with omissions that each followed one particular aspect, resulting in many divergences.
Furthermore, as time passed since the Sage’s passing, such was the natural course of the Dharma’s destiny.

For this reason, while the Tathāgata was still in the world, there appeared the omen of a dream of a layered-wool staff breaking; the Buddha gave a prophetic prediction that the Sūtras and Vinaya would eventually be divided into five schools.
Regarding the eighteen branches [of the lineage], as the Heavenly Being replied to Nanshan:

"Thirty-eight years after the World-Honored One attained enlightenment, he took the old alms bowl left behind by Kāśyapa Buddha. Having attended the royal feast in Rājagṛha, he commanded the Venerable Rāhula to wash it at the Dragon Pond.
Losing his grip, he dropped it, and it shattered into five pieces. Furthermore, there was a householder who dreamed—"
A single bolt of wool split itself into five pieces, and both [incidents] were reported to the Buddha. The Buddha then prophesied:
"After my parinirvāṇa, the Sūtras and Vinaya shall be divided into five schools. Furthermore, King Bimbisāra dreamed that a golden staff broke into eighteen segments;
filled with fear, he questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said: "More than one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a King Aśoka whose majesty..."
Furthermore, Jambudvīpa, at that time the various bhikṣus shall teach eighteen divisions that lead to the gate of liberation; their ultimate goal is one and the same. This is the omen;
therefore, O King, do not grieve over it. Thus, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says:
"Although these five schools differ in name, none of them obstruct the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas or the Great Nirvāṇa. By relying upon them to practice, all [attain the goal]."

They attain liberation. Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, “In the future, my disciples shall consist of twenty schools (*nikāya*), which will be able to cause all dharmas to abide.
These twenty schools shall all attain the four fruits [of the śramaṇa];
the Tripitaka shall be equal, without distinction of inferior, middling, or superior. It is like the water of the ocean, whose taste is no different; it is as if a person has twenty [fingers].”
"Son, this is what the Tathāgata has truly spoken. Mañjuśrī, the two fundamental divisions arise from the Mahāyāna;
they arise from the Prajñāpāramitā. Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas—all emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā.
Just as earth, water, fire, wind, and space are the dwelling places for all sentient beings, so too is the Prajñā..."
The pāramitās, as well as the Mahāyāna—the source from which all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas emerge—are described in verse:
"The eighteen and the two original schools All emerge from the Mahāyāna; There is neither 'is' nor 'is not'; I say they will arise in the future.
Regarding the statement "the two original schools," these are the Mahāsāṃghika and Sthavira schools. As for the Mahāsāṃghika school, it split...
Seven schools emerged from the Sthavira [School]. From the Sthavira, eleven schools branched out; together with the two root schools, they constitute twenty schools in total.
However, regarding the names and numbers of these various schools, as found in various sūtras, śāstras, and biographical records, the designations differ from one another.
The numbers vary, sometimes increasing and sometimes decreasing. Some derive the eighteen schools from five, while others claim they emerged from four.
In some accounts, within a single millennium, they gradually increased to five hundred. Since these explanations are not uniform, it is difficult to provide a detailed account based on them.
Here, I shall adopt the general consensus and what is commonly heard; speaking of them both collectively and individually, approximately:

It consists of six schools. As stated in the *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Preface): "There are six schools in total and in distinction. The *Mahāsāṃghika* is the general [school], while the preceding five are the specific ones.
Because the practitioners and understanding of this *Mahāsāṃghika* school are open and pervasive, they do not give rise to biased attachments;

they universally accord with the five views because their practice is universal. Thus we know that the *Mahāsāṃghika* is the general [school] and the five schools are the specific ones. Taken together, there are six schools. Now, regarding this...
Regarding the versions currently transmitted, only four *nikāyas* remain; the *Kāśyapīya* and *Vātsīputrīya* texts are missing.
However, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* was classified by various masters of antiquity as an abridged version, not a complete manuscript from India.

This is because its text is sparse, consisting of only forty fascicles, and its meaning does not encompass the doctrines of the five *nikāyas*. Furthermore, it should not be considered [the full canon].

The *Jixuaji* (Collection of Predictions) is likely an abridged version of the *Guang* (Extensive Vinaya). Other texts such as the *Shanjian*, *Vinayamātṛkā*, *Mātṛkā*, *Pinaye*, and the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* are all branches of the Vinaya, or perhaps one or two among the five hundred [Vinaya texts]. These various schools have all been personally prophesied by the Buddha; there is no need for laborious doubt that they might be right or wrong based on differences in their names and titles.
It is like one lamp producing hundreds of thousands of lamps: though the lamps differ according to the objects they illuminate, the light itself is one.
In its function of destroying darkness and dispelling gloom, there is no duality. Thus, throughout the various kingdoms of the Five Indias, [they follow...]
By upholding this single Dharma, all shall attain the fruits of the Way. Throughout the Eastern Land (China) since ancient times, the fourfold assembly has practiced it entirely;

they have maintained the traces of the precepts in unison and all have ascended to the realization of the sages. Truly, this is like nectar cast among humanity; as long as one partakes of it, there is none who does not have their hunger and famine removed.
(Upagupta—also called Upagupta; this translates as "Near Protector. The Buddha formerly prophesied: "After my parinirvāṇa, Upagupta shall be a Buddha without marks.")
He performed great deeds of Buddha-work. After my passing, he will be the foremost in teaching and transforming disciples. Aśoka—translated here as "Sorrowless"—is King Aśoka.
