The Vinaya Piṭaka is called *piṭaka* in Sanskrit, which is translated here as "basket" (*zàng*). This carries the meaning of "containing" and "upholding. Without a basket, there would be no way to accumulate wealth;
without a basket, there would be no way to store texts and meanings. The *Śāstrasaṃgraha* asks: "What is meant by 'basket' (*piṭaka*)? Because it is able..."
Because it encompasses; that is to say, it encompasses all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) so as not to allow them to be dispersed.

Therefore, it is called a "pitaka" (*piṭaka*). Furthermore, "pitaka" means a "receptacle" (*bhājana*). A receptacle is that which can gather together many meanings. (These initial explanations will not be repeated later; readers should take note of this.)
Buddhayaśas—whose name means "Awakened Fame" in the language of Qin—was a native of Jibin in Northern India, born into the Brahmin caste. In his youth, he followed the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas).
Once, a śramaṇa came to his house to beg for alms; his father became enraged and ordered someone to beat him. Consequently, the father’s hands and feet [became paralyzed].
He was unable to walk or stand. He then consulted a diviner, who said, "You have offended a worthy person; it is the work of spirits and ghosts.

He immediately invited this śramaṇa to sincerely repent for his transgression, and after several days, he recovered. Consequently, he caused Yaśas to leave the household life as the śramaṇa’s disciple.
At that time, Yaśas was thirteen years old. He constantly accompanied his teacher on long journeys through the wilderness.
They encountered a tiger. The Master wished to flee and hide, but Yaśas said, "This tiger is already full; it will certainly not harm people. Shortly thereafter, the tiger departed.

As they proceeded further, they indeed saw the remains of meat. The Master marveled at this in secret. When he reached the age of fifteen, he could recite fifty to sixty thousand words of scripture each day.
However, because he went out daily to beg for alms, his practice of recitation and study was neglected. There was an arhat who held him in high regard.
He was intelligent and quick-witted. His patrons constantly provided him with alms. By the age of nineteen, he had recited several million words of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras.

However, because his character was simple and haughty, he was not highly regarded by the other monks. When he reached the age for full ordination (*upasampadā*), no one came forward to preside over the ceremony;
thus, until nearly his twentieth year, he remained a *śrāmaṇera*. He then followed his maternal uncle to study the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). In the world...

He was well-versed in various arts and incantations. His deportment was elegant and his speech refined; he possessed a gentle smile that caused those who saw him to forget all sense of strangeness or reproach.

At twenty-seven, he received full ordination and made the recitation of scriptures his primary task. He never let go of his scrolls from his hands, and whenever he sat upright to contemplate their meaning, he would remain unaware as the time passed unnoticed.
Such was his single-minded devotion. Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Śākala. At that time...
Prince Dharmaputra (which in the language of Qin means "Son of the Dharma") observed that his appearance and attire were dignified and elegant, and asked where he had come from.
Yaśas responded with lucid eloquence, and the prince was delighted by him; he subsequently invited him into the palace to provide for his needs, treating him with great honor and generosity.
Kumārajīva arrived later and studied under him; they held one another in profound respect.
Kumārajīva returned to Kucha with his mother, while Guṇabhadra remained behind. Shortly thereafter, the king passed away and the crown prince ascended the throne.
While the king’s grandson was still the prince, Fu Jian dispatched Lü Guang to attack Kucha. The King of Kucha urgently sought military aid from [Guṇabhadra].
Shache. King Shache personally led his troops to rescue him. He sent Yaśas to remain and assist the crown prince, entrusting him with future governance.
Before the relief army had arrived, Kucha was already defeated. Upon returning, the king recounted in detail how Kumārajīva had been captured by Lü Guang, whereupon he sighed and said:
"Although I have known Kumārajīva for a long time, we have not yet fully shared our inner thoughts."

Suddenly becoming a captive, when shall we meet again? After staying for more than ten years, the King passed away; he then traveled to Kucha, where the propagation of the Dharma was very flourishing.

At that time, Kumārajīva was in Guzang (present-day Suzhou Road, within the domain of Yongzhou). He sent a messenger to invite him, and as he prepared his provisions to depart, the people of the country requested that he remain.
He stayed for another year or so and said to his disciples: "I wish to seek out Kumārajīva; you may [proceed]."
They packed their belongings secretly and set out at night, ensuring no one knew of their departure. A disciple said, "I fear that if we are pursued by dawn, we will not avoid having to return.
Guṇavarman then took a bowl of clear water, cast medicinal herbs into it, and recited several dozen words of incantation.
He gave the water to his disciple to wash his feet, and they immediately departed in the night. By the time dawn arrived, they had traveled several hundred li. He asked the disciple:
"What did he perceive? He replied, "I heard only the sound of a violent wind; tears simply flowed from my eyes.

Yaśas then gave him consecrated water to wash his feet, and they rested. The next morning, the people of the country pursued them, but having already traveled several hundred li, they could not catch up.
They reached Guzang, but Kumārajīva had already entered Chang'an. It was heard that Yao Xing had pressed him into service with concubines and handmaidens.
He urged [the king] to act contrary to the Dharma, sighing, "Kumārajīva is like fine cotton; how can one allow him to enter among thorns?

When Kumārajīva heard that [Fu] Xing had arrived in Guzang, he urged Xing to welcome him. Xing did not yet accept this. Shortly thereafter, he commanded Kumārajīva to translate the scriptural canon (*sūtrapiṭaka*).
Kumārajīva said, "In propagating the teachings of the Dharma, it is fitting that both the phrasing and the meaning be perfectly realized. Although I have memorized..."
Regarding the text, its principles have not yet been fully mastered; only Buddhayaśas has profoundly penetrated its subtle depths. He is currently in Guzang.

I pray that an imperial edict be issued to summon him. Let his words be deliberated three times over before being committed to writing, so that these subtle teachings do not fall into oblivion and may be trusted for a thousand years.
Emperor Xing followed this advice and immediately dispatched an envoy to invite him, offering him generous gifts, all of which he refused to accept.
He then smiled and said, "Now that the imperial decree has been issued, one ought indeed to set out at once.

However, since the patron treats scholars so generously, should my situation prove to be like that of Kumārajīva, I dare not yet accept the command. When the envoy returned, he related this in detail; Yao Xing sighed in admiration of his prudence.
Firm in his faith and earnest in his exhortations, Kumārajīva finally arrived in Chang’an (in the ninth year of Hongshi). Emperor Yao Xing personally went out to welcome and inquire after him;

he established a new monastic office within the Xiaoyao Garden and provided the fourfold offerings, all of which Kumārajīva declined. When it was time for the alms-round, he would take but a single meal.
Thereupon, Kumārajīva produced the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. For over a month, there were still doubts and hesitations regarding its difficult passages.
Before he had yet taken up his pen, Guṇabhadra arrived; they deliberated together until the principles of the arguments were finally settled.
More than three thousand monastics and laypeople all marveled at the excellence and precision of his insights. Guṇabhadra was a man with red eyebrows who was highly proficient in the *Vibhāṣā*;
thus, his contemporaries called him "The Red-Browed Vibhāṣā Master. Since he served as Kumārajīva’s teacher, he was also honored as the "Great Vibhāṣā Master."
The offerings from the fourfold assembly—robes, alms bowls, and ritual implements—filled three rooms; yet he did not set his heart upon them and sold them for profit.
With the proceeds, he constructed a saṃghārāma south of the city. Previously, in Kaśmīra, Guṇavarman had recited the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* without bringing the Sanskrit original with him.
Yao Shuang, a subordinate general of the Qin army, wished to invite Guṇavarman to translate it.

Lord Yao considered that since there was no Sanskrit original, it would be difficult to verify and believe; furthermore, as many members of the Sangha held differing views, he did not yet grant his permission.
Kumārajīva urged him, saying, "Saṃghavarman possesses great mnemonic skill; I have often heard him recite and practice [the text], and he has never made a single error.
Thereupon, Lord Yao immediately provided one scroll of medical prescriptions and one scroll of census records, each approximately forty [characters long].
He was given a sheet of paper and had him recite it for one day. He then assembled the monks and examined the text against the original;
down to the minute details of weight, the number of people, and their ages, there was not a single character that did not match. Thereupon, the assembly all believed and submitted.
Consequently, in the twelfth year of Hongshi, he translated [the work] into forty-five fascicles, and also produced the *Dīrgha Āgama* and other texts. A monk from Liangzhou...
Translated into the Qin language by Zhu Fonian of the Gate [Monastery], with Daohan receiving the dictation. By the fifteenth year, the assembly was adjourned.
Yao Xing presented Kumārajīva with ten thousand rolls of silk as a religious gift (*dakṣiṇā*), but he would not accept any of it.

Zhu Fonian and Daohan each received one thousand rolls of silk, and five hundred śramaṇas of renowned virtue were all likewise given generous offerings. Later, Kumārajīva traveled to Mount Kuang in the Jin territory.

He was held in high esteem by Master Huiyuan. In the year Jia-yin, the tenth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the Venerable One personally carried iron up Mount Zixiao Peak to cast a stupa, in which he enshrined the true-body relics of the Tathāgata.
Later, he returned to foreign lands and reached Jibin (Kashmir), where he obtained one fascicle of the *Gaganagañja-sūtra*.

He entrusted it to a merchant to transmit to the monks of Liangzhou; his final whereabouts thereafter remain unknown. (It is said that the original Vinaya text was translated in forty-five fascicles, or perhaps forty-four; it has now been divided into sixty fascicles.

According to the biography of the Tang dynasty Vinaya Master Yuanzhao, later Zhi Falin again brought Sanskrit manuscripts from the Western Regions to Chang’an’s Zhongsi Temple, where they were meticulously collated and retranslated into sixty-two fascicles. However, the number of fascicles is considerable.)
[This is] a small portion from a later period).
Zhu Fonian was a native of Liangzhou.
He entered the monastic order in his youth; his aspirations and practice were firm and refined. He was harmonious outwardly and lucid inwardly, possessing great intelligence and quick wit.

He took this as his mirror for self-reflection. He recited and studied various sutras and had a general familiarity with secular learning; he was particularly well-versed and practiced in the glossaries of the *Cangjie* and *Yayue*.
From his youth, he delighted in traveling to distant lands and thoroughly mastered their customs. His family lineage was from Xihe, so he was intimately acquainted with local dialects;

there were no meanings of either Chinese or Sanskrit terms that he did not understand simultaneously. Thus, although his reputation for scholastic expertise (*yixue*) was lacking, his fame for extensive erudition was very prominent.
During the false Jianyuan era of Fu Jian, the foreign śramaṇas Saṃghabhūti and Dharmanandi entered Chang’an.
Zhao Zheng, the Secretariat Director of Fu Jian, requested that Saṃghabhūti translate the *Bāshumì jīng* (Pusyamitra Sūtra).

At that time, among the renowned and virtuous masters, none were able to transmit the translation from the Sanskrit original. The assembly all recommended Dharmarakṣa; thereupon, Saṃghabhūti held the Sanskrit text.
Hui-nian translated the Chinese text, resolving difficult points and clarifying doubts regarding the phonetics and characters.

Dharmaratna also produced the *Princes Dharmavardhana’s Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Losing One’s Sight*, which Hui-nian proclaimed and translated, composing a preface for the scripture as well.
In the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era, the ruler again requested Dharmaratna to produce the *Ekottarika Āgama* and the *Madhyama Āgama* at Chang’an.

Within the inner city of Anxi, he gathered śramaṇas who were experts in the study of meaning and requested Dharmakṣema to act as the translator. Through detailed exposition, analysis, and rigorous examination, the work was completed over two years.
Both Sengxian and Senglüe brought it to prominence; this was due to the merit of Dharmakṣema’s proclamation and translation. This occurred at the beginning of Yao Xing’s Hongshi era.

The study of the sūtras flourished greatly. Dharmakṣema translated the *Bodhisattva-avaivarta-maṇi-alaṃkāra*, the *Daśabhūmi-saṃyojana-prahāṇa*, as well as the *Udānavarga*, the *Garbha-sūtra*, the *Antarābhava-sūtra*, and others.
During the reigns of the Fu and Yao dynasties, he was the preeminent master among translators;
from the time of An Shigao and Zhi Qian onwards, none surpassed him. Consequently, the monastic community in Guanzhong all held him in high esteem. He later passed away at...
In Chang’an, both the clergy and the laity, far and near, all sighed with regret.
"Yi" (in the rhyme of *yì*) is pronounced like *yì*. "Yi" means to transmit and to explain; it refers to the mutual interpretation of the languages and sounds of two different countries. And...

This refers to the transmission and proclamation [of words]. According to the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou) and the *Wangzhi* (Institutions of the King), there were officials in charge of the languages of the four quarters, each having a "xiangxu" (elephant-mouthed) official to facilitate communication.

Those from the east were called *ji* (meaning they could transmit the differences of local customs here); those from the south were called *xiang* (meaning they could emulate the differences of local customs there);

those from the west were called *didi* (*di* meaning they could distinguish the differences in their clothing and ornaments); and those from the north were called *yi* (meaning they could interpret the differences in their speech and translate them).

These four [titles] were all official designations. Today, they are used interchangeably with the Western term. As for the title "Translator" (Yi), it is because during the Han dynasty, affairs with the north were frequent, and the translation officials were also proficient in Western languages.
Thus, when Kāśyapa Mātanga first arrived, he translated the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*; consequently, the title "Translator" was adopted.
From the Han through the Tang dynasties, the masters who translated the Tripiṭaka followed one another in succession, and all were referred to as "Translators."

This refers to translating the language of the Western Region (Sīnyan) into the speech of the Eastern Land (Dongxia), and conveying the script of the Brahmā Heaven to produce the writing of the Flower-Womb Realm (Huafang).
As for the origin of written characters, it arose from three individuals. The eldest was named Fan (Brahmā); his script ran from right to left.
The next was named Qielou (Kharoṣṭhī); his script ran from left to right. The youngest was Cangjie; his script...
Descending [the lineage], Brahmā and Kharoṣṭhī resided in India; Huangdi and Cangjie were in the Eastern Land (China). Brahmā and Kharoṣṭhī adopted their methods from the Brahma Heaven;
Cangjie derived his inspiration from the tracks of birds. While the written characters differ, the principles they transmit are the same.
Looking up to the scripts of Brahmā and Kharoṣṭhī, their phonetic rhymes correspond to those of the Brahma Heaven; the Brahma sounds serve as their speech, whether in single or multiple syllables.
They lack constancy. Sometimes a single character subsumes a multitude of principles; sometimes several words constitute a single meaning.

Examining their radical characters, there are forty-seven. Encountering objects, they combine to form [words]; according to circumstances, they are applied and transformed. Their pronunciations undergo seven shifts, following the eight grammatical rules.
Observing how they produce speech and modulate tones, they turn and assist one another; some are produced from the root of the tongue or the tip of the lips.
It is determined either by length, shortness, lightness, or weight. Within the sevenfold revolutions of sound, all sounds possess them;
within each individual sound, three segments are distinguished: namely, the singular, the dual, and the plural. Altogether, these constitute twenty-one forms of speech.
For example, calling one man "puruṣa," two men "puruṣau," [and so on].
*Lu shao*. Three types of names are called *puruṣa*. Within these, there are differences in the breath and weight of the sounds.

Beyond the seven cases (*vibhakti*), there is further the sound of the vocative, which constitutes the eighth pattern. Since the first case already has three [subdivisions], the others are all modeled accordingly;
fearing prolixity, they are not set forth here. These eight patterns comprise a total of three eights, or twenty-four sounds. The ancients called them "sounds" (*śabda*).

Regarding the discussion of the eight case endings (*vibhakti*): first is *puṃsa*. This is the direct indicative case (*nirdeśa-vibhakti*), as when one says "the man cuts the tree," it directly points to that person;
it is the case of the present entity (*bhāva*). Second is *puṃsām*. This is the case of the object of action (*karman-vibhakti*).

As in the act of cutting the tree, it is thus called the "object" (*karman*) (the old translation renders this simply as "that which is done"; "person" [*puruṣa*] is a term of honor for a male). Third is *puṃsi jñānam*. This is... [text fragment].

1. The "instrumental" (karaṇa) case is the expression of the instrument by which an action is performed, such as "cutting with an axe"; therefore, it is called "the instrument. (The old translation renders this simply as "the agent. 2.

The "dative" (sampradāna) case is the expression of that for whom an action is performed, such as "cutting for someone"; therefore, it is called "for the sake of. (The old translation renders this as "the recipient. 3.

The "ablative" (apādāna) case is the expression of the source from which something arises, such as "building a house because of [or from] a person"; therefore, it is called "from. (The term "from" [zōng] is synonymous with "cause" [suīn].)
1. *Puruṣa* (formerly translated as "the person from whom one follows"): this is the term for the object of following. 2. *Pratyaśraya* (formerly translated as "the person to whom one belongs"):

this is the term for the sound of belonging, like a servant belonging to a master; hence it is called "belonging. 3. *Pratiśaraṇa* (formerly translated as "the person upon whom one relies"): this is the term for the sound of reliance, like a guest relying on a host;
hence it is called "reliance. 4. *Āhvāna* (formerly translated as "the person who calls"): this is the sound of summoning; hence it is called "calling."

According to the laws of the Western Regions, those who wish to study the inner and outer scriptures must first understand the eight case-terminations (*vibhakti*) within this *śabdavidyā* (phonology/grammar);

only then will they know the precise boundaries of the textual meanings. Furthermore, there are distinctions between masculine and feminine inflections, as well as divisions between the technical terminology of *śabdavidyā* and common vernacular speech;

these need not be debated at length here and will be briefly presented according to the specific context later on. Nevertheless, their phonetic pronunciations are entirely different [from those of India].
The various kingdoms do not resemble the Hu (barbarian) language. Furthermore, a single phoneme of the Hu script cannot form a word;
it must rely on other words to complete the sentence before the meaning is established. Thus, we know that the Hu language does not participate in the Sanskrit sounds (*brahmanī*).

The Sanskrit sounds are inherently profound and mysterious, with meanings intersecting and details interlocking. For translators to transmit their intent may truly be called a difficult task. Nevertheless, from the Han to the Tang, [the transmission] proceeded...

Regarding previous translations where the Chinese and Sanskrit sounds differed: this was largely because when the scriptures and Dharma first reached China during the Han dynasty, the Sanskrit phonology was profound and the interpreters (*xiangxu*) were not yet proficient in it;
thus, there arose the variations between "Sengmen" and "Shamen," and between "Futu" and "Fotu.
As for the three sages Kumārajīva and Master Xuanzang, they further remarked that these were erroneous and abbreviated. I shall now, by way of private critique, [address] them as well.
Due to the five regions of India, their lands differ; the boundaries of the Qiang and Hu peoples are distinct.

Within the territories of the Eastern Xia (China), eras have shifted and ancient and modern pronunciations diverge. As for these translators, some arrived from the Hu lands, while others came from the Five Indies to the Rong (Western Regions).
They translated the Chinese language using the Rong dialects as a medium; furthermore, the languages of the Five Indies themselves are each briefly divided into various dialects.

Only the words of the Central Heavenly King (Madhyadeśa) are correct; they are no different from the voice of Brahmā. Within this single realm of the Eastern Land (China), regional dialects differ naturally:

for instance, when the Later Han dynasty was centered in Luoyang and the Eastern Jin moved to Jianye, if Buddhist scriptures had been transmitted to India earlier during the Han period, the northern accent would certainly have been considered the standard. However, it was people of the Jin dynasty who later traveled to India.
One must take the Southern language as the standard. Therefore, regarding what has been explained here, there is no lack of contradiction; though their words differ, their meaning is truly uniform.
By this it is clarified that the ancient Sanskrit language was not necessarily subject to corruption or abbreviation. (Now, this *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* was translated by Buddhayaśas.

Buddhayaśas was originally a man from Northern India who had long resided in foreign lands translating the Tripiṭaka. Later he arrived here [in China], and thus his text contains much mixed with non-Chinese (Hu) terminology, making it truly difficult to investigate in detail.)
Regarding any sentences containing omissions or uncertainties, they shall await future verification before being inserted.

As for the protocols of prostration and reverence, customs differ between regions and practices vary between the Central and the Borderlands; in India (i.e., Tianzhu), one bows with the head uncovered and the feet bare.
To show reverence: in China, one prepares the headcloth and shoes to manifest respect; in the Middle Kingdom (India), joining the palms and touching the feet is considered supreme.

In this land (China), clenching the fists and bowing the head is called the highest form of honor. The term "kneeling with the head to the ground" (*jiǎoshǒu*) used here is intended to follow local customs as an expression of devout veneration.
However, the practice of *jiǎoshǒu* originally derives from the Office of the Grand Sacrificer (*tàizhòu*) in the *Zhou Lǐ*.
Thus the nine types of prostration are distinguished. The first is called *kṣeśu* (pronounced *jī*, with *kṣi* as *jiān xī*). It means to linger;

it refers to lowering the head to the ground and lingering there for a short duration before rising. The second is called *dùnshǒu* (bowing the head): this means placing the head on the ground with the hands and rising immediately.
The third is called *kōngshǒu* (empty-headed): this means lowering the hands while the head does not reach the ground. The fourth is called *zhèndòng* (vibrating/shaking). This means...
The *jingzhong* (reverent) bow refers to lowering the hands with a sense of trembling urgency. Fifth is the *jibai* (auspicious bow), which refers to lowering the hands with dignified composure.
Sixth is the *xiongbai* (inauspicious bow): bowing first and then prostrating with the forehead to the ground is called the *jibai*;

prostrating with the forehead to the ground first and then bowing is called the *xiongbai*, which is the manner of bowing for those in three-year mourning. Seventh is the *qibai* (odd bow), which refers to first bending one [knee].
The *xī* (knee-bow). Some say this refers to performing only one bow and not repeating it. Eighth is the *bāo-bài* (bow of recompense);

"bāo" is written as "bào," meaning a bow in return. Ninth is the *sù-bài* (solemn bow), which means straightening the body with a solemn countenance while slightly lowering the hands, like the bowing of women today;
it is also called the "mere downward bow," which is what constitutes a modern-day *yī* (salutation). These are the nine types of bows.
These are all the ritual protocols of this region. As for the etiquette of the country of India, there are likewise nine grades.
The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "The forms of paying respect consist of nine levels: first, greeting with words of inquiry; second, bowing the head to show reverence."
1. Raising the hands high in a formal bow; 2. Joining the palms with the hands level and hollowed; 3. Bending the knees; 4. Kneeling upright; 5. Placing the hands and knees on the ground; 6.
Bending all five wheels (the two feet, two knees, and two elbows) together; 7. Prostrating the entire body to the ground. These nine grades constitute the utmost single prostration.

To kneel and praise the virtues is called "exhausting reverence. At a distance, one performs the *keshang* (bowing the forehead) and *baishou* (bowing the hands)—that is, prostrating the five limbs while the two palms support the air.

[They] manifest the appearance of touching [the teacher's] feet. When approaching closely, they lick the feet and rub the heels. Whenever they present their words or receive instructions, they lift their robes and kneel for a long time.

When honoring the worthy or receiving their prostrations, the teacher must offer words of consolation; sometimes he strokes the crown of their head or pats their back, instructing them with kind words to demonstrate his affection and intimacy.
Once ordained śramaṇas have received such reverence, the teacher merely adds virtuous aspirations for them and does not stop there.
They prostrate themselves, performing circumambulations according to the object of their devotion; these may be one circuit or three circuits.
For special requests made with a long-standing intention, the number follows one's desire. Examining the Western Regions (India), there is no rite of three prostrations;
rather, one simply spreads the ten fingers upon the ground and performs three bows with the head touching the ground, without rising in between. Master Wenyi said: "What we see now in the West..."
When a monk comes before the Buddha to pay homage, he must lift his lower robe, rest his knees upon the ground, join his palms while kneeling with full length, and offer verbal praise to the Buddha;
only then does he perform a prostration with his head to the ground. This is a surviving tradition that still persists; you should respectfully take it as a standard for practice.

The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "There are three kinds of salutation. The first is verbal salutation, such as joining the palms and inquiring after one's well-being while vocally uttering 'vaṃdanā' (homage).
The second is kneeling, wherein the knees are bent but the head does not touch the ground; this is mutual kneeling (*añjali*). The third is when the head touches the ground;
this is the supreme salutation, namely prostrating with the five limbs (*pañcāṅga-praṇipāta*). One should understand the significance of these expressions of reverence."

This pertains to the three karmas. If one bows the head, it is called paying respect through the karma of the body. If one extols the virtues and titles [of the Buddha], it is called paying respect through the karma of speech.
If the mind dwells in visualization, it is called paying respect through the karma of the mind.
When these three karmas pay respect in this manner, one achieves true offering. Were it otherwise, it would be nothing more than stumbling upon level ground. Furthermore, the five...
One should keep the wheel touching the ground to eliminate unwholesome physical karma; one should chant the Name and sing praises of the Buddha’s virtues to eliminate unwholesome verbal karma;
and one should constantly bring the Buddha to mind as if he were before one's eyes like a mirror to eliminate unwholesome mental karma.

Furthermore, through the vocal action of recitation, the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) is accomplished; through the mental action of mindfulness, the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is accomplished;

and through the bodily action of prostration, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is accomplished. Through the bodily action of prostration, the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) is accomplished;

through the mental action of mindfulness, the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) is accomplished; and through the vocal action of recitation, the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*) is accomplished. According to this...
From a general perspective, among the three types of action (trikarma), all three trainings (triśikṣā) are subsumed. The remainder is as described in the *Vinaya-ekottara-dharma*.
(The verses for chanting and praise, as well as the phrases for salutation, both appear in the *Vinaya-ekottara-dharma* below.)
"Buddhas" (zhū fó) is a collective designation for those of the ten directions and the three periods of time. "Buddha" (fó), in its complete Sanskrit form, is *buddha*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that in the language of Qin it means "the Knower" (*zhī zhě*), one who knows sentient beings and non-sentient beings of the past, future, and present.
Regarding the number [of categories] such as the permanent and the impermanent, he has clearly and fully awakened to all phenomena beneath the Bodhi tree;

therefore, he is named Buddha (or *Buddha*, where *da* may also be written as *dha*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Buddha" (*buddha*) means "awakened" (*jue*) in the language of Qin, because he has awakened to and understood the characteristics of all phenomena.
Furthermore, all sentient beings have long been slumbering within the three realms; since the Buddha’s Dharma-eye has already...

"Open. Because it awakens itself and awakens others, it is called "Awakening" (jue). The *Miaoyaoji* states: "In contrast to delusion, it is called 'knowledge' (zhi); in contrast to ignorance, it is called 'awakening' (jue).
The *Houhan shiji zhaosizhi* states that awakening possesses three meanings: first, self-awakening—realizing that one's nature is truly eternal and understanding that afflictions are empty and false;
second, awakening others—employing unconditioned compassion to deliver the realm of sentient beings; third, [awakening the Dharma].
His awakening and practice are perfected; he has reached the source and exhausted the depths. His conduct is fulfilled and his fruition is complete. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The nature of all dharmas is neither born nor extinguished. How marvelous! The Great Teacher awakens himself and is able to awaken others. Master Sengzhao said: "What is a Buddha?
He is the title for Great Awakening, having exhausted principle and fully realized nature. His Way is empty..."
The Mysterious is already wondrously transcendent of the ordinary realm. The mind cannot be known through wisdom; its form cannot be fathomed through images.
It acts as all things do, yet dwells in the domain of non-action; it resides within the sphere of speech and calculation, yet halts in the land beyond words.
It is not "existent," yet it cannot be called non-existent; it is not "non-existent," yet it cannot be called existent. It is profound stillness.
Vast and empty, no being can fathom it; not knowing by what name to designate it, we have arbitrarily called it "Awakening" (*jue*). Its attainment is also the ultimate limit.

(This extensive explanation is intended for those who practice the *vinaya* while simultaneously mastering the textual meanings and characteristics of the Dharma, so that later students of the sūtras and śāstras need not trouble themselves with other readings.)
"Bhikṣu" refers to a monk.
This is translated as "beggar" (qishi), or "one who eliminates hunger" (chujin), and also as "pure livelihood" (jingming).

The new term is *bhikṣu*, translated as "one who has received full ordination" (jin yuan), meaning that by receiving the great precepts (*mahā-śīla*), one draws near to *nirvāṇa* and perfect stillness. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-vyākhyā* states:

Some say there is an etymological translation (*fan*), while others say there is none. As for those who say there is a translation, they render it as "remover of scarcity" (*chujin*). Sentient beings have little merit;

while in the causal stage, they lack the means to sustain themselves, and thus, when receiving retribution, they encounter much want and deprivation. The monastic precepts and conduct are a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*);
they can produce wholesome qualities in sentient beings and thereby eliminate the scarcity of both cause and effect. Furthermore, Kang Senghui translated the *Fajing jing*.
The Sūtra states: "Ordinary people are greedily stained by the six sense objects, like a hungry man eating rice, never knowing satiety.

Now, the Sage has severed greed and eliminated the famine of the six passions; therefore, he is called 'the Remover of Famine' (Arhat). Regarding the statement that there is no [Sanskrit] equivalent, the name contains three meanings.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: first, the destroyer of evil; second, the terrifier of Māras; third, the mendicant. First, as for the destroyer of evil:

Just as one first receives the precepts and is immediately called a *bhikṣu*, so too, through the three *karmavācanās*, one gives rise to the wholesome discipline (*kuśala-saṃvara*) and breaks the unwholesome discipline (*akuśala-saṃvara*);

thus it is said that "evil is broken. If we speak generally in terms of practice and understanding: the precepts prevent physical transgressions, meditative concentration removes mental distraction, and wisdom awakens one to the emptiness of conceptualization;
thus, they are able to break the evils of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and are therefore called "breaking evil. As for the phrase "frightening Māra": since one is already...
He destroys evil. Māra thought to himself: "This person will not only leave my realm;
he may transmit the lamp of the Dharma, convert my followers, and empty my palace. Therefore, I feel fear. Generally speaking, the three Māras likewise experience fear.
Regarding the term "beggar" (*bhikṣu*): "begging" (*bhikṣā*) is a name for seeking; "person" (*puruṣa*) is a designation for one who is refined and pure.
A person who has left the household life must internally cultivate refined and pure virtue, necessarily distancing themselves from the four wrong livelihoods and dwelling in a pure way of life.
They benefit sentient beings, shatter the mind of arrogance, and remain humble and self-effacing. By requesting the necessities for sustaining the body, they thereby achieve refinement and purity.
Because he possesses virtue, he is called a "beggar" (bhikṣu). Furthermore, it is said that *bhi* means "to destroy" and *kṣu* means "afflictions";

because he is able to destroy afflictions, he is so named. Moreover, *bhi* means "to destroy" and *kṣu* means "able"; because he is able to terrify Māra and the followers of Māra, he is called "Terrifier of Māra.
The *Śāstra* states: "Terrifier of Māra," "Destroyer of Evil," and "Beggar. Māra delights in birth and death; since he has left the household life and further transforms others, [he is so named].

He is completely detached from the three realms and acts contrary to the will of Māra; yet when Māra attempts to subdue him with force, he instead becomes bound by the five fetters and can do nothing but grieve and fear.
For this reason, he is called "Terrifier of Māra" (Bhīṣma-māra). A renunciant must destroy the seven evils of body and speech; therefore, he is said to be "Destroyer of Evil" (Pāpamardana).
Now, for those living at home, there are three types of lawful means of livelihood: first, agriculture; second, commerce; and third, service. These are used to sustain one's body and life.

For those who have left the household life, the Buddha did not permit these; rather, they must sustain themselves solely through alms. When the body is at ease, the Way endures, thereby benefiting the donors (*dānapati*).
These three principles support one another, which is precisely the meaning of a *bhikṣu*. Now, the term *bìqū* (苾芻) is phonetically close to *bhikṣu*; there were those in ancient times who...

The five meanings of fragrant herbs are explained as follows: First, their substance is soft and supple, which is a metaphor for those who have left the household life, for they are able to subdue the coarseness and wildness of body and speech.
Second, their trailing vines spread out to the sides, which is a metaphor for those who have left the household life, for they transmit the Dharma to save others in an unbroken succession.
Third, their fragrance is heard from afar, which is a metaphor for those who have left the household life, for the perfume of their preceptual virtue is pervasive and is perceived by the multitude.
Fourth, it can cure pain; this is a metaphor for those who have left the household life, as they are able to sever the poisonous harm of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Fifth, it does not turn its back on the sun’s light; this is a metaphor for those who have left the household life, as they always face the sun that is the Buddha. As for "Saṃgha," the full term is *saṃgha*.
This is translated as "assembly" (saṃgha), meaning a harmonious gathering; it is a designation for four or more bhikṣus. One, two, or three bhikṣus are not called an assembly.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When many bhikṣus gather together in one place, this is called a saṃgha.
It is like a grove formed by a dense clustering of great trees; a single tree does not [constitute a forest]."
It is called a "forest" (*vana*). Apart from each individual tree, there is no forest. Likewise, each individual bhikṣu is not called the Saṃgha;
apart from each individual bhikṣu, there is no Saṃgha. It is because all the bhikṣus are in harmony that they are called the Saṃgha.

Tiantai says: "The term 'multitude' (*gaṇa*) signifies harmony. Those who practice the three vehicles of the renunciant path have minds that accord with the phenomena and principles taught by the Buddha."
Because they are united, they are called the *saṃgha*. The *Vinaya-chao* states: "This is translated as the 'harmonious assembly' (*sāmagrī-saṃgha*). There are two meanings of harmony:

first, harmony in principle (*li-ho*), which means that they equally realize *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*; second, harmony in practice (*shi-ho*), which has six specific aspects: namely, harmony in precepts through collective cultivation;

harmony in views through shared understanding; harmony in person through dwelling together; harmony in benefits through equal distribution; harmony in speech through the absence of dispute; and harmony in mind..."
[The assembly] was harmonious and joyful. Master Kumārajīva said, "To desire that the community be harmonious requires six dharmas:
first, to initiate bodily action with a mind of loving-kindness; second, to initiate verbal action with a mind of loving-kindness; third, to initiate mental action with a mind of loving-kindness;
fourth, when receiving food, to set aside a portion of the rice from one's bowl to offer to one person of superior standing and one person of inferior standing; fifth, to maintain the precepts."
Purity. Fifth is the wisdom of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*). If one practices these six dharmas, then the community will always be harmonious and there will be no discord or contention.
Master Zhaoluo said: "Without the true mind, one cannot possess the six dharmas; without the six dharmas, one cannot harmonize the multitude.
If the multitude is not harmonious, it is not the way of reverent obedience. Furthermore, the name *saṃgha* signifies a field of merit.

As the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states: "The Sangha is the field of merit that transcends the three realms. This means that bhikṣus possess the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*).
Since the precepts are the root of all wholesome virtues, worldly people take refuge in them with faith, making offerings and planting seeds of merit."
Just as fertile soil can produce excellent crops, it is therefore called a "field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there are five kinds of saṃghas:
first, the "sheep-like saṃgha," meaning those who do not know how to perform the *poṣadha*, the distribution of voting sticks, the recitation of the precepts, the *pravāraṇā*, or any *karmavācanā*;
they are entirely ignorant of all monastic affairs, just like a flock of sheep, and are thus named the "sheep-like saṃgha. Second, the "un... [text truncated]

The *hrī-apatrāpya-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha possessing shame and dread) refers to a community where the entire assembly collectively practices what is contrary to the Dharma, such as engaging in impurity, drinking alcohol, eating past midday, or any other violation of the precepts and unrighteous conduct;
all who dwell together in this manner are called the *ahrī-anapatrāpya-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha lacking shame and dread). Third is the *pṛthagjana-saṃgha* (the Saṃgha of a separate assembly).
That is to say, any *karmavācanā* performed by a separate assembly that acts according to its own will is called a "separate assembly" (*bhedasaṃgha*). Fourth, the pure *saṃgha*:

this refers to all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who maintain pure precepts and whose assembly is free from unrighteousness; this is called the pure *saṃgha*. Fifth, the *saṃgha* of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya-saṃgha*):
this refers to the four fruits and the four paths; these are called the *saṃgha* of ultimate truth. (The "four fruits" refers to the attainment of the four stages of fruition.)
"Towards" (xiàng) refers to being directed toward the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
*Vinaya* is the correct Sanskrit name; it is also called *Viniya*. Master Ying stated that it is sometimes called *Vibhāṣā*.
*Niga*, *vinaya*, or *piṇāya*—these are all corruptions resulting from the shifting of light and heavy sounds in the Sanskrit original.
This is translated as "leaving conduct" (*li xing*), where "conduct" (*xing*) also means "path. It is so named because this practice can cause one to leave the evil realms;
hence it is called by that name. Alternatively, it is translated as "extinction" (*mie*), meaning that it can extinguish the evils of body and speech. — Śikṣānanda’s Dharma [Translation]

The Master said: "Vinaya" in the language of Qin means "skillful governance. This refers to governing one's own lust, anger, and ignorance, as well as being able to govern the evils of sentient beings.
Guxiang said: "By means of this method, the name *lǜ* (vinaya) was translated from the word *naiye* (naya) used in that land [India]."
Mount Nan said: *Vinaya* is translated as "extinguishing" (*mie*). This is a name derived from its functional efficacy; it is not the primary translation.

The correct translation is "law" (*lü*). "Law" means "dharma. This is a name derived from the teaching. It involves the adjudication of gravity and lightness, as well as what is permitted, prohibited, maintained, or transgressed.

What is not dharma is not fixed. In the secular world there are nine schools of thought, and the school of Dharma occupies one of them. Therefore, worldly laws and regulations all rely upon penal statutes. [The Way...]
It differs from worldly conventions; its terminology is distinct. However, as for adjudication, one must necessarily rely on established law. The *Śīla-pratyaya-sūtra* states: "Vinaya.
"Vin" (鼻) means "to remove" (去) in the language of Qin; "aya" (奈耶) means "truth" (眞). Because it removes that which is non-true and proceeds toward the true, it is called "truth" (眞).
Furthermore, because it subdues this mind and causes this mind to rest, and because it endures so that [afflictions] do not arise, it is called "truth."
...Furthermore, subduing is the precept; cessation is concentration; and forbearance is wisdom. The *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) states:
"The Buddha taught the precepts for the purpose of stopping evil. Because evil is stopped, a mind free from regret arises.
Because of this mind free from regret, joy arises. Because of joy, tranquility arises. Because of tranquility, samādhi arises. Because of...
Because of samādhi, the eye of wisdom (prajñā-cakṣus) arises. Because the eye of wisdom arises, revulsion (nirveda) arises.
Because of revulsion, dispassion (vairāgya) arises. Because of dispassion, liberation (vimukti) arises. Because of liberation, the knowledge of liberation (vimukti-jñāna) arises.
Because of the knowledge of liberation, one sequentially attains entry into nirvāṇa. This is for the purpose of speaking and for the purpose of explaining.
Therefore, for the sake of providing a basis, and for the sake of desiring to hear [the Dharma], the mind attains liberation through wisdom in this sequential manner.
For this reason, one should diligently study the Vinaya; this is the fundamental teaching regarding the locus of the Vinaya.

Upāli is also called Upavali, or alternatively Upāli. This is translated as "Transformation-Born" (Huasheng) or "Foremost" (Shangshou), because he maintained the Vinaya as the guiding principle for the assembly;
thus he was named Upavali. It is also translated as "Attendant" (Jinchi), meaning that the Buddha [relied upon him].
When he was a prince, [the Buddha] was his attendant and minister.
Among the Tathāgata’s five hundred great disciples, all of whom were Arhats each renowned as foremost in their respective fields, the Venerable Upāli was preeminent in the mastery of the Vinaya.
The treatise states that the reason Upāli is called foremost in the mastery of the Vinaya is because, from the time he first...
Since the Buddha attained the precepts, he has never violated them even by so much as a hair’s breadth; therefore, he is called the foremost. The Buddha said:
"For the sake of future bhikṣus, you are able to establish the prohibitive laws so that they may know what is light and what is heavy, and thereby be delivered from peril and distress.
You truly uphold the Vinaya; I entrust the Vinaya to you. Do not let it be lost or leaked. It must not be shown to śrāmaṇeras or laypeople. He further praised him, saying:
First: (Regarding the term "reverend" [chánglǎo]: it refers to translating the language of the Western Regions into the speech of this Eastern Flower [China]).

Because his years are advanced, his seniority is great, and his learning and understanding are vast and profound, he is called a "reverend. In the new terminology, he is called "one endowed with longevity" (āyuṣmat). *Ekottarika Āgama*...
The Master said:
"If one perceives the Dharma of the Truths, And brings no harm to any living beings, Abandoning all defiled and evil conduct—this is called an Elder.
As for what I now call an 'Elder,' It must first be one who has left the household life."

One who cultivates the roots of wholesome deeds and discriminates between right practices— even if they are young in years and their faculties are not yet fully developed— such a person is called an elder (*sthavira*).
As stated in the *Mahāpuruṣa-vyākaraṇa-śāstra* (The Great Treatise on the Dharma of Discriminating Right Practice):
"What is called the mark of an elder does not necessarily depend on advanced age."
Though one’s form is emaciated and hair and beard are white, aging in vain without inner virtue— One who can relinquish the fruits of both sin and merit,
who practices with vigor and purifies their conduct, And who has already detached from all phenomena— such a person is called an elder of the precepts.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *śīla*; here it is translated as "prohibitory precept" (*jinjie*). "Prohibit" (*jin*) means to restrain, to regulate, to be cautious, and to cease.
It is called "restraint" (*zhi*) because it is able to restrain all unwholesome dharmas. "Precept" (*jie*) takes the sense of prevention;

that is, it is able to prevent the faults of non-virtuous conduct (*akuśala-avijñapti*) and to cease the evils arising from the three karmic actions. Therefore, it is named "prevention. "Cautious" (*jin*) refers to...

"Vigilance regarding righteousness" means being careful not to commit offenses. "Cessation" (śīla) is a Sanskrit term; its literal translation is "attainment through cessation," meaning the cessation of evil and the attainment of goodness.
Although there are many such etymological explanations, their essential meaning is one and the same.
Dharma Master Xuanzang stated: *Sumeru* is translated in the Tang language as "Wondrously High" (*Miaogao*). Formerly it was called *Xumi* or *Xumilou*, both of which are erroneous.
The *Abhidharma* and *Kosa* treatises state that it is composed of the seven treasures; therefore, it is named "Wondrous. It rises above the seven golden mountains.
It is high above the mountains, hence its name "High. It enters the water for eighty-four thousand *yojanas* and rises above the water for eighty-four thousand *yojanas*.
The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states: "Its height is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*; its length and breadth are likewise."
The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: It is composed of four precious substances and is situated within the great ocean, resting upon the golden wheel (*suvarṇamaṇḍala*).
It is where the sun and moon revolve and moor, and where the various devas dwell and rest. Seven mountains and seven seas stand encircling it in formation.
The seawater between these mountains possesses the eight meritorious qualities (*aṣṭāṅgopeta*). Beyond the seven golden mountains lies the salt sea. On each of the four sides of this mountain...
There is one color: the east is golden, the south is lapis lazuli, the west is silver, and the north is crystal.

According to their respective directions, the waters match the colors of the mountains, and the colors of the heavens are likewise. If one follows the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, the east is silver and the west is gold;
thus, when the people of the four continents look toward the heavens, each perceives it as being of a single color (lapis lazuli is a gemstone of blue color).

To be "fully equipped with the three types of action" means to be endowed with wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind. At that time, when the Venerable Rāhula had first gone forth, he was prone to telling minor lies.
The Buddha took a water vessel and poured out the water repeatedly to bring him to realization. He then asked Rāhula: "In your opinion..."
"How so? "People use a mirror, Venerable Sir, to observe their faces and see whether they are clean or unclean.
The Buddha said, "In this same way, Rāhula, when you are about to perform a bodily action, you should examine that bodily action:
'I am about to perform this bodily action; will this bodily action be pure or impure? Will it be for my own sake or for the sake of another? Rāhula, if you examine [it]..."
At that time, one knows: "I am about to perform a bodily action;

that bodily action will be impure, whether performed for myself or for another, unwholesome, resulting in suffering, and leading to the experience of a painful retribution. Rāhula, you should abandon such a bodily action as you are about to perform.
Rāhula, if upon reflection you know: "I am about to perform a bodily action; that bodily action will be impure, whether performed for myself..."
"Or for another; it is wholesome, yields the fruit of happiness, and one receives a pleasant retribution.
Rāhula, you should undertake that as bodily action. Rāhula, if you currently perform a bodily action, you should examine this bodily action:
'If I am currently performing this bodily action, is this bodily action pure or impure? Is it for myself or for another? Rāhula, if you examine it..."
At that time, one knows that one is currently performing a bodily action (*kāyakarman*). This bodily action is pure, whether performed for oneself or for another;
yet it may be unwholesome, resulting in suffering and leading to the experience of a painful retribution. Rāhula, you should abandon such currently performed bodily actions. Rāhula!
When observing at the time [of action], one knows: "I am currently performing a bodily action; this bodily action is impure, whether performed for my own sake or for the sake of others.
It is wholesome and yields the fruit of happiness, resulting in the experience of pleasant retribution. Rāhula, you should accept this currently performed bodily action.
Rāhula, if you have already performed a bodily action, you should immediately observe that bodily action, as if I myself had performed it.
Karma. That bodily action has already passed away, ceased, and changed. Is it pure or impure? Is it for oneself or for another?
Rāhula, when one observes it, one knows: "I have performed a bodily action; that bodily action has already passed away, ceased, and changed.
That bodily action was pure, whether for myself or for another, yet it resulted in unwholesomeness and suffering."
As a result, one undergoes the retribution of suffering. Rāhula, you should approach spiritual friends and those who practice the holy life.
They have already performed physical actions; you should sincerely confess them, repent for your transgressions, and be careful not to conceal them. Furthermore, guard yourself well.
Rāhula, when you observe it, you will know: "I have already performed this bodily action; that bodily action has passed away, ceased, and changed.
That bodily action was impure, whether performed for myself or for another; it was wholesome and yields a pleasant fruit, and its pleasant retribution is experienced.
Rāhula, you should dwell day and night with joy, established in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. It is the same with verbal action.
It is likewise. Rāhula, because of past formations, a mental action has already arisen. He then contemplates that mental action:
"Is this mental action, which has arisen because of past formations, pure or impure?
Is it for oneself or for another? Rāhula, when he contemplates in this way, he knows that the mental action has already arisen because of past formations.
Karma. That mental karma of his has already passed away, ceased, and changed. That mental karma was pure;
yet, whether for himself or for another, he performed what was unwholesome, resulting in a fruit of suffering and experiencing a retribution of suffering.
Rāhula, you should abandon that past mental karma. Rāhula, if one observes at the present time, one knows that because of past conduct, mental karma has already arisen.
The past has ceased, perished, and changed; that mental karma was impure, whether performed for oneself or for another.
It yields wholesome and pleasant fruits, and one experiences a pleasant retribution. Rāhula, you should regard that past mental karma.
Rāhula, because of future formations, mental karma will arise; thus, you should observe that mental karma. If, because of future formations...
When one intends to perform a mental action (*manokarman*), that mental action may be pure or impure; it may be for oneself or for others.

Rāhula, when you observe it, you will know that because of future formations (*saṃskāra*), one intends to perform a mental action. That mental action may be pure, or it may be for oneself or for others;
yet if it is unwholesome, it results in suffering and one experiences a painful retribution. Rāhula, you should abandon it.
“Rāhula, regarding that future mental karma, when it is observed, one knows that because of future formations, mental karma will arise.
That mental karma is impure; whether performed for oneself or for others, it is wholesome and results in happiness, receiving a pleasant retribution.
Rāhula, you should accept that future mental karma. Rāhula, it is because of present formations.”
A mental action arises in the present. One then contemplates this mental action: "Is this mental action that has arisen in the present due to present formations?
Is this mental action pure or impure? Is it for oneself or for others? Rāhula, when one contemplates in this way, one knows that the mental action arising in the present is due to present formations;
and one knows whether this mental action is pure, or for oneself, or for others.
...it is unwholesome and results in suffering; one experiences the retribution of suffering. Rāhula, you should abandon this present mental karma.
Rāhula, when observing it, one knows that because of present formations, present mental karma arises;
this mental karma is impure, whether performed for oneself or for others, and it is wholesome, resulting in happiness; one experiences the retribution of happiness. Rāhula...
“Rāhula, you should undertake this present mental action.

Rāhula, whatever past śramaṇas or brahmins had already examined and then further examined their bodily, verbal, and mental actions, and had already purified and then further purified them—all those were precisely these same bodily, verbal, and mental actions, which they had already examined and then further examined, and had already purified and then further purified. Rāhula, as for whatever future śramaṇas or brahmins [there may be]...”
Regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind, one should observe them as they ought to be observed and purify them as they ought to be purified.
All those [actions] are precisely these actions of body, speech, and mind; one should observe them as they ought to be observed and purify them as they ought to be purified.

Rāhula, if there are present śramaṇas or brahmins whose actions of body, speech, and mind they currently observe as they ought to be observed and currently purify as they ought to be purified, all of them are precisely these [actions of body, speech, and mind].
“Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall contemplate my bodily, verbal, and mental actions through clear comprehension; I shall purify them through clear comprehension.
Rāhula, I too contemplate these very same bodily, verbal, and mental actions through clear comprehension; I too purify them through clear comprehension. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
"Rāhula, you should constantly observe The bodily, verbal, and mental actions As being either wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.
Knowing that false speech arises from yourself, Rāhula, do not speak it. Since you originally depend on others for your livelihood, How could you utter falsehoods?"
To conceal the Dharma of a śramaṇa, to be empty and devoid of truth, and to speak false words—this is not the way.
Because one does not guard the mouth, one speaks falsely; therefore, the son of the Perfectly Awakened One follows the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Rāhula, you should train in this so that every direction may be prosperous and joyful, peaceful and free from fear. When you reach those places, do not cause harm to others.
Rāhula is also called Rāhula; in the new [translation], he is called Rāhula. Master Kumārajīva said: "When the asuras consume the moon, it is called Rāhula;
in the language of Qin, this means 'obscuration,' referring to the obscuring of the moon's brightness. The *Wenju* states that in the past, he blocked...

A rat's burrow. Furthermore, because he did not look upon the Brahmin for six days, by reason of this karmic cause, his retribution was such that he remained in his mother’s womb for six years before being born;
thus it is called "obscured. At that time, the Prince sought to leave the household life, but the King, his father, did not permit it.
When he persisted with earnestness, the King said, "If you have a son, I shall allow you to leave the household life. The Bodhisattva then pointed at the Consort with his finger.
[The Buddha said: "In six years from now, you shall give birth to a son. After the Buddha had left the household life, Yaśodharā became pregnant.

All the Śākyas were incensed, asking, "By what cause has this occurred? They wished to punish her and wished to kill her; rumors of her ill repute filled the roads. The noble lady Gopikā testified on her behalf, saying, "It is not so.
Because she was nearly burned in a pit, she made a great vow: "If I have done wrong, may mother and child both perish together."
"If these are truly my remains, let Heaven bear witness. Thereupon, she embraced her son and threw herself into a pit; the pit was transformed into a pond, and lotus flowers supported her body.
Only then did the King and the people cease their doubts. Yaśodharā was thus cleared of slander. The Grandfather King rejoiced, thinking:
"Though I have lost my son, I have gained this grandson. He shall become a Cakravartin; what cause for regret could I have? Thus she reflected.
When he grew up, he hoped for the arrival of the divine treasure; however, the Buddha summoned him and commanded him to leave the household life. His father, the King, did not permit it.
Yaśodharā was about to ascend to a high tower when Maudgalyāyana flew through the air to take her away. The Buddha ordained them both and left them as disciples under Śāriputra.

Once they had left the household life, they also lost their royal status; therefore, it is said that [Yaśodharā] was obstructed. (According to the Vinaya text, the Buddha entered the city himself and bestowed his finger-ring upon Rāhula. Rāhula...

[The Buddha] said, "I shall seize his finger," and led him to the vihāra, commanding Śāriputra to ordain him as a śrāmaṇera. The Buddha decreed that the four great arhats must not enter parinirvāṇa until my Dharma has completely vanished;
thus they remain to uphold it and have not yet entered nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) even to this day.
Therefore, he is said to be "obstructed. The *Xiyu ji* states: Rāhula—formerly called Luohouluo, and also called Luoyun—all [of these names refer to the same person].
This is an erroneous abbreviation. Here it is called "clinging to the sun. The Sarvāstivādins say:
while the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities for six years, Yaśodharā also practiced austerities within the royal palace. Due to these circumstances, the fetus remained hidden within her womb.
At that time, the Bodhisattva realized that the practice of austerities was of no benefit, and he immediately began to breathe normally at his own will. Thus...
She partook of exquisite delicacies. Having heard of these matters, Yaśodharā likewise relaxed her body and mind within the palace, conducting herself in the same manner as the Bodhisattva.
Through this pleasure, her pregnancy gradually developed, and before long, she gave birth to a son.
At that time, Rāhula seized the bright moon (as the common folk say, during a lunar eclipse) and gathered his kinsmen, requesting—
Regarding the bestowing of a name, the deliberation says: "When this son was first born, Rāhula grasped the moon with his hand;
therefore, this child should be named Rāhula. The *Mahopāyakauśalya-sūtra* states: "Doubting that the Bodhisattva was not male but a eunuch, he took as his wife Gopī, the daughter of the Śākya clan.
Rāhula appeared through miraculous transformation in the heavens and did not arise from [ordinary] birth."
He was born from the union of his parents. As the Sūtra says: "Rāhula’s appearance is upright and handsome; all who see him are filled with joy.
His skin is yellowish-white, like the color of pure gold. Furthermore, the crown of his head is shaped like a parasol; his nose is high and prominent like that of a parrot;
his two arms are long and slender, hanging down past his knees; and none of his limbs or joints are deficient."
[His faculties] were not deficient; all his sense organs were complete and fully endowed. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost disciple in being able to uphold the prohibitive precepts is the bhikṣu Rāhula. Sometimes he is called the foremost in forbearance, and at other times the foremost in secret conduct (*guhyacaryā*);
each of these titles has its own specific causes and conditions, which I shall not record here at length. Master Kumārajīva said: "Among the śrāvakas..."

Their natures are not all-encompassing; each possesses a specialized capacity, which is why they are called "foremost. Thus, among the five hundred disciples, each is designated as foremost in their respective field.
These four matters cannot be remedied.
This refers to the four *pārājika* offenses: sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying. If one commits these, it is like a person whose head has been severed;
there is no remedy that can restore them to life. Since there is no further method by which they may regain the body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*), it is said that they are "incorrigible."
There are thirteen [offenses] that may be saved, namely the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas. If one commits them, it is like a person whose head has been severed yet whose throat remains;
if one quickly finds a skilled physician, one can be restored to health. Therefore, twenty pure monks are required to perform the *karma*.
By polishing [the transgression], the offense is finally eliminated; this is not like the previous four cases where the vessel of the precepts has already been shattered.

Although one may encounter hundreds or thousands of pure assemblies, it is difficult to provide a cure. Compared to the preceding categories of precepts, this is said to be "redeemable. The *Mahāyāna-sūtra* clarifies three types of illness:
first, easily cured; second, difficult to cure; and third, incurable. The *Hongming ji* states: "An illness that is certain to cause death cannot be cured even by a sage."
That which cannot be cleared away is like a curable illness that must wait for a physician before it can be healed;

this is the case here. As for the rest, there is no need for rescue—meaning, with the exception of the precepts in the preceding chapter, if one violates any of the precepts in the subsequent chapters, one may confess before a single person or a small group.

If one confesses according to the Dharma, one immediately attains purification; this is not like the previous thirteen cases which require the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha to collectively remove the offense.
Therefore, it is said that no further rescue is required.
*Biao* (飈): pronounced *biao*. It refers to a violent wind blowing from below upward. The *Jīng yīn yì* (Phonetic Meaning of the Sūtras) states it is "small fire.
According to the character's form, it should be written as *biāo* (熛). *Biāo* means flying fire; it is also called "bursting fire" (*biāo* is pronounced *piāo*).
The Dharma of the Great Ocean of Corpses does not harbor corpses. The Buddha-dharma is like the ocean; those who commit grave offenses are like corpses.
Should there be such offenders, they are expelled from the pure assembly. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "It is just as the great ocean does not accept corpses; should there be..."
A corpse. Just as a great wind blows it onto the shore, so it is within my Dharma: we do not accept corpses. What is meant by "corpse"?
It refers to one who is not a śramaṇa yet calls himself a śramaṇa; one who does not lead the holy life (brahmacarya) yet calls himself one who leads the holy life;
one who violates the precepts and is of evil character, impure and defiled; one with wrong views who conceals unwholesome deeds within.

Carrying within one a rotting corpse, like a tree in the midst of space, though one may sit among the assembly, one is always far removed from the Sangha, and the Sangha is likewise far removed from such a person.
The text states: "The Buddha is the teacher of devas and humans; as a teacher, he is solemn and his Way is honored.

Regarding whatever he has taught, if there is any transgression, no sin could be greater. How could one possibly violate or disregard the rules of the first category and the subsequent clusters? Thus..."
To deceive the Buddha and betray his heart is, furthermore, to betray the Three Masters and the Seven Monks.

This person is a corpse in the ocean of the Buddhas and rotten flesh in the garden of flowers (referring to the four grave offenses of the first category [āpatti] and the subsequent category of *duṣkṛta* [dukkaṭa]; if discussed according to the five categories of offenses, then both the beginning and the end belong to the same category; if according to the six groups of offenses, then both the beginning and the end belong to the same group. These various texts appear interchangeably, hence it is said:
"the first category and the subsequent group").
*Elāpattra*, *elā*.

This is translated as "foul odor. This is the name of a tree. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a bhikṣu practicing meditation, out of a mind of anger, damaged its foul leaves and was reborn among the nāgas;
a foul-smelling tree grew from his head for hundreds of thousands of [eons].
"Ten thousand years! Having received this retribution of suffering, he awaits Maitreya, the World-Honored One, to receive his prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
He shall be liberated from that dragon body" (the causal conditions for this are found in detail within the *Śīla-vastu* of the *Kṣudraka-vastu*).

Phonetic Glossary:
*Kashmir* (罽賓) means "low-born" (賤種).
*Dào* (打-丁+暴) is the sound of a sharp strike. *Qiūcí* (龜茲):
the first character is pronounced *qiū* and the second *cí*.
*Hōng* (薨) is pronounced like *hōng*; it refers to the death of a Duke (*gōng*) or Marquis (*hóu*).
*Yìng* (pronounced *yùn*) means to escort a woman on her wedding journey.

*Fēnwèi* is the Sanskrit term *piṇḍapāta*, which here means "begging for food. As for *fēnwèi*, it refers to dividing the food obtained through begging and giving a portion to fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*).
By obtaining and maintaining this [food], one sustains the cultivation of the Path.
*Zī* (髭): Pronounced *zī*. It refers to the hair above the mouth.
*Gǔ* (詁): Pronounced *gǔ*. To provide a *gǔ-hùn* (exegesis) is to communicate the speech of antiquity with that of the present, thereby clarifying its underlying causes.
*Cǎi* (崽): Pronounced *zǎi*.
Dàn (sound shài).
Qì (cut by jié): sound qiè.
The vulgar form is written as é.
Lì (慄): the sound is lì; it means to fear. It also means to shrink back in terror.
Qiān (褰): the sound is qiān; it means to lift up one's clothes.
Jué (蹶): the sound is jué; it means to stumble or fall.

The Nine Schools: First is the Confucian School (Rúliú). This refers to those who follow the principles of Yin and Yang, expound upon education and transformation, recount the governance of the ages of Tang and Yu, and take the Way of Confucius as their primary tenet.

Second is the Daoist School (Dàoliú). This refers to those who maintain the principle of weakness, humble themselves, extol the virtue of Yao and Shun’s yielding of the throne through ritual bows, and uphold the humility and reverence of the *Zhou Yī*.
Third is the School of Yin and Yang (Yīnyángliú). This refers to those who follow the heavenly calendar and celestial phenomena, and practice reverence and love.

1. The Stream of the People (*min-liú*): This refers to the timely administration of the populace. 2. The Stream of the Four Laws (*si-fǎ-liú*): This refers to clarifying rewards and enacting laws in accordance with ritual regulations. 3. The Stream of Names (*míng-liú*):

This refers to rectifying names and establishing ranks so that speech accords with the accomplishment of affairs. 4. The Stream of Ink (*mò-liú*): This refers to the ancestral sacrifices in the Clear Temple (*qīngmiào*) and the bestowing of kindness upon the aged.

5. The Stream of the Vertical and Horizontal (*zònghéng-liú*): This refers to receiving titles and mandates, handling diplomatic missions, and exercising discretion in affairs. 6. The Miscellaneous Stream (*zá-liú*).

The *Liuliu* (Flowing Currents) means that it encompasses the standards of Confucianism and Mohism and contains the teachings of the School of Names and Legalism; it understands the fundamental principles of statecraft and penetrates every matter.
The *Jiunliu* (Nine Agricultural Currents) means that it encourages agriculture and sericulture and provides a comprehensive exposition of food and wealth.
"Qin language" refers to the terminology used for translating scriptures during that specific period. If a scripture was translated during the Qin era, it is designated as "Qin language.
Likewise, whether it be the Han, Jin, Sui, Liang, Tang, or Song eras, these terms are all based on the contemporary language of the time;
collectively, they refer to the Chinese language of this region.
*Zhì* (峙) is pronounced with the third tone; it means "towering," as in a mountain standing upright.
*Sǎn* (繖) is pronounced with the third tone; it means "parasol.
*Yōng* (傭) has the sound *chōng*; it means "equal" or "uniform."
