[The Three Defilements]
They are also called the three defilements (*trimala*) and the three poisons (*triviṣa*), namely greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*).
The *Chanmen* states: "The mind that draws things toward oneself is called greed; the mind of resentment and anger is called hatred;
the mind of confusion is called delusion. The *Śāstra* says: "If the mind can cause the continuity of birth and death, it is termed a stain (*mala*). This stained mind...
Distinction: Greed, hatred, and delusion, and so forth, are defiled states of mind;

they are called *kleśas* (afflictions), and are also termed "dharmas of transgression," "dharmas of decline," "dharmas of concealment," "dharmas of feverishness," and "dharmas of remorse. Such are their names.

When these defiled states of mind are cultivated and accumulated, they are termed *anuśayas* (latent tendencies). It is not merely at the moment a defiled state of mind arises that it is called an *anuśaya*.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are named greed, hatred, and delusion; along with doubt, pride, and the five views—due to these various distinctions, there are ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
These are the fetters and proclivities.
"Knots" (*saṃyojana*) has the meaning of binding; that is to say, they bind the practitioner and do not allow for liberation. "Fetters" (*paryavasthāna*) has the meaning of driving and employing;
that is to say, they are able to drive and employ the mind and spirit of the practitioner, causing them to transmigrate through the three realms.

Briefly stated, there are three knots; explained extensively, there are eighty-eight fetters. If one abandons the three knots—view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—...

When [the three fetters] are exhausted, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala). If the three fetters are exhausted and greed, hatred, and delusion are attenuated, one attains the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala).
If greed and hatred are exhausted, one attains the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). If all afflictions (kleśa) are forever exhausted, one attains the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala).
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Nir" means non-arising; "vāṇa" means non-extinction. Taken together, it signifies non-arising and non-extinction. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"What I have taught is that the cessation of the consciousness of false conceptualization is called nirvāṇa. The new [translation] says: "In the Sanskrit original..."
The correct name is *parinirvāṇa*, which is translated here as "extinction" (*mièdù*). Master Sengzhao’s treatise states:

"Nirvana is called 'the unconditioned' (*wúwéi*) in the Qin language; it is also called 'extinction. 'The unconditioned' refers to its emptiness, stillness, and silence, which are wondrously transcendent of the conditioned.
'Extinction' means that the great afflictions are forever extinguished and one has transcended the four currents. This is truly like a mirror-image..."
It is the ultimate refuge, the profound abode beyond all designation. Furthermore, it has been newly translated as "Perfect Quiescence" (yuánjì). Xianshou said:
"Because there is no virtue that is not complete, it is called 'Perfect' (yuán); because there are no obstructions that are not exhausted, it is called 'Quiescent' (jì).

Some call it *nirvāṇa*, some call it *nirmāṇa*, and others call it *nirvāṇa*. Master Sengzhao said: "As for *nirvāṇa* being the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), how could it merely mean the exhaustion of fetters? It is [the cessation of] birth..."

Death is eternally extinguished; therefore, it is called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*). It can also be translated as "peaceful bliss," because one has already departed from the thieves of the fetters of affliction (*kleśa*).
The *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* states: "Nirvāṇa is eternal, constant, and cool; there is no further birth and death."
The mind cannot be known by wisdom; its form cannot be fathomed by images. No one knows why it is so named, yet we forcibly call it "quiescence" (*jì*).
Its attainment is indeed ultimate! This is explained in detail as in the *Śīla-vinaya-kaṇḍa* (Section on Receiving the Precepts).
Regarding the life-preserving float (*uragaḍa*) used by those crossing the seas in the Western Regions: many fashion it from bird feathers and down; some make it from sheepskin or oxhide;
others carry the bladder of a large ox. Should their sea vessel be lost, they blow air into it to buoy themselves up and thereby cross the great ocean.
A parable in a Great Sūtra says: Suppose there were a rākṣasa who, following those crossing the sea, asked them all for their life-preserving bags (uḍupa).

Those crossing replied, "We would rather sacrifice our own lives than give up our life-preserving bags. The rākṣasa spoke again, saying, "If you are unwilling to give them in full, please grant me half.
At that time, the person still did not give it. In this manner, the request was made in succession until [the rākṣasa] asked for as much as a speck of dust; he—
At that time, even for something as small as a mote of dust, a person would not give it away; likewise, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva maintains the prohibitive precepts, it is also thus.
When Rākṣasas of affliction attempt to convert the Bodhisattva, urging him to commit the four pārājika offenses while guarding against other minor ones, the Bodhisattva does not comply.
When they urge him to commit saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, the Bodhisattva does not permit it. When they urge him to commit pāyattika offenses...
The Bodhisattva was unwilling to comply. [They] urged him to commit a *pāyantika* offense; the Bodhisattva was unwilling to comply. [They] urged him to commit a *duṣkṛta* offense;
the Bodhisattva did not follow. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva upholds the four grave prohibitions as well as the *duṣkṛta* offenses."
They are revered with firm resolve and are equal without distinction; how much less could one who is a śrāvaka, urgently seeking liberation, be treated with contempt or disparagement?
[The Hall of Śakra]
As for Śakra, in the Sanskrit language it is fully called Śakradevendra, and is also called Śakradevendra.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Śakra" in the language of Qin means "able"; "deva" in the language of Qin means "heavenly being"; and "indra" in the language of Qin means "lord."
Taken together, this refers to his ability to serve as the lord of the thirty-three gods; he is now briefly called Śakra, which is a combination of the Chinese and Sanskrit names.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: The Buddha said, "When he was originally a human being, he practiced immediate giving (*tun-shi*) and was capable of acting as a lord;
therefore, he is named Śakra-devānām-indra. The *Saṃyukta Āgama Sūtra* further states: "Śakra was originally a human being..."
At that time, he was exceedingly brilliant; when adjudicating matters, he could resolve a thousand cases in a mere instant.
For this reason, he was named Śakra. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If you firmly maintain the seven practices, you will certainly attain the state of Śakra."

Why is this? Formerly, when Śakra was a human being, he first practiced the path by being filial and obedient toward his parents, revering his elders and superiors, speaking with gentle words, abandoning double-tongued speech, delighting in giving without stinginess, constantly cultivating truthful speech, never deceiving or betraying others, and not giving rise to anger;
even if resentment should arise, he would immediately contemplate its cessation. This is the True Dharma.
The *Smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "Śakra is a *srotāpanna* of the first fruit; in his present body he has a thousand heads. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"In his present body he has a thousand eyes; in his hands he holds a vajra, from which flames of fire issue forth. The *Ratnakoṭi Sūtra* states:
O Śakra, you shall now surpass the collective merits and practices of a thousand Buddhas and their brothers;

even the name of the "Auspicious Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpa) will no longer exist, for it will be forever cut off for twenty-four intermediate kalpas (antarakalpas). Only thereafter will a Buddha appear in a land named Universal Endurance (Samanta-kṣānti).
That Buddha’s lifespan will be seven kalpas, and his bequeathed Dharma will likewise endure for seven kalpas. Once that Dharma has completely vanished, there will again be a vast interval.
Five kalpas. In that buddha-field, you shall succeed to the rank of Tathāgata, and your name shall be Venerable Asaṅga. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
Long ago, there was a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan who, together with thirty-two companions, jointly repaired a stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha.
At the end of their lives, they were all reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru; Kauśika became the Lord of Devas, while the other thirty...
The two serve as ministers, together constituting the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa). Śakra resides in the center.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that Śakra is the lord of two realms (the Heaven of the Four Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven). The *Sūtra on the Original Causes* states:
"At the summit of Mount Sumeru is the Great City of Sudarśana, ten thousand *yojanas* in circumference. Its double gates are one and a half *yojanas* high. The city has a thousand gates."
It was magnificently adorned and magnificent. In its center was a golden city with five hundred gates;

within it stood a multi-storied pavilion named Piśācayan (also called Vaijayanta, which is the Palace of Supreme Victory). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The Palace of Supreme Victory is one thousand yojanas in circumference.
Its ground is adorned with pure gold and various jewels, and is as soft as tūla-cotton, rising and falling according to the touch of the feet. The Āgama says:

The Venerable Maudgalyāyana traveled throughout the small chiliocosm, yet there was nothing as magnificent and stately as the Vaijayanta Hall (the remainder is as explained in the *Pravrajyāvastu* [Section on Ordination],
under the section on the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven).

Regarding the seven treasures mentioned in various sūtras, their specific enumerations differ slightly, and the Chinese translations vary as well. Here, they are presented according to what appears in our own Vinaya:
first, gold; second, silver; third, pearls; fourth, lapis lazuli; fifth, coral; sixth, conch shell; seventh, amber.
Agate. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: first, gold; second, silver; third, vaidūrya; fourth, sphaṭika (which is translated here as "water-jade" or "crystal").

Five, *śaṅkha* (its color is bluish-white; some say it is a large shell resembling the *śaka* of a chariot; *śaka* refers to the chariot’s axle-pin; because its shape resembles this, it is named *śaka-śaṅkha*).

Six, *musāragalva* (this gemstone is colored like a horse’s brain, hence its name; its color is reddish-white). Seven, red pearls (*rakta-muktā*). The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states they are produced by red insects.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that pearls come from within the bellies of fish, or from within bamboo, or from within the brains of snakes; they do not necessarily arise solely from the womb of oysters. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* mentions coral but does not mention pearls. Constantly...
The *Shui jing* (Water Classic) mentions the *candrakānta* (moon-pearl), the *maṇi* jewel, and the *muktā* (true pearl).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that these jewels are of three kinds: human jewels, celestial jewels, and bodhisattva jewels. Human jewels possess little power;

they merely have pure radiance and color, and they can eliminate poison, ward off demons, dispel darkness, and also relieve hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and various other forms of suffering. Celestial jewels... [text continues]
It is also great and superior. It constantly follows the celestial body; it can be commanded and conversed with. It is light and not heavy.
The Bodhisattva-jewel surpasses the celestial jewels and can also encompass the qualities of human jewels.
Furthermore, it enables all sentient beings to know their death here and birth there, as well as the beginning and end of the causes and conditions—just as one sees one's own face in a clear mirror.
Furthermore, these images can emit various sounds of the Dharma and rain down banners, flags, flowered canopies,
and all manner of offerings to worship the Buddhas of the ten directions. They also rain down all necessities of life and provide the four requisites to sentient beings—
namely, food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine— to eliminate their poverty and suffering.
The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are also called the seven limbs of awakening (*sapta-bodhipakṣa-dharma*). *Bodhi* is translated here as "awakening.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "When a Tathāgata appears in the world, there then appear the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment."

At that time, what are called the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of dharma-discernment, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity appear in the world.
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, these seven jewels of the awakening factors appear in the world. Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should seek skillful means.
"Cultivate these seven factors of enlightenment. Thus, O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves. [The character] yī (猗) means "beautiful"; according to the *Yupian*, it is a term of praise.

The character is also written as *huī*. Guo Pu says: "*Huī* refers to the appearance of being exquisite, elegant, light, and beautiful. Now, this awakening of the mind (*bodhyaṅga*) arises from the preparatory application of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because it is free from lethargy and agitation, it draws forth a state of lightness, beauty, tranquility, and harmony within both body and mind. This corresponds precisely to the meaning of "light and beautiful.

Therefore, for one who has attained concentration, it is not only the mind that becomes peaceful, harmonious, and refined, but one's physical appearance also becomes full and radiant. (The rest is explained below).

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are also called the five heaps (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). They are form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Aggregate" (*skandha*) takes the sense of "covering" or "obscuring.

This means they can cover and obscure the wisdom of supramundane true illumination, thereby increasing birth and death so that their accumulation and dispersal continue without interruption; hence the name.
These are the aggregates (*skandha*). If these five are complete, it is called birth; when they disintegrate and perish, it is called death.

"Form" (*rūpa*) has the meaning of being substantial and obstructive; it refers to the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body. Because these sense faculties are combined and accumulated, they are called form.
"Feeling" (*vedanā*) has the meaning of experiencing and receiving; it refers to the six consciousnesses corresponding with the six objects. And...
There are six types of feeling (*vedanā*). Because they are a harmonious accumulation, they are called "feeling. As for perception (*saṃjñā*), it has the meaning of conceptualization;
that is to say, when the mental consciousness corresponds with the six sense objects, the six perceptions are formed. Because they are a harmonious accumulation, they are called "perception."
"Formations" (*saṃskāra*) has the meaning of migrating, flowing, and constructing.

This means that because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) conceptualizes various objects and constructs various formations of good and evil, which then combine and accumulate, they are called "formations. "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) has the meaning of discernment.

That is to say, because the six types of consciousness—those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—illuminate, discern, aggregate, and accumulate with respect to their respective sensory objects, they are called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
Form is not the self. If form were the self, illness and suffering would not arise in relation to form;

furthermore, one would be able to command form, saying, "Let it be thus," or "Let it not be thus. Because form is not the self, illness and suffering arise in relation to form, and one is unable to command form, saying, "Let it be thus," or "Let it not be thus.
This is also the case for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It is likewise so. Form is impermanent. That which is impermanent is suffering. That which is impermanent and suffering is of a nature to change and pass away.
Would a well-taught noble disciple therein perceive a self, or something distinct from a self, or the two existing together?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha, "No, World-Honored One. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Therefore, bhikṣus, [do not perceive them as such].
Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; beautiful or ugly;
far or near—all that is not-self, is not distinct from the self, and does not exist within the self. One should observe it in this way.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Thus, the learned noble disciple...
Regarding these five aggregates of clinging, one observes them as they truly are: "This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.
Having observed them thus, one grasps at nothing in the entire world. Because of non-grasping, there is no attachment. Because of non-attachment, one realizes Nirvana for oneself:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
Aṅgulimāla is also called Aṅgulimān or Aṅgulimāra. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) calls him Aṅgulimāra;
in the language of Tang, this means "Finger-Garland. The older transcription, Aṅgulimāra, is erroneous. According to the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish):
This was King Prasenajit’s son, born of a queen whose natural disposition had never been virtuous. Since she became pregnant with this child, however, her character became respectful and compliant;
she delighted in proclaiming the virtues of others, took pity on those in distress, and took no pleasure in speaking ill of anyone.
Consequently, he was given the name A-xin-ze-qi (which means "Free from Annoyance"). Later, following the instructions of a false teacher, he killed a person.
He wore fingers as a garland, and thus people called him Aṅgulimāla. The *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra* states that his clan name was Kāḷaka and that he was a native of Śrāvastī.
His teacher was a brahmin who instructed five hundred disciples, of whom Aṅgulimāla was the foremost.
His physical bearing was fierce and powerful; his strength surpassed that of a mighty warrior. He could catch flying objects with his hands and outrun a galloping horse.

He was intelligent, talented, and eloquent, possessing a gentle and refined disposition. He was composed, quick-witted, and reached a state of total freedom from doubt or obstruction. His appearance was unsurpassed.
When his teacher’s instruction arrived at midday, he was ordered to kill one hundred people and take a finger from each, so that he might fashion a garland from the fingers of a full hundred.

Āyuṣmat Aṅgulimāla was born as a Brahmin deity in the Brahma Heaven. When he had obtained ninety-nine fingers and lacked only one to complete the hundred, he intended to harm his mother to take her finger.
The Buddha, moved by compassion, went before him. Upon seeing the Buddha, he abandoned his mother and sought to seize the Buddha’s finger;

though he pursued the Buddha, he could not catch up. The Buddha spoke a verse for him, and his mind immediately attained awakening. He left the household life and realized arhatship. When the time came, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and departed.
He entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms and arrived at the house of a certain elder. It happened that the elder’s wife was in labor with great difficulty, whereupon he thought:
"The suffering of sentient beings is infinite; they endure such torment. The elder said to him, "You are a most holy one;

what dharma do you possess that could free her from this laboring distress? He replied, "I have only recently left the household life and am not yet acquainted with this dharma. I shall go and inquire."
The Buddha returned and informed him; he immediately went back and reported the circumstances to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Go now to that woman and speak these words: 'Since my birth from the noble ones, I have never killed a living being.
By the power of this word of utmost sincerity, may the mother’s womb be free from harm. Then Aṅgulimāla went at once to the woman's place."
He spoke these words: "From the time I was born from my noble and holy parents, I have not taken life. By this truthful word, may the womb be liberated.
At that moment, the woman’s fetus was delivered, and both mother and child attained peace. The Buddha said: "Among my disciples..."
The most intelligent and swift-witted among the wise was the bhikṣu Aṅgulimāla (as recorded in the *Ekottarika Āgama*).

Regarding the character *jìbié* (記莂): the pronunciation is *bié*. According to this script, the radical "grass" (*cǎo*) is added; its original meaning refers to the planting and transplanting of seeds.

[This is] a name. It is borrowed here for the time being. The *Jīng yīnyì* (Phonetic Meanings of the Sūtras) states: "Bié" means "to distinguish. The sūtra text uses the character for "grass" (艸) with "bié" [below it];
this is incorrect. Old editions of the sūtra often say "yìn zhù" (seal-stay); these are one and the same. The *Wénjù* (Textual Commentary) says: "In Sanskrit it is *vyākaraṇa*;

this is translated as 'bestowal of prediction' (*shòujì*), also called 'receiving prediction' (*shòujì*), 'receiving decision' (*shòu jué*), or 'receiving resolution' (*shòubiè*). 'Bestowal' (*shòu*) has the meaning of giving; 'receiving' (*shòu*) has the meaning of obtaining."

"Vyākaraṇa" (prediction) means "recording" (*vyākarana*). "Decisive" (*niyata*) means "determined. "Vyākaraṇa" means "discernment" (*vibhāga*). That is to say, it refers to the Buddha’s truthful words;

he bestows upon [the disciple] their future fruit, determining the time and circumstances, and discerning whether [the realization] is near or distant. Because it is named after what is bestowed by the Buddha, it is called "vyākaraṇa" (prediction).

The *Śāstra* on the Royal Seal (with an allegorical explanation according to the Vinaya texts) states: "Just as a person who carries the royal seal is fearless wherever he goes, so too is the practitioner who holds the seal of the precepts;
he is unimpeded wherever he reaches and cannot be disturbed by any māras or enemies, proceeding directly to nirvāṇa."
"Only hold it firmly and do not let it be lost or destroyed; you need not seek its meaning therein.
The 'three evils' refer to the three evil realms: hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. As for hell, it refers to this place being located within the earth."
Below that, sentient beings who have committed extremely grave evil karma fall into this realm. As for the hungry ghosts (*preta*), there are three types:
first, those whose sinful karma is most heavy, who do not hear the names of water or drink for many kalpas;
second, those who merely wait and seek out the washings of humans, as well as pus, blood, excrement, and filth to eat; and yet another type, who [at times...]
"Or [those who] eat but once. This refers to sentient beings who have committed evil karma; due to their stinginess and greed, they are born into this realm.
As for animals (*tiryag-yoni*), these are those with hair, horns, scales, shells, feathers, four legs, many legs, legs, or no legs.
Those sentient beings who commit evil deeds through the waters, on land, or in the air— due to their ignorance— are born into these realms,
as described in detail below. [The section on] the Five Supernatural Powers of the Immortals (*ṛṣi*).
In Sanskrit it is *muni*; here it is translated as "seer" (*xian*). The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "To be old yet not die is called a seer; 'seer' (*xian*) means 'to ascend.
To ascend means to enter the mountains. *Zhuangzi* says: "One who has lived a thousand years grows weary of the world, departs, and ascends. *Baopuzi* states:
"Those who seek to become seers must take loyalty, filial piety, harmony, compliance, benevolence, and trustworthiness as their foundation. If virtue is not cultivated..."
Yet, by devoting themselves solely to various arts and techniques, they ultimately fail to attain longevity. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, there are those who do not rely on true awakening but cultivate *samādhi* through other means; they cultivate deluded thoughts and fix their mental conceptions to preserve the physical form, roaming in mountain forests and places inaccessible to humans.
There are ten kinds of such immortals (*ṛṣi*). The rest is as explained in the sutra and need not be recorded here at length. *Sragdharā*.

The Sūtra says: "The spirit is named the Heavenly Mind; its penetration is named the Nature of Wisdom. This innate wisdom illuminates all things without obstruction; therefore, it is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
There are five: first, the supernormal power of the divine eye; second, the supernormal power of the divine ear; third, the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others;

fourth, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives; and fifth, the supernormal power of psychic mobility. In the *Caitra-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Miaosheng addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva..."
"What dharma must one cultivate to attain the way of the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)? The Buddha then explained for him the five supernormal powers within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
First, the feet do not touch the ground; this means the body is able to fly, walking upon the void as if it were solid earth, and walking upon solid earth as if it were the void.
Second, knowing the minds and lives of others; this means being able to know the minds of other beings, whether they perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds, and where they will be reborn.

Third, the power of turning the eyes across a thousand *li*: regarding all classes of sentient beings throughout the world—whether beautiful or ugly—as well as city walls, houses, mountain crags, and trees, by the power of turning his eyes, he can see them all without distinction of distance.
Fourth, the power of calling by name so that they arrive immediately: regarding the men and women of the world, as well as elephants, horses, and all things great and small...
Regarding the word "equal" (or "all"): there is nothing he cannot hear. If anyone calls his name, whether from afar or nearby, he arrives immediately.
Fifth, he is unimpeded by stone walls; that is to say, as he moves about and comes and goes throughout the world, mountains, rivers, and stone walls do not obstruct him.
There is no obstruction whatsoever. As stated in the *Zongjing lu*, among the five types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the third is the power of reliance (*niśraya-abhijñā*).
This refers to relying upon esoteric arts and methods to move about at will without hindrance, such as traveling by means of talismans or through the miraculous transformations of medicinal elixirs;
these are all the arts of the immortals (*ṛṣi*). The Buddha spoke in verse:
The supernatural powers attained by ordinary beings are like those of flying birds; some are near and some are far, yet they do not transcend the path of birth and death.
The Buddha’s powers are unhindered dharmas; true and free from defilement, his mindfulness reaches the ten directions.
He travels back and forth without weariness, for he regards all sentient beings with loving-kindness.
Attaining supernormal powers without obstruction, the seer’s fivefold supernatural wisdom— though it may regress or fail to be perfected—
I possess the firm dharma of these powers. Now, regarding the "fivefold supernatural wisdom of the divine seers" mentioned here,
this refers specifically to that which is attained by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

The *Śīla-vinaya* (Sūluopo guó) refers to it as "Shanjian" (Good View), but the name of this country is not found there. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* (Wufen lü) calls it "Xulaiduo" (Su-laipo), while the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* (Mujing) calls it "Xiulaizha" (Xiulaiduo);

these are all one and the same. (According to the phonetic analysis, the three characters Su, Xu, and Xiu share the same Indic sound; here it is translated as "Good" [shan], while Laizha translates as "country" [guó]).
The *Vilanyā-sudṛśa* states: "Vilanyā" is the name of a country. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* refers to it as the town of Vilanyā.
The *Daśabhāṇaka-vinaya* calls it Virāṇa. The *Vinaya-mātṛkā-vaibhāṣya* calls it the country of Virāṇa; because it is near the Snow Mountains, it is named "Vi."
Rāyaṇa. This was the place favored by the śramaṇas and brahmins of the non-Buddhist paths. The *Madhyamāgama-sūtra* (Zhong benqi jing) states:
"Within the borders of the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a city named Sālāraṇya. There lived a brāhmaṇa named Ajātaśatru."
Regarding the *Nalinabindu* island, the *Sudṛśa* states:
"Nalinā" is the name of a yakṣa; because yakṣas and ghosts dwell in this tree, it is called Bīnu-zhou (the Island of the Forest).
The *Śīlakāraṇa-sūtra* states: "In the kingdom of Vairanya, there were no houses or halls. To the north...
There was the great mountain Śiśumāra, with vast valleys and deep woods, filled with various flowering trees and many kinds of birds.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus stayed there, dwelling beneath the trees on that mountain.
The *mandāra* tree is translated here as "satisfying the mind" (*shiyi*). It is also called the "white-flowered" tree. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that this is the *liàn-mù* (gymnocladus) tree.
[This was asked by] the Brahmin Vairaṇya.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that he was born in the country of Vairaṇyā, and thus named after the country.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that in the town of Vairaṇyā there was a brāhmaṇa named Vairaṇya, whom King Prasenajit enfeoffed with this town.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that in the country of Vairanya there was a brāhmaṇa king named Ajātaśatru. The *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* states:
As for Ajita, he was called Ajita because he made offerings to the sacrificial fire. He was a brāhmaṇa—here translated as "Pure Conduct" (Jingxing) or also as "Brahmacārin.
He belonged to the most noble of the four castes and was a lineage from the beginning of the kalpa.

Because he dwelt among the mountains and wilds, people referred to him by the title "Pure Conduct. His clan possessed its own distinct scriptures, which were transmitted from generation to generation.
They take the study of the Way as their profession; whether they remain at home or have left the household life, they mostly rely on their own spiritual arts and are people of arrogance (*māna*).

(The rest is explained as in the *Śīlaskandhaka* [Receiving Precepts] section). The *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: "This Brahmin king has, from time immemorial, been blinded by the darkness of ignorance and pays no heed to good or evil.
Furthermore, this man has long been steeped in wicked and heterodox views; he is an enemy and a thief of the Dharma. Although...
Furthermore, they invited the Buddha, yet they lacked faith and reverence; for this reason, he did not take their invitation to heart.

Moreover, because the Buddha wished to manifest the experiencing of past karmic retribution, he accepted their invitation. That is to say, in a past life, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin and a king named Bandhumat.
They prepared various kinds of sweet and delicious delicacies and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha. After the Buddha and the great assembly had finished eating, [the text continues].
They returned to their original place. At that time, there was a brahmin named Śaila who was instructing five hundred youths.
Seeing that the food was fragrant and delicious, he became envious and said, "These shaven-headed śramaṇas ought to eat nothing but horse fodder."
"One should not eat this sweet delicacy. He addressed the youths, saying, "Do you see this shaven-headed mendicant eating such sweet delicacies?
The youths replied, "We truly see him. "These masters of yours should likewise eat horse-grams," the Buddha said.
"At that time, the Brahmin Śailarāja was none other than my own self. At that time, the five hundred youths..."
"Those sons are now these five hundred arhats. At that time, I was jealous and reviled you, saying, 'You should eat horse fodder.
You also spoke likewise. Because of these causes and conditions, I and you all have passed through the hells for countless thousands of years.
Although we have now attained Buddhahood, due to those residual karmic conditions, I and you all ate [horse fodder] at Piraṇya."
During the ninety days of the horse-barley [fast], at that time I did not say, "Give the horse-barley to the Buddha," but rather said, "Give it to the bhikṣus.
For this reason, I am now permitted to eat pounded barley; had you added the words, "One should give the barley to the Buddha," [the result would have been different].
Therefore, today you all eat and wear only skins and barley (as stated in the *Udānavarga*).
Gautama—also called Kautama or Kautamī—is explained in the *Wenju* as meaning "pure and virtuous" (*chúnshú*). [Anciently...]
It was translated as "mud. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "Gautama" (formerly transcribed as *Qiutan*, which is an erroneous abbreviation).
Master Yuan stated: "In full, it is *Gautama*. *Go* means 'earth' in this language; *tama* means 'supreme.'"
This refers to those among the human race on earth, other than the gods; as this clan is the most preeminent, it is called "the most excellent on earth" (*di zuìshèng*).
It is also called *Gautamī*, *Kauṭamī*, or *Gopī*; these are all feminine vocatives. Nanshan says:
regarding *Gautama*, as the *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* states: "In the past, at the beginning of the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, the Bodhisattva..."
He became a king, but as his parents passed away early, he abdicated the throne to seek the Way. His teacher’s surname was Gautama;
[the prince] took this as his own clan name (thereby receiving the surname and being named *Kṣudra-Gautama*). In the Sanskrit language, "Gautama" is the name of a star.

Just as the Zhang clan established its surname based on a star, so too has it been transmitted from antiquity that Gautama refers to a mud-washer (*mṛttikāva-hāraka*); however, this is merely a trivial interpretation by the translators.
This has further led to error. I have now questioned Indian monks: they say that *Gautama* means "mud" (*mṛttikā*), while *Gautama* [as a proper name] is the name of a star.
Thus we know that he acquired his clan name because of a star; it certainly does not mean "mud.
As for later generations, they changed the clan name to Śākya (the claim that *Gautama* was pronounced with a feminine tone as *Gopī* is likely not correct).
"Śramaṇa" is sometimes called *sāngmén* (桑門) or *shājiāmǎnnà* (沙迦懣曩); both are erroneous. The correct term is *śramaṇa*, which means "one who exerts effort.
This refers to the fact that in practicing the Way, there is much labor involved. Master Kumārajīva said: "Whether it be the Buddha-dharma or external [teachings]..."
Regarding the term "Dao" (Path): All who have left the household life are called śramaṇas. Master Zhaolun stated that this is the general name for those who have renounced the world.

In the language of Qin, its meaning is defined as "diligent practice," for through diligent practice one attains nirvāṇa. It is also translated as "diligent rest. The *Āgama Sūtra* states: [text follows].
Having renounced affection and love, he leaves the household life to practice the Way. He restrains his sense faculties and remains unstained by external desires.
With a heart of universal compassion, he harms nothing. Meeting with joy, he does not rejoice; encountering suffering, he does not grieve.

He is able to endure like the earth; for this reason, he is called a śramaṇa. In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "There are two kinds of śramaṇas: there is the śramaṇa who practices [the path]..."
Gate. The aspirant śramaṇa. How is one called a śramaṇa who practices?

In this regard, a bhikṣu’s coming and going, his movements and halts, his gaze and demeanor, and his wearing of robes and holding of the alms bowl are all entirely in accordance with the Dharma; he is not attached to sensual desire.
Free from anger and delusion, they merely maintain their precepts with diligence, do not transgress what is unlawful, and train equally in all the precepts;
these are called śramaṇas who practice through habituation. What is meant by a śramaṇa by vow?

There may be a bhikṣu whose deportment and discipline, his coming and going, advancing and stopping, his gait and appearance, and his gaze and movements are all entirely in accordance with the Dharma.
Having exhausted all taints (*āsrava*), they become taintless (*anāsrava*). In this very life, they personally realize it and dwell therein;

birth and death have been ended, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—this they know as it truly is.

This is what is called a "śramaṇa by vow. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are four types of śramaṇas: first, the śramaṇa who has excelled on the path (*mārgajina*), namely the Buddha and others;
second, the śramaṇa who teaches the path (*mārgadeśaka*), namely those who proclaim the True Dharma;

third, the śramaṇa who lives by the path (*mārgajīvika*), namely those who cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities; and fourth, the śramaṇa who defiles the path (*mārgadūṣaka*), namely those who practice false views. (The Buddha is...)
"Great Śramaṇa. Thus, those who have left the household life following the Buddha are called Śākya-śramaṇas. Regarding the term "Śākya," its full form is Śākya;
this translates as "Capable One" (Nengren). The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that in the past there was a king...

His name was Yima (the tenth *cakravartin* king; he lived one hundred lifetimes prior to the birth of the Bodhisattva, as explained in the *Śīlaskandhaka*). He banished his four sons, ordering them to leave the country (the fourth son was named Śobha, from whom King Śuddhodana descended).
After the sons had received the king’s command, they went to the Northern Snow Mountains and dwelt in the Forest of Upright Trees (*ṛju-vana*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "They resided north of the Snow Mountains in a vast and remote region where vegetables and fruits flourished. They halted there.

For several years he ruled; those who returned to his virtue gathered like a market, and he flourished as a powerful state. His father went to summon him, but he declined on the grounds of his transgressions and did not return.

The father-king sighed three times, saying, "My son possesses great capability," and thus named him Śākya. Furthermore, it is said that because he dwelt in a grove of *śāla* trees, he was also called Śākya.
Since he established his kingdom within that grove, he took the grove as his clan name; therefore, *Śākya* is translated as [the one from the *śāla* grove].
Zhilín. Nánshān says: "According to the Sanskrit pronunciation today, 'Zhí' (Direct) is called 'Shì' (Śākya). Among the various things in India, a single object often has many names;
this [surname] was likewise derived from a grove. If one follows the *Biézhuàn* (Separate Biography), there is a tree in that land named Śākya, whose roots and trunk are lush and flourishing.
The *Fó-zǔ-tǒng-jì* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) states: "The people of the world all know the Tathāgata as..."
The royal lineage of the Kṣatriyas does not know the reasons for the establishment of the surnames Gautama and Śākya before and after [the Buddha's time].
There are four meanings of "Gautama": some say "Pure Tranquility," while others say "Supreme Earth"; these are names derived from his original virtues.
Others say "Sugarcane," or "Solar Lineage"; these are spoken in reference to his original conditions. Śākya...

The meaning of "Śākya" is threefold. When established as a title based on virtue, it is called "Able Sage" (Nengren). When designated as a name according to its location, it is called "Sāketi Forest" (Shāiyí Zhílín).
However, although the origin of the Śākya clan is attributed to the four sons of King Ikṣvāku, [the specific etymology remains as follows:]...
In reality, they both originated from Gautama. Although the appellations Gautama and Śākya differ, their clan name is one and the same.
When "Ikṣvāku" or "Śākyavardhana" is added, they are categorized as five clans; thus, while the branches and roots are distinct, their source and current flow as one.
Thus it is known that the two clans of Śākyas and Śākyas (Śākyas) both originate from Ikṣvāku; Ikṣvāku originates from Gautama.
In reality, they are all one clan of Kṣatriya kings (note: "Śākyas" is also the name of a tree).
The ten titles are: first, Tathāgata; second, Arhat; third, Samyaksaṃbuddha; fourth, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna; fifth, Sugata; sixth, Lokavid-anuttara;
seventh, Puruṣadamyasārathi; eighth, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām; ninth, Buddha; tenth, Bhagavat.

Regarding the title "Tathāgata": Just as the Buddhas of the past practiced the six pāramitās, attained all dharmas, and came to the path of Buddhahood according to the nature of reality (dharmatā), so too does the present Buddha come by way of this path. Because he comes just as the Buddhas have come, he is called the Tathāgata.

Regarding the title "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings): it signifies that one has perfected the ten thousand practices and is fully endowed with merit and wisdom, such that they are worthy of receiving offerings from gods and humans;

because they benefit sentient beings, they are called "Arhat. Furthermore, at the time of realizing nirvāṇa, they have exhausted all afflictions, rendering their body, speech, and mind pure, untainted, and unattached; thus, they are also named "The Unattached One" (Arahan). [They are] Samyak-saṃbuddha...
"One who knows the designation" refers to one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) and has no lack of understanding regarding any phenomenon;
therefore, he is designated as the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). Furthermore, by equally awakening all sentient beings to all phenomena, he achieves unsurpassed enlightenment.

Furthermore, he is titled the "Equally and Perfectly Awakened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha) and the "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna). Regarding the title "Perfected in Knowledge":

"Knowledge" refers to the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), namely, the divine eye, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Regarding "Perfected in Conduct": this refers to the Tathāgata’s actions of body, speech, and mind, which have been well-cultivated and fulfilled, being perfectly true and pure.
Because he has cultivated all practices through his own power of aspiration until they are fully perfected, he is titled "Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct."
The epithet "Well-Gone" (*Sugata*): "Well-Gone" has the meaning of "wondrously departed. It refers to the Tathāgata;

because his correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) can sever all afflictions and he has wondrously transcended the world to reach the fruit of Buddhahood, he is called "Well-Gone. Regarding the epithet "Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Being":
"Knower of the World" means that he has attained perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena of cause and effect, both mundane and supramundane.
He possesses correct knowledge; there is nothing he does not understand. As for the term "Unsurpassed Being" (*anuttara-puruṣa*):

among all sentient beings within the three realms—whether ordinary persons or noble ones, whether humans or devas—the Buddha alone is foremost, supreme, and peerless. Therefore, he is titled the "Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Being.
Regarding the title "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣa-damya-sārathi*): it means that the Buddha possesses the power of a Great Man and is thus able to...

He tames the two classes of sentient beings—those who are virtuous and those who are evil—by means of the ultimate truth, the Dharma of Nirvāṇa, manifesting himself as a trainer and guide to cause them to leave behind defilement and attain the supreme Nirvāṇa; therefore, he is called the "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi).
Regarding the title "Teacher of Gods and Humans," it means that he is not merely the teacher of Ānanda alone, but of all fourfold assemblies and...
In the heavens and among men, śramaṇas, brahmins, Māras, non-Buddhists, Śakras, Brahmās, nāgas, and devas all take refuge in him and practice according to his teachings;
they all call themselves his disciples. Therefore, he is titled the Teacher of Gods and Men (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*).

As for the title "Buddha," it means that his wisdom is fully perfected and his three types of awakening are complete and luminous; thus he is called Buddha (the three awakenings being: self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of the practice of awakening). Worldly...

Regarding the title "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān): it refers to one who, by means of dharmas such as untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), has destroyed all afflictions (*kleśa*)—including greed, hatred, and delusion—as well as all unwholesome dharmas;
who has extinguished the suffering of birth and death and attained unsurpassed enlightenment; and who is thus revered by gods, humans, ordinary beings, and sages, both mundane and supramundane.
For these reasons, he is titled the World-Honored One. The explanation above is derived from the *Daśottara-sūtra*.
If one were to provide a brief explanation according to their meaning: first is the title that emulates the traces of predecessors; second is the title of being worthy as a field of merit;
third is the title of universal knowledge of the dharma-realm; fourth is the title of manifesting the fruit through the virtues of the cause;

fifth is the title of wondrously proceeding to bodhi; sixth is the title of penetrating the false to reach the true; seventh is the title of gathering and transforming others toward the Way; eighth is...

The name for bestowing the Dharma according to capacity is the ninth; the name for awakening and returning to the truth is the tenth; and the name for being uniquely honored throughout the three realms is the eleventh.
Furthermore, the *Wenju* (Exposition of Terms) states: "One who is free from falsehood is named Tathāgata; one who is a field of excellent merit is named Arhat;

one who knows the dharma-realm is named Samyaksaṃbuddha; one who possesses the three types of knowledge is named Sugata; one who does not return again is named Sugata; and one who knows sentient beings..."

He is called the Knower of the World because he understands all realms; he is called the Unsurpassed One because none can equal him; he is called the Tamer of Men because he disciplines the minds of others;

he is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans because he serves as the eye for sentient beings; and he is called the Buddha because he knows the three categories of beings. Possessing these ten virtues, he is so named.
He is named the Honored One of the World (the three groups refer to the group of those fixed in rightness, the group of those fixed in error, and the group of those not yet fixed).
Regarding "all devas, māras, and brahmās":
"devas" is mentioned as a general term. In Sanskrit it is *deva*, which means "heavenly. As for "heavenly," it refers to being naturally so. It is pure.

They are pure, radiant, and clean; they are most excellent and most venerable, and for this reason they are called "devas" (heavenly beings). If one were not the cause of the most excellent, how could one be born in the most excellent place?
What is called the "most excellent cause" refers to the ten wholesome actions: the three of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind.
By means of these three types of karma, one prevents transgressions and non-virtue; because they accord with principle and righteousness, they are named the "ten wholesome actions. This is because...
These ten wholesome actions propel one out of the five realms of existence; therefore, these ten precepts are called the "Vehicle of the Gods" (*devayāna*). The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states:
"If sentient beings fully cultivate the superior ten wholesome actions, they obtain the retribution of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If they cultivate the ten wholesome actions associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) in conjunction with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they obtain the retribution of the form realm gods (*rūpadhātu*). If they cultivate the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), they obtain the retribution of the formless realm gods (*ārūpyadhātu*)."

Regarding the term "māra": in its full Sanskrit form, it is *māra*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that in the Qin language it means "able to snatch away life," because it can snatch away the life of wisdom.
It is also translated as "obstruction," because it can create obstacles for the practice of the Path. Master Sengzhao said:
In the language of Qin, it is called "the slayer" (*shāzhě*) or "the ultimate evil. One who severs the wholesome causes of others is called a "slayer";

one who opposes the Buddha and disrupts the Sangha commits no greater sin, and is thus termed "ultimately evil. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary* states: "Relying upon the Buddha-dharma, one obtains wholesome benefits;
yet failing to remember this debt of gratitude, one instead seeks to inflict harm—hence, 'ultimately evil. Chuiyu says:

It is capable of destroying the supramundane roots of goodness. Above the sixth heaven of the desire realm, there is a separate heaven inhabited by Māra, which is subsumed under the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). As stated in the *Mūlasūtra*:

"Below the Brahmakāyika Heaven, there is the palace of Māra Pāpīyan" (the Brahmakāyika Heaven is the lowest heaven of the form realm). The *Loutan jing* states: "Within both the desire and form realms..."
There is another palace of Māra, six thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, with seven tiers of palaces, and so forth. Regarding the term "Brahmā": "Brahmā" is a Western (Sanskrit) sound;
here it is translated as "Free from Desire" (*vītarāga*) or "Pure Conduct. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states:

"Because one removes the fetters of the lower realms and ascends to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is called 'Free from Desire'; it is also termed 'High Purity' (*brahmaśuddhi*). Furthermore, *Zhengzhen* says: "At the beginning of the kalpa, [it] was formed..."
At that time, the Great Brahmā King dwelt alone for an eon without any fellow Brahmās. Later, he gave rise to this thought:
"May all sentient beings come to be born in this place. Having formed this thought, the sons of Brahmā were immediately born.

The non-Buddhists, unable to fathom this, then clung to the notion that the Brahmā King is eternal while his sons are impermanent. The *Jingming shu* states: "The Brahmā King is [the ruler] of the Sahā world."
The Lord of the Realm dwells in the intermediate stage of the first dhyāna; that is, the intermediate dhyāna itself. This means he resides between the two pillars of the first and second dhyānas.
The Abhidharma states: "From the second dhyāna upward, there is no faculty of speech; therefore, no lord is established."

The Chan-men (Gate of Dhyāna) says: "In the first dhyāna, there is the mind of vitarka and vicāra; thus, there are the dharmas of speech and language, which serve as the means for presiding over the sentient beings of the lower stages.
The Wen-ju (Text on Phrases) says: "The Brahmā King dwells in the intermediate stage of the first dhyāna; internally he possesses vitarka and vicāra, and externally he possesses verbal expression.
By presiding over [the realm], he becomes a king. Those who practice dhyāna alone become Brahma-ministers (brahmapurohita); those who add the four immeasurable minds (apramāṇa-citta) become..."
O King. *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states: "Brahmā is the lord of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and also the lord of the three realms.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Śakra is the celestial lord of two places (the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven); the Māra King is the lord of the desire realm (because he dwells at the summit of the desire realm); and the Great Brahmā King is the lord of the three realms.
The *Gantong zhuan* (Records of Spiritual Resonance), in response to Nanshan, states: "Although the Māra King is the lord of the desire realm, Śakra [is the lord of the heavens]..."
O King, if one practices the Buddha-dharma, Māra cannot restrain them. Furthermore, regarding Maheśvara, the lord of the Sahā world:
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that he is the lord of a trichiliocosm; "Maheśvara" (translated here as "Great Sovereign"). The *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Maheśvara dwells at the summit of the Form Realm and presides over the great trichiliocosm. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Notes) says: "Maheśvara..."
Maheśvara is able to cover the great trichiliocosm and lifts up the World-Honored One as the basis for his transformations. (Within the great trichiliocosm there are ten billion Brahmā kings;

the Brahmā king in this location is named Śikhin. He resides in the center of the great trichiliocosm and acts as its sovereign ruler, though in reality he governs only a small chiliocosm. Maheśvara, because his retribution is most supreme, dwells at the summit of the realm of form and is able to cover the great trichiliocosm, serving as the lord and master of the world.)
"Excellence in the beginning, middle, and end" is also referred to as "excellent in the first, middle, and last parts. The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "The Buddha-dharma is never not excellent;

it is good throughout the three stages of youth, maturity, and old age; it is good when entering, while practicing, and when emerging. Furthermore, it initially restrains evil, in the middle abandons merit..."

The retribution is later entirely relinquished; this is called the three excellences. Furthermore, the Buddha constantly teaches the True Dharma throughout the three periods [of time], never mixing it with what is not the Dharma.
From the beginning, middle, and end, it is always cherished by the wise.

Moreover, during these three periods, it is entirely profound and unlike other sutras, which are coarse at the beginning, subtle in the middle, and trivial at the end. For these reasons, [it is superior].
Therefore, it is called the "Threefold Good" (in other sutras, this refers to various non-Buddhist texts).
"Brahmacarya" is a Western [Indic] term; its full form is *brahma*, which means "purity" or "cleansing. In its correct pronunciation, it signifies "quiescence."

*Śānti*. The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "Brahman" refers to *nirvāṇa*. Because this practice can lead toward it, it is called the "practice of the brahma-faring," and is thus termed *brahmacarya*.
The *Abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* states: "The brahma-faring is the Eightfold Noble Path;

it is called the brahma-faring because it is the path to *nirvāṇa*, and because it can reach [that goal], it is named the brahma-faring. (The "Eightfold Noble Path" is the Eightfold Holy Path, as explained in detail below.)
"Questioning" (wèn xùn) means "to speak. Its intent is to take speech as a means of offering consolation and inquiry, thereby extending one's sincerity and respect;

it is not like the practice of the present day, which merely involves joining the palms, bowing the head, and remaining silent without speaking—this is what is called "questioning. This, however, can barely be considered a form of harmony.

This follows the Southern tradition; it is not related to the formal etiquette of inquiry. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When prostrating, one must not be like a dumb sheep; one should exchange greetings. The *Dharmadhātu-śāstra* states:

"One should offer comfort with a relaxed countenance, speaking first while looking levelly at the other, with a harmonious expression and right mindfulness, and inquire after their well-being beforehand.
The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "When a bhikṣu arrives at the Buddha’s dwelling, he inquires after his well-being, saying:"

"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Inquiring after one’s health, [one asks]: 'Are you free from affliction? Are you free from illness?
Is your daily life light and easy? Is your strength and well-being secure? Why does one inquire whether there is little affliction and little illness?
It is because there are two kinds of illness: first, illness caused by external conditions; second, illness caused by internal conditions. The external refers to cold, heat, hunger, and thirst."
Weapons, blades, and staffs; falling, being pushed, or being crushed—such various external calamities as these are called external illnesses.

As for internal [illnesses], they include irregularity in eating and drinking, lack of constancy in sleeping and rising, and the four hundred and four diseases; such various [conditions] as these [are internal illnesses].
This is called internal illness. Such being the case, for one who possesses a body, there is suffering; therefore, one asks whether they have little affliction and little illness.
Why does one not ask whether they are without affliction and without illness, but rather ask whether they have little affliction and little illness?
It is because the body is the root of suffering; there is no time when one is not ill. Why is this? Because this body is a composite of the four great elements: earth, water, fire, and wind.
The winds are by nature incompatible; each harms the other. It is like a malignant ulcer that is never free from pain.
If one applies medicine, it may be slightly relieved, yet it cannot be cured. The human body is also like this: it is constantly ill and constantly treated.
Because it is treated, one lives; if not treated, one dies. For this reason, one does not inquire whether there is no affliction or no illness. Externally...

There are afflictions: one is constantly troubled by wind, rain, cold, and heat. Furthermore, there are the four bodily postures—sitting, lying down, walking, and standing—and each becomes a source of distress if maintained for too long.
If it were sufficient simply to ask whether one has little trouble or little illness, why then ask specifically about the ease and comfort of one's daily life?
This is because even when a person has recovered from an illness, they have not yet attained full restoration; for this reason, one asks whether their daily life is light and comfortable.
Why does he ask whether one’s strength and well-being are intact? It is because there may be someone whose illness has been cured;
although they are able to walk, sit, and rise, their strength is not yet sufficient to undertake tasks or perform activities. Therefore, he asks about their strength.
As for "well-being," it refers to someone who, though their illness has been cured and is able to undertake tasks and perform activities, has not yet attained true well-being. For this reason...
"May you be at ease? Furthermore, there are those who are free from illness and possess strength, yet still suffer from poverty, fear, and sorrow, and thus do not find peace and happiness.
Moreover, there are two methods of inquiry: inquiry regarding the body and inquiry regarding the mind.
To say, "Are you free from affliction and free from disease? Are you light in your movements and comfortable in your daily life, and are you strong? is inquiry regarding the body. If one says...
"Are you at ease?"—this is the inquiry concerning the mind. Various internal and external ailments are called "bodily illnesses.
Lust, anger, jealousy, stinginess and greed, sorrow, fear, and so forth—these various afflictions and the ninety-eight fetters [are the illnesses of the mind].
The five hundred fetters, various desires, aspirations, and so forth, are called "diseases of the mind. Because he inquires after these two types of illness, it is said:
"Are you free from affliction and disease? Are your daily activities light, easy, and peaceful? Question:
It is appropriate for humans to inquire in this manner, but even among the devas such inquiries would not be fitting, let alone toward the Buddha. Answer: Regarding the Buddha’s body—
There are two kinds: first, the body of supernatural transformation; second, the body born of parents. Because [the latter] receives human dharma, it is not like that of the devas.
Therefore, one should inquire after their well-being according to human custom.

"Rounding the Buddha" (dàofó dàor) means to circumambulate together; it is synonymous with "encompassing. Some say it is "revolving" (xuán). "Revolving" refers to moving about in a circular fashion, desiring that it be as perfect as a compass-drawn circle.
The ritual of revolving and circumambulating originated in India (Tianzhu). The rites of India comprise many varieties. Or...

Prostration is taken as an expression of reverence, or alternatively, circumambulation serves to manifest respect. There are two directions for circumambulation: clockwise and counter-clockwise; there are also distinctions between auspicious and inauspicious.

Circumambulating clockwise is called auspicious, while circumambulating counter-clockwise is called inauspicious. Therefore, in all the sūtras and śāstras, it is consistently stated that one should circumambulate clockwise.
For this reason, circumambulating counter-clockwise is censured by the deities, and even circumambulating clockwise at Maijishan was rebuked by the laity. Thus, regarding the left and right...
The ritual for this must be clearly distinguished. Specifically, regarding those who perform the rites here in this land [China], it is as follows:

acting in accordance with the seasons of heaven, one turns toward the northwest, bared the right shoulder, and circumambulates facing the Buddha; this is the correct procedure. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states that what is called "right circumambulation" (*pradakṣiṇa*)—the etymology of the word *pra* has many meanings, among which...

Regarding the intention: the term *dakṣiṇa* signifies "turning to the right" (*pradakṣiṇa*). It is precisely this [term] that refers to the right.
Because it is a designation that generally clarifies what is honorable and convenient, people of those times called the right hand the "honorable hand" (*dakṣiṇa-hasta*).

The meaning is that by taking the right side as honorable and convenient, one then accords with the ritual protocol of circumambulation. In the five regions of the West, all designate the east as the "front."
Regarding the directions: the south is the right direction. As the Sūtra says, "circumambulating three times to the right" strictly conforms to this ritual protocol.
Alternatively, it may say "circumambulating hundreds or thousands of times" without specifying "to the right," which is an abbreviation.

However, when performing circumambulation, whether it be a thousand, a hundred, ten, seven, five, or three times, each has its own symbolic significance. To discuss the common practice of three circumambulations first: it symbolizes...
One makes offerings to the Triple Gem, ceases the three poisons, purifies the three karmas, extinguishes the three evil realms, and attains the fortune of encountering the Three Jewels.
Other matters may be understood as one sees fit; they need not be described in detail here. As for the fruits of such merit, the *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā-sūtra* states:
"In the past, the Buddha and Ānanda entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. At that time, within that city, there was..."
A certain brāhmaṇa came from outside and saw the Buddha leaving the city, his radiant marks majestic and sublime.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he circumambulated the Buddha once, paid homage, and departed. The Buddha then smiled and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"This brāhmaṇa, seeing the Buddha, was filled with joy; with a pure mind, he circumambulated the Buddha once."
From this point forward, due to these merits, for twenty-five kalpas he shall not fall into the evil realms; among gods and humans, his happiness shall be boundless.
At the end of those twenty-five kalpas, he shall attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, named Kṣuṇāgiri.
For these reasons, if a person circumambulates a Buddha or a Buddhist stūpa, they will obtain immeasurable merit in whatever place they are born.
[The summer retreat lasts for] three months.
The "three months" refers to the ninety days [of the rainy season]. Summer is the time of rain. The *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is briefly divided into three types, namely:
the early, the middle, and the late. If the retreat is entered on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, it is called the "early *varṣā*.
From the seventeenth day onwards, until the retreat is entered on the fifteenth day of the fifth month, it is called the "middle *varṣā*. Only on the tenth day of the fifth month... [text ends]

The "sixth one-day binding" is called the *paścima-varṣā* (latter retreat). The first is the formal [retreat]; the latter two are for those who, due to circumstances or difficulties, are unable to enter the former binding.
Out of compassion for the assembly and in accordance with the needs of beings, the Tathāgata permitted a one-month period:
from the seventeenth day of the fourth month to the sixteenth day of the fifth month. Within this one month, the binding may be continued to completion; outside of this, it is not permitted.
Because it is not established as a formal rule (*dharma*), these three periods must all be observed for a full duration of ninety days.
As for the first period of confinement, one should remain until the fifteenth day of the seventh month when it is released.

As for the middle period, it begins from the sixteenth day of the seventh month and ends on the fourteenth day of the eighth month; if there are matters or circumstances that arise during this interval, provided the total count reaches ninety days, it is permitted.

Having understood this, one may depart. If it is not for a legitimate reason (*pratyaya*), one must remain together with those who have completed the subsequent retreat until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, when the retreat is concluded.
Based on these three periods, the focus is specifically on the summer months due to three considerations:

first, wandering about without purpose hinders the practice of the path; thus, the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "During the summer, unless there is a legitimate reason, one should not request a seven-day leave."

Regarding the Dharma: during the winter months, there is no such occasion [to travel], and one should not do so. Second, it would harm living beings, which would deeply contradict the spirit of compassion;
for throughout the summer, even a single square foot of ground contains insects. Thus, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"During the summer, except for the times of defecation and urination, one should remain in the full lotus posture. Third, since the purpose of the journey is improper, it will invite public censure.
Because the various donors complained, saying, "The heterodox practitioners who observe the precepts do not even travel during the summer retreat for fear of harming living beings;
how much less so the disciples of the Buddha who possess a compassionate heart? They never grow weary of seeking alms in both winter and summer, just as birds rely upon forest trees."
Wild beasts dwell in the mountains; they all have their seasons for dwelling. Why, O bhikṣu, do you not rest for even a moment?
It was because of this fault that the teaching arose here. Now, the Tathāgata, in accordance with sentient beings, observes the three-month summer retreat at Piraṇya.
The country of Bālā (or Bālī) is located outside of Northern India, west of the Snow Mountains, and is the name of a city in the kingdom of Bāhlika;
it is not the country of Bālā situated in the South China Sea. Some say it is the country of Vārāṇasī. Bā... [text fragment]
Roruka. This is within the territory of Central India and is far removed from Pāṭaliputra;
this is due to the phonetic similarity between "Pāṭala" and "Pāṭali," which led to a corruption of the name. Māra Pāpīyān.

There are four kinds of Māras: the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the Māra of the five aggregates (*skandha-māra*), the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*), and the Māra of the sons of gods (*devaputra-māra*).

The "Māra" mentioned here specifically refers to the celestial Māra. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) states: "In ancient translations of the sūtras and śāstras, the character for 'Māra' was written with the 'stone' radical. Since the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty..."

This means that Māra is able to afflict people; thus, the character for his name should follow the radical for ghosts (鬼). This is not the original meaning of the character itself, but is rather a transliteration of a Sanskrit term.

In full, it is *Māra*; in the language of Qin (Chinese), it means "one who can snatch away life. *Pāpīyan*—the correct pronunciation—is translated as "Evil" (惡); this is the name of the King of Māras. Master Kumārajīva said:
"In the language of Qin, he is called 'The Killer,' because he constantly desires to sever the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*) in others. He is also named... [text ends]
The worst among evils. There are three kinds of evil. The first is called "evil": if someone treats one with evil, and one returns evil in response, this is called evil.
The second is called "great evil": if a person does not encroach upon oneself, yet one harms them without cause, this is called great evil.
The third is called "the worst among evils": if someone comes to provide offerings and show respect, one fails to consider repaying their kindness, and...
Instead, they harm them; this is called the worst among evils. It is most extreme even for the Mara Kings.
While all Buddhas constantly desire to bring peace and security to sentient beings, these beings instead destroy and disturb that aim; therefore, it is said to be extremely grave.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana is also called Maudgalyāyana, or Maudgalyāyana. The *Chanyi chao* states: "Maudgalyāyana is a clan name;
it is translated as 'Praise-reciter' (*saṃstuti*). The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* translates it as 'radish' (*mūlaka*). Paramārtha calls it 'Mugala'."

It is a translation of *mudga*. Both of these items were favored by ancient seers (*ṛṣi*), and thus they named their clans after them. In the new [translation], it is called *Maudgalyāyana*, which means "Bean-Gatherer.
In antiquity, there was a seer who dwelt in a secluded mountain retreat; he constantly gathered mung beans (*mudga*) for food, and consequently took this as his surname.
The Venerable One’s mother belonged to that clan; she took her maternal surname, and thus [the lineage is so named].

Regarding the name "Mahā" (Great): it was given because the Venerable One had attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, it was intended to distinguish him from others of the same clan (*gotra*) so that there would be no confusion in his title.
Master Kumārajīva said: "He possessed great wisdom from birth; therefore, he was named Mahā-Maudgalyāyana.
He was also called Kautūlya. *Kautūlya* is the name of a tree. His father prayed to the deity of this tree, and...
Because he obtained a son, he is also called Kṛtaka; both names refer to the same person. According to the new translations, he was named Kūṭika after his father’s original name.
Master Kumārajīva said: "People of the time mostly called him by his clan name (gotra) and rarely by his personal name.
Among the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples, he was the foremost in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). [His father’s name and place of birth are explained as in the *Śīlaskandhaka* of the *Pravrajyāvastu*.]
Uttarakuru is also called Uttara-videha, and again Uttara-matya; this is translated as "Superior Place" (勝處), also "Superior Birth" (勝生), and "High and Exalted" (高上).
The *Dīrgha Āgama* asks: "What is the meaning of Uttarakuru? [It is explained] among the three heavens...
Below [the heavens], its land is most supreme and most excellent; therefore, it is named Uttarakuru, or Kurudvīpa. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) calls it Kuluo Island;
the old transliteration "Yudan Yue" and the variant "Jiulu" are erroneous.

It is situated to the north of Mount Sumeru. Its land is abundant and joyful, comparable to the heavens above. The people have no sense of self (*ātman*) or possession (*mama-kāra*), and all things are provided spontaneously.

Without requiring human labor or effort, there is naturally growing non-glutinous rice (the character *gēng* is pronounced like *gēng*; it is commonly written as *jīng*, and both are identical; for details, see the explanation in the "Thirty Matters").
Śāriputra: *Śāri* means "body" (*kāya*) or "śāli" (rice); *putra* means "son. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Śāriputra’s mother was named Śārī;
he was given this name based on his mother, hence he is called Śāriputra. This is translated as "Body-Son" (*Shenzi*). [End of] Text.
The verse says: "This girl had a beautiful form; because she was born from the body [of Śāri], she is called Śāriputra.

As for the term "Śāriputra," it means that her mother’s eyes were clear and pure like those of the śārika bird (the white egret). The *Chanyi chao* states: "In the new terminology, he is called Śāradvatīputra.
Śāradvatī here means 'śārika,' which refers to the hundred-tongued bird, also known as the spring oriole. *Putra* here..."
Regarding the term "Son" (Śāriputra): because his mother’s eloquence was like that of a śāri bird, he was designated as her son by way of this analogy;
thus, he is called Śāriputra. The Venerable One was originally born in the village of Nālada in Magadha.
He was the son of Tiṣya, a great master of treatises from South India, and at the age of eight, he ascended the debating throne and vanquished all the great [opponents].
Therefore, the Master said: "The Sūtra states that the Venerable One is the second Buddha in the world.
He is a general of the Dharma, able to follow the Tathāgata and turn the wheel of the Dharma. Among the disciples of the Buddha, he is foremost in wisdom;
all the wisdom possessed by the entire world does not equal even one-sixteenth part of his, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata. Now, the Venerable One..."
"I request that the Tathāgata proactively establish the precepts for the bhikṣus.

Although the Tathāgata had not yet established precepts for those disciples who had not yet given rise to the defiled states (*āsrava-dharma*), the Venerable One did not only now request the Tathāgata to formulate the precepts in advance;
he had also done so in a past life when he was a great minister under King Mahāyaśas in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. His name was...
Dhauli. Wise and intelligent, at that time the populace had not yet committed any transgressions, yet they requested that the King establish various punishments.
The King considered that since the common people had not yet committed any offenses or evils, he did not establish such punishments.

Likewise, at this present time, although the bhikṣus have not yet developed the dharmas of outflows (āsrava), they request that the World-Honored One preemptively establish prohibitions and precepts. The Buddha knows his disciples.
No impure phenomena had yet arisen, so no precepts had been established.
It is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), who does not impose punishments upon brahmins or householders for having committed no transgression. The Buddha was likewise.
At that time, the king named Mahāyaśas was the World-Honored One; the minister Tāḷi was the Venerable Śāriputra.
(The remainder is explained as in the *Śīlaskandhaka*).
