*Vipaśyin Buddha*.
He is also called Vipaśyin; in this language, it means "Victorious Vision.
He appeared in the world ninety-one kalpas ago, during a time when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years. He was of the Kṣatriya royal lineage, with the clan name Kauṇḍinya.
His father was the Kṣatriya king named Bandhumat, and his mother was named Bandhumatī. The kingdom ruled by the king was named Kṣemadṛśa. The Buddha had a son.
His name was Fangying (Phalguna). His attendant was named Wuyou (Aśoka). He had two great disciples: the first was named Qiantu (Khaṇḍa), and the second was named Tishē (Tiṣya).
The Buddha’s body was sixty yojanas in height, and his halo was one hundred and twenty yojanas in circumference.
He attained enlightenment while sitting beneath a pāṭala tree. He preached the Dharma in three assemblies; at the first assembly, he ordained one hundred bhikṣus.
In the first assembly, there were one hundred and sixty-eight thousand; in the second assembly, one hundred and sixty thousand;

and in the third assembly, one hundred thousand bhikṣus, all of whom had attained the path of arhatship. The Buddha’s lifespan was eighty thousand years, and for a hundred years the community remained entirely pure.
He constantly established the precepts by means of a single verse. (This was the ninth hundred and ninety-eighth Buddha of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*.)
Śikhin Buddha is also called Śikhi;
this means "Fire. He appeared in the world thirty-one eons ago, during a time when the human lifespan was seventy thousand years.
He was of the Kṣatriya royal lineage, his clan name was Kauṇḍinya, and his father’s name was Araṇābha, a Kṣatriya.
The king’s mother was named Parāhvatī. The kingdom ruled by the king was called Aruṇavatī.
The Buddha had a son named Amita; his attendant was named Kṣānticārin. He had two great disciples: the first was named Abhibhū, and the second was named Tripiṭaka.
The Buddha’s body was forty yojanas in height, and his halo was forty-five yojanas [in circumference].
His halo extended for one hundred *yojanas* throughout his entire body. He sat beneath a *pāṭalī* tree and attained enlightenment. He preached the Dharma at three assemblies:
at the first assembly, he delivered sixteen thousand bhikṣus; at the second assembly, fourteen thousand;
and at the third assembly, ten thousand. All of them attained the state of Arhat. The Buddha’s lifespan was seven [years].

"Ten thousand years! For eighty years, the assembly was entirely pure. He constantly preached a single verse as the prohibitive precept (this was the nine hundred and ninety-ninth Buddha of this *Sambhava-kalpa*)."
Suśobhita Buddha is also called Viśvabhū; this means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. He appeared in the world thirty-one eons ago, during a time when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years.
He was of the Kṣatriya royal lineage, his clan name was Kauṇḍinya, and his father’s name was...
Subāhudhara was a Kṣatriya king. His mother’s name was Yaśovatī. The kingdom ruled by the king was named Anūpama.
The Buddha had a son named Sujāta; his attendant was named Śānti. He had two great disciples:
the first was named Bhadrayaśas, and the second was named Uttara. The Buddha’s body was thirty-two yojanas in height and perfectly round.
His radiance extended for forty-two *yojanas*, and the light from his entire body reached sixty-two *yojanas*.
He sat beneath a *pāṭali* tree and attained enlightenment. He also preached the Dharma in three assemblies: at the first assembly, he delivered ten thousand people; at the second, eighty thousand;
and at the third, seventy thousand—all of whom became *arhats*. The Buddha’s lifespan was seventy thousand years.
For seventy years, the assembly remained entirely pure. Furthermore, he established a prohibitory precept with a single verse.
(This was the first of the thousand Buddhas of the Auspicious Kalpa.)
Krakucchanda Buddha—here translated as "That Which Should Be Severed"—is also rendered as "Adorned with Function.
He appeared in the world during the ninth minor kalpa of decrease within this Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years. He was of the Brahmin caste and the Kāśyapa clan.
[He was] included [in the lineage]. His father’s name was Ajita; his mother’s name was Śākyā. The kingdom was named Luṃhāritina; the king’s name was Sukhāti.
The Buddha had a son named Uttara; his attendant was named Sujñāta. He had two great disciples:
the first was named Sani, and the second was named Vīra. The Buddha’s body was twenty-five yojanas in height and perfectly round.
His light extended for thirty-two *yojanas*, and the light from his entire body reached fifty *yojanas*.
He attained enlightenment while sitting beneath a *śirīṣa* tree and preached the Dharma on two occasions. At the first assembly, he delivered seventy thousand beings;

at the second assembly, he delivered sixty thousand beings, all of whom became *arhats*. The Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand years, and throughout those sixty years, the assembly remained [in harmony].
Pure. At that time, two verses were established as the prohibitive precepts (this refers to the first Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa).
Kanakamuni Buddha—translated here as "Golden Silence"—appeared in the world during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was forty thousand years. Vipaśyin... [text ends]
He was of the Brahmin caste, with the family name Kāśyapa. His father’s name was Yaśasvanta, and his mother’s name was Uttara.
The country was named Cāmaveṭī, and the king’s name was Cāma. The Buddha had a son named Vinetāra, and his attendant was named Saumya.
He had two great disciples: the first was named Subhānu, and the second was named Udraka. The Buddha’s body was twenty-five *yojanas* in height;
his halo was thirty *yojanas* in circumference, and his light pervading his entire body was forty *yojanas*.

He attained enlightenment while sitting beneath an Udumbara tree. He preached the Dharma at two assemblies; at the time of the first assembly, he delivered sixty thousand people across [to liberation].
In the second assembly, he delivered three hundred thousand followers, all of whom became arhats. The Buddha’s lifespan was forty thousand years.
For thirty years, the assembly remained entirely pure, observing a single verse as their precept. (This is the second Buddha of this Bhadrakalpa.)
Kāśyapa Buddha—here translated as "Drinking Light"—appeared in the world during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
He was of the Brahmin caste, with the clan name Kāśyapa; his father’s name was Ajita and his mother’s name was Dhanavatī.
The country was named Pārśva; the king’s name was Kṛkin. The Buddha had a son named Jayasena. His attendant was named Sumitra. He had two great disciples:
the first was named Tiṣya, and the second was named Bharadvāja. The Buddha’s body was sixteen *zhang* tall, and his halo extended twenty *yojanas*.
He attained enlightenment while sitting beneath a nyagrodha tree. He also held two assemblies.
He preached the Dharma. At the first assembly, he delivered forty thousand beings; at the second assembly, he delivered thirty thousand beings, all of whom were Arhats.
The Buddha’s lifespan was twenty thousand years, and for twenty of those years, the assembly remained entirely pure.
He constantly used a single verse as the code of discipline. (This is the third Buddha of this Bhadrakalpa.)
Having already set forth the causes and conditions of the six Buddhas above, we shall now proceed to set forth the causes and conditions of our own Teacher, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni appeared in this world during the Bhadrakalpa when the lifespan of humans was one hundred years.
He belonged to the Kṣatriya royal lineage and had the clan name Gautama. His father’s name was Śuddhodana, a Kṣatriya king, and his mother’s name was...
The mother of the Buddha was Mahāmāyā. The kingdom ruled by the king was named Kālapinī.
The son of the Buddha was named Rāhula. The attendant was named Ānanda. His two great disciples were one named Śāriputra and the other named Maudgalyāyana.
The Buddha’s body was sixteen feet tall, and his halo extended one fathom. He sat beneath the Ajapāla tree.
He attained enlightenment under the Pippala tree. During his first assembly for preaching the Dharma, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty people, all of whom were Arhats.
The Buddha’s lifespan was eighty years. For twelve years, the community remained free from any faults or impurities, and they observed the precepts by means of a single verse.
Later, because there were those who violated the Vinaya, he established two hundred and fifty rules accordingly.
This is the Dharma of the Ten Precepts (the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa).
From the previous Buddha Vipaśyin down to the Buddha Śikhin, these three Tathāgatas appeared in the world at the end of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*.
Within that *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*, one thousand Buddhas appeared in succession in the world; this was the first.
Thus, Prabhūtaratna Buddha is the first, and Roca Tathāgata is the last.
From Krakucchanda Buddha down to Śākyamuni World-Honored One—these four Tathāgatas appeared at the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa.
Within this Bhadrakalpa, one thousand Buddhas will appear in succession in the world; Krakucchanda Buddha is the first, and Ruci is the last.
Tathāgata, in the future Star宿劫 (Nakṣatra-kalpa), there will likewise be one thousand Buddhas appearing in the world in succession.
The first shall be the Tathāgata Sunlight (Sūryaprabha), and the last shall be the Buddha Sumerudhvaja.

Regarding the fact that the first six Buddhas are cited extensively throughout various sūtras and vinayas, there are two reasons: first, they lived within the [final] hundred kalpas and possessed long lifespans.
Because they have been seen by gods and humans. Second, it means that the World-Honored One cultivated the causes for the primary and secondary marks beginning from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.
Regarding why these seven Buddhas now emerge from the same two lineages, this refers to [their emergence] from among the four clans.
The upper two castes are noble, while the lower two types are base. Since their lineage is base, they are not esteemed by the world;
therefore, all Buddhas and Tathāgatas appear only from noble lineages. The Brāhmaṇas possess pure and lofty virtue, while the Kṣatriyas possess far-reaching majesty and grace.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In accordance with what the world honors, the Buddha is born among them. Śākyamuni emerged from the Kṣatriya caste.
In an age of strength, he took birth in a royal lineage to manifest his majesty; Kāśyapa was born in a time of goodness and compliance, dwelling in pure conduct to manifest his virtue.

Thus far, according to various sūtras and śāstras, there are slight differences regarding the appearance of the seven Buddhas and the extent to which they taught the Dharma and delivered sentient beings.
Now, I have merely recorded those accounts that provide the most extensive explanations. However, as for the Buddha—
World-Honored One, you respond to beings according to their capacities and manifest transformations; the Dharma is not fixed and cannot be fathomed by ordinary people. Thus, a sutra says:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "If you now think that the disciples of the Tathāgata are few, do not hold such a view.
There are countless billions of disciples in the eastern direction, and countless billions of disciples in the southern direction. Therefore, Ānanda, you should establish this [conviction]."
"Consider this: I, Śākyamuni Buddha, possess an exceedingly long life span. Why is this so?
Although my physical body (rūpakāya) undergoes parinirvāṇa, the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) remains; such is the meaning. The Fayuan states:

According to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, when the Tathāgata first attained Buddhahood, he initially converted the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), turning them away from error and leading them into the Right Path. At that time, his śrāvaka disciples thought..."

Because he served [the Buddha] personally, the number [of his disciples] was limited. However, if one were to calculate those who, throughout the Tathāgata’s lifetime of teaching, were delivered by means of the Three Vehicles and attained entry into the Way, they would be immeasurable and boundless. Master Xuanzang said:

"According to the Western Regions, the Dharma taught by Śākyamuni during his single lifetime consists of three periods. During the first period, for the sake of the śrāvakas, he taught that phenomena possess characteristics (sanimitta)."

The Dharma. To shatter the attachments of non-Buddhists and cause them to realize the attainment of the Way, during the second period, he taught the Dharma of signlessness (*animitta*) for the sake of bodhisattvas of minor practice, in order to shatter the śrāvakas and cause them to realize the signless Mahāyāna.

During the third period, for the sake of bodhisattvas of great practice, he taught both the Dharma of signs and the Dharma of signlessness simultaneously, in order to shatter [the attachment to] both the Dharma of signs and the Dharma of signlessness, and cause them to...

Awakening to the Middle Way constitutes the ultimate Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Throughout these three periods, [the Buddha] extensively transformed immeasurable beings according to their individual capacities;
some even attained the Way by hearing the Dharma successively from disciples of the Three Vehicles, as numerous as motes of dust or grains of sand.
Therefore, it cannot be determined by a single passage, nor can it be restricted to a single meaning.
The sūtra is called *sūtra* in Sanskrit; this is translated as "契經" (*qi jīng*, "Sūtra of Accordance") or alternatively as "線經" (*xiàn jīng*, "Thread Sūtra").

"契" (*qi*) means that it accords with the principle of all Buddhas above and accords with the capacities of sentient beings below. "經" (*jīng*) has the meaning of "to string together" and "to encompass," signifying that it threads through [the teachings].
The meaning that should be known is the gathering and sustaining of those beings to be converted. Master Zhao said: "Sūtra" means "constant.
Although ancient and modern times differ, the path of awakening does not change; it cannot be obstructed by the various heterodoxies, nor can it be altered by the multitude of sages.
Therefore, it is called "constant. Cien (Xuanzang) said: "Sūtra" means constant and dharma; it is that which gathers and that which penetrates. Being constant, it is the Way.
It provides a model for the hundred kings; its Dharma serves as a paradigm of virtue for the ten-thousand chariots. "Gathering" refers to the collection of these wondrous meanings;

"pervading" refers to the guidance of those ordinary beings. It is hoped that all may together emerge from the ford of suffering and ultimately reach the shore of enlightenment. Now, this sūtra possesses a universal application.
There is a distinction. Generally, *sūtra* is the collective name for the sacred teachings.

Specifically, it refers to prose that directly explains the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), which follows the length of its meaning and principles rather than being restricted by the number of syllables;

this is the specific *sūtra*, such as the teaching on the Four Noble Truths and so forth. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "It refers to prose compositions that provide a concise exposition of what is to be taught."
Regarding the explanation of the meaning: the *Mahā-śāstra* states that those sūtras within the various scriptures which teach directly are called *sūtra*.
These include the four Āgamas, the various Mahāyāna sūtras, and the two hundred and fifty precept sūtras; furthermore, there are others existing outside the Tripiṭaka.
All of these are called *sūtras*. Within this context, from the *sūtra* (契經) up to the *upadeśa* (優波提舍), they are collectively termed the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
These were all spoken by the Tathāgata with a single voice; it is simply that the ailments of sentient beings are not uniform.
Since medicine employs manifold methods, the categories of the teachings are opened into twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). *Geya* (Sanskrit;
here translated as "Verses") refers to verses that restate the prose *sūtra* previously spoken; it is also called "Verses of Response" (*geya*), meaning...
One should restate the meaning through verses following the preceding prose text. These may consist of six lines, four lines, three lines, or two lines;
the number of lines is not fixed, yet all such compositions are termed *gāthā*. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"In various sūtras, based on the prose passages previously explained in detail, the concluding verses are composed and recited. This refers specifically to the texts of the formal compilation (*saṃgīti*).
In the Saṃgīti-varga and other sections, as the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I declare that through knowledge and vision one can exhaust all outflows (āsravas).
It is impossible that there could be knowledge and vision by which one cannot exhaust the outflows. After the Buddha had spoken these words in prose, they were later compiled into verse:

One who possesses knowledge and vision exhausts the outflows; one without knowledge and vision does not. When one penetrates the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, the mind is liberated from afflictions.
— *The Sūtra on Receiving the Prediction* (Āśvalāyanavyākaraṇa-sūtra)
In Sanskrit it is called *vyākaraṇa*; this is translated here as "prediction" (*shouji*). Dharmottara says: "The holy speech that bestows a name is called 'bestowal' (*śāsana*);

when the fruit is taken as the intended goal, it is called 'prediction' (*vyākaraṇa*. This refers to the Tathāgata’s conferring upon various bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and others, the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood.

Regarding the term *gāthā*, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "Formerly it was called 'jie' (偈), which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit original. Some call it 'jietuo' (偈他), which is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound.

Following the correct pronunciation now, it should be called *gāthā*. In the language of Tang, this means 'verse' (*song*); it is also called 'recited verse' (*fengsong*). It is further termed 'isolated verse' (*giqu*)."
The *Miaoxuan* states: "That which is not followed by a verse commentary is called 'isolated' (*gūqǐ*). This refers to verses that are spoken directly without reciting the prose (*chángxíng*);
examples include the 'Chapter on Emptiness' (*Kṣānti-parivarta*) and others in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: 'That is to say, among the various sūtras...'"
The concluding verse is a didactic stanza. Regarding what has been said therein, it refers to the *khaggavisāṇa-sutta* (Rhinoceros Stanzas) and others:
"Because intimacy with loved ones and association with those who are hateful give rise to desire and aversion, the wise avoid both alike;
they dwell alone and practice walking meditation like the horn of a rhinoceros."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is called 'do no evil,' and so forth, up to 'this is the teaching of all Buddhas'— this is named a *gāthā*,
a verse."
The sutras and śāstras frequently refer to these as "Self-Explanations" (*udāna*). In Sanskrit, this is called *udāna*, which here means "unasked self-explanation.

This refers to instances where no one has asked a question, yet the Tathāgata, through his knowledge of others' minds, observes the capacities of sentient beings and proclaims the teaching himself, such as in the *Shorter Amitābha Sūtra* and others.
These may be spoken in prose or in four-line or eight-line verses; the verses are derived from the *Dharmapada*.
This refers to the *Sūtra*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Udāna" means that there is a dharma which the Buddha must necessarily teach, yet no one asks about it;
therefore, the Buddha briefly provides the opening for a question. For example, when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, in the hall of the Vaiśya householders.
While walking in meditation in the shade, he himself uttered this udāna: "Truly excellent is this matter: there is no self, and nothing belonging to a self.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: "In what way is it that there is no self and nothing belonging to a self?

How is it that this matter is truly excellent? The Buddha said: "Ordinary persons have not yet attained the untainted path; because their minds are shrouded by perversions, they [grasp at] the non-self..."
There is no "mine. The mind is greatly terrified. If the Buddha and his disciples hear these auspicious sounds, they will joyfully practice them;
because they are free from inversion, they shall not create [further karma] again.
The *Nidāna-sūtra* is called *nidāna* in Sanskrit, which here means "causal occasion. The *Miaoxuan* states: "In the *Sūtras*, because someone asks a question, the Buddha explains this matter;
in the *Vinaya*, because someone commits such an act, he establishes this precept. This applies to all [cases]."
The Buddha’s discourses on the events of dependent origination are all termed *nidāna*. The *Jātaka*—
in Sanskrit called *jātaka*, which here means "born from a tree"— refers to accounts of the Bodhisattva’s practices based on past events.

It is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Bhikṣus, you should know that in the past I was born as a deer, a bear, a roe deer, a rabbit, a dragon, and as a golden-winged bird (*garuḍa*), a minor king, and the likes of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). This refers to such instances.

The *Sūtra on Wholesome Courses* refers to the narration of others' virtuous deeds. All sūtras speak of "past events" (*itivṛttaka*). In Sanskrit, this is called *itivṛttaka*, which here means "past events.
The *Vibhāṣā* states that it refers to those sūtras within which the matters previously seen or heard in the past are proclaimed.
The *Xianyang lun* states: "The 'Past Deeds' (*itivṛttaka*) refers to the Tathāgata’s teaching of such matters as the previous lives of the noble disciples.
The 'Birth Stories' (*jātaka*) refers to the Tathāgata’s teaching of the practices originally cultivated by the Bodhisattva. The *Miaoxuan* states: [as above].
This refers to another matter: it is like when the Buddha was about to bring King Śuddhodana and five hundred others back to his kingdom, he spoke a verse on the three causes and conditions.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "King Śuddhodana forcibly compelled the Śākyas to leave the household life and become disciples of the Buddha."
The Buddha selected five hundred people who were capable of attaining the Way and led them to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to teach and transform them.
During the first and last watches of the night, they applied themselves with single-minded diligence and did not sleep; through their tireless cultivation of vigor, they attained the Way.
Having attained the Way, the Buddha led them back to his native land and stayed in the Forest of the Rishis. This forest was fifty *li* from the city; these were the Śākyas.
In the Playful Garden (Kūṭāgāra-śālā), these Śākya bhikṣus, while staying in Śrāvastī, remained diligent and sleepless during both the first and last watches of the night;
thus, they perceived the night as being long. Coming from the forest to enter the city for alms, they felt the road was far and weary.
At that time, the Buddha, knowing their thoughts, had a lion come to pay homage at his feet and stand by his side. By means of these three causes, the Buddha [manifested the miracle].
For this reason, he spoke these verses:
"The night is long for one who does not sleep; The road is long for one who is weary; Saṃsāra is long for the fool Who does not know the True Dharma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu: "Before you went forth from the household life, you were negligent and slept much; you did not perceive that the night was long. Now, for the first time..."

In the latter part of the night, one who seeks the Way finds sleep scarce; thus, the night feels long. This forest was once a place where you traveled by carriage for pleasure, and you did not perceive it as distant.
Now, carrying your alms bowl and walking on foot, you are utterly exhausted; thus, the path feels long. This lion, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, was a teacher of brahmins.
He came to the Buddha’s presence to listen to the Dharma, while the assembly was listening to the Dharma without [interruption].
As soon as they spoke together, he conceived an evil thought and reviled them, saying: "What difference is there between these shaven-headed fellows and beasts?
They cannot distinguish the good from the bad, nor do they know how to speak.

Because of this karma of harsh speech, from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha until today, for ninety-one kalpas, he has constantly fallen among the animals. At that time, this person should have immediately attained [the fruit].
The Way: Because of ignorance, one creates for oneself the long duration of birth and death; now, because the mind is pure in the presence of the Buddha, one shall attain liberation.
Thus it is said in the Vaipulya Sūtra.

"Universal" (*fang*) refers to the fact that it universally benefits all capacities; "equal" (*deng*) refers to the fact that the four teachings are discussed together. Many sutras and śāstras speak of "Vaipulya.
In Sanskrit, it is called *vaipulya*, which here is translated as "universal-extensive" (*fangguang*). The *Miaoxuan* states: "This is named according to what it represents.

The principle of the universal-extensive is 'universal' because it is the correct principle, and 'extensive' because it is richly encompassing. This refers to the Mahayana Vaipulya scriptures, the meaning of which is as follows:
It is vast, equal to empty space.
The *Adbhuta-dharma* is called *a-fu-da-mo* in Sanskrit; this is translated here as "unprecedented phenomena" (*abhūta-dharma*) or also as "rare phenomena. The *Miaoxuan* states:
The Buddha manifested various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), which caused sentient beings to marvel at such an unprecedented occurrence. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Rare phenomena (*adbhutadharma*) refers to those accounts within the sūtras that describe extremely rare events concerning the Three Jewels and the like, as well as the disciples' praises of the World-Honored One’s rare merits.
For example, when Śāriputra praised the World-Honored One’s unsurpassed merits, the Venerable..."
Ānanda, he praised the World-Honored One’s most rare and extraordinary teaching.
The *avadāna*,
which in the Indic language is called *avadāna* and here is translated as "parable" (*píyù*), refers to the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata for those of dull faculties.
Through various metaphors and expressions, he instructs and clarifies them, causing them to attain understanding. As it says in the *Zhiguan*:
"When the moon is hidden behind heavy mountains, he uses the metaphor of raising a fan; when the wind ceases in the vast void, he uses the instruction of the swaying tree."
*Upadeśa-sūtra*: here translated as "Successive Analysis" (*zhù fēnbié*).
It refers to the meaning of what is taught; it may also be rendered as "Exegesis" (*lùn yì*). The *Mahā-śāstra* states:

"It answers various questions, explains their underlying reasons, and further elaborates upon various meanings. For example, when the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths, [it explains] what they are."
Four. These are the Four Noble Truths. What are the four? They are the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
This is called the exposition of the meaning. What is the Noble Truth of suffering? It refers to the eight kinds of suffering, beginning with the suffering of birth. What is the suffering of birth?
It refers to the various sentient beings who experience suffering within their respective places of birth. Such is the case.
Question and answer, providing a detailed explanation of its meaning—this is called *upadeśa*.
*Kontei* (恐畏) is an Indian name for *śabara*; here it means "fear" (*we*) or "terror" (*bu*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* refers to it as the "Forest of Terror."
When those who have not yet abandoned desire enter this forest, their hair stands on end; for this reason, it is called the Forest of Terror (*Bhaya-vana*).
It is also called *Śītavana*, which translates as "Cold Forest," meaning that its groves are deep and secluded and cold.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This forest has many corpses; when people enter it, they fear the cold.

However, in the Western Regions, wherever there are cities or villages, the king invariably provides a separate forest for the disposal of corpses. The *Faxian zhuan* (Record of Faxian) calls it *Śmaśāna*, which in the Han language means "burial field for the abandonment of the dead.
Various sutras and śāstras often refer to it as the Āṭavī Forest, and it is also called... [text continues].
"Dark Forest by Day" (Zhòu'ànlín) is identical in all respects.

Regarding the expression "exposing the right shoulder," some say it means exposing one shoulder, some say it means exposing one arm, and others call it "baring the shoulder" (biāndǎn). "Baring" (tǎn) refers to the flesh.
This refers to baring the shoulder. According to the customs of India, standing with the shoulder exposed and the upper body bare constitutes a rite of profound respect;
this is further completed by the removal of sandals. As for hats and veils, they originally do not exist [as part of the rite]; however, if one suffers from cold, they may temporarily be permitted.
When performing the ritual of prostration, these must be removed, as only then does it accord with the proper form. The Vinaya regulations for the three robes likewise require...
One should wear the robe covering both shoulders. However, upon seeing a superior elder, one must immediately bared the right shoulder and expose the arm.

This is not like the śramaṇas of this region who casually leave one shoulder bare while still wearing a shirt or tunic underneath; to call such a person "one who has bared his shoulder" (pratyaṃśuka) when it is actually covered by clothing is a profound error.
Nevertheless, because this practice has been followed for a long time, it is difficult to reform it all at once. For those who are disciples of the Buddha:
One must understand that this was originally established by the Buddha. Various sūtras and śāstras frequently state that one should place the right knee on the ground;

they also speak of *hukuì* (half-kneeling), *hùkùì* (cross-kneeling), or *chángkùì* (long-kneeling). These differences arise from the distinct transliterations and translations between the Hu (Central Asian) and Brahmanic (Indian) traditions, which have led to many variations in China.
"Hu" refers to the regions of the Qiang and Rong peoples. "Hù" means to kneel with the left and right knees alternating positions.
"Ground" (*bhūmi*) indicates that there is something to be requested. Regarding the meaning of the term, the *Yīngyì Zhǐguī* states: "It is incorrect to say 'kneeling on the floor' (*hùguì*).

This is because it is a term inherited from the Indian world, where it refers to those dwelling in the Five Indias and north of the Pamir Mountains—namely, the various tribes of the Rong, Qiang, and Hu.

In current translations of the Sūtras and Vinaya, it is frequently rendered as 'mutual kneeling' (*hùguì*). Because three parts of the body are raised like wings, it is called 'mutual kneeling'; that is, the right knee touches the ground."
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* clarifies three meanings: first, the right knee has strength, enabling one to remain kneeling for a long time;
second, the right knee has strength, making it easy to rise and sit; third, the right knee is restless, and placing it on the ground brings stability.
If both knees touch the ground, this is called *dīrgha-jānu* (long-kneeling). The *Yijing’s Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "As for 'long-kneeling,' it refers to crouching on both knees."
Regarding the posture on the ground: one supports the body by standing with both feet upright. What was formerly called "hukui" (kowtowing on one knee) is incorrect;

this is practiced throughout the Five Indies, so why refer to it specifically as "Hu"? As for "placing the palms together," some call it "crossing the hands," while others say "joining the ten fingers and nails.

All these terms denote a composed countenance and an expression of reverence, intended to restrain the mind from wandering and scattering. However, since the impulses of the mind are difficult to guard against, the practice of placing the palms together is prescribed.
And it is for the sake of single-mindedness. The *Commentary on the Meaning of Avalokiteśvara* states: "In this land [China], one shows respect by folding the hands;

in India (Tianzhu), one shows reverence by joining the palms. The hands originally occupy two sides; now they are joined as one to signify that one is not distracted or negligent, but is instead focused and single-minded.
The *Fayuan* states: "Nowadays, among those who prostrate to the Buddha, many join their fingers but do not join their palms, or there are some who..."
To join the palms and then let them open is due to arrogance and indolence. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"When joining the palms, they must not be hollow in the middle; the ten fingers must not be uneven. Yet, while one’s original intent was to seek merit, one instead incurs the fault of arrogance.
This is the protocol for joining the palms while kneeling with bared shoulders; as for the rite of prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, it is even more so.
One must understand this thoroughly. The *Sūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra* (Chí dì lùn) states: "When the five wheels reach the ground, one performs prostration.
The *Āgama-sūtras* and the *Mūla-vinaya* clarify that the two elbows, both knees, and the crown of the head are called the "five wheels" (*pañca-cakra*).
A "wheel" refers to a circular form; since all five points are circular and can rotate upward and downward, producing ever-increasing merit, they are termed "wheels. Now...
When observing Western monks prostrating, they frequently lift their robes to expose their knees first as they descend to the ground;
they then rest their elbows on the floor while supporting themselves in mid-air with both palms, demonstrating the gesture of receiving the feet [of the honored one].

Recently, I have seen those in this land who perform the prostration by pressing both hands down on the ground and planting both feet behind them, yet failing to touch their heads to the ground; such is a manner of irreverence and negligence.

Alternatively, some stand before the Buddha, waiting for a mat before they prostrate; others spread out their sitting mats (*kaṭhina*) as if intending to seat their own bodies upon them, and only then perform their prostrations.
These are all great errors of the Dharma-ending age. The Tripiṭaka Master Yijing stated:
"Spreading out one's sitting mat while prostrating is a practice not seen in the Five Indias. For those who prostrate, the intention lies in showing reverence to the superior."
Regarding self-abasement: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "Of the human body, the head is the highest and the feet are the lowest.

To prostrate with the head at the feet is the ultimate expression of reverence. If one were to first place an object upon the body before performing prostrations, how could this constitute a ritual of self-abasement?

(One should know that the sitting cloth was originally prescribed for the purpose of sitting and reclining; it was not intended from the outset for use during prostrations. That this practice has now become widespread in this land is not due to the effort of a single individual.)

This is capable of rectifying the erroneous customs that have long prevailed. However, when members of our own wise community enter among those who follow such errors, they cannot avoid being influenced by them. One should instead treat the Tathāgata’s three robes with reverence; fearing thoughts of dust and defilement, one may hope to avoid the transgressions of violating the teachings and harboring arrogance or hatred.
One must surely aspire to the correct standard and reject [the errors] as appropriate.

Regarding the text on the formulation of the precepts, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, in the future there will be people of false views who shall slander the Buddha, speaking these words: 'If the Tathāgata is omniscient, for what reason does he wait...'"
Sentient beings commit offenses, and only then are the precepts established. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This is precisely the mark of omniscience.
If I were to establish the precepts preemptively, people would slander me. Why is this? Because I have committed no offense."
How can this be asserted with such force? This is not the teaching of one who possesses all-knowledge. Why is this? Because I am without fault;
the Tathāgata lacks compassion, does not benefit others, and does not embrace sentient beings.
It is like a man who has no son yet says he has a son who will be born at a certain time—such empty words, how can they be trusted? Why is this? Because they are not true.

Therefore, if one were to see the actual production of an offense, then faith would arise. Thus, Mañjuśrī, since people and devas do not see the offenses that have not yet been committed, how could they be prohibited by a precept?
It is necessary to see the offense before a precept is established (and so forth).
The *Sūtra of Good Observance* (*Śariputra-bhikṣu-vinaya*) states: "If the Tathāgata were to establish a precept before a defilement had arisen, sentient beings would conceive thoughts of slander."
"How is it, Gautama, that the śramaṇas are like the śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are of noble lineage or former kings;
who have renounced their wealth, palaces, wives, children, and retinues; who do not spare even their own lives; and who are all content?"
"They have no desires for the world; why then, Gautama, do you instead bind them with the *prātimokṣa*?
Thus you speak because you, Gautama, have not skillfully distinguished the people of the world.

If one were to establish precepts [in such a manner], the people of the world would likewise not give rise to a mind of reverence, just as when a physician who is unskilled in treating diseases sees a person..."
When a boil was first about to form, although it possessed the nature of a boil, it had not yet fully developed; he immediately lanced it.
Once lanced, blood flowed profusely and he suffered great agony. When the physician applied medicine to it, the wound healed immediately.
The physician said, "I have treated your illness; you must give me my fee. The patient replied, "This is a foolish physician! If this were truly my illness..."

"You should treat me; I was originally without illness. Yet you forcibly tore my flesh, causing blood to flow and giving rise to great agony, only to then demand payment from me—is this not madness? The śrāvaka disciples are also like this:

if they first establish precepts and then give rise to slander, saying, "I am myself without fault, yet you have forcibly established these precepts," for this reason the Tathāgata does not [permit it].
First, the precepts are established. If there are those with outflows (*sāsrava*), at that time the Tathāgata shall establish precepts for his disciples and point out the *Prātimokṣa*.

It is like a skilled physician who prescribes medicine according to the disease, enabling recovery and causing [the patient] to receive great rewards and praise, saying, "This excellent King of Physicians has skillfully treated my ailment. The Tathāgata is likewise.
Thus it was. According to each transgression, the rules were established; they received and upheld them with joy, without a single word of complaint.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: "The Tathāgata has long known such matters; why did he not establish the prohibitions beforehand?
Is it not the case, World-Honored One, that you wish to cause sentient beings to enter the Avīci Hell? It is like a great multitude of people who, wishing to go to another land, become lost."
They have lost the right path and follow deviant ways. Because these people do not know they are lost, they all claim this [deviant way] to be the path;
furthermore, they see no one whom they may ask about what is right or wrong. Sentient beings are thus deluded regarding the Buddha-dharma and do not perceive the true and correct.
The Tathāgata should therefore first proclaim the right path and instruct the bhikṣus: "This is a violation of the precepts; this is..."
Regarding the observance of the precepts, they should be established in this manner. Why is this? The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, is the embodiment of truth;
he knows and perceives the true path and is able to expound the ten wholesome actions, their superior merits, and their essential meaning.

Therefore, one should request that the precepts be established first. The Buddha said: "If it is said that the Tathāgata is able to proclaim the ten wholesome actions and their superior merits for the sake of sentient beings..."
This is the merit [of the Tathāgata]. Thus, the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as he does Rāhula.
Why do you challenge me by saying, "Could it be that the World-Honored One wishes to cause sentient beings to enter hell"?

I see that for even a single person who possesses the causes and conditions to fall into the Avīci Hell, I would remain in the world for one kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa, for the sake of that person. As for me, regarding the multitude...
He has arisen with great compassion; for what reason would he ever deceive? Regarding those who regard him as a child:
if they were to cause him to enter hell, it would be like a mendicant within a kingdom who, seeing a hole in his robe, subsequently mends it. The Tathāgata is likewise;
seeing that sentient beings possess the causes and conditions for entering the Avīci Hell, he immediately uses the goodness of the precepts to mend them.

Although the Tathāgata has something to teach, he does not establish precepts prematurely; rather, it is only after monks have gradually engaged in unrighteous conduct that he subsequently establishes them according to the specific circumstances.
Thus, sentient beings who delight in the Dharma follow and practice these teachings. Such is the assembly of these [beings].
Only then can one perceive the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states: "Stop, stop, Śāriputra!

Only after the tainted dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*) have arisen will the World-Honored One establish the precepts. (Thus, although the two hundred and fifty rules of the Dharma were already established when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment...)
It is only because the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings were not yet capable of being restrained all at once that [the rules] were established only after they had committed the offenses.

Regarding the meaning of "existence" (*sāsrava*) in the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it asks: "What is the meaning of 'existence'? It refers to all phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). The Buddha said: "If..."

Karma is that which causes the continuity of future birth; this is called *bhava* (existence). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "It is called an outflow (*āsrava*) because it causes one to lose the Path.

The *Abhidharmapitaka* states: "It flows down into birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "What is the meaning of 'outflow' (*āsrava*)? It means the sense of remaining and dwelling [within cyclic existence]."

The meaning of stagnation and storage; the meaning of branching streams; the meaning of confinement and maintenance; the meaning of enchantment and delusion; the meaning of intoxication and confusion—these are the meanings of *āsrava* (outflows).

The meaning of dwelling and remaining is also the meaning of *āsrava*. As for the meaning of dwelling and remaining, it causes sentient beings to dwell and remain in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The meaning of "soaking and storing" is the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*).

Just as seeds soaked and stored within a moist vessel are able to produce sprouts, so too, within the vessel of a sentient being's afflictions, the seeds of karma are soaked and stored, capable of producing future existence. This is the meaning of "streaming forth."

Regarding the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*): just as water flows from a spring or milk from a breast, so too do the various outflows stream forth from the six sense bases of sentient beings. Regarding the meaning of "binding":
just as a person who is bound by others cannot travel freely in the four directions as they please, so too are sentient beings bound by the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because they are maintained, one wanders through the various realms, destinies, and births, lacking self-mastery and failing to proceed toward the realm of nirvana.
Regarding the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*) as "delusive bewitchment": it is like a person who has been bewitched by a spirit; such a person speaks what should not be spoken.
One performs what should not be performed and thinks what should not be thought.

Because sentient beings are thus deluded by the various afflictions (*kleśa*), they give rise to the three types of misconduct of body, speech, and mind. The meaning of "intoxication" (*mada*) is the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*);
just as when a person drinks much wine made from roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits, they immediately become intoxicated and confused, unable to discern what should be done.
One should not perform improper actions. Being shameless and lacking remorse, such sentient beings are intoxicated by the wine of afflictions;
they do not discern what should be done and what should not be done, remaining intoxicated by shamelessness and lack of remorse, even unto such afflictions.
They cause sentient beings to transmigrate up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); therefore, they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are of two kinds: cause and fruit. Uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are likewise of two kinds:
cause and fruit. The fruit of the contaminated is called suffering (*duḥkha*); the cause of the contaminated is called origination (*samudaya*). [The uncontaminated...]
The fruit is termed "cessation" (nirodha). The untainted cause is termed the "path" (mārga).
Regarding the four *pārājika* dharmas:
*pārājika* is the head of the five categories of offenses and the first of the seven groups of transgressions. To protect them is like guarding a bright pearl; to violate them—
To those who do so, [the precepts] are like spoiled meat. To respectfully guard them is the path to Nirvana; to abandon them is a worn-out sack in the ocean of suffering.
To violate even one of them is to cease being a bhikṣu. The devas will not protect you, and the sages and saints will all reproach you.

As you walk, ghosts will sweep away your tracks; as you lie down, demons will bewitch your mind. Even on the grounds of a saṃghārāma, there is no place for you to set foot. Throughout the ten directions...
Regarding almsgiving (*dāna*): even a drop of water does not go to waste. As stated in the *Sudarsana-vinaya*:

"If one wraps the outer *kāṣāya* around one's neck while internally practicing impure acts—having committed such evil deeds—one will fall into hell immediately upon death. It would be better to swallow red-hot iron balls amidst blazing flames and die;
if there is one who has broken the precepts, they should not consume the offerings of the faithful. The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "O Śramaṇas..."
Entering the gate, one beholds the Buddha’s luminous precepts. One discards the old and renews oneself;

refining the mind and extinguishing desire, one becomes pure within and without, like a clean cloth that takes on color when dyed. Thus observed by the multitude, the śramaṇa beholds the light; his conduct is lofty and his wisdom complete.
The world offers him service, providing clothing, food, and dwellings; he accepts these without fault, and the merit of the donor is great. He advances in practice and meditative concentration.

They attained the first fruit of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the second fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the third fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and the fourth fruit of arhatship (*arhat*).

People also heard of this. Although these śramaṇas had not yet attained the Way, they were clear in their understanding of the meaning of the Buddha’s scriptures; they maintained upright minds and were filial toward the teachings.

They propagated great compassion to nurture all things, and their benevolence reached all living beings. Taking themselves as a measure for others, they brought peace to them; they viewed enemies as their own children. Upon seeing women...
When people come, treat them as sisters. If you behold those who are destitute and suffering, you should contemplate the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
May all living beings find peace in body and joy in mind; may they encounter the Triple Gem, have their defilements removed and their darkness extinguished, and with pure hearts perceive the light.

Returning to the original non-existence, one attains eternal peace and boundlessness. With such resolve and conduct, one remains free from transgression from beginning to end regarding fine food and elegant clothing.

As for the fundamental nature of all beings—greed, lust, anger, hatred, ignorance, and jealousy, which are the filthiest among filths and the darkest among darknesses—the śramaṇa’s mind opens to receive illumination;
the defilement of delusion is utterly stilled. Though dwelling in a defiled world, he is like a lotus.
A lotus dwells within the mud, yet the mud cannot defile it; therefore, receiving offerings incurs no fault.

However, if one harbors the three poisons, does not eliminate the ten evil deeds, indulges the heart in desire, seeks gratification through flattery and deception, and does not uphold the Buddha’s precepts—then it would be better to swallow hot iron or drink molten copper.
Such death is but momentary, whereas receiving offerings with impurity leads to rebirth in the Great Mountain Hell (Mount Tai), where one must drink that copper.
They eat charcoal; the years [spent there] are difficult to calculate (Mount Tai is, indeed, a place of hell).
△ First: Impure Conduct (this is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for bhikṣuṇīs).

Vaiśālī is here translated as "Extensive and Adorned" (Guǎngyán). The *Jìngmíng lüèshù* states: "This term means 'vast, extensive, adorned, and pure. Because the kingdom is broad and level, it is called 'extensive' (guǎngbó);
because the cities and towns are magnificent and elegant, it is called 'adorned and pure' (yánjìng). It is also called Vaiśālī. Furthermore, it is also said:
Regarding Vaiśālī, Master Kumārajīva said: "Vai" refers to the suitability of the soil for rice cultivation;
"śālī" means "extensive and magnificent," as the ground there is level, vast, and adorned. The *Sudarśana-sūtra* states: Long ago, the king of Vārāṇasī had a queen who became pregnant.
When the queen realized she was pregnant, she informed the king, and the king immediately provided her with all necessary attendants and provisions.

She was nurtured until all her faculties were fully developed and harmonized. When the full month had passed, she entered the birth chamber. If one possesses merit and virtue, they give birth at dawn;
this lady likewise gave birth at dawn, but produced a single piece of raw flesh, red as the hibiscus flower.
Furthermore, when other women gave birth to children whose complexion was like gold, this lady saw the wives of her attendants giving birth.
The child was handsome and exquisite; she felt shame in her heart and thought to herself:
"If the King sees that other wives have given birth to handsome children, yet my son is but a lump of flesh, devoid of hands and feet, he will surely feel loathing and contempt upon seeing him.
Having had this thought, she immediately took him and placed him in a vessel, then struck gold to make a thin plate.
He wrote a title in vermilion ink stating: "This was born of the Queen of the King of Vārāṇasī.
He covered the top of the vessel and sealed it with the royal seal. He inscribed [the title] with gold leaf and placed it on the exterior of the vessel before sending it down into the river.
After the messenger had discarded it, various spirits and deities protected it so that it would not be blown away or submerged by wind and waves. At that time, there was a certain Daoist master.
Relying on a cowherd, he lived by the riverbank. One morning, this practitioner went to the river to wash himself and saw this vessel from afar.
Thinking to himself, "I shall pick up this vessel," he approached and took it.
Upon seeing that it was inscribed with golden letters and marked with the royal seal, he opened the vessel to look inside and saw nothing but flesh.
He had this thought: "If this were dead meat, it should have long since rotted and stunk; there must surely be some extraordinary sign.
He immediately took it and returned to his dwelling. He carefully set it aside for a period of over half a month, during which it became two pieces.
When the Daoist saw such an auspicious sign, he placed it in a favorable location. From that time forward, another half-month passed, and the two pieces...
Each produced five embryos. Furthermore, after another half-month, one portion became male and one portion became female;
the male was the color of gold and the female was the color of white silver. When the Daoist saw these signs, his heart gave rise to love and esteem for them.
As if toward her own child with no difference, by the power of her mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*), milk spontaneously flowed from the thumbs of both hands.
One finger fed the boy and one finger fed the girl; as the milk entered the children's bellies, it was like clear water entering a *maṇi* jewel.
He was transparent both within and without. The Daoist named the two sons "Lichizi" (in the Han language, this means "thin-skinned," or also "same-skin").

The Daoist raised these two sons with extreme hardship; he would enter the village to beg for food while simultaneously seeking various provisions for the two sons, returning only when the sun had set.
At that time, a cowherd saw the Daoist on behalf of his two sons... [and so forth].
Suffering was thus. He came forward and said, "Virtuous one who has left the household life, you ought to cultivate the Path.
Why do you hinder and neglect your spiritual practice for the sake of these two children? You may give them to me; we shall raise them. The practitioner replied, "Excellent!"

Thereupon, the cowherd returned home. On the following day, together with his companions, he leveled the road, erected banners and streamers, scattered flowers of various colors, and beat drums to welcome the two sons.

Upon arriving at the place where the practitioner resided, he addressed the practitioner, saying, "These two sons are now ready to depart. The practitioner replied, "Excellent. The practitioner then further entrusted them [with instructions].
These two sons possess great merit and virtue that is immeasurable.
You should attend to them well and provide for them with the five kinds of dairy products: milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and ghee.
When these two sons have grown up, they will seek out a fine, level, and spacious location to establish their own residence together; you may then install the son as king.
The daughter was made a lady. Having received these instructions, the cowherds and others immediately returned to their original dwelling place.
As the two sons gradually grew up, they went out with the sons of the cowherds to play.
These two boys then kicked the cowherd boys; the cowherd boys wept and returned to tell their parents, "These two have no father."
The mother and sons trampled and struck us. Their parents replied, "You all should each avoid this place.
Because of this, the site was named Vatsa (Vatsa meaning "avoidance" in the Han language).

When the two sons reached the age of sixteen, the cowherd saw that his sons had grown up and observed a level and broad expanse of land, one hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth; he then [established] its center.
They erected houses. The cowherds gave their daughters in marriage to the men, establishing them as husband and wife, and immediately installed the men as kings and the women as queens.
Subsequently, they became pregnant and gave birth to twins—each a boy and a girl.
In this manner, sixteen sets of twins were born. When the cowherds saw that the number of princes was gradually increasing, they each began to do so again.

They constructed houses and built various gardens and ponds. When the dwellings of thirty-two people were joined together, expanding and spreading out until they reached three times their original size, it was therefore named Vaiśālī. This is the fundamental causal origin.
The *Xiyuji* states: The kingdom of Vaiśālī (within the borders of Central India) is over five thousand li in circuit.
Its soil is fertile and its flowers and fruits are abundant. The āmra and mocā fruits are both plentiful and highly prized. The climate is mild and pleasant.
The customs are pure and simple; they cherish merit and value learning (and so forth).
Regarding Kalandaka Village and Upatiṣya, the son of Kātyāyana (also written as Kā):
*Kalandaka* is translated here as "the bird with a beautiful voice. The *Sudarsana* states: "As for Kalandaka..."
This is the name of a mountain mouse. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī, accompanied by his female entertainers, entered the mountains for recreation.
The king became weary and fell asleep beneath a tree; the entertainers scattered in all directions to play.

At that moment, within a cave beneath the tree, there was a large venomous serpent which, smelling the scent of the king’s wine, emerged intending to bite him. A mouse from atop the tree descended, making a sound.
He called out, "Wake up, King! and the snake immediately retracted. After the king had awakened, he fell back asleep; the snake emerged once more, intending to bite the king.
The rat cried out again, causing [the king] to descend from the tree to wake him. Once the king had risen, he saw a great venomous snake in a hole beneath the tree and was struck with terror.
He looked around in all directions for his attendants, but they were nowhere to be seen. The king thought to himself:
He said, "I have now returned to life through the kindness of a mouse. The king then reflected on how he might repay the mouse's kindness.

At that time, there was a village near the mountain; the king immediately summoned the villagers and decreed, "From this day forward, my entire royal stipend shall be diverted to provide for the mouse.
Because of this mouse, the village was named the Village of Kalandaka. At that time, within the village...
There was an elder who possessed four billion gold coins. The King immediately conferred the rank of elder upon him;
because of the name of his village, he was called the Elder Kalandaka. Sūdena was the son of the Elder Kalandaka.
Twelve years after the Buddha attained enlightenment, Sūdena went forth into the religious life. Sūdena remained in another country for eight years.
He studied the Way for eight years. Later, he returned to the village of Kalandaka.

According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun), because his parents sought and petitioned the deities until they obtained him, he was named "Obtained by Seeking" (*Sudinna*). Thus, Sudinna is translated here as "Obtained by Seeking.
If following the Sanskrit pronunciation, *su* is translated as "good," and according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is translated as "Good Wealth" (*Sudhana*).
My son, this man, at the beginning of the eon when the world was first formed, became defiled by desire even before the phenomena of outflow (*āsrava*) had arisen.
Furthermore, in the present time, among the disciples of the Buddha, he has given rise to the phenomena of outflow even before such phenomena have existed.
Using skillful means, he led his mother to engage in improper conduct. In a past life, that mother had also been the chief consort of the King of Kāśī;
using skillful means, she smeared honey upon the leaves of a nyagrodha tree.
Because of a defiled mind, he lured away the golden deer king and touched him; immediately, the deer lost his golden color.
Furthermore, at this present time, by means of skillful expedients, he has led his son astray and caused him to lose his brahmacarya. As for that deer king of that time—
Sudinnas (according to other sūtras and vinayas, this is often *Kalandaka*, which is the name of a bird).

*Arhat* means "one for whom there is no further birth" (*anutpāda*). It is also called "one who is unattached" (*asaṅga*). It is translated as "one worthy of offerings" (*arhat*). It is also called "one of proper deportment" (*yogya*) or "one worthy of [veneration]. It is also called "worthy."
True. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ara" means "thief," and in the Han language it means "to destroy.

Because all thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been destroyed, and because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, one should receive the offerings of all devas and humans in the world. Furthermore, "A" means "not."

The term *arhat* means "one who is born. Because they will not be born again in future lives, they are called *arhats*. Alternatively, it is said that there is no direct equivalent in Chinese; the name contains three meanings.
Because the chaff of ignorance has been shed, they will not receive the retribution of birth and death within the field of future lives; thus, they are called "unborn" (*a-jāti*).
Because the ninety-eight latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) have been exhausted, they are called "slayers of thieves" (*vītarāga*). Possessing the merits of wisdom and abandonment, they are capable—

Because he is a field of merit for humans and devas, he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat). Since it encompasses these three meanings, the Sanskrit name is retained (the remainder is explained as in the fourth precept).
The *Huashui shanjian lü* (Sūtra on the Flower-Water Good-Seeing Vinaya) states: "Flower-water" (*huashui*) refers to blood; this is a term for blood.

It is the natural law of women that when they are about to conceive, a mass of blood forms at the site of the embryo. After seven days, it breaks spontaneously, and from this, blood flows out. If the blood flows out...
Regarding "non-interruption": the male seed does not remain stationary but flows out together [with the female element].

If it has been completely discharged, the male seed returns to its original place, and only then is conception formed. It is like a farmer who has plowed, prepared, and matured the field, yet it is suddenly flooded by excessive water.
When grain is placed in water, it sinks to the bottom; when grain floats on the surface of the water, it flows out in all four directions.
Why is this? Because the water is excessive and the grain does not adhere to the mud, it cannot form roots or stalks. It is the same with women:
if the blood has ceased, the male seed can remain, and thus conception occurs.
"Thus, 'the two' refers to the former [wife]. In the Sanskrit language, it is *pūrvabhāryā*; this is translated here as 'the former second' or 'the original second,' which means the former wife.
This implies that once one has abandoned secular life to leave the household, the title of 'wife' no longer applies, yet she remains his original [consort] from when he was still in the world."
At that time, because his wife was second in rank, she was called "the Former Second.
Regarding the "heat of sensual thoughts":
although the body and speech do not move, one merely contemplates beautiful features in the mind. As for "sensual desire," the mind becomes clouded and deluded.
"Intoxicated" means the body is dazed and confused. "Desiring heat" refers to the union of two bodies.
"Torch" (tǔchì):
the second character is pronounced as *jù* with the rising tone; it refers to burning bundles of reeds. This is used as a metaphor for desire being like a torch.
It can burn away the bodies and lives of sentient beings and brings about various other calamities; therefore, the Buddha employs various metaphors to explain this.
Regarding the metaphor of the torch: the Buddha said that it is just as if a person were to hold a torch in their hand and walk against the wind;
if they do not discard it quickly, they will surely burn their hands and other limbs. It is also like a tree.
As for the fruit: it is like a foolish person who, craving delicious fruit, climbs a tree to eat it and refuses to descend in time.
When others cut down the tree, he falls as it topples over; his body and head are shattered, and he dies in agony. Furthermore, there is the fruit of the tree.
Once matured, it immediately falls to the ground and rots away; it is not a lasting phenomenon. Furthermore, it is like a borrower:
suppose there is a person who borrows articles of pleasure, such as palaces, chariots, horses, the seven treasures, famous garments, and fine clothing.
If anyone sees them, they all praise their beauty together; yet later, the owner takes them back at will. Others [are likewise].
When people see this, they say: "That which was borrowed is truly a deception; it is not a borrowing at all. Why is that?
Because the owner of the object seizes it back according to his own will. Furthermore, it is like a metaphor for a dry bone.
It is like a starving dog that gnaws upon a dry bone; it may tear its lips or break its teeth, or even wound its throat, yet it cannot thereby alleviate its hunger.

Furthermore, it is like a piece of meat: suppose there is a small morsel of flesh fallen on the open ground, which a crow or an owl seizes and carries away, while other crows and owls compete and pursue it. If...
If this crow quickly abandons this small piece of meat, the other crows will no longer pursue it in competition.
Furthermore, it is like that which is seen in a dream: for example, there may be someone who, in a dream, obtains all five objects of desire and amuses themselves;
yet once they have awakened, not a single one of them is to be seen. Therefore, desire is like a dream.
*Vajjiputtaka* is also called *Vajji*;
this means "to avoid. The causal conditions for this are found in the previous section on Vaiśālī. [Regarding] "weak in the precepts" (*dubbala-sīla*).
[The character is] pronounced *luí* (rhyme with *léi*). It means illness, emaciation, and exhaustion.

This refers to one who lacks the power to uphold the Tathāgata’s precepts and teachings, whose mind gives rise to weariness and longing for domestic affairs—like a foolish person who is unskilled in eating and drinking.
He ate raw milk mixed with meat and immediately fell ill with leprosy, jaundice, and emaciation; his limbs were so exhausted that he could not support himself.
Without any sense of remorse or resolve to seek a skilled physician, he thought only of applying arsenic, excrement, and urine as a remedy.
Yet their suffering only increases further, with no possibility of recovery. It is just the same for them: within the Buddha’s precepts, they lack the mind of superior progress;
they feel weary and disenchanted, yet do not reproach themselves to seek noble practice.

Instead, they turn their thoughts back toward the pleasures of household life, like that leper who does not repent and seek a physician, but hopes instead to consume excrement and urine—vainly exhausting himself in suffering.
It will never improve. It is impossible for one to abandon the joy of the Tathāgata’s noble and holy precepts and yet obtain another form of happiness;
such a thing cannot exist.
(The female macaque...)
*Ci*: pronounced like *cha*. It means a female animal that acts as a mother. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "In general, there are three kinds of offenses:
first, offenses against the paths of karma (*karmapatha*); second, offenses of misconduct (*duṣcarita*); and third, offenses against the precepts (*śīla*).

Sudinna committed an offense of misconduct among these three; because sexual intercourse is an evil dharma, it does not constitute an offense against the paths of karma. [He did not commit it] himself.
Because his wife was deceased, he incurred no offense of violating the precepts, as the Buddha had not yet established the rules of discipline. The bhikṣu in the forest incurred two offenses:

he incurred the offense of misconduct (*duṣkṛta*), because sexual intercourse is an unwholesome act; and he incurred an offense of the course of action (*karmapatha*), because the female macaque belonged to the male macaque.
He did not incur an offense of violating the precepts, as the Buddha had not yet established the rules of discipline. Both of these bhikṣus are termed "those who acted first."
Therefore, there is no offense of violating the precepts.

Regarding the "bhikṣu by name," the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu by name is one who is designated by name. The *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "It is like a person establishing a personal name."
One is called a *bhikṣu* either because it is a name commonly granted by the world, or because one belongs to the clan of *bhikṣus*; for these reasons, one is addressed as a *bhikṣu*.
This is what is meant by a "nominal *bhikṣu*. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"Just as people in the world establish names when they wish to call out to men, women, and so forth, and thus address someone as a *bhikṣu*."
A "semblance bhikṣu" refers to one who has shaved off his hair and beard but has not received the Buddha’s precepts; because his physical appearance, deportment,
and manner of movement resemble those of a bhikṣu, he is called a semblance bhikṣu.
The *Mūla-bhikṣu-śāstra* states:

"If a person is not actually a bhikṣu, yet claims for themselves, 'I am a bhikṣu,' or is one who dwells as a thief (*caura-vāsika*) while claiming to be a bhikṣu—this is called a 'bhikṣu by self-claim'.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* further states: "Moreover, there is the bhikṣu who dwells as a thief..."
One who has shaved off his beard and hair, dons the *kāṣāya*, and declares of himself, "I am a bhikṣu," is called a "bhikṣu by self-assertion.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one shaves his own head and claims for himself the title of bhikṣu, he does not take birth within my Dharma;
he should not be granted ordination or the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*). If he has already received the full precepts, he must be expelled."

Regarding the phrase "Welcome, Bhikṣu," the *Śālistambasūtra* states: When a layperson comes to the Buddha’s presence desiring to leave the household life, the Tathāgata immediately observes their faculties.
If the causes and conditions are complete and they are one who may be delivered, he then calls out, "Welcome, Bhikṣu! and their hair and beard fall away of their own accord.
He fell [into the order] and became a bhikṣu. As for "calling": the Tathāgata extended his right hand from within his saṃghāṭī robe;
his hand was golden in color. With a Brahma-voice, he called out, "Welcome! You may practice the holy life (brahmacarya) to bring an end to the source of suffering.

Before the Buddha had finished speaking, he immediately became a bhikṣu, having attained full ordination (upasaṃpadā). His three robes and earthenware bowl were already suspended over his right shoulder.
The color of his almsbowl was like that of a blue *utpala* flower; his *kāṣāya* robe was as brilliant as a red lotus.
He was fully equipped with a needle, thread, a small knife, and a water-strainer—these eight items being the daily requisites of one who has left the household life, which appeared spontaneously.
His deportment was perfect. As for the "Well-Come" (*svāgata*) bhikṣu, he was first Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
From Yaśas until Subhadra, all those whom the Tathāgata summoned with the words “Come” (ehi) and thereby received the precepts were called *ehibhikṣus*.

If a person possessed karma that obstructed the Path, or was unable to realize the fruit of *aśaikṣa* in their present body, the Buddha did not ordain them as an *ehibhikṣu*. Those who were ordained by the Buddha [in this manner]—
All of them were in their final bodies as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Why is this? It is because it was spoken by the Tathāgata’s own divine mouth;
others could not have attained it.
"Bhikṣu" in the sense of "one who begs":

just as worldly people, such as brahmins and others, constantly beg for alms in order to sustain their own lives, when they beg from others, they also say, "I am a bhikṣu. This is what is meant by a "bhikṣu" in the sense of begging.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding the bhikṣu who wears cut-and-sewn robes, the *Sudarsana* states:
'As for one who wears cut-and-sewn robes, the value of the robe may be as much as ten million [gold pieces]. Once the bhikṣu has obtained it, he then cuts it.'"

Having cut [the cloth] and joined it together, one destroys the value of the garment by stitching it with needle and thread; thus ruining its fineness and softness, it becomes a coarse and worn garment.
Originally bright white, its original color is ruined by tree bark, and it thus becomes an old garment.
One who is able to wear such a cut-and-sewn garment is called a bhikṣu; this is what defines a bhikṣu.

Regarding the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* (The Vinaya Compendium on the Questions of Upāli) concerning the "bhikṣu who has destroyed the fetters" (*kṣīṇasaṃyojana-bhikṣu*): the term "bhikṣu" carries the meaning of "one who destroys. All afflictions (*kleśa*) are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).

If a person has left the household life, destroyed all afflictions, exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), and attained the fruit of Arhatship—or has reached twenty years of age [as a novice]—[he is a bhikṣu].
Or, even if one is less than twenty years of age, because they have attained arhatship, they are said to have received the full precepts;
this is also called "receiving the full precepts through superior attainment. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"Sentient beings who are bound by the fetters of outflows and afflictions are able to receive subsequent bodies and undergo the ripening of suffering and retribution, wandering through birth and death in a continuous succession of causes and conditions. If one can know and see [this], one severs them as such..."
These are the outflows. Having uprooted them completely, like cutting off the head of a tāla tree so that they never arise again, he is called a bhikṣu who has destroyed the afflictions,
a bhikṣu by means of the formal ritual of the white-fourfold motion (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

This refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), whose person is free from obstacles, who seeks the complete precepts with a perfect mind, and who generates the superior resolve (*adhyāśaya*).

Having made a formal declaration through speech, manifesting the action of vocal karma, they request the threefold petition before the Sangha. Thereupon, the community of monks performs the *jñapti-tri-karman* (one motion and three proclamations).
Regarding the matter at hand, it is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma, reaching its ultimate fulfillment and perfection. This is...

One should be rebuked. Having attained the nature of a bhikṣu, it is called "receiving the full ordination through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. When accomplished according to the Dharma, one becomes a bhikṣu who has obtained his place.
Among these eight types of bhikṣus, only the bhikṣu ordained by the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is taken as the basis for the method of establishing the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*).
As for those who come by invitation (*svāgata*), those who have broken the bonds, and those who have already realized the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*), they possess spontaneous [attainment].

Regarding the precepts: they consist of the eternal abandonment of the transgression of violating prohibitions. As for those who wear the cut-and-sewn robes (*khaṇḍa-cīvara*), these are gathered from discarded refuse (*pāṃsukūla*).

Their status applies to those who attained through spontaneous arrival (*svayam-āgata*), those who broke their fetters (*saṃyojana-bheda*), and those ordained by the formal motion of four parts (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Originally, this was not part of the canonical text; therefore, no other school possesses this designation.

If it were not included therein, it would be subsumed under the ranks of external sectarians. The remaining three [categories] are all merely provisional names; they do not constitute the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"Zhong ye" (The assembly; having attained the locus, this is to attain the essence of the unconditioned precept and to perfect the nature of a bhikṣu).
*Sifenlü mingyi biaoshi*, Fascicle Three, Phonetic Glossary.
*Qi* (pronounced *ji*) means to repair or mend.
*Ju* (with the second tone) means "how could it be" or "is it not.
*Mei* is the same as *mei*.
"Meng" (夢): the upper character is pronounced *dèng*; the lower character is pronounced *méng*.
"Luan" (臠): the pronunciation is *luán*; it refers to a piece of meat.
"Qi" (鵄): the pronunciation is *chī*.
