○ Regarding the Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas:

As for the gravity of these precepts, they consist of two sections from beginning to end. If one commits an offense in the first section, one is expelled without further deliberation; if one violates the latter section, one is subject to communal instruction.
Should the offense be concealed, one must undergo *parivāsa* (probation) in addition; if it is revealed, one is immediately made to perform *mānāpya* (rehabilitation). Furthermore, one must...

The four conditions must be fulfilled; at the very least, twenty monks must gather together to perform the removal [of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense]. Since these conditions necessarily depend upon the assembly, one must be diligent, firm, and cautious.
This is especially true in this degenerate age when circumstances are difficult to fulfill and pure monks who know the Dharma are hard to find.

If one does not act according to the teachings, one’s confession will be in vain. Should one treat the words of the Vinaya with contempt, one will incur grave transgressions, depending on whether the violation of the precepts was light or heavy.

The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "If one lacks shame and remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is like the lifespan of the Nirmāṇarati devas, which is eight thousand years.
Yet, when calculated by human reckoning, this corresponds to two hundred thirty billion and forty thousand years.
If one is even more obstinate and does not believe in the Buddhist sūtras, it is as in the case of [the hell of] Avalokita."
The *Samādhi Sūtra* states: "The transgressions of killing eighty-four thousand parents and others are so profound and grave as to be incalculable;

they cannot be eliminated. The *Kāśyapa Sūtra* states: At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, in the future final age, during the last five hundred years, there will be semblance śramaṇas who, though wearing the kāṣāya robe, will destroy the [Dharma]..."
"Throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they have accumulated [the causes for] *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The Buddha said to Kāśyapa: 'Do not ask about this. Why?
Because those foolish people truly possess faults and evils; they believe in and accept all demonic activities (*mārakarman*).
The Tathāgata does not say that such people will attain the Way. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, [they would not be able to plant...]"
He manifests various supernormal powers and preaches the Dharma to transform and teach others, yet he cannot cause those evil desires to cease. Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:

“World-Honored One, I would rather carry all sentient beings, mountains, rivers, and villages of the four continents upon my head for an entire kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa, than I could bear to hear the voices of those foolish sentient beings who do not believe.”
“World-Honored One, I would rather sit upon a single sesame seed for a full kalpa, or even less than a kalpa, than hear the voice of that faithless,
deluded person who has broken the precepts. World-Honored One, I would rather remain within the great fire at the end of a kalpa—
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down— for hundreds of thousands of billions of years, than hear that [faithless person]...”
"World-Honored One, I would rather endure all manner of anger, abuse, beatings, and injuries from all sentient beings than hear the voice of those faithless,
deluded people— those great thieves of the Dharma who steal the teachings and violate the prohibitions.
As it is said in the sutras, should one not be fearful?"

△ First: Emission of Semen (This is an *asaṃvara* [exclusive] precept. For bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pāyattika*. Because the afflictions of women are deep and heavy, they are difficult to restrain and control. If the Buddha were to impose a heavy penalty upon them, it would cause distress to sentient beings.

Furthermore, for a woman, emission of semen generally requires a private, secluded place and much effort; whereas for a man, it can occur spontaneously according to circumstances. Therefore, the regulations are not the same).
Śrāvastī, also known as Śāvatthī, is translated here as "Source of Renown," meaning that precious objects abound in this city.

It is also translated as "Abundant Virtue," which encompasses four meanings: first, the possession of wealth and treasures; second, the excellence of the five sensual pleasures; third, the abundance of learning; and fourth...
[The Buddha] explained the meaning of "Abundance" (*Puṇya*). Tiantai said: "Śrāvastī is also called Śāvatthī. In the past, there were two rishis;
the younger brother was named Śāva, which means 'young,' and the elder brother was named Abhadda, which means 'invincible.
The city was named after these two individuals combined. The *Sudarsana* says: "Śrāvastī is the name of a practitioner of the Way. In the past..."
There was a Daoist practitioner residing in this place. In ancient times, there was a king who, seeing that this land was excellent, requested of the Daoist that he establish a kingdom there.
He named it after the Daoist’s own name, calling it Śrāvastī.

It was also called Bahuputra, meaning "Many Sons," because the precious treasures and various rare items of all nations were gathered and accumulated in this country; thus it was named Bahuputra. As the verse says:
Śrāvastī is exceedingly sublime; those who behold it never tire of doing so.
Amidst the sounds of ten kinds of musical instruments, it calls out for food and drink. Abounding in many precious treasures, this city-state is like the palace of Śakra.
Within its borders, there are five hundred and seventy thousand households; as for those outside the city belonging to the kingdom of Śrāvastī, [they are likewise numerous].
There were eighty thousand villages, and the kingdom measured one hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"The country of Śrāvastī—formerly called Shewei, which is an error—is within the borders of Central India.
It is over six thousand *li* in circuit, and its palace city is over twenty *li* in circuit. Grain crops are abundant, the climate is temperate, and the customs are simple and sincere."
Śikhaṇḍī is the name of the capital city ruled by King Mahāsena;
it is the designation for the royal capital of the kingdom of Kośala. Kālodāyin...
He is called "Black Light" (Kṛṣṇābhāsa) and also "Coarse Black" (Karkaśakṛṣṇa), because his face was black and his eyes were red.
His former name was Udāyin, which means "Appearance," signifying that he was born at the time of sunrise. According to the *Sudarsana*, he is Kālodāyin.
He was born on the same day as the Buddha and was originally a high minister. Before the Buddha had renounced the world, he constantly served as his attendant.

Regarding the matter of the schism in the Saṅgha, it is said: At that time, a venomous snake emerged from a hole by the roadside. Seeing this venomous snake, Udāyin feared it would harm the Bodhisattva;
he immediately drew a sharp sword and cut it into two pieces. The snake then spat out its venomous breath, which struck Udāyin.
His body turned black; for this reason he was named Kṛṣṇa-Udāyin (when the Buddha had not yet left the household life, he was called Bodhisattva).
Because the World-Honored One had left the world and attained enlightenment, his father the king, longing to see him, dispatched Udāyin to go and welcome him.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him and called out, "Welcome, Bhikṣu! Whereupon his beard and hair fell away naturally, and he became a bhikṣu by nature.
He was full of desire. Later, in Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin woman who pressured him into committing an unrighteous act;
however, the Venerable One did not comply with her wishes. She, harboring malice and anger, maimed her own body and falsely accused the Venerable One, reporting this to her father.
Her father assembled a crowd of five hundred Brahmins to drag the Venerable One away, but the Venerable One possessed great strength.
He was even unable to move his feet. At that time, the Buddha perceived through his insight that this was the final instruction for Udāyin.
The Buddha withdrew his spiritual power, and the assembly of brahmins beat him nearly to death and dragged him before the king.
Although the king knew thoroughly that the matter was false, he nevertheless rebuked the Venerable one three times. The queen also earnestly admonished him. The Venerable one—
Upon hearing this, he felt profound shame and remorse. He then went to the Venerable Śāriputra, prostrated at his feet, and related the matter in detail.
At that time, Śāriputra observed his faculties and disposition, and taught him the Dharma according to his capacity, providing him with further instruction.
Having heard this, he disciplined himself, gave rise to a courageous and resolute mind, eliminated all fetters and afflictions, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Having realized the fruit of the path, he reflected upon repaying the Buddha’s kindness and engaged in the work of teaching and transforming others.
The Buddha said, "Among all my śrāvaka disciples who teach and transform sentient beings so that they attain the noble fruits, Udāyin is the foremost.
Thus, the Venerable One, in the city of Śrāvastī, taught and transformed eighteen hundred million people, leading them to attain the noble fruits. Later, for the sake of [subduing] the violent...
The wicked daughter-in-law consorted with a thief and cut off the life of the Venerable One. She took the corpse and discarded it in a heap of refuse.
This was the ripening of karma previously committed by the Venerable One; now that the fruit has matured, he experiences it within his own aggregates and physical vessel, and not in any other place.
There is no other thing that can take the retribution in his stead. At that time, on the fifteenth day, when it was the time for the Poṣadha ceremony, the great assembly had all gathered.
"Only the Venerable One was not seen. Could it be that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have forgotten their mindfulness? They must know he has been killed and cast into a heap of filth.
Then the Buddha, surrounded by the great assembly, arrived at the city gate at night and emitted a great radiance that filled the entire city.
The gate opened of its own accord. The King, the Queen, the ministers, the commoners, and the women were startled awake and rushed forth in haste.
Following the Buddha, they went to the place where the refuse heap was located. They brought forth the Venerable’s body, bathed it with fragrant water, and placed it within a precious carriage.

With music, banners, and streamers, they escorted it out of the city together. Arriving at an excellent location, they cremated him with fragrant wood and collected the relics, placing them inside a golden jar.
At the side of a crossroads, they erected a stūpa as an object of veneration, serving as a field of merit for humans and devas.

[It is also said: "The Venerable One, having already realized the fruit [of Arhatship], vowed to repay the Buddha’s kindness by converting a thousand households of married couples so that they might all realize the holy fruit. He had already converted nine hundred and ninety-nine households; as for the last household, the husband had already attained the fruit."

She went out. The wife had an illicit affair with a thief; fearing her husband's return, the Venerable One disclosed the matter, thereby causing the thief-husband to kill her (the details of this prior karmic connection are found in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*).
"One who dreams within a dream" refers to the spirit wandering during sleep. *Liezi* classifies six types of dreams: first, the "true dream" (dreaming while in a state of tranquility);

second, the "terrifying dream" (dreaming from a state of shock or alarm); third, the "recollection dream" (dreaming of what one has habitually thought about); fourth, the "awakening dream" (dreaming of what was spoken while awake); fifth, the "fearful dream" (dreaming from a state of dread...).
And there are dreams [of joy]. Sixth, joyful dreams (dreams of delight). The *Śubhadarśana* states: "There are four kinds of dreams:

first, dreams caused by the disharmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as dreaming of mountain collapses, or soaring through the void, or seeing tigers, wolves, lions, or bandits pursuing one."
Second is the dream resulting from prior perception; that is, having seen white or black forms, or the features of men and women during the day, one sees them in a dream at night.
Third is the dream granted by devas; if it is a deva who is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they manifest a good dream to cause the person to obtain what is wholesome;
if it is one who is a bad influence, they manifest a bad dream to cause the person to have unwholesome perceptions. Fourth is the dream of conceptualization; that is to say—
Regarding the previous lives of people: if one possesses merit and virtue, one will now see auspicious dreams; if one has committed transgressions, one will now see inauspicious dreams.
For example, when the Bodhisattva’s mother dreamed that he was about to enter her womb, she saw a white elephant descend from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and enter her right side;
this was a dream of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, if one dreams of prostrating to the Buddha, reciting sutras, or upholding [the teachings]...

Precepts, generosity, and various other virtues—these too are like dreams. Dreaming of paying homage to the Buddha, listening to the Dharma, or preaching the Dharma, and so forth, constitutes a virtuous dream.
If one dreams of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, this is called an unvirtuous dream.
If one dreams of colors such as blue, yellow, red, or white, these are indeterminate dreams. Question: If that is so, then one must experience their karmic fruit.
[The questioner] replied: "One does not receive the karmic fruit. Why? Because the mental karma is weak, it does not induce retribution.

Therefore, the Vinaya states: 'Except for that which occurs in dreams, there is no offense. Since the Buddha established the precepts to regulate physical action (*kāyakarman*) and did not regulate mental action (*manaskarman*), there is no fault in dreams.
The Buddha said: "If what occurs in a dream were real, then no one at all would [be able to escape the consequences]."
One can attain liberation. Regarding the *Mūla-vinaya*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "I do not say that those bhikṣus have no mental activity or conceptualization;
however, what occurs within a dream is not a reality. One should exclude what happens in dreams. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"Although there is consciousness within a dream, there is no fixed, real entity to be found; therefore, there is no offense. [Nirvāṇa]...

The *Pan jing* (P’an jing) states: The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying, “If there is a bhikṣu who engages in sexual intercourse in a dream, does this constitute a violation of the precepts?
The Buddha said, “No. One should conceive of sexual desire as foul and impure, not giving rise to even a single thought of purity.
One must distance oneself from women and the afflictions of craving. If one engages in sexual intercourse in a dream, upon waking one should give rise to [a sense of revulsion].”
[One should feel] remorse. When receiving offerings, one should regard them as eating the flesh of one's own son during a time of famine. If lustful thoughts arise, one should quickly abandon them.
One who can act in accordance with what the Buddha has taught is called a Bodhisattva. *Pañcavargīya-vinaya*: The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If one has not yet abandoned desire, hatred, and delusion, and sleeps with a distracted mind, one will inevitably discharge impurity. Although...
One has not yet been able to leave it behind; one sleeps with a mind bound by mindfulness. If there were no such fault, the *Sudarsana* states:
"Sleeping with a distracted mind" means sleeping with an unconcentrated mind. If one sleeps during the day, one should first resolve: "At such and such a time, I shall arise.
As it is said in the Sūtra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If, after you have finished bathing, you wish to sleep, you should..."
One should form this thought: "I shall rise before my hair has even dried. If one sleeps in this manner, it is virtuous. Furthermore, at night, one should know the time:
"When the moon reaches such-and-such a position, I shall rise. If there is no moon, one should think: "When the stars reach such-and-such a position, I shall rise.
One should first bring the Buddha to mind, and then, among the ten wholesome dharmas, reflect upon each dharma according to one's inclination before falling asleep.

Regarding "essence" (*śukra*): The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that because the winds of deluded thought and false recollection blow upon the fire of lustful desire, the flesh, marrow, and fat flow and undergo a thermal transformation to become essence.
There are five types, seven types, and ten types of essence, as detailed in the Vinaya texts.
(The phrase "taking mindfulness of the Buddha as the first" means that among the six recollections, mindfulness of the Buddha is primary.)
Regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Saṃgha" refers to the four *pārājikas*. "Āvaśeṣa" means that this offense has a remainder;
it should be remedied through *karma* (formal ritual action). Therefore, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Furthermore, this offense must be confessed within the Saṃgha.
It is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring confession before the community). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
“*Saṃgha* means that if one commits this offense, one must rely upon the *saṃgha* to undergo the prescribed procedure, and rely upon the *saṃgha* to attain purification from the offense;
it does not depend on any individual. *Āvaśeṣa* has the meaning of ‘remainder. If a bhikṣu [commits an offense] among the four *pārājika*..."
Within the Dharma of the Kāśyapa [tradition], if one commits even a single [of these offenses], there is no remnant remaining; one may not dwell together [with the community].

These thirteen dharmas, although committed by a bhikṣu, still have a remainder because they can be remedied; therefore, they are called *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṃghāvaśeṣa). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: first, the matter depends upon the Saṃgha; second, its nature is residual, requiring the Saṃgha for its removal.

This indicates it is not among the initial grave offenses (*pārājika*). "Saṃgha" refers to the community; "avaśeṣa" means remainder. Because one follows the instructions of the community, the offense is only then extinguished.
Furthermore, while the nature of the preceding four precepts is non-residual, this one is residual. This is because...
Because it can be cured. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "It is like a person who has been mangled by another; as long as the throat remains, it is called 'mangled.
It is like two people who have entered together into the midst of battle: one is struck down by another and his life has ceased;
the other is struck down by another, yet a small portion of the life-faculty remains unsevered. If he obtains a skilled physician and excellent medicine, he may be healed. If...
That which is "non-existent" cannot be cured. It is the same for one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; there is a slight principle by which it may be repented.
If one obtains a pure assembly that performs the method for confessing and removing the offense according to the Dharma, this offense can be removed.
If there is no pure assembly, it cannot be extinguished. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. (*Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*)
It is said: *Saṃgha* means "the Saṃgha. *Ādi* means "the beginning. *Śeṣa* means "the remainder.
Why is it called the "beginning of the Saṃgha"? The answer is: when this bhikṣu has committed an offense and desires purification, he goes to the place where the Saṃgha is;
the Saṃgha grants him *parivāsa*. This is called the beginning. Once the *parivāsa* has been completed, next the six-night *mānāpya* is granted.
The *nāṭa* (probationary period) constitutes the middle [offense]; for the remainder, an *āpattipariśuddhi* (rehabilitation) is granted. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
As for "Cakravartin," in Sanskrit it is *cakravarti-rāja*, which here means "Wheel-Turning King. Master Xuanzang says:
Now, when a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) is about to ascend the great throne, a great wheel-treasure appears in response to his merit, floating through the air to manifest before him.
There are distinctions among these wheels—of gold, silver, copper, and iron—and consequently, differences in the extent of his realm: four, three, two, or one continent.
Because this serves as a prior auspicious omen, it becomes his title. A Golden Wheel-Turning King’s transformative influence extends over the four continents; a Silver Wheel-Turning King, however...
The rule of the copper-wheel-turning king excludes Uttarakuru; the iron-wheel-turning king excludes both Uttarakuru and Aparagoyānī, and thus pertains only to Jambudvīpa.

The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "In the world there is a wheel-turning sage-king who possesses the seven treasures and four divine virtues. What are the seven treasures? First, the golden wheel."
The seven treasures are: first, the wheel-treasure; second, the white elephant-treasure; third, the dark-blue horse-treasure; fourth, the divine jewel-treasure; fifth, the jade woman-treasure;
sixth, the householder-treasure (in other sūtras called the steward-treasure); and seventh, the military commander-treasure. How is the golden wheel-treasure accomplished?
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King emerges from the land of Jambudvīpa, born of the Kṣatriya caste consecrated by water, on the fifteenth day when the moon is full—
At that time, having bathed in fragrant water, he ascended a high palace and enjoyed himself together with his assembly of court ladies.

Suddenly, the divine wheel-treasure appeared before him; it had a thousand spokes, was complete in radiance and color, was made of celestial gold, and was fashioned by celestial artisans—unlike anything found in the world.
The diameter of the wheel was fourteen feet. Upon seeing it, the Wheel-Turning King immediately summoned his fourfold army.
Facing the precious golden wheel, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and stroked the golden wheel with his right hand, saying:
"Proceed toward the eastern direction and turn according to the Dharma; do not deviate from the established rule. The wheel then turned eastward.
At that time, the king immediately led his fourfold army to follow behind it. Wherever the wheel came to rest, the king halted his carriage. At that moment—
The minor kings of the eastern regions, seeing the Great King arrive, came before him carrying precious bowls filled with precious grain.
They prostrated themselves and addressed him, saying: "In this eastern region, the land is fertile and prosperous, abounding in various rare treasures. The people are numerous and flourishing;
their natures are benevolent and harmonious, and they are compassionate, filial, loyal, and obedient. We pray only that the Holy King will govern and rule here. We..."
When acting as attendants on his left and right and receiving his governance, the Wheel-Turning King at that time says to the minor kings: "Stop, stop!

O worthy ones, you have already made offerings to me; you must now govern by means of the True Dharma (saddharma), ensuring there is no partiality or injustice, and that no unlawful conduct occurs within the realm.
Do not kill living beings yourselves, and teach others not to kill."
Those who commit theft, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, lying, frivolous talk, greed, anger, jealousy, and hold wrong views—these are the ones for whom I provide governance.

When the minor kings heard these words, they followed the Great King on a tour of the various kingdoms, reaching as far as the eastern sea, and subsequently traveling through the south, the west, and the north. Following...
Wherever the wheel arrives, the various kings each offer their kingdoms, just as the minor kings of the eastern regions did (and so forth).

This is the accomplishment of the Wheel-Treasure (the remaining six treasures are explained at length in the sutra; the four divine virtues are: first, long life without premature death; second, a strong body free from illness;

third, a handsome and upright countenance; fourth, overflowing treasuries). If it is an iron-spoked wheel, it has two hundred and fifty spokes; a copper wheel has five hundred spokes; a silver [wheel]...

The wheel has seven hundred and fifty spokes; the golden wheel has one thousand spokes. According to the origin of this *cakravartin* emperor, when he appears in the world, he is endowed with a full thousand sons.
The land is as level and smooth as the palm of a hand, peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, free from all calamities and epidemics.
Food and clothing appear spontaneously without the need for seeking or labor. The king transforms and guides solely through the ten wholesome deeds, nurturing all with compassion.

The people and all things are like a father’s love for his children; the citizens admire the king as children look up to a father. They follow the king’s transformative guidance; thus, the treatise states:
"All wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) never inflict harm; they subdue others through victory so that each may dwell in peace.
They exhort and transform them to cultivate the path of the ten wholesome actions. Therefore, when a wheel-turning king dies, he is certain to be reborn in heaven."

Regarding internal form and external form: "internal form" refers to one's own body; "external form" refers to the bodies of others; "internal and external form" refers to both one's own body and the bodies of others.
The *Suvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "When internal form and external form come into contact, they become functional and move within space; yet even so, there is no 'internal' [substance]."
Furthermore, there is no external form; because one moves of one's own accord, one incurs an offense.
*Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*—this term means "skirt. Its color, substance, dimensions, and the rules for wearing it are all as explained in the section on the "One Hundred Matters."
△ Section Two: Physical Contact with a Female Body (This is an exclusive precept:
if a bhikṣuṇī makes physical contact with a male, she incurs a pārājika offense).
*Menmo*: *men*, with the *qie* (phonetic guide) *ben*; the pronunciation is *mén*. It means to stroke or grasp. *Mo*: *mo*, with the *qie* *mo*; the pronunciation is *mò*.
Regarding the character *menmo*, it refers to stroking or feeling with both hands.
"Mou kou mou" (鳴口鳴) means to chirp or whistle at someone's mouth. Furthermore, "mou" (嗚) should be written as "mi" (歍), meaning for the mouths to draw near one another. This refers to verbal abuse.
*Mà* (罵): pronounced with the *mò* (莫) initial and the departing tone of *má* (麻). It means evil speech. *Lì* (詈): pronounced with the *lì* (力) final. To directly rebuke is called *mà*;
to indirectly assist [the rebuke] is called *lì*.
*Nàbǐ* (捺髀):
*nà* is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "nuǎi" (乃八切) and carries the departing tone (*rùshēng*). It means to press down with the hand. *Bǐ* (髀): pronounced *bǔwěi* (補委切), sounding like *bǐ*.

Master Ying stated that in ancient script it was written as *bì* (蹕), which shares the same pronunciation as *púmǐ* (蒱米切). The *Shuowén* states it refers to the outer part of the thigh. If pronounced *bì* (陛), it is a Northern Chinese usage.
The pronunciation of this character is *fāng'ěr* (方爾). This pronunciation is current in the Jiangnan region. In the Vinaya texts, it was formerly written as *bǐ* (髀), which is a vulgar character.
*Niśīdana*.

This is called the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat). It is also called the "clothing for sitting" (*anuvāsanaka*) or the "clothing for following the feet" (*pādānuvāsanaka*), because it must be carried along and never separated from one.
Regarding the intent behind the regulation of the *niṣīdana*: its primary purpose is to protect the monastic bedding as well as one's own belongings from becoming stained or greasy.
Whenever one wishes to lie down or sit, one must first spread the *niṣīdana* over the bedding, and only then slowly [sit or lie down].
He sat down slowly and lay down accordingly. The Buddha said: "It is for the sake of the body, for the sake of the robes, and for the sake of the bedding that I have prescribed their possession.

It is called 'for the sake of the body' because it wards off venomous insects, thorns, and the like. It is called 'for the sake of the robes' because one fears that dust and grime might soil the Dharma-robes.
It is called 'for the sake of the bedding' because it is spread upon the bedding to block grease and filth, fearing they might soil the bedding."
[The text] is complete. Master Jing says: The Sanskrit term *niṣīdana* is translated here as "reclining mat" (*wòfūjù*), and it is also called "sitting-and-reclining mat" (*zuòwòjù*).
The *Jiètán jīng* (Sutra on the Precept Platform) states: "The *niṣīdana* is like the foundation of a stupa.
Your present reception of the precepts is the very foundation of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*). This is because the fivefold [Dharma-body] is accomplished through the precepts. If...
There is no sitting mat; by using your own body as a seat, the fivefold concentration and wisdom will have no place from which to arise (the remainder is explained as in the Ninety Matters).
*Cǎo jié* (grass straw): *jié* is pronounced *jià* (as in *qìjià*). *Jié* refers to the stalks of grain after the husks have been removed, used to make mats. Alternatively—

The characters 作 (zuò) and 鞂 (jié)—the latter being the vernacular form of 秸 (jié)—are both incorrect. In the old versions of the Vinaya texts, it was written as [卄/告] (jiá). Master Yìng refuted this.

[卄/告] is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* (from the rhyme category *gǔ*) and the tone *yù*; it refers to the husk of grain. [戞] (jiá) has the pronunciation *jiǎ*. The term for the husk of grain is [卄/告] (jiá).
● Vinaya Piṭaka, Volume Three △ Third [Section]:
Harsh Speech (This is an exclusive precept; for a nun, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*).
Maheśvara is translated here as "Great Sovereign" (Dàzìzài). In the correct Sanskrit sound, it is *Mahāmaheśvara*.
He has eight arms, three eyes, rides a white ox, and holds a white fly-whisk and a trident. As stated in the *Īśvaradevaputra-sūtra*:
Eighty-four thousand kalpas ago, he was the son of a tranquil Brahmin named Śaṅkha.
He dwelt in a grass hut within a mountain valley when he encountered a Tathāgata named Guṇasāgara.
He then lit three lamps and offered three needles, making his offering with a sincere heart and making this vow: "I offer these three lamps..."
Three needles. May I be endowed with the three eyes and obtain the trident. In birth after birth, may I constantly practice the vow of generosity and become a sovereign of the world.
May I attain the eight masteries, fulfill my desires, and possess sharp and keen faculties of mind and consciousness. Furthermore, it is said:
"In the past, throughout countless koṭis of kalpas, I practiced giving and made offerings at the feet of the Great Muni Buddha."
One maintains precepts for the sake of merit and perfumes the mind with wisdom. From that point onward, one attains the retribution of mastery.

Within eight lifetimes, one obtains eight kinds of mastery. Throughout my successive births, I have practiced giving, maintained the precepts, and engaged in asceticism, seeking sovereign mastery, the joy of liberation, and even ultimate quiescence and peace; it has been thus. Therefore, [I practice] giving...
Generosity. Observing with wisdom, guarding with a single mind, and practicing without interruption. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states:

"Beyond the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, there are Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes known as Maheśvara, lords of the trichiliocosm. The *Abhiṣeka Sūtra* states: "His name is Wéilíngdì (Vaiśravaṇa). The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* states:

"I travel through the ten directions by means of my supernormal powers, visiting the lands of all Buddhas to assist them in spreading their transformation. By the power of divine mantras, I manifest bodies throughout the six realms to deliver and liberate sentient beings."

Born [into this state], they internally cultivate the bodhisattva precepts and practices, dwelling for a long time within the flow of the Dharma. Reaching the level of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), their merits are perfected (the remainder is as explained in the second fascicle).
"Deluded person" (癡人): in Sanskrit, *moha*; here it means "delusion. As stated in the *Sūtra on Right Practice* (*Samyak-caryā-sūtra*), the Buddha sat in contemplation and reflected:
"Because of human delusion, there is birth and death. What is delusion? Originally one came from within delusion; now, having been born as a human, one is again deluded in mind."
They do not understand or comprehend; they do not know where death will lead them, nor do they even contemplate the suffering of the world.
They do not know the severity of the tortures in hell; this is called ignorance (*moha*). Thus, birth and death continue without ceasing.
Birth and death occur in the interval of a single breath; human life does not last longer than that. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "The Buddha possesses great compassion..."
There is no harsh speech. Why then does he say "foolish person"? The answer is: The Buddha’s words are expressions of reality;
they are not harsh speech. Because these sentient beings are bound by all afflictions and are fully possessed of ignorance, the Buddha speaks thus out of his heart of compassion.
Reproaching and subduing them— just as a present-day preceptor or ācārya may address a disciple as a "fool" for the sake of instruction,
which is not harsh speech— so too does the Tathāgata, with a heart of great compassion, act for the purpose of disciplining his disciples.
And he rebuked him. △ Fourth:
Praising One’s Own Body to Solicit Offerings (This is an *asādhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*; for a nun, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*).

This is the matter. Some have erroneously written it as *bōzhé*. Master Ying stated that the Sanskrit term is *vāśī*, which means "praise. As for the term *baini*, it is likely a corruption.

"Set aside [your hesitation]. Speak as you wish regarding the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Yet, you still harbor doubts: if you were to explain them in sequential order, the text would be vast;

For these reasons, report this fully to the World-Honored One. The Buddha immediately granted the bhikṣus permission to cite the sūtras.
The essential points and wondrous phrases directly reveal their meaning. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: There was a bhikṣu named Bhadrika who was foremost in chanting.
This bhikṣu possessed a beautiful voice and addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, please permit me to perform vocal chanting.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to chant. There are five benefits to chanting: the body does not grow weary, and one does not forget what has been learned..."
One’s memory is retained; the mind does not grow weary; the voice does not deteriorate; and speech is easily understood. Furthermore, there are five benefits. Four are as previously stated;
the fifth says that when the devas hear the sound of the *bhāṣya*, their hearts are filled with joy. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
When there is sound that possesses five kinds of purity, it is called the Brahma-voice (*brahmasvara*).
What are these five? First, its tone is upright; second, its tone is harmonious and elegant; third, its tone is clear and penetrating; fourth, its tone is profound and full;
fifth, it is heard everywhere at a great distance. Possessing these five qualities, it is named the Brahma-voice. This is the analogy of Brahmā.
The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata’s voice when preaching the Dharma has eight qualities: first, the most excellent sound; second, the easily understood sound;
third, the soft and gentle sound; fourth, the harmonious and well-adjusted sound; fifth, the venerable and wise sound; sixth, the unerring sound; seventh, the profound and wondrous sound."
Eighth, he does not use a female voice. His speech is without omission or flaw, and no one can find fault with it (and so forth).

Regarding the precept-keeper, the Vinaya states: "A precept-keeper is one who is without deficiency, without breach or leakage, and without defilement. As for "without deficiency," this refers to [the lifting of...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated here.*
The foremost of these heavy precepts consists of upholding the four *pārājika* rules. To guard them with purity, as one would cherish a bright jewel, is called "being without deficiency.
If one violates them, it is like a vessel that has already been broken; it is no longer fit for use.

Such a person is on the periphery of the Buddha-dharma, is not a *śramaṇa* or a son of the Śākya, and has lost the dharma of a *bhikṣu*; this is termed "deficiency. As for "not being pierced or leaking," it means:

To cite the beginning of their majestic deportment, they maintain the *pāyattika* rules and so forth; because they protect them as one would a small air-bladder, it is called "without breach or leakage.
If there is any transgression, it is like a vessel with holes or leaks that cannot receive the Way, and is thus called "breached and leaking.
Regarding those who are "unstained," this means that although they maintain the discipline (*vinaya*) without breach or defect, they must nevertheless possess meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Maintaining a shared mind, one does not give rise to lustful thoughts; therefore, it is called "untainted. If one thinks of matters concerning the breaking of precepts, it is then termed "defiled.
Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "Although one does not physically join with that woman, yet converses with her in jest and flirtation."
Outside the wall, the sound of bracelets was heard; men and women were seen pursuing one another, all of them defiling the pure precepts. Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Although the matter has been prohibited, [monks] still allow women to wash, wipe, massage, speak with lustful minds, and gaze at one another."
To observe the precepts for a limited number of days, or to expect wealth and happiness in future lives or unrestrained enjoyment in the heavens—all such instances are termed impure.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "One who purely observes the precepts is able to receive and uphold every precept established by all Buddhas without the slightest transgression;
therefore, this is called 'observing the precepts. One who attains the precepts of the pure mind possesses the precepts of dhyāna."
It is so. To maintain the mind without distraction and thereby attain concentration is called the "precept of pure mind.
As for the "precept of pure wisdom," it means to uphold this wisdom and not allow it to become distracted, thereby attaining the vision of the Four Truths; this is called the precept of pure wisdom.
All people who possess faith and uphold the precepts should apply their minds and give rise to this thought: even if one commits a minor [offense]...
Even minor precepts give rise to a sense of dread, no different from the weighty precepts.
One who maintains the precepts in this manner possesses pure brahmacarya, and the prātimokṣa-saṃvara they uphold is likewise pure.

They should cultivate all bodily, verbal, and mental actions to bring virtuous conduct to fulfillment, even to the point of being able to restrain body, speech, and mind so as not to commit transgressions.
The Ten Evils.

The bhikṣu Kāla is sometimes called Kālu or Kālu; this means "black. Sometimes his name is pronounced by including his father's name, as Kālāma-putra (Son of Kālāma).
According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, this refers to the bhikṣu Kṛṣṇamṛgīputra (the Son of the Black Deer). Some say: [text continues].
"Ruru" (Lu-zǐ) is the name of his mother. Therefore, the *Pinaiye* (Kṣudrakavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya) states: "Kālā is the son of Rurupāraka; 'Ruru' is the mother's name.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "The son of the householder Ruru was named Kāla. He was intelligent, wise, and of keen faculties;
whenever people came with questions, he constantly resolved their doubts. When he had other urgent affairs, if there were women—such as daughters or sisters—who came to seek him..."

He would go to ask Kāla whether it was appropriate or not appropriate to give [a girl]. If someone sought a wife for themselves, or sought one for their son, they would likewise go to ask Kāla whether she was suitable to be taken.
Later, Kāla left the household life out of faith, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and became a bhikṣu; yet he remained preoccupied with other affairs just as before.
(As stated above). *Shì* (適) means "to suit" or "to satisfy.

"Flower garland" (*mālā*) is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "garland" (pronounced *mán*). A sutra states: "That which is worn upon the forehead is called a garland. According to this...
In the Western Regions, garland-makers (*mālākāra*) frequently use *sumana* flowers, stringing them in rows to form garlands.
Regardless of whether they are male or female, noble or humble, all adorn themselves with these, either on the head or the body, as ornaments.
In the Vinaya texts, the character [is] used; this is not the correct form. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* asks: "What are the flowers for making garlands and necklaces?"
1. The *utpala* flower; 2. the *vārṣika* flower; 3. the *campaka* flower; 4. the *atimuktaka* flower; 5. flowers fashioned from beaten gold; 6.

Upāsaka is also called *īpūsa*; this is translated as "near male" (*jìn shì nán*). Master Zào said: "The meaning of the name is 'faithful male' (*xìn shì nán*). It is pure.

It is also rendered as 'One Who Dwells Near' (*upāsaka*), meaning that by receiving the precepts and practicing them, one is capable of dwelling near an Arhat. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:

*Sogaka* (Sogha) means that one draws near to and cultivates all wholesome dharmas; that is to say, one’s body and mind become intimately familiar with wholesome dharmas.

It means that because he sincerely accepts and upholds [the teachings], guarding the Dharma and Vinaya of all Buddhas and not begrudging his own body or life, he is called an *upāsaka*.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "Receiving the eight precepts and the fast is called *upoṣadha*. *Upoṣadha* is the Qin (Chinese) term for 'good lodging' (*śubha-vāsa*).

The country of Āṭavī is called *āṭavī* in the Sanskrit language; this means "wilderness. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "In the country of Aṭavi, there was a bhikṣu who built a private dwelling;

Between the two kingdoms, in a vast wilderness, there were five hundred bands of bandits who slaughtered traveling merchants;
because of this, the passage of people between the two realms was cut off. When King Bimbisāra heard of this matter, he commanded his great general, saying:
"You should go to that wilderness between the two kingdoms, eliminate those bands of bandits, and remain stationed there for the time being. At that time...
Having received the king’s command, that great general led his attendants into the wilderness. Upon seeing the band of thieves, he advanced alone;
as their spears and arrows clashed, he struck down one hundred men. Although four hundred remained, they still came forward to fight.
The general addressed them, saying: "Do not advance! Let us not all die together. You should cast off your armor and weapons and leave the wounded."
"This is an arrow. Observe whether he is alive. When the bandits heard this, they examined the one who had been shot and attempted to remove the arrow; however, he immediately passed away.
Only then did they realize that the general was highly skilled in the art of archery, and they dared not fight again. The remaining four hundred men...

They sought mercy and begged for their lives. The Great General took pity on them; with a heart of compassion toward them, he immediately built a new city at the junction of the two realms and gathered all the people together to dwell there.
From that time forward, it was named the City of the Wilderness (Khaṇḍava-pura).
The Ganges is also called the Gaṅgā River, or the *Kiṅga* River. *Kiṅga* means "coming from heaven";
this is because its source is seen to come from a high place. Alternatively, it is said to be the name of a river deity, after which the river is named.
The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "The Gaṅgā River was formerly called the Henghe (Gaṅgā); 'Hengga' is an erroneous transcription. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Among the four great rivers, the Gaṅgā is the largest. People from all distant regions regard the Gaṅgā in their scriptures as a river of merit and auspiciousness.
If one enters it to wash, all sinful defilements and evils are entirely eliminated. Regarding people...
It is an object of veneration. Furthermore, while the names of other rivers change from age to age, this Ganges remains constant throughout successive lifetimes.

Its bed contains golden sand. Flowing from Lake Anavatapta through the Elephant Mouth in the east, it passes through the central regions of Central India and flows horizontally into the southeastern sea (some say it flows from the Silver Ox Mouth;
its sand is as fine as flour and its water white as milk, which is why it is frequently used as a metaphor in various sūtras). As for the four rivers: first, the Gaṅgā; second...

Mahākāśyapa.
He is correctly called Mahākāśyapa, or sometimes Mahākāśyapa. *Mahā* means "Great.
*Kāśyapa* is translated as "Drinking Light" (飲光), meaning that the radiance of his body can outshine all other objects. Some say: "The Venerable One is a primordial ancestor from antiquity;
he is a Great Seer (*ṛṣi*) whose body possesses such brilliance that it can swallow and obscure the light of lamps and fires."
The people of that time found this extraordinary; thus, he was called the Rishi Pītabhāsa (Drinking Light). It was from this that his clan name was established.

The text states: Regarding the term "Great" (*Mahā*), if explained according to what it represents, it may be because his wisdom was great, his virtue was great, or his mind was great, and for these reasons he is called Mahākāśyapa.
If explained according to the literal fact, among the Buddha’s disciples many were named Kāśyapa, such as the Ten Powers (*Daśabala*) and the Three [Kāśyapas].
Among those of the same clan, Kāśyapa and the others were the most venerable and eldest; therefore, the term "Great" (Mahā-) was prefixed to distinguish him.
Among the ten great disciples, he was foremost in dhūta practices. The Vinaya states:
In the kingdom of Magadha, there was a great city named Nyagrodha. Within this city, there was a great brahmin also named Nyagrodha.
He possessed vast wealth and many servants; his granaries were filled with the seven treasures, and he held eighteen villages as his fief and sixteen great towns to provide for his retinue.
Furthermore, he possessed sixty billion pieces of the finest, most exquisite gold.
Due to his past causes, moved by his meritorious goodness, and as the fruit of his karma matured, he planted seeds of ordinary wheat that grew into golden wheat.
Every harvest yielded more than two hundred *shi* of grain. Later, he took a woman from a prominent clan as his wife;
though many years passed, they had no offspring. Constantly seeking an heir, he made offerings to all the deities everywhere.
Although he had prayed for a long time, his wish was not fulfilled; harboring sorrow and distress in his heart, he rested his cheek in his palm and sighed. His mother said to him:
"Formerly, when I had no son, I prayed at the Nyagrodha tree and you were born. Now, you should likewise pray at that sacred tree."
He prayed with all his might, seeking only a single son, and his wish was certain to be fulfilled.
Having followed his mother’s instructions, he prepared a vast array of delicacies beneath a *pipala* tree (the Bodhi tree) in the rear garden and offered this prayer:
"I prostrate before the deity of this tree; grant me a son at once. If my wish is granted, I shall establish a grand temple for you right here."

He further organized a great assembly to express his gratitude for this extraordinary favor, declaring, "If my wishes are not fulfilled, I shall cut down the tree by its very roots, leaving you with no place of refuge.
At that time, the deity, perceiving the intensity of his resolve, felt fear arise within him and thought, "I am powerless; what shall I do?
He immediately went to the presence of the Northern Heavenly King Vaishravana and reported the aforementioned matter in detail. The deity...

Having heard this, the king reflected that he lacked the power [to save himself] and immediately ascended to the heavens, where he piteously addressed Śakra. Upon hearing this, Śakra told his attendants:
"If any deity manifests the signs of impending decline, you must come and report it to me. Later, a certain devaputra manifested the five signs of decay;
he was quickly sent to report it to the Lord of Devas. When the Lord of Devas arrived, he said to him: "Now, you ought—"
He went to the city of Nyagrodha within Jambudvīpa, to the house of a great brahmin, and there took birth.
The son of heaven addressed him, saying: "Great Deva, you should know that this brahmin, relying on his own noble status, has become deeply negligent."
However, when the Great Teacher, the Buddha, appears in the world and his work of conversion is completed, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
I have a long-standing vow to cultivate pure conduct under the World-Honored One; I fear that being born there might become an obstacle for me.
The Lord of Devas said to him, "Do not worry. I shall assist you at all times, ensuring that you remain ever vigilant. He [the deity] gave him this command.
When his life there had ended, he went to the Nyagrodha clan and took rebirth by entering a womb.

When the months were complete, a son was born whose appearance was transcendent and whose radiance was brilliant, like Jambū-nada gold. His head was rounded, his arms long, his nose prominent, his eyebrows high, and his forehead broad.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks, after twenty-one days had passed, his kinsmen gathered in joyful assembly and conferred upon him a name.
They said, "This child was obtained beneath a *piyāla* tree; therefore, he should be named Piṇḍola. Furthermore, according to his clan lineage, he may be named Kāśyapa.
For this reason, people of that time called him Piṇḍola or Kāśyapa. As he grew older...
Great indeed! He was entrusted to an enlightened master to study various arts and skills as well as all the scriptures.

Once they passed through his ears or eyes, he memorized and retained them without forgetting. Regarding the four Vedas (*veda*—translated as "clear wisdom" or "the four treatises on clarity"; formerly called *Veda*;

all Brahmins in India recite and study them, transmitting them orally rather than writing them down on paper)—he understood them all thoroughly. Having studied these treatises, among all the worlds, he dwelt upon the earth.
[Śāriputra] examined all auspicious omens and transformations; there was nothing he did not master. He was able to manifest his own school’s tenets and skillfully refute the arguments of others.
Once he had attained complete clarity, the brahmins appointed him as their leader and teacher, and he instructed five hundred brahmin youths (and so forth).
At that time, the Bodhisattva [having taken the name of the Buddha] departed the city at midnight and went forth into homelessness, dwelling in the Forest of Austerities. At that time, Kā...
At that time, Upāli also abandoned his household affairs and practiced the path of renunciation, thinking to himself:
"If there is anyone in the world who is an Arhat, I shall rely upon him and serve him with a respectful heart. Having thus gone forth, he...
At that time, people called him the Recluse Kāśyapa. He resided near the Śāṇakavāṣṭa Caitya (the *caitya* being a stūpa).
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having practiced austerities for six years while dwelling in an araṇya, attained perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
He then traveled through the human world and arrived at Vaiśālī, where he sat beneath a tree near the Śāṇakavāṣṭa Caitya in order to lead [others].
In order to guide Kāśyapa, the Buddha emitted light from his entire body, which shone brilliantly and pervasively.

Upon seeing this, Kāśyapa followed the light until he reached the presence of the World-Honored One. From afar, he beheld the Tathāgata, whose countenance was upright and dignified, whose marks and signs were peerless, and whose faculties were serene and tranquil.
With a single mind free from distraction, he was like the King of Mountains, resplendent with a golden hue; Kāśyapa was filled with joy.
He leaped for joy and cried out in a loud voice, "This is my Teacher! I am his disciple! The World-Honored One said, "So it is, so it is, Kāśyapa.
I am your Teacher; you are my disciple," and so forth. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"Kāśyapa was a śrāvaka disciple who had attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and was endowed with the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*)."
When the Tathāgata had completed his work of transformation and was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed Kāśyapa, saying:

"Throughout kalpas of vast duration, I have diligently practiced asceticism for the sake of all sentient beings, seeking the unsurpassed Dharma. That which I formerly vowed and expected has now reached its full fruition.
I shall now enter great parinirvāṇa; I entrust the treasury of all dharmas to you, that you may uphold and maintain it."
"Proclaim this so that it may not be lost or neglected. This gold-threaded *kāṣāya* robe offered by my maternal aunt shall be preserved and transmitted until Maitreya attains Buddhahood.
Within my bequeathed Dharma, all practitioners—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—shall first be delivered and caused to transcend the cycle of rebirth.
Kāśyapa received these instructions and took charge of them.

Having upheld the True Dharma and completed the compilation of the scriptures, in his twentieth year, weary of the impermanence of the world and intending to enter parinirvāṇa, he proceeded to Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
Ascending the northern slope of the mountain, he took a winding path toward the southwestern ridge. The mountain peaks were steep and treacherous, and the cliffside trail was rugged and narrow;
thereupon, he struck the rock with his mendicant’s staff until it split open as if it had been cut. Once the mountain path was opened, [he ascended].

Advancing along the various paths, winding and turning in complex curves, intersecting and opening through oblique passages, one reaches the mountain summit. From there, one emerges toward the northeast.
Having entered between the three peaks, one stands holding the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*. By the power of his vow, the three peaks contract and cover him over (*Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"The Venerable One enters within, sits cross-legged, and makes this solemn declaration: 'May this body of mine, together with my bowl and staff, remain long without decaying,' continuing until fifty-seven *koṭis* of years have passed...").

For sixty hundred thousand *koṭis* of years, when the Tathāgata Maitreya appears in the world, he shall perform the work of a Buddha. Having made this vow, he immediately entered meditative absorption; thereupon, those three peaks merged into one, covering the Venerable One as he remained in solemn stillness.
Therefore, this mountain now has its three ridges rising high. When the World-Honored One Maitreya arises in the future, [he shall reveal him].
After the Dharma was preached during the three assemblies, there remained immeasurable sentient beings of haughty pride who were about to ascend this mountain;
upon reaching the place where Kāśyapa was, Maitreya snapped his fingers, and the mountain peak opened of its own accord. When those sentient beings saw Kāśyapa, [they were filled with faith].
His stature was short and small, which further increased his arrogance. At that time, Mahākāśyapa presented him with the robe and delivered his words;

once the rites of veneration were completed, [Mahākāśyapa] ascended into the void and displayed various supernatural transformations. He then manifested fire to cremate his own body and entered parinirvāṇa.

As the assembly gazed up in reverence, their arrogant minds were eliminated, and they were thereby moved to realization, all attaining the fruits of sainthood. Now, a stūpa has been erected upon the mountain.
This is a stūpa (a tower). When gazing from afar on a quiet night, one may sometimes see bright torches. Yet, those who ascend the mountain find nothing at all to behold.

(This mountain is located in the kingdom of Magadha, more than a hundred *li* from the Mahī River. In Sanskrit it is called Kukkuṭapāda-giri; this translates as "Chicken's Foot Mountain. Because the Venerable One entered parinirvāṇa while residing there, people did not dare to refer to it directly, so it was subsequently renamed "Venerable's Foot Mountain").
Regarding the *Līxiàng* and the *Zhou Lǐ*: five households constitute a *lín* (neighborhood), and five *lín* constitute a *lǐ* (village), which refers to twenty-five households.

It refers to dwelling. A "fang" (ward) is within one *li* square. "Xiang" (lane)—the initial is pronounced as in *hu jiang*; the final is the departing tone (*qu sheng*). It refers to the lanes within a *li*.
Those that are straight are called "jie" (street); those that are curved are called "xiang" (lane).

The Śravaṇa-jaṭila (Conch-crested Ascetic) was a non-Buddhist practitioner from the western regions. He either wore his hair in a conch-shaped topknot or piled his hair into a crest resembling a conch shell.
"Brahmacārin" (Vanzhi) is a specific designation for a Brāhmaṇa; as for his lineage, he claimed that his ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā, and he followed their traditional practices.
This is the dharma of Brahmā; therefore, "Brahma" was taken as its name. It exists only in the five regions of India and is found in no other countries.
Whether they be householders or renunciants, those who receive and practice this dharma are also called *brahmacārins* (the term *brahma* refers to...).
[It means] "pure.

There is this jewel. If a person obtains it, poison cannot harm them and fire cannot burn them.
*Ganda*—the correct pronunciation is *Gandha*, which means "fragrance. In Sanskrit it is called *Nāga*, which means "dragon."

The *Piṇḍola Sūtra* states: "The Prince of Thousand Merits was named Udāyana. His physical appearance was upright and handsome, and he was endowed with majestic characteristics.

He was valiant, heroic, and martial, like Rāma or Aśvatthāman. Because the King had planted various roots of goodness in the presence of a Pratyekabuddha during a previous life, he obtained such a retribution.

Within the country was an elder named Sandhaning, whose family was immensely wealthy. He immediately dispatched his storekeeper to provide grain for offerings.
The storekeeper was delighted and provided sufficient grain. Furthermore, five hundred messengers were appointed to prepare and serve food and drink, providing them constantly.
There was one man who knew when the time had come. This man kept a dog that would always follow him wherever he went.
One day, this messenger forgot to go and inform [the sages]. The dog, knowing that the time had already arrived, went alone to the mountain location and barked loudly toward the pratyekabuddhas.
The pratyekabuddhas, knowing that he had come to invite them, immediately went there to receive their meal.
The elder Sandhana of that time is now the Buddha. The treasurer of that time is now the elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
The person who went daily to announce the time for the meal is now King Udayana.
As for the puppy of that time, because it barked, it has obtained exquisite and wondrous voices in every lifetime; he is now the elder Surūpa.
The five hundred people who prepared food at that time are now these five hundred arhats. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Among the upāsakas who direct their whole hearts toward the Buddha with minds that never waver, King Udayana is the foremost."
