[The first [section] (and so forth). In the past, there was a Buddha named Pāṭhikaputta. At that time, this son of a Malla was born into a householder’s family.
The people of the kingdom and the towns collectively held a great assembly and invited the Buddha to enter the country, surrounded by sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus.
They made offerings at the great assembly and practiced giving for seven days. At that time, there was one...
The Arhat Bhikṣu, amidst the great assembly, used his supernormal powers to arrange the seats and prepare the food and drink.
At that time, Māraputra, seeing such supernormal power, was filled with great joy;

he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: “I pray that in my future life, during the time of a future Buddha, I may leave the household life.”
He practiced the Path and swiftly became an Arhat. He distributed rooms, bedding, seats, and various foods and drinks for the assembly of monks;

his supernormal powers were no different from those of an Arhat today. At that time, the World-Honored One contemplated whether the aspirations of this good man would indeed be fulfilled in a future age.
Having observed the future, the World-Honored One spoke to Mālakīmāta:
He said, "After a hundred thousand kalpas from now, there will be a Buddha named Śākyamuni. At the age of seven, you shall leave the household life;
as soon as your hair falls to the ground, you will become an arhat named Trapuṣa Malla-putra, endowed with the six supernormal powers.
You will surely attain this vow. From this point forward, Malla-putra, through practicing generosity and observing the precepts, you shall be reborn in heaven."

Above, he passed away from his life in the heavens and was reborn below in the human world. Thus, through successive cycles, he eventually reached the time when Śākyamuni Tathāgata appeared in the world.
Descending from heaven to be born among humans, he left the household life and attained the Way.

Among the śrāvaka disciples, he was foremost in distributing bedding and requisites for the Saṃgha. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "When the Venerable Upagupta held the relics in his left hand..."
Guang [the Buddha] divided the bedding and requisites among the monks with his right hand, instructing that those bhikṣus who were of similar standing should stay together in one place,

engaging in discussion or remaining in silent meditation, harmonizing with one another, and practicing all wholesome dharmas without anxiety or distress (other circumstances are detailed in the root Vinaya).

*Āraṇya* (阿練若) is also written as *ālan*. It is sometimes called *āraṇī*. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is translated as "a place of seclusion" (*dūrībhāva-sthāna*) or "the absence of contention" (*araṇa*).
This means that the dwelling is not in conflict with the world; specifically, it refers to a location five *li* away from a village or town. Fearing that...
If the path were too far, begging for alms would be laborious and obstructive; if it were too near, people and things would create a clamor.

Because begging is convenient when the distance is neither too far nor too near, five *li* (approx. 2.5 km) was established as the limit. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) translates this as a "secluded place" (*antara-vihāra*).

The *Fourfold Teaching Ritual* (*Sijiao yi*) states: "Not performing various worldly affairs is called 'interval' (*antara*); a place free from clamor and bustle is called 'seclusion' (*vihāra*). This accords with the Dharma.
Master [Seng]shi translated it as "emptiness and stillness. The *Śīla-pratyaya-sūtra* translates it as "a place of open space. Master Sengzhao said:
"Anger and contention arise in crowded assemblies; non-contention emerges from open spaces. Therefore, the Buddha praised those who dwell in *āraṇya*, stating that they obtain eight kinds of merit."
The *Cizhi biqiu shanjian lü* (The Good-Seeing Bhikṣu Maitrībala Vinaya) states that among the group of six bhikṣus, he was the most wicked;
throughout successive lifetimes, he was constantly at enmity with Māraputra. The *Gengben lü* (Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya) states that Śrīgupta, because of his evil deeds in former days...
Because he slandered his mother, for many thousands of years he suffered the torment of being burned and boiled in hell.

Due to the remaining residue of that karma, throughout five hundred lifetimes he constantly encountered malicious slander; even today, though he has attained arhatship, he is still subjected to malicious slander.
From this one should know: purely black karma yields purely black retribution, and purely white karma yields purely white retribution.
Pure white karma yields pure white retribution; mixed black-and-white karma yields mixed black-and-white retribution.
One should abandon purely black and mixed karma and diligently cultivate the white category [of wholesome deeds], as detailed in that Vinaya.
*Dānapati* is sometimes called *dāna*. The *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* states: "In Sanskrit it is *dānapati*, translated as 'donor' (*shizhu*). *Dāna* means 'giving,' and *pati* means 'lord.
To call them *dānyue* (dānapati) is not the original, correct translation; it is a truncated form that omits the syllable *na*."

Regarding the character [for *dāna*]: take the upper sound *ḍa*, change it to *da*, and further add the character *yue*. This implies that by practicing the giving (*dāna*) of renunciation, one can personally transcend and cross over poverty.
Although this is a skillful translation, it ultimately deviates from the original source. As the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:
Because it can destroy stinginess, envy, and the suffering of poverty and low status, it is called *dā* (this is translated as "giving" [檀] in this region).

Furthermore, because it subsequently brings about great wealth and can lead to the accumulation of merit and provisions (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*), it is called *nā* (the term *dāna*, meaning "giving," is a word specific to this region).
*Vyāpāda* in Sanskrit is translated here as *chēn-huì* (瞋恚). *Chēn* (瞋) is pronounced with the initial *qīng* (切) and the rhyme *chēn* (嗔); it refers to being angry and staring with wide eyes.

*Huì* (恚) is pronounced with the initial *hú* (胡) and the rhyme *guì* (桂), yielding the sound *huì* (惠); it refers to anger and resentment. The *Wénjù* (文句) states: "To be angry with oneself is *huì*; to be angry with others is *chēn*."
It is because of anger. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Anger is not the way of one who has left the household life; the way of one who has left the household life is patience.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu’s appearance and robes differ from those of the laity, yet his mind is filled with anger, it is not appropriate for him.
If he practices patience, he will personally possess the merit of compassion. Moreover, by cultivating patience, one can accomplish [the goal] for oneself.
Why is this so? Because those who harbor anger desire to harm others, yet they end up harming themselves.

Whatever evil they inflict upon others through body or speech, the evil they receive for themselves exceeds that by a hundred-thousandfold. Thus one knows that anger is a great source of self-destruction.
Therefore, the wise person who desires their own benefit, seeking to escape great suffering and grave transgressions, [should abandon anger].
"One ought to practice patience. Master Kumārajīva said: "If one can practice patience, then internally one does not weary oneself, and externally one does not harm others;

this is to protect both oneself and others. When Master Wuzhuo traveled to Mount Wutai, he encountered Mañjuśrī, who had manifested as an old man along with the youth Candraprabha. For Wuzhuo, the youth spoke a verse:
No anger on the face is the offering; no anger in the mouth emits sublime fragrance;
no anger in the heart is the precious treasure—untainted and stainless, it is the true permanence.
*Vinaya Piṭaka*, Fascicle Four.
△ The Ninth: Taking a Piece [of Cloth] and Slandering (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
The Ram.
*Dí* (都黎切, *dūlí qiè*; pronunciation: *dī*). It refers to a ram. The *Sāncāng* states: "Dí means a solitary ram. A solitary male is a stallion ram (*mǔyáng*).
(The character *mǔ* is pronounced *mǔ*; it refers to the father of livestock. For birds, one says *cí* [hen] and *xióng* [cock]; for running animals, one says *pǐn* [female] and *mǔ* [male]).
Regarding "taking a portion from a category of matters that belongs to a different category":
this refers to the *pārājika* rules, which are not the cause of liberation and belong to a category distinct from *nirvāṇa*, because *nirvāṇa* is diametrically opposed to *saṃsāra*.
"Taking a portion" means taking minor offenses among the various modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) and accusing others of having committed them.
It is "heavy" (*guru*). Some say it refers to "other parts" (*avaśeṣa-bhāga*). "Other" refers to matters that are not *pārājika*;

yet, by means of such other matters, one is treated as having committed a *pārājika*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "As for 'different parts,' these are the four *pārājikas*. If among these one commits even a single matter..."

He is not a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya; he has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu, and is therefore called "one of a different class" (vibhanga). As for "a fragment" (khaṇḍa), it refers to matters among the various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Regarding 'matters of a different and non-fragmentary class' (*vibhangakhaṇḍārtha*): 'different' (*vibhanga*) means that nirvāṇa is contrary to saṃsāra.

The four *pārājika* dharmas are not the cause of that [nirvāṇa], and are thus termed 'non-fragmentary' (*akhaṇḍa*). To slander by means of such non-fragmentary matters is precisely what constitutes this dispute."
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "As for 'substitutes' (*avaśeṣa*): *Tāpa* is a human being, while a sheep is a non-human being;
to place a sheep in the position of *Tāpa* is called a substitute. To place a ewe in the position of a *bhikṣuṇī* is also called a substitute.
Why? Because the matters are similar."

Xiǎng (響) is pronounced with the two initials xǔ and liǎn; its sound is xiǎng. That which is substantial and refined is called *shēng* (sound); that which is simple and pure is called *xiǎng* (echo). Furthermore, it refers to a resonance.
△ Chapter Ten: Schism in the Saṃgha (This is a shared precept; it is likewise established for nuns).
In the kingdom of Mithilā, within the boundary of Anupiya.
The kingdom of Mīnīso is the city of the Śākyas. Anupiya, also called Antivā, is the name of a forest.
This forest is not far from the city of the Śākyas.

Aniruddha, also known as Aniruddhadatta, means "The Undying" (Wumie) in Chinese. This refers to the fact that the merit from his past gift of food, through which humans and devas have enjoyed happiness, has not perished even until now;
hence he is called "The Undying. The *Xiyuji* states: "Aniruddha; formerly called A..."
The term "Nili" (尼律) is an error. The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) states: "Some call him Aniruddha, while others call him Anuruddha;
these are like the differences between the dialects of Chu and Xia. This [name] means 'Wish-fulfilling' (Yìrú) or 'Free from Poverty' (Wúpín).
In a past age of famine, he once offered millet porridge to a Pratyekabuddha. For ninety-one kalpas, he experienced [the fruits of this merit] among gods and humans."

Because his intentions were as he wished, he was named "As He Wishes" (Cintāmaṇi). Because from that time on he lacked nothing and was free from want, he was named "Free from Poverty" (Anāthapiṇḍada).

He was the younger half-brother of the Buddha and the son of King Droṇodana. Among the disciples of the Buddha, he was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
Formerly, at the site of the *caitya* of Kāla-kaṇḍa Buddha, a great offering was being performed. At that time, there was a band of thieves who intended to commit a robbery.
He entered into the *caitya*. One thief, seeing that the lamp was dim, went to light it.
Beholding the honored countenance of the Buddha, joy arose in his heart, and he immediately made a great vow: "May I, in a future life, encounter the Great Teacher and serve him without weariness;
may I obtain a wondrous divine eye, foremost among men. By the power of that vow, he has now obtained the divine eye, which is most excellent.
The first was Kāla-kunda Buddha (i.e., Krakucchanda Buddha).
Mahānāman—translated here as "Great Name"—was the eldest son of King Droṇodana. He was born one month before the previous Buddha and attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
The Way.

Regarding the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*): these are the objects of desire required by the five sensory faculties (*pañca-indriya*). First is the desire for form (*rūpa*), which refers to the handsome physical appearance of men and women.
1. Desires for forms (*rūpa-kāma*) include garments, as well as worldly precious objects of various wonderful colors, such as black, yellow, red, and purple.

2. Desires for sounds (*śabda-kāma*) refer to the two types of musical sounds: those of stringed and wind instruments and bells and pendants, as well as the sounds of men and women singing and chanting.

3. Desires for fragrances (*gandha-kāma*) refer to the bodily scents of men and women, as well as all worldly perfumes. 4. Desires for tastes (*rasa-kāma*) refer to various kinds of food, drink, delicacies, and dainties.

Delicious flavors; the five tactile desires (*spraṣṭavya-kāma*). These refer to the softness and smoothness of the bodies of men and women, their bodies being warm in cold weather and cool in hot weather, as well as various excellent tactile sensations such as clothing and so forth.
These five kinds [of objects] are all capable of causing sentient beings to delight in them and become attached without satiety.
The *Zhiguan* states: "The five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are not themselves desire, yet within them there are flavors that can give rise to active engagement (*saṃskāra*)."
Human beings possess a mind of desire; therefore, they are called the "five desires" (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). This is because they constantly entice people into the realms of Māra.
In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There was a mountain where humans and wild animals lived together.
At a place frequented by monkeys, a hunter smeared birdlime upon the grass. A wise monkey avoided it from afar and departed."
The foolish monkey was unable to avoid it from afar; as he touched it with his hand, his hand immediately became stuck.
Seeking release, he tried to loosen it with both hands, whereupon both hands were stuck. He sought release with his feet, and his feet were stuck as well.
He bit the grass with his mouth, and his mouth likewise became stuck. With all five limbs stuck together, he lay on the ground with his fists clenched. The hunter then took a staff...

He pierced it, took it upon his shoulder, and departed. Monks, you should know that this foolish monkey abandoned its own domain and the dwelling place of its parents to roam in another’s domain, thereby bringing about such suffering and distress. In the same way, monks, foolish worldlings dwell in dependence upon a village settlement;
at dawn they put on their robes and take up their bowls to enter the village for alms, yet they do not skillfully guard their bodies and do not maintain restraint.

Regarding the sense-gates: having seen forms with the eye, one gives rise to defiled attachment; likewise with sounds for the ear, odors for the nose, tastes for the tongue, and tangibles for the body—all give rise to defiled attachment.
A foolish bhikṣu, once his internal faculties and external objects have been bound by these five fetters, follows whatever the Māra desires.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "Abide depending upon our own sphere of activity, the domain of our parents;
do not follow the sphere of others or the activities of their domain. Monks, what is meant by "one's own sphere of activity, the domain of one's parents"?
It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness: abiding in the contemplation of the body as the body, and abiding in the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.

(As stated above). According to the *Huayan jing suishu yanyi chao* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra Following its Sub-commentary), the five kinds of desire consist of wealth, form, food, fame, and sleep;
these will not be described in detail here (the five sense objects are, namely, form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch).
Bhadrika— here translated as "Worthy" (賢) or "Virtuous and Good" (賢善)— was the son of King Śuddhodana. According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, at that time the World-Honored One,
in accordance with King Śuddhodana’s spiritual capacity (*indriya*), preached the Dharma for him, causing King Śuddhodana to [attain] the gold of wisdom.
With the vajra, he shattered the high mountain of the twenty-fold view of a self and attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Having realized this fruit, he went to King Śuklodana and said, "Prince, you may accept the royal throne. He replied, "What is the reason for this?"
The king said, "I have now seen the Truth; I am unable to remain as king. He asked, "On what day? He replied, "Today.
The other then reported, "I attained the vision of the Truth at the very moment the World-Honored One first arrived here."
Next, he went to the residences of King Droṇodana and King Amṛtodana to inform them that they should accept the royal throne.
They both replied, "We have already seen the Truths. King Śuddhodana said, "If this is so, whom do I now wish to anoint on the crown of the head and install as king?
They replied, "The Śākya youth named Bhadrika should be called to the royal throne. At that time—
King Śuddhodana immediately performed the consecration and bestowed the royal throne upon Bhadrika. In the *Śatavarga-sūtra*, Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"What merit did this Bhikṣu Vādi of the Śākya clan plant in his past lives, such that he was born into a noble family and, not long after leaving the household life, attained the fruit of Arhatship?
The Buddha said: "In the distant past, immeasurable eons ago, in [the city of] Pāṭaliputra..."
In the country of Nala, there was a pratyekabuddha who was wandering for alms.

At that time, there was a man, impoverished and starving, traveling along the road with only a few cakes which he intended to eat himself. He saw the pratyekabuddha, whose deportment was dignified and composed.
With a heart full of joy, he immediately took the cakes and offered them to the Pratyekabuddha. After the Pratyekabuddha had accepted the cakes, he manifested eighteen miraculous transformations.
When the donor saw this, his faith and reverence were profound; he made a vow and departed.

By virtue of this merit, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he did not fall into the three miserable realms, but was born among gods and humans, enjoying honor, nobility, and wealth, and constantly experiencing happiness.
It was thus until now, when he encountered my renunciation and attainment of the Way.

That person who gave the cakes at that time is none other than this Bhikṣu, King Bāhula of the Śākya clan. Among the Buddha’s śrāvaka disciples, he is foremost among those of noble and prestigious lineage who have gone forth.
Nandi is translated here as "Joy. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "One who begs for alms and endures humiliation, avoiding neither cold nor heat—this refers to the bhikṣu Nandi."
*Kumbhīra* is translated here as "Majestic Like a King" (*Weiru Wang*). It is also called *Jinbilu*. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"One who dwells alone in quietude, sitting in meditation and focusing the mind on the Way—this is what is meant by the Bhikṣu Kumbhīra. The *Fenbie Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) says: "Kumbhīra..."
The bhikṣu Vīra always went to seven houses to beg for alms and never exceeded seven. The reason for this was that he had made a vow to limit himself to seven.
When begging for food, he wished to bring blessings and joy to all sentient beings; he focused his mind on the Way and was free from thoughts of greed.
Whether he received good or bad food, he did not allow it to increase or decrease his resolve. He begged for food in regular order, making no distinction between the poor and the wealthy.
If, when obtaining food from one or two families, there is another donor, one stops if it is sufficient; if it is insufficient, one accepts more.

If one reaches seven families and still does not obtain food, one returns to one's dwelling to contemplate and practice the Path, without thinking about tomorrow—whether one should go to such-and-such a house or not go to such-and-such a house. Because there is no thought of discrimination at all, it is called "seven."
He was a śramaṇa of the householders. Upon returning, he would sit in meditation, withdrawing his mind to dwell in the Way; thus he was called Kumbhīra.
Among those who beg for alms from seven households, he was the foremost.
Nanda, here translated as "Joy," was the elder brother of Upananda; he was not the same as the Nanda who was the Buddha’s younger brother.
After he left the household life, he became one of the group known as the Six Companions.
Bhadanta is translated here as "Worthy Joy" (Xiánxǐ). He is also called Upānanda or Upananda, which means "Near Joy" (Jìnxiǎo).
Among the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*), he was the most greedy. (The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "Next to the elder Vāśpa, Udāyin, Devadatta, and Bhadanta...")
*Ānanda*. *Ānanda* is abbreviated as *Ān*.
This means "Joyous" (*qingxi*) or "Delightful" (*xinle*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Qin language, it means 'Rejoicing' (*huānxǐ*)."
These are matters of past causes and conditions. Furthermore, names given by parents are also established based on causes and conditions.
What are the causes and conditions from previous lives regarding Śākyamuni Buddha? In a former life, he was a potter named Mahāprabha (Great Radiance).
At that time, there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni, whose disciples were named Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Ānanda. [The Buddha] went to the potter’s [dwelling].
They stayed for one night, and the potter made offerings to them, making this vow: "May I become a Buddha in the future age of the five turbidities.
May my name and that of my disciples be no different from those of the present Buddha and his disciples.
By virtue of the Buddha's vow, he received the name Ānanda. Furthermore, from lifetime to lifetime, he made a vow: "I shall be a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha."
"Son, among those of great learning, you shall be foremost; your name shall be Ānanda.

Furthermore, because you have practiced patience and eliminated anger throughout successive lifetimes, you were born naturally handsome, bringing joy to all who see you; for this reason, your name is established as Ānanda. As for how his parents gave him this name:
at the time the Buddha attained enlightenment, the gods informed King Śuddhodana. The king’s heart was filled with great joy, and at that moment—
The messenger of King Droṇodana came and addressed the king, saying, "Your younger brother has fathered a son. The king’s heart was filled with joy, and he said, "Today is most auspicious;
it is a day of great delight. This child shall be named Ānanda. How was this name established based on causes and conditions?
Ānanda was handsome and pure, like a fine, bright mirror; those who saw him felt joy in their hearts and minds. Therefore, [he was named Ānanda].
He is named Ānanda. He is called "Joyous" (*Kīrti*) because at the time of his birth, the entire nation rejoiced. Alternatively, it is translated as "Untainted" (*Anāsakta*);

although residual thoughts were not yet fully exhausted, he followed the Buddha into the palaces of devas, humans, and *nāgas*, and even upon seeing women, his mind remained free from defilement or attachment.
Thus, in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Ānanda possesses great merit; his wisdom is perfected."
Indeed, Ānanda is now on the stage of training, yet there is no one whose wisdom equals his. Why is this so?
Whatever an Arhat ought to know, Ānanda knows it; whatever the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, ought to learn, Ānanda understands it all with clarity.
Among my śrāvakas, he is the most extensively learned, courageous, and diligent.
His mindfulness was undisturbed, and he was foremost in extensive learning; he was capable of performing administrative duties—namely, the bhikṣu Ānanda.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "The bhikṣu Ānanda is my younger brother.
He has served me for over twenty years, fully receiving and upholding all the teachings he heard, just as one pours water from one vessel into another."
Place it in a single vessel. After my parinirvāṇa, that which the bhikṣu Ānanda has not yet heard, the Bodhisattva Mahāviśuddha shall be able to propagate;
that which Ānanda has heard, he himself shall be able to proclaim and disseminate.
Mañjuśrī, the bhikṣu Ānanda is endowed with eight qualities. What are these eight? First, his faculty of faith is firm and solid. Second, his...
1. His mind is upright. 2. His body is free from the suffering of illness. 3. He is constantly diligent and energetic.
4. He is endowed with mindfulness. 5. His mind is free from arrogance. 6. He has accomplished meditative concentration. 7.
He is fully possessed of the wisdom born of hearing. Mañjuśrī, the attendant disciple of Vipaśyin Buddha was named Aśoka.
They likewise possessed these eight qualities. The attendant disciple of the Tathāgata Śikhin was named Kṣemakara.
The attendant disciple of Viśvabhū Buddha was named Upaśānta.
The attendant disciple of Krakucchanda Buddha was named Badhri. The attendant disciple of Kanakamuni Buddha was named...
It is said that Sūti, the attendant disciple of Kāśyapa Buddha, was named Parvata;
he too was fully endowed with these eight qualities. I, Ānanda, am likewise so endowed with the eight qualities.
For this reason, I declare the Bhikṣu Ānanda to be the "Treasury of Much Learning. As the Mahā-śāstra verse says:
His face is like the pure full moon; his eyes are like blue lotuses. The waters of the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma flow into Ānanda’s heart.
He can cause the hearts and eyes of people to rejoice upon seeing him.
To all who come seeking to see the Buddha, he manifests himself in accordance with their needs without failing propriety.
The *Dvādaśayātra-sūtra* states: "The height of Ānanda was one zhang, five chi, and three cun. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there were three men who possessed the greatest strength. The first was Ānanda; the second was Kūṭadanta; and the third was a son of the Śākya clan.
Among these three men, none could surpass them in great strength. Ānanda was able to turn [the wheel of the Dharma]."
Forty *li* of stone.
Devadatta is abbreviated as Tiáodá (調達); it is also called Típódōu (提波達兜). *Devā* here means "heaven" (*deva*), and *datta* here means...
*Devadatta* is also called *Yü* (Given) and *Shih* (Bestowed); these three meanings are identical. It means that his parents requested a son from the heavens, and the heavens bestowed him upon them;

thus he was named Devadatta. Alternatively, it is translated as "Heavenly Heat" (*Tianre*), because at the time of his birth, the hearts of the assembly of humans and devas were all struck with awe and agitation.
He was the younger cousin of the Buddha and the biological elder brother of Ānanda. Having left the household life, he recited and mastered sixty thousand [stanzas].
The *Dharmasaṃgraha* states that he was fully learned in the twelve Vedas. The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* says that Devadatta’s height was one zhang,
five chi, and four cun,
and that Upāli was his barber.
This means that because he originally served as a barber for the Worthy King (Bhadra-rāja), he was called a "hair-cutter" (*kṣaurika*).
The *Saṃghabhedavastu* states: "The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying: 'By what karma did this Upāli formerly become a barber for the king?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: 'In the past, there was a king who had a barber. A Pratyekabuddha came and stood before him.'"
At the gate, he said to that man, "Noble son, shave my head; you shall obtain a virtuous fruit.
That barber had a nephew, to whom his uncle said, "I have been sent as a messenger for the King;
after I am gone, you must shave this man according to the proper rite, just as you would for the King himself. Then that nephew heard what his uncle had said.
He said, "I shall think it over myself and then give him to this man; by shaving his head according to the Dharma, he will surely gain much merit.
Having formed this thought, he then carefully considered [the man] as a Pratyekabuddha and shaved his head according to the Dharma.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha further reflected, "That man has shaved my head for me according to the Dharma; I shall protect and assist him, and ensure that..."
This person has gained great benefit. Having formed this thought, the Pratyekabuddha immediately ascended into the void and manifested various supernatural transformations.
Upon seeing these, the man was filled with a sense of wonder; he joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and made this vow:
"Since I have now shaved the head of this person, who is like a king..."
"I pray that in my future lives, throughout every birth, I may always serve as a barber for kings, no different from my maternal uncle.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "That nephew is none other than Upāli here.
Because he made this vow while shaving the head of a pratyekabuddha in a previous life, he has now become a barber for the king, and so it shall continue until he eventually encounters [the Buddha]."
The five Pratyekabuddhas all made this vow: "May I, in every successive life, serve as a barber for various kings.
Later, during their four births, they encountered the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and likewise made this vow. At that time, the bhikṣus again harbored this doubt:
"What meritorious deeds did Upāli perform to realize arhatship and become foremost in upholding the Vinaya? The Buddha said:
Regarding Upāli, there is another causal occasion; listen well, and I shall now explain it to you.

Long ago, in the past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles.
At that time, the Buddha had a disciple who was an Arhat.

Among those who upheld the Vinaya in the land of Han, he was the foremost. At that time, Upāli was his disciple; though he maintained the holy life (*brahmacarya*) for the rest of his life, he did not attain the fruit of his practice.

As death approached, he made this vow: "By the merit, karma, and roots of virtue from the precepts I have upheld, may I, in a future age when the Tathāgata Śākyamuni appears in the world, serve as the upholder of the Vinaya for that Blessed One."
"In terms of being a disciple of the Vinaya, he is no different from my own upādhyāya. As for that disciple, he is none other than Upāli.
Because he made a vow in the past, he has now obtained this fruit."

The city of Kapilavastu is translated here as "Red Marsh City" (Chize Cheng) or alternatively as "Yellow City. In ancient times, there was a rishi named Yellow-Head (Huangtou) who practiced the Way in reliance upon this place.
Master Jing said: "The city of Kapilā is located on the borders of the Snow Mountains; its boundaries were divided [there]."
On the riverbank, at the place where the rishi Kapila resided. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"The country of Kapilavastu—formerly called the country of Kāpiśī, which is an error—is within the borders of Central India.
It is over four thousand *li* in circuit. Zhu Falan replied to Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty: "Kāpiśī [Kapilavastu] is a trichiliocosm..."
The Sahā World is the center of ten billion suns and moons. All Buddhas of the three periods of time are born therein;
likewise, all devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits who possess practice and vows are born there, receiving the Buddha’s true transformation and all attaining enlightenment.
As for sentient beings in other places, because they lack the karmic conditions to move the Buddha, the Buddha does not go there. This applies to both the Buddhas and the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings.
O King, all [these people] are born in the Central Land and not in the borderlands (as explained in detail in the commentary on the *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules).
"White *karpāsa*" (*bái dié*; *dié* is pronounced *tié*) refers to fine cotton cloth. In the Western Regions, they weave it from wool; its width is two or even three *zhǒu*.
It is five *zhǔ* long, up to nine *zhǔ*. It is worn as a garment draped across the body. The *Nan shi* states:
"In the kingdom of Gaochang, there is a plant whose fruit resembles a cocoon. The silk within the cocoon is like fine *lú* (the character *lú* refers to the threads of cloth;
*jiǎn* refers to a cocoon). The people of the country of Anzi harvest it and weave it into cloth that is exceedingly soft and white."
The *Vīraṭa-vinaya-mūla* states:
"The Elder Vīraṭa ordained Ānanda separately. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda* school states: "Daśabala-Kāśyapa was Ānanda’s upādhyāya.
Regarding the fact that the Tathāgata now dispatched Vīraṭa to ordain Ānanda: [this refers to the latter case].
Because Ānanda had not attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) while in the presence of the Tathāgata, he only realized arhatship after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Generally, those whom the Buddha himself converts are "Come, monk" (*ehi bhikṣu*) bhikṣus; their hair and beard fall away spontaneously, and they attain the exhaustion of outflows in the very presence of the Tathāgata.
Since Ānanda did not attain it in that way, the Buddha did not convert him himself, but sent an elder to ordain him.
The kingdom of Champa is also transcribed as *Jambā*; the character *pó* is also written as *bō*. The *Xīyùjì* states:

"In the kingdom of Jambū, within the borders of Central India, the circumference is over four thousand *lǐ*. The capital city of the kingdom lies with its northern side facing the Gaṅgā River; its circumference is over forty *lǐ*."
The soil is damp and humid, and crops flourish in abundance. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest.
The capital city is built with layered bricks, reaching several *zhang* in height; its foundations are lofty and steep, and its defensive walls are high and formidable.

In the distant past, at the beginning of the kalpa when human beings first appeared, people lived in the wilds and dwelt in caves, as they were yet ignorant of palatial dwellings. Later, a celestial maiden descended to appear among men and wandered...

The Gaṅgā River flows with natural grace; moved by its spiritual power, [the queen] conceived and gave birth to four sons. They divided the kingdom of Jambudvīpa among themselves, each ruling their own domain.
They established capitals and built cities, demarcating borders and defining frontiers. This, then, was the capital city of one of those sons.
Jambudvīpa is the origin of all cities. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"The city of Campā was populous, flourishing, and prosperous. King Prasenajit conferred this city upon the Brahmin Gotiputa as his *brahmadeya* (Brahman’s portion)."
The country of Kauśāmbī is also called Kauśāmbi, or sometimes Kauśāmbī; it is explained as in the section on the *Mahallaka-śikṣāpada*.
[There was] Kātyāyanīputra.
Some call him Kākuḷa; others call him Kākuda. *Kāhu* is his name, and *Kula* is his clan.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī there was formerly a son of Kauṇḍinya named Kakkhū, who practiced the pure Brahma-faring and attained the fruit of Anāgāmin, being reborn in the Brahma-heaven. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* calls him Kāpuṭa.
Bhikṣu Kulaputra was a disciple of the Elder Maudgalyāyana. This bhikṣu abandoned the five desires and cultivated the four brahma-vihāras;

at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. The Brahma-world is a heaven within the realm of form (rūpadhātu). The Vinaya-mūla states that he was reborn in the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).
Mastery over Transformations is the fifth heaven of the desire realm (kāmadhātu). [The four brahma-vihāras are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. (Xuán)
Yinxiu). Regarding Ajātaśatru, the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"Ajātaśatru; in the language of Tang, this means 'Unborn Enemy' (*Weishengyuan*). Formerly [it was] called 'Ajā'..."
"World" (*loka*) is a corruption or abbreviation. Miaole (Miaole Dashi) says: "While still in the womb, his mother already harbored an evil heart toward King Bimbisāra;
he was already wicked even before birth, and thus this became his name. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Aja means 'unborn' (*anutpanna*), and loka means 'enemy.
Because the Buddha-nature has not yet arisen, the enemy of afflictions (*kleśa*) arises. Because the enemy of afflictions arises, [he is called Ajātaśatru]."
He beheld the Buddha-nature; because he did not give rise to afflictions, he immediately saw the Buddha-nature. He was also called Pārlu-ci (波羅留支), which was formerly translated as "Fingerless" (無指).
The Miaole (妙樂) commentary states: When he was born, a physiognomist predicted that his fate would be ominous. The king ordered him to ascend the palace tower.

He was struck but did not die; he merely lost a finger, and thus his name was given. The palace attendants protected him and called him Sudarśana (Good Appearance). It is also said that Devadatta addressed Prince Sudarśana, saying, "The people of the country revile you as 'Unborn Enemy' (Ajātaśatru). Sudarśana asked, "Why am I named 'Unborn Enemy'? Who gave me this name? Devadatta replied: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "Devadatta," but based on the context of the narrative, the following would typically follow: Devadatta said, "Because you have not yet been born when your father died, you are therefore called 'Unborn Enemy. Sudarśana then said, "I shall kill my father and become king. Devadatta said, "If you kill your father, you will be reborn in hell. You should instead give the kingdom to your younger brother, Viśākha, and retire to the forest to practice the Way. Sudarśana followed this advice and became a *śramaṇa*. Later, King Ajātaśatru killed his father and ascended the throne. He then sent for Sudarśana, but Sudarśana had already attained the fruit of Arhatship and would not return. King Ajātaśatru then imprisoned him. When Sudarśana was imprisoned, he recited verses, saying: "Though I have committed no offense, I am now bound in fetters. My mind is filled with resentment, Yet I do not harbor anger toward others. King Ajātaśatru heard of this and sighed deeply, saying, "This man’s virtue is truly great; though I have imprisoned him, he harbors no ill will. He then released him and restored him to his former status. Sudarśana then returned to the forest to continue his cultivation of the Way. Later, King Ajātaśatru fell ill. His ministers consulted the physicians, who said, "The king’s illness is incurable; it can only be cured by the blood of an Arhat. The king then summoned Sudarśana and said, "I am suffering from a grave illness. You must provide me with the blood of an Arhat to save my life. Sudarśana replied, "I am indeed an Arhat. However, the Buddha has taught that one who takes the life of an Arhat commits a heinous crime and will fall into the Avīci Hell. Your Majesty, please do not harm me. The king said, "I have no choice but to take your life. Sudarśana thought to himself, "If I do not give my blood, the king will surely die. If I give it, I will fall into hell. What should I do? At that moment, the Four Heavenly Kings appeared before him and said, "Do not worry. We shall protect you. Sudarśana then drew his sword and cut his own throat. Blood flowed from his neck like a spring. The king drank it and recovered. Sudarśana then entered Nirvāṇa. Because he did not wish to cause the king to fall into hell, he took his own life. This is why he is known as Sudarśana. Furthermore, Devadatta addressed Prince Sudarśana, saying, "The people of the country revile you as 'Unborn Enemy'. Devadatta said, "If you kill your father, you will be reborn in hell. You should instead give the kingdom to your younger brother, Viśākha, and retire to the forest to practice the Way."
He said, "Before you were born, all the physiognomists predicted that once this child was born, he would kill his father;
for this reason, outsiders all called you 'The Unborn Enemy' (Ajātaśatru), while those within the palace, out of concern for your heart, [called you otherwise]."

"It is said that you were well-observed. After Queen Vaidehī heard these words, once you had been born from her body, she cast you down from a high tower onto the ground, breaking one of your fingers. For this reason, people further called you Bālāñjika (and so forth).
At that time, King Ajātaśatru contemplated forms as the Buddha had instructed, and so on."

Having contemplated consciousness, he addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, it is only now that I have come to know that form is impermanent, and so on, up to consciousness being impermanent.
Had I been able to contemplate in this way from the beginning, I would not have committed these offenses. He further said:
“World-Honored One, I see in the world that from the seed of an *eranda* tree grows an *eranda* tree; I do not see an *eranda* tree growing from a *candana* [sandalwood] seed.”
“Regarding *candana* (sandalwood): I have only now seen it—how from the seed of an *elā* tree grows a *candana* tree.
The *elā* seed is my own body; the *candana* tree is my mind, which is faith without roots.

‘Without roots’ means that I previously did not know how to revere the Tathāgata, nor did I believe in the Dharma and the Saṅgha; this is called being without roots. At that time, the King and his wife...
The people and the ladies-in-waiting of the inner palace all together gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*).
They then made offerings to the Buddha with various jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies, as well as incense, flowers, necklaces, and exquisite music. The Buddha said, "Great King,"
In the past, you first gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*) before the Buddha Vipaśyin.
From that time until my appearance in the world, during all this interval, you have never again fallen into hell to undergo suffering.
Great King, you should know that the mind of enlightenment possesses such immeasurable karmic fruits and rewards. This is clarified in the *Rājāvavādaka-sūtra*.

The Buddha spoke for him; Mañjuśrī explained that the king’s grave offenses were like Mount Sumeru, yet all were extinguished except for a portion the size of a mustard seed, which would still lead him into the Piṇḍa hell. Although he was within it, he experienced no suffering.
Furthermore, he was granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. As for those with "rootless faith," at the original time their five faculties had not yet...
[He] stood up. Having now finally attained faith, it is therefore called "rootless. The *Puchao jing* (Sūtra on Universal Transcendence) states:
"Ajātaśatru repented before Mañjuśrī and attained the *anulomikī-kṣānti* (patience of conformity). At the end of his life, he entered the Piṇḍala hell;

as soon as he entered, he was reborn in an upper Buddha-field and attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). When Maitreya appears, he will return to this realm, named 'Immovable' (*Acala*)."
This Bodhisattva shall later become a Buddha, named Śuddhaviṣaya Tathāgata (according to the Sanskrit *Bharadvāja*, this translates as "Protector";
perhaps because his finger was seen to be damaged at that time, this name was given to protect his dignity; if translated directly as "Fingerless," it would likely be an error).
*Chòu* (嗽):

*chòu* is pronounced with the initial *chù* and the final *shuò*. Its sound is like *shuò*. It is identical to *shù* (數). It means to suckle. The *Tōngsúwén* (通俗文) states: "To inhale by holding [the mouth] is called *chòu*."
In the old version of the Vinaya text, it was written as [口*數]. This is a vernacular character.
"Xiōng" (兇) is pronounced with the *xǔ* and *róng* finals, sounding like "xiōng" (胸). It means "wicked" or "violent."
*Mòxiè* (莫懈切):
The pronunciation is *mài*. It also means "to grow old. The *Shijing* says, "The sun and moon advance (*mài*). The *Guǎngyá* says, "To *mài* is to return and go toward [a destination]."

*Lǎomào* (老耄): pronounced *mào*. It means to be dazed and forgetful; it also refers to being confused in old age. The *Zuozhuan* states: "As one grows old, wisdom becomes senile (*mào*). The *Quli* says:
"Those in their eighties and nineties are called *mào*."
The cave-dweller is like a pig in a pit;
this is the stone grotto where the yakṣa Kimpila resides, located on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Beside a small mountain, the *Faxian zhuan* states: "Going fifteen li southeast, one reaches Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Three li before reaching its summit, there is a stone cave on a southern ridge where the Buddha formerly sat in meditation.
Furthermore, thirty paces to the northwest, there is another stone cave where Ānanda sat in meditation; there, a celestial Māra transformed himself into a vulture."
There was a vulture dwelling in front of a cave that terrified Ānanda; thus it was named the Vulture Cave (*Gṛdhra-kūṭa*).
In front of this mountain cave were the seats where four past Buddhas had sat, as well as several hundred stone caves where various arhats practiced meditation.
While the Buddha was walking back and forth east and west in front of the stone chamber, Devadatta hurled a rock across the treacherous slopes to the north of the mountain, wounding the Buddha.
"Foot-toe" (zúzhǐ). "Bèng" (迸) means to scatter or fly forth;

it is pronounced with the *bìng* rhyme group (as in *qǐ-bìng*). "Bēng" (崩) is in the departing tone (*qùshēng*); it means to rush or to pursue. It also means to disperse and run away. [End of] section.
The mind looks back to the right, like the gaze of a great nāga;
it is a backward glance. In Sanskrit, *nāga* means "dragon" (*long*) and is also translated as "elephant. The majestic deportment of the World-Honored One is thus.
Regarding the "Great Elephant" (Mahānāga): The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that one who possesses the mark of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) gazes like an elephant king.

When he wishes to turn his body to look, his entire body rotates together. Because his body and mind are focused and unified, whenever there is something to be observed, both body and mind turn toward it together.
This is, for example, like a lion: when it seizes its prey, it does not alter its majestic power because the object is small.
The Buddha is also like this. Whether he observes something or speaks something, his body and mind are always together and never dispersed.
Why is this? Because from incalculable kalpas past, he has cultivated the dharma of single-mindedness;
by virtue of these karmic causes and conditions, the skull and the body are one, without any separation or division. Furthermore, it is because he has destroyed pride life after life.
Do not disparage sentient beings; when observing them, [the mind and wisdom] revolve together.
"Zi" (襞) is pronounced with the initial *bi* (必) and the final *li* (歷), sounding like *bi*. It refers to folding or pleating clothing.

*Si-dié*: the initial *dú* is pronounced with the *xié* tone; the phonetic value is *dié*. It means "layered" (*chóng*). It is also written as *xiè*. The *Zílín* states: "A double-layered garment. It is also written as *shè*, likewise pronounced *dié*; it means "to fold.
In older versions of the Vinaya texts, it was written as *dié*. *Dié* refers to a "tablet" or "slip"; it refers to a written document on a tablet. This is not that meaning here.
Usage: Trivandita is also called Trivendradā; alternatively, it is called Trivadrādatta, or Triven.
Dharmaruci was the most wise and highly talented among these four men;
therefore, he occupied the foremost position among them.
*Krandaka-dāpata* (the "da" is pronounced as *tu*, though it is also written as *ta*; alternatively, it is called *Krandara-dāpa*, or *Krandaka-dāpā*).
This was a close friend of Devadatta; some say he was his disciple. The *Śatopama-sūtra* (*The Sutra of One Hundred Parables*) states: "In the past, there was a man..."

He had taken two wives in marriage. If he favored one, the other would become resentful; unable to adjudicate between them, he remained positioned between the two wives, lying flat on his back with his body upright.
It happened that there was a great rain from heaven; the roof leaked, and both water and mud poured down.
It fell into his eyes; because of a prior commitment, he did not dare to rise and avoid it, and consequently caused both eyes to lose their sight.

Ordinary worldlings are just like this: by associating with evil friends, practicing what is contrary to the Dharma, and creating karmic fetters, they fall into the three evil realms and dwell long in birth and death, losing the eye of wisdom—just like that foolish man.
Because of those two wives, he lost both eyes. Now, Khaṇḍa and Devadatta were friends with Trayastrimśa;
they have lost both their eyes.
[Likewise] Kūbara...
He was also called Gopālī, which means "Cowherd," and is also translated as "Evil Age.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Kokālika was a great disciple of Devadatta who slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana;
after his death, he fell into the Padma Hell (as detailed elsewhere).
*Kāruḷadīśa* (also transcribed as *Kāruṭadaī* or *Kaṭamulokadīśa*; its precise translation remains uncertain). According to the *Kāruḷa*, this is translated as "Golden Flanks" (*Suvarṇapakṣa*).
*Dīśa* is the name of a constellation. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that this person...
There were seven sister bhikṣuṇīs: first, Thullanandā; second, Cūḷanandā;
third, Tiṣyā; fourth, Upatiṣyā; fifth, Tiṣyāyudhā; sixth, Tiṣyāphalā; and seventh, Tiṣyarakṣitā.
(Tiṣyā may also be translated as "Square" [diś]; upa- is translated as "near" [upa-]).

The four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are: first, the noble lineage of contentment with clothing; second, the noble lineage of contentment with food and drink; third, the noble lineage of contentment with bedding and seats;
and fourth, the noble lineage of contentment with medicine. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, medicine is subsumed within the [category of] the former three.
The fourth is the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*) of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation. The treatise states: "Noble" (*ārya*) refers to all non-erroneous wholesome dharmas.
Because these four can produce [them] and cause them to continue, they are called "lineages" (*vaṃśa*). Furthermore, "noble ones" (*ārya*) refers to Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas;
since [the wholesome qualities] arise from these and continue without interruption, they are named "noble lineages. Moreover, the name "True Dharma" (*saddharma*)...
"Noble ones, these are able to sustain and maintain [the Dharma], causing it to continue for a long time; therefore, they are called 'noble lineages' (āryavaṃśa).
Thus, that the True Dharma remains in the world for a thousand years without perishing is entirely due to the power of the noble lineages, just as rafters and beams support a house."
They prevent [the mind] from being scattered or destroyed. It is by virtue of these conditions that they are called the "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*).

Namely: first, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever food one obtains; second, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever robes one obtains; third, the noble lineage of contentment with whatever bedding one obtains;
and fourth, the noble lineage of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation, based on whether there is or is not [existence].—The Blessed One.

For the sake of establishing the livelihood and the activities for his disciples, [the Buddha taught] that the first three types constitute the establishment of livelihood, while the fourth constitutes the establishment of activities. Regarding the establishment of livelihood through the first three:
this means abandoning four kinds of occupations and practicing one kind of occupation. As for abandoning the four kinds of occupations: first, agriculture as an occupation; second, commerce...

[The first] has occupation as its activity; the second has seeking alms as its activity; the third has hired labor as its activity; and the fourth has mastery as its activity. In all these cases, [the noble ones] renounce them.

One who practices a single type of activity takes only begging for alms as his activity. These noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) all have the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Question: Why is the contentment arising from medicinal requisites for the sake of illness not described as a noble lineage? Answer: [Because it is dependent on external conditions.]
It is said: These are already included within what was previously explained. That is to say, there are two kinds of requisites for a physician and medicine:
those that are edible and those that are inedible. Those that are edible are included among food; those that are inedible are included among clothing and bedding.
Furthermore, because one wishes to benefit the sick bhikṣu, it is not taught that contentment with medicine and requisites constitutes the noble [dharma].
Regarding the [noble] lineages: suppose there is a bhikṣu who, although afflicted by illness, does not seek medicine because his duties are few.
If the Buddha were to establish this as a noble lineage, he would then remain fixed in his illness and be unable to diligently cultivate the application of the Noble Path.
To benefit him and cause him to diligently cultivate the Path, it was for this reason that this was not declared a noble lineage. As the Blessed One said:
These four noble lineages are the most excellent knowledge, the knowledge of the spiritual lineage, the knowledge that is delightful, and are untainted by defilement.

They are beyond reproach; among all the world—whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, brahmās, or anyone else in the world—none can rightfully speak of their faults. Thus said the Venerable Vasumitra.
The commentary states: The Buddha knows these four, which enable entry into the noble embryo (*āryagarbha*); therefore, they are called "supreme knowledge. All noble ones (*ārya*) arise from them;
therefore, they are called "knowledge of the lineage" (*gotrajñāna*). These are what practitioners delight in day and night; therefore, they are called "delightful knowledge.
They are free from the four types of worldly activities; therefore, they are called "unadulterated. All merits...
Because virtue is perfected through this, he is called "one who cannot be censured.
Since he causes no harm to himself or others, none among the world—including śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, and brahmās—can rightfully speak of his faults.

Regarding the phrase "delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation," it means delighting in the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*) and delighting in the cultivation of the noble path (*āryamārga*). Furthermore, [it refers to] being without interval...

The Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is called "delight in abandonment" (*prahāṇa-rati*); the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is called "delight in cultivation" (*bhāvanā-rati*). Furthermore, the Path of Seeing is called "delight in abandonment," and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is called "delight in cultivation.
Moreover, "delight in abandonment" manifests the various Patiences (*kṣānti*), while "delight in cultivation" manifests the various Knowledges (*jñāna*).

They are also termed the "Four Stainless Natures" (*catur-vimala-dharmatā*). The *Cittaviśuddhiprabhāsa-sūtra* (Mind-Ground Contemplation Sutra) states: "Regarding these four matters of the Four Stainless Natures, according to whatever..."
It is attained. Being coarse or subtle according to one's mind, it is free from greedy seeking; this is the stainless nature (*vimala-dhātu*).
From this, all the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas arise. The Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha is never interrupted.
For this reason, it is named the "stainless nature."

"Being one as water and milk" means that when water and milk are mixed, they become a single substance, with no distinct color or flavor; this serves as a metaphor for the present Tathāgata’s twelve [links of dependent origination].
The essence of the various sections of the sūtras has no distinction; their practice accords with the principle because they are of a single characteristic without divergence.
Now, all bhikṣus study together within the single dharma-gate of the Tathāgata; you should not form factions.

The increase of morality, mind, and wisdom—this is called the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One trains in the increase of morality; one trains in the increase of mind; one trains in the increase of wisdom. Question:
Since there are many types of training, why are they precisely equated with the three trainings? Answer: The three trainings encompass all training. For example...
These five categories of precepts prevent evil in body and speech and purify body and speech; there is no dharma that is not exhausted therein.

For one whose training in the mind increases, the mind rests within defilement; there is no dharma that is not encompassed. For one whose training in wisdom increases, they clearly perceive the characteristics of dharmas and eradicate evil at its root.

Training in the increase of the precepts means studying the Vinaya Piṭaka; training in the increase of the mind means studying the Sūtra Piṭaka; training in the increase of wisdom [means studying the Abhidharma Piṭaka].
As for this, "increasing study of Abhidharma" means studying the Abhidharma. Furthermore, "increasing study of the precepts" means studying the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpattinikāya*).

"Increasing study of the mind" refers to attaining the five factors of the first dhyāna, the four factors of the second dhyāna, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna; this is called increasing study of the mind.
"Increasing study of wisdom" means clearly seeing the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, it means extinguishing the non-restraint of evil conduct as well as all forms of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Purity regarding the five categories of precepts is called the increase of training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā-vardhana*). Because of this purity of training in morality, one attains purity of mind;

this is called the increase of training in mind (*citta-śikṣā-vardhana*). Further investigating the profound principle and increasing wholesome qualities is called the increase of training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā-vardhana*). Furthermore:

In the Sūtras there are three cultivations: the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the cultivation of the mind (*citta*), and the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, one knows that the three trainings encompass all training.

The Vinaya-mūla states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "When they increase the training in ethical discipline, increase the training in the mind, and increase the training in wisdom, they attain the subduing of greed, hatred, and delusion, and their exhaustion.
Having attained the exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion," [they proceed to liberation].

One does not commit unwholesome deeds and does not associate with evils. Furthermore, by training in these three trainings, one attains the fruits of stream-entry (srotāpatti), once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), non-returning (anāgāmin), and arhatship.
Therefore, one should diligently apply oneself to training in these three trainings.

An illegal separate assembly refers to a case where, within a single residential boundary (*sīmā*), at the time of a formal act (*karmavācanā*), there are those who do not attend and should have granted their consent (*chanda*), yet do not grant it;

and when those present ought to be censured, they are censured [despite the rule]. (The *Ekottarakarmaśataka* states: "Even though all have assembled together, if those who ought to be censured are censured and do not desist, one forcibly performs the formal act. That...

To perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), yet to proclaim this matter while performing the formal act for that other matter, constitutes an illegal *karman* performed by a separate assembly (*adharma-bhinna-saṃgha-karman*). As the *Samantapāsādikā* states: "In a single residence, there are four bhikṣus.

One person receives the consent (*chanda*), and three persons recite the *Prātimokṣa*. Or, three persons receive the consent, and two persons recite the *Prātimokṣa*. This is called 'illegal' and also called 'separate assembly. This is termed an illegal separate-assembly *karman*."

An illegal assembly in concord refers to those residing in the same dwelling place who perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) together in one location; they grant their consent (*chanda*) to those who ought to grant it, and those who ought to be censured in person do not censure them.

[The *Baiyi jiemu* states: "Those who ought to be censured shall be censured; at the time of censure, they shall then desist. They then perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation).

To perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) by making the motion for this matter, yet performing the *karman* for that other matter, is an illegal *karman* of a harmonious assembly (*adharmika-sāmagrī-karman*).
(The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "In a single residence, there are four bhikṣus. The four should recite the *Prātimokṣa* in full;
instead of reciting it in full, they perform the procedure for three persons, each speaking face-to-face with the others. This is called an illegal *karman* of a harmonious assembly.")

Regarding the "separation of the Saṃgha by means of the Dharma": it refers to a case where, within the same residential boundary (*sīmā*), at the time of a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), there are those who do not attend and fail to provide their consent (*chanda*).
Furthermore, those present who ought to voice a censure do so; yet, that [group] proceeds to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* in accordance with the Dharma.

This constitutes a formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed by a separate assembly according to the Dharma (*dharmabhinnasaṃghakarma*). (The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "In a single residence, there are four bhikṣus, or three; one receives the consent (*chanda*), and three perform the face-to-face recitation.
Or, there are three; one receives the consent, and two perform the face-to-face recitation. This is called a 'separate assembly according to the Dharma' [*dharmabhinnasaṃgha*].")
Regarding the distinction of a separate assembly based on similarity of dharma:
this refers to those residing in the same dwelling place. At the time of a *karmavācanā*, if there are those who do not attend, they should grant their consent (*chanda*); yet they do not grant it.

Furthermore, regarding those present who ought to be rebuked, they are rebuked; and when performing a formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) or a formal act with a fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), the formal act is performed before [the assembly is complete].
Afterward, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made. This constitutes a *karmavācanā* that is similar in form but performed by a discordant assembly (*vibhakta-saṃgha*).

A "harmonious assembly" (*saṃgha-sāmagra*) that is similar in form refers to those residing in the same dwelling place. At the time of the *karmavācanā*, there may be those who do not attend but have granted their consent (*chanda*), and they should be present before the assembly.
To reprove one who should not be reproved; to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya* or a *jñapti-caturtha* *karmavācanā*;

or to perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) after having already performed the *karmavācanā*—these constitute a semblance of dharma and a concordant assembly’s *karmavācanā* (as explained in detail in the Cāpala-khandhaka).

△ Thirteenth: Not Abandoning a Malicious Disposition (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
The Noble Lord.

The Buddha is the most honored among all sages; therefore, he is called the Holy Lord (*ārya-svāmin*). Furthermore, because Channa was a minister who served the Buddha while living as a householder, he said, "I am the Holy Lord.
The *Sudharman-vinaya* states: Channa spoke to the bhikṣus, "You should not instruct me;
I should instruct you. Why is this? Because the Buddha is my family Buddha. Why is this? [He continued: "I..."
Together with Qin-zhe, I followed the Buddha into the mountains to study the Way.

Not a single one of the elder monks was there to attend upon the Buddha when he attained the Way and turned the Wheel of Dharma; therefore, the Buddha is the Buddha of my own house, and the Dharma is the Dharma of my own house.
For this reason, I should instruct the elders, and the elders should not, in turn, instruct me.
"Not receiving admonitory words" means not accepting them; "receiving" refers to internalizing them. The *Fayuan* states: "If one internalizes the principle, then speech ceases;
if one deviates from its intent, then disputes arise. Thus, straightforward speech is the root of virtue, while acceptance is the source of practice. Therefore...

When words are recorded, virtue becomes manifest; when teachings are received, conduct becomes complete. This is like eyes that are too short-sighted to see on their own, requiring a mirror to observe one’s form;
or hair that is too clumsy to manage itself, necessitating a comb to facilitate its care. Thus, it is by means of these things that the face is given its shape.
It is the power of the bright mirror that makes the hair orderly; it is the merit of the dark comb that makes the hair smooth.
That conduct becomes fragrant is due to the benefit of speech. Therefore, when the body is about to perish, one will certainly not accept words of upright admonition.
When one's life is about to end, it is impossible to remain in the care of a skilled physician. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī and a kingdom named Kāśi.
At that time, there was a brāhmaṇa who constructed a public well in the wilderness for the sake of those tending cattle and those traveling on foot, so that they might all resort to the well."
They drank and bathed together. As evening approached, a pack of jackals came toward the well and drank the water remaining on the ground.
There was a leader of the jackals who did not drink from the water on the ground; instead, he thrust his head into the jar to drink the water.
Having drunk, he lifted the jar high and dashed it to pieces, so that the mouth of the jar remained pierced through his neck. The other jackals said to the leader:
"Jackal Lord, if even a moist tree leaf that is fit for use should be protected, how much more so this jar, which benefits travelers?
Why have you broken it? The jackal lord replied, "I do as I please; I simply seek my own gratification—how could I care for the affairs of others?
At that time, a traveler said to the brahmin, "Your jar has been broken; put another one on."
Just as with the previous incident, the jar was broken by a jackal. This happened up to fourteen times;
though the various jackals repeatedly admonished him, he still would not heed their words. Then the brahmin thought to himself, "Who is it that breaks my jars?
I shall go and watch for them. It was indeed a jackal. He then thought, "This is a hindrance to my well of merit."
He then fashioned a wooden jar, sturdy and difficult to break, with an opening large enough for the jackal’s head to enter but narrow enough to make it difficult to exit.
He placed it by the well, then took up his staff and waited in a secluded spot. When the traveler had finished drinking, the jackal chief entered as before to drink; having finished, he emerged.
It struck the ground but could not break it. Then the brahmin seized his staff and beat him to death.
A deva in the sky spoke this verse:
"The wise speak words of compassion, But the obstinate refuse counsel; By stubbornness, he invited this calamity."
Having thus lost his own life, this foolish jackal suffers the misery of this wooden jar.
One should know that he who accepts admonition is called a wise person; he who does not accept admonition is called a fool.
When his body perishes and his life ends, he falls into the three evil realms, suffering immeasurably for a long night. (Note: "Bei" [pronounced zhí] is the general name for a comb and a hairpin.)

He is revered, trusted, and honored by humans and devas. Fourth, it is for the purpose of severing evil karma through the sequential application of the Dharma.
Since [the offense] begins in a secluded place and gradually becomes entangled and pervasive until there is no limit to its reach, this precept was established to prevent it.
The term for "indeterminate dharma" (aniyata-dharma) in Sanskrit is *aniyata-dharma*; this refers to the indeterminate dharmas. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"Regarding the indeterminate dharmas, it means that the substance of these offenses lacks a fixed characteristic; thus, while multiple offenses may be contained within them, they cannot be said to be fixed. This is according to the Sarvāstivāda school.

It is said: When the Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment, he had already definitively established the five categories of precepts; their relative gravity and their application or suspension were such that there was no law left unsettled.
The reason it is called "indeterminate" (aniyata) is simply that a trustworthy person may not recognize the specific characteristics or the relative weight of an offense.
Furthermore, they do not recognize the name of the offense.

Even if they see [a monk] sitting in the same place as a woman, they do not know what he was doing—whether he engaged in sexual intercourse, whether he committed physical contact, whether he spoke evil words, or whether he taught the Dharma by exceeding the limit of five or six words;

This translates as "near-lady" (近士女); it is also translated as "near-service-woman" (近事女). In terms of its meaning, it is translated as "near."

This is because it is the nature of all Buddhas' teachings. That is to say, once a laywoman has received the three refuges and the five precepts, she is then able to personally serve the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
Some say that one who receives the eight precepts is called a "near-dwelling woman" (upāsikā).
This refers to dwelling near an Arhat. It is also called "the girl Sunakṣatrā. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states:

"One who observes the eight precepts for one day and one night is named Sunakṣatrā. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Because this person’s wholesome mind remains apart from a night of broken precepts."
*Píngfù* (屏覆). *Píng*:

She was named Migāramātā (Mother of the Deer). Thus, the Vinaya-mūla states: "Migāramātā," or sometimes "Makara.

She gave birth to thirty-two sons, all of whom were *malla* (wrestlers). Miga-ra was the name of her eldest son.
This woman attained the third stage of the path (*anāgāmin*). The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states that she was the daughter of Dhamma-ha-sen, the younger brother of King Prasenajit.
Sen had formerly fled to the kingdom of Takṣaśilā due to a crime and settled there.
She was taken into the household as a wife, and this daughter was born. This girl possessed exquisite talent, wisdom, and eloquence.

Later, she married the seventh son of the minister Liqi-mi from the kingdom of Śrāvastī as his wife. King Prasenajit, having heard of her wisdom and eloquence, immediately appointed her as his sister-in-law (king’s sister).
Subsequently, she gave birth to thirty-two eggs; from each egg emerged a son, all of whom were handsome and dignified in appearance, and valiant.
Kien-wu-shuang (Keṇa-a-dvaya) was a man of singular strength; with the power of one person, he could match a thousand men. At that time, Viśākhā’s faith was awakened and her understanding opened.
She invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for them. The entire family attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Later, the Buddha further expounded the teaching for them.
He immediately attained the stage of Anāgāmin. Among the upāsikās, he was foremost in wisdom, talent, and eloquence.

Regarding the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules:
if one examines this section on forfeiture, it clearly arises from greed and accumulation. Greed is the foremost of the three poisons and the precursor to the five hindrances.
Accumulation serves as the turbid cause for the three realms and the fruit of suffering within the six destinies. For this reason, sentient beings are unable—
Transcending these faults and afflictions, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, took pity on those of greedy and voracious nature and rescued those of deluded and hoarding minds.

Like the garuḍa possessing wings, or a boat possessing a sail, he praised the virtue of *dhūta* and envied the practice of the *araṇya*, reprimanding those who lacked it.
I am weary of this. I lament those who possess few desires. Why do you store these things in chests and bags without shame, and pile them high upon the upper shelves without remorse?

You turn your back on the four noble lineages and contravene the prohibitions of the Tathāgata. You plan only for the abundance and pleasure of the present moment, without considering the calamities left behind after death.
Once the four elements have separated, how can these myriad objects remain? From this point on, you will utterly lose the way to Nirvana.
This is the wondrous cause for the long-term accumulation of the suffering of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Thus, the Mahā-sūtra states:

"There are four kinds of illnesses for those who have left the household life that prevent them from attaining *nirvāṇa*: first, desire for clothing; second, desire for food; third, desire for bedding and requisites;

In future ages, at the time when the Dharma is about to perish, during the final five hundred years, when the community of those who uphold the precepts and the faction of the True Dharma are on the verge of being extinguished;
when the faction of those who break the precepts and follow what is not the Dharma flourishes; when they slander the True Dharma; when the lifespan is shortened;
at the time when sentient beings are decaying, when the Dharma is perishing, and when the Saṃgha of bhikṣus is disintegrating—Ānanda, you should...

At that time, being struck with alarm, fear, and dread, there were certain bhikṣus who did not cultivate the body, did not cultivate the mind, did not cultivate morality, and did not cultivate wisdom.
