What are these six? First, attachment to the alms bowl; second, attachment to robes; third, attachment to food; fourth, attachment to... [the rest of the sentence is truncated in the source].

They become attached to their beds and seats. Fifth, they become attached to their dwellings. Sixth, due to the causes and conditions of illness and emaciation, they become greedily attached to medicinal decoctions.

Because they greedily seek out superior robes and alms bowls, as well as the finest varieties of medicinal flavors, they further engage in mutual strife and contention, litigating against one another even up to the official courts;
their mouths are like swords and blades as they slander one another. They [slander] each other...
They harbor hatred and envy. Thus, for the sake of robes, alms-bowls, food and drink, bedding and seats, dwellings, and medicinal requisites, they harbor mutual hatred and envy;
their minds are not matured, and they face one another with turbid hearts.
Furthermore, Ānanda, you should observe these evil bhikṣus who, having left home out of faith, have become attached to robes and bowls once they have gone forth. Six...
Through these various causes and conditions, one falls into the three evil realms, as described in the sūtras. A wise person should therefore give rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.
△ First: Keeping Extra Robes (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
The three robes are: first, the *saṃghāṭī*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*; and third, the *antarvāsaka*. These three dharma-robes are collectively called *cīvara* in India;
in the Hu kingdoms of the north, they are referred to as *kāṣāya*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
The reason for establishing these three distinct names is the desire to manifest a previously unheard-of dharma (*apūrva-dharma*).

Among all ninety-six types of [non-Buddhist] schools, none possess these three names; thus, this distinction is made because they differ from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The *Pinfen gongde lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merit) states:
"Some say that the maker of the three robes [did so] because of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma (*trivartana-dharmacakra*); others say it was for..."
Because of the three periods of time—or as some say, for the sake of the three seasons—one provides the three robes. In winter one wears the heavy ones;
in summer, the light ones; and in spring, the medium ones. It is for these three seasons that one possesses the three robes.
During times of great cold, one may wear the three robes layered thickly to ward off the chill. Others say they are also for the sake of mosquitoes, gadflies, and dragonflies.
Therefore, the three robes were established. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that they were instituted for five reasons: to ward off cold and heat; to eliminate shamelessness and lack of modesty;
and to produce virtuous deportment and purity when entering a village or traveling on the road.
Only then were the three robes prescribed. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "The three robes are the insignia of the śramaṇas and the noble ones; therefore, my disciples shall be uniform in these."
Robes are sufficient to ward off great cold and great heat, to keep away flies, mosquitoes, and gadflies, to cover one’s sense of shame and modesty, and to preserve the noble lineages.

If by nature one cannot endure the cold, it is permitted to wear old and worn-out garments; one may, according to one's inclination, have them quilted or layered. This is precisely what is meant by having few desires and few concerns.
The Vinaya states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and disciples of the Buddhas of the past wore such robes as I do today.
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and disciples of the Buddhas of the future shall wear such robes as I do today.
Cut with a blade to form the robe of a śramaṇa, it cannot be plundered by enemies or thieves. It is *pāṃsukūla*.
If the sūtras clarify the twelve *dhūta* practices, there are two kinds of robes: first, the *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that because of the causes and conditions of fine robes, one pursues them in all directions and falls into wrong livelihood. If one accepts fine robes from others, attachment arises;
if one does not become attached, the donor will feel resentment. Furthermore, fine robes are for those who have not yet attained the Way.
Wherever greed and attachment arise, the cause of fine clothing leads to the calamity of bandits, or even to the loss of life.
Because there are such afflictions as these, one accepts the practice of wearing coarse hempen robes. Second, regarding "only three robes," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains:

"The practitioner has few desires and is content; their clothing merely serves to cover the body, being neither too much nor too little. Therefore, they accept only the three robes. As for laypeople seeking [fine garments]...
Because they delight in pleasure, many store various kinds of clothing; whereas some non-Buddhists practice asceticism and thus go naked without shame.
Therefore, the disciples of the Buddha abandon these two extremes and abide in the Middle Way. The *Jietan jing* (Sutra on the Ordination Platform) states:
"The five-strip lower robe severs greed for the body; the seven-strip middle robe severs anger of the mouth; the great robe, the upper robe, severs delusion."
It is the mind. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Those who don the *kāṣāya* cast off the three poisons" (*naīe* refers to the triple-layered *tricīvara*, not the head-wrap worn today).

The "Six Groups of Bhikṣus" (Ṣaḍvargika), also known as the "Six Multitudes," refers to those who gathered in groups to perform various acts contrary to dignified decorum, entering and departing in large parties.
They were: first, Nanda; second, Upananda; third, Kālodāyin; fourth, Channa; [fifth, Svāgata; sixth, Udāyin].
Pañcaśikha and Pūrṇa—these six individuals were such that there was no dharma they did not master.

They had attained a thorough understanding of the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and were proficient in the various arts and techniques of the five vidyās and the hundred crafts. Nanda and Upananda were both excessively greedy, and it is also said they were excessively wrathful;
they were skilled in mathematics, the shifting movements of yin and yang, and in preaching the Dharma and engaging in debate. Kātyāyana...

Dhāyī was full of desire and was deeply proficient in the way of archery; he was skilled in understanding the Abhidharma and later attained the destruction of the outflows, entering the Nirvana without remainder.
Chandana was full of anger (also said to be full of delusion) and was also proficient in the way of archery;

he understood the Abhidharma and later attained the destruction of the outflows, entering the Nirvana without remainder. Aśvaka and Punarvasu were full of delusion (also said to be full of anger) and were skilled in music.
They were capable in all manner of jests and diversions, and were likewise skillful in preaching the Dharma and engaging in debate; they also understood the Abhidharma.
These four men were all from noble families who influenced one another and became friends, propagating the Buddha’s teachings.
Internally, he was the main pillar of the Dharma-gate; externally, he was the great protector of the Buddha’s teachings.
This was what is called a manifestation of great spiritual power (*mahopāya*). Each had nine disciples, totaling sixty.

At that time, Kālodāyin had already severed his afflictions (*kleśa*), and Channa went to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī to attend to his affairs and reside there. Then there were Aśvajit and Pūrṇa—these two.
They both passed away, leaving only Nanda and Upananda, who remained until they reached old age. The Mahāmegha Sūtra states:
"Devadatta was able to instruct and reveal the path to countless, immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to dwell securely in the roots of goodness.
All that pertains to Devadatta’s sphere of activity is truly beyond the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. 6.
The assembly of bhikṣus, as well as the great bodhisattvas and Devadatta, all traveled together with him. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said, "I have also manifested in Jambudvīpa as one who does not maintain the prohibitive precepts and commits the four grave offenses."

All people see this and say that I have truly committed an offense. However, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have firmly upheld the prohibitive precepts without any lapse or deficiency. Furthermore, I manifest in Jambudvīpa as an icchantika;
all people see me as an icchantika, yet in reality I am not an icchantika. What is meant by an "icchantika"?
"How could I possibly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi?
Furthermore, I manifest in Jambudvīpa as one who breaks the harmony of the Saṃgha, and sentient beings all claim that I am a schismatic.
Yet, when I observe among humans and devas, there is no one capable of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha. He continued, "Furthermore, I manifest in Jambudvīpa as a Māra..."
"Pāpīyan! All people say that I am Pāpīyan. However, for immeasurable kalpas, I have been free from the deeds of Māra;

I am pure and untainted, like a lotus flower. (Since the Buddha manifests himself in this way to benefit sentient beings, how could the group of six, including Devadatta, ever fathom or understand it?
The *Śata-avadāna-sūtra* says: "Long ago, there was a man who wished to gain the favor of a king. He asked others, saying..."
"How did you obtain this? Someone said to him, "If you wish to attain the appearance and features of the king, you must imitate him.
Upon seeing the king's eyes, the man then imitated the king's eyes. The king asked him, "Are you ill? Or are you afflicted by wind? Why are your eyes like this?
The man replied to the king, "I am not ill in my eyes, nor am I afflicted by wind. I wish..."

Having gained the king’s favor and observed the king’s glances, they imitated him. When the king heard these words, he became greatly incensed and ordered his men to inflict harm upon them, banishing them from the country.
People of the world are just like this: within the Buddha-dharma, they desire to draw near and seek its wholesome teachings for their own growth;
yet once they have drawn near, they do not understand the Dharma-king, the Tathāgata.
For the sake of sentient beings, they employ various skillful means to manifest their own deficiencies, thereby giving rise to derision and slander, and imitating what is improper.
Because of this, they forever lose their goodness within the Buddha-dharma and fall into the three evil realms;
just as that man imitated the king, so it is with these people.
*Chángyī* (畜長衣):

*cháng* is pronounced with the second tone (*zhōngliángqiè*), and *chǎng* is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). It means "surplus" or "remnant. As the *Book of Jin* states: "In my whole life, I have had no surplus possessions (*wú chángwù*).
This refers to it. The *Mātṛkā* says: "As the Buddha taught, if a robe exceeds ten nights [without being processed], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

How does one come to possess an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*)? It is said that if it enters one's hand, or rests upon one's knees or shoulder, and one forms the thought, "This is my robe," then it becomes an extra robe.
In the *Madhyama Āgama*, the Buddha said: "I say that one must not keep any robes at all; yet I also say that one may keep all robes.
If one keeps robes, it causes unwholesome and evil dharmas to increase and wholesome dharmas to decline."

Regarding such robes, I say they must not be kept. If, however, by keeping such robes one increases wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) and causes unwholesome and evil qualities (*akuśala-dharma*) to decline, I say that such robes may be kept. As it is with robes, so it is with food, drink, bedding, seats, and villages.
Furthermore, it is said: "Outflows (*āsrava*) are abandoned through use. If a bhikṣu uses clothing... [text fragment ends]

It is for the sake of benefit, not out of arrogance, nor for the sake of adornment; it is merely for protection against mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, rain, cold, and heat, and it is done out of a sense of shame and modesty.
If one uses food and drink, it is not for the sake of profit, nor out of arrogance, nor for the sake of corpulence and pleasure;
it is merely to enable the body to endure for a long time and to eliminate afflictions, anxieties, and distress.

It is for the sake of practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*). It is because one wishes to eliminate old ailments and prevent new ones from arising, so as to abide for a long time in peace and freedom from illness.
If one uses dwellings, houses, beds, bedding, or furniture, it is not for the sake of profit, nor out of pride, nor for the sake of adornment;
rather, it is solely so that exhaustion may find rest and tranquility may be attained.
It is because of [the need for] sitting. If one uses medicinal decoctions, it is not for the sake of profit, nor out of pride, nor for the sake of physical plumpness and pleasure;
rather, it is solely to eliminate the affliction of illness, to sustain the life-faculty, and to abide in peace and freedom from disease.
If one does not use them, then afflictions, distress, and grief arise; if one uses them, then afflictions, distress, and grief do not arise. This is what is meant by...
It is with outflows (*sāsrava*). It is abandoned through its application. The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states: "The offense of a bhikṣu who covets material requisites is extremely grave.
Long ago, there was a bhikṣu who was greedily attached to a bronze gong. After he died, he became a hungry ghost (*preta*).

Once the distribution of the communal property was finished, he appeared before them in his true form, appearing utterly dark and gloomy like a mass of pure black clouds. The bhikṣus were struck with wonder and alarm."
"What is this object? Among the assembly was one who had attained the eye of the Path, who said, "This is a deceased bhikṣu who, out of greed for this gong, fell among the hungry ghosts (preta).
Now, still craving it, he has come to seek it. The bhikṣus immediately returned the gong to him;
he then seized the tongue of the gong and licked it, after which he set it down and departed. The bhikṣus picked it up again, but it was utterly foul-smelling.
It cannot be approached. Furthermore, he had others recast it into vessels, yet it remained foul-smelling and unusable.
By this evidence, one knows that greed is a great affliction. Moreover, in the past, there was a bhikṣu who delighted in making robes;

day and night he was obsessed with dyeing them. He fell gravely ill and knew he was about to die. He then raised his head to look at his robes, and within him arose a poisonous thought, saying: "When I die..."
Afterwards, who would dare wear these robes of mine? Before long, he passed away and was reborn as a *nirmāṇa-kāya* snake, which returned to coil around the clothes.
When the assembly carried the corpse out for cremation, they sent someone to retrieve the garments;

seeing the snake coiled around them, it hissed poison from near its throat, and no one dared to approach. The assembly went together to look, but none among them dared to draw near. There was, however, one bhikṣu...

Having attained the Way, he entered the four immeasurable contemplations (*catur-apramāṇa*), whereby poison could no longer affect him. [The snake] then approached him and said, "This was originally your garment;
it is no longer yours. Why do you protect it? He then immediately cast it away and entered into a thicket of grass.
The poisonous fire breaks out and burns the grass; it then turns back and burns one's own body. At the end of life, one immediately enters hell.
Within a single day in hell, one is burned three times; all this is due to the harm caused by greed.
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: *Naiḥsargika* means "to relinquish" (*śe*).
*Pāyattika* means "falling" (*duō*). According to the phonology (*śabdavidyā*), *naiḥ* is translated as "exhaustion" (*jìn*) and *sargika* as "relinquishment" (*shě*).
The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states: "The object must be relinquished and the offense must be confessed. This refers to that which has been transgressed.
The object must be relinquished entirely to the Saṃgha, whether it consists of many people or a single individual; one may not relinquish it to a separate group.
Once it has been relinquished, any remaining offense of falling (pāyattika) must be confessed before others. The *Śīla-pratyaya-sūtra* states: Upāli addressed the Buddha.
What is meant by *niḥsargika*? The Buddha said: "If one loses the three robes three times, they may no longer be received, nor may they be worn.
Whether one trades them away or begs for them [to replace them], this is called *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

It is called 'burning the roots of the Noble Path. For one who sells them, samādhi cannot arise; this is called 'shifting and falling' (*śikṣāpada-niḥsarga-pātayantika*). Within this, there is the offense of falling (*pātayantika*), which, together with the nine..."
The ten matters are identical; they differ only in that among the ninety offenses, there is no forfeiture of material goods (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*), which is why they are distinct.

Regarding the offenses involving falling away (*pārājika*) for the Great Saṃgha, there are one hundred and twenty types in total. Thirty types are excluded because they arise from material goods, as the transgressions therein stem from strong greed and arrogance.
Because one must relinquish it and enter the Saṃgha, it is called a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
*Kāṭhina* (also transliterated as *kejichina*) means "firm and solid" in its literal sense; it was formerly translated as the "Cloth of Merit," because by receiving this cloth...
Furthermore, during the five-month period, one obtains five beneficial merits: first, the permission to keep extra robes; second, the permission to stay overnight apart from one's robes;

Here, the *saṃghāṭī* is translated according to its meaning as the 'Robe of Many Fragments,' because it consists of many strips. If named according to its function, it is called the 'Robe for Entering Royal Palaces and Villages,' as it is worn when begging for food and when preaching the Dharma."
The Vinaya Master Jing said that *uttarāsaṅga* is translated as "upper robe.

It refers to the body’s dwelling [garment]. Some call it the inner garment (*antarvāsa*). Master Yijing states that *antavastra* is translated as the lower garment;
it is also called the inner garment. Nanshan says: "The lower garment is named according to its function; it is the garment worn when walking within the monastery or performing miscellaneous tasks.
The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "One should know that the three robes have distinct functions for use. When performing work or on the road..."

When walking about or while inside the monastery, one should always wear the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*). When performing prostrations or during meals, one should don the seven-strip robe (*saptakaṣāya*).

*Chǎnglù* (敞露):
*chǎng* is pronounced with the second tone (*shǎng*). It means vast or open. It also means to open. The *Cāngjié piān* states it refers to being high and prominent;
that is, leveling the high ground so that one can look out over a great distance. Master Ying says that the old version of the Vinaya text uses the character *chāng* (閶), which is pronounced *chǎng*.
The *Chuci* refers to it as the "Gate of Heaven" (*tiānmén*). It is also the name for the west wind. Furthermore, there is "Chánghé," which people today call a great gate;
all such gates are termed "Chánghé. However, "cháng" does not carry this meaning [in the original sense].

Regarding the miscellaneous matters concerning the relinquishing of robes, it is said: if one intends to return immediately upon going elsewhere for a short time, one need not take the robes with them.

Furthermore, if one goes out briefly intending to return, but reaches the point where evening falls and returns after night has already fallen, fearing harm from insects or thieves, one should stay overnight there.
One should not travel at night. One may borrow one of the other three robes from a fellow practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) and maintain it for the purpose at hand.

The robe previously maintained should be mentally relinquished, after which the new one should be maintained. According to this Vinaya text, this refers to cases where there is another robe available.
One may borrow [a robe] for the purpose of maintaining it, so as to avoid the offense of being separated from one's robes overnight and the transgression of failing to maintain them.
If there is no fellow practitioner of the holy life with whom one can borrow a robe, one should perform a mental relinquishment (*cetanā-tyāga*).

It is better to be without a robe and incur the *duṣkṛta* offense of violating the rules of decorum than to incur the heavy downfall (*pārājika*) of being separated from one's robes overnight. One should understand that this precept concerns robes already [in one's possession].
One incurs an offense by failing to relinquish [the robe] after staying overnight. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "There are cases where one relinquishes the robe and incurs no offense.

For example, when a bhikṣu goes beyond the boundary to stay elsewhere, he borrows a robe and maintains it; once he has passed through the designated area, he relinquishes the robe and returns it to the other person.
This is called relinquishing the robe without offense. There are also cases where one incurs an offense without relinquishing the robe. For example, when a bhikṣu goes beyond..."

Regarding the boundary: when one travels to another location for the night and borrows a robe to maintain [the precepts], at the moment the boundary is crossed, one must immediately return that borrowed robe.

One does not perform the formal rite of relinquishing it; rather, one returns it and receives one's own robe again. Because one has not relinquished the previous robe yet receives one's own robe once more, the dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) is impaired, resulting in a *duṣkṛta* offense.

This is what is meant by "incurring an offense. There are cases where one incurs an offense even without relinquishing the robe, and there are also cases where one both relinquishes the robe and incurs an offense, as follows:
If a bhikṣu possesses his own robe and stays overnight outside the boundary, at the conclusion of the night, it is an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
This is called both forfeiting the robe and incurring an offense. Alternatively, there are cases where one does not forfeit the robe and incurs no offense;

for example, when a bhikṣu personally maintains possession of his robe and does not stay overnight apart from it. This is called neither forfeiting the robe nor incurring an offense. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* asks: "May it be used?"

[Question: May one accept the robes of the Saṃgha as one's three robes (tricīvara)? [Answer: One may accept them. [Question: Once they have been accepted and kept, if one stays apart from them overnight, must they be relinquished?

[Answer: They need not be relinquished; one need only perform a *pāyattika* confession. (This means that if there is a valid reason and one temporarily borrows the robes of the Saṃgha to accept and keep them, there is no need to relinquish them if one stays apart from them overnight.)
This is because the robe originally belongs to the Sangha. The Vinaya states: "There are five causes and conditions for retaining the saṃghāṭī:
if there is fear; if one suspects there will be fear; if it is raining; if one suspects it will rain; or if one is engaged in making or washing the saṃghāṭī."
If the robe is stained or deeply soiled and tucked away, this is called "temporarily leaving it behind" and not taking it with one when traveling; it does not mean being separated from it overnight.
If one dwells in a forest hermitage (āraṇya) where there is doubt or fear, then one follows the precept regarding staying overnight separated from one's robes for up to six nights.

(Tang Dynasty: Zen Master Wuzhuo traveled to Mount Wutai. On his way to visit the Vajra Cave to pay his respects, he encountered Mañjuśrī, who had manifested as an old man. The old man led him into the Prajñā Temple. The grounds of the temple were entirely made of lapis lazuli, and the halls and buildings all shone with a golden hue.)

The old man sat upon a white-toothed couch and pointed to a golden stool, commanding Zhe to sit upon it. They conversed, and Zhe wished to stay for one night. The old man asked, "Do you carry the three robes? Zhe replied, "Since receiving the precepts, I have carried them. The old man said, "This is a matter of attachment. Zhe replied, "There is also sacred teaching regarding this;

if you permit me to stay overnight, I shall mentally relinquish them, for the Buddha himself permitted this in cases of urgent necessity. The old man said, "If there is no difficulty, one must not relinquish the robes; you should guard them with urgency. He then dismissed him. Alas!
That people nowadays do not consider it a fault to sleep apart from one's robes—upon seeing this, they should reflect for themselves.
"Eight trees" refers to the case where a bhikṣu stays overnight in an unbounded araṇya; the space between eight trees constitutes his robe-boundary (cīvara-sīmā).
Furthermore, regarding the space between eight trees: the measurement is based on the human cubit (*hasta*) and the bow (*dhanus*), where four cubits constitute one bow.
According to the method for planting mango trees (*āmra*) taught by Śrutavān the Brahmin, one tree is planted at intervals of seven bows so that the flowers and fruit may flourish.
Between eight trees, the total distance is fifty-six bows. If calculated in *śu* (chi), according to the ancient Zhou standard...

One chi (尺) is one chi-eight cun (寸); this constitutes one *hasta* (肘). Between eight trees, the total distance is four hundred three chi and two cun (which is forty *zhang* and three chi and two cun).
There are those who take twenty-four finger-widths of an average person as one *hasta*;
this corresponds to one chi-five cun by the *hugui* (笏尺) standard. Between eight trees, there would thus be three hundred thirty-six chi. If compared with this...

The Buddha placed his robe between these eight trees and stayed overnight in another location. When the dawn appeared, he incurred an offense of expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya), as explained in detail in the Sikkhāpada-khandhaka.

*Si-zhou* (四肘): *zhi* is pronounced as in *zhǐ-yǒu* (止酉); *zhou* is pronounced with the third tone (*shàngshēng*). It refers to the elbow joint. From the elbow joint to the tip of the fingers is called one *zhou*.
In the country of Cāmara, the method for making bows is such that they are four *zhou* long by the standard of an average person’s elbow; some say they are five *zhou*. The old [translation] used...
One *hasta* (cubit) is one foot-eight inches in length according to the *mūla-saṃgha*. According to the *Vinaya-viniścaya*, twenty-four finger-widths (*aṅgula*) constitute one *hasta*.
Seven *paramāṇus* (ultimate atoms) form one *aṇu* (minute particle); seven of these form a water-particle; seven of these form a copper-particle;
seven of these form a rabbit-hair particle; seven of these form a sheep’s-hair particle; and seven of these form a cow’s-hair particle.
Seven *rajas* (dust particles) make one *taraṇa* (mote in a sunbeam); seven *taraṇas* make one *likṣā* (nit); seven *likṣās* make one *yūka* (louse);
seven *yūkas* make one *yava* (barley grain); seven *yavas* make one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). Twenty-four fingers make one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits make one bow (*dhanus*);
five hundred bows make one *krośa* (the meaning of *krośa* is explained below).

She is called Mahāprajāpatī, and is also called Mahāmāyā. The *Wénjù* states that she is translated as "Mahāprajāpatī.
She may be addressed by her clan name as Kautamī, or as Gautamī; she was the Buddha’s paternal aunt and the elder sister of Lady Māyā.
Seven days after the Buddha’s birth, Lady Māyā passed away and was reborn in the heavens. Her aunt—
She was nourished by her maternal aunt, Āmrapālī, who was the biological mother of Nanda. She was born in the city of Devadṛśa to King Suprabuddha.
According to the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, she lived for one hundred and twenty years, yet her body showed no signs of aging, appearing like a sixteen-year-old maiden.
This was because, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, she had been the chief queen of King Kṛkī and had planted [the seeds of merit].
Because she offered various fragrant flowers and exquisite foods as an offering to the stūpa of the relics of Kāśyapa Buddha and made this vow,
she has now obtained this retribution (the remainder is as explained in the *Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka* and in the commentary on the phrase "Māyā").
The *Mūla-vinaya* of the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā states: In the city of Takṣaśilā, there was an elder who, not long after marrying his wife, gave birth to a daughter.
Her body possessed three virtues, like a blue utpala lotus: first, her body was golden-hued, just as...
1. His eyes are like the filaments of a flower. 2. His eyes are a deep blue color, like the petals of a flower. 3.
His fragrance is rich and pervasive, like the scent of a flower. After twenty-one days had passed since his birth, his relatives gathered for a meeting, intending to bestow a name upon him.
They said, "This child’s body is like a blue lotus; we should give him the name 'Blue Lotus' (*Utpala*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Her appearance was upright and her complexion was the color of the *utpala* lotus. In the distant past, during kalpas long ago, this person was a Brahmin girl.
When her parents and family members went to sea to gather treasures, she remained behind;
unable to support herself, she lived together with various courtesans in one place, providing for herself by selling her beauty. This woman’s beauty...
Her appearance was not beautiful, and no one came to visit her. She constantly reproached herself, wondering why she alone was so unfortunate.
At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha whom everyone revered with deep respect.

Someone said to her, "If you can make offerings to the Pratyekabuddha, whatever you desire will be fulfilled according to your heart's wish in every lifetime. Thereupon, the woman followed these words and prepared exquisite food and drink.
She covered it with *utpala* flowers and offered them to the Pratyekabuddha, making this vow:
"May I, in every successive life, always obtain the form of a woman, peerlessly beautiful and upright, respected by all, such that none may surpass me.
Furthermore, may I attain the merits obtained by this śramaṇa. For this reason, she has now been born as a woman in this life.
She was foremost in physical appearance. By virtue of her original vow, she has now attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and is praised by the Buddha.
Among the bhikṣuṇīs, she possesses great supernormal powers and is the most preeminent. The *Mahā-śāstra* cites this bhikṣuṇī’s *Jātaka-sūtra*, which says:
"I recall that in a former life, I was a female entertainer who wore various kinds of garments."

Furthermore, *Kapilavastu* is also rendered as *Kapiḷavastu*. This translates as "Yellow-Headed" (*Huangtou*) or, alternatively, as "Tortoise-Caste" (*Yuanzhong*;
for details, see the explanation in the *Bhikṣu-saṃghabheda-vinaya*). *Nyagrodha* is explained as in the *Mahāvihāra-vinaya*. It may also be translated as the "Park of the Many-Rooted Tree.
This park is located three or four *li* south of the city of Kapilavastu; it belongs to the Śākyas.
After attaining *samyak-saṃbodhi*, he returned to his kingdom to see his father, the King, and this was the place where he preached the Dharma for the King.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard that the Bodhisattva had attained *samyak-saṃbodhi*, felt a deep yearning and longing; he dispatched an envoy to invite the Buddha.
Knowing that the Buddha would not reside within the royal palace, the King immediately constructed sixteen great monasteries in this very garden. Its...
The smaller [monasteries] total sixty-four. Within each courtyard, there are multi-storied pavilions, exactly like those in the Jeta Grove, without any difference.
Having welcomed the Buddha back to the kingdom, they resided here.
It was at this very place that the Buddha converted the eight princes and five hundred members of the Śākya clan (the eight princes excluding the ninth, Upāli).
*Ran* (染) is pronounced *bo* (博) with the tone of *bai* (伯). It means to wave or gesture. To "wave" (*hui*) is to split or divide. The *Guangya* states: "To *bi* (擘) is to split apart.
[This refers to] Gautamī.
The meaning is as explained in the first fascicle. She is Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī.
Master Yuan states that "Gautamī" or "Kauṭamī" are both feminine vocatives; if spoken with a masculine inflection, one says "Gautama."
△ Chapter 18: Receiving Gold, Silver, and Coins (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
The Minister Zhujì.
Some call him Ratnaśikhin (Jewel-Crest), while others call him Manicūḍa (Wish-Fulfilling Topknot); the meaning is the same.
In the Sanskrit language, *maṇi* means "wish-fulfilling jewel" (*cintāmaṇi*), and furthermore, *maṇi* is the general name for jewels.
This minister was the head of a village in the city of Rājagṛha.
The sun and moon have four afflictions;
these four afflictions are the asuras, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist. Sometimes they are considered to have five afflictions by dividing smoke and clouds into two separate afflictions.
As the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The orbs of the sun and moon are obscured by five veils and thus lack clarity."
It is not illuminated; it is not vast; it is not pure. First, clouds; second, smoke; third, dust; fourth, mist; fifth, the hand of the *Grahā* Asura. Regarding "clouds":

it is like when, during the height of summer, a small cloud arises and in an instant increases, completely covering the void and obstructing the disks of the sun and moon so that both are made invisible.
Regarding "smoke": it is like when grass is burned in a forest or wild thicket.
Regarding "wood": suddenly, smoke spreads to cover the entirety of space, obscuring the disks of the sun and moon so that neither appears. Regarding "dust":

it is like during a great drought when a powerful wind swirls and strikes, causing a tumultuous cloud of dust to rise suddenly and cover the entirety of space, obscuring the disks of the sun and moon.
Both are made to disappear. As for "mist" (*nīhāra*): it is like when autumn and winter arrive and mist rises from mountains and rivers.

Furthermore, it is heard that in foreign lands, when rain first clears and the sun shines upon the valleys and plains, the vapors of the earth surge upward; these fine particles disperse and spread, completely covering the void of space.
They obstruct the disks of the sun and moon, causing both to become invisible. Regarding the hand of the asura Hraḥhu:
when the asuras fight with the devas, the devas take the sun and moon as their banners; by the majesty of the sun and moon, the devas always prevail over them.
At that time, the asura Hraḥhu constantly harbors resentment toward the sun and moon, desiring to destroy them. Because of this—

The asuras—*asura* being the term for *asura*, and *hrahū* being the name of the asura king—were unable to destroy [the mountain] by any means of their skillful artifice, owing to the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings;
they then used their hands to shield it, causing it to vanish for a moment.
Regarding the relinquishment therein:
one should have it delivered to a trustworthy upāsaka or to a park-keeper, saying, "This is not for me;
you should know this. If that person takes it and returns it to the bhikṣu, [he] should accept it.

Regarding those items belonging to individuals, one should therefore accept them and instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle pure goods) to take charge of them. If one obtains pure robes, bowls, or other such items, one may trade for them and then formally accept and maintain them.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, one is required to relinquish them within the Saṃgha and place them among the Saṃgha’s inexhaustible assets (*akṣaya-nīvi*).

One may use [the proceeds] to make clothing for the dwelling, but they must not be used for food. It is permitted for a sick person to have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure attendant) keep them, provided one does not become greedily attached.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Sangha should perform a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint a single bhikṣu to discard them in water or fire.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if the items are few, they should be discarded; if they are many, one may entrust them to a like-minded *kappiya-kāraka*.
[Regarding] the border [of the monastery], the speech: "Because it is impure, I should not accept it; you should accept it.
Once the *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) has accepted it, he says to the bhikṣu: "This object is given to the bhikṣu. The bhikṣu says: "This is an impure object; if it were pure, I would accept it.

(This is called *viśuddhi-vāda*, declaring purity). If one cannot find a *kappiya-kāraka* who shares the same mind, one should make it into bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions. One should...
One should enter the midst of the Saṃgha to repent. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If there is a gift of cloth-money offered by another, one may accept it as needed.
Having accepted it, one should regard it as belonging to that person and keep it; one should entrust it to a *śuddhaka* (pure person) to hold."
One should not hold it oneself. If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), one should stand before a single *bhikṣu* and speak these words:
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind: I, [name], have obtained this impure object. I shall hold this impure object."
"Exchange it for pure wealth. Thus he says three times. One may use it according to one's needs; do not harbor doubts. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states:
"If, during the rains retreat, a donor offers the price of robes to the community of bhikṣus, one should accept them while maintaining the mental attitude that this gift is entrusted to the donor.
One should seek out a person of faith and respect—whether a *karmadāna*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a lay follower (*upāsaka*)."
If one acts as a pure donor and perceives the object as the property of a donor, there is no offense in taking hold of it.
If no donor can be found, one should take gold, silver, or other such items and say before a single bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, please attend to me.
I, [name], have obtained this impure wealth; I shall now use this impure wealth to exchange for pure wealth. This should be repeated twice.
3. One should carry it oneself or have another person carry it.

If a bhikṣu obtains gold, silver, or the like while on a journey, for the sake of provisions for the road, he should carry it himself or have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) or a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) carry it.

The Sarvāstivādins say that money, precious gems, grain, and rice are all treated the same as "extra robes" (*atireka-cīvara*); they must be formally declared pure (*śuddhi-uddeśana*) after ten days. The rest...

As explained in the *Cīvara-vastu* (Section on Robes) within the section on "Pure Gifts" (*śuddha-dāna*), this method of declaring an object pure was established by the Buddha’s great compassion out of pity for disciples of inferior faculties, so that they might dwell securely in the cultivation of the path.
However, one must give rise to deep shame and remorse, with a mind free from greedy attachment;
only when using it without producing defiled results does one accord with the intention of the Compassionate Honored One. Should there be emotional attachment...
[This] defiles the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The Buddha did not permit it. A true seeker of liberation should rely upon the Great Teaching.

As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If one says that the Buddha permitted bhikṣus to keep male and female slaves, impure things, gold, silver, and precious treasures, granaries of grain, cattle, sheep, elephants, and horses, or to trade for profit—even in times of famine, out of compassion..."
Out of compassion for his disciples, [the Buddha] further permitted the bhikṣus to store up old provisions and to eat food prepared by their own hands without receiving it through formal acceptance.
Such statements as these should not be relied upon; therefore, they are cautioned against. This refers to the impurity of the eight types of wealth, which increase greed and destroy the Path.
Thus, the *Shishi Yaoyong Chao* (Essentials of the Vinaya) is cited, stating: "First, fields, houses, and gardens; second, planting and cultivating seeds; third, storing..."
1. Accumulating grain and silk; 2. Keeping domestic animals and servants; 3. Raising and tethering birds and beasts; 4. Hoarding money, treasures, and precious objects; 5.
Possessing felt rugs, mattresses, cauldrons, and cooking pots; 6. Using beds adorned with ivory and gold, as well as other heavy articles.

These eight categories are extensively enumerated in the sūtras, śāstras, and vinaya as common counts of prohibited items, clearly manifesting their faults and the fact that they should not be kept. Furthermore, the Vinaya and Sūtras state: "If there is one who keeps [these], it is not [permissible]."
My disciples, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* also states: "They will certainly not believe in my Dharma and Vinaya.
For these eight reasons, they all increase craving, destroy the Path, defile the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and bring about impure fruits; therefore, they are called "impure. It further says:

"In the Vinaya, because it concerns practical matters and the capacities of those with inferior faculties are narrow, there is much allowance for keeping [possessions]. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "If..."
"O disciples, there will come a time when no one provides for your needs, and during a famine when food and drink are difficult to obtain.
Desiring to protect and uphold the True Dharma, I permit my disciples to accept and possess gold, silver, vehicles, fields, houses, grain, rice, and whatever else is required for trade.
Although I permit the acceptance and possession of such things, they must be given through pure offerings from donors of sincere faith."

The commentary states: "The preceding clarifies that for the Mahāyāna, both the capacity (the practitioner) and the teaching are urgent; the following clarifies that for the Hīnayāna, both the capacity and the teaching are lax.

Regarding the Vinaya, which concerns matters: if one violates a matter, the offense is light, as this is evident. The Sūtras take principle as their core: because one violates principle, the offense is grave.

Because the capacity of the Hīnayāna is narrow and insufficient, it permits [violations] contrary to the above. Because the Mahāyāna is capable of such endurance, its offenses are grave. Yet worldly people conversely claim that the Hīnayāna..."

One must rely upon the precepts; the Great Teaching pervades all quarters. How many errors have there been! (The explanation provided here should properly appear later within the commentary on the Vinaya texts;
however, as I wish to provide it immediately so that beginners may understand, it is presented here. All such instances follow this same principle.)
△ Chapter Nineteen: Buying and Selling Precious Objects (This is a shared precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
Gold, whether refined or unrefined.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "That which is 'formed' refers to vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth; that which is 'unformed' refers to gold ingots and fragments of gold. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"Whether formed or unformed, whether with characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) or without characteristics: 'formed' means making various vessels out of precious materials;
'unformed' means it is merely the precious material itself, not yet made into a vessel; 'with characteristics' refers to precious materials that have been fashioned into vessels."
It may take the form of written characters or the form of seals. "Non-appropriation" means not making vessels or treasures, not making written characters, and not making seals.
Furthermore, it is said: "The essence of this precept should properly be called 'the use of various treasures,' and one must not say 'buying and selling.
This precept constitutes an offense immediately upon its occurrence; it is not like the precept against trading. The precept against trading is for the sake of profit."
Therefore, having purchased [an item] and then reselling it constitutes an offense.
△ The twentieth [offense]:
Buying and Selling (This is a shared precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
The term "seller" (fàn) is pronounced with the *jiàn* (諫) radical and the fourth tone (*qùshēng*). To buy low and sell high is called "selling" (*fàn*).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that among all the *pāyattika* offenses, the offense of selling is the most grave. It is better to be a butcher than to engage in trade.
He sells them. Why is this? Butchers specifically harm animals;

those who trade in all manner of goods deceive and harm others regardless of whether they are monastics or laypeople, noble or foolish, observant of precepts or violators of precepts—there is nowhere they do not practice deception. Furthermore, they constantly harbor evil intentions.
If they deal in grain, their minds are always filled with the hope that the world will suffer from famine, frost, hail, and pestilence. If they deal in salt, they hoard it.

Other goods [are likewise affected]. The mind is constantly filled with longing, and disturbances arise from the four quarters. The royal roads are blocked and cut off. Such are the evils of those who engage in trade.
Even if these traded goods are used to prepare food for the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should not consume it.

If they are used to build monasteries for the Saṃgha of the four directions, one must not dwell within them. If they are used to construct a stūpa or an image, one should not pay homage toward them. Furthermore...
The Buddha said: "If a monk who observes the precepts merely makes a mental salutation, he should not accept or use these items.
If this monk dies, the Sangha should perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to divide these items. Question:
"Since he did not accept or use these items while alive, why is a *karmavācanā* performed upon his death? Answer: "This business of buying and selling involves a profound transgression."

This is grave. If one is alive when the Saṃgha consumes these items, although one has violated the precepts and incurs guilt, because they are within the field of merit that is the Saṃgha, they are permitted to be used.

Because they are used, the continuity of the practice remains unbroken. If one were not permitted to use them within the field of merit that is the Saṃgha, there would be no merit in this life and one would incur heavy punishment in the next. For this reason, [I] do not dare [to consume them].
It is made anew. Since the bhikṣu has already died, there is no longer any reason for buying or selling; therefore, it is permitted to take the goods through *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).

*Dǎo* (擣): pronounced with the tone of *duō gǎo qiè* (都槁切); it means to push with the hand, or alternatively, to strike, to pound, or to thresh. *Zhì* (治): to process or refine. *Chén* (陳): to lay out or arrange.
The character 知 (zhī) is pronounced as *chí* (as in "pool"). It means to process or refine. Alternatively, it is pronounced as *zhì* (as in "child") when read with the *zhíyì* (直意) initial.

When referring to processing something that has not yet been refined, it takes the level tone (*píngshēng*). When referring to the act of refining itself or its resulting efficacy, it takes the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

Regarding "timely medicine" (*kālabhojana*): "time" refers to the period from dawn until midday. There are two kinds of timely medicine: first, that which is swallowed (*khādya*), and second, that which is chewed (*bhojya*).

There are five types of swallowed food: namely, boiled rice, parched grain flour, dry cakes, fish, and meat. There are also five types of chewed food: namely, roots, stalks, leaves, [flowers, and fruits].
Flowers, fruits, and fine powdered foods, etc., which may be consumed from dawn until midday, are called "timely medicines" (*kālabhaiṣajya*).
Regarding "non-timely medicines" (*akālabhaiṣajya*, also known as *yāmika*): there are two types. First, from midday until dusk; second, from dusk until the appearance of the morning light.
It has not yet emerged; this constitutes "improper time. Regarding medicines for improper time: this refers to making a gruel from pears, dates, parched grain, sugarcane, and so forth.
If it does not cause intoxication, drinking it during improper time is permitted. However, it is not permitted to receive it on one day and keep it until the next day.

This is called "medicine for improper times" (*akālabhaiṣajya*). (The *Ekottarakarma* states: "As for 'further medicine,' it should be consumed throughout the day; if it reaches the night, it may only be taken until the first watch. The commentary notes:

"According to the Vinaya teachings, one night is divided into three sections. The first section is called the 'first watch. Beyond this, it should not be consumed. If there are only five watches, it should be during the latter half of the first watch. The traditional term "medicine for improper times" is not a literal translation.)

Regarding "seven-day medicine" and "eighth-day [medicine]": this means that from the first day, once the medicine has been received and placed in one's hand, it may be taken and consumed by oneself within the seven-day period.
There are five kinds of seven-day medicine: namely, clarified butter (*sarpis*), oil, fresh butter (*navanīta*), honey, and rock sugar (*phāṇita*). These are for those who are ill.
Regarding the causal conditions: whether taken at the proper time or not the proper time, if one takes them oneself within seven days, these are called "seven-day medicines.
As for "lifelong medicines": [they may be taken] as long as life lasts.
"Throughout one's life" refers to those who have a chronic illness.
If they obtain medicine appropriate for their ailment, from the time they first receive it until the end of their life, they are permitted to take it themselves.
"Medicine for life" includes pills, powders, decoctions, ointments, and extracts; all things that are salty, bitter, sour, or pungent, and which are unfit to be used as food.
Even regarding ashes, soil, and so forth, if there is a cause for a chronic illness, one may take them oneself and consume them for as long as one lives;

these are called "medicines for the duration of one's life" (*yāvajjīvika*). The *Mūlakalpa* states: For instance, sugarcane itself is a "timely medicine" (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*), its juice is a "renewed medicine" (*yāmika-bhaiṣajya*), and its molasses is a "seven-day medicine" (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*);
the ash may be taken for the duration of one's life. Curd is included among the "timely medicines," whey is subsumed under the "renewed medicines," and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) [is likewise].
If [the substance] is curdled milk, it lasts for seven days; once burned to ashes, it lasts for the remainder of one's life. Meat is included at this time; if it is fat, it lasts for seven days;

once burned to ashes, it lasts for the remainder of one's life. One should consume these according to the specific circumstances (as with the three aforementioned medicines, they must all be formally received and maintained before being permitted to take them oneself;
the rest is explained in the section on the administration of medicines).

● Vinaya Piṭaka, Volume Nine △ Section Twenty-one:
Keeping an Extra Alms Bowl (This is an *asādhāraṇa* precept;
if a nun keeps one for more than one night, she incurs a *nissaggiya pācittiya*).
The country of Soma is called *pātrasoma*;
this is translated as "moon," though the precise etymology remains uncertain. In this country, there was a potter who possessed faith and devotion.

The Buddha instructed him step by step, teaching him how to fashion bowls. Following these instructions, he produced them accordingly, and they were immediately completed with extraordinary excellence.
The bowl was thus named *sumā-pātra*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When the Buddha was in the country of Suma, he himself fashioned a mold for a bowl to serve as a model for later use and had a potter fire it. The potter then made many more and fired them together.

Upon opening the kiln door to inspect them, he saw that they had all become golden-colored bowls. Terrified, he said, 'This is the supernatural power of the Great Śramaṇa. If the King hears of this...'"
[The people] thought, "He must surely possess much gold and treasure," and they took [the bowls] and buried them. The Buddha again caused them to be fired, and they all became silver bowls.
They were again afraid and buried them. The Buddha again caused them to be fired, and they then became copper bowls, with a fine blue color like that of the Jambu tree.
He gave them to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not dare to accept them. The Buddha said, "I permit you to keep them."
Now, according to the Vinaya texts, there are six kinds of almsbowls, ranging from the *sumana* to the red bowl. However, their essential types do not exceed two:
namely, iron and earthenware (other copper bowls are not permitted to be kept; they are permitted because they were transformed by the Buddha’s supernatural power).
Uggāra (sometimes written as Yougala or Yūgala; also called the village of Ugāra) is all one and the same name.
The Buddha permitted the possession and use of alms bowls from this country.
Oukaśa (sometimes written as Oukaśa or Oukaśa) refers to the same country. This land produces alms bowls, which the Buddha permitted [his disciples] to possess.
The three types of bowls mentioned above are given their three names based on the country of origin; alternatively, they may differ in color and appearance, ranging from coarse to fine.
In reality, they are simply of one category: earthenware.
The large and small bowls are called *pātra* in Sanskrit, or *patra*; this is translated as "bowl" (*bo*). In terms of meaning, it is rendered as "receptacle appropriate [for a monk]."
The *Fazhen* (Clouding the Chariot) states: "It must be a vessel that accords with the Dharma. This refers to the substance, the color, and the dimensions—all three must accord with the Dharma.
Regarding the substance: it is either clay or iron. Regarding the color: it is to be fumigated to produce a black or red hue, or the color of a peacock's throat or a pigeon.
Regarding the measurements: as stated in the Vinaya texts, the large [bowl] is three *dou* and the small is one and a half *dou*.
Nanshan says that this refers to the *dou* of the Zhou dynasty; according to the Tang *dou*, the upper bowl is one *dou* and the lower bowl is five *sheng*. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states:

Regarding standard measures: from one and a half *śronas* up to two and a half *śronas* is considered a standard measure; anything less than one and a half *śronas* or exceeding two and a half *śronas* is not a standard measure.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The maximum amount received is three *pātra*s of rice and one *pātra* of soup."
If there is half a *karṣa* of other edible food and half a *karṣa* of soup, this is called a "superior bowl" (*uttama-pātra*).

The inferior one (*hīna*) receives one *pātra* of rice, half a *pātra* of soup, and half a *karṣa* of other edible food; this is called an "inferior bowl. That which lies between the superior and the inferior is called a "middle bowl" (*madhyama-pātra*).
If it is larger than the large bowl and smaller than the small bowl, it is not called a "bowl. Regarding the term *pātra*, the Vinaya Master says: [text continues].
It is said: "The various masters of the treatises have many differing explanations, yet they take one principle as correct:
namely, that one *pātra* receives fifteen *liang* of rice—what is called thirty *liang* in the Qin language—which is the measure of a pot of non-glutinous rice from India at that time.
People of the period all collectively calculated that the superior bowl receives three *pātra* of rice and one *pātra* of soup; the remainder may be eaten."
The "thing" (the food item) consists of half a *gong* of soup and three *pattha* of rice—equivalent to two *sheng* of the Qin measure.
One *pattha* of soup and the remaining edible food amount to half a *gong*, which is one and a half *pattha*; this further equals one *sheng* of the Qin measure.

A superior bowl (*shang-po*) has a capacity of three *sheng* of the Qin measure. The Vinaya master says: "There is no remaining edible food; it simply means that the superior bowl receives three *pattha*."
He receives one *pātra* of rice and half a *pātra* of soup. He leaves an empty space at the top of the food so that his fingers do not touch the food within.
