For this reason, sages and worthies have appeared there in succession without end. Now, I shall briefly cite the measurements of one continent.
This is the general outline. The remaining details are fully set forth in the sutras and śāstras, so they will not be described here at length.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is formed through immeasurable causes and conditions, and so too is the great earth.
The water wheel rests upon the wind wheel; the wind rests upon space; space has no support.
It is through the karmic retribution of sentient beings that the world remains stable. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The trichiliocosm all takes the wind wheel as its foundation.
This wind wheel is so solid and firm that it exceeds even diamond (*vajra*). By the power of the minds of sentient beings, [it is thus sustained]."
It is produced by the power of karma and is able to sustain the world, preventing it from collapsing.
From below the wind down to this point is empty space; above the wind is water; above the water is gold; above the gold is earth; and upon the earth are the mountains.
The Cakravāḍa Mountains encircle it on all sides. Outside the mountains is also emptiness, which is unfathomable. That which is contained within the mountains is as follows:
As for the lands, there are ten billion. How is this known? As the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"The sun and moon revolve around the four continents; the area illuminated by their radiance constitutes one world-system (*lokadhātu*).
Within such a thousand world-systems, there are a thousand suns and moons, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, four thousand continents, and four thousand great oceans."
There are four thousand evil realms, one thousand kings of the Yama hell, one thousand Four Heavenly Kings, one thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, and so on up to one thousand Brahmā heavens;
this constitutes a small chiliocosm. One thousand such small chiliocosms constitute a medium chiliocosm.
One thousand such medium chiliocosms constitute a great trichiliocosm. Within it, there are four Sumeru mountains...
From the continents, the sun, and the moon, up to the Brahma heavens, there are ten trillion of each; they all form together when formed and perish together when destroyed.
This constitutes a single trichiliocosm, collectively known as the Sahā world, which is in total a single Buddha-field.
For now, I shall briefly clarify this one set of four continents, as illuminated by a single sun and moon, according to [the established standard].
Within these ten thousand billion suns and moons, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest their transformative teachings;
it is the locus where they appear and disappear, and where they guide both the sages and the ordinary.

Within this realm, beyond Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there are seven layers of golden mountains and seven layers of fragrant water-seas, surrounding one another in succession. These are the seven mountains and seven seas.

Beyond this is the Great Salt Ocean. Within the Salt Ocean, there are four great continents, eight intermediate continents, and tens of thousands of minor islands, all distributed and situated throughout.
Surrounding the exterior of the Salt Ocean is the Small Iron Rim Mountain (Cakravāḍa), which encircles it completely.
These four continents and the rest are all supported by the earth-element wheel; this constitutes a single world-system. Its...
Regarding the four continents: according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, there is a world south of Mount Sumeru named Jambudvīpa.
This land is narrow in the south and broad in the north, measuring seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth. The faces of its inhabitants resemble the shape of this terrain.
There is a great tree named Jambū, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.

The human lifespan is one hundred years; few exceed this, while most fall short, and those who die prematurely are many. (The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states: "In the southern continent, clothing and ornaments are of various kinds and not uniform.

There are countless instances of sexual desire throughout a lifetime, yet there are also those who practice cultivation until death remains free from desire. Their body height is three and a half cubits, or four cubits. The *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "At the beginning of the kalpa, [in] Jambū...")

The people of Jambudvīpa have a lifespan of eighty-four thousand years and a height of five hundred bows (*dhanus*). During the second period, their lifespan is forty thousand years and their height is two hundred bows. During the third period, their lifespan is ten thousand years and their height is one hundred bows.

By the time of the age of strife, their lifespan is reduced to one hundred years and their height to one bow; one bow is equal to four cubits (*hasta*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "There are two intermediate continents: first, Cāmara, and second, Avaracāmara; both are inhabited by humans.
To the east of Mount Sumeru is a continent named Pūrvavideha (translated as "Victorious," because it excels Jambudvīpa; it is also called "East," meaning it is situated at the eastern direction).

It is also called "the beginning" (ādi), meaning the place where the sun first rises. That land is narrow in the east and broad in the west, shaped like a half-moon, measuring nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
the faces of its inhabitants resemble this shape. There is a great king of trees named Kalpavṛkṣa, with a circumference of seven yojanas.
Its branches and leaves spread fifty *yojana*s in all directions and it rises one hundred *yojana*s high. The lifespan of its inhabitants is two hundred years;
they consume fish and meat, and they engage in trade with each other using fine silk, gauze, pearls, and gems. There are rites for marriage [the *Abhidharma* states: "In Pūrvavideha..."].

Those with many desires reach [the state of non-desire] six or seven times in a single lifetime; there are also those who practice until death and remain without desire. They eat the flesh of fish that have died of themselves; they do not kill living beings themselves, nor do they cause others to kill. Their hair is cut short in front and hangs down behind.

Having put on their lower garments, they wrap the upper garment around their bodies. They are eight cubits tall. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "There are two intermediate continents: first, Deha; second, Videha; both are inhabited by humans.
To the west of Mount Sumeru is a continent named Godānīya (also called Aparagodānīya), which means "Cow-Wealth" (*go-dhānya*). The *Lokotpatti-sūtra* states: "Beneath a Kiṃpaka tree, there is..."
There is a stone ox, one yojana in height; for this reason, it is named Aparagoyānī. The shape of that land is like a full moon, and the faces of its people resemble it.

It is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth. There is a king of trees named Kiṃpaka, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.
The lifespan of its people is three hundred years. They [exchange] cattle, horses, pearls, and jade with one another.

Regarding commerce (the *Abhidharma* states: in that land they eat meat and kill living beings; when people die, they cremate their corpses, or place them in water or bury them in the earth; their marriage customs are the same as those of the people of Jambudvīpa;

those with many desires have ten or twelve wives, though there are also those who have no desire; for adornment, they all wear their hair loose, wearing garments both above and below; their height is sixteen cubits).
To the north of Mount Sumeru is a continent named Uttarakuru (this means "Supreme" or "Exalted Place"). Its terrain is square.
The human faces resemble those [of the gods]. It is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth.

There is a king of trees named Āmra, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions. The lifespan of humans is one thousand years. There is no commerce;
they sustain themselves by what they possess. There is no sense of "I" or "mine. The mountains and bathing pools abound with flowers and fruit.
Various birds warble in harmony. On all four sides are the Anavatapta Pools, from which flow the four great rivers.
There are no ditches, pits, thorns, mosquitoes, gadflies, or venomous insects. There is naturally growing non-hybridized rice (which grows without being sown), replete with every flavor.
By placing a *jvālā-prabhā* maṇi-jewel beneath the cooking pot, it boils and cooks spontaneously; when the rice is cooked, the light vanishes. There are those who remain in a crouching posture.
There are trees with leaves so densely packed that they do not leak when it rains from heaven. Men and women sleep beneath them.
When the fruits of the fragrant trees ripen, they naturally split open to reveal various garments, vessels, or food. There are jeweled boats upon the rivers; they board these for recreation.
When entering the water to bathe, they leave their clothes on the bank, board the boats to cross the river, and put on whatever clothing they encounter, seeking no original garments. Next...
Upon reaching the fragrant trees, the trees bowed their trunks. The people there took up musical instruments in their hands and walked along, tuning the strings;

they were free from all ailments, and their physical appearances were identical. Their hair was a deep blue-black, cut level with their eyebrows. Whenever a person gave rise to a desire for sensual pleasure...
He gazed intently at the woman. She followed him into the grove.

If that woman was a relative—such as a parent or a maternal uncle’s kin—and thus one with whom he ought not to engage in sexual desire, the tree would not bend its shade over them, and they would each depart separately.
If she were not a relative and such conduct were appropriate, the tree would then bend to cover their bodies, and they would enjoy themselves as they pleased for one day, two days, or up to seven.
On that day, they departed. After being pregnant for only seven or eight days, she gave birth. Whichever child was born, whether male or female, was placed at a crossroads.
As passersby emerged, they extended their fingers into the child's mouth, and milk flowed forth, completely suffusing the child’s body. After seven days had passed, the child grew up;
the boys went among the assembly of men, and the girls went among the assembly of women. When their lives ended, there was no weeping (because the human lifespan is fixed at a full thousand years).

They do not offer condolences for those who have died. [The deceased] are placed within the four paths. There is a bird named *Uvīśāna* (translated as "Grief-Comforting") that carries them away to other regions (the *Qishi jing* states:
"When a person dies, there is a bird that seizes their hair and places them in another world"). That ground is soft; it sinks when stepped upon and rises again as the foot is lifted.

When one voids excrement or urine, the earth opens up to receive it, and once finished, it closes back together. This is because they cultivated the ten wholesome deeds in previous lives and were thus born here.
Continent. The people of that land and continent do not commit the ten unwholesome deeds; their every movement naturally accords with the ten wholesome paths.

When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the heavenly realms or other auspicious places. (The *Abhidharma* states: "Those with much desire reach [the heavens] four or five times in a single lifetime, while there are also those free from desire.

Their height is thirty-two cubits. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "There are two intermediate continents: one is Kuru, the other is Kaurava; both are inhabited by humans. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Among the eight intermediate continents of the four great continents, the human forms are short and small. Furthermore, there are five hundred smaller [islands].")
[These] continents are inhabited either by humans or by non-humans (non-humans being *pretas*), and some are even empty. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:
"The people of the Northern Continent see through mountain obstructions without hindrance; whatever they hear with their ears—whether distant or near, large or small—they all perceive.
The people of the Eastern Continent likewise see various forms even in total darkness, and everything that serves as an object for their auditory consciousness [is perceived]."

Within the range of a single arrow-shot, the people of Aparagoyānī perceive objects through their visual consciousness without obstruction by mountains or walls, and they are likewise able to hear sounds.
Just as the species of vipers and snakes in Jambudvīpa hear sounds with their eyes, so too it is for the people of Aparagodānī.
It is likewise with hearing various sounds and seeing various forms and images across intervening obstacles.

According to the *Benjing* (Original Scripture), among the five kinds of excellence in Jambudvīpa compared to the other three continents, up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), there are two: first, valorous strength; second, correct mindfulness.
The three places where Buddhas appear in the world; the four grounds for cultivating practice; and the five places for practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Among the various heavens and the three continents, each possesses these three qualities, which surpass those of Jambudvīpa: first, longevity; second, superior physical form; and third, superior land.
According to a comparison of the sūtras and śāstras, those who excel in Jambudvīpa do so by means of the Path (mārga); those who excel in the other three continents do so by means of merit (puṇya).

Nevertheless, the northern continent (Uttarakuru) possesses the most excellent meritorious happiness. The sūtra refers to it as a "difficult place" because, although its inhabitants possess the merit of longevity, they lack wisdom;
thus, they are unable to increase their cultivation of the practices of the Path. For this reason, the Buddhas are not born in that land, and the True Dharma does not exist there.
"Difficult to hear" (durlabha-śravaṇa) is so named because it is one of the eight difficulties (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa). As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:

"The three matters of Jambudvīpa are superior even to those of the heavens, let alone those of Uttarakuru. First, the ability to sever sexual desire; second, the power of mindfulness and recollection; third, the capacity for diligence.
For these reasons, the Buddhas appear only in Jambudvīpa. This brief summary provides the general outline to enable one to understand the four continents.
Regarding the characteristics of regions: if one wishes to explain them extensively, one should consult the sūtras and śāstras.
As for the statement that "the Buddha does not grant wishes that exceed human limits," what constitutes an exceeding wish? It is, for example, as when a king... [text fragment ends]
Regarding human laws: if there are requests made according to one's vows, the ritual must certainly not be violated. If one seeks wives, concubines, slaves, fields, or houses, these are all granted.

However, because the Buddha considers such things to be transgressions and not in accordance with the Dharma, he does not grant them; thus it is said that he does not grant improper wishes, but grants only those wishes that accord with the Dharma.
The country of Aṇapiṇḍa (also transcribed as Aṇagapiṇḍa; its etymological translation is uncertain).
The river Ajiravatī.
It is also called the Ajiravatī River. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) calls it the Aciravatī River;
in the language of Tang, this means "Unconquerable" (*Wusheng*). The older transcription as "Ailuo bati River" is erroneous. Other details are as in the account of the Council of Five Hundred.
The explanation of the term "City of Kuśī" is as follows.

Regarding the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-bath robe): it is so called because one bathes in heavy rain while wearing this garment; thus it is named the "rain-bath robe. The rest is as in the ninety matters.
Commentary on the Middle [Section].
△ The Twenty-eighth: Keeping an Urgently Offered Robe (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
King Prasenajit, also known as Boli-xian-ni; the *Xiyu ji* states that his correct name is *Bālāsena*, which in the language of Tang means "Victorious Army.
Master Jing translated it as "Victorious Light. The *Renwang jing* states: "This King Prasenajit has already..."
Ten thousand kalpas ago, during the Dharma of King Nāgaprabha Buddha, he was a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage (*caturthabhūmi*).

He rebelled—*fan* (pronounced *fǎn*, with the third tone) meaning to turn back or repeat; it signifies being contrary. He was disloyal—*pàn* (pronounced *bàn*, with the fourth tone) meaning to revolt.
"Sheng" (Sound/Name) means to rebel and act with overbearing arrogance (*hù*; *hù* is pronounced with the third tone; "bá-hù" carries the meaning of being violent and defiant).
*Li-shi-da-duo* (Liśidatta) and *Fu-na-lo* (Punara):

*Li-shi-da-duo* is translated here as "Bestowed by the Immortal" (*xiānshòu*), or alternatively as "Immortal Bestowal" (*xiānshī*), or also as "Immortal Remnant" (*xiányú*). This refers to one who follows an immortal.
This was because he sought to obtain a son from another person. Pūraṇa—also called Pūrṇa—is translated as "old acquaintance" or "long-standing friend.
He was the elder brother of Śakradatta. These two brothers were ministers of King Prasenajit;
in the kingdom of Kośala, their wealth was so vast that there was no one equal to them, and they were able [to serve] the Buddha.
...and the fourfold assembly shall all together enjoy it, without claiming it as "mine. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:

He himself said, "When King Prasenajit wished to enter the park for an excursion, he had me ride upon a great elephant with the foremost palace lady seated before me and another behind me, while I sat in the middle. When the elephant descended the slope, [the one] in front..."
Those in front embraced my neck, while those behind clung to my back. When the elephant ascended the slope, those behind embraced my nape and those in front clung to my collar.
Those court ladies, for the sake of entertaining the King, wore garments of fine silk and brocade, applied various exquisite perfumes, and were adorned with jeweled necklaces.
I traveled together with them, constantly guarding three matters: first, the driving of the elephant, fearing...
[He would] lose the right path. Second, he guards his own mind, fearing the arising of defiled attachment. Third, he guards his own integrity, fearing a fall into ruin.
At that time, I did not entertain improper thoughts regarding the king’s ladies for even a single moment.
The Buddha praised the elder: "Excellent, excellent! You are able to skillfully guard your mind. However, Pūraṇa is exclusively practicing the holy life."
Purity through freedom from desire; not clinging to perfumes or flowers; distancing oneself from all that is vulgar and base—these are the preeminence of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Līṣadatta, though not exclusively devoted to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), was contented and realized the Four Noble Truths—this is the preeminence of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Later, both passed away. The Buddha declared of these two persons: "One was preeminent in ethical discipline; the other was preeminent in wisdom. Both were equal in this regard.
They are born in a single realm, sharing the same mode of birth, and in a future life, they attain the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
They are born in Tuṣita Heaven and, returning once more to this world, bring an end to the limits of suffering. As stated in the *Guṇavat-sūtra*:
"Among those with faith, he who is able to possess great wisdom is the lay follower Upāsaka Śiṣyadatta; among those with faith, he who is able to maintain the holy life is..."
"Daśāha-upāsaka" means: an upāsaka (lay follower) who has ten days remaining—meaning that during the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*), it is not yet finished;
there are still ten days left before reaching the time for the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*).
This refers to the period from the sixth day of the seventh month until the fifteenth.

"Urgent robe-giving" (*ātyayika-cīvara*) means that when a donor (*dānapati*) encounters urgent or difficult circumstances, they offer robes to the community of monks (*saṃgha*) in order to seek merit and blessings. As it says:
When intending to set out on a military expedition, or when a woman is about to give birth—during such times as these, one gives. If this period has passed, one does not give again thereafter;
therefore, it is called "urgent robe-giving" (*ātyayika-cīvara*). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "There are five kinds of urgent robe-giving: giving when one has fallen ill oneself;
giving for the sake of a sick person; giving at the time of impending death; giving for the sake of a deceased person; and giving when about to depart. Sa...
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Whether it be a king who gives, a queen who gives, a prince who gives, or a high official or general who gives—
if they have a heart of faith and joy toward the Saṃgha and give material goods to the monks—

because such noble persons are difficult to encounter with a virtuous mind and difficult to see frequently, and because there may be other urgent causes and conditions, this is therefore called 'urgent robe-giving' (*ātyayika-cīvara*)."
If one does not accept it, the merit of the former person will not be realized and the Saṃgha will lose the robe; therefore, its acceptance is permitted.

If a woman, when about to be married and going to her husband’s house, gives property to the Saṃgha so that she may attain independence because she lacks it, or if a sick person gives property to the Saṃgha out of a virtuous mind, it shall benefit both the living and the deceased. As...
These are all termed "urgent robes for distribution. Once the Saṃgha has received the robes, they shall be divided according to seniority.
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If there are five kinds of urgent robes for distribution, they should be accepted and divided accordingly.

If a donor says, 'I wish to give this with my own hands,' it should be accepted even if the time limit has not yet arrived; there is no offense, provided that [the recipient] has already been appointed."
Regarding the person in charge of robes (*cīvaradhara*): if a donor says, "Please keep this robe until my return;

I shall offer it with my own hands," then it should not be divided. (The person in charge of robes refers to one person appointed by means of a formal motion and announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to serve as the guardian of the Sangha's clothing and requisites.

If, during the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), a lay donor (*dānapati*) offers robes to the Sangha, they should be entrusted to him for safekeeping. Once the retreat is concluded, the community of monks shall divide them among themselves.)

Regarding the time for keeping robes, one should keep two types of robes during the robe season, as explained previously in the commentary on the precept concerning robes exceeding one month. That is to say, these robes given in haste may be kept during two periods of the robe season:

either for fifteen days or until the end of the season. If [the period] exceeds this, the robe must be relinquished; otherwise, it should be purified (*pariśuddha*) or formally accepted (*parigṛhīta*).

If one does not relinquish it, does not purify it, and does not take formal possession of it, then upon reaching the sixteenth day at the appearance of the dawn light, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
With the exception of the ten-day urgent gift-cloth (*daśāha-ātyaya-dāna-cīvara*), all robes obtained during the rainy season retreat must await the time of the *pravāraṇā*.

If one divides [the robes] during the retreat, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If there remain nine days, or even down to one day, before the time of the *pravāraṇā*, and one receives an urgent gift-cloth, then beyond the two types of robe-periods, [it is an offense].
The sixteenth day. The number of days for reduction or increase is as clarified in the *Vinaya-mūla* (the Root Vinaya).

"Pravāraṇā" (Self-Indulgence) is also called "Suī" (At Will); this refers to performing the Pravāraṇā ceremony at the conclusion of the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*). Now, regarding the retreat...
There are two types. If one observes the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer) retreat, the fifteenth day of the seventh month is the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony;

if one observes the *paścimavārṣika* (late summer) retreat, the fifteenth day of the eighth month is the time for the *pravāraṇā*. The *Shishi Yaoyong Chao* states: "For ninety days, one cultivates the Way."

To refine body and mind, many people are deluded regarding themselves; they do not recognize their own faults. It is therefore appropriate to rely upon the pure assembly to bestow compassionate instruction.
One should freely declare one’s own transgressions and allow the monks to openly point out one’s errors. Thus, one’s inner lack of integrity is revealed and one’s outer flaws are made manifest.
Since body and speech are entrusted to others, it is called *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence). The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "Whenever the summer retreat has concluded..."
At the end of the year, this day should be called *suīyì* (following one's will). This means that, regarding the three matters, one may raise any issue at will;
it carries the sense of confessing offenses and eliminating transgressions. The old term *zìzì* (self-indulgence) is a literal translation of this meaning.
In Sanskrit it is called *pravāraṇā*, translated as "according to one's wish" (*suīyì*). It also carries the meaning of "satiety.
Furthermore, it refers to following the wishes of others by bringing forth the offenses one has committed. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* asks: "For what reason is the *pravāraṇā* performed?
It is so that the bhikṣus shall not be left alone; so that each may remember their own offenses and confess them with sincere words."

Because they have been subdued and attained purity, they naturally remember [their transgressions] with joy, as they are free from guilt. As for why this is established at the end of the summer retreat:

if one considers the beginning of the summer when the community first gathers, they set their intentions together and establish a solemn commitment for the ninety-day period to practice the path of renunciation in unison.

If one were to accuse another of a fault prematurely, there would likely be resentment and contention; these would then spread among one another, causing the abandonment of the Path and the disruption of spiritual practice. Therefore, [the rule is set for the end of the summer].

The regulations were established at the end of summer. One should undertake the practice in the third month; while residing together to advance in one’s studies, when the time has concluded, one should announce one’s departure.

Each person should then proceed according to their own direction. If there are necessarily unwholesome karmic actions, one must not proclaim them alone. Since the grave transgression of obstructing the Path admits of no concealment, it is necessary to request instruction;
this is precisely what is intended here. Therefore, the Vinaya permits the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) once the *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat) is completed; this is a matter of self-accusation.
To allow others to raise charges against one’s faults is not to act according to one's own self-will; such an act constitutes negligence. The *Zhihuachao* states:
"In various sūtras and vinayas, the sixteenth day of the seventh month is regarded as the year of birth for the bhikṣu’s fivefold dharma-body (pañca-dharmakāya).
Thus, the fifteenth day of the seventh month is the end of the year. When a bhikṣu leaves the secular world, he does not follow secular conventions.
The calculation is by years; it refers merely to the counting of *śīla-lakṣa* (rainy-season retreats). *Lakṣa* means "to join," signifying the transition between the old and the new.
29. Leaving One’s Robe for More Than Six Nights (This is a unique precept, as nuns do not have the rule regarding forest hermitages).
*Kārttika* was formerly translated as "Merit" (*guṇa*). According to the *Xiyuji*, it is translated as "Pleiades" (*mǎoxīng*), because the Pleiades constellation governs this month.
It refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month; this one-month interval is called the *Kārttika* month.

The Vinaya states: "When the three months of the summer retreat have ended, if one remains in an *āraṇya* (forest hermitage) for the final month of *kārttika* in a place where there is doubt or fear, this is called a person who observes the 'later' retreat (*paścimavarṣa*).
One must remain for the full month of *kārttika* in order to complete the year [of the rains retreat].
This does not mean that the month of *kārttika* has already passed. The *Nanshan Jieben* (Nanshan Code of Precepts) refers to the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

"Once it is full. This is an error, as it contradicts various Vinayas. Alternatively, the character "wei" (未) may have been omitted before the character "man" (滿). As the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"When three months have passed, but one has not yet reached eight months, one has not completed the year. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: [omitted].
"The three months of summer not yet being complete" refers to the period before the final month of the summer retreat. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The summer retreat lasts for three months;
it does not reach eight months. The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "After three months, during the final month, a bhikṣu may dwell in an open space."
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One should practice the latter *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) while staying in an *araṇya* (forest hermitage).
Based on this, it should be understood that those who undertake the latter *varṣā* must remain for this full month.

Furthermore, those who follow the assembly of the former *varṣā* must likewise remain for this full month after performing the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony) on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, so as to complete the ninety-day period.

If it is claimed that once the full moon of the month of Kārttika has passed, one may dwell in an araṇya (forest hermitage) and thus remain separated from one’s robes for eight months and six nights during the course of a year—excluding only the four months of the summer retreat—this is certainly not correct.

Due to various causes and conditions involving distressing matters, one may stay together for two nights out of compassion;

however, for the sake of protecting the Buddha-dharma, staying for a third night is not permitted. If one has already stayed together for more than two nights, on the third night, one must stay with a different person.

This constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika). Because it involves a continuous succession with a previous person, if one has stayed together for two nights and then moves to another location, and after staying there for one night returns to stay together again, there is no offense.
However, if it is with a eunuch or a hermaphrodite, staying together for one night is a minor offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
staying for more than two nights is an offense of falling (pāyattika).

first, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly; this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision."

Because the circumstances are identical, even when the Saṃgha has assembled, if there are women—whether many or few—and no wise man is present, [the teaching] must not be delivered.
However, it is permissible to preach the Dharma to nuns; since this is done for the sake of instructing the entire community of nuns according to the Dharma of exhortation, there is no fault.

The *Fajie Cidi* (Successive Order of the Dharma Realm) regarding the Five Precepts states: After the Buddha had conferred the Three Refuges upon his lay disciples, such as Trapusa and Bhallika, he immediately bestowed the Five Precepts upon them, making them *upāsakas*.
If a lay disciple of the Buddha violates these five precepts, they are no longer [a true disciple].
For laymen and laywomen of pure faith, the sutras therefore state: "The five precepts are the great prohibitions of the world.
If one violates the five precepts, in heaven one opposes the five stars; on earth one opposes the five sacred peaks; in the quarters one opposes the five emperors;
and in the body one opposes the five viscera. In this way, there are immeasurable violations of worldly order. If we consider the supramundane, violating [them]..."
The five precepts destroy the fivefold Dharma-body and all the Buddha-dharmas. Why is this so?

The five precepts are the root of the *śīla* (ethical discipline) for all Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. If one violates the five precepts, one may not receive the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna precepts again.
If one can uphold them firmly, they constitute the five great gifts. These five are collectively termed...

Regarding the precepts (*śīla*), their essential meaning is prevention. They are able to prevent the non-virtuous non-manifesting actions of improper discipline and to restrain the evils arising from the three types of action;
thus, they are called "prevention. First is the precept against killing. What is meant by "killing"?
It refers to when one truly knows that it is a sentient being, forms the intention to kill, takes its life, and subsequently initiates a manifest physical action.
This is called the transgression of killing. If one does not perform this act, it is called the precept of non-killing.

Other acts such as confinement, imprisonment, flogging, and so forth, are the preliminary means (*upāya*) to killing and are not the actual transgression itself. 2. The Precept of Non-stealing: What is called stealing?

Knowing that something belongs to another, giving rise to a thieving mind, taking the object and moving it from its original location, and considering the object as one's own—this is called stealing. If one does not...

To perform such an act is called the precept against stealing. Any other calculations, up to and including grasping with the hand or lifting [the object] off the ground, are the preliminary means (*upāya*) to theft, not the actual offense.
Third is the precept against sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*). What is called sexual misconduct?
If a woman is under the protection of her parents, brothers, sisters, husband, sons, or by worldly law, royal law, or a guardian—
[It is protected by] the protection of the precepts for those who have left the household life, and so forth, even down to one’s own wife who has received the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*).

[The same applies to intercourse with] one who is pregnant, one nursing an infant, or in a non-vaginal location; all eunuchs, men, spirits, animals, and so on—if one commits [the offense] with such as these, it is likewise [a transgression].
This is called sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*). If one does not perform such acts, it is called the precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct.

Other instances—such as flirtatious speech, making appointments by means of objects, or even holding hands and touching the body—all constitute sexual misconduct before the act of intercourse is consummated; these preparatory efforts (*prayoga*) are not the actual transgression.
The fourth is the precept against false speech (*anṛtavāda*). What is called false speech? It is when, with an impure mind, one desires to deceive.
To conceal the truth and utter deceptive words, thereby giving rise to verbal karma—this is called false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
To refrain from such an act is called the precept of abstaining from false speech. The offense of false speech arises from the mutual understanding of the sounds of one's words;

if there is no such understanding, although the words may be untrue, they are merely the preliminary means (*upāya*) to false speech and do not constitute the actual offense. Fifth, [the precept] against drinking intoxicants.
The Precept Against Alcohol. What is meant by "alcohol"? There are three kinds of alcohol: first, grain-based alcohol; second, fruit-based alcohol; and third, medicinal alcohol.
Whether dry or moist, turbid or clear—any such substance that can cause the human mind to become agitated and negligent, giving rise to the thirty-six faults.
To refrain from drinking these is called the precept against drinking alcohol. This...

Regarding these five precepts: the first four are *prakṛti* (intrinsic), while the last one is *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibitory). Prohibitory offenses are those that can be expiated through repentance;

intrinsic offenses are those that cannot be expiated. As stated in the *Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*: "As for intrinsic precepts, whether one has received them or not, they are both offenses."

This differs from other prohibitive precepts, such as the bhikṣu’s precept regarding grass and trees, where one incurs an offense if one has formally undertaken the vow, but does not incur an offense if one has not.
The *Chao* states: "Regarding natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), their nature is inherently good when observed and inherently evil when violated;
they do not acquire goodness or evil solely through the Buddha's injunctions. Therefore, when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world..."

One transforms people by means of this Dharma. If, after receiving the Buddha’s precepts, one commits an act such as killing, one incurs an additional offense of violating the regulations (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Therefore, it is said that whether one has received them or not, both [situations] constitute an offense. Regarding the precept against [harming] grasses and trees:
this is not prohibited at all; however, because non-Buddhists and laypeople believe that grasses and trees possess life, they see bhikṣus cutting or felling them and say:

Lacking a compassionate heart, [the Buddha] sought to quell the world's censure and thus established the precepts. Therefore, if a bhikṣu accepts them and then violates them, it constitutes an offense of transgressing the regulations.
Laypeople do not accept them; thus, if they violate them, there is no offense. Hence it is said that by not accepting them, one does not incur guilt.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-śāṭhyāyanīputra-sūtra* states: "Regarding all meritorious qualities and practices that assist the Path, to summarize the essentials..."

I shall speak of this. Taking the precepts as the foundation and upholding the precepts as the beginning—if one does not uphold the precepts, one will not even attain the body of a wild jackal afflicted with scabies and sores, let alone attain a body of merit.
You should know that because the precepts are pure, the lineage of the Buddha is not severed and one achieves equal and perfect enlightenment;
the lineage of the Dharma is not severed and one discerns the nature of phenomena; the lineage of the Sangha is not severed.
One cultivates the unconditioned path; because one maintains pure precepts in an uninterrupted succession, one’s merit is inexhaustible.

The *Upāsaka-śīla-varga* states: "If an upāsaka can wholeheartedly receive and maintain such precepts, this person is called a *puṇḍarīka* flower among upāsakas, a subtle and supreme fragrance among upāsakas."
A pure lotus among laymen (*upāsaka*), a genuine jewel among laymen, a true hero among laymen.
Good son, as the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas: the first is the householder.
Second is the renunciant. A renunciant bodhisattva is called a bhikṣu; a householder bodhisattva is called an upāsaka.
For a renunciant bodhisattva to uphold the monastic precepts is not difficult.
For a householder bodhisattva to uphold the lay precepts is indeed difficult. Why is this? Because a householder is entangled by many adverse conditions.
Because it is observed as a circumambulation (as detailed in the *Upāsaka-śīla-saṃgraha*, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, and other texts).

Regarding the method of the Eightfold Fasting Precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), various sūtras and śāstras refer to it either as the "Eightfold Fasting Precepts" (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*), the "Eightfold Precepts" (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), or simply the "Eight Precepts" (*aṣṭa-śīla*).
*Upavāsa*. It is also called the "Eightfold Dharma for Cultivating Merit. Although these names are not uniform, the precepts (*śīla*) are the same.
This means that the first eight dharmas are termed the "fasting" (*upavāsa*), while the final one—abstaining from eating at improper times—is termed the "observance" (*poṣadha*).

"Fasting" (*upavāsa*) refers to closing off the eight evils so that no transgressions arise; "observance" (*poṣadha*) takes the meaning of "leveling" or "aligning" with the midday meal. That is to say:
This prohibits the eight unwholesome deeds and causes one to cultivate the Middle Way. Furthermore, another explanation states: "Zhai" (齋) means "to align" (*qi*).
It refers to aligning the actions of body and speech. The *Fayuan* (法苑) says: "Zhai" means "alignment. This means prohibiting the six sense-faculties so as not to be defiled by the six sense-objects;
it is called "zhai" because one aligns the severance of all evils and fully cultivates all virtues. Thus, the essence of "zhai" and "jie" (precept) is one, though their names differ.
If one seeks the definitive essence [of these terms], their essences may differ slightly. "Upavāsa" (fasting) is defined by the name "not eating after midday.
"Śīla" (precept) has the meaning of "preventing what is wrong and ceasing evil. Thus, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The first eight are precepts; the ninth is fasting.
Because the fast and the precepts are counted together, there are nine. It is also called the "Eight-limbed Precepts" (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*). "Limbs" (*aṅga*) refers to constituent parts. Because...

These two are combined into one; therefore, they are called the eight branches (*aṣṭāṅga*). This means that abstaining from anointing with perfumes and wearing garlands, and abstaining from singing, dancing, and theatrical performances, both pertain to the category of adornment;
thus, they are established together as a single branch. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Now, the essence of the fast (*upoṣadha*) is non-eating after midday, which is supported by eight matters. The essence of the fast and these factors mutually sustain one another."

This is called the Dharma of the Eightfold Uposatha. Question: Within the eightfold restraint (*aṣṭāṅga-saṃvara*), how many are branches of ethical discipline (*śīlāṅga*), how many are branches of heedfulness (*apramādāṅga*), and how many are branches of seclusion (*vivekāṅga*)? Answer: Five are branches of ethical discipline, namely:
abstaining from taking life, up to abstaining from drinking intoxicants. One is a branch of heedfulness, namely: abstaining from eating at improper times. The remainder...

The second is the factor of distancing (*viveka-aṅga*). Furthermore, the first four are factors of ethical discipline (*śīla-aṅga*), because they involve abstaining from natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

The fifth is the factor of non-negligence (*apramāda-aṅga*); for even if one has received the precepts, if one drinks various intoxicants, the mind becomes negligent and one is unable to maintain protection.
The final three are factors of distancing, because they accord with the mind of weary detachment (*nirveda-citta*); through weary detachment, one is able to realize [the goal].
Because it is the fruit of restraint (*saṃvara*). By means of this one-day observance (*upavāsa*), there are eight branches:
three are added to the five, and one is subtracted from the ten, because two are combined into one and one is divided into two. Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* asks:
"For what reason are eight things correctly abandoned? It says: "These eight are the gateways; by means of these eight dharmas, one abandons all evil."
Among these, four are actual evils; drinking alcohol is the gateway to all evils; the remaining three are the causes and conditions for negligence.
For such a person to be free from these five kinds of evil is a cause and condition for merit; to be free from the remaining three is a cause and condition for the Path.

Furthermore, this is the precept that possesses five kinds of purity: first, practicing the ten paths of wholesome action; second, severing all sufferings of the past and future; third, [the third point].
One is not troubled by an evil mind. Fourth, one guards it through mindfulness. Fifth, one dedicates the merit toward *nirvāṇa*.
If one can observe the fast in this manner, even the four great treasuries of jewels cannot equal even a fraction of its value, nor can the karmic rewards of a heavenly king surpass it.
Therefore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to obtain the eight precepts..."

The Eightfold Fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*). Those who are free from all suffering shall exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) and enter the city of Nirvāṇa; one should therefore seek skillful means to accomplish these eight fasts.
The honorable positions among humans are not worthy of being esteemed as noble, and the pleasures of the heavens are beyond measure.

One who seeks unsurpassed merit should seek this fast. If one wishes to be born in the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one must observe this fast.

O Celestial Beings, one who observes this fast shall attain their wishes: whether they seek the rank of a Heavenly King of the first, second, third, or fourth direction, or the position of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), they shall achieve that vow.
Whether they seek the vehicle of the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha-vehicle, all their vows shall be fulfilled.
I have now achieved success through the observance of these precepts; by means of the eightfold fast and the ten wholesome actions, there is no wish that is not obtained.

Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "If there is a person who takes four great treasuries filled with the seven precious jewels and offers them as a gift to others, the merit obtained by that person does not equal that of another person who observes the eight precepts for one day and one night.

[The former] eliminates all five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*) so that they are entirely extinguished; this results in immeasurable karmic rewards, culminating in the unsurpassed [enlightenment]."
[This refers to] the bliss [of nirvāṇa]. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "Between the five precepts and the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), which is superior?

It answers: "Due to specific causes and conditions, the two sets of precepts are equal. However, the five precepts are maintained for a lifetime, whereas the eight precepts are maintained for one day.

Furthermore, in the case of the five precepts, the duration is long but the number of rules is few; in the case of the one-day precepts, the duration is short but the number of rules is many. If there were no...
The Great Mind: though one might observe [the precepts] for the rest of one's life, it is not equal to observing them with the Great Mind for a single day.
It is like a weakling serving as a general; though he may lead troops for his entire life, he ultimately achieves no fame or merit.

If, however, a hero exerts himself, the calamity and disorder are immediately settled; with the merit of a single day, his name covers the whole world. Comparing the Eight Precepts to other precepts, it is likewise so.
It is so. Regarding the characteristics of the precepts herein, the first five are identical to what is explained in the context of the five precepts;
they differ only in that while the five precepts merely abstain from sexual misconduct, these require the complete cessation of all lewdness and promiscuity.

As for the latter three precepts—refraining from wearing garlands of fragrant flowers and refraining from anointing the body with perfumes—this means not using various flowers as garlands nor using incense as powder.
Regarding "anointing, perfuming, wearing ornaments, and adorning oneself with garments and accessories":
this means not personally practicing singing, dancing, or performing various musical entertainments, nor watching or listening when others perform them.
Regarding "not sitting on high, broad, or large beds": this means not sitting on beds that exceed the prescribed limits or are elaborately decorated and adorned.
Regarding "seats" and so forth, as stated in the *Āgama Sūtras*: "A high, wide, and large bed" refers to one where the legs are sixteen inches long—this is not "high";

four feet wide—this is not "wide"; and eight feet long—this is not "large. Only when exceeding these measurements is it termed a "high, wide, and large bed. Furthermore, there are eight types of beds;
the first four are distinguished by their material and are considered precious, such that it is improper to sit upon them. The latter four...

Distinguishing the "great" according to persons: even if one were to spread out the ground as a seat for a person of honor, it is still improper to sit upon a single gold bed, a silver bed, an ivory bed, a horned bed, a Buddha’s bed, a Pratyekabuddha’s bed, an Arhat’s bed, or a teacher-monk’s bed.
Regarding "not eating at improper times," this means not consuming food after midday.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "These eight precepts are called the *upavāsa-saṃvara* (the discipline of near-dwelling).

They are termed 'near-dwelling' because one dwells near the Arhats by receiving this discipline and training in accordance with them. Some say they are called 'near-dwelling' because they dwell near the lifelong precepts (*yāvaj-jīva-śīla*).
Others call them 'nourishing' (*puṣṭi*), for they nourish the roots of goodness of householders and cause them to draw near to renunciation.
Because the roots of goodness of the household remain. Question: How is the near-dwelling restraint (upavāsa-saṃvara) obtained? Answer: It is obtained from the instruction of another;
that is, following the teacher’s instruction, one personally utters sincere words and receives it with reverence. Furthermore, as for the one who receives the restraint:

One must follow the teacher’s words and speak exactly as the teacher speaks; only then can one receive [the precepts]. If one speaks first oneself, or speaks simultaneously with the teacher, the discipline (vinaya) will not be obtained.
Question: What kind of clothing and ornaments should one wear when receiving this discipline? Answer:
One receives this discipline (*saṃvara*) by wearing the clothes and ornaments that one habitually uses;

however, if they are intended merely for temporary adornment of the body, they must be discarded before receiving this precept. One should understand that the same principle applies to items such as beds and seats.
When receiving [the precepts], the duration should be exactly one day and night, neither more nor less; that is, at the time of dawn, from the teacher.

It is received. Upon reaching the dawn of the following day, the discipline (*vinaya*) is then relinquished. Question: If one receives this precept after midday, does one still obtain the precept? Answer:
One should say that it is not obtained, except in cases where there was a prior commitment for the eighth day of the month and so forth.

He constantly observes the fast and precepts. Due to other circumstances, he does not remember [the precepts] before midday; it is only after eating that he remembers them and feels deep shame and remorse.
If he then invites a precept master and receives them according to the Dharma, he may indeed obtain them. These precepts should be received from one of the seven classes of practitioners;
they can be obtained from any of them, but not from elsewhere. Why is this? Because if one lacks the lifelong precepts, they are incapable of [acting as a precept master].
Regarding the precept master, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "As for the method of receiving the fast (*upoṣadha*), it must necessarily be received from another.

From whom should one receive it? From among the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*). Furthermore, it says that if there is no one present to receive it from, one may simply perform mental recollection and verbal declaration, taking refuge in the Triple Gem and saying, 'I uphold the eight precepts,' and this is likewise permissible.
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* also states: "If there is no one present, one should simply perform mental recollection."

He speaks thus: "I shall observe the eight precepts," and so forth. Based on this intention of receiving the precepts, it is permitted to receive them by oneself if no teacher is present; however, if a teacher is nearby...

If one conceives a mind of pride and does not go to receive [the precepts] from another, but receives them by oneself, one does not obtain the precepts. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "If one is not respectful, the restraint (*saṃvara*) is not produced. This must be received from a teacher; there is no room for self-reception.

Furthermore, later on, if one encounters conditions for violating the precepts, it is because of shame toward the precept-teacher that one is able to avoid transgression. If one does not receive them according to the Dharma in this manner, only a sublime conduct (*kuśalacaryā*) is produced, but the restraint is not produced. Having received the eight precepts:
If one lashes or strikes sentient beings, the fast is not pure; even if one does not lash them on that very day, if one intends to lash them the following day, it is likewise not pure.
To state the essential point: if one’s body or speech acts lack dignified decorum, the fast is not pure even if the formal precepts have not been broken.
Furthermore, even if body and speech are pure, if the mind gives rise to thoughts of greed, sensual desire, or anger, [the fast is not pure].

Thoughts of malice and harm are also called impurity of the fast (*upoṣadha*). Even if the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are pure, if one does not cultivate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), it is also called impurity of the fast.
Having received the eight precepts, to cultivate the six recollections with diligence is called purity of the fast.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "The discipline of the one-day vow (*upavāsa-saṃvara*) may consist of either the fundamental paths of action (*mūla-karmapatha*)..."

The fundamental [precepts] are pure, whereas the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are impure. For example, when one who possesses mastery receives this discipline (*saṃvara*), there may be a cook who intends to kill living beings for their food.
That person then says: "I have now received the precepts; I must not take life.
Leave it until tomorrow to be killed for my meal. This applies equally to acts such as execution and the like. This is what is meant by [the distinction between the pure and the impure].

The fundamental courses of action (*maula-karmapatha*) are pure, while the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*) are impure. The Blessed One has said that although the precepts one has undertaken constitute a superior action, they do not yield a great fruit.
Alternatively, there are cases where both the fundamental courses of action are pure and the preliminary stages are also pure.
Yet they are harmed by evil discursive thoughts—namely, discursive thoughts of sensual desire, discursive thoughts of ill will, and discursive thoughts of harm.
The Blessed One has said that although the precepts one has undertaken are indeed superior karma, they do not yield great fruit.

There may be cases where both the fundamental paths of action are pure and the proximate stages are also pure, such that one is not harmed by evil discursive thoughts, yet [the practice] is not fully encompassed.
The cultivation of right mindfulness refers to the six recollections: the recollection of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, ethical discipline (*śīla*), renunciation (*tyāga*), and the devas.

The World-Honored One has taught that although the ethical discipline one undertakes is a superior action, it does not necessarily yield a great fruit; for there may be cases where the fundamental courses of action (*karmapatha*) are pure.
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are also pure; they are not impaired by unwholesome discursive thoughts (*vitarka*).

While they maintain right mindfulness, they do not dedicate [the merit] toward liberation—meaning, for instance, seeking rebirth in heaven or the pleasures of desire—and thus observe the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*).

The Blessed One has said that although the precepts observed therein constitute superior karma, they do not yield great fruit. This is provided that the fundamental paths of action (*mūlakarmapatha*) are pure.
...up until the dedication toward liberation. The World-Honored One has taught that the precepts one receives are a distinguished karma capable of yielding great fruit.

From this, one should know that according to the superiority or inferiority of the mind, the retribution obtained will differ. Therefore, one should resolve upon the Great Mind (mahācitta) in order to seek supreme fruit.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, after receiving the precepts, one makes a vow, saying: "I, [Name], having received and practiced the Eight..."
Observing the precepts and following the training of all Buddhas is called *poṣadha*. I vow that by means of this merit, I shall not fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions.

Furthermore, I do not seek the pleasures of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) or a Brahmā king within the world. I vow to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*), attain *sarvajñatā*, and accomplish the path of Buddhahood.

(*Poṣadha* means "dwelling together" in the language of Qin; it is also called "pure dwelling" in the language of the heavens, or "progress" in human speech, and is also termed "nurturing. It refers to the path and...)

In the mundane world, both [the ordinary person and the practitioner] receive and practice the training, which consists of purifying body, speech, and mind, abiding according to the precepts. *Sarvajñā* (薩雲若) is translated in the Qin language as "the aspect of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*). Because it is the cause, it is called *prajñā*; because it is the fruit, it is called *sarvajñā*.
Furthermore, in the *Sūtra on the Eightfold Cultivation of Merit*, one makes this vow: "I uphold the practice of the precepts to adorn my own mind and cause it to rejoice.
I shall extensively cultivate all corresponding and superior practices, seeking the fruit of Buddhahood until it is ultimately perfected."
Furthermore, he spoke these verses:

"I have generated the supreme, non-dual mind; For the sake of all sentient beings, as an uninvited friend, I shall practice the excellent conduct of the path to supreme enlightenment, To become a Buddha and bring vast benefit to the world."

"By virtue of this wholesome karma, may I, in this very life, before long attain perfect enlightenment and preach the Dharma for the benefit of the world, liberating sentient beings from the suffering of the three realms of existence.
The *Āgama* states: The Buddha told the upāsaka, "On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month..."
One should go to where an elder bhikṣu resides and receive each of the eight precepts one by one;
receiving them one by one, do not allow the sequence to be lost. The *Upāsaka-śīla-varga* states:

"If an upāsaka, having already undertaken the observance of the precepts, is unable to observe the eight precepts for six days within a single month to make offerings to the Triple Gem, that upāsaka incurs a loss."

Regarding mental transgressions: do not give rise to them, and do not fall into decline. Impurity arises from intentional action (on the third day of the waxing moon and the third day of the waning moon—these together are called the "six days"—one should observe the eight precepts as detailed in the *Essentials of the Refuges and Precepts* and other sources;
these are not set forth here at length).
The Eightfold Noble Path is also called the Eightfold Right Path, as explained in detail in the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on the Ordination Rite).
The ten unwholesome courses of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*).
They are also called the ten unwholesome dharmas (*daśākuśala-dharma*). The *Fajie Cidi* states: "Unwholesome" takes the meaning of being contrary to principle;

these ten all arise in contravention of principle, and are therefore called unwholesome. They are also called the ten unwholesome paths (*daśākuśala-mārga*), because they lead to retribution of suffering and are thus not wholesome paths.
First is killing (*prāṇātipāta*), which means the taking of the lives of all sentient beings.
1. Killing: This is called taking life. 2. Stealing: This refers to seizing the property of others;
therefore, it is called stealing. 3. Sexual misconduct: This refers to engaging in sexual acts with those who are not one’s wife or concubine; therefore, it is called sexual misconduct. 4. Lying:
This refers to deceiving others with one’s speech; therefore, it is called lying. 5. Divisive speech: This refers to inciting strife.
To speak words that cause others to be divided and lead them to discordant gains and losses is called *paiśunya* (slanderous speech).
Sixth is *pāruṣya* (harsh speech): to address others with evil words so as to cause them distress is called harsh speech. Seventh is *saṃbhinnapralāpa* (frivolous speech):
to use artfully adorned and pleasing words that deviate from reason is called frivolous speech. Eighth is *abhidhyā* (covetousness)...
1. Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*): This refers to the greedy attachment to and longing for objects that accord with one's inclinations, such that the mind knows no satisfaction;

this is called sensual desire. 9. Ill will (*vyāpāda*): This refers to the arising of anger and resentment toward objects that conflict with one's inclinations and do not accord with one's own wishes;
this is called ill will. 10. Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): This refers to the denial of cause and effect and the practice of a path of wrong views, such that the mind lacks correctness.
Faith is called wrong view. As the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"At the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Great Heavenly Wheel-turning Sage King (*cakravartin rāja*) who possessed long life and freedom from illness, ruling according to the True Dharma.

His descendants succeeded one another, holding the position of Wheel-turning Sage King for eighty-four thousand years until the lineage of virtuous seeds was never severed. This was the final Sage King."
His name was Rintshi. He also transformed the world through the True Dharma and delighted in giving. He had a crown prince named Zenjin.
At a later time, the king entrusted the affairs of state to the crown prince, then shaved off his hair and beard, left the household life to study the Way, and cultivated the four Brahma-vihāras:
loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. When his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven. As for that King Zenjin—

They did not inherit their fathers' vocations, and the True Dharma declined and fell into ruin. Consequently, the people became short-lived, their complexions grew pale, they lacked strength, were plagued by many illnesses, and were devoid of wisdom;

they further fell into poverty and destitution. Driven by desperation, they resorted to theft and mutual entanglement. Because of this taking of what was not given, the King issued a decree to execute them.
When the people heard that the King would invariably put them to death for taking what was not given, they all detested that evil and each strove to acquire wealth.
The sword. The sword is fashioned from this; by means of it, killing arises. From this, two evils emerge. Furthermore, one commits adultery with another’s wife, and the husband quarrels with him.
He says of himself, "I did not do it," and thus four evils are formed. Sowing discord with double-tongued speech constitutes the fifth evil.
Quarreling leads to mutual abuse, which is the sixth evil. Speech that does not reach sincerity constitutes [the seventh evil].
The seventh evil is to envy the harmony between others. This constitutes the eighth evil. To harbor resentment such that one's facial expression changes is the ninth evil.
For the mind to be clouded by doubt and confusion is the tenth evil. Due to the root of these ten evils, external things decline and waste away; how much more so internal dharmas!
That is to say, as a retribution for killing, the lifespan of sentient beings becomes extremely short; as a retribution for taking what is not given...

Therefore, sentient beings are born into poverty and low status due to the retribution of sexual misconduct; the family members of sentient beings are not chaste and virtuous due to the retribution of false speech;
and the breath of sentient beings is foul and unpleasant, failing to be fresh and clean, due to the retribution of frivolous speech.

It causes the earth to become uneven; this is due to the retribution for divisive speech (*paiśunya*). Thorns and brambles grow upon the ground; this is due to the retribution for harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).

Speech becomes manifold and discordant; this is due to the retribution for envy (*īrṣyā*). It results in the failure of crops to ripen in abundance; this is due to the retribution for malice and harm (*vyāpāda*).
It causes all external things to wither and decline, let alone internal things. One should therefore mindfully abandon these ten [unwholesome paths of action].
The dharmas of evil. To practice the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśa-kuśala-dharma*).

The ten wholesome dharmas are the opposite of the aforementioned ten unwholesome dharmas; they are thus called the ten wholesome dharmas, or alternatively, the ten wholesome paths (*daśa-kuśala-mārga*). Tiantai says:

The ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) are of two kinds: first, abstention (*virati*); second, practice (*caryā*). Abstention consists merely in ceasing prior unwholesome acts and not harming others.

Practice consists in cultivating superior virtues and bringing benefit and happiness to all. These two are collectively termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*). "Wholesome" takes the meaning of "conforming to principle" (*yathārtha-anuloma*);
because it quiets perversion and returns to the truth, it is called "conforming to principle. Abstention, therefore, quiets the grave perversions of evil.
When practiced, they gradually lead one toward the goodness of the supreme path; therefore, both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) are termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
Alternatively, they are designated with the name "the Path" (*mārga*), because they are able to lead one to the fruit of ultimate bliss. As stated in the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above*, the Buddha said:
"After my parinirvāṇa, if the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings wish to be reborn in the fourth heaven, they should for one day, or even up to seven days, focus their minds..."
One should mindfully recollect those devas, uphold the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, contemplate the ten wholesome actions, and practice the path of the ten wholesome deeds.

By dedicating these merits, one makes the vow to be born before Maitreya Buddha; by recollecting this, one will be reborn there accordingly. As for the mention of "seven days," this is spoken merely from the perspective of the near term;
if even this can induce rebirth in that heaven, how much more so will one who does so throughout an entire lifetime surely attain it. Thus says the *Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra*.

There are those who receive the dharma of the ten wholesome paths. These are not set forth in detail here. (The fourth heaven is named Tuṣita Heaven. It is there that Maitreya Bodhisattva teaches and transforms the devaputras.
If one is born in that place, one will immediately become non-retrogressive.)

● Vinaya Piṭaka, Volume Twelve △ Digging the Earth,
Number Ten (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
Regarding "ground already dug" and "ground not yet dug":
"ground already dug" refers to ground that has previously been excavated, where insect species have dispersed and grasses and trees no longer grow;
thus it is called "already dug ground," which in meaning is termed "unproductive ground. "Ground not yet dug" refers to ground that has not yet been...

Because it has not been dug, it is called "undug ground. Alternatively, even if it was previously dug, if four months have passed and it has been saturated by rainwater such that insects, grasses, and trees have regrown as they were before, it is again termed "undug ground. In meaning, this is called "native soil" (*jāti-bhūmi*).
As stated in the *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā*: "Native soil refers to that which has never been dug; or, if it was previously dug, it has been moistened by rain."

If it remains moistened by rain for three months, this is called "land where [plants] grow. If there is no rain or moisture, yet it remains moistened by water for six months, this is also called "land where [plants] grow.
Other than this, it is not "land where [plants] grow. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In lands with heavy rainfall..."
In the eighth month, the earth gives birth [to plants]. In lands with little rain, the earth gives birth in the fourth month. Excluding these times is called "non-arising ground.
The Sarvāstivādins say: "The fourth and eighth months are the rainy season; the earth is continuous and its moist power permeates it, enabling grasses and trees to grow.
Therefore, by definition, these are 'arising grounds. At other times, when there is no rain, the sun scorches the land until it is parched, and the wind..."
The wind blows up the soil, yet no grass grows; therefore, its meaning is named "the ground of non-arising" (*ajātabhūmi*).

Furthermore, regarding "the ground of arising," the Hu-ben (Hui-lin’s version) states it is "the real ground" (*bhūtā bhūmiḥ*), while "non-arising" is stated to be "the unreal ground. The *Sudarśana* [Vinaya] states: "the true ground and the non-true ground."
As for "true ground," it is that which is free from sand, stones, and gravel, consisting purely of earth; this is called true ground.
As for "not true ground," it is that which abounds in sand, stones, and gravel with little earth; this is called not true. If the ground has been scorched by fire, it is also called not true ground.
If the ground contains sand and stones, how can one know whether it may be excavated? One should take a small amount of soil and [test it] with water.
Examine it closely. If four parts are stone and one part is soil, it may be dug. If there is soil on top of the stone four inches thick and it is dry, it may be taken.
If rain has already fallen for four months, it must not be taken (even if the stone constitutes four parts, it may be dug provided there are certainly no insects or grass).
*Jué* (钯): pronounced *jué* (with the *qiu* and *fú* initials; a *kuāng* rhyme in the entering tone). It refers to a large hoe. *Zuó* (斵): pronounced *zuó* (with the *zhú* and *jué* initials).
It means to pare or shave. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To hew or chop."
*Ken* (sickle) means "to cut with force. Its pronunciation is *ken*. It is as the ancients said: "The new moon resembles a whetted sickle. This refers to pinching and wounding [the fingernails].

[The character] is pronounced with the initial *qia* (from *ku* and *qia*) and carries the sound of an embedded [nail]. It means to prick with the claws. The original form was 掐 (*qiā*), but it was erroneously written as 掐 (*qiā*).
[The latter] is pronounced with the initial *táo* (from *tāo*) and does not have this meaning.
"To know it and to see it;

to know it and to see it"—this is the pure expression. That is to say, when a bhikṣu wishes to take something, he should cause that attendant (kappiya-kāraka) to know for himself and see for himself what is to be dug up and where it is to be placed. However, this is the rule for bhikṣus.
One must not speak directly, saying "dig this" or "place this. Therefore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If a bhikṣu requires anything, he says to the *kappiya-kāraka* (the attendant): 'You know this. If he does not understand, he speaks again, saying: 'Look at this.
If he still does not understand, he speaks again, saying: 'I need this. If he still does not understand, he speaks again, saying: 'Give me this. [The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* also says...]

The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: Whenever one wishes to take vegetables, grass, or soil, one should speak from a distance, saying, "There is something good at such-and-such a place; bring it here purified.
If one goes to the edge and points it out, one commits an offense.
△ Chapter Eleven: Destroying the Village of Ghosts and Spirits (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
The Village of Ghosts and Spirits.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Preta" means "fearful. This refers to those who are timid and full of dread.

It also means "majestic," for they can cause others to stand in awe of their majesty. Furthermore, it says that "preta" means "one who seeks," because these hungry ghosts constantly seek food and drink from others to sustain their lives.
"Śrī" (Spirit) means "capability. Those of great power are capable of moving mountains.

Reclamation of land. Those of lesser power can manifest and conceal themselves through transformations. A "village" (*grāma*) refers to a gathering; all ghosts and spirits dwell by relying upon trees, just as humans have villages.
Those with merit and spiritual power are called "gods" (*deva*); those without merit and who are dull-witted are called "ghosts" (*preta*).
Furthermore, those with merit rely on large trees, while those without merit rely on small trees, even down to medicinal herbs. [Thus ends the] Precept.
The *Nidāna-saṃyukta* states: There is a spirit that dwells in the roots of a tree; there is a spirit that dwells in the branches of a tree;

there is a spirit that dwells within the bark of a tree; there is a spirit that dwells within the fissures of the bark; there is a spirit that dwells in the buds of a tree; and there is a spirit that dwells in the leaves of a tree.
There are spirits who dwell upon the flowers of trees, and spirits who dwell upon the fruits of trees; indeed, all medicinal herbs, shrubs, and trees possess spirits.
The reason these spirits dwell there is that they consume their fragrance. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"As for the ghosts who dwell beneath trees, it is because they saw people planting trees to provide shade for others, yet with an evil mind they cut them down to take the timber."

Because they were used [for fire], they fell among the trees and are constantly afflicted by cold and heat (this too is but one retribution; it is not the case that all those who cut down trees with an evil mind fall among the trees).
Regarding "destroying a village," the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "Destroying" is a general term for twisting, pulling, uprooting, digging, cutting off, and inflicting injury.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "I shall now explain the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu engaged in construction."

Regarding this: whenever a person appointed for a task intends to fell a tree for the purpose of construction, seven or eight days prior, they shall establish a maṇḍala beneath that tree, arrange incense and flowers, provide various sacrificial offerings, and recite the Three-Part Sūtra (Tri-saraṇa-gāthā).
The senior bhikṣus should perform the *te-khi-na* (tikīṇa) incantation and blessing, proclaim the ten paths of wholesome action, and praise virtuous deeds.
Furthermore, they should announce: "If there are devas who have long resided in this tree, you should seek another place to dwell.
This tree is now for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha Jewel; after seven or eight days have passed, [the construction] shall proceed."
One should cut them down. However, if at the time of felling a tree some unusual sign appears, one should praise the merit of giving and renunciation and explain the faults of stinginess and greed.
If the sign still appears, one must not cut it down; but if there is no such special sign, one may proceed.
"You should cut it down. If a bhikṣu engaged in construction does not act in accordance with my regulations, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharma-āpatti).
As stated above, if no other signs appear, cutting it down is permitted; however, this must always be done by a lay agent, and not by the bhikṣu himself.
The *Pañcaśata-praśna* states: "A bhikṣu may personally cut trees or dig the earth to construct a stūpa or monastery for the Buddha."
"And as for creating images [of the Buddha], is there merit? He replied, "One will still not escape the great suffering of punishment in hell;

how could there be any merit? This is because one has fundamentally violated the precepts. (Maṇḍala—this is translated as *tán* [altar]. *Tarkyaṇa* means the act of offering ritual objects; it is also a verse of offering.
The verse appears in the phrase concerning the discarding and washing of bowl-water among the "one hundred matters" that follows. It is manifested by this mantra.)
Ārdraka-sudṛśa is said to be yellow ginger (haridrā). Uśīra—
Some call it *uśīra*, which here means "root of *máoxiāng* (cyperus grass). The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that this is the name of a cooling medicinal herb.
The *Samantapāsādikā* says that *uśīra* is *xiāngfú* (the sound *fú* is pronounced as *fú*). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* calls it *xiāngfùzǐ* (nutgrass root).
[The characters] *wě* and *yōu* are identical in their Sanskrit pronunciation.

lukkha is... [the resin of the *śallakī* tree].

*Tuólóulóu*;
