*Mao-liao* (hairy dockweed) does not die at its roots in winter; there is hair on its leaves. There are also *bai-liao*, *hong-liao*, *xiang-liao*, and *he-liao*.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śīla-saṃgraha*, *liao*, indigo, *luole*, and coriander are called "self-falling seeds," because they are obtained through their own natural falling.
Because they grow from what has been split open, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* designates them as "splitting seeds," such as coriander, dill, and so forth;

this is because the sprouts emerge only after the seed has been split open. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, basil and *mālatī* (blue flax) are called "heart-born seeds" because they are produced from the heart [of the plant].
When purifying these, if one uses the hand to rub and crush them, it is considered purified.
The *pūtila* species are those that grow from the void; this refers to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, lotus roots, *uṇḍuka* (water-cress), and other things that grow from the void.
Other Vinayas classify sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and lotuses under the category of "knot-born seeds" (*parvaja-bīja*), as they all propagate from their joints.

They are able to grow. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The *huìzǐ* (the character is read as *jié*, but pronounced *jiē*; it refers to the *bójié* jujube, the *zǎo* date, the *lí* plum, and their like) produces seeds, and these seeds in turn produce further seeds.
This is what is meant. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "This refers to rice, wheat, barley, various beans, and mustard."

...and so forth. These various types of seeds are called "seed from a child" (*putra-bīja*) because they arise from a child. The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "Seeds different from a child" refers to grains such as rice and wheat;

that is to say, these are seeds of a different species from the child. Another explanation is that grains such as rice and wheat produce sprouts only after their husks have split open, and thus they are categorized as "seeds that split open.
As for those seeds different from a child, it is like the horn of a cow, which is capable of [producing a calf].
Reeds and the like grow [from such causes], or perhaps green sprouts grow from sheep’s wool, and blue lotuses grow from a heap of cow dung.
When things arise from dissimilar origins, they are called "seeds of different offspring. Therefore, the treatise says:
"If a thing arises from a similar cause, it is like rice arising from rice, or barley arising from barley; if a thing arises from a dissimilar cause, it is like planting ox-hair upside down. Thus...
There is the *pu* plant; it grows from seeds and sprouts from reeds. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "By what causes and conditions do five types of seeds appear in the world?
A great chaotic wind blows the five seeds from the world of *Abhavya* (the Indestructible) and brings them here to grow in this land;
thus, the five seeds emerge in the world. The *Lokotpatti-sūtra* says: "At that time, there was the *Anabhi*..."
A great wind arises from another world-system currently in the stage of formation and abiding; it blows five kinds of seeds and scatters them throughout this world-system.
Having scattered them once, it scatters them again, and so on until they are widely scattered—namely, root-seeds up to seed-seeds.
These constitute the five types of seeds (in this region, cow dung produces only green fungi and does not give rise to lotuses).
*Hei piao*:
"piao" is pronounced with the third tone (rising tone). It refers to a bluish-white color. The *Shiming* states that it is a light blue color.
If one brushes it...
[The character is pronounced] with the *bei* (北) radical and the final *mo* (末) tone;
it is a voiced aspirated consonant (*pan* [般]). It means to twist open. △ Twelfth:
Annoying Others with Discordant Speech (This is a shared precept; for nuns, it is likewise prescribed).

"Eating in a single sitting" means that a bhikṣu who has undertaken the dhūta practices does not eat repeatedly, nor does he take morning meals and so forth, but accepts only the practice of eating in a single sitting.
Within that single sitting, he eats until he is fully satisfied; there is no further sitting for food. Even if he has not yet reached full satisfaction [within that sitting], [he must not rise].
Regarding those who eat from a single sitting due to specific causes and conditions: they likewise do not sit down again to eat, and are thus called "those who eat from a single sitting.

As for "eating leftover food without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (formal ritual)," this refers to when a bhikṣu has finished eating the formal meal (*prāsaṅgika-bhojana*) and there is still some remaining food, or food sent by a donor.
If it is not yet past midday, and a bhikṣu has not yet finished eating, or has already finished eating but wishes to eat more,
he should take that food to another bhikṣu who has not yet finished eating, or to one who has finished eating but has not yet risen from his seat.

To renounce craving is true joy; to subdue the conceit of "I am" is the supreme joy.
Cūḷapanthaka heard this verse from afar and immediately attained the fruit of arhatship. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"The elder brother gave him a single verse, which he could not master after four months of recitation. His brother rebuked him and expelled him. At that time, the World-Honored One saw him weeping and took pity on him;
using his supernatural powers, he transformed the verse he was reciting and taught it to him anew. He mastered it instantly."
After four months of diligent service, he was further granted the *Vimala-gāthā* (Verses on the Removal of Dust and Defilement), and was told:
"Whenever a bhikṣu comes from outside today, you must wipe away all the dust and defilement upon his leather sandals.
Kṣullaka respectfully assented and wiped them as instructed; one sandal became perfectly clean, while the other, despite being scrubbed with great effort, would not.
He thought: "Even external objects, when stained by dust and grime for a mere moment, cannot be cleansed;

how much less so the internal stains of greed, hatred, and delusion, which have defiled the mind throughout the long night? By what means can these be purified? While he was reflecting thus, [he attained purification].
The contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) then appeared before him, and he immediately attained the fruit of arhatship in due order.
Question: For what reason was the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka so utterly dark? Answer:

Venerable Cūḍapanthaka, in the past, during the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha, had fully mastered and upheld that Buddha’s Tripiṭaka; however, because of the defilement of stinginess regarding the Dharma (*dharmamātsarya*), it obscured his [understanding].
In the past, he never taught others the texts or explained their meanings, and he neglected and forgot the principles [he had learned].
Due to that karma, he has now obtained such an extremely dull-witted result. Some say that the Venerable One was once a pork-butcher in the city of Vārāṇasī;
he bound the mouths of five hundred pigs and transported them on a boat to the other shore, and then disembarked them.
At that time, because his breath was obstructed, the pig died. Due to the power of that karma, he became so dull-witted.
Some say that in a previous life, that venerable one had once blocked the entrance to a *gūḍha* (boar) cave, preventing the animal from escaping.
He died while still in the womb. Due to that karma, he was thus dull-witted. Furthermore, various sūtras state that the Buddha said:
"In the past, the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka studied the sūtras for twenty-four years and mastered only five verses.
Yet, he understood them deeply and felt no distress. Why was this? Because in his previous lives, he had encountered five hundred Buddhas. All [of these were due to his past roots of virtue]."

This is notified in various sutras: if one merely conceals the path of the scriptures and refuses to teach others, yet later suffers from illness for twenty-four days and only upon the brink of death feels remorse, calling out to others to teach them—this constitutes a single merit.

If even this five-word [instruction] yields such results according to what is known, how much more so when teaching others in full; the merit obtained would be incalculable. Thus is the distinction of merits explained.
The treatise states: "This bhikṣu was able to conceal his form and transform it so that he did not appear; therefore, he is called the foremost.
(Although what has been said above is not uniform, there is no one among men who, throughout many lifetimes, has not acted in this way.)
The Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī is explained as in the section on *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* [offenses]. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣuṇī, who has long practiced the life of renunciation and is honored by kings, is Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. (Gautamī)
"Mī" (彌) is her family name.
Bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā is also called Caṃmā;
this translates as "Peaceful Security" (An-yǐn). It is also rendered as "Patient Practice" (Rèn-xíng). She was the daughter of King Prasenajit. Formerly...
King Prasenajit and King Brahmadatta were constantly at odds with one another; each leading the fourfold army, they stationed themselves on opposite banks of a river and established boundary markers.
At that time, the queens of both kings each gave birth to a son and a daughter, who were exceptionally handsome and beautiful.
The King was greatly delighted and sought to reconcile with him. They agreed to form a marriage alliance and made this solemn covenant:
"From this day forward, let us never again offend one another, even unto our descendants. Later, when Prince Brahmā was seven years of age, [the following occurred].

He sought to take her as his wife. Upon hearing this, the girl addressed her father, the king, saying: "A human body is difficult to obtain, and even more so is the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
I only pray, Great King, do not cast my person into such hardships, causing me to be forever separated from virtuous friends.
I beseech you with compassion to grant me permission to leave the household life. The king replied: "While you were in the womb, I..."
"I grant you this; because of you, the two kingdoms have reached a reconciliation. Now, if you betray your word of honor, he will surely become my enemy once again.
Thereupon, the king immediately sent a messenger to King Brahmadatta with these words: "Within seven days, come quickly to take her in marriage."

When the princess heard this, her heart was filled with grief and distress. She put on soiled and greasy garments, immediately ascended a high tower, knelt upright with palms joined, and addressed the Jetavana:
"Tathāgata, World-Honored One, you who are compassionate and pity all sentient beings; I am now beset by suffering and calamity;
I pray that you will look upon me with mercy and grant me deliverance. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing from afar the princess's plea...
Moved by compassion, he appeared before the woman and preached the Dharma to her in various ways. Her mind was opened and her understanding clarified;
she attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*. When seven days had passed, the prince led several million people, bringing treasures to take her as his bride.

At that moment, she suddenly became aware that her body was in mid-air, where she manifested eighteen miraculous transformations. When the father-king saw his daughter, he was struck with deep terror.

The Buddha immediately granted her permission to leave the household life. Her husband, who was a prince, also gave rise to faith and reverence; repenting of his own faults and transgressions, he likewise permitted her to leave the household life.
Upon hearing these words, the woman went at once to the Jetavana Grove to seek ordination from the Buddha. The Buddha immediately granted her permission, and she became a bhikṣuṇī.
She practiced with diligent effort and attained the fruit of arhatship. At that time, the bhikṣus requested the Buddha to speak of her.
Regarding their past affinity, the Buddha said: "In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a woman who constantly quarreled with her husband.
Later, on one day, they exhorted one another to go to a bhikṣu and receive the eight precepts of the fast. Thereupon, they made a vow together:
'May we, in whatever place we are born, be honored, illustrious, and noble; and amidst disputes, may we always reach reconciliation. Having made this aspiration..."
Having made this vow, according to the length of their respective lifespans, they each reached the end of their lives and were reborn together in a royal family. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that husband’s father was at that time, he is now King Brahmadatta. As for the wife’s father at that time..."
The King Prasenajit of today is that person. The husband at that time is the Prince of today.
The wife at that time is the Bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā, the daughter of the king (as recorded in the *Śatavarga-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*). The *Ekottarika-āgama* states:
"As for the one who was wise and intelligent, she was the Bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā; among the five hundred Arhat bhikṣuṇīs, she was the foremost."
She was the foremost among them.
The bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā Gautamī— Tiṣyā, also called Kṛśā, or Kṛtīśā, or again Kṛtīśā Gautamī.
Some call her Gotamī; others call her Gopikā, as explained above. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When the bhikṣuṇī Śiśukā Gotamī was still a laywoman, all seven of her sons died. Because of her great grief and sorrow, she lost her mind and went mad.
The Vinaya of the Sarvāstivādins states: "In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was an elder named Ghoṭamukha."
He was very wealthy and possessed great riches. Not long after he had married his wife, she became pregnant. When the months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter.
Although her features were upright and handsome, she was thinner than ordinary people. All her relatives gathered together to give her a name, and they all deliberated, saying:
This woman was thin of form; she was the daughter of Gautama. A name should be established for her, and she was called Śrī-Gautamī (according to this, *tiṣya* is translated as "thin").
The World-Honored One observed her faculties and nature, and preached the Dharma according to their capacities, causing her to realize and understand the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
She attained the fruit of a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and requested ordination. The Buddha granted his permission and entrusted her to Mahāprajāpatī.
The Master immediately caused him to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). He taught him the *Vinaya* and instructed him according to the Dharma.

He, in turn, applied himself with diligence, single-mindedly and without weariness, contemplating and understanding that the five destinies revolve without ceasing and that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
Having returned [to the world], she attained extinction. She severed the delusions of the three realms, shattered the wheel of the five destinies, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, she was endowed with the eight liberations. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Among my disciples, the bhikṣuṇīs, Śrī-Gautamī is foremost in upholding the Vinaya. As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*: [text continues].
Regarding the practice of the dhūta-precepts, there are eleven restrictions;
namely, the bhikṣuṇī Kṛśā Gautamī (she is said to have "eleven" because she does not observe the rule of dwelling in an araṇya).
The *Pāriyātra-āraṇya-bhikṣuṇī-saṃyukta-āgama* states:
"The bhikṣuṇī Śrīṣācārā. The *Separate Translation of the Saṃyukta-āgama* states: [the same].
The bhikṣuṇī Cāpā entered the Akṣavāṭa grove and sat beneath a tree.
At that time, Māra transformed himself into a young brahmin (māṇava) and approached her, saying, "Of the ninety-six kinds of paths, which path do you delight in?
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "I do not delight in any of these paths at all. Thereupon, Māra spoke this verse:
"By whose instruction did you have your hair shaved, that you now call yourself a bhikṣuṇī? You do not wish to delight in the non-Buddhist paths;
you are utterly foolish.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī spoke this verse:
Furthermore, all those of other paths are bound by false views; bound by various kinds of views, they ultimately fall into the net of Māra.
The Great World-Honored One of the Śākya clan, the peerless Great Being, supreme among all things—having subdued Māra and sat at the site of enlightenment, he has transcended everything above.
Liberated from all things, having tamed them and reached the end of existence—his teaching is for me;
he is my World-Honored One. I delight in his Dharma. Now that I know him, I have utterly eliminated all fetters and outflows;
I have severed all craving and extinguished the darkness of ignorance.
Having attained cessation and abiding securely in the untainted dharma, one should know that because of this, Pāpīyān has fallen into defeat.
At that time, Māra thought: "The bhikṣuṇī knows my mind; she is now filled with grief and has vanished."
The bhikṣuṇī Sūmi (also transcribed as Sōumi; its translation is unknown);
the bhikṣuṇī Śūna.
The translation is not yet certain.
*Sura* bhikṣuṇī is sometimes called *Sumā*. This means "good," or "well-restrained," or "handsome. It is also translated as "moon."

The *Saṃyukta Āgama* translated by another [school] states: When the bhikṣuṇī Sumā had finished her almsround and was about to head toward the Forest of Attaining the Eye (*Cakṣur-lābha-avana*), the Māra King immediately manifested as a brāhmaṇa, stood by the side of the road, and asked, "Where do you wish to go?
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "I am now going to that place of tranquility. Thereupon, the Māra spoke this verse:
It was said:
"This place attained by seers and sages is difficult to reach; it cannot be obtained by your base and defiled intellect."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī entered meditative concentration. Perceiving through insight that this was Māra, she immediately spoke these verses:
"The female form is devoid of agency; it is only the mind that cultivates meditative concentration.
If one perceives superior dharmas through the lens of male or female characteristics, one may speak of a 'woman,' yet within the Dharma, such [characteristics] have no power."
If there are no signs of male or female, how could discrimination arise?
Having severed all craving and extinguished the darkness of ignorance, one attains the realization of cessation and abides in the untainted Dharma.
For this reason, you should know that Pāpīyān has fallen into defeat.
At that time, Māra thought, "The bhikṣuṇī knows my mind well. Filled with anxiety, he returned to his palace. As stated in the *Sūtra on Endowed with Virtue*:
"Regarding her cultivation and practice, she has well attained the divine eye; she is the bhikṣuṇī Sumā."
Cārā is the name of a bhikṣuṇī;
this translates as "one who moves" (xing) or "one who acts" (dong). The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
The bhikṣuṇī Cārā entered the Andhavana forest to practice dhyāna. At that time, Māra Pāpīyas transformed himself into a youth and approached Cārā, speaking a verse:
"Perceiving birth as happiness, one experiences the five desires upon being born.
Who has instructed you thus?
At that moment, Ccharā recognized that this was Māra, who intended to cause her distress, and she spoke this verse:

Those who are born must surely die; being born, one undergoes manifold sufferings. The pain of flogging and all such afflictions arise from conditioned existence. One should sever all suffering and transcend all rebirth.
With the eye of wisdom, observe the Noble Truths as taught by the Muni: Suffering itself, the origin of suffering, and the cessation of suffering.
Cessation extinguishes all suffering; one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path.
This is the Dharma of the Great Teacher, leading peacefully to Nirvana and characterized by equanimity. I rejoice in that Dharma;
because I know that Dharma, I no longer delight in rebirth. Having abandoned all craving and joy, I have cast off all darkness.
Having realized cessation through direct experience, she dwelt securely with all taints exhausted.
When the evil Māra perceived that she had understood his intent, he became sorrowful and vanished from sight.
The bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā—
also called Vatsalā, which means "Virtuous Conduct," or Upabhadrā, translated as "Near Conduct"—
at that time went to the Nyagrodha Forest and sat in meditation under a tree with her body upright. At that moment...
At that time, the Māra king transformed himself into a young brahmin (maṇava) and went to where the bhikṣuṇī was, asking: "Noble lady (āryā), where do you intend to take rebirth?
The bhikṣuṇī replied: "I have no place at all for taking rebirth. The Māra then spoke this verse:
The Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens, the Tuṣita and Nirmāṇarati heavens, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven—these places are the height of bliss;
you should aspire to and delight in them. When she was experiencing these most excellent and wondrous things, the bhikṣuṇī spoke again in verse:

In the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens—though they enjoy pleasures in these various realms—they do not escape the view of self. Bound inevitably by Māra, the world wavers;
even they must pass away and perish. There are no such beings among the ordinary worldlings.
The realm of liberation— where the world is ablaze, where the world emits smoke,
and one has emerged from all agitation— in such a place I find delight.
Having severed all craving and extinguished the darkness of ignorance, I have attained cessation and abide in the untainted Dharma.
For this reason, it should be known that when Pāpīyān fell into defeat,
Māra thought to himself, "The bhikṣuṇī well knows my mind," and he returned to his palace filled with anxiety (as recorded in a separate translation of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*).
*Śīlavatī* (尸羅婆遮那) is the name of a bhikṣuṇī.
*Śīla* means "coolness" (*śītala*) and also means "purity. It is also called *sīla*, which means "fine jade. Fine jade also carries the sense of being pure and clean.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "To uphold the teachings of the Vinaya without committing any transgression constitutes [the first] *pātimokkha*..."
According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the bhikṣuṇī Śīlā entered the Andhavana forest and sat beneath a tree.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas immediately transformed himself into a youth, approached the bhikṣuṇī,
and spoke this verse:
"How are sentient beings born? Who is their creator? From where do sentient beings arise, and to where do they go?
The bhikṣuṇī, knowing this to be Māra, the Evil One, who wished to create obstacles, immediately spoke a verse:
If you think there is a sentient being, this is merely the manifestation of Māra. There is only a collection of empty aggregates;

no such thing as a sentient being exists. Just as when various materials are assembled, the world conventionally calls it a "chariot," so too, through the combination of causes and conditions of the aggregates, we provisionally name them a "sentient being. When they arise, suffering arises.
Abiding in this, suffering arises; there is no other dharma that gives rise to suffering. When suffering arises, suffering itself ceases.
Free from all sorrow and suffering, and having departed from all darkness, you have realized nirvana and abide with all taints exhausted.
Knowing you thus, O Evil Māra, you shall vanish of your own accord.
At that time, Māra thought, "The bhikṣuṇī has already known my mind," and harboring inner grief and distress, he immediately vanished and disappeared.
The *Araḷavā Bhikṣuṇī-mahā-śāstra* states:
While the Buddha was traveling with the fourfold assembly, among the community of bhikṣuṇīs there was a bhikṣuṇī named...

Āravā. This refers to those born by transformation within the earth (this demonstrates that among humans there are four modes of birth: those born from eggs, such as Viśākhā’s mother, who gave birth to thirty-two eggs;
those born from moisture, such as the woman Āmrapālī, who was born from within a flower; those born from a womb, such as ordinary humans; and those born by transformation, such as these bhikṣuṇīs).
The bhikṣuṇī Mālāpī has not been clearly translated;
the bhikṣuṇī Unni.
The translation is not clearly known. Bhikṣuṇī Vanī;
*vanī* here means "eloquent" or "articulate."
The precepts are the methods for restraining body and speech. This means that if one can uphold the precepts with firmness and purity,
then the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) is accomplished, such that there is neither upholding nor violating.

"Samādhi-samādhi" refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This means that when one cultivates untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentration, the sense faculties and their objects are purified and extinguished,
and one becomes free from all distraction.
"Wisdom,
wisdom" refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*). This means that by cultivating this untainted wisdom,
one is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms and transcend tainted birth and death (*sāsrava-saṃsāra*).

It is called "liberation" (vimukti) because one is released from bondage and attains freedom. That is to say, by not performing further karmic actions, one is freed from all burdens and fetters, thereby attaining mastery.
There are two kinds of liberation: first, conditioned liberation (saṃskṛta-vimukti), which refers to that which is untainted (anāsrava).
Wisdom severs the out-flowing afflictions (*āsrava-kleśa*). Second is unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*), which refers to the total extinction of all afflictions without remainder.
Since the afflictions have been exhausted, the principle is fundamentally unconditioned.
Knowledge of the vision of liberation is known through wisdom; vision belongs to the eye. This is precisely the eye of the knowledge of non-arising, which illuminates with sovereign clarity.
That is to say, if one illuminates and realizes that consciousness and mind are all merely false conceptualizations, then the eye of the knowledge of non-arising is sovereign.
This is clearly understood. As for the aforementioned fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*):

if sentient beings can uphold the precepts, cultivate concentration and wisdom, and practice various pure deeds, they will be able to transform the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the physical body and thereby accomplish the fivefold Dharma-body.

That is to say: transforming the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) accomplishes the body of morality (*śīlakāya*); transforming the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) accomplishes the body of concentration (*samādhikāya*); transforming the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) accomplishes the body of wisdom (*prajñākāya*). Transforming...

The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) becomes the body of liberation (vimukti-kāya), and the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) becomes the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya). This is explained at length in the sūtras and śāstras.
[Distraction] is tumultuousness.
*Kuì* (古外切): Pronounced like *kuài*. It means disorder or clamor. *Náo* (奴教切): The departing tone of *niáo*. It means lack of stillness; it means to disturb.
The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
It is also called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and again, dependent arising. That is to say: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises.

From ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise; from volitional formations as a condition, consciousness arises; from consciousness as a condition, name-and-form arise; from name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases arise;

from the six sense bases as a condition, contact arises; from contact as a condition, feeling arises; from feeling as a condition, craving arises; from craving as a condition, clinging arises; from clinging as a condition, existence arises; from existence as a condition, birth arises... [birth]...

Conditioned by old age and death, there arise sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair; thus this entire great mass of suffering accumulates and comes into being (this is called the primary meaning of dependent origination).
Master Fa-sheng said: "Cause" means that previously the thing did not exist, yet it arises from that [condition]. "Condition" (pratyaya)...
This means that although one originally possesses the potential, it arises from those [conditions]. Tiantai says:

These twelve factors are called "causes" because they can successively induce results; they exist by mutually depending upon one another, which is termed the "conditioned continuity of causes and conditions."

Thus, the cycle of birth and death continues without end. If one understands ignorance and does not give rise to grasping for existence, then the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms and all cycles of birth and death will cease.
This is the essential method for transcending the world. (Next, the meaning of differentiation shall be explained.)
First is ignorance (*avidyā*). This refers to all the delusions of the afflictions in past lives that shroud the fundamental nature, such that nothing is clearly understood;
hence it is called ignorance.
Second, formations (*saṃskāra*). This refers to all wholesome and unwholesome karma performed by means of body, speech, and mind in past lives;
these are called formations.

Third, consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness is the mental consciousness; it refers to this consciousness being driven to enter [the womb] due to the mutual牵引 (attraction/pulling) of past afflictions and karma.
Entrusting oneself to the mother’s womb, in a single kṣaṇa, with defiled craving as the seed, one receives the *saṃjñā* (perception) and forms the embryo;

this is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). The fourth is *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form): "name" (*nāma*) refers to the mind, meaning that the mind exists only as a designation and lacks substantial essence or characteristics.
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to material substance, namely the physical body. This means that by virtue of entering the womb, one gathers the two drops—the red and white—of the father and mother. Up to...
In the fifth seven-day period thereafter, it is called the stage of form (rūpa). The various sense organs and physical forms arise, along with the differentiation of the four limbs.

It possesses both the body faculty (kāyendriya) and the mind faculty (manendriya), yet the other four faculties, such as the eye, do not yet exist. Since the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are not yet complete, these are all subsumed under name-and-form (nāmarūpa);
therefore, it is called "name-and-form."

The five and six bases are also called the six sense entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*). This refers to the period following *nāmarūpa* up until the sixth seventh-day interval, which is termed the stage of hair, body hair, nails, and teeth.

In the seventh seventh-day interval, it is termed the stage of possessing the faculties (*indriya-sampanna*). At this point, the six sense organs unfold and possess the function of entering the six objects;
these are called the six sense entrances.
The six contacts (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*). This refers to the period from birth onwards when the six sense faculties encounter their respective six objects.
Although this encounter occurs, there is as yet no arising of conceptual discrimination or cognitive awareness that gives rise to perceptions of suffering or pleasure; this is termed contact.
The seven feelings (*vedanā*). This refers to when, due to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), there is contact with the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*);

if one then gives rise to discrimination and cognition, one experiences the objects before one, such as matters of beauty or ugliness. Although one thus discriminates, one has not yet given rise to thoughts of lustful craving and so forth;
this is called feeling.
Eight: Craving (*tṛṣṇā*). This refers to the gradual arising of passionate attachment through the conceptual discernment of various sensory objects.
One then covets diverse and excellent requisites, as well as objects such as sexual desire, yet has not yet engaged in extensive or universal pursuit; this is termed craving.
Ninth, grasping (*upādāna*): this refers to the mind becoming increasingly intense due to craving, such that it incessantly pursues the objects of the five sensory realms;
this is called grasping.
Tenth, existence (*bhava*): this refers to the arising of wholesome and unwholesome karma due to the pursuit of various objects, which accumulates and draws forth the three [types of] future births.

The fruit of existence is called "existence" (bhava). This means that cause and effect do not perish; thus it is termed existence. The three existences are: the existence of desire (kāma-bhava), the existence of form (rūpa-bhava), and the existence of formlessness (ārūpya-bhava).

Eleventh, birth: this refers to taking birth again within the six destinies and four modes of birth in future lives, due to the wholesome or unwholesome karma performed in the present life; this is called birth.
Twelfth is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). This refers to the fact that after birth has occurred, the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) matures and then disintegrates;
this is called old age and death. *Wenxuan* asks: Why is illness not taught as a link (*aṅga*)? Answer:
A factor is established as a link only if it exists at all times and in all places. Furthermore, there are people who are born free from illness, such as Bakula, who was born [without disease].

One who has not yet experienced [the suffering of] birth does not recognize the pain of a headache, much less other ailments; therefore, it is not established [as a link]. Question: Are sorrow and lamentation (*śoka-parideva*) branches [of dependent origination]?
Answer: No. This is merely to reveal the end by way of the beginning. Just as with old age and death, sorrow and lamentation necessarily follow. Thus, Tiantai said:
"Old age and death give rise to sorrow, lamentation, weeping, and various forms of grief and suffering; a multitude of afflictions gather together. If one correctly contemplates all phenomena...

The purity of the true mark (*dharmatā*) means that ignorance is exhausted. Because ignorance is exhausted, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted, and so on until all the aggregates of suffering are exhausted.
That is to say: because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this ceases, that ceases. From the cessation of ignorance...

Then volitional formations cease. With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases. With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease.

With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases. With the cessation of existence, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age and death [cease].
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress are extinguished; thus, this entire mass of pure suffering that has accumulated is all extinguished.

If one can thus correctly contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time, one will give rise to true outflow-free wisdom and become a pratyekabuddha. As the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
There are four kinds of wisdom for contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination: first, the inferior; second, the middling; third, the superior; and fourth, the supreme.
Those who contemplate with inferior wisdom do not perceive the Buddha-nature; because they do not perceive it, they attain the path of the śrāvaka.

Those with middling wisdom observe [the twelve links of dependent origination] and do not see the Buddha-nature. Because they do not see it, they attain the path of the Pratyekabuddha. Those with superior wisdom observe it but do not see it clearly.
Because they do not see it clearly, they abide in the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Those with the most superior wisdom observe it and see it clearly;

because they see it clearly, they attain the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time, these refer to ignorance (*avidyā*)... [and so forth].

The two links of *saṃskāra* (volitional formations) constitute the past cause. The five links of *vijñāna* (consciousness), *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form), *ṣaḍāyatana* (the six sense bases), *sparśa* (contact), and *vedanā* (feeling) constitute the present effect. The three links of *tṛṣṇā* (craving), *upādāna* (clinging), and *bhava* (existence) constitute the present cause. The two links of *jāti* (birth) and *jarāmaraṇa* (aging and death) constitute the future effect.

Beyond these, the remaining factors across the three times function as mutual causes and effects, even down to two lifetimes or a single moment of mind in the present, which fully possesses the twelve links of dependent origination, as explained extensively in the treatises.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: In the past, when the Buddha Vipaśyin appeared in the world, he preached the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
After that Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, there was a king who erected a tower made of ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*), adorned with all manner of ornaments.
This king had five hundred wives who made offerings to this tower, each making a vow, saying: "May we, in the future, from this..."
At that time, the king was none other than Nanda; the five hundred ladies were these five hundred nuns.
Due to the causal conditions of this original vow, they ought to attain liberation through Nanda.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: What is the difference between *avavāda* (instruction) and *anuśāsana* (admonition)? It answers: That which prevents what is unbeneficial is called instruction (*avavāda*);
that which provides what is beneficial is called admonition (*anuśāsana*). Furthermore, it is so called because it teaches one to abide in right mindfulness.
It is called "instruction" (*avavāda*). Because it teaches one to abide in correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*), it is called "admonition" (*anuśāsana*).
Furthermore, because it causes one to cultivate the manifest (*vijñapti*), it is called "instruction"; because it causes one to cultivate the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), it is called "admonition.

Furthermore, because it causes one to cultivate *śamatha*, it is called "instruction"; because it causes one to cultivate *vipaśyanā*, it is called "admonition. Furthermore, because it causes one to cultivate the Noble Path...
It is called "instruction" (*anuśāsanī*). It is called "teaching" (*avavāda*) because it causes one to cultivate the fruits of holiness (*āryaphala*).

Furthermore, it is called "instruction" because it causes one to cultivate mundane wholesome dharmas (*laukikakuśaladharma*), and it is called "teaching" because it causes one to cultivate supramundane wholesome dharmas (*lokottarakuśaladharma*). This is what is meant by instruction.

The distinction between the teachings (*śamatha*, here translated as *zhi*; and *vipaśyanā*, here translated as *guan*). "Jia" (賈) is pronounced like *gu* (古), with the phonetic components *gong* (公) and *tu* (土).

Within this state, one should subdue the mind, constantly examining one's own faults and not speaking of the shortcomings of others.

He said to the bandit, "You should shoot this belly. It was for its sake that I left the forest; therefore, it is the fault of this belly that has brought about this distress.
To reflect upon oneself and show leniency toward others is just like this.

a bhikṣu must not travel along a road with a bhikṣuṇī. However, when traveling with other bhikṣus or with a caravan of merchants, it is permissible.
One must carefully examine one's companions—whether they are virtuous or unvirtuous, beneficial or harmful—before proceeding together.
As stated in the *Vinaya-viniścaya*: "When bhikṣus are about to set out on a journey, they should inform their two teachers in advance, one day prior."

"O, we should consider whether there is anything we have forgotten and ensure that it is not neglected.

If there is a compelling reason that necessitates traveling with such a person, one should first offer an act of confession (*kṣamāpanā*) and only then go along with them."
Whenever traveling on a road, one should engage in Dharma-discourse and avoid uttering evil words, or else maintain noble silence so as not to allow the mind to become distracted.
If one arrives at a shrine or temple of a deity, one should recite a Buddhist *gāthā* (formerly called a "verse") and proceed while snapping the fingers.
A *bhikṣu* should not make offerings to deities. If, while on the road, one pauses briefly to rest, or...
Upon reaching a spring or pool, one should recite a *gāthā* when drawing water. At the place where one stays overnight, one should recite the three invocations (*tri-śaraṇa*), and so forth.
Whenever one reaches a resting place outside the monastery, one should shake the dust from one's robes, wash the body, and bathe the feet to ensure complete purity.
Next, one should replenish the water in the flask. As for leather sandals used while traveling, they should be wiped with a piece of torn cloth, but never against pillars or walls.

Having struck [the door] and caused no injury or damage, he should again wash his hands thoroughly and put on his robes completely. With a dignified and composed demeanor, he should then enter the monastery.
Proceeding to a single cell, he should speak but little and adjust his own deportment. He should then inquire after a place to stay.
When a resident bhikṣu sees a visiting bhikṣu—if the resident is younger than the visitor—he should rise to welcome him, calling out "Welcome! from afar with palms joined.

He joined his palms and said, "I pay my respects. The guest replied, "Welcome most graciously. [The host] took up the robe and bowl and led him into the room, offering him a seat and requesting him to sit.
He removed his garments and massaged the guest's calves and feet to relieve his fatigue. He brought a basin for washing the feet and bathed them for him.
After conversing for a long while, he finally performed the rites of respect: adjusting his robes, prostrating once, and joining his hands.
He should press both feet [of the visitor] and ask if they are well. If they have never met before, he should inquire about their seniority and pay respects according to their rank.

If the visitor is junior, the procedure for questioning and answering follows as before; if the visitor is senior, he should instruct the junior monk to receive the visitor’s robes and bowl, provide a seat at the appropriate time, and relieve him of his fatigue.
If there is kindness and compassion, the senior monk may occasionally press the shoulders and back of the junior. In all cases...

When visiting bhikṣus first arrive at another location, they should first pay homage to the senior elder (sthavira) who heads the community. The senior elder, in turn, should greet them with "Welcome" and other such words.
Furthermore, if guests arrive, one should assess whether one possesses bedding, mats, and sleeping requisites, and provide for them accordingly as prescribed above.
Should one fail to act in accordance with these regulations, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).

This refers to those among the four castes who are of noble lineage and high repute, who abide by the teachings of the world, and are designated as "virtuous ones.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "In the kingdom, superior persons are called 'elders' (*gṛhapati*). Originally, the designations used in the Western Regions differ from those of this land.
There, those of noble birth and prominent clans, as well as wealthy merchants and great traders who have accumulated tens of millions in wealth, are all collectively termed [elders]."

"Householder" (*gṛhapati*) is a title used for those who possess virtue. It refers to one who is advanced in years and mature in merit, who is senior to others in worldly affairs, and is thus designated as a "householder.
According to the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), one is called a householder by virtue of possessing ten kinds of qualities:
first, noble lineage; second, high status; third, great wealth; fourth, majestic power; fifth, profound wisdom; sixth, advanced age; seventh, [right] conduct...
1. Purification; 2. The eightfold etiquette; 3. Praise from above; 4. Return to below.
"Virtuous One" (*bhadanta*) is called *bhadanta* in Sanskrit, which means "Virtuous One. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: "A junior bhikṣu should address an elder..."

One who is of great virtue should be addressed as "Venerable" (Bhadanta). One who is older should address a younger person as "Long-lived One" (Āyuṣmat). If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "From this day forward, those of lower standing should address their seniors as 'Venerable Elder' (Upādhyāya)."
The senior monk should address the junior monk by the title "Venerable Life" (*āyuṣmat*). In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "From this day forward, I command all bhikṣus:
you must not treat one another with a disrespectful mind. Those who are senior shall be addressed as 'Venerable' (*bhadanta*), and those who are junior shall be addressed as 'Worthy One' (*āyuṣmat*).
You should regard one another as brothers. From now on, you must not use the names given to you by your parents."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "How should the bhikṣus address one another from now on? The Buddha said:
"If a junior bhikṣu addresses a senior bhikṣu, he should call him 'Elder' (sthavira). A senior bhikṣu may address a junior bhikṣu by his clan name or personal name.
Furthermore, if the bhikṣus wish to establish a title, it should be based upon the Three Honored Ones. This is my [instruction]."
Regarding these instructions on the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
At one time, the group of six bhikṣus addressed one another using the terminology of laypeople, calling each other "Father," "Mother," "Elder Brother," and "Younger Brother. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should address one another and exchange greetings in this manner: when speaking together, you must not call one another 'Father,' 'Sir,' or 'Māhala' (old man)."
It should be said: when speaking with one's mother, one must not say "Amma" or "Āvā";
one should say "Bāludīti. When speaking with one's elder brother, one must not say "Āvuso"; one should say "Sāludī."
When speaking with one’s sister, one must not say *pabbajitā*; one should say *pabbajitāye*.
When speaking with a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), one must not say *vattantī*; one should say *upajjhāya* (this is translated as "Preceptor").
When speaking with an instructor (*ācariya*), one must not say *vattantī*; one should say *ācariya*. If there is...
Regarding many *ācāryas*: one should say, "The *ācārya* named so-and-so. When conversing with them while seated on the same level, one may address them by their personal name, as "Candita" or "Vatsa.
When conversing with them while seated on a higher level, one should address them as "Bhadanta," or as "Āyuṣmat," or as "Ācārya.
If someone calls out to you, you must not respond by saying, "What path? or "What thing? If...
When the Upādhyāya calls you, you should respond with "Yes. When the Ācārya calls you, you should respond with "Yes.
When an Elder (sthavira) calls you, you should likewise respond with "Yes. When a junior calls you, you should ask, "Why do you call me?
When a woman or a man calls you, you should ask, "Why do you call me? If someone asks, "What is the name of your Upādhyāya or Ācārya? [you should answer accordingly].
What is this? One must not directly state the name of one’s *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*. One should say, "By reason of his [spiritual] significance, his name is so-and-so.
Such is the proper manner of speech according to the Dharma; if one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*).
The Tripiṭaka Master Yijing states that the Vinaya says: "If one is not an *upādhyāya*, yet one calls him 'Upādhyāya'; if one is not an *ācārya*... [and so forth].
If one addresses someone as "Ācārya," or translates these two terms [as "Preceptor" and "Teacher"], or directly utters the name of an Upādhyāya, in all such cases one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
However, if someone asks, "What is the name of your Preceptor (*upādhyāya*)?
or asks, "Whose disciple are you?", or if one must state the teacher's name due to some personal business, in all such instances [it is not an offense].
One should say: "I have come for a certain matter; I shall state my preceptor’s name. My preceptor’s name is so-and-so.
In the Western Regions and the Southern Seas, calling oneself by name is not a word of pride. Even if one were to address you directly, it is not a term of disrespect;

it is merely intended to distinguish between self and other, entirely devoid of any conceited heart. This is not like the land of China (Shenzhou), where such a practice is regarded as vulgar and contemptible.
If you have any objections, you may change "I" to "now. These are all the teachings of the Sage and should be put into practice.
You must not follow others blindly or fail to report your concerns early.
△ The thirty-first offense: Accepting an offering of food more than once (this is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
A village without a fixed residence.
At that time, there was a village in the kingdom of Kosala where there was no monastery (*saṃghārāma*) nor any lodging for travelers.
A householder, for the sake of merit, constructed a dwelling and provided all manner of food and drink to supply the community of monks who came and went.
One may provide only a single meal and a single night’s lodging, as one cannot offer more; because it is established through the merit of such giving, other Vinayas all refer to it as a "merit hall.
For the sick person...

△ Section 33: Eating in a Group Apart from the Community (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns). Kāla.
He is called Kṛṣṇa (Black) and also Kāla (Time). He was the son of King Bimbisāra’s sister.
The *Pañcavargīka-vinaya* states that King Bimbisāra had a younger brother named Kāla; "Kāla" and "Kālu" are phonetically similar.

Four persons constitute a "group of four. If they form a separate group—whether numbering four or more—and go out for alms or accept an invitation, it is called "eating in a separate group" (*pṛthaggaṇabhojana*).
Furthermore, regarding eating in a separate group: if one is apart from the community... [text truncated]
Down to a single person, all are termed "eating in a separate group" (*pṛthag-bhaktika*). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"Eating in a separate group means eating separately. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "A 'separate group' refers to those who do not eat in the same place.
If four bhikṣus within the same boundary—even down to one person—do not eat together, they are all termed 'a separate group. This term 'eating' refers to..."

This constitutes a formal meal; eating other food does not constitute an offense. If among four persons, one has a permissible cause (*kṣaṇa*), or if there is one *śrāmaṇera* together with three fully ordained monks (*upasampanna*), or if a small amount of food is sent—down to a single spoonful of salt or a handful of grass or leaves.

If the original donor intended the offering specifically for a particular room, thinking, "I shall provide for the person residing here," then whether one eats by manifesting supernatural power in mid-air, or if it is food belonging to the Saṃgha, or food for private use, there is no offense in any case.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Whenever one eats separately from the assembly, it must be within the boundary (*sīmā*). There are various kinds of boundaries; some are established by the community of monks."

Regarding boundaries (*sīmā*): there is the village boundary (*grāma-sīmā*), the household boundary (*kula-sīmā*), and the wilderness area (*araṇya-sthāna*), which naturally constitutes a boundary of one *krośa*.
Within such a boundary, one must not eat separately, nor perform the *poṣadha* separately; however, this does not apply to the clothing boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).
Thus, monks, whoever is within such a boundary must not eat separately, provided it is food offered by a donor (*dānapati*) and [eaten] by four or more [monks].
Eating together in one place is called "eating as a separate group" (*pṛthaggaṇabhojana*). Furthermore, it is said:

if, during a communal meal, the *karmadāna* (steward) takes property belonging to the Saṃgha and separately prepares rich and excellent food for four people to eat together—even though those four are in two different locations—it constitutes [the offense of] eating as a separate group.
There is no offense of eating separately from the assembly; however, if one eats what is impure, one incurs the offense of stealing from the Saṃgha.

When consuming food belonging to the Saṃgha, four kinds of signals should be given: first, striking the ghaṇṭā; second, blowing the conch; third, beating the drum; and fourth, making a public proclamation.
One must ensure that these four kinds of signs are heard and known within the boundary; they must invariably have fixed limits.

One must not, at times, strike the *gandi*, beat the drum, or blow the conch shell, causing the proceedings to become confused and lacking definite rules, thereby failing to establish the monastic dharma.
If one consumes the communal food (*saṃghika-bhikṣā*) without employing these four kinds of signs, it is not pure; this is called [impurity].
To consume the property of the Saṃgha is to steal from the Saṃgha;

it does not matter whether there are bhikṣus within the boundary or not, whether they are many or few, whether they are barred or not barred, or whether one knows that bhikṣus are present or knows that no bhikṣus are present—all such acts are termed "improper consumption" and are also termed "stealing from the Saṃgha.
This is not termed the offense of eating separately from the assembly (pārivāsika). If one performs these four characteristics while consuming the food of the Saṃgha...
Suppose that within the boundary there may be monks or no monks—whether many or few—and whether one knows there are monks or no monks, or whether they come or do not come;
provided that there is no obstruction, there is no fault whatsoever.
If there is an obstruction, even if the *gandī* gong is struck, the meal is impure and is termed "stealing from the Saṃgha. If within the great boundary there are two...

Regarding the three locations, each has its own beginning and end of the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa, yet they share a single *poṣadha*. At the time of the meal, one should simply strike the *gandī* drum at each location;
no one should obstruct anyone else. Thus, there is purity and no fault. The *Mūlakalpa* states:

"If the person in charge of supervision, prior to the midday meal, takes his own portion first, there is no fault. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "There are five causes and conditions for [eating] early..."
Please come to eat. One may eat in one's own room under these circumstances: first, when one is a newly arrived guest; second, when one is about to depart;
third, when one’s body is afflicted by the suffering of illness; fourth, when one is a caregiver for the sick; fifth, when one serves as an administrator (*karmadāna*).

According to these rules, eating apart from the community (*pṛthag-bhakta*) is not permitted without such causes. If there is a donor who wishes to invite virtuous persons (*bhadanta*) separately, they must necessarily also invite the Saṃgha.
Gā. From the lowest member of the assembly, each person shall receive the invitation in turn. If it concerns the *saṃghika* daily meal, the *gandī* gong must be struck;

those who beg for food must each depart individually. Regarding invitations to private residences, the Vinaya provides specific allowances (*kappiya-vatthu*). If one makes a request based on a vague pretext, [it is not permitted].
Eating [in such a manner] inevitably incurs transgression. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:

"For what reason did the Tathāgata prohibit eating in a separate group, yet permit three people to eat together in one place? The intention behind this was to protect and preserve all persons so that they would not suffer diminution;
furthermore, it was to subdue monks of evil desires and to sever their excessive attachment to large retinues."
They call out the names of the monks and seek much from them, thereby diminishing the households and destroying the Sangha by causing it to split into two factions;
consequently, they ensure that monks who act in accordance with the Dharma do not receive offerings of robes, food, or drink, while those who act contrary to the Dharma do.
They obtain great gain and support. Once these bhikṣus of evil desires have received such offerings, they engage in disputes with those who practice pure conduct.
Therefore, the *Śāriputra-vinaya* (Ten Recitation Vinaya) states: "For two reasons, one should prohibit eating separately from the assembly:
first, to protect and care for the donors out of compassion; second, to break the power and influence of those bhikṣus of evil desires."
△ Thirty-fourth: Receiving an Invitation for More Than Three Alms Bowls (This is a common precept; it is likewise prescribed for nuns).
The woman Gaṇakā.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "This girl has a squint; therefore, she is named 'Squinting Eyes' (*lòu-àn*). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "This girl is blind in her right eye" (*miǎo*).

[Note: *Lòu* (洛代切) is pronounced *lài*; it means to look askance or side-long. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "The pupil of the eye is not straight. *Miǎo* (弭沼切) is pronounced *miǎo*; it means one eye is small.]
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: A bhikṣu who goes for alms should carry a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) and shake it to make a sound before entering a person’s house.
If the village dwellings are situated in a cluttered manner, he should make a mark to avoid losing his way; he may place a cake or some flour [on the threshold].

At the entrance of a gate, there are five places where one should not beg for alms: namely, the house of a professional crier, the house of a courtesan, a tavern, the royal palace, and the house of a caṇḍāla.
Furthermore, if one knows that a woman is by nature prone to excessive lust and defilement, one should likewise not beg from her.
This is because it may give rise to harm. Furthermore, it is said that there are three kinds of vain waste of offerings given in faith.
First, a donor gives with faith, knowing that this bhikṣu is one who upholds the precepts; having received the gift, the bhikṣu then takes this object [for his own use].
1. To give to one who has broken the precepts; 2. Knowing that this bhikṣu possesses right view, to bestow a gift with faith, yet then take that object and give it to one of wrong view; 3.

To accept in excess and not consume it oneself, even accepting as much as a single handful of food beyond what is permitted, unless the donor has previously expressed their consent. These three matters are all termed "wasted and lost."
Faith-based offerings shall bring about evil retribution.

(This is a unique precept; for a nun, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. If a nun has already finished her meal and subsequently eats the five types of solid food, it is a *pāyattika*.)
*Khañja* (Sanskrit) is here translated as "improper food" (*asana*) or "chewed food. This refers to roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
According to the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*, oils, sesame seeds, rock honey, and steamed foods all belong to the category of *khañja*, as in the following three [examples].

The nineteenth precept: furthermore, because oil, honey, and so forth constitute *sāyānīya* (soft food), these oils and other such items, although not "proper food" (*bhojana*), do not carry the meaning of being something to be chewed. For this reason, they are mostly not included in other Vinayas.
Some say it is *khādaniya*, which is translated here as "food that may be eaten," as will be clarified below. Master Jing says: "Half-ka-dan..."
*Ni-ban-je* means five. *Kha-dan-ni* has the meaning of "masticating"; it should be translated as "five masticable foods.
These are: first, roots; second, stalks; third, leaves; fourth, flowers; and fifth, fruits. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"All fruits are called *khādaniya* (masticable food)."
The five kinds of *praṇīta-bhojana* (proper food).
In Sanskrit, it is called *praṇīta*, or alternatively *bhojana*; this is translated here as "proper food.
These refer to rice, parched grain flour (*maṇḍa*), dry cakes, fish, and meat. Master Jing says: *Ban-zhe-pu-shan-ni*. *Ban-zhe* means "five," and *pu-shan* [refers to] *praṇīta*.

*Ni* (niṣyanda) carries the meaning of "chewing and swallowing. It should be translated as the "five types of chewed food" (*pañca-kavaḍīkārāhāra*). The older term, "five types of formal food" (*pañca-bhojanāni*), is a semantic translation.
These are: first, rice; second, barley and bean porridge; third, parched grain flour (*maṇḍa*); fourth, meat; and fifth, cakes. Fish is included within the category of meat.
Therefore, they are not mentioned separately. If one has first eaten the five kinds of chewed foods (*khādya*), one may later eat the five kinds of masticated foods (*bhojya*).

If one has first eaten the five kinds of masticated foods, one should not further eat the five kinds of chewed foods; if one eats them again, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
This should be understood by analogy. Milk, curd, and so forth are not included within either of these two sets of five; there is no further mention of them in the Vinaya text.

Regarding alternative names: those that are not subsumed under "proper food" (bhojana) include various noodle dishes; if a spoon placed upright does not fall over, they are all categorized as cakes or rice.
Dry parched flour mixed with water such that traces remain when drawn across with a finger is likewise subsumed under "eating.
Generally, all thin gruels and thin parched flour preparations are not "proper food," because they cannot satisfy one's hunger. For instance, in the Five Indias...
The territories and regions are vast and far-reaching. To speak in general terms, they extend for more than four hundred stations in each of the four directions—east, west, south, and north.
Excluding the remote frontiers, although it is not possible to witness everything firsthand, one may inquire into them in detail. As for all that is eaten and chewed:

The varieties of delicacies are manifold. In the north, wheat flour is abundant; in the west, parched grain flour (*piṣṭa*) is plentiful. In the kingdom of Magadha, wheat flour is scarce while rice is abundant.
The southern frontiers and the eastern borders are similar to Magadha. Ghee, oil, milk, and curd are found everywhere.
Foodstuffs such as cakes and fruits are beyond counting. Among the common people, even meat and pungent-smelling foods are rare.

In all the countries, non-glutinous rice is abundant while millet is scarce; there is no sorghum. Sweet melons are plentiful, along with sugarcanes and taro, but leafy vegetables like *huai* (Amaranthus) are lacking, whereas turnips are sufficient.

However, these seeds are of two colors—black and white—and have recently been translated as "mustard seeds" (*sarsapa*). They are pressed for oil and used as food; this is the practice in all countries.
As for the flavor of the leafy vegetable, it is no different from that of the turnip (*mūlaka*) in the Divine Land (China). Yet its root is hard and woody, which differs from the turnip.
Its seeds are coarse-grained when they form, and thus it is not the mustard seed either. It is like the *karka* and the tangerine, whose forms change according to the soil.
At Nālandā, [the Master] deliberated on his doubts together with the Meditation Master Wuxing, yet they were unable to reach a definitive resolution.
Furthermore, the people of the Five Indias do not eat various types of pickles or raw vegetables;

consequently, these people suffer no afflictions of abdominal pain, their intestines and stomachs remain harmonious and supple, and they are free from the distress of indigestion. (According to the commentary: *màn jīng* refers to *wú jīng*; it is also called *wú gēn*, or *fēng cóng*. It is also known as...)

The large *jiāngqiàn* has various names. Some say that when the turnip stem is short and the leaves are large, growing close together upon the ground, and the broad leaves are red, it is the *mànzhēng*. Zhuge Liang, when stationed at his camps during military expeditions, would always order his soldiers to plant it.

It was used to provide provisions for food. Consequently, the people of the Three Shu and Jiangling today call it "Zhuge Vegetables" (Guo-ge cai). If they wither during the summer, they plant them again; these are called "Chicken-feather Vegetables" (Ji-mao cai). After harvesting the remainder, the seeds are taken to produce oil. Its other medicinal uses are explained in the Bhaiṣajyavastu (Section on Medicine).

*Qi* (sauce): same as *qi*. Pronounced *ji*. It is minced raw meat with vinegar. One theory states it is made by pounding pungent ingredients. Pungent ingredients refer to ginger, pepper, and the like.

The *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakta-vidhi*, also known as the *ucchiṣṭa-bhakta-vidhi*. At one time, there was a bhikṣu who entered a village to beg for food and obtained a great quantity, which he ate together in one place.
He then took the remaining food and brought it back to the monastery to give to the other bhikṣus; however, those bhikṣus had already finished their meals.

[He said,] "I dare not eat it; I shall discard it. The Buddha said, "I permit the bhikṣus to take food from that place back [to the monastery], perform the *kṛtāvadāna* (the ritual for leftover food), and eat it" (the procedure for the ritual is as stated in the Vinaya text). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:

"If one obtains leftover food and eats it after performing the ritual, one dwells in comfort oneself and the donor gains merit. When wishing to perform the ritual, first wash the hands clean and receive [the food]."
Having finished eating, he takes the food and approaches a bhikṣu who has not yet eaten enough, or one who, though having eaten enough, has not yet left his seat.
Crouching before him, he says: "Venerable sir, please attend to me. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have finished eating and am satisfied;
yet I now wish to eat this excellent, perfect food. May you perform for me the ritual of 'leftover food' (vighasa-kalpa). Then that bhikṣu...
Śrāmaṇera, you should take two or three mouthfuls, eat them, and then reply to him, saying: "This is your property; you may eat it as you wish.
(He replies, "So be it. If you have already eaten enough, it is not proper for you to eat more; you should press down with your hand and tell him: [as follows].
"This is your property; eat it as you please. There are five circumstances under which the ritual for designating food as "leftover" (*atirikta-bhakṣaṇa-vidhi*) is not valid:

first, when one is within the boundary (*sīmā*) while addressing someone outside the boundary; second, when they are out of reach of one another; third, when one is at their side; fourth, when one is behind them;
fifth, when the person in front has left their seat. If these conditions are reversed, the ritual is successfully performed. Even if one person performs the ritual, others may eat the food.

In all these cases, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu brings food and wishes to perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual of leftover food), if he performs the ritual over a bowl while it is inside a vessel, then only what is in the vessel is designated as 'leftover food';
what is in the bowl is not so designated. If the liquid from the food in the vessel flows into the bowl, both may be designated as 'leftover food. If [both are]..."

Regarding two alms-bowls: if one requests that food be made into *vighasa* (leftover food), and the person before one has finished eating the food in only one bowl, it is only when that single bowl is [filled] that it may be designated as *vighasa*.
If there are two bowls, or if cakes or vegetables are placed across and covering both, both may be designated as *vighasa*.
It is the same for various other types of vessels. If a bhikṣu has already eaten his fill... [text continues].
When a great donor arrives bringing various kinds of food and drink, one should go to the *karmadāna* who is on duty that month or to an administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) to inform them.

In one region alone, there are more than a hundred countries whose scripts, languages, and pronunciations are identical to those of the present Tang state. However, because the sea routes are so vast and distant, they often take hundreds of thousands [of days] to traverse.

[The text] was translated through multiple layers of interpretation and never transmitted [to this land]. Thus, it is not surprising that those in this region remain bound to their old ways like those guarding a stump.

Did you not open [this work]? It is the *Dàxué dàzhuàn* (Great Commentary on the Great Learning) by Gu Yewang of the Liang dynasty. He extensively investigated the origins of characters, though their appearances were inconsistent;
therefore, the preface to the *Yùpiān* states: "There was one who opened the tomb of Lord Chūnzhōng and obtained its inscription; these were all in the clerical script (*lìshū*)."
Regarding the characters: examining those of Chunshen, they are the *liwen* script contemporaneous with King Wu of Zhou and the Six Kingdoms; thus, they were not from the day of the annexation.
Since the various scripts of this country, including seal and clerkly styles, still remain obscure, how can one possibly know of the events during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha?
History is not something that can be heard or seen with one's own ears and eyes. He asked again: "Now, to the west of the Western Capital, there is a high earthen mound four *zhang* tall;
popular legend says this is the 'Tower of Cang Jie for Creating Writing. How can it be said that the *lìshū* script already existed in ancient times?
He replied: "Cang Jie built up the earth on this site to construct a tower; it was not here that he observed the tracks of birds."
There is no factual basis for this. Furthermore, regarding the tradition concerning Cang Jie, its origins are rarely known within this land. Some say he was a minister of the Yellow Emperor;
others say he was an ancient sovereign. As for the script of bird tracks, it has changed into various forms over time, and what remains today is but a fragment.
Words that are of no benefit need not be elaborated upon.
*Jùqú* (鉅渠) has the third tone; it means "great. *Ài* (艾) is pronounced *ài*;
it means "old. Furthermore, there is the expression "fifty days of *ài*," which refers to the hair turning gray and white like the color of *ài* grass.
"Yǔ" (齲) is pronounced with the second tone of "qú"; it means decayed.
"Pān" (潘) is pronounced like "fān"; it refers to rice-water.
*Kǎn* (穬) is pronounced like *gǒng*.
*Xiā* (鰕) is pronounced like *xiá*.
The *kalaviṅka* is an aquatic bird resembling a water duck but smaller; its body is rounded and its tail is very short. It floats on the surface.
The *xiāngsè* (fragrant-colored) lives in the rivers and marshes of Lingnan. It does not travel in large groups; usually, there are only two or three pairs at most.
When people approach it, it immediately submerges into the water and emerges several *zhàng* away. The common folk call it "water crystal," while those who do not recognize it call it a "water duck.
It always swims and rests together with its mate, never parting from one another.
