If one receives a plain *antarvāsa*, one should add the following words: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with single-mindedness. I, the bhikṣu [Name], accept and maintain this plain *antarvāsa*. (Recite this three times.

If one intends to make an *uttarāsaṅga* or a *saṃghāṭī*, follow the same procedure as for the *antarvāsa*; the only difference lies in adjusting the wording according to whether it is an upper or lower robe.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there is a reason to relinquish it, one should assume the proper dignified demeanor and add: 'Venerable sir, please attend to me with single-mindedness.'"
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], this saṃghāṭī robe is among my three robes; having previously maintained it, I now relinquish it.
(Recite this once and then stop. The same applies when relinquishing the other two robes, or even the five robes of a Bhikṣuṇī, etc.). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If a bhikṣu living alone has a need to exchange one of his three robes, he should perform the proper deportment, hold the robe in his hand, and apply the ritual formula with both mind and speech."
[He] says: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], this saṃghāṭī robe of so many strips, now relinquish" (having spoken thus three times, he then receives the extra robe;

with the same deportment as before, he adds the formula): "I, the bhikṣu [Name], this saṃghāṭī robe of so many strips, receive" (having spoken thus three times). For the other two robes and so forth, the receiving and relinquishing are likewise.

The extra robe that has been relinquished should be treated by means of the mental act of pure giving (*cetanā-pariśuddhi-dāna*). The receiving and relinquishing for the remaining four assemblies are all conducted according to this standard. Regarding the mental act of pure giving, one should bare the right shoulder... [Sanskrit term: *huhu*].
Kneel. Holding the robe with your hands, speak these words with your mouth: "I, the bhikṣu [name], offer this extra robe as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) to [name] among the five assemblies."
(Give it to him as he wishes). As he takes and uses it (it may continue until the eleventh day. Again, with the same dignified demeanor as before, say):
"I, [Name], this extra robe, I take back from [Name]" (it may continue until the tenth day. Again, say as at the beginning): "I, [Name], this extra robe, I purify by giving to [Name]."
One may take and use them accordingly (since one discards the old in this way, one receives new ones; every ten days, one changes). The Vinaya-mūla states:
"If making new robes, it is permitted to make a single-layered *antarvāsa* (inner robe), a single-layered *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe), and a double-layered *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe).
If they are old robes, it is permitted to make a double-layered *antarvāsa* and *uttarāsaṅga*, and a four-layered *saṃghāṭī*. If they are *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robes)..."

Regarding robes: they may be worn in whatever number of layers one desires. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If the three robes are torn, provided the seams remain unbroken, the formal undertaking (*samādāna*) is not lost.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the lower edge of a robe is damaged, one should wear it inverted and secure the upper and lower parts with hooks and buttons.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "Wearing them inverted as one pleases constitutes no offense. However, if the seams of the robe are broken or severed, [the rules differ].
One should patch it with material or bind it with thread. If a garment is about to tear, one should sew it together with long thread.
If a hole is seen, it should be mended and patched. If the interior is rotted, one should fold the two layers together;
if it is completely ruined and unfit for repair, one should make it into a lamp-post or cut it into small pieces and mix it with cow dung.
Clay: It is used to fill the holes of pillars or to plaster walls. When used in this manner, it causes the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) offered by the donor to increase spontaneously.

(For example, if a torn cloth is made into a whisk and later becomes worn and shattered, it should likewise be mixed with clay and so forth for use. If a floor mat is ruined, it should be mixed with clay to coat and sweep the walking path.)
A bhikṣu should not enter a village without his robes hemmed or without fastening them with hooks and ties, except in cases of unavoidable circumstances.
If he enters the dwelling of a non-Buddhist renunciant, there is no offense if his robes are not hemmed.

If he wears his robes, he should not sit down by relaxing his body on rough or hard ground, wood, stone, refuse heaps, or any place lacking a seat; rather, he should prepare a wooden block or a piece of bark for rubbing and polishing.
Clean it. Alternatively, make a grass cushion, wrapping it with cloth; its size may be as one desires, and it should be used as a seat.

When performing manual labor, one must protect it well so that mud does not soil the robes. When traveling through places with thorns, one should lift the hem of the robe so that it does not hang down and tear.
If it should be washed, do not fail to wash it; if it should be sewn or dyed, do not fail to do so.
Sewing or dyeing [the robe] both constitute an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

When wearing the *saṃghāṭī*, one should not perform manual labor, walk on the road, sit with it wrapped around the thighs, or lie down while wearing it. One should not wear it while naked; when prostrating, the robe must not brush against the ground.
One should not wrap the knees [with the robe]. Nor should one sit or lie down upon the two lower garments. If there is no other object available, it is permitted to use them as an under-layer;
sitting or lying down in this manner is not an offense. In putting on robes, one should abandon three types of mind:

first, the mind that delights in adornment; second, the mind that uses them with contempt; and third, the mind that seeks fame through pretense, such as falsely wearing tattered clothing while desiring...
One should not harbor these three thoughts: thinking that others will recognize one’s virtues and conduct; seeking only to change the color of the robe;

or thinking that by merely obtaining enough to cover the body, one is following the Great Master’s teaching and progressing in the cultivation of wholesome qualities. Instead, one should give rise to five kinds of thoughts:
first, the thought of moderation—measuring the use so as not to cause damage; second, the thought of intervals—not wearing the same garment repeatedly.
First, it smells foul and quickly decays. Second, one should know that reflecting on the extreme difficulty from which it came gives rise to a mind of gratitude;

when using it, do not act contrary to the Dharma. Third, know the proper time: use it appropriately according to the seasons of cold and heat. Fourth, know the proper measure. Fifth, know the proper quantity.
The thirteen requisites are sufficient to sustain the body; to store away many extra robes increases greed and causes one’s practice to decline (the thirteen requisites are recorded elsewhere).
○ Regarding the four *prātideśanīya* dharmas: examine these four rules in detail.

Their substance is identical to greed and affliction; because they give rise to two faults, the Buddha prohibited them. First, by means of food and drink, one increases one’s own afflictions and delusions.
Second, due to a lack of contentment, one causes others to lose their faith and respect. Although this section on confession follows [the preceding rules],...
Chapter on Falling [into Defeat]. However, as for the nature of this offense, it exceeds that of a *pāyattika* (expiable offense). As the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"This bhikṣu should return to his residence, go to where the other bhikṣus are, and address each of them individually, saying: 'Venerable sirs, I have committed an evil dharma that must be confessed;
it was not something I should have done. I now confess it before you. The *Vinayavibhaṅga-praśna* asks: "Are the remaining offenses also permitted [to be confessed] in this manner?"
Regarding the term "confession" (*pratideśanīya*): how does it receive this name? The answer is:
because at the place where one resides, there must be a monk present to whom one must individually and separately confess; unlike other offenses, it receives this distinct name.
Furthermore, once the offense has been committed, it must be confessed immediately and may not be delayed; this too differs from other offenses. Thus should it be understood. All [of these]...
Due to the burden of greed: indeed, among all afflictions, greed is the foremost; it is the root of birth and death and the cause for future existence.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Sentient beings, when their minds are shrouded by food, drink, sexual desire, and so forth, are able to undergo rebirth.

Furthermore, this greed is termed "sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) within the ten unwholesome paths of action and the four bonds (*bandhana*). "Sensual desire" refers to the longing to obtain what belongs to others.

Furthermore, this craving is harmful to wholesome qualities. Why is this? One who is deeply attached to desire pays no heed to ethical discipline, lineage, the teachings, dignified conduct, or reputation;
they do not accept instruction and fail to perceive decline or suffering.

They do not discern between sin and merit; they are like the insane or the intoxicated, unable to distinguish the beautiful from the ugly, and like those who are blind, they do not see benefit or fortune.

Because they do not eliminate greed, the harms they suffer are manifold. If one gives rise to greed regarding food and drink, one should immediately contemplate it with revulsion and form the perception of impurity.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One should contemplate that this food arises from impurity."
Just as flesh arises from semen, blood, and the urinary tract, serving as the dwelling place for pus-worms;
and just as ghee, milk, and curd are formed through the transformation of blood and are no different from putrid pus;

and just as the sweat and grime of a cook are various kinds of impurities—if these were placed in the mouth, the brain would have two channels through which putrid saliva flows down, which then mixes with the spittle before becoming flavor. Its appearance is as follows:
It is like vomit: having entered through the gate of the abdomen, it is held by earth and moistened by water; moved by wind and boiled by fire, it is like millet being cooked in a cauldron.
The dregs and turbidity sink to the bottom, while the clear portion remains above. It is like the brewing of wine: the dregs and turbidity become feces, and the clear portion becomes urine.
The waist has three apertures. When wind blows upon the oily sweat, it disperses into the hundred vessels and mingles with the pre-existing blood.

This coagulates and transforms into flesh. From this new flesh, fat, marrow, and bone are produced. From within these, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) arises. From the union of the new and old flesh, the five sensory faculties arise.
From these five faculties, the five consciousnesses arise. Following the sequence of the five consciousnesses, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises.
One discriminates and grasps at signs, deliberating upon the beautiful and the ugly; thereafter, afflictions such as the notions of "I" and "mine," as well as various sinful karmas, arise.
Furthermore, when reflecting on this food, one realizes that the labor expended is immense; consider, for instance, a single bowl of rice.
The laborer sheds sweat; gather it and measure it. If the food is meager yet the sweat is profuse, such is the bitterness of this sustenance.
As soon as it enters the mouth, it becomes impure; within a single night, it transforms into excrement and urine. What was once a delicious flavor becomes something one loathes to behold.
The practitioner reflects on such wretched food: "If I harbor greed and attachment for it, I shall fall into the three miserable realms," just as...
This is the contemplation of food. One should cultivate revulsion for the five desires. For example, there was once a brahmin who practiced the dharma of purity.
Due to certain circumstances, he arrived in an impure land and thought to himself, "How can I avoid this impurity?
Only by eating dry food can I attain purification. He saw an old woman selling cakes made of white marrow and said to her: "I..."
"There is a reason. He has been staying here for a hundred days, and I have constantly made cakes and sent them to him, giving you much payment for them.
The old woman made cakes every day and sent them to him. The Brahmin, being greedily attached to them, ate his fill and was delighted.
As the cakes the old woman made gradually lost their color and flavor, he asked her, "For what reason has this happened? The mother replied:
Because the abscess had healed, the brahmin asked, "What does this mean? His mother said, "The lady of our great house developed an abscess in her private parts.
I treated it by applying flour and ghee; when the abscess ripened, pus came out, and I mixed it with ghee and made cakes.
I did this every day, and gave these cakes to you. That is why the cakes were so good. Now that the lady's abscess has healed, I shall [no longer do so]."
"Where else could I have obtained it? Upon hearing this, the Brahmin struck his head with both fists, beat his breast, and retched dryly.
"How shall I violate this pure dharma? I am finished! Abandoning his business, he hurried back to his own country. The practitioner is just like this:
becoming attached to these foods and drinks, he delights in eating them without contemplating their impurity; later, he will suffer the retribution of his actions.

What regret can avail now? (The four bonds: first, the bond of sensual desire; second, the bond of ill-will; third, the bond of attachment to precepts and rituals; fourth, the bond of the view of self). △ First:
Receiving Food from a Nun Who Is Not a Relative (This is an uncommon offense; for a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*).

The character 讓 (ràng) is pronounced with the level tone (qiè) as liàng, or with the departing tone (qùshēng). It means humility. To place others before oneself is called "yielding" (ràng); furthermore, because one does not dare to accept [the honor] for oneself, one yields.
*Xiǎn-zhuó* (浣濯):
Pronounced *xiǎn* (with the initial *zhí* and final *qiè*) and *zhuó* (pronounced *zhúo*).
It means to wash until it is lustrous, bright, and pure. *Prāyaścittika*.
This term has no direct equivalent; by way of meaning, it is translated as "to confess toward another.

The *Upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra* translator explained it as either "one should preach the Dharma" or "one should reveal [the offense]. The *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: "The essence of this precept carries no formal name for the offense;
one confesses the transgression once before a single person. The rest is as explained above.
△ Second [Offense] of Eating Food Directed by a Bhikṣuṇī (This is a unique precept; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta).
If there is not even one bhikṣu present...
If there is not even a single bhikṣu—meaning that the minimum limit has been reached—one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
This precept constitutes an offense when a bhikṣu accepts food offered by the instruction of a bhikṣuṇī. The Vinaya-mūla states:
"There was a bhikṣuṇī who pointed out [the food] and gave it; if there is not a single bhikṣu, he speaks to that bhikṣuṇī. This refers to the bhikṣu.
One should confess this transgression before the bhikṣus. Other vinayas all state:
"If among the bhikṣus there is not even a single bhikṣu who speaks to that bhikṣuṇī, then all those bhikṣus should confess this transgression before the bhikṣus.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If there is a bhikṣuṇī who instructs a bhikṣu to provide him with food, [this constitutes] the first [offense]."
The presiding elder (sthavira) should speak. If he does not heed the words of the presiding elder, the second elder should speak next;

in this manner, it proceeds down the line until it reaches those who have newly received the precepts. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one eats without having been rebuked three times, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya (*vinayātikrama*).
If one continues to eat after being rebuked three times and still does not stop, there is no offense. Once one person has rebuked [the offender], everyone may eat.

There is no offense. The *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: "If two groups of the Saṃgha are seated together, if even one person among one group speaks to that bhikṣuṇī, the second group is also said to have spoken.
If they enter separately, sit separately, eat separately, and exit separately, then the bhikṣu who entered the donor’s gate should question the bhikṣu who exited."
"Which bhikṣuṇī? [The questioner asks. "In this matter, she instructs the donor to give food to the bhikṣus. [The respondent] answers: "So-and-so. [The questioner] should ask:
"Has she been instructed? [The respondent] answers: "She has been instructed. This person who enters the bhikṣu-saṃgha is also called "instructed.
When there are bhikṣus leaving the city gate, the bhikṣus entering the city should ask those leaving. If those leaving have already been instructed, [they are considered instructed].
Entering is also called "restraining. What is meant by "restraining" should be expressed as: "Sister, please stop for a moment;
wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating," or "Please stop for a short while; wait until all the bhikṣus have finished eating," or "Please stay a little longer."
Waiting for the bhikṣus to finish eating, some said, "Please wait a moment. Waiting for the bhikṣus to finish eating.
△ Third [Section]: Receiving Food from a Family Home (This is a unique precept;
for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta. The Sarvāstivādins say that this precept is shared with the bhikṣuṇīs).

"Those who are still training" (*śaikṣa*) refers to those in the remaining three fruits [of the path] whose afflictions and outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted; they must still train in order to sever them.

As for the Arhat, their outflows are already exhausted and what was to be done has been accomplished; thus they are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*). "Family" (*kula*) refers to the four castes. *Vinaya-saṃgraha*.

It is said: "Those who are householders" refers to those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*)—namely, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*).
It is only these persons in training who reside in the household; it does not refer to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If the wife is a noble one (*āryā*) and the husband is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or if the wife is an ordinary person and the husband is a noble one, in either case, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a householder should not be performed for them."

If both husband and wife are noble ones (ārya) and free from the mind of stinginess and greed, only when their wealth is completely exhausted should the *śaikṣakula-karman* (the formal act regarding a family under training) be performed for them. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If the Saṃgha performs the *śaikṣakula-karman*, one must not avoid going there like a bird dodging an arrow; rather, one should go at appropriate times to visit them, preach the Dharma, and engage in discussion."
Regarding Dharma-affairs: if members of a family wish to give a gift, one should say, "Set it aside for a while; I myself shall know the proper time.
If the members of the family say, "Venerable sir, why do you not accept this gift? Do you consider us poor? at that time one should say, "You are not poor.
As the World-Honored One has said, a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is endowed with four qualities... [regarding] the voice-hearers (*śrāvaka*).
Among those who hear [the Dharma], they are the greatest of the wealthy. What are these four?
First, they give rise to a firm root of faith toward the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—a faith that cannot be destroyed by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, or worldly people.
Second, they give rise to a firm root of faith in the Dharma. Third, they give rise to a firm root of faith in the Saṅgha. Fourth...
One who gives rise to firm roots of faith in the precepts—faith that cannot be destroyed by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, or people of the world—is said to have accomplished these four dharmas.
Among the Tathāgata’s śrāvakas, such a person is not poor, but is the most wealthy of all.

△ Fourth: Receiving Food in a Frightening Place (This is a unique precept [not shared with nuns]. For nuns, it is a *dukkaṭa*, because nuns are not permitted to dwell in forest hermitages that are frightening places).
Kūli is also called Kūlī;

this is his clan name (*gotra*). According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-daśādhyāya*, in places where there is fear or perilous difficulty, one must perform a formal act of notification and motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to appoint a single bhikṣu as an observer and guardian. As...
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: The Buddha said, "In a dangerous forest area, one should appoint a bhikṣu endowed with five qualities to act as a guardian:
he must be free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; and he must be well-acquainted with the roads. First, one should inquire whether he is capable and exhort him with the matter at hand.
If he says he is capable, he should be dispatched by means of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation). As for that guarding bhikṣu..."
There is a practice regarding the Dharma that I shall now explain. A monk on guard duty should thoroughly inspect the area within half a yojana (fifteen li) around all four sides of the monastery.
If there is any place of danger, he should either raise smoke or hang up banners and flags.
Or one may spread tree leaves crosswise across the path, or write characters to inform [others]. If there is no place of fear, one should hoist a white banner.
If one does not follow this ritual procedure, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. If the guardian is hungry, [one should provide for him].

Regarding those who require food: at the time of the morning meal, they may eat cakes according to their inclination. If a companion is required, one should grant [permission] through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), which should be performed as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of proceeding to the perilous forest, a place of fear."
Regarding that road, he is well able to observe it. If the Saṃgha deems the time right and grants permission, the Saṃgha should authorize it.
The Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as an observer in that perilous forest and place of fear. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal ritual (*karman*) is established according to the motion. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The person for whom the ritual is performed..."
One must certainly employ those who are brave, strong, and capable of repelling the enemy. If they are unable to repel them, the entire Saṃgha should go to the place where the enemy is.
If they are still unable to do so, one should inform the donor (dānapati) and have many people provide protection.
Regarding the *Śikṣāpada-dharmas*:

Now, as for the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya, their four modes of deportment accord with the regulations and their myriad practices conform to the rules. They avoid the five heterodox paths that deviate from the right way and enter the level thoroughfare of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Internally they concentrate on true wisdom; externally they take others as their model. Thus they benefit both themselves and others.

The conduct of his vast mind overflowed with loving-kindness; he emptied himself of notions of "I" and "mine. He entered deeply into the gate of Prajñā, cultivating both the Great and Small Vehicles simultaneously, and guarding equally against both the nature and the prohibitions.
He feared even the slightest leak in his life-buoy and was cautious of the grave transgressions that arise from a single drop.

He followed the right livelihood to adorn the noble lineage and upheld the Bequeathed Dharma to alert and propagate it. Beholding the age of the Semblance Dharma, he remained as if still in the world, observing it with clarity.
As if the *caityas* were still present, they looked up to the original model of the Dragon City (Nālandā) and reverently honored the solemn entrustment of the Crane Grove (Śrāvastī).
Their learning encompassed the Tripiṭaka, and their wisdom penetrated the Five Vehicles. They abandoned the mind of solitary wandering and bore the practice of the two fields of merit.

Having fully traversed the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* without weariness, they bore the burden of rescuing those drowning in the six realms of existence without fatigue. Possessing such wondrous conduct, these are truly sons of the Śākya; they are also called—
The Bodhisattva’s vast mind: if one studies in a biased manner, then phenomena and principle will fail to be harmonized.

One may either cling to the Great [Vehicle] while slandering the Small, or practice the Small while misrepresenting the Great; or uphold phenomena while discarding principle, or preserve principle while denigrating phenomena.
When these views diverge from one another, they revert to becoming those of external paths. Therefore, within the Mahāyāna, the narrow mind is censured as that of an outsider and a thief.
Such a person, disparaging those with great learning and calling them biased or evil, is termed one of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). As the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"If bodhisattvas should think thus: 'Only by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā* does one attain liberation.'"
To think that there is no other dharma through which one can attain liberation is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To think that "this dharma is profound" or "this is not profound" is called overweening pride. To think that "this dharma is pure" or "this dharma is not pure" is called overweening pride.

To think that "these are the dharmas of the Buddhas," "these are the dharmas of the *pratyekabuddhas*," or "these are the dharmas of the *śrāvakas*" is called overweening pride. To think that "this dharma should be practiced" or "this..."
One should not act [in such a way]; this is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride). To think, "This is a profound dharma" or "This is not a profound dharma," is called *adhimāna*.

The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva, regarding the prohibitions established within the Tathāgata’s *prātimokṣa* and *vinaya*, acts for the sake of protecting sentient beings—causing those who lack faith to believe and increasing the faith of those who already believe"—[this is likewise].
This is the training of the śrāvaka. Why is this? Because a śrāvaka, at the very least, seeks to cross over himself;

he does not fail to protect others, causing those without faith to have faith and those who already have faith to increase and broaden their study of the precepts. How much more so for the bodhisattva, whose crossing is that of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Furthermore, a bodhisattva perceives things in this way and speaks thus: "A bodhisattva should not listen to the sūtras and teachings of the śrāvakas;
they should not accept them, nor should they study them. Of what use are the śrāvaka teachings to a bodhisattva? This is called an offense.
It is a frequent offense, an offense arising from defilement. There is no offense if one is exclusively studying the Bodhisattvapitaka and has not yet been able to master it completely.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva does not employ skillful means regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, but instead abandons it and fails to study it, exclusively practicing the sūtra-dharmas of the śrāvakas, this is called an offense; it is a grave offense. This offense arises from non-affliction.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva commits a *duṣkṛta* (minor transgression) and does not confess it, it obstructs the bodhisattva precepts. [As stated in] the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, he skillfully knows all modes of deportment and preceptual conduct;
he skillfully studies the precepts of the Śrāvakas, the precepts of the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Bodhisattva precepts.

Having cultivated such preceptual conduct, if he sees that his deportment does not accord with the assembly, he should immediately distance himself from it and refrain from acting in inappropriate places. If there is a śramaṇa..."
Regarding the conduct of precepts and dignified demeanor, one should associate with those who possess them. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If someone were to say that there are no four *pārājika* offenses, thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, two *aniyata* rules, thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, ninety-one *pāyattika*, four *pratideśanīya* rules, numerous *śaikṣa* rules, or the seven methods for settling disputes;
and that there are no *sthūlātyaya* or the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*)," [such a person should be known as a false teacher].
And as for the icchantikas: if there were bhikṣus who committed such offenses and fell into hell, while those of external paths (tīrthika) would all be reborn in heaven.
Why is this? Because those of the external paths have no precepts to violate;
therefore, the Tathāgata manifested these teachings to terrify people and thus proclaimed these precepts. It even says: "Although the Tathāgata has spoken of committing the *duṣkṛta* offense..."

Ānanda, for example, according to the calculation of years, months, and days in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, eight million years [in hell] is likewise a manifestation by the Tathāgata intended to terrify people.
To say that from a *pārājika* offense down to a *duṣkṛta*, there is no difference in gravity, is a false statement made by various Vinaya masters.
They claim this was established by the Buddha; one must certainly know that this was not spoken by the Buddha.
Such discourse is the sūtra and vinaya of Māra. Furthermore, if it is said that regarding the various precepts,
even if one violates a minor precept, down to the most subtle, one shall undergo retribution for suffering without limit— and having understood this,
one guards oneself like a tortoise withdrawing its six limbs— if there is a vinaya master who further says that whatever precepts are violated, none...
There is no karmic retribution for such a person; one should not associate with them. As the Buddha has said:
"If one transgresses even a single dharma, this is called lying; seeing no future world, there is no evil they will not commit.
Therefore, one should not associate with such people. Within my Buddha-dharma, purity is thus; how much more so for those who possess it?
One may commit a *sthūlātyaya*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or even a *pārājika* offense, yet it would not constitute a transgression.
Therefore, one must guard oneself deeply. If such dharmas as these are not protected, what other dharma could be called "prohibitory precept" (*vinaya*)?
In the sūtras, I have also taught that there are those who commit the four *pārājikas*, down to even the most subtle [offenses].

Those who commit *duṣkṛta* and other such offenses should be strictly disciplined. If sentient beings do not protect and uphold the prohibitive precepts, how could they ever perceive the Buddha-nature?
Although all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, it must be through the observance of the precepts that they subsequently perceive it.
By perceiving the Buddha-nature, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. As the sūtra says:
What has been stated is, in truth, not false. Since these are the personal words of the Great Master, how could one dare to disbelieve them?
If one knowingly violates them, then one’s own downfall is near; if one is indolent and fails to study, then liberation will have no foreseeable end.

Since you possess such a magnanimous mind and extensive wisdom, why fear minor matters of ritual conduct? Even the hundred schools of external arts require broad learning, let alone the internal scriptures.

Regarding these various rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*): according to this [text], there are one hundred such rules; however, when compared with other schools (*nikāya*), their numbers are not fixed—some increase and some decrease. The circumstances for their establishment are manifold, and the specific matters differ slightly from one another.

Nevertheless, these are primarily for protecting one’s deportment (*īryāpatha*) and thus differ from the preceding four sections (*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, and *pāyattika*). Regarding transgressions, there are two categories: intentional and unintentional. For intentional offenses, one must confess them before others; for unintentional ones, they are extinguished through self-reproach. These one hundred rules are all prescribed for both monks and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), though there are only one or two that are not common to both.

These exceptions will be noted in the commentary below as they appear in the text. As for this present section on training, it is not possible to list each rule individually with its specific characteristics; therefore, based on approximately one hundred rules, ten general categories are described here to form two verses.

This explains the sequence: (1) the matter of putting on robes; (2) the matter of entering a village; (3) the matter of sitting and rising; (4) the matter of eating and chewing; (5) the matter of protecting the alms bowl; (6) the matter of defecation and urination; (7) the matter of preaching the Dharma; (8) the matter of stupas and images;
(9) the matter of walking on the path; (10) the matter of climbing trees.

(1) Properly adjusting the lower robe and the saṃghāṭī; (2) entering a village; (3–11) the eleven matters concerning sitting; (12–32) the twenty-one matters concerning eating and chewing; (33–34) the two matters concerning protecting the bowl; (35–37) the three matters concerning defecation and urination; (38–57) the twenty matters concerning preaching the Dharma while holding [the bowl];

(58–83) the twenty-six matters concerning revering the stūpa, the vihāra, and the image; (84–85) the two matters concerning walking on the road; (86) climbing a tree—these are all the dharmas that a śramaṇa should study.
*Śikṣā-karaṇīya* (or *karaṇa*) is also rendered as *kailai*. In the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, it is written as *śiṣa-karaṇīya*. *Śiṣa* means "to learn.
*Karaṇīya* means "that which should be practiced. Thus, according to its meaning, it is translated here as "that which should be learned" (*yīngdāngxué*). One should learn.
This refers to matters that ought to be studied. A foreign corruption of the sound is *śikṣāpada*, which the Hu-seng (Central Asian monks) translated as "guarding the precepts.
This means that because these offenses are subtle and extremely difficult to maintain, one establishes them by studying and guarding them accordingly.
The *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* asks: "In the other sections it is not said 'one should study,' yet this precept alone is so; why is this?"

The answer is: The other sections are easy to uphold, yet their offenses are grave; if one commits them, the offense is established, and one must either repent before the assembly or repent face-to-face.

This precept, however, is difficult to uphold, yet its offense is light. Should one happen to commit a transgression, if the mind feels regret and one resolves to train, no formal name for the offense is incurred;
it is simply stated that "one should train. Even if one were to intentionally violate these rules of training within this section, [the consequence is as described].
All should perform the confession for a *duṣkṛta* offense. As the *Vinaya-mūla-sūtra* states: "If one acts intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta* that requires confession;
because it was done intentionally, one also commits a *duṣkṛta* of improper conduct (*anācāra*). If it was not done intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta*."

According to the various Vinayas and Śāstras, both intentional and unintentional acts are clearly distinguished. For an intentional act, one should perform confession (*pratideśanā*) before another person;
for an unintentional act, one need only reproach one's own mind and repent, vowing to be careful in the future. As the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"If a bhikṣu does not rely on the Buddha’s teachings, disregards shame, and intends to commit an unrighteous act, he incurs [the offense] upon grasping and spreading out his robe."
This constitutes a mental offense of regret (*kaukṛtya*). If one puts it on over the body, one incurs an offense of regret that must be confessed.
If a bhikṣu has a compliant intention but wears the robe improperly—whether due to negligence, forgetfulness, or ignorance—and thus wears it in an unrighteous manner, [he incurs an offense].

One merely incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) through self-reproach. Furthermore, according to various Vinayas and Śāstras, it is frequently stated that the Buddha established the five categories of precepts (*pañca-varga-śīla*).

This is the first of these categories. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Since its establishment occurred at the beginning, why does it now appear later? It answers: "The Buddha established it at the beginning;
however, those who compiled the Dharma-piṭaka placed it later in their systematic arrangement. Why is this? Although the name of the offense..."
First, there are five degrees of gravity. Because the heavy precepts come first and the light precepts follow, this precept is the lightest among the five categories and is therefore placed last.
Furthermore, one is an actual offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) while the other two are prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*);

since the actual offense comes first and the prohibited offenses follow, it is placed first. Moreover, one is an offense without remainder (*anavaśeṣa*) while the other two are offenses with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*); for this reason, it is considered grave.
Those that are heavy come first; those that are light come last.
*Nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* is sometimes called *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī*, sometimes *nīpasaṅghāṭī*, and sometimes *nirva-sanna*. (From the *Xiyu ji*)
It is called *nīvāsana*; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "skirt. The old term *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* is an error.
As it has neither straps nor loops, when one is about to wear it, one gathers the fabric into pleats and secures it with a cord. Regarding the pleats, each school differs;
as for the colors, they vary between yellow and red (the rest is explained below). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: When the Buddha was at Vārāṇasī, there was a rishi...
While staying in the Deer Park at Rṣipatana, the five bhikṣus, though they had left the household life, still wore the dress of laypeople;
their deportment and appearance were far from dignified. At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself: "The Buddhas of the past..."
"How should the assembly of śrāvakas be instructed regarding their clothing? At that time, the devas came forward and said to the Buddha, "It should be as the clothing worn by the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
The World-Honored One then used his divine eye to observe and know that it was exactly as the devas had described;
there was no difference in the matter. He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "From this day forward, you should be like the Śuddhāvāsa devas."
He put on the nivāsana (undergarment) with a neat and rounded fit. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* asks:

Among the five categories of precepts, why did the Buddha specifically prohibit [the wearing of] the nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī (outer robe) and the three robes [only] when observing the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities?

The answer is: When the Buddha established the five categories of precepts (*pañca-pārājika*), one should in all cases contemplate the Buddhas of the three periods of time as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
However, because a great deal of time has passed, the written records have been lost; thus, while they are entirely absent from the other categories, they alone remain here.

Furthermore, when the five categories of precepts were established, this [category] was originally at the very beginning, but those who later compiled the Dharma-treasury arranged it toward the end. For this reason, this category...

Because it is fundamental, it is not mentioned in the other chapters. Furthermore, if this precept were considered minor compared to the others, future disciples would fail to develop a sense of profound respect for it.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, observing with his Buddha-eye the Buddhas of the past and future as well as the Śuddhāvāsa deities, subsequently established it so that sentient beings of future generations would not give rise to the sin of arrogance. Moreover, throughout the three periods of time...
The precepts established by the Buddhas have both common and differing aspects; among the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*), they do not necessarily all coincide.
However, this practice of wearing the *nivāsana* (undergarment) and the *kāṣāya* (robe) is entirely the same for all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Therefore, regarding this precept, one should observe the example of the Buddhas and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, whereas for the other categories of offenses, one need not do so.
The *tāla* tree leaf was formerly called *baidu* (貝多) or *baiduo* (貝多羅); this translates as "bank" (*tīra*).

Its shape is like that of the *zōnglǐ* (椶櫚) palm found here in this region, and it also resembles the *guīshàn* (葵扇) tree of Lingnan. It grows straight and tall; the largest reach a height of seventy or eighty feet.
The flowers resemble yellow millet seeds; their leaves are long and broad, and their color is lustrous. When writing in India, there is nothing that does not employ them.
What is currently called "palm leaf" (*baïyè*) is merely an abbreviated name. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to it as the *tālī* tree.
It is over a hundred cubits high; its upper branches have few leaves, and its shape is like an umbrella. Although its trunk is tall, its fruit is very scarce.
The Vinaya states that when making a *tāla* leaf for wearing as a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, one should let the two front corners hang down.
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, letting the two corners hang down is the "fish-tail" style of wearing it. As for the *tāla* leaf style of wearing it, the folds rise up like...

Regarding the *tāla* leaf: the *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states that this refers to grasping the edge of the lower garment (*nivasana*), folding it finely into pleats, and tucking them all together at the waist so that its shape resembles a *tāla* leaf—gathered at the top and spreading out below.
This is similar to the secular skirts of this region, which are likewise pleated at the top and spread out below;
however, the difference lies in the fact that those [secular skirts] are already pleated when worn.
