(As explained in detail in the Vinaya texts. The *Nèifǎ zhuàn* states: Regarding the method for wearing the lower robe (*saṃkakṣikā*), I shall briefly set forth its general outline.

For instance, according to the Sarvāstivāda school’s style of making the lower robe, it measures five cubits in width and two cubits in length. It may be made from silk, fine cloth, or plain cotton, whichever is available.

In the Western Regions, these are all made as single layers; in China, one may make them double-layered at will. The dimensions of the width and length are determined by one's preference. Once it has been wrapped around the body, lift it up...
Let it pass over the navel. With the right hand, pull up the upper corner on the left side, drawing it inward toward the right side of the waist.
Take the outer edge of the upper hem on the left side to cover the left flank (the side near the right hand is the right hem; the side near the left hand is the left hem).
With both hands, lift the two sides so they are perfectly level and the center is held upright; thus, three pleats are formed. Afterwards, with both hands...
Each [corner] is gathered up to the waist; all three folds are drawn back to cover it.
Each of the two corners is lifted up by three fingers' breadth and tucked toward the spine, allowing them to enter between the waist by about three fingers' breadth.

Even if the sash has not yet been tied, the robe will remain on the body and not fall off. Afterwards, take the waist-sash, approximately five cubits (*hasta*) in length, hook it at the center, and lift it upward.
Below the navel, smooth the upper edge of the skirt; draw it back, crossing the two rows in front, and pull them alongside to the left and right.
Firmly press both sides with one hand and wrap the two cords around them; this may be done three times. If they are too long, cut them off.

If it is short, add more. The ends of the sash-bands should not be embroidered with colorful patterns; this is what is meant by wearing the skirt in a neat and orderly fashion, forming the specific tradition of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Wearing the *pāṭalimandala* (the lower robe) over the *nivāsana* (inner garment) is precisely that which is authentic.
This is translated as "tying the skirt neatly. The width of the cord should be like the surface of a finger;
whether it is square or round, as in the case of boot-cords or sock-strings, either is acceptable. Cords made of hemp or similar materials are not permitted by the Vinaya texts.
Whenever one sits on a small stool or bends down, one should pull the skirt upward and tuck the lower corners of the skirt tightly under the hem of the skirt. Tuck them into...

The robe should cover the crotch, but it is sufficient to conceal both knees; leaving the shins exposed is not a fault. It must extend upward to cover the navel and downward to reach four finger-widths above the ankles;
this is the protocol for lay dwellings. If one is within a monastery, it is also permissible for it to reach halfway down the calf.

These measurements were personally established by the Buddha himself; they are not to be arbitrarily adjusted higher or lower according to human whim. How could it be appropriate to willfully violate the teaching?
The essential point is this: following ordinary sentiments, those who wear skirts (śāṭaka) that extend so long they sweep the ground commit two faults:

first, they waste the pure offerings of those with faith; second, they show contempt for the Great Master’s precepts. Even if one were to apply oneself with earnestness, who could possibly accept such a garment?
Among ten thousand people, perhaps not one would truly keep this in mind. In the Western Regions, all skirts are worn horizontally; even their white woolen cloths follow this practice.
The width is two cubits. If it is only half that size, it is difficult for the poor to obtain; in such a case, one must sew the two ends together, cutting open the interior to serve the purpose.
This is the protocol for wearing the robe, as fully detailed in the Vinaya texts. However, I have merely briefly set forth the essential points here;

a detailed discussion cannot be conducted without meeting face-to-face. Nevertheless, the distinctions among the four schools are manifested through the manner of wearing the lower garment (*saṃghāṭī*).
The Sarvāstivādins fold both edges outward in a double pleat.
The Mahāsāṃghikas gather the right skirt at the left side and tuck it inward so that it does not fall. Western women wear their skirts no differently than the Mahāsāṃghikas;
the regulations for the Sthaviras and Saṃmitīyas are likewise, differing only in that they turn the fabric outward straight and fold it sideways.

The manner of inserting [the girdle] differs; however, the construction of the waistband itself is no different. For nuns, it follows the rules of their respective schools (*nikāya*) just as for monks, with no separate form at all.

(Regarding the four schools: first, the Mahāsāṃghika; second, the Sthavira; third, the Mūlasarvāstivāda; and fourth, the Saṃmitīya. These four schools are the ones most commonly transmitted in the Western Regions.)
*Zhé* (襵):
pronounced *zhé* (質涉切), with the sound of *zhé* (摺). It refers to the pleats of a garment. *Chòu* (皺): pronounced *chòu* (側救切), with the sound of *zòu* (縐). It means to be puckered or crinkled.
"Many pleats and wrinkles" (*zhèchòu*) refers to making many fine pleats.
*Jiǎo-zhuān* (also written as *zhuàn*) is pronounced *chuán* (same as *zhù* and *yuǎn*). The *Zílín* states that it refers to the calf muscle, which is the belly of the foot.

Having properly adjusted the three robes (as detailed in the Vinaya text), Śāriputra then entered the house of a layperson, where he suffered from the wind blowing his cut-and-sewn robe off his shoulder.
The Buddha said: "I permit hooks and toggles to be attached at the corners. The *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states:

Regarding the method for wearing the dharma robes and the fashioning of the toggles and loops, these shall be set forth according to the Vinaya. One may take a robe of five cubits and fold it into three pleats.
At the folded portion of the shoulder, four or five finger-widths from the edge, one should attach a square patch measuring five fingers on each side, which is to be embroidered all around.
At the four corners, pierce a small hole in the center with a needle to secure the neck-cloth (*kaṭhina*).
This cloth may be made of cord or silk, with a thickness similar to that of a shirt’s collar, approximately two finger-widths in length. Tie it firmly; cut away the excess.
Pass the cloth through the hole and pull it out toward the exterior, crossing it in a cross-pattern to form two loops. Knot them on the inside.
In this regard, as for the pleated section at the chest, fasteners should be attached along the edge, just like the fasteners on a shirt; this is the method.
First, the original design is presented here according to its general outline. If one wishes to master the technique perfectly, it must ultimately be transmitted face-to-face.
Fasteners with loops should also be applied to the lower hem of the garment, so that it may be worn draped over either shoulder as desired; this is the permission granted by the Sage. At both ends...
Trim the corners to a length of about eight finger-widths; attach a loop and a toggle to each. These are required for the time of eating:
fold them back across the chest and fasten the toggles together; this constitutes the essential rule. This applies whenever one is within the monastery or when facing the assembly.

It must never have a fastening cord. Regarding the method of wearing it over the shoulder like a shawl: if one is traveling abroad or entering the dwellings of laypeople, one must then fasten it with a cord.
At other times, it may simply be draped over the shoulder. When attending to private or administrative affairs, one may fold it back over the shoulder as desired;
however, when facing a venerable person, it must be kept neat and orderly. One should take the right corner of the robe and drape it broadly over the left shoulder, letting it hang down the back.

Afterwards, do not rest [the robe] upon the elbows. If one wishes to fasten the ties, one must first drape it over both shoulders; then, tuck the ties inside and loop them back toward the rear of the shoulders so that they do not slip off.
With the corners resting on the shoulders, the garment will encircle the neck, with both hands emerging from below and one corner hanging down in front.
The image of King Aśoka is precisely according to this model, as is his demeanor when holding a parasol while traveling.
This is excellent; it refers to wearing the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) in a neat and orderly manner according to the instructions.

As for the umbrella, it may be woven from bamboo and made as thin as a bamboo mat. A single layer is sufficient, with the dimensions determined by one's preference, measuring two or three feet in width.
The top should be double-layered to accommodate a handle. The length of the handle should be measured according to the width of the canopy. Alternatively, it may be thinly brushed with lacquer.
It may be woven from reeds, or fashioned like a wicker hat; even when lined with paper, it becomes sturdy.
Although this was not previously practiced in the land of China (Shenzhou), its adoption is nonetheless essential.

In sudden rain, it does not soak one's clothes; in scorching heat, it truly invites coolness. Since it accords with the Vinaya and benefits the person, there is certainly no harm in carrying it. Thus...

The various discussions on this matter are numerous and largely beneficial, yet none of them were practiced in China. When the corner of the *kāṣāya* hangs down, it precisely resembles the trunk of an elephant;
even when Indian monks arrived, they all followed suit. This was truly because the silk was so smooth that it slipped off the shoulders, leading to the corruption of the correct rule.

Later, when the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty arrived, he transmitted the method of draping the robe over the shoulders; nevertheless, many ancient virtuous masters still expressed their disapproval.

The delusions of those who cling to antiquated traditions exist everywhere. If one secures the three robes with short ties and cuts the long cords, the transgression of violating the teachings is immediately avoided.
By wearing the *kaṣāya* crosswise and removing the waistband, the labor of sewing and stitching is simultaneously spared.
As for the water flask and alms bowl, each should be suspended from both shoulders so that they merely reach the armpits; it is improper to let them cross over the chest. Its...
The loops [of the robe] should not be long; they should merely suffice to pass over the shoulders. If they are crossed and draped across the chest, it will cause one to feel short of breath.
This was never the original design and must not be practiced. The people of the northern region of Suli mostly practice this crossing;

such variations follow local customs and are truly not the Buddha’s regulation. If there are other robes available, one should first drape them over the shoulders and then wear them together, covering [the body].

Regarding one’s robes and alms bowl: whether heading toward a monastery or visiting a layperson’s home, one must first reach the quarters to set down the umbrella before untying the knots and hanging the robes and bowl upon the wall in front of the room.
One should provide plenty of ivory pegs so that there will be no lack of space for placing items when needed.
Furthermore, as for those who make their *kāṣāya* from thin silk, the fabric is often too slippery to remain on the shoulder.
When performing prostrations, one should let it fall to the ground; one may use any non-falling material for this purpose, though silk, fine wool, or white felt are most essential.
As for the *saṃkakṣikā* (under-robe), it is used to cover the shoulders; adding one more cubit to its length is necessary to accord with the original ritual requirements.
Regarding the method of wearing it, one should expose the right shoulder and cross it over the left arm; it should be worn constantly within the dwelling quarters. Only...

Give this to him as a lower garment (*saṃkakṣikā*). When he goes outside to pay respects to the Honored One, he may add other robes as appropriate (the rules for wearing the *saṃkakṣikā* are explained in detail in the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya).
The *Mātṛkā-sūtra on Entering the House of a Layperson* states: Regarding the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu when entering the home of a donor (*dānapati*), he should not engage in frivolous play;
he should not harbor arrogance based on self-reliance; he should not be flighty or impulsive; he should not speak without restraint or hesitation; and he should not be confused or disorderly.

One should not speak without a coherent thread of discourse. Because it is improper to sit at a great distance, one should lower the body and approach the other person to converse. Furthermore, one should not sit too close together while talking.
One should not sit with legs drawn up in a squatting posture or on one side. One should not sit while shouting loudly. Although one maintains dignified deportment, [these faults must be avoided].
One should not sit displaying the appearance of possessing virtuous qualities. One should not sit with the thighs crossed.
One should not sit with the knees crossed. One should not sit with the feet crossed. One should not sit using the hands to feel about or search to the left and right.
One should not sit with one's feet moving or without remaining still. One should not sit upon a large jar or vessel.
One should not sit alone with a bhikṣuṇī in a quiet room. One should not sit alone with a woman in a room.
One must not sit in a lower position while preaching the Dharma to someone seated on a high seat. A bhikṣu should always practice patience amidst all forms of decline and gain.
This is called the method for a bhikṣu to sit when entering a household. Furthermore, there are nine circumstances in which a bhikṣu, knowing the mind of a donor, should not sit to preach the Dharma:
first, if a bhikṣu enters another’s house and the donor, although they prostrate to him, [does not invite him to sit].

1. If one knows that [the host] does not give rise to a mind of respect, one should not sit. 2. Although one goes out to meet and welcome [the host], if the mind is not earnest and respectful, one should likewise not sit.
3. Although [the host] offers a seat, if one knows the mind is not sincere, one should likewise not sit. 4.
Although [the host] invites one to sit, if they place one in an irreverent position, one should likewise not sit. 5. Even if there is some Dharma being preached...
1. If they speak words that are contrary to the Dharma, one should not sit with them, as their mind does not accept such speech.

2. Although one hears of those with virtue, if they do not believe or accept it, one should not sit with them. 3. If they have something to request and, knowing they possess much, give only a little, one should not sit with them.
4. When arriving at their house, if there is fine food, they do not provide it.

Furthermore, one should not sit when coarse food is being prepared. Ninth, although one may be provided with what is necessary, if it is given according to the manner of a market transaction, one should likewise not sit.
(The opposite of these nine points is when one should sit and preach the Dharma. When a bhikṣu enters the house of a layperson, he should collect his mind like the metaphor of moonlight.
When walking through a village, he should proceed with humility, reverence, and a sense of shame; he should not...
With a haughty mind and heedlessness, devoid of shame and remorse, they act with distraction. As for the method of collecting the mind:
it is like a person whose feet tread upon a high mountain, a precipice, or a sheer and perilous cliff; at every moment of thought, fear arises, and no other thought remains.
It is also like a person at the very summit of a steep height, facing a deep abyss, giving rise only to a heart of fear, and nothing else.
Without other thoughts, when entering a village, one should collect the mind so that it does not scatter; it should be just like this.
Monks, you should collect your minds when entering a village, just as Kāśyapa entered the village and walked about. As the Blessed One said:
If a bhikṣu, when wishing to enter a village, gives rise to such thoughts as: "May all that the donor possesses be given to me alone;
let nothing be given to others. May they give much to me and not little. May they give what is excellent."
"Do not give to me with ill-will; give with a mind of reverence, and do not give without reverence.
Having formed this thought, he enters the village, yet whatever he seeks does not accord with his wishes.

At those places where he seeks, he develops a sense of withdrawal, becoming sorrowful, anxious, ashamed, and distressed by suffering, finding no joy. If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to enter a village to beg for alms...
He does not form such thoughts regarding what is obtained—whether it be much or little, good or bad.
Thus, he gives rise to no mind of sorrow, anxiety, shame, or affliction. Monks, when Kāśyapa enters a village, he never forms such thoughts.
Because he does not form these thoughts, he does not fall back from any matter, whether it be good or bad, much or little.
The mind... up to the point that it does not give rise to thoughts of suffering or displeasure.
At that moment, the World-Honored One moved his hand through the air and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "This hand now revolves in mid-air without obstruction and without being bound.
Bhikṣus who walk in the world should likewise have minds that are unobstructed and unbound. If a person seeks wealth, they should act..."
The mind controls the body; only then is it attained. If one wishes to seek merit, one must bind the mind and discipline the body; only then will the retribution be obtained.

If there is a bhikṣu who maintains equanimity toward both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and upon seeing others gain benefit, feels as if he himself had gained it and gives rise to sympathetic joy—such a bhikṣu is fit to serve as a teacher for the world. O bhikṣus, Kā...
When the leaves enter the village, they are unobstructed, unbound, and ungrasped. Those who desire gain seek gain;
those who desire merit seek merit. Just as one rejoices when gaining benefit for oneself, one likewise rejoices when seeing others gain benefit, being exactly the same in both cases.
It is like a hand moving through the air: there is no obstruction and no binding.

*Xièlèi* (脅肋). *Xiè* is pronounced with the *qū* and *yè* initials; it belongs to the *xiǎn* (險) rhyme group in the entering tone (*rùshēng*). It refers to the armpits on the left and right sides of the body.

*Lèi* (肋) is pronounced with the *lì* and *dé* initials; its sound is *lē*. It means "bone. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "It is called *lèi* because it restrains (*lè*) the five viscera (*wǔzàng*). Thus, it serves to bind and restrain the five internal organs.
● Vinaya Piṭaka, Fascicle 20: "Evil Beasts" (èshòu). [The character] shū (舒) is pronounced with the *qiè* (切) tone;

[the character] shōu (收) is pronounced with the *qù* (去) tone. Birds that fly are called *qín* (禽); those that run are called *shòu* (獸). Furthermore, those in the wild are called *shòu* (獸), while those living in dwellings are called *qín* (禽).
It says: "To keep [ferocious beasts]. "Ferocious beasts" refers to all evil oxen, horses, dogs, tigers, wolves, lions, elephants, and so forth.
"Cun-zuo" (蹲坐)—the second character is pronounced *cun*—means to squat; it refers to sitting such that the buttocks do not touch the ground. In Sanskrit, this is called *utkuṭuka*.
This is translated as "squatting" (*cung-ju*). It means that both feet are planted on the ground and both knees are held upright (the character *kǔ* [尻] is pronounced with the *gāo* tone;
it is synonymous with *shuí* [脽], which refers to the very end of the spinal column).
*Jiāo* (驕):
pronounced *jiāo* (with the initial *jiān* and *yáo* as the phonetic components; the tone is *jiāo*). It means dissipation, indulgence, arrogance, and self-conceit. *Shē* (奢): pronounced *shīzhē*.
The character *yīn* (音) means "distant. It means "excessive" (*chě*) or "grand" (*tài*).

The character *kuāng* (匡) is pronounced with the *zhǒu* (肘) radical and the *qūliàng* (區亮) rhyme; *kuāng* takes the departing tone (*qùshēng*). Master Ying states that the tradition transmits it as being pronounced *qūfàng* (區放), meaning to extend the elbow horizontally.
The origin of this character is not fully detailed. The *Liji* (Book of Rites) states: "When sitting side by side, do not extend one's arms across [the other].

*Li* (戾) is pronounced with the *qie* (phonetic guide) *li ji*, sounding like *lei* (例). It means "oblique" or "crooked. The character is derived from a dog exiting through a door while its body is bent and twisted.
The Vinaya states: "One must not walk with a swaying body. To sway the body means to walk while twisting the body to the left and right.
A bhikṣuṇī who walks in this manner commits a pāyattika offense. To "walk hurriedly" [is as follows:]...
[The character] is pronounced *qū* (cut by *xū*) with the sound *zǔ*. The *Shìmíng* states: "To walk quickly is called *qū*; to run quickly is called *zǒu*.

[The character] *páo* (or written as *pào*) is pronounced *pú bào* (cut by *pú*). It means fierce, impetuous, and sudden. It is read in the departing tone (*qùshēng*). It denotes violence, haste, and urgency.
*Tuán fàn* (摶飯):
*tuán* is pronounced with the initial *dú* and the final *guān*, sounding like *tuán*. It means to form [the food] into a ball with one's hands. [This was done] because he was choking at the time.

The character *xiè* (歇) is pronounced *yè* (謁). It refers to the obstruction of the flow of food and air. When one suffers from such a choking sensation (*yē*), if they desire water, they should say, "I need water.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If the two teachers or the elder (*sthavira*) call out while one is eating and the food has not yet been swallowed, one may respond provided that the voice does not change.
If one cannot do so, one must wait until after swallowing before responding. If the person before one...
If someone objects, one should reply: "There is food in my mouth; therefore, I do not respond immediately.
If one lets the sense faculties run wild and speaks while holding food in the mouth, one violates the rule of training.
*Nie* (齧) means to bite;
it is also written as *nie* (囓). It is pronounced *nie* (same as the compound *yu-lie*). It means to gnaw. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If a cake or a ball of parched grain is large, one should divide it with the hand so that it is of a size suitable for the mouth."
The *āmra* fruit is sometimes called *āmla*, or *āmravali*; its correct name is *āmra*, which here means "pomegranate. Master Zhao’s commentary states:
"Its fruit resembles a peach, yet it is not a peach. Master Yuan says: "Its appearance is like that of [fruits] in this land."
The *nài* (loquat). Its flavor is like that of a pear. The *Zuanyao* states: "To translate it as 'nài' according to the old version is an error. This fruit has many blossoms but very few seeds.
Its leaves resemble those of the willow, being over one chi long and about three fingers wide. The shape of the fruit resembles a pear, though its base is hooked and curved;
it is difficult to tell whether it is ripe or unripe. It can be used to treat illnesses. In that country, it is called the "King’s Tree" (*rājavṛkṣa*).

This refers to planting it within the royal city; alternatively, it may be translated as "difficult to distinguish. The Great Sūtra states: "It is like the mango fruit (*āmra-phala*), whose ripeness and unripeness are difficult to differentiate.

This contains four propositions that explain the meaning of being "difficult to distinguish": first, both the exterior and interior are unripe; second, the exterior is ripe while the interior is unripe;
third, the exterior is unripe while the interior is ripe; fourth, both the exterior and interior are ripe. It further mentions the *āmra* tree.
As for the Jambu tree, it undergoes three transformations in one year: at times it produces flowers, their radiance and colors flourishing;
at times it produces leaves, lush and verdant; and at times they wither and fall, appearing as if dead.

The *jambu* fruit is also written as *yanpo*. The *Zhongbenqijing* (Sutra on the Origin of the Middle) calls it the *yanbi* fruit; because it does not exist in this land [of China], it was not translated.
If one translates it according to the sound *yanpo*, it means "pair" (*śamyā*) here.
"Stamen" (ruǐ) and "staminal column" (ruǐ):

the phonetic components are *lèi* and *qiè*, with the former having the third tone (*shēngshǎng*). It refers to the filaments at the heart of a flower. That which is outside the flower is called the calyx (*è*), and that which is inside the flower is called the stamen (*ruǐ*;
it is also written as *ruǐ*).
● Vinaya Piṭaka, Fascicle 21:
Khandhaka (alternatively called *Gandhaka* or *Vagga*). This is translated as "Dharma-aggregate" (*dharma-puñja*), meaning that [the contents] are grouped according to their common characteristics.

The term *khandhaka* refers to a collection formed into a single unit. Within this present Vinaya-piṭaka, those sections whose subject matter follows similar categories are divided into twenty *khandhakas*, beginning with the *Upasampadā-khandhaka* and ending with the *Kṣudraka-khandhaka*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: *varga*;
*varga* here is translated as "chapter" (*pin*). A "chapter" refers to a teaching, a category, or a class; it is also said that its legal principles and meanings are identical.
That which is gathered together in one place is called a "chapter" (*varga*).

The walnut is called *prāśī* in Sanskrit, which here means "walnut. During the Han dynasty, Zhang Qian was sent as an envoy to the Western Regions; upon his return, he reached the lands of the Qiang and Hu peoples.
He took its seeds back and planted them in the region of Qin. Later, they gradually spread to the eastern lands; thus, it is called "huáotáo" (walnut).

Its trunk is large, its leaves are thick and provide much shade, and it bears fruit in pods. When the fruit ripens in autumn and winter, one harvests and cracks the shells to take the kernels for food.
Eating it frequently strengthens the body and promotes hair growth, yet eating it in excess stirs the wind-element and generates phlegm. The outer covering of the fruit...
The *qīngpí* (green peel) dyes both hair and silk entirely black. The bark of this tree produces a very extraordinary brownish hue (commonly called "walnut").
The *bítáo* (read *bēi* or *bī*) is also called *bísì*; its leaves resemble those of the persimmon (*sì*), yet they are larger.

It is even thicker and truly possesses fine hairs. When it blooms, the flowers are yellowish-white; when it bears fruit, it resembles a chestnut (*dillenia*), being dark green-black, large, and shaped like a cow’s heart.
There are two varieties in the southern regions, blue and yellow; in Jingzhou, it is called *wubi*.

Eating it moistens the heart and lungs and quenches thirst, though long-term consumption causes a person to feel cold. It can also be used to make glue and lacquer. In the south of the Ling Mountains, it is called...
The *zhīniúxīn* (ox-heart persimmon) and the *fēnglí* (wind-pear).

Regarding the *ānlí* (pear), there are many varieties and their names are not uniform; these include what are known as the *élí* (goose-pear), *rùshèlí* (milk-leaf pear), and *xiāolí* (digesting pear).

Jie-li (Jujube), red-li (red pear), lu-li (deer-pear), sang-li (mulberry-pear), zi-li (purple-pear), qing-pi-li (green-skinned pear), xiang-shui-li (fragrant-water pear), and tang-li (quince) and other such pears—all varieties of pear are cold and sharp in nature.
Do not eat them in excess, for they cause "cold in the center" (internal chills) in people.
Eating pears in moderation digests wind, dispels heat, relieves vexation, and quenches thirst; it also removes phlegm. However, eating them in excess can also disturb the spleen.
Therefore it is said: "Li" (pear) means "li" (beneficial); it refers to the meaning of facilitating downward flow.

*Xi* (噏) and *xi* (歙) are two forms of the same character. They are pronounced with the initials *x* and *h*, followed by the finals *u* and *ji* (i.e., *xū* and *xī*). The sound is the same as *xi* (吸).
Exhalation is *chui* (吹); inhalation is *xi* (吸), which means to draw in or to drink—that is, to draw food into the mouth. The *Guangya* states: "To inhale food. [From the] Vinaya.
Regarding "sucking in food": to "suck" means to open one's mouth and call out from afar. This is like what the *Laozi* says: "If one wishes to contract [something], one must first expand it.
As for *supīra* juice:
[it is a fermented drink].
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: Regarding the method for treating wind-diseases (*vāta-vyādhi*), one should employ *suvikala-juice*. As for the preparation of this juice:
first, have a lay attendant (*karmadāna*) pound large barley grains and place them in a vessel. Add water and let it sit for two or three days until it becomes slightly sour.
Filter it thoroughly and drink it; however, it is not permitted to pour it onto a wound. The *Mātṛkā* states:

"Take medicinal roots, stalks, flowers, fruits, and leaves, place them in a single vessel, and after they have fermented with vinegar, strain them until they are clear and free of turbidity. One may consume them from the morning until the first watch of the night;
for the latter watch, it is as previously explained. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Regarding the method for preparing *sūpīra* (sour gruel) juice..."
Take the wheat and pound it lightly to remove the awns and dust, taking care not to break the grains. Rinse it thoroughly with water seven times and place it in a clean vessel.
When setting out this gruel, do not place it toward the east or the north; it should be placed toward the south or the west.
Ensure there is a clear passage for air so that no foul odors enter. It must not be placed within a stūpa courtyard or in an exposed location.
As for the method of preparation: place within [the vessel] *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, black pepper, *pippalī*, and other such items that constitute medicines for the duration of one's life.
Cover it with a clean cloth, tie it with a cord in the shape of a rooster’s foot, and place a wooden lid on top.
When receiving this liquid, dissolve it in water according to its quantity, and then drink; do not drink it without dissolving it.
Drinking is not permitted. If the heads of the grain have not been broken, one may drink it both at the proper time and at improper times.
If they are broken, one may drink it only at the proper time, not at improper times. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "First take *āmalaka*, *harītakī*, and *bibhītaka*."
Regarding "grains": these are the seven grains, beginning with non-husked rice (*śāli*).
[One takes] *āmalaka*, plantain fruit, all tree fruits, all bamboo shoots, fish, meat, honey, granulated sugar, rock salt, and *trisuṇṭhī*. All such substances are mixed together as one;
they are placed either in a jar or in a small vessel, the opening is sealed with clay, and it is set aside for three or four years to await its transformation.
When it is ripe, its color is like the color of honey. It is used to treat diseases such as wind-derangement and leprosy, these being the primary ailments.
When taking this medicine, one must consume rich and fatty food during meals. Among all medicines, none surpasses this as being the most supreme.
It may be taken after midday. If one is not ill, it may be taken by mixing it with water; however, one must not [consume it]...
Pour it over the ulcer (the names of the various medicinal fruits mentioned above are explained in the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* and other sections; they are not annotated here in detail).

"Bitter wine" (*kǔjiǔ*) is simply vinegar; because it possesses a bitter taste, it is colloquially called "bitter wine. According to the standard form, "vinegar" should be written as *zuò*, yet it is here rendered as [苦酒].

There are many varieties; therefore, they are given various names, namely: rice vinegar, honey vinegar, *qū* (fermenting agent) vinegar, barley vinegar, flour vinegar, peach vinegar, grape vinegar, vinegar made from jujubes, black raspberries (*yīngǔ*), and various other fruits, as well as vinegar made from dregs and chaff.
Among all these vinegars, only rice vinegar is the authentic one. When consuming these vinegars, one should add a small amount of water.
One purifies it by dripping [the liquid] through a fine silk strainer. Its color is like that of bamboo or reeds.
Having ascertained that it is free of insects, one may drink and use it at will, whether it be the proper time or not, and whether one is ill or healthy.

*Ti-fan* (literally "lick-rice") is vulgarly written as *ti*. It is pronounced with the same initial as *zhǐ* and the final tone of *shí* (the third tone). It means to take food with the tongue. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"One must not lick one's hands repeatedly while eating. If ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar has adhered to the hand, one should [return to] the bowl."
Wipe [the fingers] with the upper part [of the hand], gather [the food] together in one place, and then take it for eating. One must not eat by counting the fingers.
If soup, gravy, sweet, or oily substances adhere to the fingers, one must not count them; rather, wipe them as described above, gather [the food], and eat it.
If honey, rock sugar, or salt adheres to the fingertips, one may count them; there is no offense. (Note: *Gai* [pronounced *xi*] means to wipe.)

Regarding the handling of food vessels—that is, all vessels for food and drink—one must not grasp them with soiled hands. If one manifests defiled conduct now, one will later receive the calamity of impurity;
therefore, one must be cautious and careful, as stated in the *Jingjing jing* (Scripture on Purity). The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) says: "In the past, there was a certain person who..."
He served the bhikṣus, always attending to their needs and managing their affairs. He would prepare food and drink, constantly holding the vessels with his hands and saying, "Take this;
use this. He did this day after day without ever confessing his transgressions. At the end of his life, he fell among the hungry ghosts (preta).
There was a bhikṣu named Aśoka who, while going to the latrine at night, heard the sound of groaning and moaning. He asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a hungry ghost..."
The hungry ghost asked, "What conduct did you practice in your former life to fall among the hungry ghosts? He replied, "In this monastery, I served as an attendant for the Sangha.
The ghost asked, "You were originally diligent; by what cause have you fallen into this state? He replied, "I gave impure food to the assembly of monks.
The ghost asked, "In what way was it impure? He replied, "The monks had various jars and vessels for holding food, and I saw..."

Supporting the vessel with his finger, he was instructed: "Take this; use this object. Having committed an offense of *pāyattika*, he did not repent after the instruction had been proclaimed three times, and thus the transgression became increasingly grave.
For this reason, he fell among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). With both hands, he tore at his chest, flaying the skin and flesh;
he clutched his throat and gasped for breath. He was asked: "Why do you tear at your chest? He replied: "Because the worms devour my body and it is painful. He was asked again: "Why..."
He moaned and replied, "I am so overcome by hunger that I am on the verge of death.
He asked, "What do you wish to eat? He replied, "I wish to eat excrement, but I cannot obtain it. He asked, "Why can you not obtain it?
He replied, "Because other hungry ghosts push me aside, I cannot move forward. Venerable Aśvajit said, "I know what to do. The ghost said, "We pray that the Saṃgha will perform a spell for us."
The Venerable Aśvajit returned and recounted this to the assembly. The assembly asked, "He was originally diligent; why did he fall into an evil realm?

He replied, "Because he gave impure food to the Saṃgha and did not repent, he was reborn there. I prayed for him and offered a blessing, whereupon he subsequently obtained food from excrement and no longer groaned.
By this testimony, it is known that a great bhikṣu must not receive food with his own hands.
Preparing food and drink, or handling monastic utensils—if they are not monastic utensils—one may receive them with one's own hands, carry them, and give them to the Saṃgha; there is no offense.
[Also, there is no offense in] discarding the water used for washing the bowl.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When washing the bowl, one must not pour away even a single grain onto the ground.
If there are such grains, they should be gathered and placed upon a wooden board or on leaves. If they are fine particles or flour (*cūrṇa*) that cannot be gathered, there is no offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: There were some laypeople who had newly built a house and wished to have the water from a bhikṣu’s bowl sprinkled upon the floor.
[The people] considered it auspicious. The bhikṣus did not dare to sprinkle [water). The Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to sprinkle water from their bowls that contains no food upon the ground. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* says: The Buddha said:
"If someone comes to beg for bowl-water, one should wash the bowl clean, place pure water within it, recite the *ariṣa-gāthā* three times as a mantra, and then bestow it upon them."
If that person washes with it or drinks it, they can eliminate ten thousand ailments. The note states:
*Ariṣagāthā* refers to verses spoken by the Buddha found within the holy teachings (*āgama*). When recited, they possess great power;
wherever else such verses are to be recited, they are all of this same category. This is just as when one bathes at a river, pond, or well.
When drinking water, one may briefly rest under a tree to seek coolness before departing; or stay at a guesthouse;
or enter a shrine hall, treading upon a maṇḍala or stepping on the shadow of a Buddhist stūpa; or at times, one’s own shadow may obscure the countenance of the Honored One;
or when the great assembly disperses; or when entering a city or village; or when performing prostrations to the Honored One at dawn or at dusk.

[This concerns] ritual observances. Whether it be at the conclusion of each meal or when sweeping and cleaning stupas and temples—such matters are indeed numerous—one must in every case recite gāthās while performing these acts to obtain merit.
If one intentionally neglects or treats them with contempt, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
However, because the monastic community of the East River (Dōsen) did not previously practice this, I have provided this commentary so that they may understand the holy teachings.
Regarding its existence, as for the *gāthā*, there is a verse that says:
"The pleasures of the five worldly desires, Or even the pleasures of the various devas— If compared to the bliss of the exhaustion of craving, They do not equal even one-thousandth part of it.
From accumulation (*saṃskāra*) suffering arises; From suffering, accumulation arises again."
The Noble Eightfold Path can transcend [suffering] and reach the sublime state of Nirvana.

Whoever practices giving will certainly obtain its benefit and profit; if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely attain peace and bliss hereafter, even regarding such things as tears and spittle.
*Tì* (should be *tí*; pronounced with the *tài* rhyme; means nasal mucus). *Tì* (pronounced with the *tǐ* rhyme; means tears; not this meaning here).
*Tuò* (pronounced with the *tù wò* rhyme; the departing tone; means saliva). The Vinaya states: "One must not discharge feces, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva upon living grass or vegetables.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It should be done on ground where there is no grass," or during the summer... [text continues].
When the moon rises, the grass grows everywhere so that there is no vacant spot;
this refers to places where camels, oxen, horses, and other animals have walked, as well as upon bricks, tiles, stones, and dry grass leaves.

If, according to the sequence above, such places are unavailable, one should use a wooden branch to receive [the excrement], causing it to fall first onto the wood and only afterwards onto the ground. This applies even if one’s hands or feet are defiled by feces, urine, mucus, or saliva.
One may wipe oneself on living grass. One must not defecate, urinate, or spit into water.
If it rains and water suddenly overflows, one should do so upon a clod of earth, a tile, a stone, or on bamboo or wood—first falling onto the wood and then into the water.
If the hands or feet become soiled, they may be washed with water. Washing after defecating or urinating in water carries no offense. If...
When entering the water to bathe, one must not spit into it. If one is far from the bank, one should spit into one's hand and then discard it there.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If the water is not used by people, or if it is seawater, there is no offense. Even if the water is used [by people], [spitting in it is prohibited]."
If one uses a remote and desolate place where no people reside, there is no offense. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "There is no offense if it is a thicket of thorns.
If traveling through a great forest where branches and leaves grow densely together, one should avoid places frequented by people.

If crossing a field of living grass where there is no open space, one should spread dry grass or leaves upon it before defecating or urinating. If none can be obtained, there is no offense. In all cases..."
When blowing one's nose or spitting, one should not make a loud noise, nor should one do so frequently.
If one is naturally prone to much mucus or saliva, one should go to a secluded place. For a bhikṣuṇī to void excrement, urine, or spit upon living grass or vegetables constitutes a pāyattika offense.

The people of the five regions of India do not stand when voiding urine or excrement; whenever they perform these minor acts, they always squat. This is also largely consistent with the customs of the various countries of the barbarians and Hu peoples.
Only in the land of the Eastern Xia (China) are the practices different; matters there are not fixed, and many people stand while doing so.
Those who squat are few. If one were not from a squatting region, yet squatted, people would mock them as being "not male.

Likewise, if one were not from a standing region, those who stood would not find it strange. Furthermore, according to the Vinaya regulations, one may preach the Dharma to those who cover their heads or wear sandals;
however, in this place, those who wear formal crowns and prepare ceremonial shoes are considered respectful, whereas in the Five Indies, the opposite is true.
This is what is meant by "reverence. Based on these two approaches, how can one avoid contravening the prohibitions of the Sage? One should simply follow the local customs and conditions;
for instance, both the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and the Sarvāstivāda school possess abbreviated teachings that were established by the Buddha as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
He then explained it for them. Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Even if something is prescribed by me, if it is not considered pure in other regions, it should not be used.
Even if something is not prescribed by me, if it must be practiced in other regions, it must be practiced.
According to the intent of this teaching, one should follow what is considered pure according to the local custom. There is no [other way].
To act contrary to the Sage’s intention is to invite secular reproach; those who uphold [the precepts] will thus encounter no obstacles.

Should there be those who, upon merely hearing this teaching, fail to reflect and examine it deeply, and instead recklessly claim it accords with the Sage’s intent—taking other fixed prohibitions and parroting them as this very instruction—this would constitute imposing what was not prescribed and relaxing what was prescribed.
Such a person cannot escape the sin of abolishing the Teaching. Therefore, the wise must exercise profound caution.
Thus, the *Xingzong* (Essentials of Practice) states: "Within the great trichiliocosm, the Buddha is the Dharma King; the Vinaya is the Buddha’s decree, established solely by the Sage.

All others of lower rank may only rely upon and follow it. This is because the Tathāgata’s practice and fruition are perfectly consummate, having fully exhausted the nature of the light and heavy karma of all sentient beings;
even those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment downward are not yet capable of it, let alone other minor sages who would presume to [act otherwise]."
I venture to propose this analogy: it is like the rewards, punishments, and edicts of a state, which must necessarily issue from the sovereign.

If subordinates were to usurp authority or commoners were to violate their trust, ruin would follow before long. The Buddha-dharma is likewise; if one permits others to speak [contrary to it], sentient beings will not uphold it, and thus the Dharma will not endure for long.

*Mùjī* (木屐): the character *jī* is pronounced as *jí*. Footwear made of grass is called *fēi*; that made of leather is called *lǚ*; that made of hemp is called *jiè*; and that made of wood is called *jī*.
There are also *bàojī* (帛屐), which refers to footwear made of silk. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu [wears such footwear] for the sake of the stūpa or for the affairs of the Saṃgha..."
One should approach the king or the local lord and say, "Please teach me the Dharma. One should not tell him to remove his sandals, for fear that he might become suspicious.
If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure attendant) nearby, one should intend to speak to the *kappiya-kāraka*, while the king listens; thus, there is no offense.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If many people are wearing wooden clogs or leather sandals and cannot be made to remove them, one may preach the Dharma solely to those who are not wearing them;
there is no offense. (Note: *fēi* is pronounced *fèi*; *jiǎo* is pronounced *jué*)."
"Pura" is also called "Abula" or written as "Fulo. Master Ying states that the correct term is "Puo-lo," which is translated here as "short-collared boots.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should not make the leather cuff too deep; it is permitted to reach up to the ankle, but the cuff must not be like [a high boot]."
Shoes. One should open the front [of the boot] (the character for "front" is pronounced *yǎo*; the character for "leather" is pronounced *yōng*).

*Fó tǎ* (Buddha-stūpa)—the character *tǎ* is pronounced *tà* (with the initial *tuó jiǎ* cut). The *Jiètán tújīng* (Diagram Sutra of the Precept Platform) says: "As for the origin of the character *tǎ*, in the word-books of this land..."
This refers to the sound of an object falling (meaning the sound of an object dropping). It was originally not a designation from the Western Regions.
According to the Sanskrit texts, the place where the Buddha’s relics are enshrined is called *stūpa*; in the new terminology, this is *sōtōba* (stūpa).
The *Xiyu ji* states that *sōtōba* is what is known as a *futu* (pagoda). In older translations, it was called *yūba*, also *tōba*, and also *shi-yū*.
"Bō" (簸) and "shù dòu bō" (數斗波) are both erroneous transcriptions. Some translate it as "square mound" (方墳), while others translate it as "round [rǒng-jiá + shì]" (圓[冗-几+豕]).
Alternatively, it may be translated as "highly manifest. In terms of meaning, it is translated as "spiritual temple" (*lingmiao*). The *Weishu*, "Shilaozhi," states:
"After the Buddha had passed away, his body was cremated with fragrant wood. His spiritual relics were broken into fragments, large and small like grains of rice.

Striking them did not destroy them; burning them did not scorch them. Yet they possessed radiant light and divine efficacy, and were thus called *śarīra*. Kings and ministers collected and enshrined them, exhausting their offerings of incense and flowers."
Out of reverence and admiration, they constructed palatial halls and called them *stūpas*, which are like ancestral temples;

thus, it is correct that they were at times referred to as "stūpa-temples" (*tamiào*). Now, *bútú* (stūpa) is translated as "accumulation of forms," and is also named *caitya*, or alternatively *cetiya*.
Some call it *ci-mei* (支微), some call it *zhi-di* (脂帝), and some call it *zhì-duō* (制多). These are all phonetic corruptions resulting from the varying weights of the Sanskrit sounds.
It was formerly translated as "a place worthy of offerings" (*pūjā-sthāna*), or as "a place where evil is extinguished and goodness arises.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* state: "That which contains relics is called a *stūpa*; that which lacks relics is called a *caitya*. (From the *Wénjù*).
It is said: "A *caitya* is that which possesses no skeletal remains. According to this, its name cannot be established by distinguishing between the presence or absence [of relics].
Generally, wherever the Buddha or his *śrāvakas* preached the Dharma or entered *parinirvāṇa* in the West, monuments were erected there;
these are called *stūpas* and also *caityas*. Master Jing says: "After the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, had entered *nirvāṇa*..."
Humans and devas assembled together and burned [the body] with fire. The multitude gathered fragrant wood until it formed a great pile;
they then designated this place as a *caitya*. Since *caitya* carries the meaning of "accumulation," the name *caitya* arose based on the principle of its formation.
Furthermore, it is said that first, one contemplates how the World-Honored One’s manifold virtues are all gathered here; second, it was constructed by piling up bricks and earth.
Such is the detailed explanation of the meaning of the term. It is also called a *stūpa*, the meaning of which is the same as this.

The old practice of using "tā" as a general term and "zhītí" (caitya) as a specific designation is entirely erroneous. Alternatively, both may simply be common names understood by the public, regardless of their etymological distinctions.

Regarding its meaning: there are briefly two types of explanations for names in the Western tradition [India]. First, names with meaning; second, names without meaning. As for names with meaning, the establishment of the name has a basis;
that is, one explains it by relying on the relationship between the name and its referent. The essence of the name and its referent are consistently congruent.
For example, in explaining the name "Skilfully Entering" (*Suvikrānta*), first one relies on the traces of his virtues; this is establishing a name based on its meaning. Next...
It is said: "Or they understand it collectively. This means that one does not discuss its specific meaning;

rather, it refers to what people in the world commonly call "skillful entry," which is a name devoid of [specific] meaning. The *Āgama* Sūtras clarify the four sites of sanctity (*catuḥ-sthāna*), namely:

the place where the Buddha was born, the place where he attained enlightenment, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, and the place where he entered parinirvāṇa. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā* states: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada invited the World-Honored One..."
The Venerable One said, "I wish to construct a stūpa with the hair and nail-clippings of the Tathāgata. If the Buddha permits it, I shall build one.
The Buddha told the householder, "You may do as you wish. [The householder] did not know how to proceed with the construction.

The Buddha said, "From the time he descended from Tuṣita Heaven to be born in Jambudvīpa, through his conversion and guidance of sentient beings, until his parinirvāṇa—[this is the sequence of] his birth stories and holy deeds."
Regarding the traces [of the Buddha], one should act according to one's inclination. The *Sūtra on the Eight Great Sacred Stūpas* states:
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, "I shall now proclaim the names of the eight great sacred stūpas; you should listen attentively. What are the eight?
The first is the Lumbinī Garden in the city of Kapilavastu, the place where the Buddha was born. The second is the kingdom of Magadha."
Third, the place where the Buddha realized the fruit of the Way at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River.

Fourth, the place where he turned the Great Wheel of Dharma in the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi. Fifth, the place where he manifested great supernormal powers in the Jeta Grove in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Sixth, the city of Kuśinagara, the place where he descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Seventh, the city of Rājagṛha.
The place where the Śrāvakas made their distinctions; the seventh, Vaiśālī, the place where the Buddha manifested his lifespan for the sake of conversion;

the eighth, Kuśinagara, between the twin śāla trees within the śāla grove, the place where he entered nirvāṇa—regarding these eight great sacred shrines (*caityas*), if there are sons or daughters of good family who give rise to great faith...
With a devoted mind, one should construct stūpas and temples, serve them, and make offerings. Such a person will obtain great benefit and reap great rewards;
they will be fully praised, and their fame will spread everywhere, profound and vast.
Even all bhikṣus should likewise train in this. (Lumbinī, that is, Lumbinīvana).
Tuṇḍila was a Brahmin village,
also known as Tuṇḍila-brāhmaṇa-grāma. It was originally the birthplace of Kāśyapa Buddha (the origins of this village and the construction of its stūpa are detailed in the *Kṣudraka-vastu*).
*Gāozuò* (high seat):

*cú* is pronounced as *wò* (second tone), and *zuò* is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). It means a seating position. The *Guǎngyùn* states it refers to a bed or seat. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states there are two kinds of seats:
first, high beds; second, low beds. There are two types [of low beds]: first, those that are low, which are called "low"; second, those that are coarse and inferior, which are also called [low].
"Low. There are two kinds of "high": that which is tall in stature is called high; that which is exquisite and fine is also called high. *Chí* (持) means to hold.

*Shǒu* (鉾) [in ancient texts written as] *máo* (矛), now written as *máo* (矛). The three forms are identical and pronounced *mò hóu* (莫侯切), with the phonetic value *móu* (謀). It is a weapon, such as...
The *tián* (a short spear) has three edges. The *qiú móu* (long spear) is two *zhàng* in length. The *shǔ móu* (staff-spear) is one *zhàng* and two *chí* in length and has no blade.
Furthermore, the *yí móu* (barbarian spear) is two *zhàng* and four *chí* in length. The *Sengqí lǜ* (Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya) states:

"If a bhikṣu is traveling through a dangerous road or a place of terror, and a guard says, 'Venerable One, preach the Dharma for me,' if he preaches it, there is no offense. (*Tián* is pronounced like *shàn*; it is a small [spear]).
It is also a spear (the *shu* [殳] is pronounced *shū*).

Regarding the holding of a parasol, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "A parasol is a parasol made of tree bark, a parasol made of *tāla* leaves, a parasol made of *tāli* leaves, or a bamboo umbrella."
A *chattra* (parasol) includes such varieties as the layered parasol and the peacock-feather parasol; all such items capable of shielding against rain and sun are called *chattras*.
If a Dharma Master or a Vinaya Master holds a parasol while preaching the Dharma during times of wind, rain, cold, snow, or intense heat, [it is permissible].
There is no offense.
○ Regarding the Seven Methods for Settling Disputes:
One who wishes to extinguish the four types of disputes must fully employ these seven kinds of methods to eliminate them according to the specific circumstances.
One must carefully observe: remove disputes by means of the two methods; settle accusations by means of the four;
apply the three for transgressions; and resolve all matters of contention.
This is the venerable Muni’s skillful method for resolving disputes; should any litigation arise, this truly can extinguish it.
Do not seek to stop strife with strife; this only causes strife to burn more fiercely.
Just as one wishing to extinguish a blazing fire would never add more fuel, so too for those who possess wisdom:

by following the World-Honored One’s admonition and constantly practicing the six points of concord, disputes will naturally dissolve. As for those who are foolish, ignorant, and blind, [strife persists].
Violating the precepts while harboring anger, Firmly clinging to the evil habit of ignorance, And abandoning the five *smṛtyupasthānas*— if resentment is not discarded,
One will seek retribution for eons to come. When the ripening fruit of suffering and its accumulation manifests like a shadow or an echo,
Those who wish to extinguish the bonds of enmity Should cultivate the teaching of harmony and patience.

Vipaśyin Buddha taught: "This is the foremost path: Contemplate that Rṣi Kṣāntivādin, who, when Kali cut his body, Attained the Way and vowed to cross over first. In the Deer Park, he first proclaimed the knowledge [of this];
Now that you are called a son of the Śākyas, You should maintain the wisdom of non-self; Do not harbor strife or long-standing enmity."
How can one be called a son of the Śākya? It requires the essential elimination of the karma of birth and death.
Guarding the precepts and maintaining meditative concentration, the sun of wisdom illuminates the Four Noble Truths and the perfection of parinirvāṇa is complete.
If you seek the fruit of perfect enlightenment, always maintain the conduct of a newborn child; for eternal kalpas, be a companion, until together you turn the wheel of Dharma.
If any matter of dispute arises, it should be settled in accordance with the seven methods, following the instructions of the Great Teacher, in conformity with the Dharma and the Vinaya;
all nuns shall study this together.
△ Regarding the first case of *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence):
at that time, some bhikṣus performed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) even though the person concerned was not present. The Buddha said: "One should not do so when the person is not present."
[One] performs the *karmavācanā* in the presence [of the assembly]. If one performs the *karmavācanā* [without such presence], it is not valid, and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

What constitutes "presence"? It is presence of the Dharma, the Vinaya, the person, the Saṃgha, and the boundary (*sīmā*). What is presence of the Dharma? It is the Dharma upheld that extinguishes the dispute.
What is presence of the Vinaya? It is the Vinaya upheld that extinguishes the dispute. What is presence of the person? It is said:

Regarding "the matter of coming and going": what is meant by "the Saṃgha being present"? It refers to those who have gathered together in one place for a formal act (*karmavācanā*), with those who did not attend having granted their authorization;
it is one who, being present, is entitled to censure but does not do so. What is meant by "the boundary being present"?
It refers to performing a formal act within the boundary and establishing a restriction thereon. If a matter of dispute has been settled and one initiates it again, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

[The Buddha said: "Ānanda, if a bhikṣu who arrives later, or one who has newly received the precepts, considers this to be the first dispute and initiates it again, or if one who has already given their consent (chandadāna) subsequently regrets it, in all such cases it is a *pāyattika* offense.
According to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, there are ten kinds of formal acts (*karmavācanā*) performed without the assembly being present:

1. the overturning of the bowl (*pātra-nikubjana*); 2. the relinquishing of the overturned bowl (this refers to when laypeople revile or slander bhikṣus, and the Saṃgha should perform a formal act against them)."

1. Punishment (daṇḍa): One who does not associate with others; if he personally recognizes his fault and acts with a compliant mind, seeking the Saṃgha’s pardon, the Saṃgha should perform a *karmavācanā* to release him.

2. The Family under Training (*śikṣādattaka*): 3. The Family Abandoned (*śikṣādattaka-viprakrānta*): (As explained in the section on the method for repentance). 4. Building a Dwelling (*kuṭī-karaṇa*): This refers to using the grounds of a ruined or abandoned monastery and, through a *karmavācanā*, granting them to a layperson so that they may build a dwelling for the Saṃgha.

5. The Śrāmaṇera: This refers to a Śrāmaṇera of evil views who has been expelled. All those listed above have not received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and are therefore not permitted to hear the *karmavācanā* methods; thus, only two types of release and the case of building a dwelling apply to the Śrāmaṇera, who is merely placed in a location where he is within sight but beyond hearing.
7. Insanity (meaning that because of ignorance, [the formal act] need not be performed in their presence). 8. Not prostrating. 9. Not conversing. 10.

Not making offerings (meaning that if a bhikṣu acts contrary to the Dharma and harasses a bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣuṇī may not deal with the bhikṣu face-to-face; she may only perform the three types of *karmavācanā* from a distance, such as not prostrating, etc.).
△ Regarding the second *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection):
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had not committed a grave offense, yet all the other bhikṣus said he had committed one. They asked him, "Do you recall committing [an offense]?"

"Is it grave? He does not remember having committed an offense and replies, "I do not remember committing an offense, Venerable Sir; do not interrogate me repeatedly. Yet the monks continue to interrogate him without ceasing.
The Buddha permits the Saṃgha to perform the *smṛti-vinaya* (the discipline of recollection) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
What is the *smṛti-vinaya*? Regarding that monk’s offense, he should no longer be accused, nor should he...
It is called "calling to mind. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "This is the Vinaya of protection;
other bhikṣus should not expose his transgressions, nor should they cause him to be reminded [of them]. This refers to being repeatedly caused to remember by others.
Therefore, the Buddha now permits the practice of the *smṛti-vinaya* (the discipline of mindfulness), so that one shall not have to be questioned again.
△ The third is the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for those who were not insane).
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was deluded and mentally deranged, whereby he committed many offenses. Later, when he regained his senses, the other bhikṣus questioned him incessantly.

The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to grant him the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one no longer insane) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
What is the *amūḍha-vinaya*? Regarding those offenses of that bhikṣu, they should not be raised again, nor should they be brought to mind.
This is the *sarvavastuka* (the "all-inclusive" category). According to the *Sarvāstivāda*, this is the *vinaya* of protection.
△ The fourth [category] is the *pratijñā-vinaya* (settlement by confession).
At that time, a bhikṣu, using his divine eye, saw another bhikṣu violate the precepts. Without accepting the other's own confession, he immediately dragged him out through the gate.
The Buddha said: "One should not act in this way. Even at another time, one should not act in this way. One must first cause the person to acknowledge their guilt, and only then assign the penalty.
What is meant by 'one's own confession'? It is when one states the name of the offense and its category, and then performs repentance."
What is the remedy? It is said: it consists of reproaching one's own mind and giving rise to a sense of weary detachment.
△ Fifth: Seeking the Offense; the Characteristics of Seeking the Offense.
At that time, a bhikṣu committed an offense, and his statements were inconsistent from beginning to end. The Buddha said:

"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of a *karmavācanā* consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to establish that bhikṣu in the place of his offense. Having assembled the Saṃgha, one should first perform the formal act of accusation (*codanā*); having performed the accusation,"
He causes [the offender] to be reminded. Having caused him to be reminded, he applies the legal procedure for the offense (according to the *Kṣudraka-vastu* on the settling of disputes).

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, thirty-five practices are carried out. What is the "locus of the offense"? It refers to that monk whose offense is subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya*) and being reminded.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* says: "seeking the intrinsic nature of the offense. The *Mātṛkā* says: "truly searching for the offense."
As for this: one who has previously committed an offense and already confessed it, but later conceals it. The Sarvāstivādins say:
"This is a *pratikarṣaṇīya-vinaya* (disciplinary measure of reconciliation). (Thirty-five lines; as set forth in the Vinaya text.)
△ Chapter Six: The Procedure for Many Monks Regarding the Search for Faults.
If various monks have a dispute arise that they are unable to settle, they should seek out many monks who are learned in the Dharma.
The settling of disputes by means of voting sticks (*śalākā*). "By means of many voting sticks" refers to speech. What is the "majority decision" (*yadbhūyasikīya*)?

It is when those who speak on behalf of the majority—those who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkā—are employed. According to the Sarvāstivādins, it is when one seeks out many who possess the Vinaya.

Because the causes and conditions for much seeking are severed, and because seeking in many places is severed—since it is severed from many places—it is called *yadbhūyovāda-vinaya* (the Vinaya of Majority Decision).
△ *Tṛṇastāraka* (Covering with Grass), the Seventh:
Like covering with grass.

At that time, the bhikṣus were disputing with one another; they frequently violated many of the communal precepts, engaging in and speaking of things that were not the dharma of a śramaṇa, and their coming and going was without restraint. Later, those bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"If we return and question them about these matters together, it may cause this dispute to become even more deep-seated and grave. It will endure for months and years without being extinguished, causing..."
The Saṃgha could not find peace and happiness. They reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "This dispute should be settled by the 'covering with grass' (tṛṇaprastāraka).

Regarding what is called "dispute" (*adhikaraṇa*), the Vinaya states that there are four kinds of disputes: disputes concerning speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*), disputes concerning accusations (*anuvāda-adhikaraṇa*), disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*), and disputes concerning matters (*kicca-adhikaraṇa*).

What is a dispute concerning speech? It is when bhikṣus engage in a verbal dispute with other bhikṣus, citing eighteen points—ranging from "dharma" and "non-dharma" to "what has been spoken" and "what has not been spoken.
If they thus engage in verbal contention based on such characteristics, resulting in mutual strife, this is [a dispute concerning speech].
Regarding verbal disputes (*vāda-kalaha*). What is a dispute arising from searching for faults (*anveṣaṇa-kalaha*)? (The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "Instruction.

When a bhikṣu searches for the offenses of another bhikṣu by means of the three grounds for accusation—namely, violation of the precepts, violation of views, and violation of conduct—and by means of what is seen, heard, or suspected, conducting such a search for faults in this manner, this is called a dispute arising from searching for faults.
What is a dispute arising from transgression (*āpatti-kalaha*)? It refers to the transgression of the seven types of offenses, from the *pārājika* down to the *duṣkṛta*. This is it.
Disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-araṇa*). What is a dispute concerning matters (*vastu-araṇa*)?

That which is enacted as a matter within a dispute concerning speech, that which is enacted as a matter within a dispute concerning searching (*mārgaṇa-araṇa*), and that which is enacted as a matter within a dispute concerning offenses—this is a dispute concerning matters. The *vinaya* (disciplinary procedures) for settling [disputes] are as follows: the dispute concerning offenses (*āpatti-araṇa*) is settled by three *vinayas*, namely:

presence (*sammukha*), confession (*pratijñākāraka*), and the "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*)—that is, either presence and confession, or presence and the covering with grass, or presence and the specific locus of the offense.
The dispute concerning matters (*kṛtya-araṇa*) is settled by all the *vinayas* according to the specific offense committed. The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: [as above].
Regarding the four types of disputes, seven methods are able to eliminate them; therefore, they are called the "Seven Methods for Settling Disputes.
Having identified the nature of disputes and the methods for their elimination, these are essential practices for a bhikṣu; thus, this Prātimokṣa Sūtra shall now be recited in its entirety.

"What I have done is wrong; my precepts are not pure. I have committed even minor and secondary transgressions and have been unable to protect and uphold them according to the Dharma in every detail, yet I continue to accept the fourfold offerings from faithful donors."

Regarding the Dharma for Bhikṣuṇīs:
Generally speaking, the female mind is weak; its emotions delight in license and indulgence, it is full of deceit and transgressions, and it is characterized by instability and immodesty. Therefore—

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, responded to their capacities, guarding them with subtlety and restraining them with firmness; thus, whenever he established a precept, it was twice as stringent for women as for men.
In every case of prohibition, the restrictions were invariably more severe for the *saṃgha* of nuns.

Were it not for having planted sublime causes in past lives, how could one have received such sacred instruction? Having renounced worldly pleasures and being called a "Śākya daughter," one ought to revere her capable father.
He was instructed [as follows]: Wear coarse clothing to cover the body; sustain yourself with simple vegetarian food. Walk little and speak sparingly; cleanse the emotions and extinguish dissipation.

Ensure that the internal faculties and external objects do not interact, just as a well-guarded tortoise skillfully hides its six limbs. By upholding the precepts, one avoids even a *duṣkṛta* offense;
by clarifying the mind, one remains unmoved when encountering external things. Within the Tripitaka, apply yourself diligently to study and cultivate the five [precepts].

They bestow the Eightfold Respectful Precepts and uproot the three poisons with the seven branches of purification. Their minds dwell upon perfect enlightenment, and their aspirations are set upon the Mahāyāna.

They regard the four modes of birth as their own infants and contemplate the three miserable realms as their own suffering. Seeking the realization of the Way at an early stage, they deliver others through the Dharma.
Possessing such conduct as this, one appears in the present as a virtuous friend to humans and devas, and ultimately serves as a vessel for crossing over the three realms.

(Once a bhikṣuṇī has received the full ordination, she should first read the *Prātimokṣa* thoroughly so that there are no errors or omissions; only then should she study the Vinaya-piṭaka to understand what constitutes an offense and its non-offense. If her intelligence is sufficient, she may then study the Bhikṣu-vinaya so as to know the distinctions between the common and uncommon rules of the two sets of discipline.

Now, the terminology of these bhikṣuṇī precepts is for the most part identical to that of the Bhikṣu-vinaya, as explained in detail previously. The *Saṃgha-vinaya* (Monastic Code) has therefore been reissued here; it is explained concisely. Where there are points of divergence within it, detailed annotations will follow the text. *Bhagavān* is the Sanskrit term *Lokanātha*, which in this [language] is translated as "World-Honored One" (*Shizun*). This is one of the ten titles of the Buddha.
It is said that because he possesses the aforementioned nine titles and is revered by all beings, he is called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).

Since he is honored alike by those in the heavens and those among humans, he was formerly referred to as "The Benefactor of the Multitude" (*Zhongyou*). This means that he possesses manifold virtues that benefit himself and is further able to benefit all sentient beings;

"Markaṭahrada" (Monkey Pond). "Mí" is the sound for *márkaṭa*; "hóu" is the sound for *kapi*. This beast has no spleen; it digests its food through physical movement. "Jiāng" (river) should properly be called "chí" (pond).

Entering the supreme dharma of noble wisdom refers to the Buddhas and those of the four fruits of the path. This is a most excellent dharma that cannot be attained through physical strength, power, or intellectual cleverness;
rather, it is realized and entered through the practitioner’s diligent and tireless application of superior and wondrous power.
"Great Sister" (*dà jìjì*): "Yīn zǐ" (音子) means elder sister. Originally written as *jì* (姉), it is conventionally written as *zǐ* (姊). As for "Sister" (*sì xìng chūjiā*, 四姓出家):
those from the four castes who have left the household life all return to the same clan name, Śākya; thus they are sisters within the Dharma.
"Overweening pride" (*adhimāna*) refers to the state where one has not yet attained realization of the noble [path], yet claims to have already attained it.
Because this noble wisdom is a superior practice, one gives rise to a mind of conceit regarding these supramundane, superior dharmas; this is called overweening pride. This is because—
Inwardly, one has indeed attained and realized [the fruit], yet, with this mind as the dominant factor, one feels conceited toward others; this is overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

If, knowing for oneself that one has not attained the qualities of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), one deceives others by claiming to have attained them, this is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
Therefore, excluding cases of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), there is no offense. (The four matters are concluded.
Śrāvastī—this means "the land of what is heard"—is the name of a city, not the designation of a kingdom; it is so called because its name is renowned.
The person was fond of practicing the Way and its virtue; because his fame was heard throughout the five regions, he was named Śrāvastī.
The name of the kingdom was Kośala. Regarding Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma: "Jeta" means "Victorious. "Anāthapiṇḍada" is the title of the elder Sudatta; Sudatta... [text continues]
The elder spread gold coins upon the ground to purchase the grove from Prince Jeta for the purpose of building a monastery for the Buddha.

The prince was pleased at heart and offered the grove’s trees to him. Because the two men shared a single intention in their act of giving, the place is commonly called the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma (the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery).
Hao-gui (Noble and Dignified). Ancient reading: gui (noble). Modern reading: gui (noble).
Da-shan-lu-le Chang-zhe (The Great and Virtuous Elder Mṛgāra).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: The son-in-law of Mother Viśākhā was named Mṛgāra; his grandson was named Śrībhadra. Śrībhadra constantly kept the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā in mind.
In Sanskrit, he is called Śrībhadra; this means "Auspicious and Good" (*Śrī-bhadra*).

"Auspicious and Good" and "Greatly Auspicious and Good" have the same meaning. "Mṛga" (Deer) is the name of his father. (Note: "Son-in-law" refers to the husband of a daughter; in current vernacular usage...)

she was also a woman of the Śākya clan. Moreover, this bhikṣuṇī was one who mastered the Tripiṭaka and was skilled and proficient in preaching the Dharma;
she was the foremost among the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and was also a Great Power Bodhisattva manifesting in this form to prompt the Buddha to establish the precepts.
"Āyī" (ā-ā-gē;
the initial sound is *è*, colloquially pronounced as *yà*). Regarding the current practice of addressing a *bhikṣuṇī* as "Āyī":
some say it is because the *bhikṣuṇī* Mahāprajāpatī was the Buddha’s maternal aunt, and thus [the term] was adopted as a form of address.
The rest is explained as in the Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka.
"Grasping and making a sound" refers to making a sound; it means kissing her mouth, that is, the drawing close of the mouths.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: He asked, "What do you require? The nun replied, "I require dried jujubes.
He then purchased them and gave them to her. The bhikṣuṇī held the jujubes in her hands and asked, "Do you see these dried jujubes? He replied.

*Zhuō bǐ* means to seize the thighs. *Bǐ* is pronounced *bǐ*; it refers to the two legs.
Asura is translated here as "Not-Ugly" (Wu-Endun). This means that while the males are ugly, the females are beautiful.

It is also translated as "Non-Gods" (Fei-Tian), meaning that although the retribution of these deities is most excellent and they rank immediately below the various heavens, they are not [actual] gods.

and may not be separated from one.
