hemp footwear is called *jù*; and leather footwear is called *lǚ*. (*Fèi* is pronounced *fèi*; *jù* is pronounced *jù*).
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa*. "Saṃgha" is translated here as "the community.
*Āvaśeṣa* means "remainder" or "residue. Taken collectively and briefly, it is called "Saṃghāvaśeṣa" (Monastic Residue).
It is like a person who has been mutilated by another but still possesses a throat; thus, they are said to be "residual. It is like two people... [text continues].

They both entered the midst of the battle array; one was killed by another and his life was severed, while the second was also killed by another, yet his life-force remained slightly present and had not been cut off.
If he were to obtain a skilled physician and excellent medicine, he could be cured; if he did not, he could not be cured.
The same applies to those who have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. There is still a principle by which it may be confessed;
if one obtains a pure assembly that can perform the ritual for confessing and removing the offense according to the Dharma, this offense may be removed.
If there is no pure assembly, it cannot be extinguished. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. (The five matters are concluded.)
Śāḷha Mṛgāra; the elder Mṛgāra, also called Mṛgaputra (Son of the Deer). He was also the son of the elder Mṛgāra.

"Xiayi" (pronounced yǐ): "yi" means to rely upon.

Smoke and flames issue from its mouth; people of the world call it a "broom-star" (Kheṭaka-tārakā). In a single thought-moment, it can travel hundreds of thousands of yojanas.

This is the Radiant Phase (*abhijit*).
This refers to when the eastern direction has already turned crimson. This defines "dawn" as the two *kṣaṇas* (two hours) prior to sunrise; it is the phase of light (*āloka-nimitta*).
Furthermore, it is limited by the point at which one can clearly discern the lines on the palm.
The "peril of life" refers to the fear of circumstances that might cause the loss of one's life.
The "peril of the holy life."
This refers to the fear that there may be causes and conditions for the breaking of the precepts. (The seven matters are concluded.
The country of Kauśāmbī is within the borders of Central India; it is over six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is over thirty *li* in circuit. Śam... [text fragment]
Yinshǎn (Sound-Flash).
Jùshīluó Yuán (Ghoṣila Garden);
Ghoṣila means "Beautiful Sound" in this language; it is the name of a householder. The garden is located to the southeast of the city. No.
Yuan. The bhikṣu Chanda,
also known as Chandaka, was the one who tended the Buddha's horse before the Buddha left the household life.
The nun Wei-ci (also written as E), also known as Uppalavaṇṇā, was the younger sister of Channa; some say she was his elder sister.
She taught [them] the increase of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

To teach the increase of morality means to teach the increase of training in the five categories of precepts. To teach the increase of the mind means to teach the increase of attaining the four dhyānas.
To teach the increase of wisdom means to teach the increase of clear vision regarding the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, to teach the increase of morality is to teach the Vinaya Piṭaka;
to teach the increase of the mind is to teach the Sūtra Piṭaka; and to teach the increase of wisdom is to teach the Abhidharma Piṭaka.

An illegal separate assembly refers to those residing in the same dwelling place who, at the time of a *karmavācanā*, have members who do not attend and should have granted their consent (*chanda*), yet do not grant it;
furthermore, those who ought to be rebuked are rebuked [in their absence]. This is called a separate assembly. They then perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

To perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) for one matter while proposing another is called an illegal act (*adharma*). This constitutes an illegal *karmavācanā* performed by a separate assembly (*bhinnasaṃgha*).
It is an illegal act performed by a harmonious assembly (*samagrīsaṃgha*).

This refers to residing in the same location, performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*) together in one place, granting consent (*chanda*) by those who ought to grant it, and not censuring those who ought to censure in the presence of others—this is called "harmony.
It includes performing the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act with one motion and one proclamation) and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act with one motion and three proclamations).
To report this matter while performing a *karmavācanā* for that other matter (this is termed "unlawful") constitutes an unlawful and concordant assembly *karmavācanā*.
This is a lawful and separate assembly *karmavācanā*.

This refers to when a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is being performed within a single residential community (*sīmā*), and there are those who do not attend and should have granted their consent (*chanda*), yet do not grant it;

and those who, being present, ought to voice an objection (a *pṛthag-jana* assembly) do so. That [assembly] then performs a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) or one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

To perform [this] act according to the Dharma is the *dharmika-vigraha-saṃgha-karman* (a formal act of the Saṃgha performed by a divided assembly that is nonetheless lawful). Regarding "similar to the Dharma" (*dharmasābhāgya*) and "divided assembly" (*vigraha*), these are explained as above.

"Similar to the Dharma" refers to performing the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) or the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), having first performed the preliminary motion (*karma-pūrva*).

Having polished [the vessel], one then performs the formal announcement (*jñapti*). This is what is meant by "resemblance of the dharma" (*dharmasādṛśya*). This constitutes a *karma* performed by a separate assembly (*bhinnasaṃgha*) that resembles the dharma.
"Resemblance of the dharma" and "harmonious assembly" (*saṃghasāmagrī*) are both explained as above. These are the five kinds of *karma* mentioned above.
All such [procedures] are contrary to the Dharma. If the Saṃgha performs these kinds of *karmavācanā*, because they are contrary to the Dharma, there is no offense.

*Vinaya* is here translated as "skillful governance" (*śubha-vinaya*); it means governing oneself regarding lust, anger, and delusion, and being likewise able to govern the evils of sentient beings. It is also called...

"Destroying evil" refers to what the Buddha taught: the *vijñapti* (informative) and *avijñapti* (non-informative) precepts are able to destroy the evils of body and speech; therefore, it is called "destroying evil.
(The eight matters are concluded.)
○ Regarding the seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas,
"rootless" refers to the absence of the roots of seeing, hearing, or suspicion. As for the root of seeing, it means actually seeing that [person] commit one of the eight *pārājika* offenses.

Regarding the middle [category]: having committed one offense, if one sees it oneself or hears of it from another, this is called the "root of seeing" (*dṛṣṭimūla*). Regarding the "root of hearing" (*śrutimūla*):

if one hears that he has committed one of the offenses among the eight *pārājika* rules concerning the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or if he says that he heard it from such a person, this is called the "root of hearing.
Regarding the "root of doubt" (*vaimatikamūla*): there are two ways in which doubt arises; first, from seeing...

Doubt arises. If one sees [the woman] entering or leaving a forest with a man, or even seeing her holding a blood-stained knife and accompanied by evil associates, this is called doubt arising from what is seen.
Second, that which arises from hearing: if [it occurs] in a dark place.
If one hears the sound of a bed, or even hears someone say, "I have attained the state of a superior person," this is called a doubt arising from what has been heard.
Apart from these three bases, to slander another by means of some other matter is called "groundless.
Whether the person before one is pure or impure, when one slanders them without these three bases, it is all termed groundless. (Regarding the latter four *pārājikas*)
The same applies to those who slander [the Dharma].
To take a portion from among heterogeneous matters refers to the eight *pārājika* offenses; if one commits even a single one of these, one is no longer a śramaṇa.
"Daughter of the Śākyas, she has lost the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī and has no share in nirvāṇa; because nirvāṇa is contrary to saṃsāra, it is called 'a different portion' (*visabhāga*).

'A fragment' (*khaṇḍa*) refers to minor matters among the various modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), meaning that one takes a minor offense within the *pārājika* rules and slanders another by saying they have committed a *pārājika*."
*Āraṇya* is translated here as a "secluded and tranquil place," meaning a location five *li* removed from a village.
A *vihāra*.

What is called a *vihāra* (monastery) is not so named because its buildings are exquisite; rather, it is called a *vihāra* because it is the dwelling place of those who practice with refined discipline.
"Yìguān" (詣官): "Yì" (詣) is pronounced "yì"; it means "to arrive at. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If someone steals a bhikṣuṇī’s robe, one must not say, 'This person is a thief.
One should only say, 'This person has taken my robe. If someone is about to plunder a bhikṣuṇī, one may approach [the authorities].
When requesting protection from the King, one must not utter his name; if one speaks his name, it constitutes an offense. Furthermore, it is said:
if a person enters a nunnery and cuts down trees, one must not seize their axes or hatchets, nor may they be broken; if they are broken, the value must be repaid.
If the value is not repaid, an offense is committed according to the amount of that value.
In the duration of a single thought-moment (*ekacittakṣaṇa*), there are ninety *kṣaṇas*. Within one *kṣaṇa*, nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing pass. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
twenty thought-moments constitute one blink (*tatkṣaṇa*); twenty blinks constitute one finger-snap (*acchaṭā*); twenty finger-snaps [constitute one moment].
One *la-yü* is called one *luo-yü*; twenty *luo-yü* constitute one *xu-yu*. At the time when the day is at its longest, there are eighteen *xu-yu*;
at the time when the night is at its shortest, there are twelve *xu-yu* (when the night is long and the day short, it should be understood as the reverse).
Prasenajit (here translated as "Victorious Army"),
a Brahmin.
These are the Brāhmaṇas. Regarding their lineage, they claim to have been born from the mouth of Brahmā;

because they are the most excellent among the four castes, they alone take the name "Brahmā" as their designation, considering themselves the descendants of Brahmā. They exist only in the five regions of India.
It does not exist in other countries.
Liśa (離奢) is here translated as "thin skin" (皮薄), and is also called "same skin" (同皮).
The city of Rājagṛha is the same as the city of Rauruka.
The saṃghārāma.
This is called a "Garden of the Multitude" (saṅghārāma), meaning a place where the roots and sprouts of the seeds of the Buddha's sons are cultivated and where the fruits of holiness are realized.
In this region, it is called a "temple" (si), also called a "monastery" (yuan), and also called a "vihāra" (jing-she).
Magadha is here translated as "the Land of Good Victory" (Śobhana-vijaya) and also as "the Land Without Affliction" (Anupadrava).
Its king was Bimbisāra.
This is King Śrīghana (translated as "Cloud-Shading" or "Victorious Body").
As for his lineage:

it is the Śākyas (a noble clan; that is, the place where the Śākyas resided, and they established their clan name based on that residence). It is also the Koliyas (also written as Kauriya; this is the clan of the people of Rāmagrāma).
... (unidentified). Mi-ning (unknown). Ba-qi (translated as "Vajra"). Man-la (alternatively written as Mo-la or Mo-la; translated as "Malla" or "Wrestler"). Su-mo (translated as "Moon").
*Karma* (羯磨) is here translated as "performing the ritual action to accomplish the task.
[He] lifted his robe.
Qiān (褰): Pronounced qiān; it refers to "lifting one's robes to wade through water.
Chù rǎo rǎo (觸嬈嬈):
Pronounced niǎo; it means to toy with or dally with.
The bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā—
also transcribed as Xianmo (讖摩), which means "Peaceful Security"— had attained the samādhi of loving-kindness and was wise and intelligent.
Among the five hundred arhat bhikṣuṇīs, she was the foremost leader.
Kosala is the name of the kingdom of Śrāvastī; it is the domain ruled by King Prasenajit (Kosala is also written as Kiao).
*Nie* (in *nièliáng*) has the phonetic value of *niǎn*; it means to ascend or to tread upon. A *liáng* is a bridge.
[This refers to] boiling soup.
Gēng (羹): Pronounced gēng. It refers to a soup in which the five flavors are harmonized.
Zhǔ (煮): Same as yù (鬻). *Vinaya Piṭaka*, Scroll 23, Tiśya-nanda.
Ti-she (坻舍) is the same as Di-she (坻舍).
Regarding "selling" (販): the pronunciation is fan (范). To buy low and sell high is called "selling" (販).
*Geng* (莖) means "stem.

Its pronunciation is *heng*. It refers to the trunk of plants and trees. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is a supporting pillar. Since branches grow from the stem, it is called a "supporting pillar" (*zhizhu*).
Sesame is also known as *jusheng* (greatly victorious). It was originally produced in the country of Hu, hence it is called *humai* (Hu-seed). It is black in color;
in common parlance, it is called "black sesame," which is indeed this plant. Among the eight grains, it is the most superior; therefore, it is called *jusheng*.
Kṛṣṇa-phāṇita (black stone-honey) is the hardened form of sugarcane syrup; it is of two kinds, black and white.
There is also rice-flour.
*Chao* (pronounced *chǎo*). This refers to parched rice, millet, wheat, and so forth, which are parched and ground into flour to make *chao*.
It may be served as loose powder or formed into balls with sugar and honey.
*Maṇi* is here translated as "wish-fulfilling jewel" (*cintāmaṇi*). It is also called "free from defilement," because the radiance of this gem is pure and cannot be stained by impurities.
This precious jewel resides upon the neck of the Dragon King; if a person obtains this jewel, poison cannot harm them, nor can they be burned by fire.
It does not burn. Upon examination, this jewel exists both in the heavens and among humans; it is only that in the human realm its marks of merit are slight and not fully complete.
Vaiḍūrya.
The character *bi* (毗) is sometimes written as *fei* (吠), or the character *bi* is omitted entirely. The character *liu* (瑠) is sometimes written as *liu* (琉);
in ancient times it was simply written as *liuli* (流離), though later generations added the "jade" radical (*yu*). This is originally a Sanskrit term; why labor to add the "jade" radical?
It is translated as "blue-colored jewel" (*nīla-ratna*) and also as "not far away. This refers to a mountain in India that is not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, where this jewel is produced.
It was named for this reason. Some say it is *gandhārī* lapis lazuli; "gān" (紺) refers to a blue color containing red. Regarding *khaḍga* (珂貝):

the pronunciation of *kha* is like that of *ke* (軻). One source says it is agate (*musāragalva*); those as pure white as snow are one type. Another source says it belongs to the class of conch shells, produced in the ocean.
Some say that the larger varieties of shell are called *ka* (agate).
Coral is called *pravāḍa* in Sanskrit; this is translated here as "coral. Its shape is like a withered tree and it is red in color. (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)
It is said that *shān'gū* (coral) is a stone-tree that emerges from the sea. A foreign tradition states:

"Seven or eight hundred li southwest of Daqin (the Roman Empire), one reaches the Coral Isle (*shān'gū zhōu*) in the surging ocean. The bottom of the isle consists of flat rocks upon which coral grows.

People harvest it using iron nets. The *Shūyì jì* (Records of Strange Anomalies) states: "The coral tree is emerald green in color and grows at the bottom of the sea; a single stem may number [several...]"
It has ten branches, with no leaves between them. The larger ones are five or six feet high; the smaller ones are over a foot.
(The Great Qin refers to the country of Persia, located outside of Western India; today, coral is also found in the Eastern Sea.)
In foreign lands, gold is called "raw" (*sheng*) and silver is termed "likeness" (*xiang*). This means that because the original color of gold is naturally yellow, it is called "raw.
As for "likeness," it signifies resemblance; since silver can be dyed to resemble gold, it is called "likeness."
Gandharva is translated here as "Fragrance-Body" (xiāngyīn) and also as "Spirit Who Soars Above the Void. They are the musical deities of the Heavenly Emperor.
[They] studied under the same teacher.
This means that within the teachings of the same Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, one studies the twelve divisions of the sūtras; for their essence is without distinction.

Just as water and milk blend together, so too the essence of the Tathāgata’s twelve divisions of the sūtras has no differentiation. Their practice accords with principle, being of a single characteristic without discrepancy.
It is like water and milk, which merge into a single substance without distinct color or flavor.
Regarding "Dharma-speech" and "Vinaya-speech":
Dharma-speech refers to speech that is perfect in its phrasing; Vinaya-speech refers to speech that accords with principle without error and is further capable of leading to reality.
The meaning is called "Dharma-discourse" (*dharmaparyāya*); the utterance of gentle and soft words is called "Vinaya-discourse.
Regarding the two bhikṣuṇīs:
the first was named Sumā (the character *su* is pronounced with a third tone, as explained above); the second was named Vappā (also called Vappa). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
The first was named Cīnā; she was a daughter of the Śākya clan. The second was named Uttarā, which here means "Superior.
*Gài* (pronounced *jì*) means to irrigate; *guàn* (pronounced *guàn*) also means to irrigate, to water, or to pour.
*Huamanman* (華鬘鬘). The pronunciation of *man* is *mán*. In Sanskrit it is called *mālā*, which here means "garland.

In India, when making garlands, they mostly use *sumana* flowers, stringing them together in rows to form a continuous wreath. Regardless of whether one is male or female, noble or humble, all adorn themselves with these.
Some [use] heads, some bodies, as ornaments for display.
"Chang" (俗作娼;
pronounced *chāng*) refers to female musicians (*nǚyuè*); "jì" (pronounced *jì*) also refers to female musicians.
"Chàng-hé-chàng" (Lead-and-response singing). "Chàng" (唱) means to lead or precede; it refers to initiating a song.
"Hé" (和), with the departing tone of the character "huò" (禾), means that the sounds harmonize with one another, following each other in succession.
"Pai-shuo" (俳說) means "pai.
It refers to "pai-you" (俳優), which denotes mixed theatrical performances involving drums and reed organs.
Huang (簧). The pronunciation is huáng. It refers to the side of the reeds at the base of the *sheng* and *yu* pipes. Thin gold leaves are used to cover them;
when blown upon, they vibrate to produce sound, and thus they are called "huang. For this reason, both the *sheng* and *yu* are referred to as "huang."
The "blown conch" (chuì bèi) is the largest of the *lí* shells; it is blown to provide rhythmic accompaniment for music.
[He] feigned lameness.
*Cháng* (pronounced like *yáng*): to deceive. *Bǒ* (the character pronounced with the third tone): to have a gait that is not straight.
Alternatively, *xiào* (pronounced like *xiào*): to whistle, which is to produce sound by puckering the mouth.
"Śramaṇa Śākyaputra Śramaṇa.
This is translated as "one who has performed meritorious labor," signifying that he has undergone much toil in cultivating the Way.

It is also translated as "one who practices diligently," meaning that he diligently performs all manner of good deeds and brings all evils to rest. Whether in the Buddha-dharma or among the non-Buddhist paths, all those who have left the household life are [called śramaṇas].

He is called a *śramaṇa*. "Śākya" means Śākyamuni; here it is translated as "Capable Benevolent One" (*Néngrén*). When we now speak of a "son of the Śākya *śramaṇas*," this is intended to distinguish him from other *śramaṇas*.
Regarding this, there are four general categories to differentiate the meaning of a *śramaṇa*: 1. One who is a son of the Śākyas but not a *śramaṇa*;
this refers to those of the royal lineage. 2. One who is a *śramaṇa* but not a son of the Śākyas; this refers to the *brāhmaṇas* (and other non-Buddhist renunciants who practice...).
[He is] a practitioner. He is a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, and indeed a bhikṣu. One who is not a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākyas belongs to one of two lower castes:
(1) merchants, or (2) farmers. In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are four castes who leave the household life;
they no longer have their original caste names, but are simply called śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas. The reason for this is that birth [in the spiritual sense] proceeds from me."

The Dharma arises; its establishment is through the establishment of the self and the Dharma. It is like the four rivers entering the ocean, where they no longer retain their original names and are collectively called the great ocean.
Furthermore, in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If someone were to ask you, 'What is your lineage?'"
One should answer them thus: "I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.

Born directly from [the Buddha’s] mouth, transformed by the Dharma, pure in the present and pure in the future, I shall be a disciple of Maitreya in the time to come; all such are called 'Sons of Compassion'."
"Brahman" (婆羅門) is here translated as "Pure Conduct" (淨行) or "Brahmacārin" (梵志). This is one of the four castes among the people of India.
Whether they have left the household life or remain at home, they take the cultivation of the Way as their primary task. The rest is as explained above.
Regarding the four kinds of disputes:

first, the dispute of speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*). This refers to when bhikṣuṇīs dispute with one another, citing eighteen grounds for dispute and engaging in contentious talk, until they eventually come to blows against each other.
Second, the dispute of investigation (*anveṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*). This refers to when bhikṣuṇīs [investigate] with one another...
The dispute concerning the search for faults (*āpattiparyeṣaṇā-vivāda*) refers to the commission of seven types of offenses (from *pārājika* down to *durbhāṣita*).

The dispute concerning matters (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*) refers to the occurrence of matters within the dispute over speech, the dispute over the search for faults, and the dispute over offenses; these are termed "disputes concerning matters.
(The eighteen matters of dispute are set forth in the *Bhikṣu-saṃghabheda-vastu*.)

*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*:

*Naiḥsargika* means "to be relinquished" (*śe*); *pāyattika* means "falling" (*duō*). This refers to the fact that once one has committed this offense, the object must be relinquished to the Sangha, or even to a single person;
as for the remaining *pāyattika* offenses, one should confess them before a single pure (*viśuddha*) bhikṣu.
The nun confesses her transgression.
"The robes are finished" means that the five robes are finished.

Except in the case of a formal monastic procedure (*saṃgha-karman*), if there is a reason such as illness, or if the refuse-rag robe (*pāṃsukūla*) is heavy and unfit to be carried while traveling, one should request the *akalpiya-cīvara* (non-forfeiture of robes) procedure from the Saṃgha three times.
The Saṃgha then performs a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and grants that person the method of non-forfeiture of robes; therefore, this excludes the case of the Saṃgha.
*Karmavācanā*. There is no offense (as detailed in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*).
Regarding "the time for non-seasonal robes":
this refers to when the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread; there is a period of one month called "the time" (from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month).
[On the sixteenth day of the seventh month]. There are five months designated as the "season" (from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month).
If one obtains robes during these two periods [the period of the kaṭhina robe and the five-month season], they are called "timely robes" (*kālacīvara*).
Apart from these two periods, robes obtained at other times are called "untimely robes" (*akālacīvara*).

"Non-relative" means one who is not a relative by blood on the mother's or father's side, extending back through seven generations without kinship. "Relative" means one who is a relative by blood on the mother's or father's side,
extending back through seven generations with kinship.
"Previously not having accepted an invitation for free offerings" means that one has never before accepted a donor’s invitation to seek whatever one desires at will. We—

"Cáo" (pronounced *zǎo* with the level tone) means "class" or "group.
It refers to those who attend to affairs— that is, the lay attendants (*upāsaka*) who perform various tasks and serve the *bhikṣuṇīs*.
The *saṃghārāmika* refers to those who guard the temple gates; they may have volunteered of their own accord or been hired by a donor (*dānapati*).
They are lay followers (*upāsaka*).
This is called an upāsaka (lay follower). It refers to one who has received the five precepts.
"Orally receiving" means verbally assenting; that is, receiving them by placing [the precepts] on the ground.

*Wǔ zhuìzhuì*. The pronunciation is *zhuì*. It means to join together and to patch. The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "The bhikṣuṇīs placed their bowls in various locations, whereupon rust formed on the iron;
furthermore, due to being struck or thrown, many were damaged. The Buddha said: "One should use thin tin [to mend them]."
He used it as a bowl-rest. He then wrapped his alms-bowl entirely with his mendicant’s staff. The Buddha said, "One should not wrap the bowl entirely with the staff;
rather, one may make a small rest that merely supports the bottom of the bowl. He then fashioned various strange and elaborate shapes for it.
The Buddha said, "It is not permitted. There are two kinds of substitutes: first, such as the leaves of the Bodhi tree or the Nyagrodha tree;
second, such as the palm of the hand (the Nyagrodha tree is the *nyagrodha* tree)."
Mao (貿) to Mao (貿).

*Sūyóu* (clarified butter) and *shēngsū* (fresh butter):

Regarding oil and fresh butter: "fresh butter" refers to the fresh butter of cattle, sheep, and other such animals. Having been purified by sprinkling and washing so that it is free from the odor of food, once accepted, it may be consumed for seven days.
Honey and rock honey.

*Dānapati* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "giving" (*dāna*). *Yue* is a word from this region [of China], meaning that if a person can practice giving, they will immediately transcend the ocean of poverty.
The five robes are: first, the *antarvāsa*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*; third, the *saṃghāṭī*; fourth, the *saṃkakṣikā*;
and fifth, the *aṃsavastra*. The *Mūla-karmavācanā* states: first, the *saṃghāṭī* (which is the *saṃghāṭī*); second, the *uttarāsaṅga*.
(That is the *uttarāsaṅga*). Third, the *saṃghāṭī* (that is the *antarvāsaka*). Fourth, the *kaṣāya* (the lower garment). Fifth, the *saṃkakṣikā* (the armpit-covering undergarment).
These five robes are those most essential for a *bhikṣuṇī*. The three robes are as previously described; the remaining two must now be discussed.

*Juesuluojiā* (厥蘇洛迦). Its correct translation is "grain basket" (*cūḍaka*). This name is derived from its shape; it is so designated because its two ends are sewn together, making its form like a small grain basket.
It is the lower garment worn beneath the *nivāsana*. It is four cubits in length and two cubits in width.

With both ends sewn together, when putting it on, one stands inside it, lifts it up past the navel, gathers the two sides at each end, folds them double behind to cover, and secures them with a waist-belt. It is located [below the waist].
Two finger-widths above the ankles; this is the manner in which the community of nuns in the West wears their lower garment (*śīrṣaka*).
There is only this single skirt and no other clothing. Because it is a warm land, this suffices for traveling long distances; it is not like a cold country where many layers must be worn.

The old translations "Jue-xi-luo" (厥修羅) or "Qi-xi-luo" (祇修羅) are all erroneous. Regarding the manner of fastening the cord: its measurement is the same as that for monks, as explained in the *Śaikṣa-dharmas*.

As for the *saṃkakṣikā*, it is equivalent to the "shoulder-covering garment" (*fubo*) used here [in China], but it is one cubit longer; this is precisely its proper measure, intended to cover the shoulders and armpits.
The Buddha established this rule because he feared the three robes might become soiled; thus, one first uses it to cover both shoulders, and then...
Above this, they generally don the Dharma robe, wrapping it around the neck so tightly that the collar fastenings rest upon the shoulders; these collar fastenings resemble those of a shirt.

The garment covers the entire body, never exposing the arms, and both hands remain tucked in front of the chest, as in the image of King Aśoka, even when performing prostrations to the Triple Gem, receiving full ordination, or partaking of food.
Regarding these protocols, it is never permitted to expose the chest or shoulders. When a *bhikṣuṇī* is in the monastery, this is the rule;
the same applies to the monks (*bhikṣu*). However, when eating or performing prostrations, the monks do expose their shoulders;

this is the custom throughout the Five Indies, where one never sees monks or nuns covering their shoulders. Within the monastery, there is no practice of wearing neck-ties or fasteners, as they are made of coarse woolen cloth.

It is light and coarse; it does not fall from the shoulders. In this region, silk is smooth, so one wears a band across the chest as a matter of local custom, which has nothing to do with the Buddha’s regulations.
This practice simply stems from previous traditions of translation and transmission;

failing to understand its proper form, some call it a *saṃkakṣikā*, while others call it a "shoulder-covering robe. However, what is called a "shoulder-covering robe" is actually a *saṃghāṭī*. To call it that is a mistake.
The term *saṃkakṣikā* is a corruption resulting from improper oral transmission; these two [terms] originally refer to a single object, yet they have been forcibly assigned two distinct names.

*Saṃkakṣikā* resembles a sash, and its original pronunciation is preserved; however, the Vinaya contains no such category for "covering the shoulders. Furthermore, the ancient *saṃkakṣikās* used here in this region are not of the original design;
they should properly be called *kūṭāgāra*, yet they are made of plain cloth with one side left open. This is the actual practice.
The current *qun* (lower robe) is likewise not authentic; each varies in its dimensions, and even when worn, it does not conform to the established rules.

"Bhagavān" is the name of the World-Honored One (Bhagavat), who possesses great merit and is most holy. Its essence contains many meanings and cannot be translated directly.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Bhaga" in the language of Qin means 'merit' (*guṇa*), and "vān" means 'to possess. Thus, it is called 'One Who Possesses Merit' (*Guṇavān*). Furthermore, Bhaga..."
*Ga* means "discrimination. *Va* means "skillful. Because he skillfully discriminates the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena, he is called Bhagavān.
Furthermore, it is translated as "Renown," meaning there is no one whose renown equals that of the Buddha. Alternatively, it is called Bhagavat;
in the new translation, it is called Bhagavan. The *Dhāraṇī-śāstra* explains: "Bhagavan" is a masculine appellation.
...and Bhagavati. "Vati" is called in the feminine voice; both [terms] convey the intended meaning. The commentary explains it as "World-Honored One" (Bhagavat).
According to the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), if analyzed through the method of opposition (*dvandva*): *bhaga* means "to break," which in the Sanskrit translation is rendered as "ability.
Because he is able to destroy the four māras, he is named Bhagavat. Furthermore, it is said to be *Bhagavan*. According to the grammatical treatises, *bha* means "to break," and *a* means...
Non-arising is the name for realization in Sanskrit. Wisdom that can realize "A" is called "A-Brahman. Because of A-Brahman, one is able to destroy the afflictions;
therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is neither born nor extinguished, neither coming nor going, neither one nor different.
Neither discontinuous nor eternal, neither increasing nor decreasing, and endowed with such virtues, he is named Bhagavān. He is also called Bhagavān;

"Bhaga" means merit and wisdom, while "Vān" means "endowed with. Interpreting the meaning according to its constituent parts, it signifies that he is so called because he is endowed with merit and wisdom.
Being adorned and perfected, he is named Bhagavat. Furthermore, "Bhagavat" is also an appellation used in the masculine gender.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The term 'Bhagavat' functions according to six meanings: first, mastery; second, brilliance; third, majesty."
Fourth is renown; fifth is auspiciousness; sixth is nobility. The verse says:
Mastery, brilliance, and physical excellence, Renown, auspiciousness, and nobility— These six qualities are perfectly fulfilled; Therefore, he is designated as Bhagavat.
What is the meaning of this? It means that because the Tathāgata is forever unattached to any afflictions, he possesses mastery.
It possesses the sense of "meaning" (*artha*) because it is refined and tempered by the fierce flames of the fire of wisdom;

it possesses the sense of "blazing" because it is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Being; it possesses the sense of "dignity" because all supreme qualities are perfected such that nothing remains unknown;
and it possesses the sense of "renown" because it is approached and venerated by all the world, who all offer praise.

It possesses the meaning of auspiciousness; it possesses all virtues; it constantly exerts skillful means to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings without ever becoming weary or negligent;
and it possesses the meaning of nobility (the above is an extensive explanation intended to make known that the Tathāgata possesses these manifold virtues).

*Kuì-nào* (confusion and clamor). *Kuì* (潰) is pronounced like *kuài* (膾); it means disorder. *Nào* (鬧) is pronounced like *náo* (鐃) with a departing tone; it means lack of stillness and disturbance. It signifies being in a state of disarray (*lángjí*).
Láng (pronounced láng): the name of a beast resembling a dog, with a pointed head and white cheeks; it is tall in the front and broad in the rear.
Its nature is largely greedy, hence it is called "greedy wolf" (tānláng). It tramples and tosses the grass, making it disordered, hence it is called "in disorder" (lángjí).
Jí (pronounced jí) means that the grass is not woven together, but is scattered and disarrayed. (Huò [pronounced huò] means to turn over and over.)

Regarding the value of four *kambala* (woolen blankets), the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that it is worth four large coins (*mahāpaṇa*). According to this, these four *kambala* are worth four *kārsāpaṇa*.
To say "coins" is incorrect; the *kārsāpaṇa* is originally a name for a numerical unit, not a designation for a coin. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "four *karṣāpaṇa*."
A *kāṛṣāpaṇa* consists of sixteen *māṣakas* (that is, sixteen parts). The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
"In winter, to ward off the cold, an extremely expensive garment may be made using four *kāṛṣāpaṇas*, but it must not exceed that [amount].
*Kārṣāpaṇa*, *kāḷāpaṇa*, and *kāriśapaṇa* are all one and the same name; they differ only due to errors in the pronunciation of the syllables."
According to the sixteen *kārsāpaṇas* of India, one *kārsāpaṇa* is divided into four parts. One part consists of five *māṣakas*.
One *māṣaka* contains eighty cowrie shells. Thus, the four parts together contain twenty *māṣakas*, totaling one [kārsāpaṇa].
One thousand six hundred cowrie shells constitute one *kāṛṣāpaṇa*;
this is the count for one thousand six hundred cowrie shells. Now, these sixteen strips are sixteen parts;
as four *kāṛṣāpaṇas* consist of four times sixteen parts, they total eighty *māṣas*, which altogether amount to six thousand four hundred cowrie shells.
"Teeth. This is the large number for four *kārsāpaṇas*. The rest is explained as in the first section of the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya.
(*Māṣa* is also a name for a number; it refers to eighty cowrie shells. If one speaks of a "part," there are five *māṣas*; five *māṣas* as a large number total four hundred cowrie shells.)

Cowrie shells are commonly called *haiba* (sea-bags) by the laity; children often carry them to ward off seizures. They are also called "seizure-warding conchs. In ancient times, they were all used as currency, but during the Qin dynasty, their use was abolished and coins were introduced. Even today, they are still currently used in the kingdom of Magadha.

"Garlic" refers to pungent, aromatic vegetables. Generally, any substance that is pungent and foul-smelling is termed "pungent. There are things that are pungent yet...

Those that are not pungent include substances such as asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). There are things that are pungent but not "fleshy" (*hūn*); these include ginger and mustard. There are things that are both "fleshy" and pungent;
these are the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*). The Buddha prohibited the five pungent roots because they are foul-smelling and impure, capable of obstructing the Noble Path.
Those who consume them will inevitably incur karma leading to the Avīci Hell. Yet, people today are unable to observe this precept.
This refers to those who are unwilling to behold the Noble Path and instead willingly commit the sins of the *ānantarya* class.
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Buddha told Mahāmati: "All such things as onions, leeks, garlic, and scallions are foul-smelling, filthy, and impure;
they can obstruct the Noble Path and likewise obstruct the pure realms of worldly humans and devas, let alone the karmic rewards of the pure lands of the Buddhas. Furthermore, [the text continues:]
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Consuming cooked food arouses lust; eating raw food increases anger.

The celestial beings of the ten directions loathe the stench and depart from afar, while various hungry ghosts lick their lips. Constantly dwelling with ghosts, one's merit and virtue daily diminish, and one will forever lack benefit.
A powerful Mara King may manifest in the form of a Buddha and come to preach the Dharma for them, disparaging the prohibitions and precepts while praising..."
Those who harbor lust, anger, and delusion will, at the end of their lives, become followers of Māra and fall eternally into the Avīci Hell. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Those who eat such things shall be born in places of suffering, defiled and impure. Furthermore, the *Jingfu Jing* (Sūtra on Reverencing Merit) concerning the Golden Coffin says:

"If those who drink alcohol, eat meat, or consume the five pungent roots create scriptures or images, they will labor in vain with little merit; the master craftsmen will gain no benefit, nor will the various devas."
[They] will not receive protection. Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: "Those who eat the five pungent roots defile the Triple Gem;

upon death, they fall into the Hell of Excrement and Filth. When they emerge, they become wild foxes, pigs, or dogs. Even if they obtain a human body, their physical form will be foul-smelling. Moreover, the *Niyata Sūtra* says:
"If a person who eats alcohol, meat, or the five pungent roots enters a monastery, they will fall into a pig's womb. Later, they may..."
Regarding human beings, they often suffer from body odor. The *Baoying jing* (Sutra on Retribution) states: "The seven classes of followers must not eat meat or pungent vegetables.
In cases of illness, it is permitted [to consume them] outside the monastery, at the homes of laypeople, for a period of forty-nine days. Thereafter, one should bathe with fragrant water."
After that, one may recite [the scriptures] without incurring an offense. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, it is permitted for a sick bhikṣu to consume garlic.

He is allowed to stay alone in a small room for seven days; he must not lie upon the beds or mats used by the Saṃgha. He must not go to the lecture hall, nor to the places for urination or defecation.

As for garlic—whether it be *rasonia*, mountain garlic, or any other variety of garlic, as well as all others, whether raw or cooked, leaves or skins—one must not eat them at all.

(The five pungent roots are: first, onion; second, leek; third, chive; fourth, garlic; fifth, *hingukṣā*. *Hingukṣā* is a slight corruption of the Sanskrit sound; correctly it is called *hiṅgu*. [He] saw [them], but did not see them in other countries. Their roots were as thick as the roots of small radishes and white; they smelled like garlic. The people of that country planted and took their roots to eat. At that time, the Tripitaka Master arrived in that country during winter;

They committed an unrighteous act. The Buddha said: "One should grant them the *karmavācanā* for training in the precepts for two years. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, there was a case where a woman who was pregnant was suddenly ordained.
The Buddha said: "Grant her the two-year *karmavācanā* so that it may be known whether [the fetus] exists or not.

This means that by means of the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*), one purifies the mind, and by means of the two years, one purifies the body. Now, according to the intent of the Vinaya, regardless of whether she is pregnant or not, the rule is established as such.

One should grant two years of training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*). It is permitted for a maiden of eighteen who has previously been married and is ten years old to each undergo two years of training in the precepts;
only when they reach the age of twenty and twelve [respectively] shall the full ordination (*upasampadā*) be conferred.

This is because a maiden of eighteen, having not yet experienced the hardships of life and her resolve not yet being fully formed, is not yet capable of receiving the Great Precepts (*mahāśīla*). One should...
One should grant the training for two years. Even if she is over eighteen years of age, one should still grant it (the remainder is explained below as in the commentary). The Buddha said:
"A śikṣamāṇā should learn all the precepts of a full bhikṣuṇī, with the exception of taking food with her own hands and giving food to others.
The *Shishi Yaolan* states: "A śikṣamāṇā fully trains in three dharmas: first, she trains in the roots, which refers to the four pārājikas; second, she trains in the six..."
The *dharmakarma* (legal procedure) regarding those with whom [one may] associate refers to: sexual contact with a defiled mind; stealing four *kārsāpaṇa*; taking the life of an animal;

minor false speech; eating at improper times; and drinking alcohol. Regarding the methods for practicing the three trainings, one should follow and learn the various precepts and deportment of the *bhikṣuṇīs*.
However, one must not disclose the names of the offenses of the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) to them. If one commits a root offense (*mūlāpatti*), [the situation is different].
Regarding the *dharma*: one should immediately expel such a person. If one commits an offense within the *śikṣamāṇā-dharma*, one is granted another two-year *karman*.
If one violates the rules of conduct, this constitutes a direct transgression of the Buddha’s teaching and must be confessed; it does not destroy the six *dharmas* originally undertaken.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: A *śikṣamāṇā* sits below all fully ordained nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*) and above all novice nuns (*śrāmaṇerī*).
Regarding impurity, what is impure for a *śikṣamāṇā* is pure for a fully ordained nun;
what is impure for a fully ordained nun is also impure for a *śikṣamāṇā*. A fully ordained nun may stay with a *śikṣamāṇā* for three nights. The *śikṣamāṇā*...

A *śrāmaṇerikā* may stay with [a bhikṣuṇī] for three nights. A *śikṣamāṇā* may give food to a *bhikṣuṇī*, except for that which has been purified by fire, that which is of living seed, and the taking of gold, silver, or money. She may receive food directly from a *śrāmaṇerikā*.

A *bhikṣuṇī* must not speak to her regarding offenses such as the *pārājika*s, nor even down to the *vinayātikrama* offense; however, she may tell her that one must not engage in sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth. The *śikṣamāṇā*...
The śikṣamāṇā, on the day of the poṣadha or the pravāraṇā, enters among the saṃgha, kneels with her right knee on the ground and joins her palms, saying:
"O noble Saṃgha, I, [name], am pure; may the Saṃgha bear this in mind. She says this three times and then departs.
Regarding those who have committed the four *pārājika* offenses later on, they must begin their training anew.
As for the nineteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and those below them, if one commits each offense individually, one shall perform a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) repentance according to the specific offense committed.

If one violates the rules against eating at improper times, eating stored food, handling money, gold, or silver, drinking alcohol, or wearing flowers and perfumes—these being among the five precepts—one must train for two years again, corresponding to the number of days the violation occurred.

Once the training in the precepts is completed and she wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), the *upādhyāyinī* (preceptor) should formally announce to the Saṃgha and request the *karmavācanā* for maintaining a disciple.
Thereafter, she shall receive full ordination within the two assemblies of the Saṃgha (*āryā*, here translated as "Noble One" or alternatively as "Venerable").

*Ōng-pì-pǒ-ōng*. The pronunciation of *ōng* is like that of *lóng*. It means being exhausted and ill. Being exhausted and ill is synonymous with having a chronic or debilitating illness. This is as the ancients said: "I have the ailment of exhaustion and chronic debility.
*Pì* is pronounced like *bì*. *Pǒ* is the third tone (rising tone) of the character *pō*. As for *pì*, both feet are incapacitated; as for *pǒ*, one [foot] is... [incapacitated].
"Zu" means to be disabled.
"Yin" (pronounced yīn) means mute; "ba" (pronounced yā) means mute. "Yinba" refers to being unable to speak.
The *antarvāsa* (安陀會) is translated here as "lower garment" (*xiàzhuóyī*) or "innermost garment" (*zhōngsùoyī*); it refers to the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*).
The *uttarāsaṅga* (鬱多羅僧)...
This is called the "upper robe" (*uttarāsaṅga*), which refers to the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*).
The *saṃghāṭī* is translated here as the "double-layered robe"; it refers to robes ranging from nine strips up to twenty-five strips.
*Saṃkakṣikā*, sometimes called *saṃghāṭī*. Master Ying states that the correct term is *saṃkacchikā*. *Saṃ* means "to cover" (*yǎnfù*);
*kacchikā* means "armpit" (*yè*). Thus, it is named the "armpit-covering garment. In the Vinaya texts, it is written as *saṃkakṣikā* or *saṃghāṭī*.
The terms *saṃkakṣikā* or *saṃkacchikā* are both corruptions. Tripitaka Master Yijing states that *saṃkakṣikā* is equivalent to what is known here as the "shoulder-covering cloth" (*fubuo*);
it is one cubit longer, which is its proper measurement, and is used to cover the shoulders and armpits.

The Buddha established this regulation out of concern that the three robes might become soiled. First, one should use a common shawl to cover both shoulders, and then, over it, one should don the formal dharma-robe.
One should wrap it around the neck and tighten it, fastening the collar-tabs over the tops of the shoulders; these collar-tabs are similar to those of a shirt.
The robe always covers the body entirely; the shoulders are never exposed, and both hands remain tucked in front of the chest.
Even when performing acts of reverence toward the Triple Gem, receiving the full precepts, or partaking in the ritual of eating, it has never been permitted to expose the chest or shoulders.
When nuns are in the monastery, the rules are always like this; the monks follow the same practice. However, when eating or performing prostrations, the monks expose their shoulders;
this is the custom throughout the Five Indies, for one never sees monks or nuns covering their shoulders.

Within the monastery, there is no rule regarding the use of neckerchiefs or toggles. This is because the woolen cloth is light and coarse, so it does not slip off the shoulders; here in this land, silk is smooth and slippery.
Wearing the *saṃkakṣikā* across the chest is the established custom of one’s own tradition and is not derived from the Buddha’s regulations;

it merely follows what was translated and transmitted by predecessors who did not grasp its proper form. Thus, they call it the *saṃkakṣikā*, yet further claim it is the "shoulder-covering robe" (*kaṭhina*).
However, the "shoulder-covering robe" is actually the *saṃghāṭī*; to call it the *saṃkakṣikā* is a corruption of the transmitted terminology. This...
The two [terms] refer to one and the same object; they are merely given two different names. *Cīvara* resembles a sash, yet its original pronunciation is not so;
the Vinaya does not have this term for "covering the shoulders. Furthermore, the ancient *cīvara* of this region is also not of the original pattern;
it should properly be a *kūṣulaka*, yet it is made with a single side open, which in fact corresponds to a lower garment (*antaravāsaka*). These are not authentic; each has its own [distinctions].
The variations are inconsistent; even in their actual use, they have not yet mastered the proper rules. In the various kingdoms of the South Sea, the community of nuns wears a distinct garment.
Although its manufacture does not conform to the Western [Indian] standard, it is commonly known as the *saṃkakṣikā* (monk’s shoulder-cloth). It is two cubits in length and two cubits in width.
Sew both ends together, leaving a space of about one chi. Stitch each corner for one cun. Lift it up, pass it through the shoulders, and pull it out over the right shoulder.
It requires no waistband; it covers the armpits and breasts, with the lower edge reaching past the knees.
If you wish to wear this garment, there is no harm in doing so. As for the thread, only two strands are required; it is more than sufficient to conceal physical deformities. If...
If one does not prefer it, one may instead return to wearing the *saṃkakṣikā* (undergarment) as worn by the great *bhikṣus*.
Within the monastery rooms, both the *kūrcaka* (waist-cloth) and the *saṃkakṣikā* suffice for these two purposes.

As for the *saṃkakṣikā*, it is made from one and a half widths of silk or cotton cloth, measuring four or five cubits in length; it is worn by draping it over the shoulder like the five-fold robe (*pañcakaṭhina*).
This is the proper ritual. If one is heading elsewhere, one must cover the body well, as if in a private room; baring the shoulders is not appropriate.
During the seasons of spring and summer, this may suffice for the body; during autumn and winter, one may wear whatever keeps one warm as one pleases.
Carrying the alms bowl to beg for food is sufficient to sustain the body. Although she is a woman, she possesses the resolve of a man. (From the South Sea)
This is the region of South India. *Kūsuluka* (also written as *Kusuluka*, as explained in the following text) refers to the shoulder-covering garment;
according to the aforementioned explanation, this is simply another name for the *saṃkakṣikā*. Since it is of two [parts]...
Regarding robes: although they constitute the same type of garment, the five robes of a bhikṣuṇī lack one. It should be understood that this missing one is the *śīrṣaka* (skirt).
As stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, among the five robes of the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha, three share the same name as those of a bhikṣu;
the latter two robes are, first, called the *saṃkakṣikā* (shoulder-covering cloth), and second, the *kuśulaka* (or *kṣudrakā*), also known as the *cīvara*. Now, regarding the *kuśulaka*:
This is the same as the sound of *kusulaka*. This refers to the lower garment (*antaravāsaka*) of a nun.
Since the present Vinaya does not mention a skirt but instead speaks of a "shoulder-covering *saṃkakṣikā*," this must certainly be an error. Therefore, the *Nidāna* states:
*kusulaka*, which is translated here as "grain basket" (*cūan*). As for what was formerly called *kicilinda*, no one recognized its meaning; this, however, is—
It is shaped like a small basket; this is the number of the five robes for a *bhikṣuṇī*. It should be translated as a "skirt" (*śāṭaka*). The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states:

The Buddha said: "If there are those who perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts, then the True Dharma has not yet perished in the world.
He further stated: "As long as the Vinaya-piṭaka remains, the Buddha-Dharma also remains. Therefore, those who propagate and uphold [the teachings] must [act accordingly].
It is especially fitting to follow the teachings so that the True Dharma may endure forever and the Prātimokṣa may remain eternally firm. (Regarding the *kai-tan* [precept altar]:

as for those such as Zhao and others who, out of doubt, received the precepts previously but—due to being of inferior or middling faculties—did not obtain them, they sought to receive them again with increased excellence; thus they did not lose their original seniority (*la*). Nowadays, people have not yet developed a sincere heart seeking the precepts, but merely covet the wearing of robes.

They do not select a teacher or a monk worthy of the Dharma; how then can the precepts be obtained? Furthermore, they constantly sleep apart from their robes, and the robes themselves have long been lost. They do not fear that the present-day *kāṣāya* will leave their bodies, nor that in the future iron leaves will wrap around them. Alas! Moreover, there are those who, having once received the precepts...)

Originally, I did not understand this. My grasp of what constitutes upholding or violating the precepts was utterly bewildered; yet I still insisted on saying that with a single *hwadu*, what is there to uphold or violate? However, where there is receiving [of the precepts], there is upholding and violating. Since there is neither upholding nor violating, what benefit is there in seeking to receive them?

Even after the Sixth Patriarch transmitted the robe and bowl, he still sought out masters like the Dharma Master Ru from the Western Regions to preside over the altar and confer the precepts upon him. Who are we, to boast so recklessly and falsely, slandering the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, and thereby incurring the burden of sin for ourselves for long kalpas?
Explanations of Terms in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Twenty. Phonetic Transcriptions:
[The character for the preface is] 亶 (dǎn). It means "partial" or "one-sided. A "she" (舍) is a dwelling.
"Hù" is pronounced like "hú.
"Tùn" is pronounced like "tún"; it refers to a small granary.
"Xiè" is pronounced like "xiè."
*La* (pronounced *la*).
*Tao* (pronounced *táo*): to weep.

The Great Man possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; his eyes are like those of a pigeon,
and his gaze is deep blue and far-reaching.
Mount Bandhuma, the clan name Ārāḍa, the forest hermitage,
the concentration of non-activity, Udraka Rāmaputra,
the village of the great general Uruvilvā, and the five bhikṣus.
The four daughters: Jambū, Nairañjanā, Bodhi, and Trinaśālā;
and Śrī and Śrīvṛkṣa.
