The Dharma of the Upasampadā-khandhaka.

I have heard that when the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) were first established, there was as yet no distinction between ruler and subject, husband and wife. Once the four clans had arisen, [the social order] consequently...
There exists the sequential order between kings, lords, fathers, and sons; therefore, when a great man takes a single step, he establishes the imperial wheel for ten thousand generations.

It is from this that the Kṣatriya clan first begins its foundation. Those who abandon worldly pursuits and accumulate wealth, concealing their traces to dwell in integrity, constitute the Brāhmaṇa caste.
Based on these causes, categories were established. Those who migrated and pursued profit became the Vaiśyas; those who exerted themselves in the fields became the Śūdras.
Thus, the four castes became manifest, yet the lineage of liberation had not yet been heard of.
Therefore, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, extended their unconditioned compassion and appeared in the world in succession to inaugurate the transformation through the Dharma—down to my own time.
The Great Teacher, the Subduer, who exercises his vast vows of compassion, manifested his wondrous and profound eternal essence and his perfect voice like an echo in a silent valley.
He descended his spirit from Tuṣita Heaven and displayed his signs within the royal palace. He revealed his majestic body of thirty-two marks and manifested his great wisdom of the ten powers.

Mounting his cloud-steed, he passed beyond the Vīra forest; treading through the grove of suffering, he remained for six years. Now that the conditions for his birth have been fulfilled, [he appears].
He moved his body to the Bodhi tree; receiving auspiciousness, he sat cross-legged. Having repelled the demonic adversaries, he settled into meditation.
Beholding the morning star, he awakened to Bodhi and was titled the "Awakened One" (Buddha). Thereupon, throughout the trichiliocosm, radiant light shone forth like a blazing torch.
The four peaks and eight mountains rose in magnificent splendor, radiating brilliance. Dragons and deities danced in competition, and the submerged lands surged with joy.

The devas of the realms of desire and form flew like clouds and shone like stars; ten billion Brahmā kings gathered in a tumultuous assembly, praising and looking up to him with one voice, entreating him to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
He accordingly shifted his posture at the Deer Park and expounded the profound mystery of liberation, whereby the five men realized the Way.
Following the traces of the Dragon River, the sublime path of Śīla was inaugurated, whereby the thousand sages attained the fruits of realization.
Reaching the royal city of Rajagṛha, those who received benefit were infinite; on Vulture Peak and by the Monkey River, those who awakened to the Dharma were beyond counting.
Thus, he rescued the nine abodes and extensively saved those drowning in the six realms. With a single voice he expounded the twelve divisions of the scriptures, leaving no hidden depth unexposed.
Though subtle, it cannot be fully described. If expanded, it comprises eighty thousand *tāla* leaves;

if condensed, it is subsumed within the Threefold Training—namely, morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Morality is the "Ganges Sword" that severs the three evil realms; concentration is the sturdy vessel that cuts off the flow of defilements;
and wisdom is the brilliant torch that destroys delusion and karma. Yet, wisdom arises dependent upon concentration, and concentration relies upon morality.

Birth arises from the merit of precepts, which depends upon their reception. If the reception is flawed, the precepts cannot be attained. The source of attaining the precepts lies in the interplay of mind and object.
If there is even a slight deficiency in this mind-object relationship, the unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) will not be encompassed.

Without such encompassment, the fruits of the Path have no cause; the Jewel of the Sangha cannot be distinguished. Therefore, the precepts serve as the vessel for crossing over birth and death and are the foundation of *nirvāṇa*.
This is the fundamental framework of the Buddha-dharma and the life-vein of the sages and worthies. For this reason, the Tathāgata established it as the foremost of the Tripiṭaka;
therefore, it must be held in the highest respect. As the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa-sūtra* states:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and leaves the household life for even one day and one night..."
They cultivate the path for two million kalpas, never falling into the evil realms, but always being born in auspicious places and experiencing supreme, wondrous bliss.
Encountering spiritual friends, they never regress; they meet with various Buddhas, receive the prediction of enlightenment, and sit upon the Vajra Seat.

One thereby accomplishes the path to perfect enlightenment. However, for those who have left the household life, upholding the precepts is most difficult. If one can uphold the precepts, that is true renunciation.
It is exactly as the Sūtras say: how could one not cherish and respect the Prātimokṣa?
"O Great Being, when this world was first formed, the great earth was a single ocean of water.
Stirred by the wind, it became unified as one mass, like boiled milk. Once it had cooled, solidification occurred; likewise upon the surface of that sea,"
Thus it was. Above, there was the "earth-flavor" (*pṛthivī-rasa*), which was fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite taste (from the *Mūla-saṃnipāta*).

At that time, among the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, some whose merit was exhausted were reborn there, while others, being fond of observing new lands and by nature fickle and restless, tasted it with their fingers.
Having done so three times, they perceived its sweet flavor. Eating it incessantly, they gradually became coarse and corpulent, and [their divine radiance] was lost.
The celestial realms possess wondrous colors and the radiance of supernormal powers. Yet, all becomes profoundly dark.

Subsequently, a black wind blows upon the waters of the great ocean, causing the sun and moon to drift forth and be placed at the edge of Mount Sumeru, established within the solar path. They circumambulate Mount Sumeru, illuminating the four continents.
At that time, when people see them emerge, they rejoice; when they see them enter, they are filled with fear. From this point onward, there are days and nights.

The transition from the new moon to the full moon, and the cycles of spring and autumn, end and then begin again. At the time when the kalpa first formed, the various devas descended to become human beings;

they were all born by transformation, their bodily radiance was sovereign, and they traveled through the air with supernormal power. There were no distinctions of male or female, nor of noble or humble.

Because they arise together in the world in great numbers, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). There was naturally occurring "earth-flavor" (*pṛthivī-rasa*), its taste like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) or fresh ghee (*navanīta*), and its sweetness like honey.
Later, sentient beings tested it with their hands and tasted it; consequently, they developed an attachment to its flavor and gradually began to eat it in morsels.
Their radiance then diminished, and they no longer possessed supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Those who consumed much of this earth-flavor became coarse in appearance.
Those who ate little became radiant in complexion, and thus a sense of competition arose. Because of this competition, disputes and right-and-wrong judgments emerged.
As the *rasa* (earth-essence) gradually faded, everyone became distressed. Then, an earth-skin (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) appeared, resembling thin cakes;
yet this earth-skin also vanished. Next, an earth-flesh (*pṛthivī-māṃsa*) appeared; when the earth-flesh vanished, natural earth-fat (*pṛthivī-puṣṭi*) appeared (as recorded in the *Āgama Sūtra*).
When the earth’s fertility ceased to produce [other crops], two branches of grapevines grew forth, their flavor likewise sweet.

After eating them for a long time in great quantities, they began to mock one another when the grapes failed to grow. Then, non-hulled rice grew spontaneously; it required no sowing and was free from husks or chaff.

It grew to a height of four finger-widths and could be harvested morning and evening, with the stalks regrowing immediately. By the time of the morning and evening harvests, the rice [was ready]. (From the *Loutan jing*)
It then reached maturity; although they consumed it repeatedly, no change occurred in their appearance. Sustaining themselves with this as food, they lived for a long time.
At that time, because those sentient beings consumed solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), impurities accumulated within their bodies. Desiring to eliminate these, two passages were formed.
From this, the male and female organs (*indriya*) subsequently arose, and passion was born. Due to this attachment, they then began to [interact] with one another...
Having become intimate with them, they committed unrighteous acts.
When other sentient beings saw this, they vied with one another to pelt them with refuse, stones, and earth, refusing to dwell together and banishing them from the community.
Because those people of that time were thus driven out, those who delighted in practicing evil subsequently gathered together, constructed dwellings, and covered their bodies [therein].
They committed unrighteous acts; this was the very first time a household was established, and thus families came into being.
At that time, when the sentient beings were at evening or at dawn, they would gather rice out of hunger, taking enough each day to satisfy their needs and leaving no remainder.
Then, one sentient being, due to laziness, rose in the morning to gather rice and subsequently took the amount for both the evening as well.
"Rice! Rice! they cried. When evening arrived, a companion called out to him, "Come, let us go gather rice together. The man replied, "You take it yourself;
I came this morning to gather rice and have already secured enough for two meals.
Upon hearing these words, his companion praised him in his heart, saying, "This is truly excellent. When I go to gather it now, I shall bring back enough for two days' provisions."
In this manner, they imitated one another, taking rice for two days, three days, seven days, and even for half a month or a full month.
Gradually, their intake doubled from the previous amount. Because of this greed, which increased day by day, husks and impurities began to grow within the rice.
Once it was harvested, it would no longer grow; and even when it did grow, [it was covered in husks].
In fact, it gradually deteriorated. Thereupon, the people vied with one another to harvest and gather it;

because they accumulated it out of greed, the rice became small and poor in quality, its husks and impurities increased, and the grain lost its vitality so that it would not grow back after being harvested. Only a small remnant might remain.
When the people saw this, they said to one another, "Let us divide up the boundaries of the land," and so each of them divided it.
For this reason, the cultivation of fields in the world first began, and thus boundaries were established.

At that time, there was a sentient being who, although he possessed his own field, privately stole the grain of others; though warned repeatedly, he did not desist. Consequently, they brought him before the assembly and presented the case.
He recounted the matter. The other, in turn, reproached him, saying, "For the sake of a few grains of rice, you have humiliated me before the assembly.
Because of this incident, the great assembly gathered together and said to one another, "We do not know which of these two persons is at fault.
We intend to select from among the assembly a sentient being who is handsome in appearance, complete in physical form, and possessed of penetrating wisdom."
He was appointed as the Lord of the Fields (Kṣetrapati). He punished those who committed transgressions and nurtured those who were faultless.
We, the multitude, each gave one-sixth of the fields we cultivated according to the law.

At that time, from among the assembly, one person endowed with complete virtues was selected and established as the Lord of the Earth (Bhūmipati); he then administered punishments according to the Dharma.

He nurtured the multitude of beings; once the multitude was established, he was made the lord of the earth, and thus he obtained the name "Mahāsammata" (Great Consent), which is to say, the Great Man-King (*mahāpuruṣarāja*).

Because he was able to protect the weak and vulnerable, he obtained the name "Kṣatriya" (as recorded in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*). By these causes and conditions, the name "Kṣatriya" came into being.
At that time, a certain sentient being had this thought: "All the family lineages and material things in the world..."
"It is like a thorn, a carbuncle, or a sore; you should now abandon it, enter the mountains to practice the Way, and contemplate in a quiet place.
Thereupon, he entered the mountains to contemplate beneath a tree, going out into the village every day to beg for food. When the villagers saw him, they said:
They offered him reverent worship, and the assembly together praised him, saying, "This man is truly able to cast off the burdens of home and enter the mountains to seek the Way.
Because he is able to abandon evil and unwholesome dharmas, guarding the Path and abiding in integrity with pure conduct, he is therefore called a *brāhmaṇa*.
From this cause and condition, there came to be the *brāhmaṇa* caste in the world. Those sentient beings..."
In the middle [class], they practiced various occupations, migrating and pursuing profit to sustain themselves. Because of this, there came to be the Vaiśya caste (merchants) in the world.
Furthermore, among those sentient beings, there were those who exerted their strength in the fields and practiced various miscellaneous arts to support their lives.
Because of this, there came to be the Śūdra caste (those of mixed occupations and farmers) in the world (as recorded in the Āgama Sūtras). Due to these causes...
For these reasons, there exist these four castes, with the Kṣatriya as the foremost. Great Beings are supreme; the Śākya clan descends from such Great Beings.
Now, following the original Vinaya, I have compiled the royal lineage so that those who consult it may easily perceive it.
(The details of the four castes are as explained in the eighty-first precept of the Pātayantika section.)
The first king was named Mahāpuruṣa (the Sūtra calls him Samatāpati);
the second king was named Kalyāṇa (the Sūtra calls him Ratna);
the third king was named Lohitya (the Sūtra calls him Surasa).
The fourth king was named Qi (the sūtra names him Jingqie; the character *qi* was originally written as *zhai*, and later people added the "heart" radical below it to distinguish it).

The fifth king was named Dingsheng (the śāstra names him Mandhātṛ, which means "I-nourish," because he was born from a lump of flesh on the crown of his father's head; thus he was called "I-nourish").
The sixth king was named Chela (the sūtra names him Zhexing; this is counted as the seventh king in that text).
The seventh king was named Vatsara (the Sūtra is titled *Sucarita*);
the eighth king was named Mīḍha (the Sūtra is titled *Mīmāṃsā*);
the ninth king was named Mīḍhila (the Sūtra is titled *Rasendra*).
The tenth king was named Vairi (Vāhyari, the External Seer);
the eleventh king was named Śakrāditya (Śakrāditya, Hundred Wisdom);
the twelfth king was named Lūṣi (Lūṣi, Lustful).
The thirteenth king was named Suruci (Good Desire);
the fourteenth king was named Parana (Severer of Bonds);
the fifteenth king was named Mahāparana (Great Severer of Bonds).
The sixteenth king was named Kṣemaka (Treasury of Jewels);
the seventeenth king was named Mahākṣemaka (Great Treasury of Jewels);
the eighteenth king was named Suprabha.
The nineteenth king was named Mahāsudarśana;
the twentieth king was named Aśoka;
the twenty-first king was named Prabhāsa.
The twenty-second king was named Li-na (meaning "Growth");
the twenty-third king was named Mi-lo (meaning "Mountain");
the twenty-fourth king was named Mo-lo (translated here as "Power," while his name in the scripture is "Divine Heaven").
The twenty-fifth king was named Viryabala (or Kṛtabala);
the twenty-sixth king was named Dṛḍharatha;
and the twenty-seventh king was named Daśaratha.
The twenty-eighth king was named Śata-ratha;
the twenty-ninth king was named Dṛḍhadhanus;
the thirtieth king was named Daśadhanus.
The thirty-first king was named Śata-dhanus;
the thirty-second king was named Siṃha-kara (in the sūtra, he is called Yang-shou);
the thirty-third king was named Jaya (in the sūtra, he is called Shan-si). After King Jaya, ten dynasties succeeded one another.
The succession of the Wheel-Turning Kings (Cakravartin):
the first Wheel-Turning King was named Kṛkin (five kings followed in succession);
the second Wheel-Turning King was named Turuṣka (five kings followed in succession).
The third wheel-turning king was named Aśvapati (seven kings followed in succession);
the fourth wheel-turning king was named Gandhāra (eight kings followed in succession);
the fifth wheel-turning king was named Kalinga (nine kings followed in succession).
The sixth wheel-turning king was named Cāṃpeya (in succession there were fourteen kings);
the seventh wheel-turning king was named Kaurava (in succession there were thirty-one kings);
the eighth wheel-turning king was named Pañcāla (in succession there were thirty-two kings).
The ninth wheel-turning king was named Mṛḍīka (in succession there were eighty-four thousand kings).
The tenth wheel-turning king was named Aśoka (in successive succession there were one hundred kings).
Following these one hundred kings after Aśoka, there was a king named Mahāsudarśana; he was the ninetieth successor after Aśoka.
The fourth king of the world was the seventh-generation ancestor of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Next follows the sequence of the Buddha’s seven generations of ancestral kings;
the name of the seventh-generation ancestor was Mahāsammata.
The sixth patriarch was named Yisimo (identical to the tenth wheel-turning king mentioned above; the sutra names him Upāla).
The fifth patriarch was named Youluotuo.
The fourth patriarch, the high ancestor, was named Jueluo.
The third generation, the great-great-grandfather, was named Bula;
the second generation, the grandfather, was named Siṃhahanu;
and the first generation, the Bodhisattva’s father, was named Śuddhodana (which means "Pure Rice" and is also called "White Pure").

The Cakravartin King of the Golden Wheel was named Bodhisattva Siddhārtha, and the Cakravartin King of the Iron Wheel was named Rāhula (from the first Great Human King down to the Bodhisattva, there were a total of eighty-four thousand two hundred and fifty-four kings; however, according to other sūtras and śāstras, the accounts vary and differ, with the numbers being inconsistent and difficult to reconcile;
only this Vinaya and the *Dīrgha Āgama*’s *Loutan jing* are largely identical).
The Bodhisattva’s ancestral grandfather, King Siṃhahanu, had four sons:
1. King Śuddhodana, who had two sons: the elder was named Siddhārtha (the World-Honored One), and the younger was named Nanda.
2. King Śuklodana, who had two sons: the elder was named Devadatta, and the younger was named Ānanda.
King Trivṛt (Three-Bushel Rice) had two sons: the elder was named Mahānāman, and the younger was named Aniruddha.
King Catur-amṛta (Four Nectars) had two sons and one daughter: the elder son was named Śakra (the Fixed Star), and the younger was named Bhadrika (the Virtuous).
The daughter was named Amṛta-rasa (Nectar Flavor); Amṛta-rasa had a son named Śephalaka, who is the one mentioned in the sūtras as the World-Honored One’s maternal cousin, the bhikṣu Tiṣya.
The Bodhisattva was born on the eighth day of the fourth month at sunrise; some say it was the eighth day of the third month, while others say it was the eighth day of the second month.
These differences arise because generations have passed and time has shifted, or perhaps because the calendar began with the month of Zi (the eleventh lunar month).

The months of Jiànchǒu (the tenth month) and Jiànyín (the eleventh month) were taken as the beginnings of the year. The translators arrived at these dates at different times and translated the scriptures according to their respective eras;

hence this discrepancy. According to the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Marvels in the Book of Zhou), in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao, the year of Jiǎyīn (486 BCE), on the eighth day of the fourth month, the rivers, streams, springs, and ponds suddenly overflowed, and the water in all the wells surged upward, flooding the palaces and private dwellings.

The mountains, rivers, and the great earth all shook. That night, five-colored vapors appeared, penetrating and threading through the Taiwei constellation and spreading across the western quarter, appearing entirely in shades of blue and red. King Zhao immediately asked his ministers, "What omen is this?
None of the ministers could discern its meaning. The Grand Astrologer Suyou divined it and obtained the ninth line of the fifth hexagram, Qian. Suyou said:
"A Great Sage has been born in the West; therefore, he has manifested this auspicious omen. The King asked, "How is it with the world?

Boyou replied, "At present there is nothing else, but beyond a thousand years, his teachings and influence shall reach here. King Zhao immediately dispatched someone to carve an inscription on stone and buried it before the Tianci Temple in the southern suburb.
Later, in the year of Xinyou during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, [the stone was discovered].
The Emperor dreamed of a golden man, sixteen feet tall, with a sun disc upon his crown, who flew into the palace courtyard.
In the morning, he assembled his ministers and ordered them to interpret the dream. Fu Yi, a man of broad learning, submitted this report:

"According to my examination of the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Records of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou), on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jiayin during the reign of King Zhao, a Great Sage was born in the West. More than one thousand years later, his fame..."
Including this teaching, calculating by the year, it has been one thousand ten years until the present *xin-you* year. Is this perhaps what Your Majesty dreamed?
The Emperor believed this to be so and immediately dispatched eighteen men, including the General of the Household Cai Yin and several *boshi*, to travel westward in search of that Way.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi, they indeed encountered Kāśyapa.

On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the year Wuchen, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna—two masters who were experts in the Tripiṭaka—brought with them a white woolen image of the Buddha made during the fourth year of King Udayana’s reign, as well as the Sūtra in Forty-two Sections. An Shigao and others welcomed them and returned home.
Upon arriving in Luoyang, Emperor Ming asked Dharma Master Kāśyapa Mātanga, "Is it possible to know the date of the Buddha’s birth?

Mātanga replied, "In the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao, the year of Jiayin, on the eighth day of the fourth month, he was born from the right side [of his mother] beneath a pāla tree within the Lumbinī Garden. Judging by this evidence, it was indeed the eighth day of the fourth month."
There is no doubt regarding this. The *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* states:

"When a bodhisattva wishes to attain Buddhahood instantaneously without passing through a womb, they manifest birth from a womb (and so forth) to prevent people from harboring doubts—fearing that [the Buddha] might be a mere transformation-body and thus not one who has received the Dharma."
The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: From the time of the Great King Mahāsammata until Rāhula, the lineage was severed. Why?
Because Rāhula realized the fruit of non-arising (*anutpāda-phala*) and thereby cut off the seed of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

For this reason, his lineage was terminated. (Lumbinī is also called Lomilini or Lambinī; it means "place of liberation," and is also called "severance" or "cessation," referring to the severing and cessation of the afflictions [*kleśa*].)

Regarding the Snow Mountains (Himavat): they occupy the northern border of the five regions of India; they lie to the east of Persia and Khorasan; they reside to the south of the Tujue (Turks) and Mount Xiangshan;
and they are situated to the west of China and the Qiang and Hu peoples. Furthermore, within the territory of the five regions of India, there are seven [mountains].
There are more than ten kingdoms. The city of Kapilavastu is located in northern Madhyadeśa (Central India) and borders the realm of Northern India.
The kingdom of Northern India lies at the side of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat). The kingdom of Kapila is the very center of the land of Jambudvīpa.
The *Lokadhātunirdeśasūtra* states that the Snowy Mountains are composed of various jewels and have four golden peaks at its summit. In the center...
First is the High Peak. On the peak is a dragon pond, fifty *yojanas* in breadth; this is the Anavatapta Lake.

Regarding the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, as found throughout various sutras where the Tathāgata himself describes these thirty-two marks, here they are presented according to the sequence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Now, let us set this forth. The body of the Tathāgata’s response and transformation manifests these thirty-two marks to signify that the myriad virtues of the Dharma-body are perfectly fulfilled, causing those who behold it to feel love and reverence, and to know that there exists a supreme virtue worthy of veneration—the Honored One among gods and humans.
As the King of all Sages, he manifests the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

1. The mark of level feet: This means that the soles of his feet rest flat and are entirely level and full, like the bottom of a casket or an incense box. 2. The mark of wheels with a thousand spokes: "Spoke" refers to the spokes within a chariot wheel;

it means that on the soles of his feet, the hub, the web, and the wheel-ridges are all perfectly complete, like a wheel with a thousand spokes. 3. The mark of long, slender fingers: This refers to the hands... [text continues]
1. The fingers are slender, round, and long; they are straight, even, and beautiful; the finger joints are well-proportioned; they are lustrous and lovely—surpassing those of other people. 2.

The mark of the softness of hands and feet (meaning that the hands and feet are exquisitely soft and supple, surpassing the other parts of the body). 3. The mark of the webbed hands and feet (meaning that between the fingers and toes there is a web-like membrane joined together, its pattern like fine embroidery;

it is like the feet of the King of Vultures (*Gṛdhra-rāja*): when the fingers are joined, the web does not appear, yet there is no wrinkling or looseness; when they are spread apart, it appears, yet there is no constriction or tightness). 4. The mark of the full heels (the heel is the back of the foot).

1. The mark of having full and well-rounded heels. 2. The mark of high and beautiful ankles (meaning the ankles are elevated and prominent; they are like the color of pure gold, and the hair upon the ankles is the color of blue lapis lazuli; they are adorned in various ways and are exquisitely perfect). 3.
The mark of calves like those of the king of the *eneya* deer (*eneya* means "golden deer king" in this context; *jangha* refers to the flesh of the calves and thighs;

it means that from the feet to the calves, the limbs gradually taper and become rounded, and the knees are all level and without joints, like the calves of that deer king—exquisite and foremost). 4. The mark of hands reaching below the knees (meaning the two...).

10. The mark of the arms being long and straight (standing upright, they reach past the knees). 11. The mark of the horse-king’s concealed organ (meaning that the male organ is hidden and secret, like that of the horse-king, such that it cannot be seen).

12. The mark of the body being proportionate in length and breadth (meaning that the physical form is upright and well-proportioned; whether measured vertically or horizontally, there is no lack of symmetry). 13.

The mark of the pores producing blue-green hairs (meaning that on all the pores of the body, there is a single hair growing from each pore; their appearance is orderly, curling to the right and pointing upward, and they are deep blue-black in color and soft). 14. The mark of the body hairs pointing upward (meaning the body...).

13. All the pores of the body have their hairs curling to the right, pointing upward, and lying flat. 14. The golden-colored body mark (meaning the entire body is golden in color with a brilliant radiance, like a mass of purple gold, adorned with all the marks, being the most subtle and supreme).
15. The mark of bodily light extending one fathom in every direction (meaning the halo of the body naturally emits light that illuminates each of the four sides for one fathom).

16. The mark of fine and smooth skin (meaning the skin is delicate, smooth, and lustrous; it does not retain dust or water, nor do mosquitoes or gadflies alight upon it). 17. The seven [convexities]...

17. The mark of the seven parts being level and full (meaning that the soles of both feet, the palms of both hands, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck—these seven places are all level, full, and well-proportioned).

18. The mark of the two armpits being full (meaning that the left and right armpits are level and full, without any depressions). 19. The mark of the body being like a lion (meaning that the body is upright and even, and its majestic demeanor is solemn, like that of a lion king).
20. The mark of the body being straight and upright (meaning that the physique is correct, even, and straight, without being hunched or crooked). 21. The mark of the shoulders being rounded and full.
(21) The two shoulders are perfectly rounded and full. (22) The mark of forty teeth (meaning that while ordinary people have only thirty-six teeth, only the Buddha possesses a full set of forty).
23. The mark of teeth that are white, even, and closely set (meaning that all forty teeth are pure white, even, and closely set, and their roots are further deep and firm). 24.
The mark of four canine teeth that are white and pure (meaning that the four canines are the whitest, being brilliantly polished, fresh, and clean).

25. The mark of jaws like those of a lion (meaning that both jaws are full and prominent, just like those of the lion king). 26. The mark of obtaining supreme flavors through the moisture and fluids in the throat (meaning within the throat...).

26. The mark of having a constant flow of exquisite, sublime flavor in the throat and armpits (like the pouring forth of nectar). 27. The mark of a broad and long tongue (meaning the tongue is wide and long, soft, red, and thin;

it can cover the face and reach up to the hairline). 28. The mark of a Brahma-voice that is deep and far-reaching (meaning the voice is harmonious and elegant, reaching both near and far, and being heard everywhere).

The Sūtra says: "In the mountain valleys there is the kalaviṅka bird, which utters a wondrous sound. Such a beautiful voice cannot be matched by gods, humans, or kinnaras, except for the voice of the Tathāgata.
Kalaviṅka means 'wondrous-sound bird'. 29. The mark of eyes with pupils like refined gold (meaning the eyes are pure, clear, and lustrous, like the essence of gold).

30. The mark of eyelashes like those of a bull king (eyelashes refer to the hair at the corners of the eyes; it means the eyelashes are exceptionally superior, just like those of a bull king). 31. The mark of the eyebrows...

The mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows (referring to the space between the two brows where there is a white hair-tuft, pure and soft like *tūla* cotton, curling to the right and constantly emitting light).

The thirty-second mark, the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) (referring to the fleshy prominence on the crown of the head shaped like a topknot; it is also called the "unseen crown" because all humans, devas, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas are unable to see it).

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains the precepts without wavering and the mind of giving without shifting, abiding securely in truthful speech like Mount Sumeru, through these karmic conditions, they attain the mark of soles that are flat like the bottom of a casket.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, toward their parents, preceptors, teachers, elders, and even down to animals..."

If one gives birth [to a child] and provides for them with wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma, through these karmic conditions, one attains the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet.

Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva refrains from killing and stealing, and always gives rise to joy toward their parents and teachers, through these karmic conditions, they attain three marks: first, the fingers are slender and long; second, the heels are long.
Third, his body is square and straight. These three marks arise from the same karmic conditions.

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings, through these karmic conditions he obtains webbed fingers like those of a white goose king.
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, when his parents or teachers are suffering from illness, washes and wipes them with his own hands; [through this, he obtains the mark of long fingers].
By grasping, holding, massaging, and rubbing [others], through these karmic conditions, one obtains soft hands and feet.

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva maintains the precepts, hears the Dharma, and practices giving without weariness, through these karmic conditions, one obtains full and well-proportioned ankles and body hairs that curl upward.
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva listens to the Dharma with single-minded devotion and expounds the true teaching, through these karmic conditions...

One attains the leaping gait of a deer king. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to a harmful mind toward sentient beings, is content with whatever food and drink they receive, always delights in giving, and provides medicine to those who are ill, then by virtue of these karmic conditions, their body will be perfectly proportioned.

Like the nyagrodha tree, his body is well-proportioned; when standing, his hands reach past his knees; he has a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head (uṣṇīṣa), such that the top of his head cannot be seen.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva provides protection for those who are terrified and gives clothing to those who are barefoot and shivering, through these karmic conditions, he attains the mark of the concealed male organ (kośagatavastiguhyatā). If a bodhisattva mahāsattva associates with the wise...

He keeps away from foolish people, delights in skillful questioning and answering, and sweeps and repairs the paths; through these karmic conditions, his skin becomes fine and soft, and the hairs on his body curl to the right.
Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly provides clothing, food and drink, bedding, and—
By giving medicine, incense, flowers, and lamps to others, through these karmic conditions, one attains a golden-colored body that is constantly radiant with light.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, they are able to relinquish their most cherished possessions without stinginess.
Not discriminating between fields of merit and non-fields of merit; by these karmic conditions, one obtains the mark of the seven parts being full.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, when practicing giving, does not give rise to doubt in the mind; by these karmic conditions, one obtains a soft and gentle voice.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and uses it for giving; by these karmic conditions—
He attains fullness of the collarbones and an upper body like that of a lion, with arms and elbows that are long and slender.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva stays far away from divisive speech, harsh speech, and a mind of malice, by virtue of these karmic conditions, he attains forty teeth that are white, pure, even, and closely set.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates great loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, by virtue of these karmic conditions—
He attains the mark of two tusks. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly makes this vow:
"To whoever comes to me seeking something, I shall give it according to their wish," through these karmic conditions, he attains the mark of a lion’s jaw.
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva provides all manner of food and drink required by sentient beings, through these karmic conditions, he attains the mark of supreme flavor in the throat.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva personally cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action and also transforms others through them, by these karmic conditions, they obtain a broad and long tongue.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not speak of the faults of others and does not slander the true Dharma, by these karmic conditions, they obtain the Brahma-voice.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, upon seeing those who are hostile or hateful, gives rise to joy...
Mind. By these karmic conditions, one obtains eyelashes of deep blue color.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not conceal the virtues of others and praises their goodness, by these karmic conditions, one obtains the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (*ūrṇā-kośa*). If a bodhisattva mahāsattva...
When cultivating the karmic causes and conditions for these thirty-two marks, one attains the non-retrogressive bodhicitta.
The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-śāstra* (or *Dhāraṇī-dhātu-śāstra*) states: "The thirty-two marks have no differentiated causes; they are all obtained through the observance of the precepts.
If one does not observe the precepts, one cannot even obtain the body of a low-born human being, let alone the retribution of the marks of a Great Man. Thus says Saccaka.
The *Kātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra* states: "If one does not maintain the precepts, one will not even obtain the body of a jackal afflicted with scabies;

how much less could one obtain a body of merit? For example, suppose all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm, born by the four modes of birth, were to simultaneously become universal monarchs (cakravartin), and their merit were increased a hundredfold;

this would then constitute the merit of a single pore of a Tathāgata. Increasing it another hundredfold constitutes the merit of a single secondary mark (anuvyañjana). Increasing it another hundredfold constitutes the merit of a single primary mark (lakṣaṇa). Increasing it another hundredfold constitutes the merit of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows (ūrṇā-kośa). Increasing it another hundredfold..."

When this is completed, it constitutes the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*). When this is increased a hundredfold, one first achieves the merit of the spiral topknot (*śikhā*). Within the body of the Tathāgata, there are furthermore eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), as explained in the sūtras and śāstras.
*Piṅśā-píng*.

(The second character is pronounced *píng*, with the phonetic component *míng* [蒲明] and the radical *qiè* [切]). This refers to King Bimbisāra, as explained in the section on the precept against stealing (*steya-virati*).
*Vēilúo* (衛邏).
*Wei*: pronounced as *yu gui*, with the phonetic value of *wei*; it means to guard and protect. *Luo*: pronounced as *lang zuo*, with the second tone (departing tone) for *luo*;
it means to patrol. *Ganqinggan*: *gan* is pronounced as *gu an*, with the departing tone for *gan*; *gan* means to contain. It refers to a deep blue that contains a trace of red.

Gù pàn (the second character pronounced with a departing tone). It means to look around. (Furthermore, when the black and white of the eyes are clearly distinguished, it is written as 盼; the common vulgar form is 盻. In the Vinaya texts, it was formerly written as 眄, which is incorrect.)
Bandhava Mountain is also called Pan-da Shan (Mount Bandha) or Ban-ta Shan (Mount Banta). In the *Buddhacarita* (The Life of the Buddha), it is translated as "White Mountain" (*Sveta-parvata*).
Its clan name is Rishi.

Regarding the lineage of the Solar Clan (*Ādityavaṃśa*), various accounts appear across the Sūtras and Vinayas, with their causal origins being manifold. Now, according to the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins:
from King Mahāsaṃmata (the Great Consensus King), who appeared at the beginning of the kalpa, the succession was transmitted in order. Later, there was a king named Kṛkin.
At that time, Tathāgata Kāśyapa appeared in the world. That king had a son named Sujāta; after King Sujāta, [the succession continued].
Thus, in the succession of one hundred and one generations, the last king was named Karṇa. King Karṇa had two sons:
the first was named Gautama, and the second was named Prasenajit.

Seeing that his father ruled the kingdom unrighteously, Gautama took leave of his father and went to the hermitage of the Black Sage (Kāla-rṣi) to renounce the household life. Prasenajit succeeded to the throne.
He became king. Later, while Gautama was in the mountains eating various fruits and herbs, he fell ill.
He then went near a city and stayed there, having built a hut. At that time, a thief’s husband had secretly killed his mistress and thrown the knife before the hut.

When the pursuers saw the knife, they immediately seized Gautama and bound him, leading him before the king. The king ordered him to be paraded through the city to be shown to the public, and placed him—
On the point of the sharp wood, the black-colored seer arrived and, upon seeing him, was deeply moved by grief.
He asked, "Now that you have been wounded, has your practice of the various dharmas declined in body or mind? He replied, "Though my body is wounded, my mind is unharmed.
The teacher said, "How may I know this? He replied, "If the course of my mind has truly not changed, I pray—"

The master’s complexion was black; it transformed into a golden color. At that moment, the rishi also transformed into a golden color and addressed his master again, saying, "When I now relinquish my life, what path shall I attain?
The master replied, "According to the teachings of the non-Buddhists, one who has no son [attains such a state]."
Unable to attain the good path, he was made to recollect the acts of lust from his past lives.
Consequently, two drops of semen and blood emerged from his body and fell to the ground. By the power of karma, these immediately became two eggs. Warmed by the rays of the sun, two boys were born.
Nearby there was a sugarcane grove, and they went into the grove to play. A seer took them [there].
He returned and raised him until he was grown, giving him the name Nanda-janman (Born of Joy). For this reason, he is called of the Solar Lineage (*Sūrya-gotra*).

Furthermore, because he is a descendant of the Gautama clan, he is also called Gautama (formerly transcribed as *Gautama*; this is correct). Because he was born from the body [of his father], he is called Body-born (*Kāyaja*).
Moreover, because he was found within a sugarcane grove, he is also called of the Sugarcane Lineage (*Ikṣvāku-gotra*). By these four [reasons]...

For these reasons, there were four titles. Later, when King Prasenajit died without an heir, the ministers deliberated together and wished to invite the king’s elder brother, Gautama, to succeed him on the throne.
Upon learning that he had already died, they invited the eldest son to return to the kingdom to inherit the throne and govern the country.
Before long, he also passed away without an heir, whereupon they again invited the younger son.
He returned to succeed to the royal throne. The multitude conferred upon him the title of King Ikṣvāku.
His descendants succeeded one another for one hundred generations, all of whom were known as the Ikṣvāku clan. The last king was named Senāpati, also called Vardhana. This king had four sons:

the first was named Ulkāmukha (the Sūtra calls him Prabhāsa-mukha); the second was named Mahākarṇa (also called Śravaṇakarṇa); the third was named Hastivikrama; [and the fourth was named]... [text fragment].
(Alternatively named Tamed Elephant). The fourth was named Ratnakaṭaka (alternatively named Ornament). Later, he took a wife and fathered a son named Priya (alternatively named Ever-Living).
Desiring to establish him as his successor, he banished his four sons from the borders of the kingdom.
At that time, the four princes, together with their four sisters and a great multitude of followers, arrived at the banks of the Gaṅgā River, where the seer Kapila resided.
At the place where they dwelt, they cut thatch to build huts and lived near the rishi. The rishi, weary of the noise, took his four sons and went to another favorable location;
there, he sprinkled water on the ground to mark the boundary. The princes followed his instructions, built a city, and settled there.
Because of the seer’s indication, it was established and named the City of Kapilavastu (formerly called Jialipoluo).
Later, as the population gradually increased and the original city became cramped, a celestial deity, having observed this, pointed out another spacious site and established a separate city.
Consequently, this city was called Devadaha. At a later time, King Mahāsaṃmata asked his ministers: "My..."
"Where are my four sons now? The minister replied, "They are beneath the Snowy Mountains, in the city of Devadṛśa, where they have extensively established cities and towns.
Upon hearing this, the king leaped for joy and, raising his hands, exclaimed, "My sons are truly capable! My sons are truly capable!
It was because of these words of praise—*śakya* in Sanskrit, which means "capable"—that he acquired the name Śākya. Later, when the king passed away, Priyadarśana...
King Vītaśoka died without issue. The ministers went to the city of Devadṛśa and installed the eldest prince, Arciṣmukha, as the sovereign of the kingdom.
He too died without issue. They then installed Mahākarṇa as king;
Mahākarṇa died without issue. Again, they installed Hastipada as king; Hastipada was childless. They then installed Ratnakaṭaka.
He became the king. Ratnacūḍa had a son named Upacūḍa, who later succeeded him to the throne.
Upacūḍa had a son named Devadundubhi, who also succeeded him to the throne. King Devadundubhi [ruled] in the great city of Kapilavastu.
The descendants succeeded one another in turn until the time of King Siṃhahanu.
Among all those skilled in archery in this Jambudvīpa, King Siṃhahanu was the foremost (he was the ancestral king of the Tathāgata). According to the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, the four sons were banished;
they took their leave of the king and departed. Reaching the borders of the Snowy Mountains, they wandered far to the east and west, and then toward the south.
To the north lies a vast expanse. The ground is as level as a whetstone and abounds in timber from the Śibi region. There, cities and settlements were built;

the population flourished, the soil was fertile, and the fields were rich, such that there was no lack of food or clothing. When the father-king heard of this, he sighed in admiration, saying three times, "My son possesses great capability.
From this, they were subsequently called the Śākya clan. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that they resided at Ṛjuka-vṛkṣa.
"Forest. He was also called Śākyamuni; because he took the forest as his clan name, the *Bodhisattva-pūrvacaryā-sūtra* states:
"Because Śākya dwelt beneath the dense shade of the branches of a great tree, he was therefore named Śākyamuni (i.e., Śāyi).
According to various sūtras and vinayas, it is sometimes called the country of Śākyas, and sometimes the clan of Śākyas; this is naming him after his place of residence.
This was the Venerable Āḷāra Kālāma (also known as Rauruka Kālāma).
This man had already attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness and had attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.

The concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*) refers to the time when one cultivates this concentration; at that time, one does not employ any internal or external objects. External objects are called "space," and internal objects are called "consciousness.

By relinquishing these two objects, one enters the sphere of nothingness (it is called "the sphere of nothingness" because one does not employ them when first beginning the cultivation). It is also called "the state of non-existence."

There are locations; these constitute the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Now, there are four such locations for the formless absorptions, collectively termed the "emptiness concentrations" (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
They are called "empty" because the essence of these four concentrations lacks form or color.
Each takes its respective realized object as its location. Because the object-dharma sustains the mind, and the mind is thus without distraction, it is called "concentration" (*samādhi*).
1. The concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*). This refers to entering concentration by taking space as the object, having extinguished the three kinds of form.

It is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (the practitioner, weary of form as if it were a prison, desires mental liberation; thus, they cultivate the wisdom of insight to break through form. Having transcended all signs of form, extinguished the signs of resistance, and no longer attending to various signs, they enter the sphere of infinite space.

The mind accords with the dharma of space; this is the concentration of the sphere of infinite space). 2. The concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*). This refers to relinquishing space and taking consciousness as the object, thereby entering [concentration].

The concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*): This refers to a practitioner of meditation who, becoming weary of space—thinking that space is boundless and that focusing on too many objects leads to distraction which can destroy concentration—abandons space and turns the mind to focus on consciousness.

When the mind is in correspondence with the phenomenon of consciousness, it is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness. The third is the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*):

This refers to one who abandons the sphere of infinite consciousness and enters concentration with the mind resting upon the phenomenon of nothingness; this is called the concentration of the sphere of nothingness. (The practitioner of meditation becomes weary of consciousness, thinking that consciousness throughout the three periods of time is boundless and that focusing on it...)

If it is excessive, it becomes distracted and can destroy concentration; therefore, one relinquishes the consciousness that takes [the lower realm] as its object and turns the mind toward the dharma of nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*), becoming associated with that dharma of nothingness—this is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

That which was realized by Ārāḍa Kālāma is the fourth, the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*); this refers to entering concentration by relinquishing the perceptions of both extremes.

It is called the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*). (For one who practices concentration, they feel weary of the perception of the sphere of nothingness as being like delusion, and they regard the sphere of perception as being like an abscess or a sore.

There is another concentration named the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; that is, having abandoned the sphere of nothingness, one takes as an object and contemplates the dharma of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

The mind becomes associated with that dharma; this is the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Furthermore, it is said: "Ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists also attain this concentration. Because they do not penetrate [the truth] and claim to have realized *nirvāṇa*, they sever all perceptions; therefore, it is called 'neither-perception. The disciples of the Buddha, however, know according to reality that subtle perception exists, and they rely upon the four assemblies."

Because one abides [therein], it is said not to be "without perception. Since the name is established by combining both attainment and loss, it is called the "concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*). Udraka Rāmaputra realized this concentration and was reborn in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, where his lifespan lasted eighty thousand great kalpas;
subsequently, he fell into the body of a flying fox.
Udraka Rāmaputra (also transliterated as You-ta-lan-fu) means "Son of Udra.

This person had already attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and achieved the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Udraka..."
Pūra and Kālāma did not undergo transformation through this profound Dharma; each met his end according to his lifespan. The World-Honored One prophesied concerning these two men:
"One has been born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), and the other has been born in the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana)."
These two individuals lived out their full lifespans and each subsequently passed away.

One was to become a king of a frontier region who would inflict incalculable harm upon the people. The other was to become a winged, malevolent wildcat that would fly and run after beasts, from which none could escape.
After their lives ended, they were both reborn in the hells. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "Mā..."

In the kingdom of Kāśī, to the east of the Mahānadī River, within a great forest, there is a stone pillar. This is the place where non-Buddhist practitioners entered meditative absorption and made evil vows.
Formerly, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Udraka Rāmaputra, whose aspirations soared beyond the mists and clouds while his body remained hidden in the grassy marshes.
He dwelt here in this Forest of Dharma, concealing his traces and settling his spirit; having attained the five supernormal powers, he reached the first [dhyāna].
There was a king of Magadha who held him in particularly deep reverence. Every day at midday, he would invite him to the palace for a meal.
Udraka Rāmaputra traveled through the air, traversing the void back and forth without fail. The King of Magadha would wait for the appointed time, gazing out in expectation.

Having arrived, she was received with honor and seated upon a throne. As the King was about to depart on a journey and wished to entrust her with the affairs of the palace, he sought among his court ladies for one capable of receiving this command.

Among all those in the palace, there was none more worthy than his young daughter, who was virtuous, prudent, and possessed of exemplary conduct; indeed, no one in the palace was more beloved or esteemed than she.
The King of Magadha summoned her and commanded her, saying: "I am now departing on a distant tour and have someone to entrust to you."
"You must apply yourself with all your heart and carefully see this matter through to its conclusion. That seer Udraka Rāmaputra has long been accustomed to receiving respectful offerings;

when his time comes, he will come to eat just as I do. Once you have issued these instructions, you may then attend to your other duties. Having received these commands, the young woman waited upon him according to the prescribed rites.
When the Great Seer arrived, she took [the food] and placed it before his seat. As soon as Udraka Rāmaputra touched the woman, he rose up.
Afflicted by the defilements of the desire realm, he lost his supernormal powers. Having finished his meal, he said he was returning home; he could no longer travel through the air at will.

Feeling deep shame in his heart, he spoke deceptively to the woman, saying: "Lately, as I have cultivated my spiritual practice, I have entered meditative concentration to harmonize my spirit and traveled back and forth through the void, leaving me with almost no leisure time.

The people of this land have long desired to see me, having heard of me for a long time. However, the teachings handed down by our predecessors instruct us that we must take the benefit of sentient beings as our primary task."

How could one cling to solitary perfection while forgetting universal salvation? Now, wishing to depart through the gate and travel upon the earth, I shall cause all who behold me to receive benefit and merit.
Upon hearing this, the princess proclaimed it far and wide. At that time, people vied with one another in their devotion;
hundreds of thousands gathered to sweep and clean the thoroughfares, waiting expectantly for her arrival. Udraka Rāmaputra—
The son walked from the royal palace to that Forest of Dharma. There he sat in repose and entered meditative concentration, yet his mind wandered toward external objects.

As he dwelt in the forest, the crows and birds warbled; as he approached the pond, the aquatic creatures leaped and splashed. His emotions were scattered and his mind was distracted; losing his spirit, he abandoned his concentration.
He then gave rise to indignation and immediately made an evil vow: "In a future life, may I become a violent and wicked beast with the body of a wildcat."
He was a bird with wings that preyed upon living beings; his body was three thousand li wide, and each of his two wings was fifteen hundred li wide.

Having thought thus, he accepted the bowls. By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he placed them nested one within another, and so they were.
It became a single bowl. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings could not see one another, and each thought, "The World-Honored One is using my bowl alone.
That bowl was pure, light, and exquisite; it was all-pervasive, fine, and dense; its form and color were dignified and solemn;
