At the age of eight, he could recite eighteen divisions of the scriptures and thoroughly understood the principles and meanings of all texts. At that time, the King of the Nāgas in the kingdom of Magadha...
At a great assembly, the king and his ministers spread out a high Dharma seat and gathered various scholars to discuss the meaning of the teachings.

At that, with a body only eight years old, he ascended the debate dais and sat cross-legged. The multitude was filled with doubt and wonder; yet, he proceeded to provide answers that captured the essential purport of their inquiries.
His rhetoric and principles were so transcendent that the various masters of treatises marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

The King was greatly delighted and immediately granted him a village as a fief, providing for his constant support. The King, riding in an elephant carriage and ringing a bell, proclaimed this throughout all sixteen great nations;
within the six great cities, there was no one who did not rejoice. At that time, there was a master of auspicious divination named Kauṣṭhila.
His surname was Maudgalyāyana; Śāriputra subsequently befriended and became close with him.

Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent and insight, while Maudgalyāyana was held in high regard for his noble and spirited character. These two men were comparable in their wisdom and talent, and equal in their virtuous conduct.
When traveling, they journeyed together; when sitting, they stayed together. From their youth, they were bound by deep affection, pledging to remain so until the end.

Later, both grew weary of the world and left the household life to study the Way, becoming disciples of a *brahmacārin*. They sought the gateway to the Path with diligence, yet for a long time there was no sign of realization.

Subsequently, they encountered the bhikṣu Aśvajit (i.e., Aśvajit), heard a verse on the Dharma-body, and immediately realized the first fruit (*srotāpatti*). Thereupon, they joined the Buddha and renounced the world.
After he had left the household life, more than half a month later, the Buddha preached the Dharma to the brahmin Dīrghanakha.
Upon hearing it, Śāriputra immediately attained the path of arhatship and became the teacher who turned the wheel of the Dharma following the Buddha;
he was known in the world as the "Second Buddha" (the remainder is explained as in Volume Two. The brahmin Dīrghanakha was Śāriputra’s maternal uncle).
Kulada is the name of a tree.
Because he obtained a son by praying to the deity of this tree, he was named after it. His clan name was Maudgalyāyana;
because of this, people of the time frequently referred to him by his clan name. He resided in the kingdom of Magadha at [the village of] Kolita.
The village of Nādikā, surrounded by forests, was not far from Rājagṛha. The *Sūtra on the Twelve Years of Wandering* states:
"In the first year after attaining enlightenment, the Buddha converted five men; in the second year, he converted the three Kāśyapas;
and in the fifth year, he converted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana" (the remainder is explained as in the second fascicle. Śāriputra is Śāradvatīputra).

The former masters referred to him as Upasena, which in this [language] means "Little Army" (Xiaojun). The *Saṃyukta-gāthā* states that in the Sui language he is called "Supreme General of the Campaign.
He was the son of Bhaṇḍu; the details are explained as in the *Cīvara-vastu*.
Shé (蝎): *xù jié* (許竭) cut; pronounced *xiè*. It refers to the scorpion, a venomous insect that stings humans. In common parlance, it is called the "Accountant Insect" (*zhǔbù chóng*).
The chameleon (*xīyì*) can eat it, and it is also eaten by the snail (*wāniú*). Therefore, when people are stung by a scorpion nowadays, they [use] the snail...
Spittle is smeared upon it. The front of a scorpion is called *chē* (螫); the rear of a scorpion is called *chài* (蠆). When a male stings a person, the pain remains localized in one spot;

when a female stings, the pain spreads to various parts of the body. (*Xī*, pronounced like *xī*; *yì*, pronounced like *yì*, refers to the *shǒugōng*, or "palace-keeper" lizard. Some say these two creatures are distinct: that which dwells on walls is called the *shǒugōng*.)

Among the grasses, there is the lizard (*xi*). Its tail is continuous with its body like that of a snake; it has four legs. Some are blackish-green, while the *shougong* (gecko) is brownish. It has four legs and a tail, and lies prostrate against walls or beneath houses.
*Jiǎo* (phonetic transcription: gǔ qiǎo qiè; *jiāo* in the third tone): to wind around; to bind tightly. It refers to wringing water from clothing.
Also used for vegetables.
*Ru* (茹): pronounced like *ren* with the final *yù* (切), sounding like *rǔ*. It refers to dried vegetables. The *Guǎngyá* states: "Rú means to eat. *Zhūkuāng* (竹筐):

*kuāng* is pronounced like *qū* with the final *wáng* (切), sounding like *kuāng*. It is a bamboo vessel; one that is square is called a *kuāng*, while one that is round is called a *jǔ* (筥) [the character *jǔ* is pronounced like *jǔ*; it can hold five *shēng*].

*Mǔ* (牡) means "male" (*mǔ*). [The character is pronounced] with the *mò* (莫) and *ǒu* (偶) initials; its sound is like *mǔ* (畝). It refers to the male bolt of a door hinge. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The male bolt inserted beneath the door hinge.
According to this, it serves as the male component of the lock; by means of it, the door is secured so that it cannot be opened.
"Shuàihuàn" (串戶串) refers to a door-bolt. In the *Cāngxiè piān* (蒼頡篇), it is written as "tán" (橝). Pronounced with the initial *dú* and rhyme *diǎn*, its sound is like *diàn*. It means "to hold.
This refers to what is called "the outer door not being bolted" (*wàihù bù tán*). In the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* (摩得勒伽論), it is written as "jiàn" (扂). What is a door-bolt? If [it is] above or below...
As for the door-bolt: it should be lowered together [with the door] once one has departed, in order to make the dwelling secure, to protect oneself,
and to protect the bedding from floodwaters.
*Lang* (cut by *dao*) has the pronunciation *lao*. It means continuous rain. It also has the departing tone (*qùshēng*), meaning submerged water.
*Cí dàn dàn*: *dàn* is cut by *du yàn*; it has the departing tone of *tán*, meaning to dread or avoid. It also has the initial *ding zǔ*; it has the departing tone of *duō*, meaning toil.

Regarding the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, it says: At that time, the Venerable Upananda rose from meditative concentration in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Disciple... [The details are as in the Vinaya text.]
"Regarding the methods for serving one's teacher, I pray that you will explain them to me. The Buddha told Bhadrika: "I shall now explain them for you.
Listen attentively, Bhikṣu, to the manner in which all disciples and followers should provide service. As for being a disciple,"
Toward one's preceptor, one should always maintain a sense of reverence and a mind of awe;
not for the sake of fame, nor seeking profit and sustenance, one should rise early and personally inquire after the two teachers regarding their well-being, physical comfort, and ease of movement.
One should remove their urinal vessel and massage their body. If the teacher says, "I am currently ill," one should ask what the ailment is and then...
Go to a physician and explain the origins of the illness in detail, requesting a method for treatment. Act according to the physician’s instructions and provide the treatment.
If the teacher possesses medicinal substances, they should be used to compound the remedy. If he does not have them, one may ask a close relative.
If there are many relatives, one should ask the teacher, "From which relative should I seek [the medicine]? Having received the teacher's instruction, one may go as directed.
If there are no relatives, one should go to other households and seek [medicine] as instructed, or go to a hospital or a place where medicine is distributed.
If these are unavailable, one should attend to the patient's recovery by means of their own provisions for food and drink. When the illness permits, one should provide a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).
Before the teacher intends to chew the tooth-stick, the place where he will do so should first be swept clean. One should prepare...
In the maṇḍala, arrange a stool, a water vessel for rinsing, as well as cleansing powder and earth, tooth-sticks, and a tongue-scraper.

Once he has finished washing and rinsing his mouth, remove the necessary items. If the master suffers from eye ailments, one should consult a physician to prepare an ointment for the eyes and apply it to them.
Next, one should offer him his robes; any remaining robes should be folded and stacked, not left [in disorder].
In a state of disorder. When the Master pays homage to the stupa, he should enter the room and sweep the floor.
If there is dust or dirt, he should use cow dung or wipe it clean with green leaves. Next, he should personally pay homage to the sacred image and to his preceptor.

Someone asked about the procedures for daily affairs: one should perform prostrations three times each day according to one's own ability, and likewise extend respectful greetings to fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
Next, one should exert oneself in seated meditation and the recitation of scriptures. Every half-month, one should...
One must inspect the bedding and mats for sun-drying. When it is time for the meal, one should wash both alms bowls.
If one is a bhikṣu who goes on alms-round, one should carry the heavy bowl oneself and give the lighter one to the teacher.

If it is cold weather, one should give the heavy saṃghāṭī to the teacher to wear and carry the lighter one oneself. If it is hot weather, one should give the lighter one to the teacher and carry the heavier one oneself. If...
If traveling against the wind, request that the teacher go in front and you remain behind. If traveling with the wind, you should go in front and let the teacher follow behind.
When crossing a river, support them so they may pass safely. When it is time to beg for food, you should ask the teacher whether you should travel together or go separately.
If he says to travel together, you may then follow him. If [he says to go separately...]
If one has dry flour, bean porridge, or sour gruel placed in the bowl, or if one obtains rice, cakes, granulated sugar, milk, curd, or rock honey, one should place these within the Master’s bowl.
Having begged for food and returned to the original location, one should prepare two small altars, spread various leaves upon them, and arrange two seats.
Sitting cross-legged, one should eat the meal. If one is traveling separately, [the procedure is as follows...]
Having obtained food, he shall present it to his preceptor, saying: "I have now obtained this food; you should take what you require.
The preceptor should then receive it with due moderation. If the preceptor resides in the monastery, the disciple should first wash the vessels and go to the kitchen.
He asks the administrator, "What food and drink is being prepared for the Saṃgha?

The administrator respectfully informs him, and he returns to report to his teacher, "Today the Saṃgha is preparing such-and-such food; may I request that you partake? Following these instructions, he brings it back.
The teacher should receive it with moderation, observing the proper time. If there are two teachers, they should [wash their hands and mouths] at the place for rinsing.
Having cleared away [the impurities], one should construct a maṇḍala, arrange a small stool, a water vessel, as well as earth and a tooth-stick, and wash according to the ritual rules.
If it is necessary to wash the feet, one should wash them for the teacher;

this may be done using only water, or by applying oil and rubbing it off with a powder, followed by washing again with water. One should then offer leather sandals and inquire about his meal, and further inquire...
Is it for the purpose of practicing wholesome deeds in this place, or is it to go toward another secluded dwelling?
If one says that one may go to a daytime dwelling, one should take along a seat. That dwelling should be swept clean and, from time to time, smeared with cow dung.
If there are those studying recitation, one should provide them with the scriptures; if there are those practicing meditative reflection, [one should assist them].
Instruct him in the proper mental application (*manasikāra*). When he returns, he should inspect the bedding and mats;

having washed his own feet, he should next pay homage to the sacred images and his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*), prostrating according to his capacity. He should arrange a seat for the teacher and wash his feet as before.
If it is cold, he should maintain mindfulness and prepare warm water; if it is hot, he should hold a fan.
He did so to summon a cool breeze. The Master also understood the timing and ordered him to perform his work, so that he would not let it pass in vain.
Regarding robes, bowls, and other items, at the time of construction, all tasks were to be performed first for the Master’s property, and only thereafter for one's own.
The Buddha said, "O Exalted One, you should now know that all the disciples and followers of the assembly of Bhikṣus must be provided for."
One should regard the two teachers as one's parents, and the teachers should regard their disciples as their own children.
If there is illness, they should attend to and serve one another until old age or death. I shall now briefly explain this matter for you; you should act in this way.
If you do not comply with this, you will incur an offense against the Dharma for each such instance.

If you can act in this way, the disciple, with a heart of reverence and obedience, serves as an attendant to the teacher, enabling the succession of wholesome dharmas to continue without interruption.
Just as a lotus flower situated in a pond grows and flourishes day and night, so too should you all train yourselves in this manner.

The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "As for instructing one's disciples, this is the essential means for ensuring the flourishing of the Dharma. If one does not maintain mindfulness in this regard, the extinction of the Dharma may be expected;

therefore, the matter must be handled with earnest diligence, lest the net be too wide and let slip what should be preserved. The Vinaya says: Every morning at dawn, one should first chew a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).
Next, one may approach the teacher, offering him a tooth-stick, soap powder (*snāna-kalka*), water, and a towel, and having prepared his seat."
Once he is at ease, he then pays homage to the venerable image, circumambulates the Buddha hall, and returns to his teacher.
He arranges his robes, performs one prostration, and without rising again, joins his palms and bows three times. Kneeling with both knees on the ground, he lowers his head, joins his palms, and asks:
"O Upādhyāya, please attend to me," or he asks: "O Ācārya, please attend to me; I now request..."
[The disciple] says: "Venerable Upādhyāya, I do not know if you have spent the night in peace. Are your four great elements in harmony? Is your movement and rest light and easy?
Has your food been digested? Can you partake of this morning's meal? This [greeting] may be expanded or abbreviated according to the occasion.
The teacher, in turn, gauges whether [the disciple] is at ease and answers these matters in detail. Next, one should reside in a neighboring or adjacent room. One is able to...

One should perform the major rites first, followed by reading a small portion of scripture and recollecting what was previously received, so that with each passing day and month, old knowledge is renewed and not a single moment of time is wasted.
One should wait until the time for the morning meal to assess the state of one’s physical strength; only after making the formal announcement (*pratyāśrāvaya*) may one eat.

Why the need for such haste at dawn to seek out gruel? Without having announced it to one's preceptor, there is no way to chew the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), nor is there leisure to observe for insects.
Water—how could it possibly cleanse [this]? How could one know that for the sake of a single bowl of gruel, one would violate four kinds of Buddhist teachings?
The roots of such errors and corruptions all originate from this. I pray that those who hold the office of *zhuchi* (abbot) will carefully weigh the circumstances.

Once one has shaved the head, donned the *saṃkakṣikā*, left the household life, and received full ordination (*upasampadā*), the Vinaya states: "Except for five matters, one must not fail to inform [others]; as for everything else..."
Each and every one of these must be reported to the teacher; failure to report them constitutes an offense. The five matters are: first, chewing a tooth-stick;
second, drinking water; third, defecating; fourth, urinating; and fifth, performing circumambulation (pradakṣiṇā) of a stūpa within a distance of forty-nine fathoms inside the boundary.
Furthermore, for example, if one wishes to eat white rice, one must go before the preceptor and, according to the ritual of prostration, address the preceptor, saying:
"O Upādhyāya, please attend to me; I now request permission to wash my hands and the vessels, as I wish to partake of food. The preceptor says:
Be cautious. Other matters of a virtuous nature should be understood in this same way. The teacher shall then weigh the circumstances and the timing, and direct whether one may proceed or remain.

If one knows there are many matters, they may be reported all at once. If one has mastered the Vinaya and completed five summer retreats, one may leave one’s original teacher to travel among people and seek further training;
however, wherever one goes, one must still rely upon a preceptor. Once ten summers have passed...

[The period of] full [observance] ends only upon returning to one’s place of residence. The Great Sage’s earnest intent lies herein: if one does not understand the Vinaya, one should rely on another for as long as one lives;
even if there is no senior, one should abide by the minor rules. With the sole exception of prostrations, all else should be performed for them.
How could one possibly inquire after their well-being at dawn without ever relying on the Vinaya? When matters arise, how can one know when to offer a formal announcement (*jñapti*)? There may be...
At the two times of morning and evening, one requests their instruction and admonition. Although such instructions may be provisionally extended, the intent of the Vinaya texts is not thus.

Why is this? Because a formal motion (*jñapti*) does not specify the matter itself; as for the response (*karmavācanā*), what would there be to deliberate? Such is the nature of the words used in a formal motion.
Therefore, this is not the case. It is simply that because [the practice] has been followed for so long, people have become negligent; who would willingly undergo such toil and trouble?
If one can indeed follow and practice according to the teachings, then the continuity of the monastic community will be maintained.

If one regards this as trivial, then what else could be considered important? Thus, the Vinaya text says: "It would be better to be a butcher than to bestow the full precepts upon another and then abandon them."

This is the teaching. Furthermore, according to the tradition inherited in the Western Regions (India), regarding the etiquette for serving one's teacher: during the first watch and the last watch of the night, one goes to the teacher’s quarters.

The teacher then first instructs the disciple to sit down comfortably. From among the Three Piṭakas, he provides instruction at appropriate times concerning both phenomena and principles, ensuring that time is not spent in vain.
He observes the disciple’s observance of the precepts and ensures they do not fall into violation; should he perceive any transgression, he immediately orders [the disciple to confess].

When performing the *zhichan* (confession and repentance), the disciples shall then massage their teacher’s body, fold and arrange his robes, sweep and wipe the rooms and courtyards at times, observe for insects before pouring water, and perform every minor task on his behalf; this is the ritual of honoring one's superior.
If a disciple falls ill, they shall all personally attend to them, supporting them and providing whatever is required for medicine and nourishment, showing deep concern.
They are like one's own infant. Yet, the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma take instruction as their foremost priority.

Just as the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning King is nurtured without neglect, the Vinaya contains explicit statements; how could one possibly permit such arrogance? Master Nanshan said: "The Buddha’s benefit is vast and great precisely because of the mutual support between teacher and disciple.
Through their constant encouragement and assistance, they provide both material and Dharma aid; thus, day by day, their practice deepens and endures for a long time."

Virtue is indeed firmly rooted; all depend upon this. Lately, as the True Teaching has declined and the wind of wisdom has been stilled by the fanning of the world, commoners harbor contempt and the Way has strayed into what is unlawful.
This is entirely because the teachers lack the heart to lead and inspire, while their disciples lack the will to practice and uphold it.
When these two abandon one another, they flow into base realms through delusion; how then can the light of the Way be made to shine? (The maṇḍala is this very principle.)
Explanations of Terms and Meanings in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Twenty-three.
Phonetic Transcriptions: *zhì* (the sound of 晢) and *guāng* (the sound of 目).
*Xiàn* (pronounced with the departing tone): to fall into the earth; to sink.
*Nì-yì* (upper character pronounced *xiè*, lower character pronounced *yì*): to chew; to eat. *Chǐ* (pronounced *chǐ*):
to be extravagant; to be excessive.
Fā (髮) is pronounced as fà;
jié (駃) is pronounced as kuài, meaning the rapid flow of water;
lí (犛) and máo (茅) have both pronunciations.
Máo (pronounced as in "máo") means hair.
Yù (pronounced as in "yù") means to drive horses.
*Catalogue of the Explanations of Terms and Meanings in the Four-Part Vinaya*, Volume Twenty-Four.
Turtles, turtles, ābhoga, śalabha insects,
increasing delusion, prātimokṣa,
poṣadha, tīrthika, apaya, nandika.
A stallion resembling a house-prefect;
one who has been taught to wear the *kāṣāya* to drive away crows; an image made of gold and silver;
a small boundary established by tying [robes]; a *nāṃsi* (hempen) robe; an official.
One who has violated a bhikṣuṇī, one who entered the Path with a thieving mind, one like the udumbara flower,
one exempt from taxes, one with a variegated body,
one who is paralyzed or crippled, one with webbed fingers, or one who is epileptic.
Warts, strabismus, eyes with spots,
scabies, lameness, chronic skin diseases,
hare-lip, and two types of fistulae.
The Putrid Medicine Dragon, Receiving the Full Ordination,
Measuring Shadows with a Meditation Staff,
The Ghaṇṭā, Mahākapphiṇa, The Rishi, Mount Vipula.
Hot springs, śara grass, heaps of wood,
tree stumps, boundaries, the site of the precepts (sīmā),
small precincts, and bridges.
