● Vinaya Piṭaka, Volume 34:
Turtle and Tortoise.

(The character 鼈 is pronounced *gui*, with the radical for "tooth" [龜] and the phonetic *jū* [居]; it is read as *gui*. According to the classification of turtles, there are many species, and their physical forms also differ.)
In the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*, ten kinds of tortoises (*kūrma*) and turtles (*kamaṭha*; *bì* is pronounced with the final consonant *-t*, an entering tone;
those with shells on the outside are tortoises, while those with shells on the inside are turtles) are clarified. *Ābhāṣaṇa*.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* (Good Vision Vinaya) translates [the term] as "calling in" (*āhvāna*) and also as "extracting offenses.

This refers to when a bhikṣu has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and, after having performed the *parivāsa* and even the *mānatva*, is "called in" before the assembly to have the *āpattivyutthāna-karman* (ceremony for emerging from the offense) performed for him.
Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one may then participate in the *poṣadha*—the recitation of the precepts—and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together with the Saṃgha.
The *Mātṛkā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "To lift one from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state is called *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation)."
*Āpattāyana*. This is the merit and benefit of *mānatva*. Why is this? Because he has already been disciplined and seeks purity;
he himself seeks release from his offense. The monks said: "This bhikṣu seeks purity and seeks release from his offense;
he is a virtuous and excellent bhikṣu. We shall perform the *āpattāyana* for him. Therefore, it is called *āpattāyana*.
This is the merit and benefit of the *mānāttā*. Why is this? The *ābhāṣaṇa* (rehabilitation) arises once purification has been achieved;
one attains purity and is free from offense. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "The *ābhāṣaṇa* is the arising of pure precepts; one attains pure liberation.
Within these precepts, one is pure and without transgression; having maintained them well, one departs. This is called *ābhāṣaṇa*."
Regarding that meaning:
the *śalabha* insect is a venomous insect;
its precise translation is not yet known. It is one of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), called the "difficulty of venomous insects."
It is also called the "peril of evil insects. The *Mātṛkā-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The peril of belly-crawling insects; they are called belly-crawling insects because they move on their bellies.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* asks: "What is the peril of belly-crawling insects? [They are] dragons, snakes, centipedes, and so forth."
Regarding "one who releases poison": according to the Sanskrit sound, it is *śilindhra*. Its pronunciation is identical to *śirīṣa*, which is translated as "he-hun" (合昏).
If explained according to the characters: *lín* (林) is pronounced with the *shī* radical added, yielding the sound *shā* (砂). *Líng* (蠅) is the name for a type of insect.
*Zēngjù* (增劇):
*jù* is pronounced with the *jié* and *jí* finals; it means to increase, to intensify, or to be extreme. It also denotes hardship and toil, as well as ignorance and folly.
The *Mūla-vinaya* states: "To think evil thoughts, to speak evil words, and to perform evil deeds is called 'delusion' (*mūḍha*).
Not upholding the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras is called 'ignorance' (*bāla*). It further states: "To delude oneself is delusion; to delude others is ignorance."
The *Prātimokṣa-vinaya* states:
"Prātimokṣa" means precepts (*śīla*). It is also called *vinaya*. Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says: "Prātimokṣa and *vinaya*:
these two dharmas are identical in meaning but differ in name. [The term] *zhìhuā* (Gathering Flowers) translates it as...
Prātimokṣa (Individual Liberation) refers to the three types of action and seven branches, each preventing what is non-virtuous and bringing about liberation individually and separately.

The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Prātimokṣa means that by relying on the Prātimokṣa Sūtra and practicing according to its instructions, one gradually abandons the nine grades of afflictions—ranging from the lowest of the low to the highest of the high—and because one never regresses, one attains liberation from all afflictions."

It is called "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*). Furthermore, because it enables one to abandon and separate from the various categories of afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), which are each numerous in kind, it is termed "individual liberation.
Moreover, it is translated as "preserving liberation," for it can sustain the practitioner so that they emerge from the ocean of birth and death.
As the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "Prātimokṣa is the name for the most supreme meaning; it is the [foundation] of all virtues."
Fundamentally, it takes precepts as its root; because all manner of wholesome qualities can arise from them, they are called the "most supreme" in meaning.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* asks: "Is this *prātimokṣa* precept an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precept, or is it a dhyāna precept?
It answers: "It is neither an outflow-free precept nor a dhyāna precept. As for this *prātimokṣa* precept, if the Buddha is in the world..."

It exists when the Buddha is present in the world, but it does not exist when he is not. The dhyāna-precepts and the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts exist at all times, whether the Buddha is in the world or not.
The prātimokṣa precepts are obtained through the teaching and are also obtained from another.

The meditative (*dhyāna*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precepts are not like this. Furthermore, the *prātimokṣa* precepts exist at all times—whether one is asleep or awake, and whether the mind is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
The meditative and outflow-free precepts, however, necessarily exist only within an outflow-free mind or a meditative mind;
they do not exist within any other state of mind. This applies even to the *prātimokṣa* precepts alone.
The disciples of the Buddha possess both the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts; non-Buddhists possess neither.

Indeed, it is the Prātimokṣa that maintains the Buddha-dharma, ensuring that the seven assemblies remain in the world and that the fruits of the three vehicles continue in succession without interruption.
This is because the Prātimokṣa serves as the root, whereas the dhyāna-precepts and untainted precepts do not. Therefore, among the three types of precepts, it is the most excellent and sublime.
There is none who can equal it. Since the wise know that such supreme and wondrous merit exists, they should personally treasure and uphold the precepts they have received;
do not treat them with indifference. Regarding each and every prohibited act, one must sever them so as not to commit them.

If there is no commission, there is no cause. If there is no cause, the fruit is cut off. That is to say, if there is no cause for each individual [transgression], then there will be no result for each individual.

The fruit is called "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*). Regarding the nine grades of afflictions (from the lowest-of-the-low to the highest-of-the-high): across the three realms and nine stages, there are a total of eighty-one grades.

Taking the desire realm as one stage, the four dhyānas of the form realm as four stages, and the four emptinesses of the formless realm as four stages, these together constitute the nine stages. Within the single stage of the desire realm, there are nine grades of the four afflictions—greed, hatred, delusion, and pride—namely, the superior, middling, and inferior grades.

Each category consists of three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—thus forming nine grades. In the two upper realms (*dhātu*), there are likewise the three afflictions of greed, delusion, and pride; since the affliction of anger does not manifest in the two upper realms, each of the nine stages (*bhūmi*) possesses its own nine grades of delusions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*). Together, these constitute eighty-one grades.

Because these afflictions are difficult to sever, they are subdivided into nine grades so that those who have attained the second, third, and fourth fruits may sever them sequentially. "Lower-of-the-low" refers to the ninth grade. Regarding the terms "seeing" (*darśana*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*): for one who has attained the first fruit, the severing of afflictions and the realization of principle is called the "Path of Seeing" (*darśana-mārga*).

"Severing" here refers to the elimination of the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions of seeing within the three realms. For those attaining the second and third fruits, the cultivation of truth to sever afflictions is called the "Path of Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga*). By means of this...

This is because the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the afflictions of volition within the three realms. Regarding these ten underlying tendencies: there are four afflictions in the desire realm, as explained above; each of the two upper realms possesses three, namely, with the exception of hatred (*dveṣa*). As for the "nine grades" such as the lowest-of-the-low and so forth:

since each of the nine stages (*bhūmi*) has its own lowest-of-the-low grade, when the lowest-of-the-low grade of afflictions in the desire realm is exhausted, one realizes the third fruit (*phala*); when the lowest-of-the-low grade of the two upper realms is exhausted, one realizes the fruit of Arhatship. As for the two types of afflictions—those of view (*dṛṣṭi*) and those of thought (*vitarka*)—they give rise to afflictions such as greed (*rāga*) toward all objects, whether adverse or favorable, following them without abandoning them.

Regarding the afflictions of view: "view" refers to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). This means that when the mental faculty (*manas*) encounters mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it engages in irrational calculation and gives rise to various false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), such as the non-Buddhists' calculations of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*) or eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*), and so on, up to...

This refers to equal views. Regarding the "afflictions of thought" (*si-huo*): "thought" (*si*) refers to craving and attachment. This means that the five faculties—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—encounter the five objects—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—and become greedily attached, deluded, and lacking awareness.

Regarding the *poṣadha* of the non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika), "Poṣadha" being translated in the Qin language as "Śubhavāsa" (Good Abiding): the Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit [a monk] to dwell together with the assembly of non-Buddhist practitioners for four months.
Regarding the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), the *Mūla-karman* states: the Buddha said, "If there are non-Buddhist practitioners..."
When someone comes seeking to go forth, their preceptor should inquire about the obstructing conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*). If they are found to be pure, they should be accepted;

one should then confer the three refuges and the five precepts (*pañca-śikṣāpada*), thereby establishing them in the protection of a lay follower (*upāsaka-vrata*). [According to the Vinaya-mūla, they should be made to receive the ten precepts.]
He should request [permission] three times within the Saṃgha (this is followed by the formal ritual, *karmavācanā*).

If this non-Buddhist has already lived together with the Saṃgha for four months, he should be assigned duties according to the example of a *śrāmaṇera*. During those four months, he shall wear the robes of his preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
Regarding the consumption of the Sangha’s regular food, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

After the *karmavācanā* has been performed, if one is able to serve the Sangha like a śrāmaṇera, one may take food in the order following the śrāmaṇeras. If one is unable to do so, one should be told: "Seek food for yourself.
One should daily speak before them in disparagement of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), their lack of faith, and their heterodox views. If they...
"Do not say this, Venerable One! There are also those there who are virtuous and maintain the precepts, even up to Arhats.
You should say: 'Go back to that place and seek Arhatship. If they say, 'It is truly as the Venerable One has said;
we are outsiders with wrong views, even performing the deeds of hell-beings,' then, Venerable One, please deliver us."

If, after a trial period of four months, his mind remains unshakable, he should be granted ordination. If, during that interval, he attains the noble Dharma, it is said that the trial is then completed.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "As for those who are hair-tied heretics or fire-worshipping heretics..."
Parivāsa (separate residence) is not required. Why? Because these two non-Buddhists possess karma and believe in cause and effect;
when the Buddhas of the past were bodhisattvas, they went forth into homelessness and studied the pāramitās on this very path.

*Ōng* (in *tū-yù*, "to break out of prison"). Pronounced with the *tǔ-mù* rhyme and entering tone (*rùshēng*). It refers to a dog hiding in a den waiting for someone; when the person does not expect it, the dog suddenly emerges.

Thus, the character is composed of the radical for "den" (*xué*) and the character for "dog" (*quǎn*). To speak of "breaking out of prison" (*tū-yù*) means that those prisoners, [waiting for an opportunity...]
The person did not realize it and suddenly fled.
Nandi is translated here as "Joy" (歡喜), or sometimes as "Dhyāna-nandi. This refers to a bhikṣu who dwells in an araṇya (forest hermitage) and constantly...
He delighted in sitting in meditation. Because he practiced meditative concentration (*samādhi*), people of the time called him "The One Who Dwells in Joyful Concentration.
As the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: There was an elder in Śrāvastī named Nandi who left the household life to become a renunciant.
Although there were many others with the name Nandi, this man was such that he practiced meditation even while walking, and even while lying down. Therefore, people of the time gave him this title.
For the sake of Cūḍapanthaka, he practiced his own discipline during the first, middle, and last watches of the night and attained mundane concentration (*laukika-samādhi*).

This continued for seven years. After those seven years had passed, he fell away from that meditative absorption. A celestial *māra* woman, luring him with a dead horse, destroyed his holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Furthermore, in a past life, this Panthaka was named the Seer Mṛgapatra; he had attained the [attainments] of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Regarding the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*): while dwelling in forests and wilds, he was caused to break his pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) by celestial maidens (*devakanyā*) of variegated colors.
Those celestial maidens at that time are the demonesses (*mārakanyā*) of the present day (the remainder is as explained in the *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* of the *Śīlaskandha*).
Wūlánlán (屋闌闌).

[The character] lí (離) is pronounced with the *qián* (閑) initial; [the character] lǎn (懶) has the level tone (*píngshēng*). It refers to the wooden railings of a terrace or steps. It is incorrect to write it as 欄.
[Also: "A stallion."]

Pronounced *cǎo* (the phonetic component being *cāng* and *lǎo*). It refers to a female horse. "Female" (*pǐn*)—with the second tone on the initial syllable—refers to a mother animal. Among those that fly, they are called "female and male" (*cí-xióng*);
among those that run, they are called "female and male" (*pǐn-mǔ*).
"Similar" means a transgression that resembles the original offense. "Arising from this" means arising from the original offense.
"Worse than this" means a fault more grave than the original offense. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
It is said: *pārājika*, that which resembles a *pārājika*; *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, that which resembles a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
*pāyattika*, that which resembles a *pāyattika*; *pratideśanīya*, that which resembles a *pratideśanīya*;
*duṣkṛta*, that which resembles a *duṣkṛta*. This is called "resemblance of offense. It is said:
Why are they not similar? A *pārājika* is not similar to a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*.
A *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is not similar to a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *duṣkṛta*, or a *pārājika*. A *pāyattika* is not similar to a... [and so forth].
Pāṭidesanīya, duṣkṛta, pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa; non-corresponding pāṭidesanīya, with duṣkṛta, pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, and pāyattika;
non-corresponding, duṣkṛta, with pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, and pāyattika.
Pāṭidesanīya. This is not similar [to the other categories].
It is taught that one should wear the *kāṣāya*;
it is called by the name *kāṣāya* because of the color of the garment; that is, it refers to dyed (ruined) clothing. According to the *Chujing*...
The robes of the five groups within the household [of the monastic community] all have their colors altered; therefore, they are collectively termed *kāṣāya*. This will be explained in detail below.

However, that which a *śrāmaṇera* should wear consists of the *man-tiao* (plain-strip) and the *saṃkakṣikā* (under-robe). One must understand that *kāṣāya* does not refer exclusively to the three robes (*tricīvara*) of a *bhikṣu*.
Because this point was not understood here [in China], it resulted in *śrāmaṇeras* being made to don the five-strip and seven-strip robes.

Item: Regarding the robes of the Great Bhikṣus, one may perhaps see in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) the statement that a śrāmaṇera should possess two sets of upper and lower garments:
first, a garment to be worn constantly, which corresponds to the *antarvāsaka*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*, which is to be worn when entering the assembly for purification or when traveling.
The original Sanskrit term for *antarvāsaka* is translated as "lower garment" (*xiaduo yi*). The *uttarāsaṅga*...
*Tāraṃga* is translated here as "upper garment. This refers to the distinction between the upper and lower parts of clothing for practical use;
it has no relation to the names "five-strip" (*pañcaka*) or "seven-strip" (*saptaka*) robes. That treatise itself states: "The lower garment is worn at all times;

the upper garment is worn when entering the assembly and on other such occasions for the sake of purity. Therefore, Master Xuan of Nanshan, relying on that treatise, clarified that a *śrāmaṇera* receives the *maṇḍala-saṃghāṭī*.
Regarding the Dharma: first is the plain *antarvāsa*, and second is the plain *uttarāsaṅga*. It never mentions the specific designations of "five strips" or "seven strips.
Some have seen the Buddha’s *Abhidharma-sūtra* stating that one must first don the three *kaṣāyas* before being conferred the precepts;
this, however, does not refer to the *bhikṣu*’s three robes made of cut-and-sewn patches. Subsequently, in the text for receiving full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), it says:
The names of the three robes are distinct; there is no need for confusion. The Tripitaka is clear and manifest, so you may examine it for yourself.
If one knows this yet deliberately acts with arrogance, persisting in what is contrary to the Dharma, they will bring upon themselves transgression and blame.

How much more so for those who, even regarding the constant regulations for food and clothing established by the Father of the Śākyas, remain complacent out of ignorance while still claiming to be sons of the Śākya—could such a thing not be called [a grave error]?
How shameful! As the *Mūla-karman* states: "The saṃghāṭī is the garment of those who seek tranquility (śrāmaṇeras).
To wear the pañcakaṣāya [of a bhikṣu] at will is a grave transgression. This custom has long been prevalent in the land of China, yet it constitutes a violation of the Dharma.
Do not allow them to don [the robes]. Whenever there is one who wishes to seek ordination, they should go to a teacher according to their inclination.

The teacher should immediately inquire about all obstructing dharmas; if they are entirely pure, the teacher should accept them according to their wish. Once accepted, [the procedure continues as follows].

He confers the Three Refuges and imparts the training in the five precepts, thereby establishing the discipline (*upāsaka-vinaya*) of protection. (Regarding this term "protection": in Sanskrit it is *saṃvara*, translated as "protection" (*yǒngù*).

By receiving the refuges and precepts, one is protected so as not to fall into the three miserable realms. The older translation "discipline" (*lǜyí*) is a literal rendering of the meaning, signifying the ritual procedures of the Dharma. If one were to speak only of "protection," there is a fear that students might not understand the full significance.)

Therefore, both [the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*] exist together. The *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* has already been translated as the *Hù* (護). This refers to the non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) that constitutes the essence of the precepts. Regarding the term "plain cloth" (*màn tiáo*): it is a single piece of cloth without any stripes, used for matters such as the altar partitions (*tán gé*).
The *Nanhai Jìguī Zhōngfǎ Chánjì* states: "Prior to this, one was not counted among the seven classes of followers; this is the foundation for first entering the Buddha-dharma."
The preceptor next prepares for him a *maṇḍala* (striped cloth), a *saṅkakṣikā* (undergarment), as well as lower robes, an alms bowl, and a water filter.
Only then does he formally inform the Saṃgha and announce the matter of his renunciation. Once the assembly has granted permission, he requests an *ācārya*.

In a secluded place, he should have a barber remove the candidate’s hair and beard. (According to the *Duren jing*, one should establish an altar, hang banners, set up a high seat, and have the candidate sit upon it while the hair is shaved. 2.

The preceptor also prepares two high and excellent seats. Once the temperature is appropriate—neither too cold nor too hot—he instructs the candidate to bathe. The preceptor then puts on the lower garment for him, examining him discreetly to ensure he is not a eunuch or otherwise disqualified.
Next, he gives him the upper robe, which the candidate receives by placing it upon his head. Having donned the dharma robes, [the ceremony continues].
The bestowing of the alms-bowl is called "leaving the household life" (*pravrajyā*). Next, before one's original teacher (*upādhyāya*), the *ācārya* bestows the ten precepts (*śikṣāpada*).
Once the ordination has been received, one is named a *śrāmaṇera* (translated as "seeker of tranquility"); this refers to the observance of dignified conduct and discipline.

I request instruction on this matter. Regarding those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), their status is essentially no different from that of others. However, within the Vinaya Piṭaka, there are twelve instances where they do not incur an offense;
yet for the female trainees (*śikṣamāṇā*), there are slight differences and reductions in these cases. What are these twelve? First, not distinguishing [the types of] robes;

second, staying overnight apart from one's robe; third, touching fire; fourth, eating after having finished a meal; fifth, harming living seeds; sixth, discarding [waste] upon green grass... [and so forth].
1. Purification; 2. Repeatedly climbing high trees; 3. Touching jewels; 4. Eating leftover or stored food;
5. Destroying the earth; 6. Not accepting food [with one's own hand]; 7. Damaging living sprouts. Regarding these twelve, two minor offenses do not constitute a transgression.

As for the *śikṣamāṇā*, she commits an offense regarding the latter five. (This is the intent of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya; if there are slight differences in the textual passages of this specific school’s Vinaya, they may be understood from the Vinaya itself. One who is able to act in this manner...
Only then does one become compliant with the Dharma; such a person is included among the five assemblies and is capable of consuming offerings and benefits.

How could it be that after one has left the household life, the preceptor does not confer the ten precepts for fear that they might be violated and the full precepts (mahāśīla) cannot be accomplished?

This would be to falsely bear the name of a *śrāmaṇera* and vainly embrace the title of a renunciant. One might seem to harbor a small benefit, yet how could one know of the great harm? As the Sūtra says: "Although..."

Regarding those who have not yet received the ten precepts but are nonetheless included within the ranks of the Saṃgha: this is merely a provisional concession for a single occasion; how could it be maintained as a permanent practice?
Furthermore, when those who leave the household life in the Divine Land (China) receive their tonsure, they provisionally rely upon a single master.

This master does not originally inquire whether the candidate has any of the "one obstacle" (the fatal impediment), nor has the disciple ever requested the ten precepts prior to advancing to full ordination. Thus it remains until the time of their formal admission.
They indulge their passions in committing transgressions. When the day arrives for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), they are made to enter the ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*);

yet, having never been previously instructed in the monastic discipline (*vinaya*), how could they possibly be disciplined and compliant at such a time? Such is certainly not the way to maintain the Dharma. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinayakṣudrakavastu* states:

"The three robes required by a bhikṣu—those śrāmaṇeras [should] wear the *saṃkakṣikā* over the shoulders and a single lower garment (*antarvāsaka*) below; these two garments are sufficient. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha-śāstra* states: "A śrāmaṇera may possess one *nirvāṇasaṅghāṭī*, one *kaṭicīvara*, and a *pūlaka* (undergarment)—these are the items worn on the body."
It is permitted to keep one [robe]. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* contains a verse regarding the wearing of robes which says:
"Great indeed is the garment of liberation, The signless field of merit robe. He who honors it according to the practice of the precepts Shall extensively deliver all sentient beings.
[The ritual for] driving away crows.
This refers to the monastery kitchen, the meditation hall, and other such places where crows and birds cause defilement and disorder.

Since they are still very young and unable to handle other tasks, they are ordered to drive away the birds to perform this minor labor, while also generating merit and virtue. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
The Buddha said, "I allow those capable of driving away crows to become *śrāmaṇeras*; the minimum age is seven years. (From the *Mūla-karmavācanā*).
The Buddha said, "Upāli, I have declared that one who has reached seven years of age and is capable of scaring away crows may be granted the going-forth.
Venerable One, if there is one who has reached six years of age and is capable of scaring away crows at the monastery kitchen, would it be appropriate for him also to go forth?
The Buddha said, "It is not appropriate; seven years must be the fixed requirement."
"Venerable Sir, if there is one who has reached seven years of age but cannot drive away crows from the monastery kitchen, is it appropriate for him to go forth [into the monastic life]?
The Buddha said, "It is not appropriate. One must be able to drive away crows; this is established as the standard. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Regarding 'major' or 'minor':
if one is less than seven years old, or even if one has reached seven years of age but does not know good from evil, in all such cases, one should not grant them the going forth."
Regarding family members: those who are too old—if they are over seventy—even if they are capable of performing tasks;
or if they are under seventy but unable to manage affairs, requiring assistance for rising and reclining—all such cases are not permitted to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*).

However, if one has reached seventy years of age and is healthy and vigorous, capable of practicing various activities, they are permitted to be ordained. Furthermore, there are three grades of *śrāmaṇeras*: the first is from the age of seven up to...
At thirteen years of age, one is called a *kūka-śrāmaṇera* (crow-expeller śrāmaṇera). Second, from fourteen to nineteen, these are called *dharmārha-śrāmaṇeras* (śrāmaṇeras worthy of the Dharma).
Third, from twenty upwards to seventy, these are called *nāmadheya-śrāmaṇeras* (nominal śrāmaṇeras).
These three types are all called śrāmaṇeras. The Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra states: "One who is sixty years of age may not receive the full precepts;
he is permitted only to remain a śrāmaṇera" (the remainder is explained as in the section on conferring the full precepts upon those under the required age).

Regarding "raw" and "refined" gold and silver, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Raw color" and "resembling color. "Raw color" refers to gold; "resembling color" refers to silver. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"Raw and refined" refers to gold and silver. Nanshan (*Daoxuan*) says: "Both foreign and Chinese designations are manifest," meaning that these are the foreign names.
"Raw" (*sheng*) refers to gold; "refined" (*xiang*) refers to silver. The retention of both names is a dual citation of the Hu (foreign) and Han (Chinese) terms.

As for "raw," it means that the color of gold is naturally yellow from birth, requiring no further assistance. "Refined" means "resembling"; it refers to silver, which can be dyed yellow to resemble gold.
Thus, the *Śrāvakabhūmi-śāstra* says: "The raw color [of gold] can be dyed. This should follow the Master’s commentary.
It is said: "Innate color" refers to gold; it is yellow by nature and cannot be changed. "Dyeable" refers to silver;
because its color can be dyed and altered, it is called "dyeable. These are all interpretations from the Hu (Central Asian) tradition and are not the authentic Sanskrit texts.
In the Indian *brahman* language, gold is called *suvarṇa* and silver is called *rūpya*. Originally, their meanings were not clearly understood;
in some cases, they possess names but no [corresponding] meaning, and thus are not translated. This is just as the terms for "gold" and "silver" here in this land likewise lack [specific] meanings.

It is simply due to the distinction between the yellow and white [versions]. Because the translators brought the Sanskrit manuscripts from afar, they traveled through many regions of the Hu (Central Asia);

having transmitted those Hu languages, they were translated into the language of China, resulting in these differences. Thus, the *Zhiguang* states: "Moreover, the language of the Kingdom of Khotan differs from the sounds of the Five Indias.
When the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* reached Khotan, it underwent one translation; once translated, it was further [revised]."

Regarding the original sūtra: by the time it reached the Tang dynasty, it was considered a weighty text (this refers to the version translated by Zhi Falin; it is not the one translated by Yaśas, though Yaśas had previously translated the Tripiṭaka in foreign lands before arriving here).
According to this school, as well as the Mahāsāṃghika, śrāmaṇeras are not permitted to hold or carry raw or cast-metal images.
Other schools merely prohibit the acceptance and possession [of precious objects], but do not forbid the grasping or holding of them. Therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"The three lower assemblies (śrāmaṇeras) are not permitted to possess jewels; to possess them constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, but to grasp them incurs no guilt.

However, since a śrāmaṇera has not previously grasped one, he must not be commanded to do so. Although the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* prohibits the grasping and holding, its underlying intent still accords with that treatise.
The meaning is as stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: At one time, there was a bhikṣu who took a śrāmaṇera with him to visit his relatives.
On their way through a vast wilderness, a non-human being manifested as a dragon, circumambulated the śrāmaṇera to the right, and scattered flowers over him.
He praised him, saying, "Excellent! You have gained great benefit by leaving the home life and renouncing the world, refraining from handling gold, silver, or money.
When the bhikṣu had visited his relatives' homes and, after exchanging greetings, was about to return, a relative's wife said to him, "You should go back now."
"The road is remote and provisions are scarce; you may take this money and go to purchase whatever you require. The śrāmaṇera accepted it, tied it to the hem of his robe, and departed.
On the way, a non-human being saw the śrāmaṇera carrying the money walking behind the bhikṣu.
He transformed himself into a dragon, came forward, circled the śrāmaṇera to the left, threw dirt upon him, and spoke these words: "You have lost a great benefit! Then he vanished.
A monk was practicing the path at home when he walked along carrying some money. A novice monk began to weep. The bhikṣu looked back and asked the novice, "Why are you crying?
The novice said, "I do not recall having committed any fault; I am being distressed for no reason. The teacher asked, "Is there something you are holding?
He replied, "I am carrying this money here. The teacher said, "Discard it. Once it had been discarded, a non-human being [appeared] as before.
Having previously made offerings, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was once sitting in meditation with the novice Śrīghana on the banks of Lake Anavatapta after his meal.
At that time, the novice Śrīghana saw golden sand along the edge of the lake and thought to himself:
"I should now take this sand and place it beneath the World-Honored One’s water-pitcher. The Venerable Maudgalyāyana [perceived this].

Having attained the realization of dhyāna, he immediately returned through the air by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). At that time, the novice Saṃtu was possessed by a non-human spirit (*amanuṣya*).
Maudgalyāyana looked back and called for the novice to come; the novice replied, "I cannot come. He asked again, "Are you being held by something?
[The novice] said, "I am holding this gold sand. You should discard it. Once it was discarded, he immediately traveled through the void.
They departed. Then, monks, for this reason, they all went to inform the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit śrāmaṇeras to hold gold, silver, or money. If a bhikṣu causes a śrāmaṇera to first take hold of gold, silver, or money, he incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense.
If he sees that a śrāmaṇera has already taken hold of it and subsequently causes him to take hold of it, [he likewise incurs an offense]."
There is no offense.

Establishing a small boundary (sīmā) in such cases is called a "circumstance of difficulty. Fearing that the reception of the precepts might be deficient, this is permitted as an allowance. In the absence of difficulty or such circumstances, one is not permitted to act arbitrarily.
[The text] concludes: However, this small boundary (*kṣudrasīman*) has no external marks; rather, the very place where the body is seated constitutes the substance of the boundary.

Therefore, the text says: "Now this Saṃgha assembles in one place to establish a small boundary. All of this is for the purpose of preventing and excluding persons; thus, there are no external marks. As the text says:
"If one attempts to exclude someone while they are outside the boundary, the exclusion is not valid. Furthermore, because the location is not for long-term residence, [there are no external marks].

Regarding the establishment of the characteristics: it is further stated that one should not depart without understanding the *dhātu* (elements). The remainder is clarified in the *Karmavācanā* (Ritual Procedures).

As for the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe), this refers to a discarded garment from a refuse heap; it is made into the three robes (*tricīvara*) by sewing them together, and is not the "patchwork of a hundred pieces" common nowadays.
An official is a subject of the king. If his stipend is exhausted, he may leave the household life; if the king grants permission, he may do so.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There are four kinds of subjects: some have titles but no stipend, while others have both titles and stipends. These are the two types [referred to].
In this country and other countries alike, some may not be permitted to leave the household life. There are those who possess emoluments but lack official titles;
they are not permitted here, yet they are permitted elsewhere. There are those who have neither titles nor emoluments; they are permitted both here and in other places.
Regarding the offense against a bhikṣuṇī, according to the laws of the land of India:

if there is one who destroys the brahmacarya of a bhikṣuṇī, her kinsmen shall change her family name and turn the door of her residence to face west (for in the Western lands, doors all face east). They shall demolish her kitchen and ruin the eaves of her house, surrounding it on all sides for a distance of one...
[The Buddha said: "For one *krośa* [or until death], one shall not converse with them, shall not dwell with them, and shall not eat together with them. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"Those who have committed crimes against the [Three Jewels], those who live as thieves [within the Saṃgha], those who have defiled *bhikṣuṇīs*, and others like them are not permitted to go forth. This is because such persons are defiled by evil karma and obstruct the Path of the Sages;
therefore, they are not permitted to go forth."

Entering the Path with a thieving mind is also called "thieving residence" (*caura-vāsa*). This refers to laypeople, non-Buddhists, or *śrāmaṇeras* who, for the purpose of theft, listen to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the performance of formal acts (*karmavācanā*), participating in the communal monastic rituals.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If princes or the sons of ministers, for the sake of avoiding danger, put on the *kāṣāya* robe themselves..."
One who has not yet undergone the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā* may be granted ordination; however, if it has already been performed, it is not permitted.
If a *śrāmaṇera* thinks, "What will they discuss during the recitation of the precepts? and enters beneath the bed to eavesdrop, if he is clever...

Regarding "being aware" and the "words at the beginning, middle, and end": if one is dull-witted, asleep, or has the mind directed toward other thoughts such that one does not remember the words at the beginning, middle, and end, one may later receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Formerly, on the fifteenth day during the time of the monastic confession (*poṣadha*), there was a young boy who, in a hidden place, eavesdropped."
When the precepts were being recited, the Vajrapāṇi spirits crushed his body with their vajra-clubs until it was like fine dust.
*Udumbara*—also called *udumbara*; in the new terminology, *utpala*. It refers to the kingdom of Magadha in Central India.
Dharma Master Cixian stated: "In Sanskrit it is called *udumbara*, which is the correct term. However, there is no direct translation for this;

its meaning is 'auspicious response' (*ruìyìng*), or alternatively 'rare' (*xīyǒu*). During the Sui dynasty, it was translated as 'Water-Vow' (*shuǐyuàn*), referring to the fact that the tree bears fruit without flowering."
If these flowers bloom, it signifies that a Buddha has appeared, or that a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) has been born into the world; thus they are called "Auspicious Responses" (*śubhanimitta*).
Because these flowers open only after a long interval, they are called "Rare. Master Ying said: "Their leaves resemble those of the pear tree, and their fruit is as large as a fist.
Their flavor is sweet, and they bear fruit without flowers. Even when flowers do appear, they are difficult to encounter; therefore, in the sutras, [they are used as a metaphor]."
It is a rare analogy. The *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Within Jambudvīpa, there is a sovereign king of trees named Udumbara;
it bears fruit but has no flowers. Only when a tree bears golden flowers does a Buddha appear in the world.
The *Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* states: "Not far from the city of Kuśinagara, there is a great flower pond named Mandākinī. Regarding this:

On the bank of the pond stood an udumbara tree. In the past, when the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita heaven and assumed the form of a white elephant to enter his mother’s womb, that udumbara flower had newly emerged from its bud. At the beginning of his birth, it gradually developed color and luster.
During his time as a youth, as the flower was about to blossom, he grew weary of old age, sickness, and death, and departed for the remote mountain forests. Its...
The flowers gradually grew larger, shaped like *cī-cī* (a type of bird). During his time practicing asceticism, they appeared withered and shriveled;
after he abandoned asceticism, his breath became free-flowing as he partook of various foods and drinks, until the attainment of perfect enlightenment, at which point the flowers blossomed fully.
When Brahmā came to request that he turn the wheel of Dharma, the tree and its flowers were radiant and flourishing, their exquisite fragrance wafting abroad.

It pervaded all directions and realms. Yet, the Buddha’s great compassion universally reached all those with whom he had a karmic connection; having extensively delivered beings throughout the worlds where they resided, he proceeded to Kuśinagara to lie down for the final time.
At that moment, this flower tree—withered in form and color—was seen by all who gazed upon it, causing them to exclaim in wonder and admiration.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*) states: "Surrounding Jambudvīpa, there is the road of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), one *yojana* in width."
When there is no Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), it is submerged by the waters of the ocean and none can see it.

When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, the great ocean recedes by one yojana, and this path of the Wheel-Turning King emerges, strewn with golden sand, adorned with various jewels, and sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water. Thereupon, the Holy Wheel-Turning King proceeds along it.
Traveling through islands and shoals, accompanied by the fourfold army, he traversed this path; at that time, these flowers bloomed.
*Vinaya Piṭaka*, Volume 35, Section on the Khandhaka.

Furthermore, there is the term *qián* (written with the radical for "hand" and the phonetic *jiàn*). It is pronounced like *jù* and *yán* combined; its sound is *jiān*. *Qián* means to harm. The *Tōngsúwén* states:
"To remove the private parts with a knife is called *qián*; this refers to castrating the male organ. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"As for those who lack the organ, they lack the root for attaining the Way because they have lost the characteristics of male and female; thus their minds are not settled due to minor causes and conditions."

They become prone to anger; their fetters (*saṃyojana*) are numerous, and thus they remain attached to the world. They harbor many webs of doubt regarding worldly affairs and take no delight in the Dharma.
Although they may perform a small amount of meritorious deeds, their wisdom is shallow and thin, preventing them from penetrating deeply. Their fundamental nature is fickle and changeable;

for these reasons, they cannot leave the household life. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Because this person’s fetters are deep and thick, it is difficult for them to attain the Path. Furthermore:
This person does not belong among the bhikṣus, nor does he belong among the bhikṣuṇīs; therefore, his ordination is not permitted.
[Regarding] taxes:
*Zū* (租). Pronounced with the *zōng* rhyme and the *sū* initial; the third tone of *zǔ*. It refers to the tax on fields. *Fù* (賦). Pronounced with the *fāng* rhyme and the *gù* initial;
the sound is *fù*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it means "to collect. The *Guangya* says it means "taxes. It also means "to measure. Guo Pu said:
"Taxes are used for the purpose of leveling and measuring. The *Fangyan* says: "To assign (*fù*) means to move. Taxes are used to stir and disturb [the people].
*Shēn bōbō*. It is also written as *bó*. Both are pronounced with the initial *bó* (as in *bó-gè*) and the final *bó*. This refers to a horse whose coat color is not uniform.

It is also the name of a tree, *zǐyú* (Catalpa). Its bark is greenish-white like a mottled pattern. The *Gōnjīnù* (Ancient and Modern Notes) states: "The wood resembles that of the *yùzhāng* (Camphor Tree); its bark is covered in many patches of lichen-like mottling."
This means that because his body resembles this [condition] and is not suitable for the monastic discipline, he is not permitted to leave the household life.
*Tián* (痶):

the second character is pronounced *tiǎn* (with the radical *thián*); *huàn* (瘓): the pronunciation is *huàn*. *Tián-huàn* describes the appearance of a disease. The *Jīngyīnyì* (Explanations of the Pronunciations and Meanings of the Sūtras) states that it has been handed down [as such].
*Chìxiǎn* (勅顯): *chì* is pronounced with the *guǎn* rhyme; it refers to a disease of the hair.
*Mànzhǐ* (縵指):
*màn* is pronounced with the *guān* rhyme, sounding like *mán*. "Connected fingers" (*mànzhǐ*) means that the fingers are joined together, forming a web-like membrane.
Alternatively, it is also written as [病-丙+貴].
It is pronounced *tuí* (with the same radical as 徒 and 回). It refers to a disease of the internal organs.
"瘊" (hòu) is pronounced with the initial *hu* and the final *gōu*, sounding like "hóu. It refers to the disease of warts and tumors. "睞眼" (làiyǎn) refers to squinting eyes.
The character for *yīn-lài* is explained as above.

The archaic form of *jiàn-yǎn* (瞷眼) is [馬*間] (*jiān*), pronounced with the *hu* and *jiān* rhymes, sounding like *xián*. When one eye of a horse is white, it is called *jiān*; when both eyes are white, it is called...
*Yú*. The *Cāngjié piān* states: "A disease of the eyes.
It has the supplement *huán* (cut with *chē*). Its pronunciation is *bān*. A variegated color is called *bān*. The *Shuōwén* states: "A mottled pattern."
*Jiè-sào* (疥瘙).
*Sào* is pronounced with the first tone (*qiáo*) and the departing tone (*qùshēng*). It refers to scabies or skin sores. The *Tōngsúwén* states: "The rising of the skin is called *sào*."
Yèjiǎoyè (曳脚曳):
Same as yè (拽). Pronounced with the *zhì* (制) initial and *yì* (裔) final; it means to drag. It refers to the disease of *pī* (癖).
The character *pì* (匹) is pronounced like *piè* (僻). It refers to *xiá pì* (瘕癖), a disease characterized by the accumulation of masses within the abdomen.
Regarding the hare-lip (*tù quē*), in Sanskrit it is called *śaśaka*, which here means "hare. There are those of white, black, or brindled color whose lips are naturally cleft.
Therefore, it is said that one with a hare-lip [is ineligible]. Now, regardless of whether the upper or lower lip is missing, none are permitted to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*).

To "damage the two paths" refers to what was previously mentioned: damaging those who follow the inner path (Buddhists) and those who follow the outer path (non-Buddhists). This refers to one who formerly practiced as a non-Buddhist and later came to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and subsequently...

Regarding those who have entered among the non-Buddhists and now return to receive the precepts: they are not permitted [to do so]. Because they were previously non-Buddhists who came to follow the path of renunciation, they first undermined the non-Buddhist path;

by returning to the non-Buddhist path again, they undermine the Buddhist path as well. Since they have thus destroyed both the internal and external paths, one is not permitted to grant them renunciation.
"Decayed medicine" refers to medicine that is putrid, rotten, old, and worn out. Master Jing said: In Sanskrit it is called *pūtimukti-vaiṣajya*.
*Pūti* means "old," *mukti* means "discarded," and *vaiṣajya* is translated as "medicine. Thus, it is...
This refers to discarded medicine. The intention is to simplify matters; it is merely sufficient to sustain the body. Its high value is naturally found within the Guanzhong region.
Consuming and taking it truly results in no harm. The *Cittaviśuddhipratyupannasūtra* states: "The sons of the Buddha who have left the household life [should regard] all medicines..."

One should not be greedily attached to them. When one is ill, if there are medicinal decoctions that others have already prepared and discarded—such as *kharjūra*, *vīraṇa*, and *āmalaka*—one should take such medicines and consume them.

Even throughout one’s entire life, one should consume discarded medicines and always maintain contentment regarding all such substances. One who acts in this way is called a true śramaṇa. Thus it is said.
The Buddha’s son, Longshen Shanjian, said:
"One cannot deliver dragons. Why is this? Because dragons do not attain the fruits of the path through meditative concentration."
Nāgas have five states in which they do not leave their nāga bodies. What are these five? First, regarding sexual intercourse:
if one engages in sexual intercourse with another nāga, one regains the nāga body; if one engages in sexual intercourse with a human, one does not regain the nāga body.
Second, at the time of rebirth, one does not leave the nāga body. Third, at the time of shedding the skin. Fourth, at the time of sleep. Fifth, at the time of death.
At that time, these are the five matters for which one cannot be separated from the dragon body.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* asks: "For what reason is it called 'receiving full ordination' (*upasaṃpadā*)? Once a wise person has received full ordination..."

Because one attains what was sought and achieves accomplishment, it is called "receiving full ordination" (*upasampadā*). The sense of being able to achieve [the goal] is termed "receiving full ordination.
For this reason, achieving all manner of wholesome qualities is called "receiving full ordination," up to and including the ability to achieve the dharma of tranquility (*śānti*);
therefore, it is named "receiving full ordination. The dharma of tranquility is also called the dharma of parinirvāṇa; that is to say, the dharma of *nirvāṇa*. Thus...
The *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states: "Once one has received the precepts, one is called an *upasaṃpanna*.
*Upa* means 'near,' and *saṃpanna* means 'round'—that is, *nirvāṇa*. Receiving the full ordination now is precisely drawing near to *nirvāṇa*.

The older term 'fully endowed' (*juzu*) expresses this general sense [and is also called 'perfectly endowed' (*yuanju*) or 'near-perfectly endowed' (*jin yuanju*); the meanings are all one]. Once the reception of the precepts is completed, next..."
The preceptor then points out the *Prātimokṣa* for him, so that he may recognize the characteristics of transgressions, before instructing him in the recitation of the precepts.

Once he has mastered these, he recites the *Vinaya-piṭaka*, reviewing it daily and testing himself every morning. Only after he has completed the recitation of the *Vinaya-piṭaka* does he study the Sūtras and Śāstras;
this is the traditional path of teacher and disciple in the West (India). Although we are now separated from the Sage by a vast distance, this method [remains].
It remains unimpaired. For these two masters, I liken them to parents.

How could it be that at the time of wishing to receive [the precepts], one undergoes such great toil and exhaustion, yet once they have been obtained, one pays no heed to the precepts? To have a beginning but no end is truly a great pity.

There are those who attend a single assembly seeking to receive [the precepts], but having received them, they do not return to consult their masters, do not recite the Sūtra on the Precepts, and do not peruse the Vinaya scriptures; this is in vain.
Having attained the rank of the Dharma, yet harming both oneself and others—those of such a kind as these bring about the extinction of the Dharma.
Now that the Dragon River has vanished and the light of Vulture Peak has been withdrawn, how many Arhats who transmit the Dharma can remain? Thus the treatise says:

"When the Great Master’s eyes have closed, those who bear witness perish accordingly. When afflictions increase, one should be diligent and not indolent. It is only right that all virtuous ones should act together [to preserve the teaching].
One must uphold and protect [the precepts]. If one follows along with negligence and indulges in arrogance, what refuge will there be for gods and humans?
The Vinaya states: "As long as there are those who administer the *karmavācanā*, my Dharma has not yet perished; if they do not uphold it, my Dharma will come to an end.

It further states: "Where the precepts abide, I abide. This principle is no empty statement. Since there is such profound significance, should they not truly be revered? The *Xi-jou jing* (The Scripture on the Mad Dog) says:
The Buddha said, "There are those who uphold the precepts and practices of the Buddha-dharma and teach others to serve the Buddha, yet cause them to enter hell.
Ānanda rose in alarm, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and asked the Buddha, "How can one teach so that they may attain the Way? For what reason would they instead enter hell?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "In the future, at the end of the age, there will be disciples who act as teachers; they will be indolent and..."
Though they are able to apply themselves diligently to study, they possess no wisdom and are defiled by craving for sensual desires.

They receive offerings of money, grain, and silk from others, using these to sustain themselves, yet they do not refine themselves in the Buddha-dharma. They flatter and follow the whims of others; seeing people who crave killing, they do not bestow the precepts upon them;
seeing people who relish alcohol, they do not cause them to abstain from it. To those who can drink only a little, they administer the dharma of the precepts, saying only "a little."

To obtain money and goods for the sake of performing meritorious deeds, or to seek out people and their belongings, constitutes the selling of the precepts (*śīla*). This causes others to become even more arrogant.
One who does not purify the precepts commits various grave offenses, such as killing. A teacher who instructs in such a manner casts the practitioner into hell;
because they have betrayed the Buddha’s clear teaching, the deities who protect the Buddha’s Way will seize upon their shortcomings and treat them as evil.
This is a disease caused by demons; the transgression is grave and may even lead to death. Once the retribution for the sin is paid, one enters the *niraya* hells. Ānanda asked the Buddha:

"If those who have newly resolved their intent encounter an evil teacher and, being ignorant and lacking understanding, believe that such is the nature of the Dharma, and thus come to accept his words out of folly and lack of comprehension—should they, upon meeting a wise teacher again, be permitted to receive the precepts once more?"
The Buddha said: "Within my Dharma, there is vastness and breadth; one can attain repentance and further purify oneself through confession.

When first resolving to attain enlightenment, the mind was constantly clouded and obscured, having been misled by evil teachers. In truth, one did not know this oneself, yet proceeded to receive the precepts.
At the beginning of entering the Dharma, when one does not know or understand, at that time one is not a disciple of the Buddha, but merely a person of minor worldly virtue."
[This is] merely [a matter of] hearing. It does not possess great merit. The *Vibhaṅga-sūtra* states: Ānanda asked the Buddha:

"If, in the future, there should be someone who has faith and joy in accordance with the Dharma, who sincerely desires to sever worldly ties and transcend secular customs by following the Right Path, yet at that time there is no master to transmit the teachings and precepts—if there were someone who could transcribe the Vinaya and bestow it upon them, would they thereby attain [the goal]?"
"Is it not so that one who has attained deliverance is a follower of the Way? The Buddha said, "Ānanda, only when all have come to know the prohibitive Dharma (vinaya) may the precepts be conferred.
They cannot be received merely through written characters; only then does it accord with the Dharma. Why is this?

Because the Buddha is the Great Wisdom of the world above and the world below, the Great Deliverance of the world above and the world below, and the Great [Teacher] of the world above and the world below."

It must be understood that one must not transmit this recklessly or lose its essential meaning. One should clearly comprehend the precepts and prohibitions of the Dharma, becoming thoroughly proficient in every detail before bestowing it upon others.
To bestow the precepts upon others while lacking clarity regarding the essential matters of the precepts and prohibitions is improper.

To violate the Buddha’s admonitions and yet believe them to be wrong, while conversely regarding [such errors] as correct, is a grave offense that is not small. One ought to investigate this with careful discernment.

The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states: "If a bhikṣu does not recite the precepts at all and is ignorant of the Dharma, yet performs various monastic affairs and ordains many people—would he incur any transgressions by acting as one of the three masters? The answer is: "Such a person should not even consume the faithful offerings of others."
How much more so regarding the salvation of others (the ritual procedures for conferring the precepts are fully contained within the *Karmavācanā*);
○ Regarding the *Poṣadha-khandhaka*:
as for the original principle of the *Poṣadha*, it is the profound regulation for rectifying the three karmas; it is through this *poṣadha* alone that the *saṃgha* is governed.
This is truly the vital pulse of the Buddha’s mandate and the fundamental principle of the Dharma. It is the great model established by Śākyamuni, and herein lies our exhortation.

Indeed, it is because the teachings have declined and people have become deluded that they treat this as something external; thus, the two classes of practitioners are left without refuge, the five assemblies lose their proper direction, and the devas and nāgas have nothing to revere.
How then can spirits and deities turn their hearts toward it? Even if one were to attempt to propagate it, [it would be in vain].
Those who see this condemn it; even if one should offer a slight extension of the argument, they revile it as biased and dogmatic. How lamentable!

That a son of the Muni should become a member of the faction of Pāpīyas, and that one should abandon the noble lineage of the Dharma King to succeed as the base legitimate heir of the Mara people—these faults and afflictions are all the fault of those who maintain the teachings.
Why do you not examine the clear texts of the Tripiṭaka and the five thousand wondrous scrolls?
Examine them to distinguish the true from the false. Some would rather be counted among those who destroy the Dharma than rejoice in being companions of Māra.
They abandon the *poṣadha* to debate points of doctrine, yet they are still driven away by divine powers. Even Arhats, considering themselves pure, did not attend the hearing of the precepts;
the World-Honored One had to go in person to summon them to assemble together. How much more so for us, mere ordinary beings, who are like sheep? If such were the case for these...
O Benevolent and Virtuous One, it is not that you harbor self-seeking thoughts; rather, you possess a heart intent on benefiting all beings.

You should stir the vast waves of the Dharma-ocean and strive to crush the precipitous fall of Māra. Raise the banner of Right View and topple the flag of false models. Thus, though the teaching is nearing extinction, it shall be difficult to extinguish;
though practice is prone to error, it shall be difficult to corrupt. Although the time since the Sage departed is remote, it remains no different from when he awakened the world.
He shall greatly propagate the sacred transformation and succeed to the dharma-seat, continuing the lamp left behind by Śākyamuni and boarding the original vessel of the Compassionate Buddha.
[The] Zen staff...
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: Regarding the method for making a meditation staff (*dhyāna-daṇḍa*), one should use bamboo or reed, eight cubits in length, with both ends wrapped in cloth.
The person who carries the staff must not seek out faults based on anger or attachment; rather, they should restrain the six sense-faculties and maintain right mindfulness and reflection.
If there is someone who is drowsy, the staff should be given to them. That person must not harbor resentment or malice, but should accept it as it ought to be.
This mindfulness now removes my hindrances for me; the benefit is no small matter. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

When taking up the meditation staff (*dhyāna-daṇḍa*), one should arouse a mind of reverence. There are five circumstances in which one may strike another with the meditation staff: first, out of compassion; second, to prevent him from disturbing others;
third, when he is asleep; fourth, when his head is leaning against a wall; and fifth, when his legs are stretched out (if they extend too far, one may use a wedge).
*Liàngyǐng* (Measuring the Shadow); in the Sanskrit language it is called *cai*, which here means "shadow. The *Zhǐguī* states that at Nālandā Monastery, the monk Śrīcandramati said:

"In the Western Regions, they set up a gnomon to measure the shadow. In the morning, as the shadow shifts toward the west, one simply counts the number of steps taken from the front to the back of the footprints."
This refers to measuring the shadow by counting steps. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "To measure the shadow by steps, one stands upright in the middle of the sun;
taking the position of the feet as the starting point, one measures the shadow by steps according to the height of the body.

The *Mūla-karman* states: "At that time, a bhikṣu stepped across, and the shadow moved past. The Buddha said: 'One should use a śaṅku (measuring rod) to measure it; take a fine tally-stick two [units] long.'"
Approximately one *chi* in length, with one end bent at four finger-widths, it is set upright in the sunlight to measure the length and shortness of its shadow;
this is called a *shangju*. Each measurement of shadow taken by means of a *shangju* is termed "one person" (thus the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"the shadows of one or two persons," which people nowadays generally do not recognize). The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* says: "As for the method of measuring shadows, one first takes a wooden strip, like a thin..."
The *śalākā* (measuring stick) should be one cubit (*hasta*) in length. One end is bent so that four fingers stand upright, shaped like a carpenter’s square;
these must not be separated. On the day of the measurement, the upright stick is placed in the sunlight while the remaining staff is laid on the ground to cast its vertical shadow.

When this vertical shadow is equal in length to the horizontal stick, one then measures the horizontal shadow with the four-finger span. When it reaches the full length of four fingers, it is called one *pauruṣa*. Thus...
At most one *puruṣa*, or one *puruṣa* less by one finger, half a finger, and so forth;

such increases and decreases can be inferred by the mind. (*Puruṣa* is translated as "person. Thus, a shadow of four fingers is called "one person" because when a staff of four fingers is held upright, at the time when the shadow is four fingers long, this person standing in the sun has a shadow length equal to his own body length.

When it is eight fingers, the two shadows [of the body and the staff] are equal to the body length. This is based on a person of medium height; it is not necessarily so for all. As for other heights and lengths, the principle may be applied accordingly.)
One should apply this accordingly). However, one must specify whether it is before or after a meal, or if it is cloudy or at night, one must then estimate and state it accordingly.
If following the method of the Divine Land (China), one may either erect a measuring rod at midday to measure the length of the shadow, or record the number of the twelve *dina* (double-hours).
This method of measuring shadows must be applied whenever receiving the precepts and so forth (the rest is explained in the section on the *Khandhaka* on dwellings regarding the counting of years).
*Kaṇḍa* (or *kaṇḍi*). Master Fashi says: the Sanskrit term is *bherī-kaṇḍa*. *Bherī* means "to strike";
*kaṇḍa* refers to the wooden instrument struck, which may be made of sandalwood or paulownia wood. There is no exact equivalent for this in Chinese. Many older translations render it as *gān* (犍).

"Chí" (遲). This should be written as "zhì" (稚). Pronounced *zhì* (with the phonetic components *zhí* and *zhì*). Both "chí" and "zhì" share the same pronunciation, *zhì*. However, because the forms of the characters "chuí" (椎) and "zhì" (稚) are easily confused, this error occurred.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Whatever makes a sound—be it made of tile, wood, copper, or iron—is all called a *ghaṇṭā* (揵椎).
Furthermore, when the bhikṣus did not know what kind of wood to use to make the *ghaṇṭā*, the Buddha said: "With the exception of lacquer trees and poisonous trees, [any other wood may be used]."

Regarding the sounding of wooden instruments, the striking should be performed by resident *śrāmaṇeras* or *karmadānas*. One must not strike them excessively; rather, they should be struck three times.
If there are no *śrāmaṇeras*, a *bhikṣu* may also strike them. Master Jingfa said: "Whenever the *ghanṭā* is struck, it shall not be done by a *karmadāna*;
the *karmadāna* himself shall strike it. All other miscellaneous duties, such as blowing conch shells and beating drums, are likewise [to be handled by him]."
This was performed by the *śramaṇera* (pure person) and the doorkeeper. The *Sìshìchāo* states: "In ordinary practice, at the beginning of striking the *zhūi*, one must gradually produce sound;
starting from faintness and gradually increasing until the sound reaches its full extent, only then does one strike a single stroke. This was the practice when the Buddha was in the world."
There were only three short strikes. Later, due to an invitation from another, the long strike was finally introduced. The *Nidāna* states:

When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada hosted a great assembly, there were times when people arrived after the meal had concluded and missed the proper time for food. The Buddha said: [the following rule was established].
He should announce that the time has arrived. [The assembly was so noisy that they did not hear him. The Buddha said, "One should strike the *gandī*. Still they did not hear him.
The Buddha said, "One should blow the conch shell and also beat the drum. Yet it was still not heard everywhere. The Buddha said, "Strike the great bell and drum."
The Buddha ordered the drum to be beaten. After beating it three times, one should then beat it continuously. One must wait for the sick person;

once they have been invited and have finished eating, as well as the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* (steward) having finished eating, only then should one beat the drum continuously. If one does not do so, one incurs an offense against the Dharma (*vyatikrama*). [Note: The *karmadāna* is the *vaiyāvṛtyakara*.

This refers to one who directs others regarding the various affairs of the Saṃgha, whether by striking the *gaṇḍī* or by supervising the food distribution; all such persons are called *karmadānas*. Because they are occupied with managing the affairs of the Saṃgha during mealtime, they are permitted [to eat later].
He ate first (as explained in detail in the *An-gu-jian-du*).
Mahākapphiṇa is also called Kapphiṇa;
this means "Lunar Mansion of the Room" (*Kṛttikā*). Formerly he was called Kimphila, which translates as "Majestic Like a King."
This is explained in detail in the two preceding chapters.
The "Immortal Mountain" (Xianren shan) is, in Sanskrit, Mount Aśvakarṇa; it is this very mountain.
Vihāra Mountain is also called Vibhāra Mountain. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:

"In Rājagṛha (the City of the King's Abode), on Vihāra Mountain, there is the Saptaparṇa Cave" (alternatively called a chamber, a house, or a grotto—these three names refer to the same thing). In the Sanskrit language, it is called *Saptaparṇa-guha*. This...
It is called the "Seven-Leaf Cave. As for the term "seven leaves," it refers to the leaves of that tree, which grow at most to a height of seven [units].
Although the tree bears flowers, they lack fragrance.
The *Record of the Western Regions* states: To the west of the northern gate of the mountain city in the kingdom of Magadha lies Mount Vipula.
On the shaded side of a cliff to the southwest of this mountain, there were formerly five hundred hot springs; today, only several dozen remain. Nevertheless, they still...
It is cold at times and warm at others, yet it has not entirely lost its warmth. Its source originates from the south of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat).
Flowing secretly from the Anavatapta Lake (Lake of No Heat or Torment), it reaches this place; the water is exceedingly clear and delicious, its flavor identical to that of the original lake.
As it flows through five hundred minor subsidiary hot hells, the upward-flaring intensity of the fires causes it to become warm and hot. The mouths of these spring outlets are all carved from stone.
Some take the form of lions or white elephants; others are stone conduits through which water flows down in cascades.
Below, stones are laid out to form a pool where people from various regions and distant lands all come to bathe. Those who bathe here often find their chronic ailments cured.
On both sides of the hot spring, stupas and the foundations of monasteries stand in dense succession; these were all built by the four Buddhas of the past.

This is the site where [the Buddha] sat and practiced walking meditation. Since this place is characterized by mountains and waters winding together, it is a dwelling for those of benevolence and wisdom;

indeed, there have been many recluses who lived in seclusion here. (As for hot springs, they exist in many places throughout China, though they are particularly numerous in Dianbai County in Lingnan.)

*Śalākā* is translated here as "counting-stick" (*chou*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that they should be made of copper, iron, ivory, horn, bone, bamboo, or wood; trees with lacquer or poison must be excluded.
They should be no shorter than the span of five fingers and no longer than one cubit (a fistful plus a forearm). Their thickness should not exceed...
The little fingers should not be thinner than chopsticks and should be lacquered. They should be kept in a tube and suspended above the Poṣadha hall.

When distributing the voting sticks (*śalākā*), they should be handed directly by hand. Another person should be appointed to collect them; once collected, they should be counted, and having been counted, the total should be announced.
The announcement should be made as follows: "There are so many bhikṣus and so many śrāmaṇeras; in all, there are so many persons who have left the household life. Thus one distinguishes their merits.
The treatise states: Generally, those who distribute the counting sticks (śalākā) record the number of people to ascertain whether they are acting with sincerity or not.

If one receives a stick with sincerity, one will obtain merit; if one receives it through falsehood, one's transgressions will accumulate until they surpass the heavens. Śalākā is also called "exhaustion" (*huài jìn*):
through merit, transgressions are exhausted; through transgressions, merit is exhausted.
