To accumulate objects is the entry for the sound *shēng*.
*Shù wù* (樹杌):
*wù* is pronounced with the fifth tone (*hū*) and the initial *wù*. It refers to a tree stump, meaning a tree without branches.
*Jiāngpàn*:

*jiāng* is pronounced with the *qie* of *jūliáng*, sounding like *jiāng*; it means boundary or limit. It refers to the edge or border. *Pàn* is pronounced with the *qie* of *bóbàn*, sounding like *pàn*; it refers to a field boundary.
This is now borrowed for use. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: Regarding the characteristics of boundaries (*sīmā-lakṣaṇa*):
as for mountain boundaries, the large are like Mount Sumeru and the small are like elephants. As for stone boundaries, the large are like oxen and the small are thirty *tola* in weight.
If the stones are scattered, they cannot serve as boundary markers; one must place them separately. As for forest boundaries, these include grass thickets and bamboo groves.
One must not establish boundary markers (*sīmā*). Why is this? Because grass and bamboo are empty in substance and lack solidity.
In the case of a large forest, it may extend even up to one hundred *yojanas*; for a small forest, it must be at least four trees joined together.
Regarding the boundary marker of trees, a withered tree cannot serve as a marker. A large one is a *Jambū* tree; a small one is eight inches high and shaped like an alms bowl.
Large. If there are no trees growing of their own accord, it is also permissible to plant trees. Regarding boundaries for paths:
paths leading into fields, paths toward wells or rivers for taking water, and dead-end paths—none of these may serve as boundary markers. As for main roads:

whether they are carriage roads or pedestrian paths, even those as short as those passing through three or four villages may all serve as boundary markers. Regarding ant-hills as boundary markers: the large ones...
Regarding earth boundaries: even those as small as eight inches in height may all serve as boundary marks. Regarding river boundaries:
if it has not rained for four months yet the current flows without interruption, and the water depth reaches two feet, it may serve as a boundary mark.
Regarding water boundaries: natural pond water may serve as a boundary mark; however, water flowing through fields or water contained in jars cannot serve as a boundary mark at all.
Characteristics. These are the eight kinds of characteristics for delimiting a boundary (*sīmā*). There are five types of boundary characteristics: first, square; second, circular;
third, drum-shaped; fourth, half-moon shaped; and fifth, triangular.
The reason this *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) was originally established is that it is difficult for a large number of people to assemble at a single residence;

therefore, this field is separately demarcated so that when there are essential matters among the assembly, they may be carried out at any time. Thus, the Vinaya states: "There are occasions where four [monks] are required," and so forth.
When a group of twenty people gathers for a *karmavācanā* ceremony, the assembly may become exhausted. The Buddha permitted the establishment of a *sīmā* (ordination enclosure).
However, regarding these enclosures, none of the various Vinaya texts prescribe a fixed standard. According to Western practice, they exist everywhere with a specific measurement;
they are barely over a *zhang* in size, constructed by encircling a level ground with bricks to a height of two *chi*, with the walls built inward.
The foundation is approximately five *cun* high, intended for the seating of monks; it has no steps or tiers.
In its center is placed a small stūpa, as tall as a person, with a small door opened on its side to allow for entry and exit.
For example, the layout of the *śīla-maṇḍala* at the great Nālandā Monastery in Central India is over one *zhang* (ten feet) in circumference, built directly upon level ground.
Stacked brick walls are about two chi high; the foundation for sitting within the wall is about five cun high, with a small *caitya* in its center.
This alone is the standard; all other locations follow this same format. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "The smallest boundary enclosure must accommodate twenty-one people;
this is intended for conferring absolution (*āpattivyutthāna*) upon others. All other [functions] are performed therein."
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) may also be successfully accomplished. However, this boundary for the precepts (*sīmā*) was originally established for essential matters.
If a large number of people can assemble together, they may naturally perform all the various rites within the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

Some say that if one encounters the hardship of rain during the performance of the rite, it is permitted to formally establish a boundary for the precepts under a roof; although there is this teaching, it was not the original intent.

The formal text of the Vinaya originally intends to provide extensive precautions, fearing that the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure) might fail to achieve its purpose. However, the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"Once the boundary enclosure has been established, if a house is subsequently built over it, the boundary is not lost. This refers to the formal method for establishing a boundary.
There are only two kinds: first, the *sīmāmaṇḍala* (precept platform); second, the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary). If one wishes to establish them, one may first establish the *sīmāmaṇḍala*.
This platform should be situated on one side within the *mahāsīmā*, placed in a location free from obstructions or difficulties. One should first set up its boundary markers (*liṅga*).
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "First, establish three layers of boundary markers; the innermost layer is called the *śīla-sīmā*."

The boundary markers for the outside of the *kṣetra* (precept field). The middle layer is called the inner marker of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). The outermost layer is called the outer marker of the great boundary.

[Regarding] the outer marker of the *kṣetra* and the inner marker of the great boundary—between these two markers, they should be separated by approximately two chi (cubits), or as some say, one *hasta* (forearm); although this is so, it is not strictly fixed.
Once the three markers have been established, all the monks within the natural boundary (*jñapti-kṣetra*) assemble inside the designated area of the *kṣetra*. First, he causes one monk...
The Master proclaims the boundaries outside the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept-field). First, one begins from the southeast corner marker (the *Mūla-vinaya* merely requires starting from the east).

Once the four directional boundaries have been proclaimed, the assembly may then proceed to perform the *karmavācanā*. When the formal boundary has been established according to the Dharma, one next proclaims the four internal and external boundaries of the *mahā-śīma* (great boundary).

Regarding this, some say: "At the time of establishing the *śīma-kaṇḍa*, whether everyone has assembled or not, it may be done regardless of the number, provided there are at least five persons; since there is no *mahā-śīma* [yet], there is no fault if the assembly does not gather."

If one does not establish the boundary for the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (the field of precepts), one simply recites the external marks of the *mahā-sīmā*. If there are necessarily curves or bends, they must be described according to the actual situation; furthermore, the specific limits, measurements, and locations must all be pointed out individually. Because the restrictions are not known, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) will fail to be established;

since the *karma* is performed in vain, rituals such as the reception of the precepts are all rendered empty. Therefore, it is necessary to recite clearly three times. The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: "If no *mahā-sīmā* is further established outside, and one establishes only a *kṣudra-sīmā*, one may not receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Once the marks have been recited, a person capable of presiding over the ritual from within the assembly shall perform the *karma* to establish it (the text is detailed in the *Karmavācanā*). Not...
One may receive the *kṣānti* (consent). Because the boundary has not yet been established, there is no inclusion within a boundary.

Furthermore, if one were to receive the *kṣānti*, one would not know the characteristics [of the boundary], which would result in the loss of robes and the violation of the summer retreat (*varṣa*). The *Nidāna* states: "The great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) should be established at a limit of two and a half *yojana*s;
if it exceeds this, it is not a boundary. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "When nuns establish a great boundary, the maximum..."
A great *krośa* is one *krośa*. When the Saṃgha establishes a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), it may extend to a maximum length and breadth of ten *krośas*.
The reason why, when establishing a great boundary, the village is included within it is that, by the power of the boundary established by the Saṃgha, evil cannot find an opportunity;
furthermore, within the boundary, there is the protection of benevolent deities. For these reasons, it is for the sake of the donor (*dānapati*) that the village is included.

This is the method for establishing boundaries. If one wishes to establish the *acīvarāpatti-sīmā* (the boundary where robes need not be kept with one), it is established based upon the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *mahāsīmā* (great boundary);

there are no other separate characteristics. Therefore, in the text, it still refers to this "residence" (*āvāsa*). If there is a village within the boundary, the village and the area outside the village must be excluded.
If there is no village, there is no need to chant its exclusion. Some say this is the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure).

Whether there be a village or not, it is excluded at all times. The reason for this is that even if a village should later enter the boundary, it need not be re-established, because when the boundary was first established, the village had already been excluded. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śīla-saṃgraha* (Sapoduo lun) correctly establishes this principle:

the village is excluded for five reasons even if it arrives later. If there was originally no village, once the ritual procedure for establishing the boundary has been completed, [it remains excluded].
Regarding the dwelling place of a *karmadāna* (lay attendant): when someone enters from outside the village, the area they occupy is not part of the robe-boundary (*cīvara-sīmā*).

If they subsequently depart back to the original village, the robe-boundary remains encompassed. However, if a village already existed there previously, it was not encompassed. When the village departs for an empty space, the robe-boundary becomes full once more.
This is because the coming and going of the village does not constitute the binding or unbinding of the boundary. The *Mūla-karman* states: "If the Saṃgha has already..."

Having completed the demarcation of the "boundary for not losing one's robes," one may travel within the boundary carrying only the upper and lower robes without incurring the fault of being separated from them (other schools do not require both).
Upāli requested of the World-Honored One, saying: "Venerable Sir, for a bhikṣu traveling on a journey, how far does the 'sphere of influence' of these robes extend?
The Buddha said: "It is like the seven *amra* trees planted by the Brahmin Jātiśroṇa."
The *la* trees stand seven *vyāma* apart from one another, their flowers and fruits flourishing; the total distance between them is forty-nine *vyāma*.
This is the extent of the robe-territory (*cīvara-sīmā*) for a wandering bhikṣu, O Venerable One. If it is the robe-territory for a resident bhikṣu—
"Furthermore, to what extent does it reach? The Buddha said: "It reaches only one fathom all around.
Whether sitting, standing, or lying down, it extends to that one fathom. Venerable One, suppose, for instance, a bhikṣu is lying down between two boundaries."
"How far must a robe extend? The Buddha said: "As long as even a single corner of the robe has not been separated from the body, it is called 'not being separated from the robe.
The *Mātṛkā* asks: "If one dwells in a place without boundaries, at what distance from the robe is it considered 'staying overnight separated from the robe'?
The answer is: "It depends on the size of the monks' enclosure, wall, moat, or ditch; if a bhikṣu places his robe within these limits, he is not separated from it."

One may act according to one's will until the appearance of the dawn. Regarding the three types of boundaries (*sīmā*) mentioned above, those who wish to dissolve them should do so in the following order:

first, dissolve the *acchinnaka-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one’s robe); next, dissolve the *sīmā-maṇḍala* (the boundary of the precept-platform); and finally, dissolve the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary).

If there is no *sīmā-maṇḍala*, then after dissolving the robe-boundary, one immediately dissolves the great boundary. The *Nidāna* states: "Whenever a visiting bhikṣu arrives at another empty residence..."
Regarding the dwelling place: after staying for seven or eight days, if no one comes, only then should you collectively establish the boundary (*sīmā*).
It is further said: if there is doubt, one must first dissolve the boundary and then re-establish it. If one recognizes the previous boundary, one may simply abide by it and need not re-establish it;

The four right efforts are also called the four right abandonments: first, to eliminate evil states that have already arisen; second, to prevent evil states that have not yet arisen from arising.

First: the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Just as when the yin and yang are in harmonious balance, all seeds sprout from their roots; therefore, they are called "roots" (mūla).
The five powers (*pañca-balāni*) are: first, the power of faith; second, the power of diligence; third, the power of mindfulness; fourth, the power of concentration; and fifth, the power of wisdom.

Regarding what is called "power" (*bala*), it refers to the capacity to destroy all that is evil and unwholesome, and to accomplish what is wholesome. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) asks: "The names are the same [as the five faculties]."

O Bhikṣu-saṃgha, during the summer retreat (varṣā), you must not interrogate one another regarding offenses, nor should you establish illegal regulations that cause the bhikṣus to dwell in discomfort.
One who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharmāpatti).

The one distributing the voting sticks (śalākā) shall hold the counting tray before him, while the one collecting the sticks shall follow behind with an empty tray. The Great Teacher and World-Honored One (Śākyamuni) shall first place [the first stick].
First, the tally stick (*śalākā*). Next, the entire assembly shall rise from their seats, squatting down to examine it closely;

having received the tally stick, they shall hold it with both hands and place it upon an empty tray. If there is a *śrāmaṇera*, his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or instructor (*ācārya*) [shall do so on his behalf].

One should take the tally sticks on their behalf. Next, the tally stick for the guardian deity of the monastery is cast. Once all have participated, one should count the tally sticks and announce to the assembly:

"In this residence, those who have currently received tally sticks consist of this many bhikṣus, this many śrāmaṇeras, the donor so-and-so, and the administrator so-and-so; such-and-such a village quarter is the place for alms-seeking."
At that time, all the bhikṣus should examine the places for alms-gathering. Having examined them, they should reflect to themselves:
"In this place, I am fit to observe the rains retreat; it will not give rise to suffering, and should suffering arise, I shall be able to dispel it.
If there is illness, there will be attendants, and I shall be provided with medicine. Whatever is required shall be fully supplied. Having thus reflected...
Having made this reflection, one should go to a secluded place before a single bhikṣu.

Fully assuming the proper deportment, squatting and joining the palms, one should receive the dharma (the text for the reception is found within that particular school and need not be recorded here; nevertheless, although this belongs to the ritual system of the Sarvāstivāda, the dharma itself is impartial. Since the procedure is complete and excellent, it may be adopted as a standard).

"Repairing and treating" means to mend and manage. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "After first having received the rules for the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*), one should then receive the dwelling and bedding.
Within the room, one should repair and plaster it; furthermore, the bed upon which one sits should each be examined one by one."

Regarding the principle: Nanshan says that if one is observing the *an-shu* (rainy-season retreat) in the residence of a donor, in a village, wilderness, forest, mountain crag, or dwelling, the ritual procedure for receiving the Dharma is identical to the others, with the sole exception that "monastery" (*gā-lán*) is substituted [for "monk"].

As for the words regarding the repair of dilapidated structures, these apply specifically to the monastic quarters and should be adjusted according to the specific circumstances. Regarding the ritual procedures for the four assemblies, one simply changes "bhikṣu" [to the appropriate term].
These words serve to distinguish [the cases]; the rest of the text is the same. A bhikṣuṇī should receive the *anvārohaṇa* (formal agreement) from another bhikṣuṇī;
a śrāmaṇera should receive it from a bhikṣu; a śikṣamāṇā and a śrāmaṇerī should receive it from a bhikṣuṇī. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"When an elder (*sthavira*) wishes to receive the *anvārohaṇa*, he should bare one shoulder, put on his robe, and remove his leather sandals. Hú... [text ends]
Kneel with palms joined. Facing those of lower rank, recite three times. If one receives the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) from a superior, one must additionally clasp their feet;

otherwise, all else is the same. If there is no person upon whom to rely and one intends to observe the retreat through mental resolve (*manasikāra*), the ritual text is identical, except that the opening phrase and the subsequent questions and answers are omitted. One should fully maintain dignified deportment in accordance with the Dharma.
Recite three times (kneeling on the right knee—that is, squatting).

According to the *Fangguang jingzhuchi shu* (Commentary on the Sutra on the Light of the Dwelling Place), one who merely constructs a monastery is called the "monastery master" (*vihārasvāmin*). In Sanskrit, this is called *vihārasvāmin*.
*Mī*. If one serves as the duty officer (*yāma*) in charge of the temple gate and mediates matters for the *saṃgha*, he is called a *vihārapāla*, translated as "Protector of the Temple.
If one strikes the *gaṇḍī* or supervises the food, he is called a *karmadāna*, translated as "Distributor of Affairs" (or "Superintendent").
The term *vinaya* is an abbreviation. (*Karmadāna* means "bestowing affairs"; *karman* means "affairs. The meaning is that one directs and assigns the various miscellaneous affairs of the community.)

Regarding the term for this office: the old translation "Weina" (維那) is incorrect. "Wei" (維) is a Chinese word meaning "to maintain the framework" (*kāraṇa*); "na" (那) is a Sanskrit sound that is an abbreviation of the word *karmadāna*. The *Sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of the Sangha) translates it as "one who manages affairs" (*zhishi*) and also calls him "one who gladdens the assembly" (*yuezhong*), meaning one who knows the matters and gladdens the assembly.

Nanshan says: according to the treatises on phonology, "Weina" is translated as "sequence" (*anupūrvi*), meaning one who knows the sequence of the Sangha's affairs). When the assembly has business, they gather to deliberate;
he is charged with protecting the monastery, making rounds to announce matters, and before each individual, he must join his palms and extend [the invitation].

Regarding this matter: if even a single person does not consent, the business cannot be accomplished. There is absolutely no method of striking the gavel or making a formal announcement before the assembly.
If one sees that someone does not consent, one should persuade them with reason; it has never been the case that one resorts to force or uses intimidation to suppress them.

Regarding those who guard the storehouses or manage the estates, even if there are only two or three people, they shall dispatch a family member in charge of the storehouse to join their palms and submit a formal report.
Only if this is done in harmony may expenses be incurred; truly, there is no blame for acting alone.

If one uses funds independently without reporting, then even for as little as half a *jin* of millet, one will immediately be subjected to dismissal and banishment. If a single person claims to be a man of status and acts alone...
To utilize the property of the Sangha or to handle administrative affairs without informing the great assembly is termed *kulapati*, translated as "householder.
This is a great sore upon the Buddha-dharma, resented by both humans and spirits alike.
Although it may appear beneficial to the monastery, in the end one incurs even deeper transgression. A wise person will certainly not do such a thing.

*Téng* (藤): pronounced *tú dēng* (徒登切), with the phonetic value *téng* (音騰). It refers to the *léi* (藟) vine. Nowadays, all grassy creepers and spreading vines resembling the *léi* are collectively called *téng*.
(*Léi*: pronounced with the rising tone of *léi* [雷]; a species of *gé* [葛] vine; *Mahīdāra*; explained in the *Śayanāsana-vastu* [房舍揵度]).
"Pútáomàn" (蒲萄蔓):
"màn" is pronounced with the *wàn* rhyme (as in *wàn*). It means "to extend.
Thus, the grape vine grows as a creeping stem that reaches great lengths, spreading extensively across mountains and valleys; many people plant it.
The *Mukha-dhaka* (Supplementary Text) states: Regarding the bedding belonging to the Saṃgha, one must not sleep naked. One who sleeps naked incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Whatever bedding belongs to the Saṃgha should be covered with a cloth; alternatively, one may use a five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*) for this purpose.
Examine it carefully and use it slowly. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states:

"Whenever using any bedding belonging to the Saṃgha, one must not, as one pleases, substitute it with a small, light sitting mat, or with anything that is soiled, greasy, coarse, thin, or of poor quality;
to do so incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* and brings about the calamity of a 'black back' (rebirth as a beast). The *Mūla-karman* states: As the Blessed One..."
The Buddha said, "O bhikṣus, you should not use the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha without placing a protective layer beneath them.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used items such as those that were soiled, greasy, thin, or tattered as protective layers for the Saṃgha's bedding.
Then, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl and entered Vaiśālī.
He went forth to beg for alms, with the venerable Ānanda serving as his attendant.
The Blessed One then saw a man whose back was entirely black and addressed Ānanda, saying: "Do you see this man’s black back?
Ānanda replied, "I see it. The Buddha said: "In the past, during the true teaching of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, this person..."
Having gone forth, he used whatever coarse and inferior materials were at hand to serve as a lining for the monastic bedding.
Due to the retribution of his past black karma, he fell into hell; furthermore, for five hundred lifetimes, he constantly manifested with a black back.
Because of this fault, monks should not use thin, tattered, or soiled materials to line the monastic bedding.
Regarding bedding: if it is a thick material, it should be used as a single layer; if it is inherently thin, it must be doubled over before use.

Should one act otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*vyatikrama-dharma*). By this proof, one should know that all property belonging to the Sangha must be carefully guarded and protected, lest one incur subsequent entanglements and receive immeasurable retributive suffering.
*Sengqi* (i.e., *saṃgha*). *Taduoma* (毾[登*毛]): the character *tu* is pronounced with the *he* rhyme (as in *tuo*);
the character *mao* is pronounced with the *deng* rhyme (as in *deng*). *Taduoma* refers to a woolen rug (*máo-xí*). *Guǎngcāng*.
It is said: *talmáo-máo* (carpet) refers to that which has patterns. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "It is spread before a large bed or upon a small couch;
because it is used for ascending onto the bed, it is named accordingly."
*Qūshū* (氍毹):
The character *qū* is pronounced with the *shāng* and *jū* initials, yielding the sound *shū*. It belongs to the class of felt rugs (*zhān*) and woolen blankets (*diǎn*).
It refers to a rope net.
*Jué* (羂): cut by *gǔ* and *quǎn*. *Juān* (涓): with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). Also identical to *juàn* (絹), cut by *jí* and *quàn*; its pronunciation is *juàn*.
Originally belonging to the category of nets, it also belongs to the category of ropes and cords.
Zàngjǔ (藏弆).
"Jǔ" is pronounced with the *qie* (反切) *jū xǔ*; its phonetic value is *jǔ*. It means to store away.
*Fàndòng jīng* (梵動經).
Extracted from the fourteenth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. "Ji-huan" (祇桓) is also written as "Ji-huan" (祇洹);
the new [translation] calls it Jetavana, as explained previously. The *Pañcavargika Vinaya* states: At that time, Śrāvastī...
The people of the country wished to dig a canal at Jetavana to conduct water there.

When King Prasenajit heard of this, he issued a decree saying, "If anyone attempts to conduct water into Jetavana, they shall be punished with a great penalty. Later, when there was trouble on the frontier, the king set out for the campaign himself.
The various non-Buddhists wished to join forces to divert the channel. The bhikṣus told the upāsakas about this.
The upāsakas said, "This is not something we can manage; you should go and inform the King.

The bhikṣus said, "The World-Honored One does not permit traveling back and forth during the retreat period for more than seven days. The King is far from here; by what means could we possibly go? They then...

They reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, if there is business concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha, or private business, beyond the seven-day limit, I further authorize you to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) to receive a period of fifteen days or one month to travel outside the boundary."

If one has received [the formal authorization] on a day when there are matters concerning the Buddha, the Sangha, or a stupa; or matters concerning one's parents, donors, or invitations from the seven classes of followers;

or due to circumstances such as illness and medicine, and it is impossible to return on that very same day, the Buddha permits one to go for seven days after receiving [the authorization]. If it is impossible to return within seven days, he permits one to receive [an extension].
[The period] departs on the fifteenth day. If one does not return by the fifteenth day, it is permitted to receive [the extension] for one month; having received it for one month, one should return.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, beyond the seven days, an additional thirty nights are permitted. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is permitted to receive it for thirty-nine nights.

According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it may extend to a maximum of forty nights. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, when the matter is concluded, one should return; whether it be half a month or [a full month].
One month, two months, and so on, until one returns for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the end. Master Xuán stated:

"In all the Vinayas of the various schools, the procedures for receiving [permission to remain] for a set number of days differ from one another. Later masters who engaged in ritual practice each adhered to a single school and did not employ those of other schools;
this was simply their own tradition. Now, examining the Vinaya texts of these various schools in detail, it is permissible to use them interchangeably. This is because..."
However, if one knows with certainty that a preceding matter requires exactly one night, one should employ the method for receiving the one-night [precept] from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
This applies likewise up to seven nights. If it requires thirty-nine nights, one should likewise receive it using that same text.
If [the matter] requires seven days, or even up to one month, one should receive the formal authorization using the ritual text of the specific *nikāya* (school) concerned.
If it is not certain how many days the preceding matter will take to conclude, one may use the ritual text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* to receive the days.

Later, some people, not understanding this, recited the *karmavācanā* text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* to receive [authorization for] matters pertaining to the *Mahāsāṃghika*. [This is addressed in] the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, fascicle 30.

The nine-night [periods] are all contrary to the Dharma and are not valid. How is this known? Because the specific matters recorded in the *karmavācanā* texts differ for each case, we know they are invalid.
Furthermore, the three types of receiving days within one's own school do not extend through the night.
This differs from the *itara-vinaya*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The five groups [of monastics] should observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*). The five groups may receive days [of leave].

If one goes on a journey, one must return to the boundary as soon as the business is finished, for there is no [legal] basis [for staying longer]. In the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, there is the method of receiving a seven-day leave repeatedly.
The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "If a matter arises during even a single night, one should receive a day's leave and depart," and so forth.
One should accept it for seven days. This is performed in the presence of a single bhikṣu. One may accept it repeatedly for one day, or accept it again for seven days;

one maintains the observance according to the requirements of the matter. If the seven days are not sufficient to complete the task, one should perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) to maintain the observance for eight days, and so on up to forty nights before departing.
At most, one may stay for forty nights; one must not exceed this limit, as prescribed by the Blessed One.

It is taught that [the *varṣā*] is mostly spent within the boundary (*sīmā*) and only rarely outside the boundary (it is not permitted to stay overnight outside during the latter half of the summer retreat).

Regarding those who request a seven-day leave, they must calculate the number of days; furthermore, it must not exceed forty nights. If there is a life-threatening danger or similar circumstance, not returning to one's original location does not constitute a violation of the summer retreat.
When members of the three lower assemblies receive the seven-day leave, a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) should address the *bhikṣu*.

The two women received [the precepts] in the presence of the *bhikṣuṇī*. The Dharma Master Jing said: "Since there is a karmic connection with those of lower status, I shall entrust [the matter] and depart.

(In all the Vinayas, it is stated that receiving for seven days is permitted, yet the text for the reception is not provided; it exists only in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*. Now, as each of the various *karmavācanā* texts has already prepared the wording, I shall follow this root text and, based on the formal announcement (*jñapti*) within the *karmavācanā*, it should be performed as follows:
having fully cultivated the dignified demeanor, one should speak to a single *bhikṣu*.)

Venerable sir, please attend to me with a focused mind. I, the bhikṣu [name], now receive the seven-day leave to go outside the boundary for a certain purpose, returning here to observe the rains retreat.
I inform the Venerable one so that he may know this. (Recite this three times. The reply should be as follows. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:)

The person being addressed should respond by saying: *aupayika* (the one who observes the day). The respondent says: *sādhu*. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if there is no bhikṣu present, it is permitted to receive [the observance] from the fourfold assembly, and it is also permitted for a solitary-dwelling bhikṣu to perform the mental recitation (*cittena*) of receiving the day.

This should be performed according to the preceding text, with the exception of the words addressed to the other party. Master Jing says: *Aupayika* is translated as "good" (*hao*) or "so be it" (*er*). It also carries the meaning of "expedient means" (*upāya*).

Because of this holy teaching, it serves as a skillful means (*kuśala-upāya*) capable of leading toward *nirvāṇa* and reaching the place of peace and security. *Sādhu* is translated as "good," and also as "well-accomplished. This refers to being good and capable of accomplishing the matter at hand. Whenever a ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is completed, or at the appropriate time...

When announcing matters, one should always act in this manner. To fail to speak thus constitutes a transgression of the Dharma (*vayadharmāpatti*). Regarding the term *bàn-hàn kuáng-shuō* (梵漢狂說), the old translation *chàng-sà* (唱薩) claims it means "excellent" (*sādhu*); this is an error.
Udayana is also called Udayibhadra,
as explained in the commentary on the precept regarding large dwellings within the "Thirteen Matters.
○ The Rules for the *Pravāraṇā* (Self-Examination) Khandhaka.

The ninety days having concluded and the three months having come full circle, at the dawn marking the end of the summer retreat and the year’s close, on the evening of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony when all are invited to offer their critiques, the assembly of the Dharma gathers like clouds.
They together purify their lives of wisdom; the *saṃgha* assembles in harmony to cleanse the body of precepts through the fivefold washing.

The king and his ministers extensively prepared offerings of alms; the lay followers widely cultivated merit and goodness. Humans and deities rejoiced together; ordinary beings and sages shared in the same delight.

The śramaṇas celebrated the Way—this constitutes the great seasonal observance. That the year of one’s renunciation is the occasion for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is precisely because in recent times, people have fallen into error and lost the proper path.
They have not heard the name of *pravāraṇā*, much less do they understand the practice of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. It is only...

To know that one is firmly sealed within minor transgressions is a grave error. To remain stubbornly closed off is a great fault. If one desires fragrant abundance, it instead becomes thorns and poison.

As soon as they begin to notice one another, they fall into resentment and contention. This leads to the point where later generations have nothing to hear, and those newly studying the path are cut off from listening.

Treating the words of the Dharma as non-Dharma, and what is not the Vinaya as the Vinaya, all of the Buddha’s teachings and admonitions are thereby lost and forgotten. That these growths which destroy the Dharma exist is truly due to...

It is so. I pray that all wise scholars will set their minds upon the holy teachings, tread the path of the ancient kings' orthodox regulations, and follow the brilliant ordinances of the former awakened ones.
Holding aloft the torch of the Dharma, may you serve as a mirror for the world. It would be better to endure the insults of a thousand fools than to pursue the currents of those who are deluded.
Let your resolve be such that you would rather die like a wild beast than desire to see those lion-maggots. If...
O son of the True Dharma, how could one simply sit by and look on?
The *Pravāraṇā-mātṛkā-sūtra* states:
"What is called *pravāraṇā*? When a bhikṣu has completed his summer retreat (*varṣā*), regarding wisdom and purity..."

Before the bhikṣus, one requests [the confession of] offenses seen, heard, or suspected. The reason for making this request is that during the ninety days of the summer retreat, one desires to clarify the observance of the precepts and other virtues so as to remain free from any transgression;
therefore, only upon the conclusion of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) does one first obtain the name of *pravāraṇā*.
For what reason did the Buddha teach the performance of *pravāraṇā*? First, so that each may admonish the others; second, so that each may remind the others.
1. Mindfulness; 2. Mutual instruction; 3. Mutual exhortation; 4. Mutual respect; 5. Speech that accords with one another; 6.
Having a basis for reliance rather than being without reliance. For these reasons, it is called *pravāraṇā*. When bhikṣus perform the *pravāraṇā*, they may perform one specific act.

First, regarding the time of the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation to point out faults): [The details] such as the confession of what has been seen, heard, or suspected are explained as in the section on the thirty matters (*triṃśan-vastu*). The *Mūla-karman* states:

The Buddha said, "O Bhikṣus, when there are seven or eight days remaining until the day of the *prātimokṣa-saṃgha-vaśī-bhāva* (the formal invitation), you should announce it in advance in the nearby villages and hamlets.
You may either speak of it orally or write it upon paper or leaves and place it high upon a rack or a cart."
He addressed them with a voice so that those far and near might all know:
"Venerable ones—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, and other such donors—young and old alike, listen attentively! The Saṃgha of a certain monastery shall perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
When the time arrives, you must all together prepare the necessary offerings. You young bhikṣus should..."

One should provide for the sweeping and sprinkling of the temple buildings where one resides, applying fresh *gomaya* (cow dung) as a clean coating. The *caityas* and incense altars should all be adorned and decorated.
Those who have long resided there should carry out these improvements. Various excellent and delicious meals should be provided at the appropriate times.
On the night of the fourteenth day, those bhikṣus who are versed in the Tripiṭaka and those who uphold the sūtras should remain awake throughout the entire night.
Recite the sūtras. When the fifteenth day arrives, one should recognize the proper time and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; do not let it pass until the dawn sign (*aruṇodgama*).
Once the assembly has granted permission, appoint one, two, or even many *pravāraṇā* monks who possess the five virtues.
They should be appointed in this manner. Having performed the preliminary formalities, once the assembly has gathered, one should first ask the candidate: "You, [Name]..."
[A] "Are you able to perform the *pravāraṇā* for the *saṃgha* during the summer retreat by means of the three matters—what has been seen, heard, or suspected?
He replies, "I am able. Next, one *bhikṣu* should be appointed; he should first make a formal motion (*jñapti*) and then perform the ritual act (*karman*).

The *bhikṣu* receiving the *pravāraṇā* should distribute fresh *mārga* grass to serve as a seat for the *saṃgha* (the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* calls this "spreading the grass"). Once the *mārga* grass has been distributed, next [the following... should be done.

Once seated, one should perform the *jñapti* (formal motion). Alternatively, the person receiving the *pravāraṇā* may perform the *jñapti*. Having performed the *jñapti*, one approaches the senior monk (*sthavira*) and performs the *pravāraṇā* face-to-face in successive order. The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "At that time, the senior monk and the other junior monks should each apply their full attention."

Having received a handful of *kuśa* grass, he spreads it crosswise. He then moves his body forward and steps upon it with both feet. Taking a small amount with his hand, he holds it up before him and recites [the formula] three times to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
If one person performs the *pravāraṇā*, they should do so starting from the *sthavira* (senior monk) down to the junior monks.
If there are two persons, one receives the *pravāraṇā* from the *sthavira*, while the other proceeds from the middle downward until the end. If three are appointed...

A person [performs the *pravāraṇā*] by arising from three places; the remaining meaning may be understood [as follows]. The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "If there is only one person, he should perform the *pravāraṇā* in the presence of another who has already performed his own *pravāraṇā*.

If there are two or three people, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony for one another. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, after the *saṃgha* has finished its own *pravāraṇā*, the person appointed to perform the *pravāraṇā* for the *saṃgha* then performs the *pravāraṇā* together with them. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If the person performing the *pravāraṇā* is the *sthavira*, he should bare one shoulder, adjust his robes, and bow his body as he speaks to the second *sthavira*."

"Today, Venerable Sir, the invitation for the *pravāraṇā* has arrived. At that time, the second senior monk (*sthavira*) should bare one shoulder, kneel on his right knee, and with both hands grasp the feet of the senior monk, reciting the invitation three times.
If it is a junior monk who performs the invitation, he should likewise bare one shoulder, kneel, join his palms, and speak thus to the senior monk:
"Today, Venerable Sir, the invitation for the *pravāraṇā* has arrived. The senior monk should also [respond accordingly].
Exposing one shoulder, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, and joining the palms, one recites the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*) three times.

Following this sequence, when the entire Saṃgha and the individual have completed the self-examination, one should go before the Elder and announce: "The Saṃgha has unanimously completed the self-examination.
The *Mūla-karman* states: "Once the formal procedure of the Saṃgha is concluded, next summon the community of Bhikṣuṇīs and cause them to enter the assembly to follow [the proceedings]."
[The Buddha] said: "The bhikṣu sits to one side. When the bhikṣuṇī arrives at his location, she performs the *pravāraṇā* rite just as a great bhikṣu does.
Next, he summons the śikṣamāṇās, the śrāmaṇeras, and the śrāmaṇerīs; each one receives the *pravāraṇā* in his presence (all of whom perform the *pravāraṇā* facing the bhikṣu).

Within the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha itself, a person is appointed to go before the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*) and announce their *pravāraṇā*, as prescribed in the original Vinaya text. As for that bhikṣu who performs the *pravāraṇā*..."
Standing before the senior elder, one should speak as follows: "Venerable One! Sisters! The two assemblies of the Saṃgha have already completed the *pravāraṇā*.
Both assemblies of the Saṃgha should together proclaim: 'Excellent! The *pravāraṇā* has been performed;
it has been very well performed. It is good for those who proclaim this. If they do not proclaim it, they incur an *dukkaṭa* offense. If [one] reaches this point..."
At that time, the five groups of renunciants, or perhaps including lay travelers, each provided knives, needles, thread, towels, silks,
and other such items to collectively perform the *pravāraṇā* offering for the assembly present. The bhikṣu receiving the *pravāraṇā* should carry a small knife,
or take up needles and thread, or hold various miscellaneous requisites of a śramaṇa, and stand before the presiding elder (*sthavira*).
He spoke these words: "Venerable sirs, may these items be given as a *yathāsukham* (at-will) gift to those who have completed their *varṣā* (rain-retreat)?
Furthermore, if other items for the benefit of the community are obtained at this place, should the harmonious *saṃgha* divide them?
The entire assembly answered simultaneously, "They should be divided. If it were otherwise, [the procedure would apply to] the *yathāsukham* bhikṣu and...
The assembly incurs an offense against the Dharma. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "All items such as clothing, knives, needles, and awls, once received, shall be divided equally.
The reason for offering knives and needles on this day is the desire to seek clarity of mind and sharp intelligence.
Once the distribution according to one's wishes is complete, each may go their own way; this signifies that the summer retreat has concluded, and there is no need to observe further formalities.

One night (this is according to the intention of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya. If following the *Xingshicao*, leaving the boundary is not permitted because it would constitute a breach of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and a separation from one's robes; since the night has not yet ended, one must wait until the fifteenth day when the night has concluded to be called "having completed the summer residence.
Only upon the appearance of the dawn light on the sixteenth day may one leave the boundary).
When living in a mixed residence— whether during the earlier or later retreat period— and being uncertain as to which [retreat] one should follow for the *pravāraṇā*,

the Buddha permitted that the *pravāraṇā* be performed according to where the senior monk (*sthavira*) is located. Whether the senior monk is in the earlier or the later [retreat], one should follow him.

Regarding those who have resided there for a long time: among those who have resided there for a long time, there may also be earlier and later arrivals. One should follow the majority and perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If within the assembly observing the rains retreat, there is one person who entered the retreat early, then on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the entire assembly should collectively receive the *pravāraṇā* from this one person.
Once the *pravāraṇā* is concluded, they remain seated until the fifteenth day of the eighth month."
If all [monks] observe the latter *anvāraka* (summer retreat), they should all perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

If a monk is observing the retreat in a village and hears that in the city there will be various offerings and the Dharma being preached throughout the night, and he wishes to go there, he may depart after performing the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day. This is not permitted by the Mahāsāṃghika school.

They observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in one location but perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) elsewhere; furthermore, they do not permit the acceptance of the *chanda* (consent) for the invitation ceremony, fearing that [the offender] might evade being charged with an offense,
and thus they alter the date and time.
The Vinaya states: "If the king changes the date, one should follow it. It further states: "It is permitted to perform the *pravāraṇā* on either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day.
It also states: "There are three types of *pravāraṇā*: on the fourteenth day, the fifteenth day, or the first day of the month. Regarding intercalary months:

if one observes the rains retreat (*varṣā*) according to the intercalary month, the *pravāraṇā* is performed on the fifteenth day of the seventh month; if one does not observe it [according to the intercalary month]...

Regarding the intercalary month: according to the *Mātṛkā*, the *pravāraṇā* is performed when ninety days have been completed. If there is an intercalary seventh month, those who performed the *pravāraṇā* during the preceding month do so then;
however, for those who did not perform the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in the preceding month, they perform the *pravāraṇā* once the ninety days are complete after the intercalary month has passed.
If the practice of the Path is peaceful and pleasant, one may extend the days of the *pravāraṇā* until the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
● *Jiào-zhào* (Vol. 38 of the Vinaya Piṭaka).
*Zhào* is pronounced with the second tone (*zhào*), meaning "to instruct" or "to admonish. It refers to teaching and guiding. The Vinaya states: "Young bhikṣus..."

Regarding the knowledge of the *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation), the Buddha said: "It should be instructed by the two masters (*upādhyāya* and *ācārya*). If they instruct [the candidate] but he is prone to forgetfulness and cannot remember, one who is to grant the *pravāraṇā* should provide the instruction.
If he still forgets, they should recite it together, phrase by phrase. The *Baiyi jiemmo* (Commentary on the Hundred-and-One Karmas) notes:
"If one is unable to recite the text from memory, copying it onto paper and reading it aloud also constitutes the fulfillment of the rite."
The sixty-two views refer to those held by various non-Buddhists who conceive of a self within the five aggregates (skandhas) of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Within each aggregate, they give rise to four types of views. For example, regarding the aggregate of form, to reckon that "form itself is the self" constitutes one view.
To hold that "the self is separate from form" constitutes two views. To hold that "form is large and the self is small, and the self dwells within form" constitutes three views.
To hold that "the self is large and form is small, and form dwells within the self" constitutes four views. The same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandhas*), totaling twenty views.
When categorized according to the three periods of past, present, and future, these become sixty views. These sixty views are caused by...
Taking the two views of eternalism and nihilism as their foundation, they collectively constitute the sixty-two views (the view that things exist is eternalism;
the view that they do not exist is nihilism, as extensively explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and other texts).

○ Regarding the Dharma of the Leather Section (Carma-vastu):

I have respectfully examined the teachings established by the Tathāgata; they deeply esteem benevolence and compassion. The Bodhisattva’s transformation and cultivation of beings result from the supreme exaltation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
If one commits slaughter without mercy, that is the craft of a rākṣasa; to harm living beings and abandon compassion is not the Way of the Śākya Sage. Great!
The Master, out of compassion for his assembly of disciples, observed that some lived in cold countries while others resided in harsh regions;

their constitutions were weak and prone to illness, and their physical frailty rendered them incapable of enduring hardship, thereby obstructing their cultivation of the Way and causing them to neglect their progress toward enlightenment.

For this reason, he provisionally permitted the acceptance of monastic requisites in accordance with local custom, provided they were necessarily required in those regions and used with care according to the regulations. However, if one resides in a temperate land, it is not appropriate to accumulate them at will.
This is not the fundamental intention of the Great Sage, nor does it accord with the essential practice of liberation. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

"If bhikṣus do not wear silks, cotton, or floss from the East, nor the boots, leather shoes, furs, or woolen garments of this land, nor consume milk, curd, or clarified butter—such bhikṣus are truly liberated from the world, have repaid their karmic debts from past lives, and shall no longer wander within the three realms. Why is this so?
Therefore, wearing parts of their bodies constitutes a causal condition for them. It is like a person who eats the hundred grains from the earth; their feet never leave the ground.

If one were to ensure that, regarding all sentient beings, neither the body nor its parts—through either the physical or the mental path—are worn or consumed, I would say that such a person is truly liberated.
How much more so, then, regarding the leather currently in existence, which does not exceed [these categories]?

The Execution of Butchery: All those belonging to the class of woolly creatures cannot escape the blade and the cudgel. Yet, due to their foolishness and ignorance, they do not recognize the world beyond;
they covet wealth and greed for profit to sustain their present desires. Craving their sweet fat, people seek their furs and robes.
Some are flayed alive to take their skins; some are beaten to death to soften their wool; some have their throats slit with knives until they die; or...
Nails were driven through the crown of his head until the pain was absolute; his cries of grief shook the earth and the sound of his resentment reached the heavens.
When a person of benevolence beholds this, can they not feel sorrow in their heart? When the ignorant see it, they only add to their joy and exhilaration.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva shed tears; how could the sons of Śākya not be pained at heart? Who could desire to divide his body and create enmity with him, harboring resentment throughout kalpas?
Repaying one another in turn, they await their retribution without ceasing; the bitter fruits of their actions are difficult to fully comprehend.
Contemplate this matter with care—it is truly painful and most lamentable.
Śrona (alternatively written as Shulunna). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Śrona Koṭīviṃśa," or "One Who Heard Two Hundred Crores.
This refers to a householder of great wealth who, having finally obtained an heir late in life, would immediately bestow gold upon anyone who reported the news.
Two hundred *koṭis* of coins; for this reason, his son was named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa. Regarding the matter of the schism in the Saṃgha, it says:
In the city of Campā, there was an elder named Ratnākara, who, after many months and years, gave birth to another son whose physical appearance was upright and dignified.
Rarely seen by others, the hair on his feet was four finger-widths long and the color of gold.
His kinsmen and assembly said, "Since he was born under a constellation with many stars, he should be named 'Star Girl' (Vasudattā)," and so forth. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin. At that time, Priyadarśanā..."
Within the city, the youths invited the Buddha to observe the three-month rains retreat, providing the four requisites as offerings.
For the Buddha and the assembly of monks, each person took their turn in preparing food for one day.

Among them was a youth from a poor family who consulted with his mother regarding how they might manage their turn to provide the offerings. His mother said, "You should take the very last turn to present your offering."
Before the appointed day arrived, he prepared everything to the best of his ability and made it sufficient. When the day arrived, he spread out a bear skin for the Tathāgata to step upon.
As the Tathāgata walked toward his seat, he prepared food and drink of five flavors to offer to the Tathāgata.
Prostrating with his five limbs touching the ground, he made this great vow: "In all places where I am born, may I always be born into a noble clan and a wealthy, aristocratic family."
His feet do not touch the ground, just like those of the Tathāgata; beneath his feet there is hair, four fingers long and golden in color.
His conduct and vows are like those of a Buddha, and he has vowed that when a Buddha appears in the world in the future, he shall offer worship.
The poor boy at that time was none other than the son of the Elder Ratnakaṇṭha. Due to the vow he made before that Buddha, the fruit of his karma has now matured.
He will possess great wealth and nobility. There will be hair on the soles of his feet, golden in color.
For ninety-one kalpas, he has never stepped upon the ground with his feet. On the day of his birth, twenty billion gold coins followed him, emerging daily from the earth (and so forth).
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Brave, diligent, and capable of enduring ascetic practices..."
This refers to the bhikṣu Viśākhāputra (also known as Śagata;

the correct pronunciation is Sugata, which means "Welcome," as explained in the section on the *Pātayantika* rules). Bhikṣu Sāketaka is also called Śagata; the correct term is Sugata, which translates as "Welcome," as explained in the *Pātayantika* chapter.
*Ān-yì*: *yì* is pronounced with the initial *y* and the final *-i*, rhyming with *yì*. It refers to an inn or lodging station for travelers. It also refers to a relay station;
this is what is known today as the "relay horse" system. It is said that one *yì* covers approximately thirty *li*, which is equivalent to one *yojana* in the Western regions.
The Śītavana is the Forest of Fear;
in its true Sanskrit pronunciation it is called Śītapavana, which refers to the Charnel Ground where corpses are abandoned.
This particular forest is situated beside five hundred hot springs.
There are three delights regarding the six sense bases:

first, the delight in renunciation (liberation from sensual desire); second, the delight in non-ill will (liberation from ill will); and third, the delight in tranquility (liberation through seclusion).

Fourth is the joy of the exhaustion of craving (liberation through the extinction of craving). Fifth is the joy of the exhaustion of the aggregates of grasping (liberation from all attachments). Sixth is the joy of non-delusion (liberation through the mind’s non-forgetfulness and mindfulness).
● Vinaya Piṭaka, Volume 39: The Country of Aparāntaka, also called Aśmaka.
Aśmaka means "horse" (aśva) in this language; in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, it is translated as...
Mābhūṅga (also transcribed as Āśmanta), which some say is the name of a river.

The *Xiyu ji* states that the kingdom of Avanda (within the borders of Western India) is two thousand four or five hundred *li* in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty *li* in circuit.
The soil is suitable for cultivation, with beans and wheat being particularly abundant; flowers and fruits are few, and the vegetation is sparse. The climate is windy and cold.
The people are fierce by nature and their speech is plain and simple; they do not value academic pursuits. Nevertheless, regarding the Triple Gem, they maintain a heart of pure faith.
Not far to the northeast of the city, within a great bamboo grove, lies the ruins of a monastery.

This is where the Tathāgata, in the past, permitted the bhikṣus to wear *kheṭavastrapādukā*—the Chinese term for which is "boots" (though these were leather sandals that covered the entire foot, not true boots).
Next, more than eight hundred paces to the south, there is a stūpa in the forest.

In the past, when the Tathāgata stayed here during a cold night, he covered himself with his three robes layered upon one another until dawn. The next morning, he instructed the bhikṣus to wear double-layered *naḷakānta* (軬, *fan*; *buǎn*, third tone; *tuó*, same as *dú*; pronounced *dú*).

Since the terrain in the region of Western India is mostly rugged and stony, and the western border further adjoins foreign lands, the ground is even harder, consisting of gravel and clods of earth where even cow tracks form a jangling sound. For this reason, he permitted the wearing of double-soled sandals.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that Mount Kukkutapāda (Mount Cock) is also called Mount Pārūṣaka, or the village of the Kukkuṭārāma Vihāra (*kukkuṭārāma* meaning "monkey").
The *Āgama* states that in the country of Aparāntaka, on the banks of the river Aśmaka, there was a settlement named "Monkey."
The Monkey’s Cave: In a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) near that village, there was a mountain cave where the Venerable Kaccāyana resided (Kaccāyana is explained as in the *Pācittiya* section).
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was also known as Śramaṇa Koṭīviṃśa. At that time, there was a very wealthy householder who had a son born to him with golden rings on his ears.
The householder’s heart leaped with joy, and wishing to give him a name, he gathered together various brahmins and householders who were skilled in...
One who knew the characteristics of gold and jewels showed him the child’s ear. The people said, "This child was born on the day of the śramaṇa;
he shall therefore be named Śramaṇa. His earrings were not made by human hands, and their value could not easily be appraised. He intended to estimate it by his own thought.
It was worth one hundred million in pure gold. The boy’s name was Śramaṇa; his earrings were also worth one hundred million.
The people immediately named this boy Śramaṇa Koṭīkarṇa (as recorded in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*). The Buddha said, "Among my disciples, he is the most swift in understanding and realization."
*Arbuda-prathama* (At that time, people often gave two hundred *arbudas*; *Arbuda* was confused with this).
*Elāyanta-mora-mora* (also written as *Eṇeyanta*).
These are all foreign types of bedding, equivalent to the *tong* (a kind of coarse woolen cloth) of this region.
It is made by lining it with leather; there is nothing similar to this in this region, therefore it cannot be translated [into Chinese]. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Covered with a hemp mat, covered with a wool mat, or covered with a flower-patterned robe."

The *Ṣoḍaśārthapada* (Sixteen Meanings) is called the *Ṣoḍaśārthavarga-sūtra* in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* calls it the *Aṣṭabhadrika-sūtra* (*bhadrika* here meaning "chapter").
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* calls it the *Pārāyaṇa-satyadharasūtra*. The *Abhidharma* calls it the *Sukhagrahaṇodāna*.
This is the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "other regions" (*anyadeśa*), it refers to the distinguishing of the frontiers of the four directions. In the east is the country of Pāṭaliputra (where *tiáo* may also be written as *tiáo*).

Outside the capital city and its districts lies this borderland (the *Śāriputra-vinaya* states it is the village of Śvetaka in the south, which is incorrect). To the south is the Caitya of Peaceful Virtue;
outside this caitya lies the borderland (the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states it is the Rāhubhadra-caitya in the east, which is incorrect). To the west is Mount Ṛṣipatana.

"Beyond the [four] quarters" refers to frontier countries (one master says *li*, which here means "mountain of immortals"; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says they dwell in Brahmin villages; *brāhmaṇa* is also translated as "immortal"). To the north is Zhuguo (Pillar Country).
"Beyond the [four] quarters" refers to frontier countries (the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says Mount Uśīra; not far from the mountain is the Puquan-saluo tree; beyond the tree is a frontier country).
In such frontier regions, it is permitted for a group of five who uphold the Vinaya to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*). The verse in the *Vinayasamgraha* says: "To the east, reaching Ben..."
The *Khadira* Forest; to the west, the two villages of *Tu-nu*; to the south, the river *Vatī*; and to the north, Mount *Uśīra*.

The regions outside these boundaries are called the "border countries" (*pratyantima-deśa*), while those within are called the "central region" (*madhyadeśa*). The *Mūla-karman* states: "In the east, there is a country..."
It is named Puṇḍravardhana. Not far to the east of the city, there is a śāla tree named Puṇḍraka; this refers to the eastern boundary.
From this point onward, it is called a border country (pratyantima-deśa). [Puṇḍravardhana is within the territory of Central India; it is a country on the eastern frontier.]

From here, proceeding eastward and crossing a great river, one arrives at the kingdom of Kāmarūpa in Eastern India. If one travels northeast, one reaches the Man-liao (the borderlands) which adjoin the frontiers of Shu. To the south, there is a city.
The name is Śrāvastī. To the south of the city there is a river named after the city itself;
this is called the southern boundary. From here onwards, it is called the borderland. To the west there is a village named Sthūṇopaka;
Sthūṇa and Upaka are two villages, both of which are inhabited by Brahmins. This is called the western boundary. From here onwards, it is called the...
Regarding the border countries: to the north there is a mountain named Uśīra (translated here as "the root of *máoxiāng*").

This is called the northern border; from this point onward, they are termed border countries. The commentary states: "In general terms, the distance between the intermediate regions and the two boundaries—east and west—is over three hundred stations (*yì*);
the two sides, north and south, are over four hundred stations. Although this was not witnessed firsthand, it has been examined in detail.
I questioned him about this. He replied that it was approximately forty stations south of the eastern border, reaching the country of Damalipti (within the territory of East India;

the kingdom borders the edge of the sea). From there, it is about sixty stations to Mahābodhi and Nālandā Monastery (both monasteries are located in Central India, as explained in detail in the *Vibhaṅga* on dwellings regarding the multi-storied pavilions).
This is the place from which one boards a ship to enter the sea and return to Tang China.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"In all frontier regions where there are few bhikṣus, it is permitted for five persons who maintain the Vinaya to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"It is permitted in frontier countries for those who maintain the Vinaya to be the fifth [member] when receiving the full ordination. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "In frontier..."
In a frontier region, one who understands the *Vinaya* serves as the fifth person and is permitted to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). The *Fuxingji* (Record of the Aids to Practice) states:
"Based on the *Karmavastu* chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, it cites the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* to establish ten ways of receiving [ordination].

Regarding the eighth way of receiving: the fifth person is a master of the *Vinaya*. This is because in frontier regions the population is sparse; among the five persons required for the reception, one must be a master of the *Vinaya* capable of performing the *karmavācanā*. This refers to...
The *Karmācārya* (the officiating master) serves as the fifth. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states:

"In general, one who acts as the *Upādhyāya* (Preceptor) must necessarily be established in the monastic rank and have completed ten years of residence (*daśavarṣa*). As for the *Karmācārya*, the one who provides instruction in private, and the other witnesses, there is no fixed requirement regarding their age;

however, they must understand the Vinaya and be pure. Regarding the required number [of witnesses], it is necessary that they be complete. (Although this land of China is not the 'Middle Land,' if there are...)"

A quorum of ten persons must be fulfilled; one may not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) with fewer than five. If ten persons are unavailable, five may confer it without fault, provided they are clear in the Vinaya and pure. The *Shangtong Fashi Zhuan* states:
"At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han, when the monks Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna arrived here, there were only two of them.

Because they could not obtain full ordination, they merely shaved the heads of monastics and laypeople, and these individuals wore the *mañca-śāṭī* (a single-layered robe), receiving only the five precepts and the ten precepts."
It is so. We humbly reflect that since the Tathāgata appeared in the world, it was eight years before the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) was first instituted.

China lies twenty-seven thousand *li* to the east of the White Wooden Strip (*śukla-dāru*). There, five persons who had mastered the Vinaya were authorized to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

From that time until the tenth Han Emperor, Huan Di, within a period of over one hundred years, the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Precepts were successively transmitted to one another.
After the time of Emperor Huan, five monks from the Western Regions arrived in the land of Han from the kingdom of Northern India.
They conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon the great monks. The first was named Zhī Fǎlǐng; the second, Zhī Qián; the third, Zhú Fǎhù;
the fourth, Zhú Dàoshēng; and the fifth, Zhī Lóuchèn. At that time, the Great Vinaya had not yet been translated. Zhī Fǎ...
[He] received [the texts]. He orally recited and produced one fascicle of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and one fascicle of the *Karmavācanā*, which circulated here.
What is known today as the "Old Karmavācanā" is this. Later, in the third year of the Huangchu era of the Wei dynasty, Dharmakāla (Dharmakāla means "Time of Dharma";

he was a native of Central India who was skilled in reciting the various Vinayas) again translated the Vinaya. Upon arriving in Luoyang, he established the ritual procedures for ordination based on the *Karmavācanā*, employing ten monks according to the rules, and thus widely propagated the Buddha-dharma. This is the Eastern... [text ends].
The summer retreat (*varṣā*) marks the beginning of the Vinaya discipline. Later, during the reign of Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei, there was the Vinaya Master Guang.

He examined the old *Karmavācanā* and the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*, finding that the texts contained additions and subtractions, and were incomplete in both length and detail. Relying on the great Vinaya root-texts, he compiled them in their proper sequence;
this became widely circulated in the world and is known as the "New Karmavācanā. At that time, the community of nuns came to request ordination, and Zhifa Ling...
It is said: As clarified in the Vinaya, the full ordination was conferred upon a group of five monks from the borderlands, without taking into account the community of nuns.
At that time, the nuns withdrew and returned home, weeping like rain and unable to restrain themselves.
Later, toward the end of the Han dynasty and the beginning of the Wei dynasty, two nuns from the kingdom of East India arrived in Chang’an and, seeing the assembly of nuns there, questioned them.
He asked, "From whom did you receive the precepts? The nuns replied, "We went to the Great Assembly (bhikṣusaṃgha) and received only the five precepts and the ten precepts.
The two nuns lamented, "The nuns in the borderlands have not yet attained full ordination; we shall return to our own country."
Fifteen people were converted and came [to China]. Three died of cold in the Snowy Mountains; two fell into a black ravine and perished.
Only the remainder reached this land, and there were ten people here. All the nuns went to the capital to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Later, they arrived in the region of Wu and completed the bestowal of full ordination upon the local nuns there as well. Then, the Western nuns began to long for their homeland.
Huixiang then boarded a ship for the South Sea and returned. Upon arriving at the vessel, there were only seven people remaining; three had passed away during the journey.

Having traveled back and forth for more than ten years, in the third year of Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty, an imperial decree was issued to convene an Unrestricted Great Assembly (*amogha-mahā-pariṣad*).
The Wei Emperor issued an inquiry regarding the origins of the precepts received by the monks and nuns of this land, and whether they possessed any spiritual efficacy.

When he questioned the various virtuous elders, none of them replied. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who requested to travel to the Western Regions to inquire of the sages regarding the origins of the precepts.
Setting out from Chang’an, he arrived in India and encountered an arhat, to whom he addressed his inquiry:
"Do the monks and nuns of China receive the precepts? The arhat replied, "I am but a minor sage; I do not [know this]."

"Know that it is so; you shall remain here. I shall ascend to Tuṣita for your sake to inquire of the World-Honored One Maitreya whether [the precepts] can be obtained or not, and then return to report.
He then entered meditative concentration and proceeded toward Tuṣita Heaven, where he inquired in detail about the aforementioned matter.
Maitreya replied, "Both monks and nuns have already completed receiving the precepts. He then requested a miraculous sign, and Maitreya immediately took a golden flower.
He said: "If the monks and nuns of the borderlands can receive the precepts, may these golden flowers enter the palms of the Arhats; if they cannot, let them not enter.
Having finished making this vow, he pressed the flowers against his hand. The flowers entered his palm, appearing with a height of one chi.
Maitreya said, "When you arrive at the place of the bhikṣu in China, you should follow this same method as I have done here.
The arhat descended and, following Maitreya’s instructions, pressed a flower onto the bhikṣu’s hand; it immediately entered his palm, appearing one foot high.
As these auspicious signs were manifested, people from distant regions—both monastics and laypeople—then came to pay their respects and seek [instruction].
Having received the three refuges and the five precepts, and so on up to innumerable [precepts], he was immediately named the Bhikṣu Huashou (Flower-Hand).
As he was about to depart, there were eighteen people; the rest remained in the Western Regions out of longing for it, while some ventured across the shifting sands, perishing from wind and cold.
Only the Bhikṣu Huashou returned alone to the land of Han. On the day he originally departed, at Kapilavastu...
The deity Luo manifested his form and said to Huashou: "The road is long and distant, fraught with many dangers and difficulties.
As your disciple, I shall escort you there, and you will return in safety and peace. Before he had yet arrived, a golden flower appeared in the air before Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty’s palace.
The Emperor asked the Grand Astrologer, "What strange omen is this? He replied, "It is the True Dharma from the Western Regions."
He intended to come here, yet less than a month had passed when the Bhikṣu Puṣpahasta saw golden flowers in his palm arrive in this land.

On the very day they first arrived, the golden flowers in the sky immediately vanished and were no longer seen. Since such a great omen has been manifested, the precepts and merit shall be transmitted forever.

(Regarding those in the "stationed" rank: this refers to those who, having received full ordination, have completed ten years of residence. When the ten-day period is complete, it is said that if a bhikṣu goes to another region and hears that robes have been obtained at that dwelling place, he then refuses to accept them, fearing he might commit an offense.

This constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Therefore, the Buddha permitted those bhikṣus that once clothing has come into their hands, if ten days are completed, they must relinquish it if the period exceeds that limit.
Having relinquished it, they must perform confession. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "There was a bhikṣu who entrusted clothing to a bhikṣu in another region.
Before the clothing had arrived, another bhikṣu spoke to the bhikṣu to whom it was sent. That bhikṣu became suspicious, fearing he might commit an offense of *aticāra* (excess)."

Regarding robes: the Buddha said that although a bhikṣu may have previously heard of or known of a robe, as long as it has not yet entered his hands, he does not commit the offense of possessing an extra robe (*dīrgha-cīvara*).

Unknown. ○ Regarding the *Cīvara-vastu* (The Section on Robes):
The protocols for robes and garments are the essential pivot of the renunciant life. Their use must strictly follow the regulations; one must wear them without being bound by attachment.

This would cause a deviation from the proper form. Liberation begins from this [observance], and transgression likewise originates from this. Whether one upholds or violates [the precepts] is clearly evident;
the Vinaya provides established rules. You should naturally examine and investigate these for yourself; do not allow yourself to fall into doubt or error.
Regarding the color of the *kāṣāya*, according to the Vinaya there are ten types of robes, all of which must be dyed the color of a *kāṣāya* before being worn.
Therefore, in foreign lands, all monastic robes are called *kāṣāya*. It is also referred to as *kālaśaya*, which means "improper color," or "discolored."
This refers to the color red. Master Jing said: "In Sanskrit it is called *kāṣāya*, which is translated as 'red.
To call it *kāṣāya* [in Chinese] is merely a colloquialism; it is actually the color of *gandha*. Originally, it has nothing to do with Eastern (Chinese) terminology.
Why laboriously append the character for 'clothing' (*yī*) at the end? According to the formal language of the Vinaya texts, all three robes are called *cīvara*, which accords with the Dharma."

The Master said: "The character for *yùn* (韻) is written as [the variant with the 'hair' radical] (i.e., *xiá*). The pronunciation is *jiāshā*. In Ge Hong’s *Ziyuán*, it was first changed to follow the 'clothing' radical (*qiánduó*, which refers to red tree bark).
As explained above, it is named 'clothing' (*yī*) because of its color. If expressed according to its meaning, its designations are not limited to one; thus, the *Zhéntí zájì* states:
'Kāṣāya is the name for the three robes of foreign lands, and the name contains many meanings. Or..."
It is called the "Dust-Free Robe" because it severs the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). It is also called the "Emaciated Robe" because it cuts through the afflictions (*kleśa*).
