This is said to have been brought by the Lord of Heaven (*devendra*). This fruit is used as medicine and possesses extremely manifold efficacy.

It is used in the Western Regions just as ginseng, *huishu* (*deshou*), and other such substances are used here [in China]; there is no ailment it cannot enter. The new [transliteration] is *harītakī*.
The *Mūla-karman* states: "Harītakī. The old translation, "hāliluó," is erroneous. The *Nanzhou ji* (Record of the Southern Regions) states:
"Harītakī is precisely the six-edged [fruit]. The *Bencao* (Classic of Materia Medica) states: "Its common name is 'hazǐ' (myrobalan);

it is also called 'suífēngzǐ' (wind-fallen fruit), because those that are not yet ripe are blown down by the wind and thus named. It grows in various countries of the South Sea as well as in Jiaozhi and Aizhou. Now...
It is found in Lingnan, where it is most abundant in Guangzhou. Its trunk resembles that of a *dàoguǐ* (a type of oak). The flowers are white;

the fruit resembles a *gǎnlǎn* (olibanum), but has ridges and furrows, and is greenish-yellow in color. The rind and flesh adhere to one another. It is harvested when ripe in the seventh and eighth months; those with six ridges are considered superior.
Originally, there were forty or fifty trees in front of the hall of Faxing Monastery in Guangzhou, which were brought there by an Indian monk.
I have come to plant it. There are still six or seven old trees remaining; their fruit is fine-textured and its flavor is not astringent. Each has six ridges.
The temple has an ancient well, and the roots of these trees dip into the water, causing the water’s taste to be free of salt. Whenever the fruit ripens, they brew a decoction to entertain guests.
The method is as follows: take five freshly picked *harītakī* fruits and one inch of licorice root, both crushed, and draw water from the wooden well.
It is boiled together with well water from the lower level; its color is like that of freshly brewed tea. This decoction is highly esteemed according to the local customs of the South Sea.

However, its preparation need not strictly follow the methods of former times (the well still exists today, though the trees are gone; it is found only at Baoxiang Forest in Nanhai and at the newly established site in Panyu).
*Harītakī* has a bitter and pungent taste and a warm qi. Its bitterness is predominant while its acidity is slight; its nature is swift, and it favors descending to subdue yin.
It digests residual food, removes abdominal distension, promotes the circulation of fluids, breaks up congealed qi, and stops chronic diarrhea.

It further expels intestinal wind, opens the appetite, astringes the intestines, drives out phlegm, and stops hiccups. Furthermore, because its flavor is sour and bitter, it possesses the power to gather and contract and to subdue fire;
thus, it can treat injuries to the lung-metal, extreme stagnation, suppression, distension and fullness, and labored breathing with coughing and wheezing.
This is the "Restoration" [formula]. Tripitaka Master Yijing states: There are three equal parts of pills that can cure various ailments and are not difficult to obtain.
Take the skin and flesh of *harītakī*, dried ginger, and granulated sugar; take these three ingredients in equal portions. Pound the first two until they are finely crushed.

Take a small amount of water and dissolve it with granulated sugar; then, pound them together into pills. Take about ten pills at dawn, taking as many as you can comfortably swallow. There are no dietary restrictions.
For those suffering from dysentery, they will recover after no more than two or three doses.
It can break up abdominal distension, eliminate wind, and digest food; because its benefits are so extensive, this is mentioned here. If granulated sugar is unavailable, [use honey instead].
Sugar and honey may also be used. Furthermore, regarding *harītakī*: if one can chew one fruit daily and swallow the juice, one will remain free from illness for the rest of one’s life.

(Now, *harītakī* is extremely precious in the Western Regions; the Buddha permitted it as a lifelong medicine. Its efficacy is vast, it simplifies medical practice, and it is not difficult to obtain. Thus, those who have left the household life should employ it; this is why it is singled out here.

According to the *Bencao*, if one treats all wind-disorders, phlegm, cholera, indigestion, or constipation, one should crush three fruits to extract the pulp and skin, mixing them with wine and drinking it all at once. If wind-heat rises up toward the neck...)

For heat-induced distress: take two pieces of *dahuang* (rhubarb) and *mangxiao* (barium sulfate), stir them together in vinegar until they dissolve, and apply the mixture by rubbing it onto the affected area. If the pain has persisted for a long time, one should take one piece in the mouth and swallow the liquid. After recovery, the mouth may feel dull and one may lose the sense of taste for food.

Immediately boil areca nut (*pūga-phala*) in water and drink it. If one suffers from nausea and inability to eat, take two *liang* of the nut, remove the seeds, and pound them into a powder. Mix with refined honey to form pills the size of *wuzi* (walnut) seeds; take twenty pills on an empty stomach.

If one constantly suffers from qi disorders, wrap three nuts in moist paper and bake them until the paper is dry; then peel off the paper, remove the seeds, and chew them finely, swallowing them down with one *sheng* of fresh milk. Furthermore, for all types of qi disorders and indigestion of residual food, place one nut in the mouth at night and chew and swallow it by morning.

If suffering from dysentery with watery stools: take three fruits, wrap them in flour, and roast them until they turn red. Remove the flour and the seeds, then pound them into a powder. Mix with cooked rice to form pills; take twenty-one pills with rice-water. If suffering from dysentery with flatulence: take ten fruits, wrap them in flour, and bake them over hot embers until the flour turns yellow and the fruit is cooked.

Remove the seeds and grind them finely into a powder. Mix with congee-water and consume in a single dose. If suffering from watery diarrhea: take two high-quality fruits; roast one and remove its skin, while taking the skin from the other raw. Combine these into a powder and add powdered licorice.

One *qián* [of the powder] contains a small amount of pus and blood; add two *qián* if there is much blood; add three *qián* if it is even more. Take one or two *hé* [of the mixture] with boiling rice-water, though plain water is also acceptable. Those [seeds] blown by the wind and fallen to the ground should be gathered once they have dried; these are especially precious.

The smaller ones are even better. They treat phlegm and throat disorders; holding several pieces in the mouth is particularly effective. The *Nanzhou ji* states that they primarily treat the five types of qi-stagnation in the chest, empty pain in the heart and abdomen, various types of dysentery (red or white), as well as vomiting and coughing.

In all these cases, one should use the bark. To treat wind-induced redness and irritation of the eyes, grind the seeds with white honey and apply it to the eyes. Taibai says: "In general usage, do not use *vīraka*, *āmalaka*, *laṅga-lekha*, or *jāluka*. If using *harītakī*, [use the variety known as] *vṛddhi*."

There are six types of *harītakī* (myrobalan), varying in size from large to small; these are all varieties of the *harītakī*. Each type of *harītakī* is round and has its surface exposed. There are also eight types, up to thirteen types, which are called *laṅjing-le*; these are mostly astringent and not suitable for medicinal use.

Generally, when preparing them for medicinal purposes, first soak them in wine, then steam them for one *fú* (a period of time). As for the *harītakī*, pare away the ridges with a knife, mince it finely, and dry it over a fire before using it.
The Dharma Master Vihelikṣṇa stated: "Vikṛtaka" (the old transcription *bi-yi-le* is an error). The *Sudarsana-vinaya* says:

"Its shape resembles that of a peach; its taste is sweet. When consumed, it can cure *sīta* (*sīta* is pronounced *sou*; it refers to coughing and wheezing). According to the efficacy of this fruit..."
The harītakī is largely the same [as the āmalaka], but it is most excellent for subduing gas. Its shape is roughly circular and lacks distinct edges or ridges.
Ālīla is a corruption of āmalaka; some call it *āmalaka*, as explained in the Cīvaravastu (Section on Robes). [End of] Miscellaneous [Notes].
The text states: There are five kinds of fruits: first, the *āmalaka* (Sanskrit: *āmalaka*; formerly called *āmla*, which is an error); second, the *harītakī*; third, the *vibhītaka*;
fourth, the *pippalī* (also called *bipali*; formerly called *bipa*); and fifth, black pepper (Sanskrit: *marica*).
These five medicinal substances may be eaten at will—whether one is ill or healthy, and whether it is the proper time or not—provided that one does not [neglect the rules].
*Vicikitsā* (the "a" sound is pronounced as *u*). *Vaira* is simply *vairi*.
It is explained in the section on homonyms (*pǔbiān*). *Ra* is an abbreviated term; in its full form, it is *phala*.
This refers to the fruit.

According to the *Sudarsana*, *citraka* is the name of a foreign medicine (note: the pronunciation of *citraka* translates here as "various" or "diverse," and also as "miscellaneous"; if one says *pāricitraka*).

*La*. This is translated as "the round-growing tree" (*yuánshēng shù*). The new [translation] calls it *śirīṣa*, which means "the tree that closes at dusk. It is also used for medicinal purposes in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Vinayaviniscaya-upāli-paripṛcchā*.
The *Kāśyapīya-vinaya* states:
"In this context, 'kāśa' refers to roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits. The *Mūla-karman* states: [the same].
All medicinal herbs and substances do not exceed these; thus concludes the comprehensive categorization of all medicinal classes. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There are five kinds of decoctions: root-decoctions, stem-decoctions, leaf-decoctions, flower-decoctions, and fruit-decoctions.
It is permitted to keep them in the same room for the duration of one's life."
The *Śāliśabdavyākaraṇa* states:
"Regarding *śāliśabda*, it refers to roots, stems, flowers, leaves, and fruits, as well as anything that is hard and firm. (Note: *rèn* [而震切] is pronounced *rèn*).
"Yinren" (音刃). [It is] hard and supple, difficult to sever.
*Śikṣānanda*’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Nichi" (膩渠) is a foreign medicine that can cure poisons; it does not exist in the land of Han."
*Ditā* is also called *dìtǔ*.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "That which is *nàtā* is a foreign medicine; it is not understood."
*Pippalī* is also written as *pippat* or *pippat-li*. The *Śata-bhikṣu-karman* states: "Pippalī is the same as *kō-zō* (vinegar made from *kō*).

Formerly it was called *pippal*, which is an abbreviation. (According to our current examination, *pippal* and *kō-zō* are entirely different. *Kō-zō* is a climbing vine, whereas *pippal* grows in clusters like *fū* grass. It originally came from foreign lands; now...)

It is found in Lingnan. It mostly grows within bamboo groves. In the first month, it sprouts and forms a clump, reaching about two feet in height. Its leaves are round-edged and more than two inches wide. In the fifth month, it flowers; the white color is on the surface.

In the seventh month, it bears fruit, as long as a small finger and shorter in shape than *chēqián* (plantago) seeds. It is harvested at the end of autumn. Those that are dark black are unsuitable; those that are purple-brown are the best. Its flavor is pungent and sharp, exceeding that of *jùjiàng* (sichuan pepper).

The root is called *bìzhóu mò*. Southerners cherish its pungent fragrance; some take the leaves raw and eat them. The commentary to the *Shǔdū fù* states: "The *jùjiàng* vine grows upon trees; its fruit is like a mulberry, green when ripe, and two or three inches long. The leaves resemble those of a cucumber but are thick and large. The fruit...

The bark is black and the flesh is white; when eaten, it is aromatic and pungent. Its sprouts are called *fúlíu* vines. The *Bencao* (Classic of Materia Medica) states: "Piper chaba (*bìbà*) digests stale food, descends qi, removes cold from the stomach, warms the interior, and treats *xiānpié* (abdominal tumors), scrotal hernia pain, choleraic disorders, and cold-gas pains—all of which it expels instantly.

It can eliminate foul odors and serves as an excellent seasoning for food. Long-term consumption may cause diarrhea and a sense of heaviness in the lower abdomen. *Jùjiàng* (vinegar made from *jù* vines) primarily descends qi and warms the interior; it treats cold-gas in the heart and abdomen, disperses knotted qi, and breaks up phlegm accumulations—it is a marvelous remedy.
(*Bìbà* is pronounced *bō*; *jù* is pronounced *jǔ*).
Hutong (Gymnocladus sinensis) is also known as Mulü and as Yutonglü. It grows in the plains, marshes, and mountain valleys west of Gansu Province.

The tree is tall and large; its bark and leaves resemble those of the white poplar, green paulownia, mulberry, and similar species, which is why it is named Hutong. Its wood is suitable for... [text truncated]

Utensils and implements: when their fluids seep into the earth and become congealed, sometimes mixed with decayed wood and appearing like yellow alum, they are called *hutong lei* (hutor tears) and are used in medicinal preparations.
The mare-ear tree (*mǎ'ěr shù*) is also called the donkey-ear tree; it is the *jījiǎ* (persimmon) tree. The wood is over ten feet high, and its leaves are shaped like donkey ears and are all hairy.
They do not wither throughout the four seasons. In mid-winter it blooms with white flowers, and from the third to the fourth month it bears fruit. Its taste is—
Sweet and sour. A small amount stops vomiting and quenches thirst; taken in excess, it causes fever and pain.

When the leaves are dried and their hairs removed, they regulate the lung organs, descend qi, eliminate persistent hiccups and retching, and treat incessant heat-induced dyspepsia. The white inner bark of the wood treats nausea and inability to eat.
(Both the leaves and the bark are used to treat illnesses by being boiled into a decoction for consumption.)

The *Śamala-ghūta-grāma-vināśana-śīla-vyākhyāna* (Explanation of the Precept on Destroying the Village of Ghosts with Śamala), from the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*. The Buddha said: "These are for treating wind disorders.
One should boil roots, stalks, flowers, fruits, bark, wood, and so forth together into a decoction, and wash the body with it to eliminate ailments. The bhikṣus [then used] the decoction...
When washing, his skin was colorless. The Buddha said, "Anoint it with oil. He then applied it excessively, so that the grease stained his robes.
The Buddha said, "Rub it with *śāṭī* (soap powder). Still, there was no color.

The Buddha said, "When you are about to finish washing, place one or two drops of oil into the bathwater to make the body lustrous. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "If one suffers from scabies..."

One should employ five types of astringent substances. Dry them in the shade, grind them into a powder, and boil them thoroughly with water. First rub the scabies sores with the powder, and afterwards wash them with the decoction. The five are:
(1) *āmra* (mango), (2) *kavaka* (a type of mushroom), (3) *jambū* (formerly called Yānfú; rose-apple), (4) *śirīṣa* (translated here as héhuīn;
acacia), and (5) *khadira* (translated here as gāokǔbójiā). These are all names of trees; as they do not exist in the land of China (Dōngxià), they cannot be translated.
"Bōjī shāshā" (簸箕簁簁).

This is precisely the word for *bì* (篦), with the phonetic component "shān" (山) and the radical "qiè" (皆), pronounced *shāi* (篩). This is a low-grade bamboo utensil used to remove coarse particles and retain fine ones.
It is written as *shāi* (簁) in the *lìshū* (隸書) script; the common form *shāi* (篩) is incorrect.
*Jingxiang* (零香):
In Sanskrit, it is called *tagara*; here it is translated as *lingzhang xiang* (零陵香). The *Bencao* (Classic of Materia Medica) states that its alternative name is *xuncao* (薰草).
Its primary functions are to clarify the vision, arrest phlegm, treat seminal emission, remove foul odors, and cure blood disorders and abdominal distension.

If "ku" (瘑) is also written as "gua" (痲), it shares the same pronunciation as "gu" (古) and "he" (禾), being pronounced "go. It refers to a carbuncle or ulcer. Those that break out in spring are called "swallow ulcers" (燕瘑);
those that break out in autumn are called "wild goose ulcers" (雁瘑).
Regarding salt, the Vinaya enumerates ten kinds: first, *ming-yen* (also called *qing-yen*; it is likely *rong-yen*); second, black salt (produced in Western India, in the kingdom of Sindhu).

3. *Sāmudra-lavaṇa* (in Sanskrit, *viḍalavaṇa*). 4. *Romaka-lavaṇa* (also called *rāmbha-lavaṇa*; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* calls it *lū-lavaṇa*, which is salt produced from salt flats; "mo" is pronounced as *ni*).

1. Pañcakaṭuka-lavaṇa (also called Cidupi-lavaṇa). 2. Lūṇa-lavaṇa (also named Tsalūṇa; the character 鹵 is pronounced *lǔ* [ru]. That which is produced by nature is called *lūṇa*; that made by humans is called *lavaṇa*.

This refers to digging salty soil from the seashore, leaching it with water, and boiling it until dry. It forms into clumps shaped like bricks; this is it). 3. Kṣāra-lavaṇa (unknown; there is a method of taking straw from salt-water fields, burning it to ash, leaching it with water, and then boiling it to produce salt).
4. Siṃhapa-lavaṇa (or Sindhapa; this means "rock salt. Master Jing says: "Siṃhapa salt" is named after a river. Formerly it was called *Xīn*...).

1. *Tuḥ* (頭): This is the name of a river in Western India. In this region (*cīfāng*), stone salt is produced from within the rocks of the mountains of Jiazhou; it is formed naturally without the need for boiling or refining. 2. *Śilūvi-lavaṇa* (施盧鞞鹽): This means "red salt.

It comes from the country of Sindhu in Western India, near the Indus River (*Xintou He*). This country has only a single peak, from which much red salt is produced; its color is like that of red stone. It also produces white salt, black salt, and white stone salt, all of which are taken from distant foreign lands and used as medicine.

3. *Sāmudra-lavaṇa* (海鹽): Master Jing said, "*Samudraka* (三沒達攞) is sea salt. Regarding the origins of all salts, they may come from the sea, from ponds, or from wells; the water is drawn up and boiled [to produce them].

It is established. Regarding those where mountain rocks emerge spontaneously, Tao’s commentary states: "There are nine kinds of salt among the barbarians: white salt, rock salt (the kind commonly consumed), black salt, soft salt, red salt, variegated salt, stinking salt, and horse-tooth salt."

Regarding the medicinal ash, the Vinaya states: "As for 'ash medicine,' *sāja* ash (also called *sāccha*; this is the name of a grass in the Western Regions; the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says that if *sāja* grass is ground and placed in milk, it immediately turns into curd;
according to the pronunciation of *sāja*, this translates as 'curable' or 'treatable')"; *piṇḍa* ash; and *parama* ash (these are all names of trees). *Vinayasamgraha*.
It is said: there are five types of ash decoctions. First, the ash of *māṣa* beans; second, the ash of *māṣa* awns;
third, the ash of sesame roots; fourth, the ash of *gojihvā* grass; fifth, various other miscellaneous ashes. These various ashes are to be soaked in water and boiled.

One may take it as desired. If there is a medical condition and a physician instructs one to take an unusual medicine, one should also take it for the purpose of neutralizing various poisons. A person of faith should procure it; this comes in four types:
first, the dung and urine of a newborn calf; second, the ash of the khadira tree, or the ash of the bodhi tree, or the udumbara tree.
1. Ashes of *aśvattha* (or *udumbara*, as explained above); 2. Ashes of licorice; 3. Earth taken from four finger-breadths beneath the surface;
4. These four ingredients are mixed and pounded together. One may either apply them externally or ingest them.

Regarding *jāba* medicine (which should be *jāva* medicine; as this is not found in this region, it was not translated. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Jāva medicine" is the name for a foreign medicine). The Vinaya says: *jāba* means "fragrant ox."
Xing’e (Cinnamomum tamala). Bodhiśīrṣāriṣṭa-puṭa. Tiyabodhi (alternatively written as Tiye-bodhi). Sājjarasa (alternatively called Sazheluo;
this is translated as "white resin"). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are five kinds of tree-resin medicines:
asafoetida resin, sājjarasa resin, tiya resin (ti is also written as di), tiyabodhi resin, and yavana resin."
(Also written as *dīpana*). It is permitted to stay in the same room for as long as one’s life lasts. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: there are five kinds of adhesive medicines:
first, asafoetida; second, molasses; third, lac; fourth, beeswax; and fifth, various other tree resins.
Regarding eye medicine, the Vinaya states: "Eye medicine" refers to *tāpasañjana* (the *Sudarsana-vinaya* says that *tāpasañjana* grows on land; it is also said that *tāpasa* is incense medicine).
*Kirāṭaja* (The *Śanjiàn* [善見] commentary states: *Kirāṭaja*. *Kira* means red stone. It is also said that *kirāṭaja* means "born in water"). The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* (*Lǜshè*) states:
If one suffers from eye ailments and a physician instructs the use of the five *añjanas* as an ointment for the eyes, there is no offense (provided it is merely an eye medicine).
All are termed *añjana*. First, *puṣpāñjana*; second, *rasāñjana*; third, *cūrṇāñjana*; fourth, *guḍāñjana*;
fifth, *sauvīrāñjana*. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "The Buddha taught the preparation of three kinds of eye medicine:
first, sheep gall; second, *kirātañjana*; third, *suvīrāñjana*. [These are ground] finely upon a stone.
Grind it and use it as an ointment for the eyes. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that Piṅgalavatsa suffered from eye pain;
his physician instructed him to prepare medicinal pills, place them over a fire, and inhale the smoke. Not knowing what substances to use for the medicine, the Buddha said:
"With the exception of *sāluka* (blue sandalwood) incense, combine all other fragrant substances, place them on the fire, and inhale the smoke through a tube."
(Anavatapta; formerly called Anacanna).
The Great Lake Anavatapta (explained as before) is situated within the Snowy Mountains. Not far from this lake, there is another lake named Mandākinī.
It is fifty yojanas in length and breadth. Its bottom is strewn with golden sand, and it is constantly filled with water of eight virtues, sweet as honey in taste.
Blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple lotuses of various colors cover its surface entirely.
Various kinds of birds warble their plaintive songs in harmony, making it exceedingly delightful. Around the four sides of the pond are various flowers and fruits.
Tree. It is beyond description.
Ilā-vani, also called Ilā-vaṇa, or Ārāvaṇa; this means "Son of the Earth. Formerly it was called...
*Airāvaṇa* is translated as "Fragrant Leaf. Master Yuan states: *Ai-ra* refers to *Airāvat*, which is a name for Śakra (Indra).
*Vaṇa* means "emitting sound. This indicates that this great elephant occasionally emits beautiful sounds to entertain Śakra.
Alternatively, it is said that *ai* means "to be able to emit," while *rāvaṇa* means "sound"; the entertainment is as described before.
It is said thus. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The elephant king Airāvaṇa has a body that is pure white, like the color of a white lotus.
His seven limbs are firmly planted on the ground, and he possesses six tusks.
His head is crimson, like the color of indragopaka insects (vermilion). On each of his left and right flanks, there are two and a half yojanas (two and a half *li*). [His] front..."
The hindquarters are each one *yojana* in length, and the circumference of the body is seven *yojanas*.
Its height and depth are both one and a half *yojanas*; this is its constant form, though its transformations are indefinite.

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven intend to go to the pleasure groves, by the power of their celestial merit, as soon as they raise their minds, they cause the Great Elephant King to manifest various colors to one another, and he then proceeds.

Having this thought—that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and his retinue now require him to mount him so they may enter the grove for recreation—he immediately vanished from this Jambudvīpa and appeared before the palace of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.

There he manifested his body, transforming it into thirty-two heads, each endowed with six tusks, the color of which was identical to that of his original head. Including the original head, there were thirty-three in total; on each tusk...
Above, he manifested seven ponds. In each pond, he manifested seven lotus flowers. Upon each flower, he manifested a courtyard made of the seven treasures.
Within each courtyard, he manifested a terrace made of the seven treasures. Within each terrace, he manifested a canopy made of the seven treasures.
Within each canopy, he manifested seven celestial maidens. Each celestial maiden manifested seven attendants. Each attendant...

He manifested seven celestial maidens who performed various musical entertainments. Having created these transformations, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with his retinue, ascended upon his original head;
the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, along with their retinues, ascended the thirty-two heads he had manifested;
and the families of devas from the ten thousand cities ascended his back. His body was so light that it rose up as if...
Like a whirlwind blowing lotus petals or drifting birch bark, they travel through the air to the pleasure groves where they sport.
At that time, the gods do not perceive one another’s presence or their relative positions; having arrived, they descend together and each proceeds to a pleasure forest to enjoy themselves in delight.
Then those nāga-elephants also transform their bodies into the forms of deva-princes and sport there.
Experiencing pleasure, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says: "Observe this great king of elephant-lords:
by what karmic conditions did he achieve such a massive body and great supernormal powers, and how did he gain great renown by fighting with the asuras?
By what karma did he receive the body of an animal? Behold this being; his lifespan among the gods was full seventy thousand years in the past."
In that age, there was a section of the Vedas called the *Brahmaṇa*. There was a brahmin who extensively cultivated merit and virtue and delighted in practicing charity.
Out of a virtuous heart, he always took pleasure in giving to those who were poor, blind, ignorant, and suffering.
To benefit sentient beings, there was at that time a king named Sudarśana.
On the day of a festival, he went out from the palace to sport, like the hosts of devas, accompanied by eighty-four thousand great white elephant kings.
They were covered with golden nets and adorned with precious bells; they were like the Tathāgata, adorned with all manner of golden bells. There were eighty-four thousand...

Surrounded by handmaidens and the sounds of eighty-four thousand musical instruments, King Sudarśana—possessing supreme majesty—experienced the fruit of great bliss as he proceeded toward the pleasure grounds and the palace in the grove. At that time, the brahmin...
Endowed with majestic power, he went to the pleasure grounds of King Sudarśana. This brahmin was named Samata.

Seeing that the great king was possessed of such majesty, [he observed] the king’s white elephant, named Meghasamgha, adorned with precious bells and necklaces of pearls and golden nets, all masterfully crafted by skilled artisans.
Adorned with white elephants and various songs and performances, he went to the pleasure grounds, being foremost in his physical beauty.
At that time, the Brahmin Samata thought to himself: "This king of white elephants enjoys supreme happiness;
I shall vow to be reborn as Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and become a king of white elephants. By the power of his generosity and the power of his vow, at the end of his life, he was reborn there.
Heaven [is the realm of] Śakra, the Lord of Devas. He manifests as the King of White Elephants (and so forth).

"Mǎjiù" (馬廐): the character should correctly be written as "jìu" (廄). It is pronounced *jiù*. It refers to a stable for horses. The *Shìmíng* (釋名) states: "It is a 'gathering' (*jù*), meaning [a place where] oxen... [are gathered].
This is where horses are gathered.
*Sūbī* (or *Xūbī*) is also written as *Sūbī*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The husband is named *Buk-bi*, and his wife is also named *Buk-bi*. There was...
The bhikṣu is also called Subhi. Because he recollects the same syllables, he constantly requests offerings. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "He constantly practices the samādhi of loving-kindness.
This refers to the upāsikā Mahā-Senā. Regarding the character *su-bi*, its translation is unknown.
Alternatively, *su-bi* may be a foreign term with a meaning identical to *senā*. *Senā* is the same as *Sena*, which in this [Chinese] language means:
Regarding the army, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: There was a husband and wife named Mahāsena who both had faith in the Triple Gem.

They constantly provided all necessary requisites to the Buddha and the Saṃgha at their disposal. At one time, a certain bhikṣu took a purgative medicine, but the purging was excessive, resulting in a depletion of his vital wind (*vāyu*).
A physician instructed him to consume meat broth. At that time, the householder’s wife sent a messenger to purchase meat. At that time, in that kingdom...

The king was named Brahmadatta. Upon the birth of his son, he rejoiced and issued a general decree throughout the city that for one day all killing must cease, so that [the meat] could not be obtained even by seeking it.
At that time, the householder’s wife thought of the sick man: "If he cannot obtain meat, he may lose his life. She then recalled the World-Honored One:
"In the past, while at the stage of a Bodhisattva, he repeatedly sacrificed his own body and flesh to save the lives of others. Now, I too should emulate him."
The Bodhisattva’s practice was as follows: he entered a quiet room, took a knife, cut his own thigh, and had a broth prepared to give to a sick bhikṣu.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was an upāsikā named Mahāśraddhā."
Having planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas of the past, there was once a bhikṣu who fell gravely ill.
The physician declared that he required a medicinal preparation of meat. Thereupon, the upāsikā took gold and traveled throughout the city.
She was unable to purchase meat, so she cut flesh from her own thigh and boiled it with various kinds of incense to make a broth.
After the bhikṣu consumed it, his illness was immediately cured. This upāsikā, suffering from the pain of her wound and unable to endure it, cried out:
"Namo Buddhāya! Namo Buddhāya! At that time, the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, and he heard her voice.
She gave rise to a heart of great compassion. The woman then saw the Buddha take medicine and apply it to her wound; it was restored to its original state.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said, "I did not actually go to the city of Vārāṇasī to apply medicine to that woman's bodily wound. You should know that all of this is my compassion."

By the power of their roots of goodness, those women were made to see such things [as this]. (Dharmodgata; "Dharma" here means "bestowal"; "udgata" is pronounced with the first tone on the syllable *pi*, meaning the thigh.)
"Birth-and-death bhikṣu" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained the fruits of the noble ones (*ārya-phala*). This is because they still abide within birth-and-death.
In the Sanskrit language, this is called *bāla-pṛthagjana*, which means "foolish worldling. It signifies one who is shrouded in the darkness of ignorance.
Although they possess wisdom, they merely give rise to the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) and do not produce the untainted (*anāsrava*) state. The old [commentators] say:

"They are born separately like small children," because their delusion is like that of small children and differs from the birth of the sages. Others say: "infant-like ordinary persons" (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), or "ordinary persons on the path of hair" (*vālaja-pṛthagjana*);
these terms indicate that their mental activities are unstable, like light feathers drifting east and west with the wind. Master Ying (應) says:
"Ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) is a term of meaning. To render it as "hair-path ordinary person" (*maodao pǎnfú*) or "hair-tip ordinary person" (*maotou pǎnfú*) is a long-standing error.
Students [should be aware of this].
These are persons who have attained the first fruit, the second fruit, or the third fruit; they still abide in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), training to sever all outflows (*āsrava*).
If one has attained the fourth fruit, they are called "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*); that is to say, having already transcended the stage of training, they abide in the supreme fruit of Arhatship.
From this point on, there is no further training required. Because all outflows have been exhausted, they are therefore called persons beyond training.
Yaśoda’s father is sometimes called Yaśu, sometimes Yaśas, and sometimes Sona; this is translated as "Precious Renown" (Ratnayaśas), which is the name of the son of a householder.
The *Madhyama-āgama* (Zhong benqi jing) states that the householder’s name was Aṅguli and his son’s style-name was Sona. This is the account of the causes and conditions.

In detail, regarding the *Pravrajyāvastu* (Section on Receiving the Precepts): [it says] "Yaśoda did not accept the invitation. This is because when the elder invited the Buddha, Yaśoda, and the attendant bhikṣus, he did not invite the entire Saṃgha, fearing that he might commit the offense of forming a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*).
*Xián* (涎): same as [盜-皿]. Pronounced *qián* (徐沿切). It refers to the liquid in the mouth. *Mò* (沫): pronounced *mò* (莫葛切).
It refers to saliva or froth.
Sihakavīra is also called Sihakavīrada.
*Sihaka* means "lion. *Vīrada*, or alternatively written as *vīrata*, is likely his clan name (*gotra*) or his father’s name;
the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* refers to him as "the son of Vīrata."
*Saṃkhyeya* (as explained in the section on *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
*Kṛti-niḥpatti* has already been explained in the section on *Pāyattika*.
*Maicanzhi* (磨飡緻) refers to thick *śarkarā* (stone honey), which is the boiled-down, viscous juice of sugarcane.
It is also called *upadaṃśanī*.
The *Sudarsana* states: "Upādā-phāṇita; *phāṇita* refers to refined sugarcane syrup. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:
"When sugarcane juice is boiled over a fire in a vessel, its initial state of being free from impurities is called *phāṇita*.
When it is boiled for a second time, it becomes gradually more concentrated and is called *guḍa*. When it is boiled for a third time, its color becomes white."
It is called *śarkarā* (stone-honey). The Great Sūtra states: "Stone-honey treats heat; black stone-honey treats cold.

Regarding the term *pātrī*, [the character] 籢 is pronounced *lián* (as in *liàn-yán*). Xu says: "The character *lǎn* means to gather or contract; it is used for the purpose of collecting and contracting. *Lǎn* is originally..."
The casket for storing mirrors is now borrowed here; it is written as *lián* (匳) in the clerical script, and colloquially as *lián* (奩).

"Medicine of the proper time" (*kālabhojya*) refers to that which should be consumed at the appropriate time; thus it is called "medicine of the proper time. There are four kinds of medicine, namely: [medicine of] the proper time, [medicine of] the improper time, [medicine of] seven days, and [medicine of] life-long duration. Regarding "medicine of the proper time": [text continues].
Regarding the duration—whether for seven days or for as long as one lives—the explanation is as given in the *Śayanāsanavastu* (the Chapter on Forfeiture).

The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "These four types [of medicine] are all capable of curing illness and are collectively termed 'medicine. They are required by the sick, not by those who are not ill.
When consuming these four types of medicine, one must first cultivate the intention to treat an illness before partaking of them. Furthermore, regarding these four medicines..."
Each should be taken according to its potency; that is to say, the preceding ones are stronger and the succeeding ones are weaker.
A longer duration of time is weak, while a shorter duration is strong. If the latter three medicines are mixed with the first, they should be taken according to their respective potencies:
the latter two follow the one, and the latter one follows the one. Once the allotted time has passed, they should not be taken at all. Master Jing notes:

The old [commentary] says: "Regarding the mixing of the four types of medicine and taking them according to their strength, this means that 'timely' and 'non-timely' medicines have their own relative strengths;

it does not depend on the quantity. Others say: "If yeast and ginger are mixed together, if the yeast is predominant one may eat it at the proper time, whereas if the ginger is predominant it is for non-proper times.

Both of these views should be regarded as mere conjecture. (The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If one uses timely medicines and so forth to assist in forming a seven-day medicine, and takes it as a seven-day medicine, there is no fault. Or, if one uses a seven-day... )

Medicines and the like may assist in forming a lifetime medicine; if taken as a lifetime medicine, there is no fault. Or, seven-day medicines and the like may assist in forming a timely medicine; if taken as a timely medicine, there is no fault, because they follow the predominant power [of the primary substance] and assist in its formation.

If the powers of the various portions are equal, one should determine the classification according to their names. This discussion concerns the "power-sphere" (*śakti-bhāga*), which does not accord with the *Vinaya-viniścaya*; fearing that confusion or error might arise, both versions are recorded here.
*Candana* is sometimes called *candanana*. It is a fragrant wood from foreign lands; as it does not exist in this region, it cannot be translated [into Chinese].
Alternatively, it is said that its meaning is translated as "medicine," because it can eliminate disease. Or it is called "heavenly wood candana," or "ox-head."
Candana (Sandalwood). Regarding the mountain peak from which it originates, it resembles a cow's head.

The *Xiyu ji* states that within Mount Malaya (located in South India) there is the white sandalwood tree. According to the various species of sandalwood, there are yellow, white, purple, and red varieties.
White sandalwood treats febrile diseases; red sandalwood removes wind-swelling and counters various malignant poisons. (Mount Cow's Head is located in [the continent of] Uttarakuru.)
Luzhou). Pilengqi—also called Bilengjia, or alternatively Bilige—is the clove (lit., "dixiang"). It is this.

"Agaru" (Aquilaria) is called *akaru* in Sanskrit; here it is translated as "sinking incense. Its substance is hard and black; because it sinks when placed in water, it is called "sinking incense" (*chen-shui*).
In China, it is produced only in Qiongzhou.

*Kāra* is also called *takāra*, or *takāru*; this is translated as "root-fragrance" (*genxiang*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that *takālu* refers to the *mukhaka* tree (wood-fragrance tree).
Regarding *śapphala* (the identity of this incense is unknown), the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states:

"If a sick bhikṣu has applied fragrant ointment to his body, he should not enter the assembly to sit, nor should he preach the Dharma to laypeople (*gṛhapati*) and others, nor should he visit the homes of the laity. Only after he has recovered from his illness may he wash it off."
He entered the assembly at will and even preached the Dharma for others. At that time, lay devotees with faith brought ointments to offer to the bhikṣus;
they did not accept them, or if they accepted them, they threw them away or used them for other purposes. The lay devotees were displeased. The Buddha said:
"One should apply it to the side of one's head or upon the wooden panels of the wall, and smell it with the nose when lying down. This applies to all fragrant substances."
When smelled, it causes the eyes to become clear; do not harbor any doubt regarding this. *Hú lǎn qiè* (for the character 檻):
*xián* is in the upper tone. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Jian" (*hán*) refers to a cage or enclosure (*lóng*). "Lung" (*lóng*) means a prison or stable. Another explanation says it is a pen or fold.
It is called a "pen" (*kuan*) because it encloses birds and beasts;
*Vairocana* is translated here as "Increase," as explained in the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (The Section on Receiving Precepts).
*Gānìng* (伽甯甯).

Correctly written as *nìng* (甯), with the phonetic components "nǎi" (乃) and "dìng" (定); the pronunciation is *nìng* (佞). The original Indic term is unknown; it should likely be a word for "ugliness. *Gautamī*.
Some call him Kṛṣṇagautama; Gautama is the new term for what was previously explained as *Gautama*.
This is the name of a nāga. *Ti* is equivalent to *sthā*. Śyāmāvatī.
Some call him Śivabhadra, and others call him Śābaputra. According to the Sanskrit, *suvīra* means "good son" (*śubhaputra*).
[He is also known as] Tārkṣyairāvaṇa.
*Takṣa*, or *Tākṣa*; *Airāvaṇa*, or *Airāvaṇa*, or *Haramani*.
These are explained as above.
Kapilavastu is fully called Kambalāśvatara;
this means "Horse with Hairy Back" (alternatively called Kanthaka, which also refers to hair).
Dhṛtarāṣṭra is translated here as "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó) and also rendered as "Governor of the Nation" (Zhìguó), as explained in the *Śīlaskandha-vastu*.
[He is accompanied by] Gandharvas and Rākṣasas.

Gandharva: translated here as "Fragrance Aggregate" (xiāngyīn), or "Smeller of Fragrance" (xiùxiāng), also called "Eater of Fragrance" (shìxiāng), because they sustain themselves by means of fragrance.
Rākṣasa: or Rākṣaśa; translated here as "Protector" (hùshì). If female, she is called Rākṣasī. Master Yuan says this translates as "Terrifying" (kěwèi).
(Alternatively, it is said that Rākṣasa means "Swift" [sùjí]. All those mentioned above are kings of the devas and nāgas.)
The name of the King [is as follows].
*Bhagavat* is a title denoting the supreme excellence of the World-Honored One’s manifold virtues, as explained in detail previously. According to the Vinaya texts, from Vairocana...
*Le-ca-mi*. Up to the phrase *bhagavān*, this is the protective mantra for self-guarding with loving-kindness.

When a bhikṣu uses this mantra to protect his own body, he is immediately spared from being harmed by snake venom. Furthermore, in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the bhikṣus, spoke a verse for removing poison and a prohibitive mantra, saying:
Toward the Lord Dhṛtarāṣṭra, As well as Hiraṇyakaśipu and Kambala,
I give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness toward them all; Toward Gautama, Virūpākṣa, Nanda and Upananda,
and those without feet or with two feet— Toward all the nāga kings, I likewise arouse thoughts of loving-kindness.
To all sentient beings who dwell upon the water, whether moving or stationary, I extend my heart of loving-kindness.
May all the hosts of humans and devas, gods, ghosts, and animals alike, obtain benefit and peace;
may they always be free from illness and filled with joy; may everything they behold be virtuous and auspicious, and may they never encounter any enemies or evils.
I extend thoughts of loving-kindness to all; may you not inflict harm or poison upon one another.
As I wander through all places, even those as perilous as cliffs and valleys, may the biting poisons and the harmful poisons never again harass me.
By the power of the true words of the World-Honored One, the Great Compassionate Father, which I speak as the Buddha’s own speech—may they be fulfilled.
May all poisons not invade me—greed, hatred, and delusion. These are the great poisons of the world;
by the true power of the Buddha, all poisons shall naturally perish. Greed, hatred, and delusion are the great poisons of the world;
by the true power of the Dharma, all poisons shall naturally perish.
Lust, hatred, and delusion are the great poisons of the world;
by the true power of the Sangha, all poisons naturally perish. Having eliminated all poisonous harms, they provide protection and acceptance.
The Buddha removes all poisons; may the harm of snakes perish for you.
Tadyathā | Oṃ | Dhūnbe li dhūnbe li | Dhūpe | Paridhūpe | Nate | Sunate | Kinate | Munaye | Sumunaye | Dantine | Rakṣe | Caruke | Vilope | Upa...

Ying ju li, svāhā. (If one uses this verse as a mantra to protect the body, one will not be harmed by snakes. Even if another has been poisoned, if one recites and maintains it, the poison will be eliminated. Should one be unable to recite the mantra fluently, one may treat the condition with medicinal prescriptions.

There are many such prescriptions, but the most concise and essential is as follows: take one *qian* and six *fen* of white alum; grind eight *fen* with wine and drink it, and grind the remaining eight *fen* with water. Dip a finger into the water and sprinkle it around the edges of the wound where the wine was applied. Once the water is exhausted, [the treatment is complete].)

It heals. Furthermore, it is even more effective when empowered with mantras. One method: grind dog-liver herb (*śvānakakṣa*) with wine and drink it; apply the dregs around the edges of the wound. The toxic vapors will emerge from the mouth; illuminate them with a lamp, and the vapor will immediately strike and extinguish the flame. Continue until the lamp no longer goes out when illuminated.
Another method for treating bites by a green snake (*nīla-sarpa*): grind *tuhina* pepper leaves with wine and drink it; apply the dregs around the edges of the wound, and it will heal immediately.
*Bi-dao-bi*. Rhyme: *yi*;
pronunciation: *pī*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "A large needle. Used by physicians to incise abscesses.
(The character for *zhēn* [needle] is commonly written as *zhēn*.)

The three medicinal herbs are ginger, pepper, and long pepper (*pippalī*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Cold qi arose within the Buddha’s body. The physician said, 'He should consume gruel made from the three pungent herbs.
Ānanda immediately entered the city to beg for sesame, non-glutinous rice, and large and small beans, which he then boiled together."
He offered the *sāntika* porridge to the Buddha. The Buddha asked who had cooked it. He replied, "I cooked it.

The Buddha commanded that it be discarded upon a grassless spot or into water where there are no insects. He then addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, a mahābhikṣu must not eat food he has cooked himself.
If he eats it, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
*Śrīghoṣa* is translated here as "Lion. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In the city of Vaiśālī, there was a great general named Siṃha (Lion).
He was immensely wealthy, possessing abundant money, grain, silks, fields, houses, and precious objects; he was fully endowed with all kinds of merit. (Vaiśālī)
*Li* (i.e., Vaiśālī). *Migan*:

the second character is pronounced with the *gu* and *nan* initials combined, yielding the sound *gan*. It means rice-water (*mipan*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "In the Zhou dynasty, they called *pan* (rice-wash water) *gan*. *Pan* is pronounced [as above].

*Fan*: The water used for rinsing rice. Furthermore, it is called *gan* in the north of the Yangtze River and *pan* in the south (the character *xi* is pronounced like *xi*; it means to wash rice). *Dàng-dì*:
The character *dàng* is pronounced with the initial *tu* and the final *làng*, sounding like *dàng*. It is identical to *dàng*. The *Tōngsúwén* states: "A vessel for washing is called *dàng-dì*."
"Sumi" is the name of this country;
the city is named Bhaddiya (translated here as "Worthy"). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are two cities in the country of Suma.
The first is named City of Bāḍī (i.e., Bāḍī City); the second is named Honey City. Within Bāḍī City, there were six persons of great merit:
first, a great householder; second, a great housewife; third, a great son; fourth, his wife;
fifth, a great male slave; and sixth, a great female slave.

*Manṭa-man*. *Min*: same as the *mi-lin* (彌鄰) cut; the pronunciation is *min*. *Ta*: the pronunciation is *tu*. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is written as *Min-da* (the *da* is pronounced *sui*).
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is written as *Wen-ta*. Some say *Wen-tu*. The name in India is *Hu* (護).
Lǒng (壟):

pronounced with the initial *chū* and the final *dǒng*, sounding like *lóng*. It refers to the ridges of a field; it means the high mounds of soil raised by plowing within a field, which are called *lǒng*.
Tāhālōuzhī (多呵樓支).
This is the name of a *pratyekabuddha*. *Tāha* is not clearly explained. *Lūzhi* translates as "lovely" or "delightful.
The country is called *Amūdra*, or alternatively *Aṅgudrā*. The city is named *Hāmāna*. However, this city has deep faith in the Buddha-dharma.
This is the dwelling place of the ancient seers.
It is called *Kīṭa*, or *Kinnara*, or *Keniya*;
these are all variations resulting from the shifting of vowel weight in the Sanskrit pronunciation. There is no other way to explain this.
*Fan* (according to the *Jinaye*, this is translated as "ear").
*Shilu* is sometimes written as *shiluo*; the correct pronunciation is *sheyiluo*. He was the son of a Brahmin. This person had planted [roots of merit] in past lives.
Possessing roots of goodness, upon hearing the Buddha’s exposition of the Dharma, he immediately realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Regarding the eight kinds of juices:

first, pear juice (the pear has many varieties, as previously explained); second, *jambu* juice (as explained in the section on the *Pātayantika* rules); third, sour jujube juice (in Sanskrit, *kola*).

This is called *jiao* (jujube). *Pōpóluóluó* (婆婆羅羅) is translated as "sour jujube. According to current research, however, this is not the sour jujube. Originally, there is a class of fruit in the Western Regions that resembles the sour jujube in shape; it is named the *guluojia* (孤落迦) fruit, which can be pressed to make juice.
4. Sugarcane juice (there are two kinds of sugarcane: the large variety is for regular consumption, while the small variety is used for sugar.

It is said that sugarcane can subdue gas, harmonize the internal organs, eliminate phlegm, quench thirst, support the spleen qi, benefit the large intestine, remove mental distress and heat, and alleviate gas-induced diarrhea). 5. *Vīra* fruit juice (as explained in the *Dharmaskandha-pāda*). 6. *Śāluka* juice (*Śāluka* refers to...)

It is the root of the lotus. The *Sudarsana-vibhasa* states: "This is the root of the *utpala* and *kumuda* flowers. One pounds it to extract the juice and clarifies it; this is called *śālukā-pāna*. *Utpala* means 'blue lotus' (*nīlotpala*), and *kumuda* means 'white lotus' (*puṇḍarīka*).
7. *Bhāruṇḍī* juice (also called *phalūśi*, or written as *phalūsa*; the correct term is *bhalūsaka*. Its fruit resembles the *yǐgǔ* [blackberry] and does not exist in this region.

The *Sudarsana-vibhasa* says it resembles the *āmra* fruit). 8. *Drākṣā* juice (*drākṣā* is explained as before). In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, and the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, there is also *moca-phala* juice. In Sanskrit, it is called *moca*."

Some say it is *mṛdvīkā* (grape), while others say it is *mora* (fig). This is translated as "plantain fruit. It is said that one places black pepper on top of the fruit and rubs it vigorously with the hands until it all turns into water; this is plantain-fruit juice (*kharjūra-pāna*).

Aside from the eight aforementioned juices, if there are oranges, pomelos, cherries, plums, pomegranates, and so forth, these may also be made into juice. However, for all such juices, one must wash one's hands clean, use clean vessels, and filter them. After sprinkling them with drops of water to purify them and having formally received them, only then may they be drunk. Thus, the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* records Upāli asking the Blessed One:

"As the Buddha has taught regarding 'timely' and 'non-timely' juices, what constitutes 'timely' and what constitutes 'non-timely'? The Buddha replied: "That which is not filtered is 'timely'; that which has been purifiedly filtered is..."

It is not the proper time [to drink them]. Nevertheless, one may purify them by sprinkling drops of water upon them). The *Ekottarakarma* states: 1. *Kāñjika* (a sour liquid resembling plum, shaped like a soapberry);
