[On] Damp Diseases.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from the disease of dampness due to excessive eating. The *Boluozhi* states:
"If one eats a mixture of foods, they become the locus where a hundred ailments and demonic influences gather. The less one eats, the clearer the mind becomes;
the more one eats, the more the body is impaired. Therefore, eating must not be excessive. The *Yao-lan* says: "Illness enters through the mouth; calamity enters through the mouth."
Therefore, the gentleman is cautious with his speech and moderate in his diet. The *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states:
"Generally, when illness arises in this body composed of the four great elements, it invariably originates from overeating, or is triggered by physical exertion;

or it occurs because the evening meal has not been digested when one eats at dawn, or because the morning meal has not been digested when one eats again at noon. It is due to these causes that [illness] is provoked."
Consequently, cholera ensues; hiccups do not cease for nights on end, and abdominal distension from *gū* does not subside for ten days.

Only then does one seek the "kidney-qi" of those with abundant wealth and search for the "Qin-glue" of high price. Such matters may be undertaken by the wealthy, but for the poor, their lot follows the morning dew.
Once the illness has taken hold, what can be done to save it? Even were Lu-yi [the legendary physician] to appear...
At dawn they arrive; they present pills and powders, yet there is no cause for their efficacy. When Bian Que comes at dusk, he leaves behind decoctions and ointments, yet peace and recovery follow.
Burning with fire or being pricked by needles is no different from being struck by wood or stone. With feet trembling and heads shaking, how does this differ from being prostrate and fallen?

This is truly because one does not grasp the root of the illness and lacks understanding of how to regulate and sustain [the body]. It may be said that one stops the flow without blocking its source, or cuts down a tree without removing its roots;
thus the branches and twigs spread ever more extensively, and there is no way to sever them. In diagnosing the source of an illness, one must...
Examine yourself every morning. If you perceive that the four seasonal signs are discordant, immediately prioritize abstaining from grain.
Even if you suffer great thirst, do not consume liquids or water; this is the ultimate prohibition. This may last for one or two days, or for four or five mornings.

One should set recovery as the goal; in principle, there is no fixed rule that binds one like a glued zither string. If one suspects there is undigested food remaining in the stomach, one should prick the navel and chest with a fork.
It is appropriate to drink hot decoctions to one’s heart’s content and use the fingers to scrape the throat, inducing vomiting until it is completely exhausted.

One should drink again and clear the system repeatedly, taking total exhaustion as the measure. Alternatively, drinking cold water is likewise not harmful; perhaps a decoction of dried ginger is even more excellent. As for this...
One must strictly observe a fast during the day and only begin eating at dawn the following morning. If this is not possible, one may adjust according to the circumstances.
In cases of intense fever, one must specifically avoid pouring water over the body; however, if the condition is severe with chills and shivering, it is best to apply heat near a fire.

In the regions south of the Yangtze and the mountain ranges—lands of hot miasma—one should not follow this rule; for in those areas, applying water when fever breaks out is what is appropriate to the local conditions.
If the wind [element] is aggravated, apply medicinal oil and use a cloth pad warmed by fire to apply as a compress; this is also beneficial for areas of fracture or injury.
Apply warm oil to the site, and you will observe daily improvement. Should you feel phlegm and mucus congesting the chest, [apply the following].
Saliva flows repeatedly from the mouth; clear water runs from the nose; the throat is constricted by dregs and grit; a corpse-like obstruction fills the gullet.
The voice cannot be modulated, and food and drink lose their flavor. This condition persists for ten days or more.

In such cases, abstaining from food leads to recovery without the need to cauterize the crown of the head or to twist the throat. This is indeed the clarity of a physician who can eliminate disease without resorting to decoctions or medicine.

This is a grand principle indeed. It seems that once the lingering food is eliminated, the high fever will naturally subside; once the flowing fluids are exhausted, the phlegm and mucus will be cured.

When the internal state is tranquil and the qi is dissipated, the "mad wind" will perish of its own accord. If one employs this method of regulation, there will not be a single failure in ten thousand attempts.
Since it does not require the labor of diagnosing the pulse, why should one rely on inquiries into yin and yang? Each [method] is, in its own way, correct.
O King of Physicians! May every person become like Jīvaka. As for Dharma Master Luan, he regulated the vital breaths to dispel illness; his practice was carried out in silent seclusion.
As for Meditation Master Si, he extracted malevolent influences while seated in meditation; this is not something recognized by the common world.

If one seeks a famous physician in Eastern Luo, the poor and destitute find their path cut off. If one seeks superior medicine in the Western Suburbs, the solitary and orphaned find themselves abandoned.
As for the discussion on fasting, it is concise yet profound, encompassing both the destitute and the wealthy; how could it not be essential?

Furthermore, it applies to cases such as when a carbuncle or boil suddenly erupts and hot blood surges forth, causing pain and distress in the hands and feet; or during epidemics and seasonal miasmas; or when the body is wounded by knives or arrows;
or when one’s person is injured by falling or tumbling; or in cases such as *shanghan* (cold-induced fever) and *huoluan* (cholera-like dysentery), or sudden diarrhea lasting half a day.
For headaches, heart pains, eyeaches, toothaches, or any illness that arises, one must strictly observe a fast.

Furthermore, there are three types of medicinal pills capable of curing various diseases (the pills are as described previously in the section on *kharjūra*). These medical sciences were transmitted from Śakra;

they are counted among the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyā*) and are universally honored throughout the Five Indias. Among them, the most essential is fasting. As the ancients have transmitted:

If one does not recover after seven days of fasting, only then should one seek Avalokiteśvara. In China, many people are unfamiliar with this practice and mistakenly believe it to be a distinct form of ritual fasting;
consequently, they are unwilling to adopt or study it. This is truly because those who transmit these teachings have not realized the principles of medical science.
For those suffering from the ingestion of cinnabar or other mineral tonics, chronic illnesses, or abdominal tumors, this method may be applicable.

Regarding snakes, scorpions, and other such poisons, these are entirely not treated by this method (fearing that those who use cinnabar or mineral stones might endure hunger, which is inappropriate; furthermore, flying cinnabar is found in no country, while the consumption of mineral stones is unique to China.

However, there are crystal and white stones that emit fire; if one consumes them, the body will burst apart. People of the time do not distinguish between them, leading to endless deaths by misfortune. From this it is clear that one must deeply understand and recognize [the difference].

To remove the poison of snakes and scorpions, there are naturally medicines such as sulfur, realgar, and orpiment to treat them; there is no need to abstain from food). Furthermore, during times of fasting, one must strictly avoid wandering about.
Regarding walking and manual labor: for one who practices long-distance walking, even if they have fasted, there will be no harm as long as they follow the path.

Once they have recovered, they must rest and recuperate; it is appropriate that they eat freshly cooked rice and drink a broth of ripe mung beans seasoned with fragrant ingredients, drinking as much or as little as desired.
If they feel cold, they may add black pepper, ginger, and long pepper (*pippalī*). If they know this...

Regarding Wind (vāta): one should consume spikenard (*śigru*) and mugwort (*sūṣa*). The medical treatises state that all pungent substances provoke wind, with the sole exception of dried ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), which does not do so;

it is even beneficial to add it. One should practice breath regulation (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the days of fasting and avoid drinking cold water; otherwise, follow the general prohibitions regarding medicine.
If one consumes congee, there is a fear that phlegm (*kapha*) and mucus may increase; however, if this is indeed Wind-Exhaustion (*vātala*), eating will cause no harm.
If one suffers from heat-related ailments, it is beneficial to boil a decoction of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (ginseng) thoroughly and drink it; tea is also excellent for this purpose.

If one refuses food and does not abandon it, one should subsequently provide treatment according to the specific circumstances. A decoction of *kūṣmāṇḍa* specifically eliminates diseases of heat, as does clarified butter (*sarpis*).

Honey and oil specifically dispel wind-related ailments. In the kingdom of Lāṭa in Western India, those who fall ill fast for either half a month or a full month, waiting until the illness has subsided before they eat again.
In Central India, this period is generally no more than seven days, while in the South Seas it lasts only two or three days.
This is due to the variations in climate and soil, which cause the four great elements of the body to differ accordingly.
Let it be more or less; do not treat all cases as one and the same. It is uncertain whether this applies to the land of China (Shenzhou); one should consider whether fasting is appropriate.

However, regarding those who die after seven days of not eating, it is because they were otherwise free from illness and yet maintained the fast. If disease is present in the body, one would not die even after many days [of fasting].
I have personally seen those with illness who abstained from grain for thirty days and subsequently recovered; if so, why should there be a need [for such a rule]?
Seeing this as strange, he abstained from food for many days. How can one merely observe the onset of an illness without examining the causes from which it arises?
To consume hot gruel while suffering from a fever that burns like fire, and to force oneself to eat while still ill, is truly terrifying.

Even if there were a chance of recovery, such a person would ultimately be unfit to instruct the laity. Since medical treatises clarify internal ailments, this is something strictly to be avoided. Such is the case here.

That is to say: when a wise person reflects and examines this, they employ the practice of relinquishing [medical knowledge] and storing it away. If one hears [the teachings] but does not practice them, how can the fault be attributed to the physician?

Through practice, the body is at peace and the Way is perfected; thus, the benefit of both self and others is simultaneously accomplished. If one relinquishes [practice], the physical frame is impaired and wisdom becomes faint; thus, the merit of both oneself and others is lost.
(The "Science of Medicine" [yiming] is one of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) in the Western lands; it is called the Science of Medicine and extensively elucidates medical arts.)

Regarding the affliction of wind: at one time there was a bhikṣu afflicted by wind. A physician instructed him to use medicinal smoke. The Buddha said, "Its use is permitted. He required a smoke tube; its making is permitted.

The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "The method for this tube is as follows: it should be twelve finger-breadths in length and made of iron; it may have either a single nozzle or a double nozzle."
If smoke enters the nose, it can cure various ailments. If nasal mucus flows out, one should immediately irrigate it with clarified butter (*sarpis*).
The *Mukha-dhāraṇī* states: At one time there was a bhikṣu afflicted by illness. When a physician prescribed that he should eat hemp porridge, the bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "I permit the consumption of hemp porridge when prescribed by a physician; this may also include the roots and stalks of radish."
The flowers, leaves, and seeds all cure wind-related ailments. All should be made into porridge and consumed. (The *Bencao* states:

"Among vegetables, none is more beneficial than the turnip (*màn jīng*). Eating it regularly makes one stout and robust; it penetrates the internal organs, benefits the vital energy (*qì*), descends stagnant qi, and digests food. Its roots treat heat-toxins, wind-swelling, and consumption (*xiāo kě*), and can also resolve these conditions. However, eating too much causes abdominal distension. It is further said that overeating excites the *qì*.

If sudden swelling or toxic eruptions with acute pain arise, take a large root, peel off the skin, and pound it into a paste. Boil it in vinegar for three boils, stir it vigorously to extract the essence, and apply it to the swelling. )

[Storage: Wrap in silk cloth and change it three times a day. For all types of hot swellings and toxic sores, take one handful of the root and a small amount of salt flower; pound them together and apply to the swelling, changing it three times a day. If a man’s penis swells to the size of a bushel and the testicles ache such that others cannot cure it, pound [the root] and apply it;

he will recover immediately. Its seeds primarily treat jaundice, promote the drainage of fluids, and also treat cholera and remove abdominal distension. They clear cataracts and treat blindness, and eliminate intestinal tumors, nodules, and accumulations. In cases of acute jaundice, press one cup of oil and drink it all at once.

For wounds from a spider bite, pound the seeds into a powder and take with wine; thus, there are no spiders in turnip gardens, for they fear it. If taken regularly, it clarifies the eyes, provides penetrating vision, and nourishes the intestines. Use three sheng of the seeds and three sheng of vinegar to boil [them].

Boil until cooked, then dry it thoroughly and grind it into a powder. Take one *fūncùn* (one square inch) of the powder with "well-water from the morning dew" (*jing-hua-shui*). If there is jaundice such that the skin and eyes are golden-colored and the urine is red, take the seeds of the *shengzi* plant, grind them into a powder, and mix with boiled water to take one *fūncùn*. If taken three times a day, the condition will be cured.

If wind-disease enters the abdomen, causing the body to become stiff and the tongue to be dry and hard, take three *liang* of the seeds and grind them into a powder. Take one *qian* at each dose with warm wine. For abdominal distension, take one large *he* of the seeds, pound them until well-ground, strain the juice through water, and drink one *zhan* all at once;

it will heal spontaneously. If there is jaundice of the yin type, accompanied by sweating and yellow nasal mucus or saliva, take the seeds and grind them into a powder. At dawn, take one spoonful with well-water; increase this to two spoonfuls per day until the symptoms cease. For wind-phlegm, grind the seeds into a powder and take one spoonful mixed with warm water. After a short while, phlegmatic foam will be expectorated.

For exhaustion from chronic labor (wasting disease) and blurred vision, collect the flowers of the third month in the shade, dry them, and grind them into a powder. Each morning on an empty stomach, take two *qian* mixed with well-water. [Continue for a long time.]

This garment may be worn while reading at night. Therefore, the practitioners of the Way of the Immortals take its seeds to manufacture this garment for the purpose of avoiding grains and attaining longevity; it possesses various other curative powers as described in that text, which need not be elaborated upon here. As for the term "fangcun" (one-inch square), it refers to a spoon. It means the method of making a spoon:
it is one inch square and is used for scooping up powdered medicine.
*Huàn* (患):
"malaria" (*jiào*). [The character is] pronounced *yuē* (cut by *yú*), with the phonetic value *nuò*. It is a disease of *shāi* (chills/fever). This illness involves both cold and heat;
it may manifest once every day, once every other day, once every three or four days, or it may recur for two consecutive days before subsiding.
Regarding "once a day": all of these cases are treated according to medical prescriptions.
If it is caused by a ghost, then there will be alternating chills and fevers, daily strange occurrences, inauspicious dreams, frequent feelings of terror, and abnormal speech and movements.
One should immediately treat this with the incantation for curing the malarial ghost. The incantation says:
Sumita (1), Anīta (2), Kacinita (3), Uhuṇasumita (4),
Cipahu-husumita (5), Icinitatsumita (6). Svāhā (7).
If one practices this method, one must take thread of five colors and recite a mantra over it to form seven knots.
If the pain descends from the head, first tie the neck, then the feet, and then the hands, making them very tight. Recite the mantra over water three times and spray it [upon the patient].

The illness will immediately be cured. (One should recite the mantra once for each knot; recite it seven times and tie seven knots, then use them to bind the patient. "Spray" [sūn] means to hold water in the mouth and spit it out. Alternatively, one may use the mantras found in the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya to consecrate the water. This applies unless the illness is caused by a spirit.)

It may be treated with medicinal formulas. There are many types of formulas, but the most concise and essential one requires no numerous drugs and involves no laborious decoction. Take one *qian* of high-quality *chángshān* (Corydalis), three parts of *dīngxiāng* (Eugenia caryophyllata), five parts for those with extreme cold, and three parts of *gāncǎo* (Glycyrrhiza).

All are to be cut into small pieces and soaked in half a bowl of the finest wine head. Seal the mouth of the bowl with paper and let it sit overnight; it is also excellent to leave it out in the dew. If the fever is due to occur the following day, soak the ingredients tonight. At dawn the next morning, when the sky is about to brighten...

When it becomes warm, take it while facing east and go to sleep; on that very day, [the affliction] will cease. This has been repeatedly verified. Dry the dregs in the sun, and they can still cure two or three people. If it is a small child who cannot swallow the medicine, one may carry a bag of the medicine around the neck, which will also stop [the affliction].
Alternatively, one may wipe the lips with medicinal wine.
When visiting the sick, there was a case where a layperson (*avadātavasana*) fell ill and came to the monastery. A bhikṣu attended to his care. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to dismiss him by means of a skillful expedient. If he praises the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, he may perform the necessary tasks."
[The Vinaya] says: At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if there is a sick bhikṣu of great virtue, how should he be attended?
The Buddha told Upāli, "A sick bhikṣu of great virtue must not be placed in a marginal, dilapidated, or small room, nor in a secluded or hidden place; he should be placed in a well-exposed room."

Among them, the fellow-practitioner disciples and the resident disciples should constantly attend upon him, sweeping and sprinkling the room, grinding [incense], and plastering the floor, burning various famous incenses so that no foul odors remain.
They should arrange beds and seats (for those who come to inquire after his illness to sit). However, those who come to inquire after his illness must not remain for long.
If a bhikṣu comes to inquire after his illness, they should provide him with food before or after the meal; if he arrives at an improper time...

To such a person, one should provide non-timely medicinal gruel. If there is someone who asks about the patient’s condition, the patient should respond; however, if the patient’s strength is too weak, the attendant should respond.
If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) comes to inquire after him, one should say, "Welcome, long-lived one," and invite them to sit while preaching the Dharma for them.
You will gain great merit, as the World-Honored One has said: "Tending to a sick person who observes the precepts."
"O Bhikṣus, you should regard me as no different [from yourselves]. If there is an offering, accept it and offer a blessing.
If a patient suffers from diarrhea, do not delay in inquiring after them; they should be quickly sent out. If the patient is unable to go out, one should keep three chamberpots:
one to give to the patient, one to carry out, and one for washing; once washed, they should be smeared with oil and dried in the sun."
They should take turns in this manner. One person should stay by the door so that no one enters abruptly;

another should stay by the side of the patient and, from time to time, preach the Dharma in accordance with their needs. That venerable bhikṣu should attend to the patient in this way. (The *Śāriputrābhidharma* states:

"The caregiver should praise the patient according to what they previously practiced and studied; he must not disparage them or cause them to retreat from their original wholesome resolve. He then asked the World-Honored One again: "What about minor [illnesses]?"
"A virtuous bhikṣu is ill; how should he be attended? The Buddha said:

"He should not be placed in a conspicuous location where his foul stench will permeate the outside, nor should he be placed in a secluded or private spot where people would not know of his death when it occurs. He should be settled among the people.
If the patient has two teachers, or a co-practitioner or a dependent disciple, they should attend him. If there is no one such as these, the Saṃgha should [attend him]."

Appoint attendants to care for the sick. If one, two, or three people are attending, if there is money for medicine outside of the patient's robes and bowl, it should be taken and used to provide for them.
If there is none, the Sangha should provide it. If the Sangha has nothing, they should exchange the patient's valuable robes and bowl for lighter ones to provide for them.
If the patient is reluctant to part with them, they should inform [the Sangha].
The assembly says: "Venerable Sangha, the sick bhikṣu named so-and-so, not understanding impermanence, was stingy with his robes and bowl and refused to trade them.
Having informed the Sangha, [the monks] spoke to him with gentle words and taught the Dharma until he attained understanding; only then did they trade for them.

If there were still none remaining, they should have begged for some to give to him. If that could not be obtained, they should have taken the best portion from the Sangha’s food and given it to him."
If, moreover, there is nothing [to give], the attendant should take two bowls and enter the village for alms; he should then offer the better one to the patient.

This is called the "Dharma for a Bhikṣu of Lesser Virtue when Ill" (the Dharma for being ill while on the road is detailed in that text). The *Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "If the patient is poor..."
Regarding the cost of medicine: the preceptor, teachers, spiritual friends, and others should provide for it;

or one may seek it from a donor, or use property belonging to the Saṃgha, or property belonging to a stūpa, or decorative items such as banners and canopies, selling them according to their value to provide the cost of the medicine.
If the illness is later cured, the price should be repaid. If one lacks the means, there is no obligation to repay.
It is an offense. Because he is the son of the Great Master and possesses his father’s wealth, if one is attending to a bhikṣu, one should provide for the patient;
with the exception of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), all other duties should be performed.

If the patient’s life is about to end, the caregiver should move the patient onto their own bedding, employing skillful means so as not to cause anger or distress. If the patient asks for robes or a bowl...
[These matters] should be presented with urgency. After death, regarding all funeral rites:
if the deceased has no property, one may use the property of the Saṃgha, or have the attendant nurse beg for it on behalf of the patient. If there is a patient, they are beset by their illness.
One should then take one's robes and bowl and offer them as alms wherever appropriate. Those who receive the offering should not divide it immediately;

rather, on another day, they should inquire whether [the donor] will come again. If the donor requests it back, it should be returned; if the donor says they will not take it, then it should be divided.
Furthermore, regarding all the rules of conduct for the sick and those who attend to the sick, one should act according to the instructions; whoever does not follow these practices [is at fault].

One incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha told Upāli, "Among sick bhikṣus, there are those who would die if not properly cared for, yet would live if properly cared for.
Therefore, one should provide careful attention, striving to ensure they are settled in accordance with the Dharma;
this constitutes the granting of life. Thus, nursing the sick brings great merit, as praised by all Buddhas."
[The Buddha] sighed. As in the *Jātakanidāna*, the World-Honored One praised him with these verses:
"One should attend to the sick And inquire after those in peril and distress. Good and evil have their retributions, Just as seeds yield fruit.
The World-Honored One is the father, And the Sūtras and Dharma are the mother."
"Students are like brothers. Regarding how one may attain ordination through specific circumstances, the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* (Zapiyu jing) states:
"In the past, there was a śramaṇa walking through a grassy thicket when a large snake spoke, saying, 'Upādhyāya, O practitioner of the Way.
The practitioner was startled and looked around him. The snake said, 'O practitioner of the Way, do not be afraid, do not be terrified. I pray that you [will act] for my sake.'"
He preached the sutra, saying, "May this cause me to be liberated from this sinful body. The snake asked, "O practitioner, have you heard of King Ajātaśatru?
He replied, "I have heard of him. The snake said, "I am he. The practitioner said, "King Ajātaśatru established Buddha-stūpas and monasteries."
"The merit of making offerings is so sublime that one should be reborn in the heavens; for what reason has it come to this?
The snake replied, "When I was approaching the end of my life, a bystander dropped a fan onto my face, which caused me to give rise to anger, and thus I received this snake body."
The practitioner of the Way then preached the sutra for him. With single-minded devotion, he delighted in listening; he did not eat for seven days and passed away to be reborn in heaven.
Several months later, he scattered flowers before the Buddha. The multitude marveled at this, and from the midst of the void he said: "I am King Ajātaśatru.
Having received the kindness of the practitioner of the Way, I heard the Dharma and attained birth in the heavens. I have now come to offer these flowers as a repayment for the Buddha’s grace."
For this reason, those attending a person at the point of death must not fail to protect the mind of the patient. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"If one has performed good deeds since birth but harbors an evil thought at the moment of death, one will be reborn in an evil realm; if one has performed evil deeds since birth but harbors a virtuous thought at the moment of death, one will be reborn in the heavens.
Master Kumārajīva remarked: "According to the customs of foreign lands, from birth until the end of life..."

One should record each meritorious deed performed. At the time of death, if others speak of these for one’s sake, it will cause them to rely upon their merit so that their mind is free from sorrow and fear.
They will think to themselves: "From birth until now, I have always maintained a right livelihood; I shall surely go to a happy realm. What, then, should I fear?
Therefore, one must properly protect oneself and not lose one's goodness, so that one may proceed according to one's wishes.
The *Sūtra on Birth* states: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Puguang:

"If members of the fourfold assembly—whether men or women—at the time of their death, wish to be reborn in the buddha-fields of the ten directions, they should first bathe their bodies, put on fresh and clean garments, burn various famous incenses, hang silk banners and canopies, sing praises of the Triple Gem, and recite the honored sūtras for the sake of the sick."
He expounded upon causes and conditions, parables, skillful expressions, and the subtle meaning of the sutras:

that suffering is empty and unreal, that the four great elements are but a provisional combination, and that the physical form is like a plantain tree—lacking any core substance within—and like a flash of lightning, unable to remain for long.
Therefore it is said: "Form is not long-lasting in its freshness; it must return to decay and ruin. By practicing the Path with sincerity and earnestness, one may transcend suffering.
According to what the mind desires, there is no fruit that cannot be obtained" (the remainder is as briefly explained in the section on the Small Hut in the *Vasā-vastu*).
"Mùdǎng" (木欓):
the first character is pronounced "táng. It should be written as "dǎng" (簜), which refers to a large hollow bamboo tube.
Master Ying stated that it is made of wood or clay and is shorter and wider than a wooden bucket.
The character "匙" (chí) is pronounced as "shí. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "In the Western Regions, the method of eating is to use only the right hand.

Only in cases of illness is it permitted to possess a spoon. As for chopsticks, they have not been heard of in the Five Indies, nor have they been seen among the four divisions of the monastic community."
Yet this practice is uniquely shared by the Eastern lands (China). It is a long-standing custom among the laity, while the monastic community employs it according to their own inclinations.
Since chopsticks are neither permitted nor prohibited, they may be considered a matter of minor precept (*sūtra-śikṣāpada*). When used, the assembly offers no criticism or debate.

"In the Eastern lands, this may indeed be practiced; yet if one clings to worldly conventions, there will be ridicule and disdain. In the Western regions, it was fundamentally not permitted to hold [the bowl].
This is the purport of the *Lüjiao* (Brief Teachings). (As for what is called the *Lüjiao*, the text is recorded below.)
The *Kathina* Robe *Khandhaka*:
The robe named *kathina* is a solid mass of meritorious qualities; Its substance is pure, wondrous, and subtle, bearing five kinds of benefits.
The World-Honored Ones of the ten directions Earnestly praise and extol it.
The heterodox cannot know its name; the donor transcends the evil realms.
In the past, the disciples of the Buddha Padmaśūta cut the kaṭhina cloth. Surrounded by ten thousand worthies, they stitched it like the alarka flower.
Spreading the robe, they were about to perform the ritual of repair for the Sugata and his assembly of a thousand sages.
Having personally approached, one receives the principle; such are the merits of the robe.
One must know the dharma regarding the profound and inconceivable receiving and relinquishing; its intent must not be proclaimed erroneously.
Receiving is permeated by the three minds, and its accomplishment lies in the present intention. Because it is fundamentally for the sake of fulfillment, the Tathāgata spoke these nine phrases.
The summary of the rules for relinquishment is divided into two parts: those concerning the Saṃgha and those concerning oneself.
One must attain knowledge of the meaning of these phrases, which are not all of one kind. The first eight are the fundamental rules; the latter two are also matters of that same category.
Within them, there are one hundred and eighteen points, from which their mutual meanings emerge. If a person understands this, [they shall not fall].
To accept with equanimity and without doubt—this is called perfect speech. It is endowed with all the flavors of the phrases.
Regarding "wrong livelihood":
this refers to gaining profit through false teachings. There are five kinds of such false teachings for seeking profit and sustenance.
[The Buddha said: "First, for the sake of gain and offerings, they falsely manifest wonders. Second, for the sake of gain and offerings, they speak of their own merits.

Third, for the sake of gain and offerings, they practice divination of good and bad fortune. Fourth, for the sake of gain and offerings, they raise their voices and display an air of authority to cause others to feel awe and reverence.
Fifth, for the sake of gain and offerings, they proclaim the offerings they have received in order to stir the hearts of people."
Because one sustains life through wrong causes and conditions, this is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). Furthermore, there are four kinds of wrong food by which one sustains life:
1. Downward-facing food (*adhomukha-āhāra*): This refers to monastics who compound medicines, sow grain, or plant trees;

such impure means of livelihood are called downward-facing food. 2. Upward-facing food (*ūrdhvamukha-āhāra*): This refers to monastics who observe the constellations, the sun and moon, wind and rain, and thunder.
Lightning and thunder; sustaining one’s life through impurity is called "looking upward for food.

Food from the three directions refers to monastics who curry favor with those of power and influence, acting as messengers to the four quarters, using clever speech to seek much; sustaining one’s life through such impurity is called "looking toward the directions for food.
Food from the four intermediate directions refers to monastics who study various incantations and arts, divining good and bad fortune; as [the text continues]:
This is livelihood; it is called "food that sustains the mouth. That which is contrary to the above is called "pure livelihood food" (*pariśuddhājīva*).

One does not manifest deceptive or extraordinary signs for the sake of seeking gain and offerings, nor does one raise one's voice or display an air of authority to cause others to feel fear and reverence.

Or one may manifest the appearance of sitting in meditation, observing the precepts, and so forth, for the sake of seeking profit; to manifest such false and deceptive displays is called "attaining by means of signs.
To not obtain profit through these means is called "not attaining by means of signs. The *Sūtra of a Hundred Similes* says: Once there was a husband and wife who had three flat cakes (*pūpa*).
The couple divided them together, each eating one cake, with one flat cake remaining. They made a mutual agreement:
"If there is anyone who speaks, you must not give him the cake. Having made this agreement, for the sake of that single cake, neither dared to speak.
In a short while, a thief entered the house to steal; he took all their possessions until everything was completely in his hands.
Because of their prior agreement, the husband and wife watched with their eyes but did not speak. Seeing that they did not speak, the thief immediately—
Her husband had previously plundered her, yet even when he saw it with his own eyes, he remained silent. The wife then called out to the thief and said to her husband, "How can you be so foolish?
For the sake of a single cake, you see a thief and do not call out! Her husband clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "Shame on you, slave!
I have certainly obtained the cake; I shall no longer give it to you. When the people of the world heard this, there was none who did not [laugh].
They mock [the noble ones]. Ordinary persons are just like this:
for the sake of minor fame and profit, they falsely manifest stillness and silence, yet they are plundered by various evil thieves—the false afflictions—and lose their wholesome dharmas.

Consequently, they fall into the three miserable realms without any fear, and instead of seeking the path that transcends the world, they remain addicted to and frolicking among the five desires. Even when they encounter...
Great suffering, yet they do not regard it as a calamity; they are no different from those foolish people.
"Ji" (激) is pronounced like "ji" (戟); it means to stir or move. It refers to what is called "gratitude and inspiration" (感激).
The *Mātṛkā* states that after the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has concluded, there are three items: robes, utensils, and the *kāṭhina* robe.
Those obtained during the *varṣā* may not be used as a *kāṭhina* robe, as the Buddha has taught. This concludes the section on "having passed one night."

Regarding robes: receiving the *kaṭhina* robe is not validly received. What is meant by "having passed the night"? It refers to either exceeding ten nights or passing even a single night with a deceitful mind.
[The character] is pronounced *chǎn* (with the initial *chū* and the final *yǎn*). Its sound is like that of *chèn*. It means flattery and sycophancy.

To follow someone’s lead with one’s face is called *yú* (sycophancy); to speak words of artful persuasion is called *chǎn* (flattery). The *Vimuktimārga-śāstra* states: "As for being crooked and sycophantic (*chǎnqū*): according to one's own mental intentions, one falsely promotes others, praises them with fine words, and traffics between good and evil for the sake of gain and profit.
One uses humor and jesting to please others, drawing profit toward oneself. This is what is called being crooked and sycophantic."

The character for "zhěn" (輾) is correctly written as "zhăn" (輾). It is pronounced with the initial *n* and the final rhyme *niǎn* (碾), meaning to crush something under a vehicle or to roll a wheel over grain.

Here, it is used by extension; it should properly be written as "zhǎn" (展), with the initial *zhī* and the final rhyme *niǎn* (輦), in the third tone. It means to unfold, to spread out, or to arrange and open.
The *Pañcavargika-śīla* (Five-Section Vinaya) states:
"A five-strip robe with ten partitions—such a robe as this, the Saṃgha should accept and make into a *kaṭhina* (功德衣).
If it exceeds this, it should likewise be accepted. As for what is meant by "exceeding," it refers to either a seven-strip robe with twenty-one partitions, or a nine-strip robe.
There are twenty-seven sections, up to twenty-five strips, totaling one hundred and twenty-five sections;
these must be cut and pieced together, and may not be made as a single uncut piece. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one uses an uncut saṃghāṭī, uttarāsaṅga, or antarvāsaka to make a kaṭhina robe, it is not considered 'accepted' [as kaṭhina]. The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states that it must be...
Regarding new robes that have already been washed and dyed, but have never yet been worn, as well as those not given as urgent alms-gifts—
whether they be saṃghāṭī, uttarāsaṅga, or antarvāsaka— one must complete the manufacture of at least one of these.
If one has not yet mastered [the technique], it is improper to stretch it out to five cubits or more; only then does it conform to the Dharma.

If the material is coarse or thin, or if it has been used for covering a corpse during transit, or if it is made of leaves or strips of bark previously worn by others—these are items subject to the offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

Furthermore, items that are torn, softened, or have been patched and replaced should not be stretched out. Even if one obtains such a finished item on the fifteenth day, it likewise [is not to be used].

One may perform the *kaṭhina* ceremony (according to the Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins: on the fourteenth day, one informs the Saṃgha; on the fifteenth day, one appoints a person to make the robe; on the sixteenth day, one spreads the robe). The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"On the sixteenth day, at the appearance of the dawn light, one brings the *kaṭhina* cloth, cuts it, and presents it to the community of monks.

The bhikṣus should inform the owner of the cloth regarding the need for needles, thread, and dye, as well as the number of bhikṣus who will make the robe. When the donor hears this, [he provides the necessary materials].
Having done so, one should provide food and drink for the bhikṣu who is making the robe. For the sake of the Saṃgha, one should receive the kaṭhina cloth;

one should know the procedure for receiving it. If the robe has already been cut, it should first be washed. One should cut, pin, and sew it together with many bhikṣus, dyeing it completed on that very day.
Once the purification marks have been applied, it should be received. If the robe is not yet finished, one should summon everyone.
The monks shall work together; they must not speak of the Path or its virtues, nor create obstacles, except in the case of those who are ill.
The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: "Even those capable of performing two or three stitches should all assist in the work.
Once it is completed, on the sixteenth day, the person who oversaw the spreading of the cloth should honor the *kaṭhina* with ointments, incense, flowers, and colorful decorations.
Having finished with that robe, place it upon a clean tray and carry it toward the head of the assembly. Standing before the *upādhyāya* (senior monk), hold the robe up and remain there (*etc.*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should fold this robe and place it inside a chest, scattering various flowers upon it.
The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "After the *pravāraṇā*, four things may be done: first, to dissolve the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*); second, to re-establish the great boundary; third, to [dissolve]..."

There are two kinds of causes and conditions for [the dissolution of] the boundary (*sīmā*): first, when it is submerged by a great flood and its marks are destroyed, such that the location cannot be known;

second, due to the danger of bandits, all the bhikṣus go outside the boundary. Therefore, it is necessary to perform the formal binding and releasing [of the boundary]. Third, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe;

fourth, the completion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) and the acceptance of bedding and utensils. These matters pertain to the causes and conditions following the *pravāraṇā*. (From the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*).
The Vinaya states: Why is such great diligence applied toward the *kaṭhina* robe? It is because it is praised by all Buddhas.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Padma (Lotus), who had a śrāvaka disciple named Sujāta.
While he was making a *kaṭhina* robe that was not yet finished, the Tathāgata Padma, surrounded by sixteen thousand bhikṣus, [appeared with him].

At the beginning of the month, one receives the *guṇa-vāsa* (merit robe); it is thus that it retains its name.
According to the correct Sanskrit pronunciation, it is *guṇa*, which is translated here as "merit" (*gōngdé*).

Now, to translate *kaṭhina* directly as "merit" is not acceptable, for we see that the names transmitted from antiquity are not uniform. Thus, we know that *kaṭhina* cannot be translated by a single meaning alone.

Alternatively, it is translated as "firm and solid" (*dṛḍha*) or "solid and substantial. It is also called "sheltering and covering" (*chādana*), and is further named "difficult to sustain," because it is difficult for the poor to sustain their livelihood.

*Shuài*. (Sōu lèi qiè; *shuāi* with a departing tone). It means "lord" (*zhǔ*). It also means "to lead" (*lǜ*) or "to command" (*tǒng lǐng*).
Generally, those who command troops are called generals (*jiàng shuài*). Today, those who command rebels are called rebel generals (*zéi shuài*).
Regarding the *stūlātyaya* (grave offense) that is repentable:

generally, those who follow one who has split the Saṃgha commit a *stūlātyaya* that is repentable; however, if they are the leader who splits the Saṃgha, they commit a *stūlātyaya* that is not repentable.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "To split the wheel of the Saṃgha constitutes a grave offense (*stūlātyaya*) of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) that is not repentable."
Remorse. To break the *saṃgha* through formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) constitutes an offense that is not a *ānantarya* (immediate) sin and is confessable as a *sthūlātyaya*.

To break the wheel of the *saṃgha* requires at least nine persons; one person claims to be a Buddha. To break the *saṃgha* through formal procedure requires at least eight persons; no one claims to be a Buddha.
Whether within the boundary (*sīmā*) or outside the boundary, all are completely broken. Breaking the *saṃgha* through formal procedure must necessarily...
Within the boundary (*sīmā*), performing separate *karmas* constitutes a schism of the Saṃgha-wheel (*saṃghabheda*). This must be done by a man;

however, a woman (referring to a nun) is also capable of causing a schism of the Saṃgha-wheel. A schism of the *karma*-Saṃgha is both a schism of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) Saṃgha and a schism of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) Saṃgha.
A schism of the Saṃgha-wheel occurs only in Jambudvīpa, whereas a schism of the *karma*-Saṃgha extends throughout the three continents. Ten.
The recitation says: "One who breaks the *karmavācanā* performs a separate *poṣadha-karmavācanā* within a single boundary (*sīmā*).
One who breaks the Wheel of Dharma causes others to abandon the Eightfold Noble Path and enter into false paths; 'Wheel' refers here to the divisions of the Eightfold Noble Path."
*Ei zì zhǐ ei*.
(The second character is pronounced with the *wū xiè* rhyme, sounding like *ài*). This is the sound produced when the breath is full from eating to satiety.
*Bājiāo* (Plantain).
*Pá*: cut with *bāngjiā*, pronounced *bā*. *Jiāo*: cut with *zīxiāo*, pronounced *jiāo*. Its leaves do not fall; they merely wither, hence it is called *jiāo*.
*Pá* has the meaning of *bā*; *bā* also carries the sense of "withering. Therefore, in common parlance, dried things are called *bā*.
When that tree once bears fruit, it dies; there is no further rebirth.
*Níng* (儜):
pronounced as *néng* (奴登切), meaning weak or, alternatively, exhausted.
"Gǔlú" (駏驢) is pronounced "jùxū. It is the name of a beast. This animal resembles a mule but is smaller; it is born from a father that is an ox and a mother that is a horse.
A mule, by contrast, is born from a father that is a donkey and a mother that is a horse. These two types of beasts both do not conceive on their own; should they conceive, [they immediately perish].
*Si* (pronounced *luo* [with the tone of a mule]; vulgarly written as *sui*).
*Xianji* (the second character pronounced with the initial *qi* and the final *ni*, entering tone): enmity or resentment.
Śrāvastī, also called Sūrattha, means "Good Country" (Sukhāvatī) in this language; it was formerly governed by King Candraprabha.
Other sūtras and vinayas mostly refer to it as the country of Vārāṇasī. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states that the king's name was Rāṇavatī (which means "Jewel Armor").
The first queen was named Soma; she gave birth to Prince Kalyāṇakāri (which means "Good Deed").
The second queen was named Upasunda; she gave birth to Prince Pāpakāri (which means "Evil Deed").
Prince Kalyāṇakāri married the daughter of the King of Rṣivadatta.

*Fúc-zàng* (伏藏). *Fú* (伏): the phonetic is *fù* (服); it means "to hide" or "to lie concealed. *Zàng* (藏): in the departing tone (*qìngshēng*), pronounced as *cái-làng* (才浪). That which things are stored in is called a "treasury" (*zàng*);

this refers to when a person conceals objects within it. If the objects conceal themselves, then it is pronounced with the level tone (*píngshēng*). As the Sūtra says: "concealed treasures" (*fùníbǎo*).
This refers to the "treasury" (gter). The precious objects within the cavern are called "subterranean treasures" (sa gter).
The manner in which the asuras seize the sun is as explained above, and is further clarified in the section on lunar eclipses in the thirty-sixth fascicle below.
*Prābhṛta* is also rendered as *sū*.
This translates as "well-guarded" (*su-rakṣita*) and also as "good armor" (*su-varman*). Armor also carries the meaning of protection.
[It is like] surging waves.
Yǒng (涌): pronounced with the initial *yǐn* and the final *sǒng*, sounding like *yǒng*. It means water overflowing on the surface. The vulgar form 湧 is incorrect. Huífù (洄澓):
*huí* is pronounced like *huí*; *fù* is pronounced like *fú*. *Huífù* refers to water swirling back upward; one gloss says it means "hidden flow" (*fúlíu*).
*Bǎozhǔ* (寶渚).
The character *zhǔ* is pronounced with the *yǔ* rhyme and has the sound *zhǔ*. The *Erya* states: "A small island is called a *zhǔ*. Others say:
"A place that stands alone high amidst water on all four sides is called a *zhǔ*."
*Khadira* is also called *kṣadira* or *khadara*. This refers to the acacia wood. Master Ying states that this wood is abundant in the regions south of this [Central India].
Master Yuan states that in this region it is the *kugeng* (Sophora flavescens) tree. (*Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra*)
It is translated as *zijishu* wood. According to this, the *khadira* wood is hard and thorny, yet it is not *zijishu*.
Because its wood is hard, it resembles the *zijiang* (mimosa). Whenever it is used within the context of mantra recitation, the *zijiang* may be substituted for it.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Once the khadira tree has been cut down, it does not grow again" (the character *jiāng* is pronounced like *jiāng*; it is also called the "ten-thousand-year tree," the purple *jiāng*, which in the local dialects of south of the [Yangtze] River is commonly called the purple *jīng*).

King Śuddhodana is also called Śuddhānana. The *Buddhacarita* states: "A descendant of the Ikṣvāku lineage, King Śākya Ajita, was named Śuddhodana because he possessed pure wealth and was fully endowed with virtuous qualities."
Māyā is fully called Mahāmāyā; this means "Great Skill" or also "Great Illusion. The Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins states:
King Siṃhahanu constantly reflected, "If within my lineage there were to arise a Golden-Wheel-Turning King..."
"It accords with my wish. The city of Devadṛśa was thus revealed. King Suprabuddha also thought: "I shall quickly become a kinsman to King Siṃhahanu;
this truly accords with my wish. At that time, the chief queen of King Suprabuddha became pregnant.
When the ten months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was so upright and beautiful as to be rare in the world. The king and...
The palace attendants and all who saw her were filled with wonder and looked up to her in awe.
They discussed it among themselves, saying, "Is this princess born of human origin, or has she been conjured by the manifestation of the god Viśvakarman?
After twenty-one days had passed, the ministers deliberated together and said, "This princess was not born of a human being; she is a manifestation created by the god Viśvakarman."

"This girl may be named Māyāvatī. The physiognomist declared, "This noble daughter of the King shall later give birth to a son who will possess all the marks of excellence, have great majesty and power, and attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (cakravartin).
Later, the queen became pregnant again; when ten months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a daughter whose radiance illuminated the entire city.

Her countenance and marks of excellence were peerless in the world. On the twenty-first day, the ministers assembled for deliberation and said, "This young girl surpasses even illusory transformations";
thus, she was immediately given the name Mahāmāyā (Great Illusion). The physiognomists declared, "Now, this is the King’s holy daughter."
"Later, she will certainly give birth to a son endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man; his majestic virtue shall be honored, and he will attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.
At that time, King Suvibuddha sent a letter to King Siṃhahanu, detailing in full the auspicious signs of his two daughters.
King Siṃhahanu thought of the birth of a Wheel-Turning King;
he first took Mahāmāyā to be the consort of Prince Śuddhodana, and subsequently took Māyā to be his second consort (and so forth).
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Lady Māyā replies to Sudhana, saying: "Good son, I have already accomplished the liberation door of the great vow, wisdom, and illusion."
Therefore, she is always the mother of all Bodhisattvas. Just as I was born from the right side of Queen Māyā in the palace of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu within this Jambudvīpa,
manifesting inconceivable and sovereign spiritual transformations, so it is throughout this entire ocean of worlds for all the Vairocanas.
The Tathāgatas all enter my body and manifest their birth through sovereign spiritual transformations.
Just as I am the mother of the Bodhisattva’s descent into birth here in Jambudvīpa, so it is likewise throughout the hundreds of millions of Jambudvīpas within the trichiliocosm.
Yet this body of mine is fundamentally non-dual; it does not abide in a single place, nor is it...
They dwell in many places. Why is this? Because they have cultivated the liberation door of the adornment of the illusory wisdom of the great vows of Bodhisattvas.
Just as I am the mother of the World-Honored One now, so too was I the mother of all the immeasurable Buddhas of the past.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable Bodhisattvas in their final existence who manifest [themselves] in this world.

"In all instances where they have manifested birth, I have been their mother. Thus, within this Bhadrakalpa of this world, during past times, I was the mother of Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha; and now, at the time when the World-Honored One has manifested birth, I am his mother.
Furthermore, in future ages, regarding Maitreya Bodhisattva, at that time as well, I shall likewise [be his mother]."

She was their mother. In this same sequence, she became the mother of all those who will attain Buddhahood within this trichiliocosm during the Bhadrakalpa, from Lion Buddha (*Siṃha*) down to Ruci Tathāgata.
Likewise, throughout all kalpas and across all the infinite worlds in the ten directions within this ocean of worlds, she has been the mother of all such beings.
To practice the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra for the sake of transforming all sentient beings, I manifest my own body and become their mother.

Good son, in ages past, beyond inconceivable kalpas, there was a kalpa named Pure Light (*Vimalaprabhā*) and a world named Sumeru Virtue (*Sumeruguṇa*), which contained ten billion sets of four continents. Within it, there was one...
In the four quarters of the world, there was a land named Siṃhadhvaja. Within it were eight billion royal cities.
Among them was a royal city named Īśvaradhvaja, where there lived a wheel-turning monarch named Mahātejas. To the north of that king’s city was a site of enlightenment named Pūrṇacandraprabha.
The deity of that site of enlightenment was named Maitreyaguṇa. At that time, there was a bodhisattva named...
Vimaladhvaja sat at the site of enlightenment, on the verge of attaining perfect awakening.
An evil Māra named Suvarṇaprabha, together with his retinue and an immeasurable multitude, came to where the Bodhisattva was.

That Wheel-turning Sage King of Great Majesty, having already attained the sovereign supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva, manifested a host of soldiers many times greater in number, who surrounded him.
At the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), all the māras were struck with terror and fled in every direction. Thus, that bodhisattva attained perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
When the deity saw this, he was filled with immeasurable joy and conceived the thought of the King as his own son; he then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
She made this vow, saying: "In whatever place this Wheel-Turning King may be born, until he attains Buddhahood, may I always be his mother.
At that time, that deity was none other than myself; the Wheel-Turning King is the present World-Honored One.
Since I first made that vow before him, this Buddha, the World-Honored One, throughout the lands of the ten directions...

Throughout all realms of existence, they take birth in every place, plant various roots of goodness, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, and transform sentient beings, even manifesting until they dwell in their final body.
In every thought-moment, throughout all worlds, they universally manifest the miraculous transformations of a bodhisattva’s birth;
they are always my sons, and I am always their mother. This great skillful means further endures for... [the kalpas].
Question: For what reason did the Bodhisattva’s mother pass away seven days after his birth? Answer:
It was because the lady’s lifespan had come to an end and her merit merited her ascent to heaven; it was not the fault of the Bodhisattva.

Previously, while the Bodhisattva was dwelling in Tuṣita, he observed that Queen Māyā’s life was nearing its end, with only ten months and seven days remaining. Therefore, he descended from Tuṣita through miraculous transformations to manifest [in the world].
Having entered the womb of his mother, by this reasoning it is not the Bodhisattva’s fault; rather, this is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

The Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins states: "It is the constant law for Bodhisattvas that once their mother has given birth to them, she passes away after seven days and is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" (the causes and conditions regarding the city of Devadṛśa are detailed in the twenty-first fascicle, under the section on the clan name; as for the *Balacakravartin*, he is the Iron-Wheel King who rules over the single continent of Jambudvīpa). Thus it is said.
Regarding those who possess the power of the wheel-position (the venerable Nanda is such a person):

if a monk who causes a schism in the Saṃgha declares what is not Dharma to be Dharma, knowing it to be the perception of non-Dharma when he breaks [the Saṃgha], and at the time of his formal proclamation, he then acts [thus].
To speak with the perception that it is not the Dharma, saying: "This is the Dharma"; or to speak with the perception that it is the Dharma when it is not the Dharma;
or to speak with the perception that it is not the Dharma when it is the Dharma—in this way one causes a schism in the Saṃgha and shall suffer in hell for an eon.
If one breaks the perception of dharma (*dharmasaṃjñā*) and speaks of dharma, saying "this is dharma," that person shall not fall into hell to suffer for one *kalpa*.

Doubts and other matters are as set forth in the Vinaya texts. Within this context, there are two occasions for breaking and speaking [of dharma]: even if it is merely a single instance of the perception of non-dharma (*adharmasaṃjñā*), one suffers the retribution of one *kalpa*.
This is because the mind is heavy, and thus it evokes the painful retribution of one *kalpa*. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* does not inquire [further].

Regarding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma: if one speaks of it as Dharma while perceiving it as Dharma, or speaks of it as non-Dharma while perceiving it as non-Dharma, one does not suffer for an eon;
this demonstrates that it is not a deceptive statement, because the mind is light and supple.
However, if one speaks of Dharma while perceiving it as non-Dharma, or speaks of non-Dharma while perceiving it as Dharma, one suffers for an eon; this constitutes a deceptive statement. Its...
Because the mental fetters are fierce and heavy, doubt is likewise so. Regarding the fundamental category:

only when one harbors the thought that one’s action is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*) at the very moment of performing the act of destruction does one give rise to the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-āpatti*) and also complete the karma of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*). Otherwise, one merely gives rise to the offense of immediate retribution but does not complete the karma of immediate retribution.

(As for the "offense of immediate retribution," it refers to the state where, upon falling into the *naraka* hell and undergoing punishment, there is never an interval [of relief]. If translated literally, it should be called "without interval" [*anantara*]; "immediate" [*ānantarya*]).

Regarding the term "Avīci" (無間): it refers to falling from the human realm directly into hell without any interval. Although the character "wújiàn" (無間) is the same, its meanings are distinct. In Sanskrit, it is called *avīci*, which means "without interval.

In Sanskrit, it is also called *ānantarya*, which means "falling without interval. "Without interval" (*wújiàn*) means being born and falling into hell immediately; "without gap" (*wúxì*) means that one must wait for another body before receiving the retribution. Because there is this distinction, the phrasing is divided differently.
There are eighteen matters concerning what is spoken and what is not spoken. As stated in the first section: dharma and non-dharma; vinaya and non-vinaya;

offense and non-offense; light and heavy; with remainder and without remainder; grave (sthūlātyaya—sthūlātyaya is termed "grave") and non-grave; that which is regularly practiced and that which is not.

"Regularly performed [rites]" (also called "ancient dharmas"; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "regularly performed rites" refers to the *jñapti-ekakarma*, *jñapti-dvitīyakarma*, *jñapti-caturthakarma*, the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the ordination rites for the fourteen types of persons).

[Regarding] "That which is not prescribed" (*a-prajñapta*): [Substances such as] salt were not prescribed by the Buddha; yet to say that eating them prevents one from proceeding toward *nirvāṇa* is to claim that what is not prescribed is prescribed. [The Buddha] did not permit long nails or hair; yet to say that nails and hair possess life is to claim that what is prescribed is not prescribed.

This applies to all precepts and *karmavācanās*: to prescribe what is not prescribed, or to permit what is prescribed. [Regarding] "That which is not taught" (*a-deśita*): [The details] are as explained in the *Ekottarika-dharma*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: there are fourteen matters that cause schism in the Saṃgha.

"Teaching what is not Dharma as Dharma" (*adharmaṃ dharmato deśayati*)—according to the commentary of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, this refers to five things that are not Dharma, yet being spoken of as Dharma.

To preach what is Dharma as non-Dharma (the Eightfold Noble Path is Dharma, yet one preaches it as non-Dharma); to preach what is not well-spoken Dharma as well-spoken Dharma (that which is "good" is the Vinaya; the five dharmas are not the Vinaya, yet one preaches them as the Vinaya);

to preach what is well-spoken as not well-spoken (the Eightfold Noble Path is the Vinaya, yet one preaches it as not the Vinaya); to preach an offense as no offense (the Buddha did not prescribe mental precepts, yet one says that the arising of the three poisons in the mind constitutes a violation of the precepts);

to preach no offense as an offense (not shaving the hair or clipping the nails, the Buddha said constitutes a violation of the precepts, yet one says that hair and nails possess life and thus to shave or clip them is an offense); to preach what is light...
Regarding what is heavy as being like the Utpala Dragon—because he plucked tree leaves, his offense was inexpiable—and on this basis claiming that killing plants and trees is always a grave offense;

regarding what is grave as being light—seeing cases such as those of Sūdena and Dhanika, where because they acted previously [under certain conditions], they did not incur a grave offense—and on this basis claiming that sexual misconduct and theft are minor offenses; regarding what involves a remainder (sa-avaśeṣa) as being without a remainder—where the four lower categories of offenses involve a remainder when committed, yet it is said they are without a remainder;

regarding what is without a remainder as being with a remainder—where the four grave offenses (pārājika) involve no remainder when committed, yet it is said they do have a remainder; and regarding the rules of constant practice as being non-constant.
To claim that the Dharma practiced (the Eightfold Noble Path, which is a practice constantly employed) is not a practice constantly employed;

to claim that what is not a practice constantly employed (the five dharmas, which are not practices constantly employed) is a practice constantly employed; to claim that what is not taught is taught (the four pārājikas are minor while the other sections are major—this is what is not taught, yet it is claimed to be taught);

and to claim that what is taught is not taught (the four pārājikas are major while the other sections are minor—this is the correct teaching, yet it is claimed to be not taught). [Note: "Teaching" (*shuo*) is also referred to as "instruction" (*jiao*).]

○ Regarding the *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (Methods for Settling Disputes):
Whenever a dispute arises, it should be settled according to the Dharma. Whether involving an individual or the Saṃgha, it should be eliminated in accordance with the Vinaya.

Originally, the four great elements have no master, and the five aggregates are not the self. Who, then, is the disputant who gives rise to contention? All phenomena are fundamentally empty. The multitude...

Conditions are but a provisional confluence; self and other are identical in essence. Where, then, is the "self" or the "person"? Since both person and self are empty, how can subject and object be established?
If one reflects deeply in this way, the dispute will naturally subside. Why rely on a sangha to eliminate it, thereby troubling the multitude with further debate?
To contemplate thus is to triumph over all Māras and enemies; how much more so for this foolish dispute, which would not otherwise cease?
A verse from the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* says:
"One might fight a thousand times within a single month, And in every fight, a hundredfold prevail over others;
Yet if one can take refuge with faith in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, One shall surpass those [victories] by sixteen times."
If one fights a thousand times within a single month, and in each fight wins a hundredfold over others,
yet another can take refuge with faith in the Dharma that is true and correct— this latter person will surpass the former by sixteen parts.

If one fights a thousand times within a single month, and in each fight wins a hundredfold over others, yet another can take refuge with faith in the Dharma that is true and correct— this latter person will surpass the former by sixteen parts.
If one can take refuge with faith in the entire Sangha,
they will surpass those who fight a thousand times within a single month by sixteen parts. If a person who fights but once can achieve victory a hundredfold,
one who contemplates the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) will surpass them by sixteen parts.
The Āciravatī River is as explained in the "Thirty Matters.
The Gaṅgā Lake.
It is also called the *Gaga* River, as explained in the *Śīlaskandhaka*.

Regarding the "place of offense," it is also called the "seeking of the characteristics of the offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu says of himself, 'I have committed this offense,' and later [returns...]"

If one says, "I did not do it," and the Saṃgha performs the *karma* of seeking the true nature of the offense for this person— this [is one of] the seven methods for settling disputes (as explained in the first section on the seven methods for settling disputes).

The *Madhyama Āgama* on the Six Roots of Dispute (*ṣaḍ adhikaraṇa-śamathāni*). The six roots of dispute are: first, malice and vexation; second, the bond of silence; third, stinginess and envy; fourth, flattery and deception;
fifth, lack of shame and lack of remorse; sixth, evil desires and false views. These evil natures are irrepressible. [From] the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
It is said: first, resentment and silence; second, an evil nature with a desire to harm; third, greed and envy; fourth, flattery and crookedness;
fifth, lack of shame and remorse; sixth, evil desires and false views. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: first, anger; second, affliction and harm; third, illusion and hypocrisy.
Fourth, stinginess and envy; fifth, adherence to views; sixth, the two views of extremes and false views. Regarding "anger" (*krodha*):
it is a change in facial expression that makes one terrifying to others. Regarding "malicious intent" (*vyāpāda*): it is the ability to harm and afflict others. Regarding "deceit" (*māyā*):

it is when the mind is not truthful and one falsely fabricates unreal matters. Regarding "stinginess" (*mātsarya*): it is to covet objects before one and not wishing to give them to others; this is called stinginess. Regarding "envy" (*īrṣyā*): it is to see... [text ends]

That which causes him distress upon obtaining [a result] is called envy (*īrṣyā*). Regarding views, "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is to grasp what one has seen as correct and what others have seen as incorrect.
Regarding extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), it is to view continuity as eternal and cessation as annihilation.
Regarding wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it is to slander and deny cause and effect (the rest is as explained in the *Ekottarikāgama*).
The six offenses that arise are as explained in the sixtieth fascicle of the Vinaya-mūla;
this concerns the four types of disputes and their erroneous interpretations.

Regarding the terms: *vacī-vivāda* (verbal dispute), *vaca* (speech), *vivāda* (dispute), *vivādavaca* (disputatious speech), *vaco-vivāda* (verbal dispute), *vaco-vivādavaca* (verbal disputatious speech), and *vivādavaco-vivāda* (disputatious verbal dispute).

These bricks or planks should measure one cubit in length and half a cubit in width. Break the earth into fine powder and arrange it in two rows, piling each portion separately.
Then, place one more lump on top; finally, take three lumps and enter the latrine with them.
Set them aside in one place. One is for wiping the body; the other is for washing the body. As for the method of washing the body:

one must first take the left hand and wash it with water, followed by cleansing it with earth (the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states that one should wash with the tips of two fingers—namely, the ring finger and the little finger—and cold water must be used.

Use one portion of earth to wash [the anus], one portion to wash the urinary opening, and one portion to wash the left hand. Once finished using them, they must be thrown outside the latrine;

Open the side latch with the right hand, then exit carrying the jar in the right hand—or alternatively, with the left.
Cradling a flask in his arms, he clenches his left hand into a fist. He may use his right hand to bolt the door and depart.
Upon reaching the site of the earth, he squats down to one side. If a seat is required, he measures out the space as needed and places the flask upon his left thigh;
he may press it down with his left arm (it is essential if there is a forked stick, which should be placed on top). First, he takes seven portions of earth from near his body and sets them aside.
Wash your left hand separately; thereafter, use the remaining seven portions, cleansing both hands with each one. You must wash the brick or wooden surface thoroughly.
When one portion remains, use it to wash the vessel; next, wash your arms, calves, and feet until they are all clean. Only then may you depart as you please.
This water from the vessel must not enter the lips. [End of section.]
In the chamber, one should rinse the mouth two or three times with water from a pure flask.
