"Bi" (蝙) is pronounced like "bian" (鞭); "fu" (蝠) is pronounced like "fu" (福). It is also called *shemishi* (蟙蟔), also called the "spirit mouse" (*lingshu*), and also called the "winged mouse. One—
It is called the "flying mouse" (*fei shǔ*). Due to regional dialects, it has many such names. Because it hides by day and flies at night, it is also called the "hiding-winged" (*fùyì*).
*Fúbiān* (bat) is its original name. Its fur is soft and gray; after five hundred years, it becomes white.

When its head grows heavy, it hangs upside down, hence the name "inverted-hanger. It is able to suppress its vital breath (*qi*); during the winter months, it does not eat because it is able to suppress its breath.
Therefore, they live for many years and are also called "Immortal Mice. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"In the past, on the shores of the South Sea, there was a withered tree in which five hundred bats lived in a hollow. A caravan of merchants stopped beneath this tree;

as it happened to be a time of wind and cold, everyone was hungry and frozen. They gathered firewood and dried butter, piling them up and igniting a fire beneath the tree. The smoke and flames gradually grew fierce."
The withered tree then caught fire. At that time, among the traveling merchants, there was a certain trader who, after midnight, was reciting the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
Although those bats were distressed by the fire, they loved the sound of the Dharma and endured their suffering without emerging.

Having passed away there, they were reborn according to their karma; all obtained human bodies, left home to practice and study, and, impelled by the sound of the Dharma, became wise and of sharp intellect, together realizing the fruits of sainthood and becoming fields of merit for the world. They lived in the vicinity of King Kaniṣka.
Together with the Venerable Pārśva, he convened five hundred worthies and sages in the kingdom of Kaśmīra to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
These were all, in effect, five hundred bats within a withered tree. (The character 柔 [róu] is pronounced róng.)
*Yàn* (燕): pronounced *yàn* (as in "elegant"). It is the swallow (*yǐ*). Its name calls out to itself as "yǐ," and thus it is called "yǐ" according to its own sound.
Those with a more frequent and slightly smaller call are named *hàn yàn* (Han swallows). Those with purple chests that are light and small are named *yuè yàn* (Yue swallows). [Their] chests...

The one with variegated black markings and a loud voice is called the *huyan* (Huhu-yàn). These birds all avoid the *wùjǐ* (Earth-Spirit) day when building their nests. It is distinct from the *jiānyàn* (Common Swallow);
they are not the same species. They are like small lattice windows.

*Li-cheng* (cut by *li* and *cheng*): the phonetic value is *ling*. It refers to the cross-bars or lattices between window frames; what is now called a *chuāng-líng* (window lattice) is this. *Héng-gài* (cut by *héng* and *gài*):
the phonetic value is *guì*. It means a staff or cane. The *Vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* states: "The window shutters were blown open by the wind. The Buddha said: "One should..."
A pivot was installed, and further, a bolt was placed above it; thus, it was difficult to open and close. The Buddha said, "One should use a 'ram's hoof' staff to open and close it.
[This concerns] the image of Maheśvara.

The character *ṭa* is also used as a head [radical], as explained above; it is now employed here as a seal (*mudrā*). A "seal" means "trust" (*śraddhā*), for it serves as a verification when dealing with objects.
Furthermore, it serves to establish a standard that cannot be altered. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:
"At that time, the bhikṣus had neither communal nor private property marked with any identifying signs. The Buddha said: "You may keep seals. In all cases..."
There are two kinds of seals: first, those for the community; second, those for private use.
If it is a seal for the community, one may have it engraved as an image of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, with two deer placed on either side, kneeling and crouching.
Beneath it, one should inscribe the name of the original donor who established the monastery. If it is a private seal, one should have it engraved as an image of a skeleton or in the form of a skull.

In order to inspire a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*) when seeing them, one is not permitted to fashion them from precious materials. One should instead use brass, red copper, white copper, ivory, or horn.
One must not carve them into images of men and women engaged in unrighteous acts (though the *Nidāna* states that wood is also permitted). The *Nidāna* says:
The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu should mark his robes with a sign of identification. [The bhikṣus asked,] "How should one mark them?
The Buddha said, "One should make a knot, or apply a spot of ink as a purification mark, or use other such signs of identification; only then should one possess them."

The Buddha said to those with three *vassa*: "I permit you to sit together on one bed if you are all of three *vassa* or more. The *Kṣudrakavastu* states: The Buddha said, "The old and the young should not sit in a mixed manner.
One who has no *vassa* may sit on the same seat as one who has two *vassa*; one with one *vassa* may [sit with one who has two]."

One may sit on the same seat as those who have completed three summer retreats (*varṣa*). If one has completed two or more summer retreats, one may sit together with those who have completed three or more;

this applies to all such cases. However, if one is in a layperson’s house and seats are difficult to obtain, one may even sit together with one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or instructor (*ācārya*), provided that an object is placed between them to prevent any doubt.
*Juàn* (pronounced *quán*, rhyme group *quán*): made by bending wood; this is called a *juàn*.
It refers to the place for washing one's feet.
The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu should not wash his feet anywhere.

The place for washing feet should be located in the southeast corner of the monastery, shaped like the back of a tortoise. At that time, the bhikṣus made it too smooth, such that it was unfit for scrubbing the feet.
The Buddha said, "It should be made rough. The commentary notes: This place for washing feet may also be used for bathing; this is the custom in the West.

These exist in all monasteries and in various places; they are neither large nor small, having no fixed size. They are constructed in the open air, sometimes as large as a bed or as small as half a mat.
Bricks are stacked around the perimeter to a height of about one chi. In the center, the bricks are laid in the shape of a tortoise shell.
It is plastered with lime and gravel, which cannot be washed away by water. A single opening is made on the side to allow the water to flow out externally for washing.
Washing the feet and the body is most essential for practical use.

Regarding the water basin, the Vinaya states: At one time, the bhikṣus suffered from the cold while washing their feet during the winter months. The Buddha said, "Place a wash-stand [to hold the water] when washing your feet."
The vessel: it should be washed inside the house. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states:
"If an elderly bhikṣu’s body is so weak that he cannot go to the place where one washes his feet, an attendant should be instructed to wash them for him. One should provide a foot-washing basin;
the vessel for washing feet must not be made of precious materials, but should instead be made of clay. It should be shaped somewhat like an elephant's foot treading upon the ground."
It should be high enough to support the feet. Alternatively, one may fashion it into the shape of a lotus pedestal. It must be rough and hard.
If it belongs to the community, after washing the feet with it, one should place it in a concealed, screened location. If it is a private item, it should be kept behind the door panel.
Sudatta, also called Sudāta, means "Good Giver" (Śubhadatta). This refers to his constant fondness for providing food to the poor, beggars, the solitary, and those without kin.
Because of this conduct, people of the time collectively praised his virtue and further named him Anāthapiṇḍada.
Anāthapiṇḍada-bhaṭṭi. This is translated as "The Elder Who Feeds the Destitute.

He was a high minister of King Prasenajit. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent; he accumulated wealth and yet was able to disperse it.
He rescued the destitute, aided the poor, pitied orphans, and comforted the elderly. At that time, people praised his virtue and called him 'Anāthapiṇḍada' (Feeder of the Destitute)."
His close friend was the elder Sudatta; his friend’s name was Sandhana, which in this language means "Pālita" (Guardian).
He was a wealthy and eminent elder of the city of Rājagṛha.
The city gate is called Śīha, or alternatively Śība, and also Śivaka; this translates as "Life-Sustainer" (Nenghuo). The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The gate is Śivaka. Regarding that gate deity, it was named Mṛdu-saṃjñāta in his previous life. The *Madhyama Āgama* states:
The deity guarding the city gate is named Madhupātra. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the deity guarding the city gate is named Madhubāhu.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* records that the Buddha said: "At that time, there was a heavenly deity at the city gate who addressed Sudatta, saying:
'Virtuous one, if you go to the place where the Tathāgata resides, you will obtain great benefit. Sudatta replied: 'Good man, who are you?'"
"Yes, O Householder," the deva said, "I am the son of the Brahmin Jyotiṣka, your former friend.

Because I felt great joy upon seeing Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana in the past, I have abandoned this body and been reborn as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Northern Heavenly King, specifically charged with guarding this city of Rājagṛha. Because of me...
"By merely prostrating before Śāriputra and the others and giving rise to a heart of joy, one can still obtain such a wondrous and excellent body;
how much more so when one shall behold the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, and prostrate to and make offerings to him. When the elder Sudatta heard these words, he was deeply moved.
He immediately returned by the same path to where I was.
"Qiáo kè" (僑客) means a traveler; "qiáo" (僑) is pronounced like "qiáo" (橋). It refers to dwelling as a temporary visitor or sojourner.
Jeta is translated here as "Victorious in Battle. This refers to his birth, as his father, King Prasenajit, had been victorious over foreign nations.
It is newly transliterated as Śītavana, or alternatively as Śīta, which means "Victory. The *Dṛṣṭānta-paryāya* (Piyu jing) states that King Bimbisāra was the first husband [of his mother].
The son of the [first] queen was named Vaiḍūrya. The son of the second queen was named Ki (this means "most excellent").

On the day Ki was first born, treasures were offered from the four quarters, all arriving at once. The King said, "Among the births of my sons, never before has there been such a thing; he may be named Ki.
Formerly, during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin, there was a man who went to a monastery and, after finishing his meal with the Sangha, gave a male and female slave.
He was given the task of sweeping the temple. From that time onward, he received immeasurable blessings among devas and humans;
now, having again become the crown prince of a king, he has encountered the Buddha and attained the Way.
"Deciding the price, deciding": this means to reach a final resolution. If a matter has been decided and finalized, there shall be no further reconsideration.
Now, as for the law for a prince, one must not speak falsely. Once words have been uttered and a matter is already determined, this is the law of former kings.
Therefore, Prince Jeta reviewed the old royal regulations and realized his words had been spoken in jest; he then set a price.

Consequently, he allowed Sudatta to cover the ground with gold coins as the purchase price. The *Record of the Western Regions* states: "Five or six li south of the city is the Jetavana, which is the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.
When the Elder heard of the Buddha’s merits, he conceived a deep sense of reverence and made a vow."
He constructed a vihāra and invited the Buddha to descend there. The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the site.
Considering Prince Jeta’s garden to be a pleasant and elevated location, he went to the prince and informed him of his intentions in full detail. The prince spoke jestingly:

He then sold the gold that covered the ground. When Sudatta heard this, his mind was suddenly opened and cleared. He immediately brought out the gold from his treasury and spread it over the ground as requested.

When there was a small portion remaining and the area was not yet fully covered, the Prince requested him to stop, saying: "The Buddha is truly a fertile field; it is fitting that he be sown with excellent seeds.
Thereupon, he established a vihāra on the empty space (the Sūtra says he spread the gold over the ground until it covered ten *qīng*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Sudatta took [the gold].
Gold was gathered and spread upon the ground. Within a single day, it had covered only five hundred paces;
before the gold had completely covered the site, Jeta spoke to Sudatta, saying, "As for the remaining unspread portion, I no longer require gold.

Please grant it to me, and I shall personally construct a gatehouse for the Buddha there, so that the Tathāgata may always pass through it when entering or departing. Thus, Jeta himself built the gatehouse.
Within seven days, the elder Sudatta completed a great monastery capable of housing three hundred people. It included sixty-three meditation halls and quiet retreats;
winter quarters and summer pavilions, each distinct from the others; as well as kitchens, bathhouses, places for washing the feet, and large and small latrines—none of which were lacking.
Regarding the matter of schism in the Sangha, it says: "The elder constructed the monastery until it was complete."
There were sixty locations. Outside the monastery, he constructed sixty-four separate courtyards, all of which were multi-storied pavilions.
Once they were completed, he provided them with all necessary furniture and requisites in full measure. He then dispatched a messenger to invite the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with a multitude of bhikṣus, traveled from the city of Śrāvastī to the monastery and sat upon the prepared seat. At that moment, the Elder...
Together with his retinue, surrounding him on all sides, they proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.

The elder filled a golden pitcher with water to wash the hands of the World-Honored One, but the water would not come forth. The elder became distressed and thought to himself, "I must have some karmic obstacles from past lives that cause this water not to flow.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew the thoughts in the elder's mind.
He then told him: "You have no karmic obstacles. This temple site was one where you yourself, in a former life, constructed a vihāra and offered it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
That you pour water here now is not at the original location of that former offering; therefore, the water from the jar does not come forth for you.
You should move and establish [the rite] at the site of the temple you formerly offered. The elder accepted this instruction.
He stood at his former place, and the water immediately gushed forth. The World-Honored One then uttered five kinds of wondrous sounds, offering extensive praise.
As he was about to pronounce a blessing, Prince Jeta thought to himself, "I pray that the World-Honored One will mention my name first.
Knowing this, the World-Honored One followed Prince Jeta's intention and addressed the bhikṣus: "This is the Jeta Grove, given by Jeta."
The Jeta Grove was given as a gift to the Buddha and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus from the four directions.
At that time, Prince Jeta, hearing the World-Honored One first call his own name, was filled with great joy and conceived a profound faith.
He constructed a temple gate for the Buddha made of the four precious substances. According to the *Faxian Zhuan*, one proceeds twelve hundred paces from the southern gate of Śrāvastī.
To the west of the road is the site where the elder Sudatta erected a vihāra. The vihāra faces east, with its gates and doors opening toward that direction.
On both sides of the courtyard stand two stone pillars; on the left pillar is carved the form of a wheel, and on the right pillar is carved the form of an ox.
The pond flows with pure water, the groves of trees remain lush, and various flowers of diverse colors flourish in a magnificent display. (Vaiśālī means "place of wandering.")
This is the monastery where the Saṃgha used to travel and reside).
The country of Vaḍḍha is also written as Vajja, as explained in the Cīvaravastu (the Chapter on Robes).

There were three close friends: first, an elephant; second, a monkey; and third, a francolin partridge (*kapiñjala*). [The character for] *kapiñjala* is pronounced with the initial *dīng* (丁) and the final *guā* (刮), followed by an entering tone (*rùshēng*).

The *Erya* states: "The *kapiñjala* is also called the *guānzhì* (crowned pheasant). Its shape is as large as a pigeon and resembles a female pheasant; it has feet like those of a rat, lacks a hind toe, and has a forked tail."
They are birds that fly in flocks with frantic haste; they are found in the desert regions of the north. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The *kāpiñjala* bird—this was when the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, took pity on the world’s lack of propriety and manifested in the body of a bird.
Śāriputra manifested as a monkey, and Maudgalyāyana manifested as an elephant; by means of these forms..."

Question: To establish the order of seniority and transform both the monastic and lay communities, so that they may know the distinctions between superior and inferior and high and low, this site still exists today, not far from the side of the pool at the Deer Park Monastery (Mṛgadāva-vihāra) in the city of Vārāṇasī;
a stūpa has already been erected there.

Regarding the matter of not bowing to laypeople, the Buddha said: "One should not bow to laypeople. The *Guang hongming ji* states: "Those who have left the household life do not maintain the etiquette of family members;

having departed from the secular world, they possess no ritual observances that would defile those remaining in the world. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "The dharma for those who have left the household life is not to [bow] toward..."
The king’s parents prostrate [to him], yet his six types of relatives do not show him respect, nor do ghosts and spirits pay him homage. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Among the various classes of celestial deities, none dare to seek or expect prostrations from a lay follower (*upāsaka*), just as no one dares to seek or expect acts of prostration from a bhikṣu who is like a sovereign ruler of a kingdom;
this is because they fear it would diminish his merit and shorten his lifespan."
As stated in the sūtras: The Northern Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa invited five hundred noble monks, including Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, to his own palace.
After providing them with offerings, he requested that they recite verses of aspiration for the merit of his gift, and further entreated them, saying:
"From this day forward, whenever monastics or lay followers come to my temple..."

"May all of you grant me this vow in verse. From this time forth, we and our retinues shall also, with single-minded sincerity, protect and uphold the True Dharma, ensuring that at all times the monastic and lay disciples of the Buddha shall never suffer harm.
At that time, the two Great Sages granted their request and proclaimed it to all monastics and laypeople.

There are those who uphold the Buddha’s precepts; from this day forward, even when entering a celestial temple, they should all offer verses of aspiration to the deities in accordance with the Dharma.
However, they have never been required to join their palms in respectful salutation. From such evidence, it is certain that the World-Honored One [did not intend for such acts].

It is not permitted to pay homage [to deities]. If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) delights in paying homage to celestial deities, they would then be no different from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), for they would be performing the actions of those who delight in and follow false followers.
Furthermore, if a lay follower pays homage to celestial deities, they would consequently come to cherish and revere the false doctrines that praise the gods;
they would thus be identical to those false followers who revere the gods, receiving false precepts and performing various [unwholesome] deeds.
Fellow laborers, through these means, they associate with false teachers; the causes for falling into evil destinies gradually become firm and increase.
From this point on, through successive lives, they continue to delight in practicing such perverse conduct extensively.
If those who serve as lay attendants worship celestial deities, they lead many sentient beings to great ruin. Those who worship the deities all say:
This lay follower is deeply conversant with the Buddha’s teachings, yet he currently comes to pay homage to the deity we serve; he must surely harbor reverence and faith toward that celestial being.
How excellent it is that we have taken refuge without error! Furthermore, there are those in the world who delight in the ultimate truth.
Investigating the Buddha’s teaching, one has not yet fathomed its truth. Upon seeing this, one gives rise to perverse attachments, claiming that the Buddha’s teaching resembles worldly secular texts;
because it cannot distinguish true principles and meanings, it causes such people to return to taking refuge in various heavenly deities.
By citing such arguments, they lead immeasurable sentient beings to increase their false attachments, which is called a great decline and loss. Furthermore—
Lay followers (*upāsaka*) do not belong to the celestial deities; rather, they are members of a heterodox faction who have joined together in submission.
They are not renunciants (*pravrajita*), and thus all [deities] ought to pay them respect. Therefore, it is logically established that lay followers should not prostrate to any celestial deities.
The *Nidāna* states: The Buddha said, "Monks (*bhikṣu*), one should not make offerings at the abodes of celestial deities. Nor...
Do not treat [the image] with contempt or arrogance. One should not damage a divine image, nor should one circumambulate a temple to the right, nor to the left.
If one happens to pass by on the road and must circumambulate to the right, one should recite a noble gāthā, clear one's throat, or snap one's fingers to alert the deity.
As the Vinaya states: "In the past, King Udayana, having been slandered by a sycophantic minister, spoke of Piṇḍola..."
When King Prasenajit received his prostrations, he did not rise to welcome him in return. Consequently, an evil thought arose within him, and he desired to go and kill him.

Piṇḍola, knowing that the king was approaching with such wicked intent, descended from his seat and walked seven paces to meet him. The king realized for himself that he had wrongly accepted the flattery of others;
he therefore requested forgiveness for his transgression and was thus spared from hell. However, because the monk had welcomed him, the king subsequently lost his throne seven days later.

Consequently, he was captured by a neighboring state that had raised an army; his feet were shackled and he was imprisoned for twelve years (the reasons for his failure to honor his sovereign and parents are detailed in the Guang hongming ji).

One should pay homage according to the sequence prescribed by the Vinaya; one should perform respectful salutation. This has not been repeated here. However, regarding the method of paying homage, it benefits both oneself and others.
How is this known? As the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "By means of paying homage and so forth, one brings about various benefits for others."
To cause others to be honored and respected by people is called benefiting others; it also causes others to follow one's example in showing respect and enables them to acquire merit.
Furthermore, when paying homage to others, one breaks down one’s own pride. Because this destroys unwholesome factors, it brings great benefit.
It also serves to manifest the virtues of others. Such are the benefits of paying homage and similar acts. In general...

In performing prostrations as an act of reverence, one must strictly adhere to the proper form; it is inappropriate to bypass the correct order, thereby constituting a breach of propriety, for both parties would incur fault.
Thus, the *Nèifǎchuán* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states: "The protocol for prostration must be conducted according to the teachings.

If a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) happens to be ahead of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), he must accept the prostration from the junior. The Buddha said: "There are two kinds of persons who deserve to receive prostrations: first..."
This refers to the Tathāgata and the two great elder bhikṣus; these are the sincere teachings from the Golden Mouth. Why trouble oneself with such unnecessary humility?
When a junior sees a senior, he must respectfully extend his homage; he should chant "vandate" and prostrate. The senior accepts the junior's prostration.

One may simply sit upright with hands folded (duǎngǒng). As for the term *kēlù* (the second character is pronounced *dì*, meaning "to extend"; it merely signifies a prayer that others may be free from illness), if one does not follow this principle, [it is improper].
Each would incur blame if they were to stand or sit according to their respective ranks without altering the established custom.

Since it is appropriate for the one of higher status to receive [the prostration], it cannot be that the junior should instead show reverence to the senior; this is the rule for the monastic community of the Five Indias.

How could there be such a thing as a junior wishing to pay homage to a senior, yet first expecting the senior to rise, while the senior receives the junior’s respect, fearing that the junior might harbor resentment? For this reason, they are hurried and constrained, firmly maintaining their dignity.
Being of low status, I do not dare to receive the prostration; how bitter, how bitter! Though I, the lowly one, seek to show reverence, I am unable to touch the ground.

Were it otherwise, it would be a violation of ritual propriety. Alas! To compromise the sacred teachings and to follow mere human sentiment—this would mean that the reception of respect deviates from the proper form.
This is truly worthy of profound reflection. Since this wave has spread for so long, who indeed could suppress it? The *Fenbie Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merit) states:
"In discussing the elder brother first and the younger brother later, Ājñātakauṇḍinya is taken as the eldest, and Subhadra as the youngest;
this is the essential principle of the stages of the Buddha-dharma. If one were to take intellectual brilliance and broad erudition as the primary criterion," [the order would be otherwise].
"This is indeed the Dharma of the Brahmins" (Kauṇḍinya is the same as Kauṇḍinya; Subhadra was the last person ordained by the Buddha at the time of his parinirvāṇa).
In the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Upāli requested of the World-Honored One:

"Venerable Sir, is it possible for one preceptor (*upādhyāya*), one instructor (*ācārya*), and one ritual master (*karmakāraka*) to simultaneously confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon two disciples? The Buddha said:
"Is it permitted? Between these two, which is greater? The Buddha said, "There is no distinction of greater or lesser. "Is it permitted for them to receive [the precepts] together with three people?

The Buddha said, "It is permitted. "Between these three, which is greater? The Buddha said, "There is likewise no distinction of greater or lesser. "Is it permitted for them to receive [the precepts] together with four people? The Buddha said, "It is permitted."
The Buddha said: "It is not permitted. Why? Because it is unreasonable to perform a *karmavācanā* for a group that does not constitute a formal assembly (*saṃgha*).
If one acts in this manner, one incurs an offense. Since these individuals have all received [the precepts] at the same time, there is no distinction between senior and junior."
"How should one pay respects? And what of those who manage monastic affairs or receive offerings? The Buddha said: "These various individuals should not be saluted by one another.
If one serves as a manager of affairs or receives offerings, one may accept them only as assigned by others.
Furthermore, the Buddha said: 'If that person's body is impure, one should not pay respects; if one's own body is defiled, it is improper to salute.'"
Furthermore, when he performs prostrations, one should likewise not accept them. There are two kinds of impurity:
first, the impurity of eating and chewing, which refers to chewing tooth-sticks or consuming various foods and drinks, such as roots, fruits, cakes, and vegetables.

Whether during the act of eating or after finishing, as long as one has not yet rinsed with pure water, it is all termed impure. Second, the impurity of defilement, which refers to [the presence of] excrement and urine...

Furthermore, when one is engaged in manual labor, attending to impure matters, shaving the hair, or until one has completed the purification of washing and rinsing the mouth—all such states are termed "impure.
When one is touched by such impurities, if one receives a prostration or performs a prostration to another...
All such acts incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Ten persons should not be saluted:
a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, an upāsaka, an upāsikā, one who has violated the precepts, one who is sleeping, and one who is eating."

If one pays homage to or joins one's palms before any of the ten aforementioned types of persons—including those who are defecating, urinating, or chewing a tooth-stick—one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
(This is the explicit teaching from the Buddha’s own mouth. In this region [China], it was not practiced, which has caused these rules of conduct to sink entirely into oblivion.

If there are those who set their hearts upon the True Teaching, they should together promote and propagate it, so that the Bequeathed Dharma of the World-Honored One does not fall into long-term decline. *Vandana* is translated here as "paying respect. The old term *vaṃdana* is an error, as explained in the *Ekottarika-āgama-khaṇḍa*).

For several years, he had not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) during the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*), counting those [extra] months as full years. The Buddha said: "It should not be done thus.
This means that from the seventeenth day of the fifth month onward, one receives the full ordination; therefore, it is not possible to receive it during the later retreat. If...
For one who receives [the precepts] during the middle watch of the night on the sixteenth day, once the three-month *varṣā* retreat is completed, it constitutes one year.

Among those of the same summer (*samanvāhara*), this is the minimum. Generally, once the three *karmavācanās* for receiving the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) have been concluded, [the year is counted].
The two teachers should immediately instruct him regarding the year, month, day, and time, so that he may recognize them: whether it be winter, spring, or summer;
on such a month and such a day; whether before or after a meal; at such a number of shadow-lengths; or by recording the count of the twelve terrestrial branches (*dvādaśa-rāśi*).
If he should later forget, they should further instruct him until he recognizes them. This is the method for the bhikṣu’s six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).

This refers to a single thought-moment within that [period]. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "Once the *karmavācanā* is concluded, one must immediately measure the shadow to record the distinctions between the five seasons.
Regarding these five seasons: first is winter, which lasts four months, from the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the first month;
second is spring, which likewise lasts four months, from the [sixteenth day of the] first month... [to the fifteenth day of the fifth month].

Six days. On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, the third is called the rainy season (*varṣā*), which lasts for only one month, from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the sixth month.
The fourth is called the concluding period (*anta-kāla*), lasting for only one day and one night, namely the day and night of the sixteenth day of the sixth month.
The fifth is the long period (*dīrgha-kāla*), from the seventeenth day of the sixth month to the ninth [day of the seventh month].
On the fifteenth day of the month—this sequence was established by the Buddha solely within the Vinaya teachings, clearly indicating an underlying intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*).
If one follows local customs, there may be three, four, or six periods.

Whenever those who have gone forth in the West or the South Seas meet for the first time, they ask, "Venerable sir, how many years of *varṣa* (rainy-season retreats) do you have? and the other replies, "So many."
If their *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) dates are the same, one asks at what time they entered; if the times are the same, one asks for how many days they have been there;
if the number of days is the same, one asks whether it was before or after the meal. If both were present before the meal, one then asks about the length of their shadow.

If the shadows differ, a distinction is made between senior and junior based on size; if the shadows are identical, there is no distinction of seniority. As for the seating order, it is determined by who arrived first, as established by the administrative officer (*karmadāna*).
One must then entrust the matter to those previously dispatched toward the West and inquire into this point; it is not like the Chinese practice of merely recording the month and day.

If one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) on the seventeenth day of the sixth month when the dawn light has just appeared, that person belongs to the same summer retreat (*vassa*) as others and is considered the most senior, because they were unable to undergo the subsequent summer retreat. If [it is] the tenth day of the sixth month...

When six nights remain until the end of the summer retreat, those who receive the precepts are considered the youngest among those of the same *varṣa* (seniority), because they have obtained the latter part of the summer.

(In this tradition, the calculation of months always counts the preceding month. Furthermore, according to the practice of the West, once one has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), one is called a *dhaureya* (translated as "junior master");
upon reaching ten years of seniority, one is called a *sthavira* (translated as "one of established rank") and is permitted to leave behind his formal reliance (*niśraya*).
He remains [in that state]. Furthermore, he may serve as an upādhyāya (preceptor). Whenever there is correspondence sent or received, it should be inscribed as:
"The śrāmaṇera [Name], the minor bhikṣu [Name], or the bhikṣu of established rank [Name]. This applies provided his learning has penetrated both the inner and outer [teachings].
When referring to one whose virtuous conduct is highly renowned, one should say, "The learned Bhikṣu so-and-so.
One must not say, "The monk so-and-so. "Monk" (saṃgha) refers to the great assembly; how could it be appropriate for a single individual to arbitrarily apply this term to four people?

In the West, such a practice does not exist. (Note: "So-and-so" [yǐ] is also written as "so-and-so" [jiǎ]. These are originally empty designations used for self-reference. Regarding the rules for clipping nails, it is stated: "The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to clip their nails at the edge of the skin. Not knowing how long they should be clipped, the Buddha said:
'They should be clipped to a maximum length of one grain of barley (the phrase *pīci* means 'at the edge of the skin'). The *Nidāna* states: "The Buddha said: 'The Saṃgha...'"
In a purified area (*śuddhasthāna*), if one discards fingernails or toenails, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The marks of an evil bhikṣu are that his head hair, beard, nails, and body hair are all long and sharp; these are the signs of one who has broken the precepts. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"There are five things that bring disgrace to a renunciant śramaṇa. What are the five? First, long hair; second, [long beard]..."
Their fingernails are long. Third, their robes are soiled and stained. Fourth, they do not know the proper timing. Fifth, they engage in much idle discourse.
As for why this is so, there are many bhikṣus who indulge in such talk. Furthermore, there are five other matters. What are these five?
First, people do not believe their words; second, they do not accept their teachings; third, they are unpleasant for others to behold; fourth, they speak falsely;
fifth, they incite strife between this party and that. These are the five things possessed by those who engage in excessive talk.
A bhikṣu should eliminate these five and be free from improper thoughts. Thus, O bhikṣus, you should act.
This is the training.

"Nián" (撚) is pronounced *niǎn* (with the radical for "beard" and the phonetic for "to cut"; the sound is *niǎn*). The *Zílín* states it means "to pinch and press. The *Tōngsúwén* states that one uses the fingers...
*Nie* (捏) means to twist or roll. *Zi* (髭), pronounced *zi*, refers to the hair above the mouth; that which is below it is called *xu* (鬚); that which is on the cheeks is called *ran* (髯).

*Lingqiao* (令翹), with the second character pronounced *qiao* (祁堯切), means "to raise up. The *Guangya* states: "Qiao means to lift up. Furthermore, *qiaoqiao* describes the appearance of something rising up beautifully.
"Painted eyelids" (huà yǎn liàn):
the character *liàn* is pronounced *jiǎn* (as in *jū-yǎn*). It refers to the skin on the outer upper and lower parts of the eyes.
Among the laypeople of the Western Regions, painting the eyelids was considered a mark of adornment; as for the Brahmins, they applied three lines across their faces as decoration.
"Ear-hanging" (ěr-chuí):
the first character is pronounced as *duō* (with the phonetic component *guǒ*). It means "earlobe.
"Anklet" (jiǎo-duàn).
*Juàn*: pronounced *chān* (as in *chān*). It refers to a jade ring. Sometimes it is made of copper, iron, or other materials. If it is made as a *chuàn*, then *chuàn* refers to an armlet.
A seal-mark (mudrā) refers to an engraved design made from precious materials that is set upon a finger ring to adorn the finger. —
The Six Teachers.
As explained in the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*, Piṇḍola is a name translated here as "Immovable" (Acala).
His clan name (*gotra*) was Bharadvāja; it is also rendered as Bharadvājaśi or [Bharadvāja]. Or...
*Tulaja* is a transliteration of a Sanskrit sound by various translators, which carries different weights of meaning.
It is translated as "swift" (*kṣipra*) or "sharp faculty" (*tīkṣṇendriya*). It is also called "Heavy Banner. Among the eighteen great clans of the Indian *brāhmaṇas*, this clan is one of them.
The Venerable One was originally a native of Kauśāmbī; his ancestors had served as royal ministers for generations.
The Prime Minister was intelligent, wise, and far-sighted; he served constantly as the National Preceptor. The *Udayana-rāja-dharma-paryāya* states:
"The son of the Prime Minister was named Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja. His appearance was full and beautiful, rare in the world.

He was intelligent and wise, widely learned and possessed of great knowledge. Benevolent and universally loving, his resolve was set upon rescuing those in suffering. He exhorted and transformed the citizens, exhausting [his efforts]..."
He practiced the ten wholesome paths of action, had faith and joy in the Triple Gem, left the household life to study the Way, and attained the fruit of full realization, and so forth.
Later, for the sake of the elder Jyotiṣka, he manifested supernatural powers and took a sandalwood bowl.
The Buddha then rebuked him with countless skillful means: "Piṇḍola, what you have done is wrong; it is not what should be done. Why did you take a piece of inferior wood?"
Pātra manifested his supernormal powers before the layperson. "From this day forth, for as long as your life lasts, I banish you; you shall not dwell in Jambudvīpa.
Thereupon, Piṇḍola, in accordance with the Buddha’s instruction, went to the western continent of Aparagoyānī to teach and transform the fourfold assembly.
He widely proclaimed the Buddha-dharma. The fourfold assembly of disciples in Jambudvīpa, longing to see Piṇḍola, petitioned the Buddha.
The Buddha permitted him to return to his seat; because he had manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the Buddha did not permit him to enter *nirvāṇa*.

He charged him to serve as a field of merit for the fourfold assembly during the age of the final dharma, to remain long as one worthy of offerings, and to protect and uphold the Buddha’s teachings until Maitreya descends to be born. Thus he was granted permission.
He entered *nirvāṇa*. He had also made a vow himself: whenever there is an invitation from anywhere within the three continents, he shall go.

Thus, the *Pinvilou Jing* (Sūtra on Inviting Piṇḍola) says: In the kingdom of India, whenever lay devotees (*upāsaka*), kings, or elders collectively arrange a universal assembly, they always invite the Arhat Piṇḍola Bharadvāja.
When making the invitation, one should burn incense and pay homage in a quiet place.
Prostrate. Facing Mount Malaya in India, call the name with a sincere heart:

"Virtuous Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, who has received the Buddha’s command to serve as a field of merit for those in the age of the Dharma's decline, I pray that you accept my invitation to eat here at this place.
If one is building a new house, one should likewise invite him, saying: "I pray that you accept my invitation to [dwell] in this house."
If one stays overnight on a bed or seat, or when the community of monks is invited for a communal bath, one should invite them, saying: "I pray that you will accept my invitation to bathe here.

Before dawn, one should prepare fragrant water, pure water, cleansing powder (*śāṭī*), tooth-sticks, and scented oil, adjusting the temperature to be neither too hot nor too cold according to the method of human bathing.
One should open the door and invite them inside, and then close the door, as one would for a person.

After the bath was finished, the assembly of monks entered. Whenever there is a communal meal or a ritual bathing, it is essential to invite all the monks, seeking liberation with a sincere heart, without doubt or delusion, and with pure faith; only then may they be entreated to attend.
Recently, there was an elder who heard it said that the Arhat Piṇḍola received the Buddha’s command to act as a guardian for the Dharma during the age of the Final Dharma.
The Field of Merit (Puṇyakṣetra). He then established a great assembly according to the Dharma and, with a sincere heart, invited Piṇḍola.

Beneath a woolen rug (*kūrca*), he spread flowers throughout, wishing thereby to verify [the truth]. When the meal of the great assembly was finished, he lifted the woolen rug and found that all the flowers had withered and turned yellow.

Distressed and self-reproaching, he did not know from where his transgression originated. Once again, with diligent and exhaustive effort, he questioned the Dharma Master and prepared another great assembly.

He held an assembly as before and scattered flowers, yet they all withered once again. He further exhausted his family’s entire fortune and held another great assembly, but it was still just as before.
Distressed and self-reproaching, he invited over a hundred more Dharma masters to seek the recovery of what had been lost and to repent for his transgressions.
He began by approaching a single elder among the senior monks; prostrating himself on the ground in four directions, he repented for his faults and failings.
The Elder told him: "You invited me three times, and I accepted each invitation. Yet you yourself had a slave block my way at the gate.
Because I was old and my robes were tattered, he thought I was a *vṛjji* or *tiṣya* śramaṇa who had been expelled and deemed unworthy to appear before him.
Since I had come because of your invitation, I intended to force my way in; your slave struck me with a staff, breaking my head and forehead."
"The sore on the right corner of my head is from that. He came for the second meeting as well, but I did not see him before;

when I again attempted to enter by force, he struck me on the head—the sore on my forehead is from that. He came for the third meeting as well and struck me as before—the sore on the left corner of my forehead is from that.
All of this was done by you yourself; why do you lament? Having said this, he vanished. Only then did the elder realize [the truth].
This was Piṇḍola. From that time onward, whenever people established merit, they all dared not again block their gates.
If Piṇḍola were to come, the flowers upon his seat would never wither.

When constructing new dwellings, rooms, beds, or couches, and wishing to invite him, one should always sprinkle the ground with fragrant water, light incense-oil lamps, and prepare new beds and new mattresses; upon these mattresses—
Spread out fine brocade upon it, and cover the cotton with white silk. At the beginning of the night, invite him according to the ritual and close the room.

Be careful not to treat him with negligence or to peek inside. Each person must be single-minded and believe that he will certainly come; when sincerity and devotion penetrate to the utmost, there is nothing that will not be realized.
When he arrives, a place for lying down will appear upon the mat, and in the bathhouse, a place for using hot water will likewise appear. [He] receives...
When invited to a great assembly, he may appear in the upper seats, the middle seats, or the lower seats, manifesting in the form of a monk wherever appropriate;
though people seek to distinguish him from others, they can never do so. Only after he has departed, seeing that the flowers upon his seat have not withered, do they realize it is he.
As stated in the aforementioned sutra, if one wishes to invite him, one may do so seven days or three days in advance.
From this day forward, having aroused a heart of sincere devotion, one must first sweep and sprinkle a quiet place, arrange seats and cushions,
bathe to purify the body, burn superior incense, hang silk banners and canopies, scatter various kinds of flowers, and hold an incense burner in hand.
With utmost sincerity and reverence, invite them as prescribed in the sūtras, requesting that they deign to descend and take their seats.

However, upon their seats, there must be no painted decorations, brocades, or ornaments of gold and silver; instead, flowers should be spread over them. Even though they are arhats, [they must be treated with such purity].
Nevertheless, one should receive the two hundred and fifty Pratimokṣa precepts together with ordinary monks. For this reason, one must not accept items such as variegated silks, gold, or silver;

nor may one exceed the measurement of one chi and six cun for beds and seats, nor place them in elevated locations (though there is no restriction on various ornamental jeweled vessels if they are for the purpose of making offerings to the Dharma-body). Furthermore, one must not fashion images in clay and place them upon these seats. Should [such an image]...
When the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) arrives, it would obstruct the seating; how could one possibly push aside a clay statue to sit?
If the monastery wishes to fashion a statue, they may establish a separate room to install the seat and perform offerings according to the Dharma; this will suffice.
If anyone offers money for the Holy Sangha, it shall be returned to the use of the Holy Sangha and used to procure alms bowls, spoons, chopsticks, bronze basins, hand towels, and fine plates.

Utensils and the like must be marked with vermilion inscriptions and shall not be used for other purposes. Nowadays, those who host vegetarian feasts often fail to treat the honored monks with sufficient reverence;
yet if one approaches this with a sincere heart, there is nothing that will not be moved to respond.

In the monasteries of the Western Regions and in the private residences of laypeople, a quiet and elevated location is chosen to construct halls and chambers for the honored monks, according to the four seasons, whether winter or summer.
The atmosphere [of this place] is such that offerings for the sustenance of beings are complete in every detail, as if serving a venerable teacher.
This is because the Holy Monk Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja is present and has not entered parinirvāṇa (some say Piṇḍola was a native of the country of Udyāna).
The Buddha Siṃhanāda prophesied that Piṇḍola would be foremost in the lion’s roar (*siṃhanāda*). The *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states:
"Among the disciples of the Buddha, he who is able to roar the lion’s roar is the foremost. The *Guṇavyūha-sūtra* states: "Regarding the sound of preaching the Dharma..."
He who possesses a lion’s roar is the bhikṣu Piṇḍola-bharadvāja. The *Pinfugongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merits) states that he is foremost among those who subdue non-Buddhists.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* likewise states that he is foremost among those who subdue non-Buddhists.
One who fulfills the True Dharma is the bhikṣu Piṇḍola.
The city of Ujjayinī is also called the kingdom of Vatsa. This country and its king are explained as in the *Cīvaravastu* (The Chapter on Robes).
"Brahmadatta" is a term from the Western [Indic] language; "Datta" is a word of this region. Combined, it is named "Pure Giver" (Jingshi). Pūrṇa.
He is also called Pūraṇa. These two elders, Pūraṇa and Rāṣṭrapāla, were ministers of King Prasenajit, as explained in the "Thirty Matters."
Guǎngbó (廣博):

*guǎng* is pronounced with the *bo* rhyme group and *gè* initial; *bó* is an entering tone (*rùshēng*) and means "vast" or "great. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a particular place where the ground was level, upright, and vast.
It was here that the World-Honored One manifested supernatural transformations to subdue the non-Buddhists. (From the *Zàshì lǜ*).
The Buddha said: At that time, King Prasenajit (King Pasenadi) entreated the World-Honored One, saying:

"I pray only that you will, out of compassion, subdue the non-Buddhists, bringing joy to humans and devas, causing those with faith to leap for joy, and extinguishing the source of sin and evil for those who lack it.
Thus he entreated the World-Honored One a second and a third time. The Buddha told the Great King: "A Buddha possesses five matters which are necessarily..."
It must certainly be done. What are the five? First, to cause sentient beings who have not yet resolved their minds to generate the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.
Second, for those who have long planted roots of goodness, to bestow the consecration and prophecy of the Dharma King’s heir.
Third, to cause [beings] in the presence of their parents to perceive the True Truth. Fourth, in Śrāvastī (that is, the city of Śrāvastī).
He manifested great supernormal powers. Fifth, it was only through the Buddha’s transformative influence that all sentient beings were fully liberated.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought: "In what place did the Buddhas of antiquity manifest great supernormal powers?"
"I am currently in Śrāvastī" (and so forth).
As for this lion throne made of the seven precious gems, it exists spontaneously through the Buddha's supernatural power. Furthermore, in various sūtras...
In the middle [of the assembly], wherever the Buddha sits, it is always called the "Lion Throne" (*siṃhāsana*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: Why is it named the Lion Throne?
Is it because the Buddha transforms himself into a lion? Or do real lions come? Or are lions made of gold, silver, wood, or stone?
Furthermore, since the lion is not a benign beast, it is unnecessary for the Buddha; nor is there any cause [for its presence].
"For that reason, you should not come. He replied, "This is merely called 'Lion'; it is not an actual lion.
The Buddha is the Lion among Men. Wherever the Buddha sits—whether on a couch or on the ground—it is called a 'Lion Throne' (*siṃhāsana*).
Just as the place where a king of the present day sits is also called a 'Lion Throne,' so too do people call a king a 'Lion among Men.'"
Furthermore, just as the lion is peerless and fearless among four-footed beasts, able to subdue all others, so too is the Buddha;
among the ninety-six types of paths, he is victorious over all and fearless. Therefore, he is called the "Lion among Men."
The *Fenbie gongde lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) states: "The reason the sūtra uses the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*) as a metaphor is that the lion is the king among beasts;

it always dwells in high places and does not occupy low ground, hence it is used as a metaphor for a high seat. Furthermore, because it takes up [the quality of] fearlessness, it is called the 'seat of fearlessness' (*abhaya-āsana*)."
*Fūsū* (枎疏).

The second character is pronounced with the *chú* (徂) radical and the *shū* (梳) phonetic; its sound is *shū*. "Fūsū" means that the branches and leaves are luxuriant. The *Yinyì* (音義) commentary to the *Hànshū* states:
"Fūsū" means distributed. The *Shuōwén* states: "Fūsū" means spreading out in all four directions.
Fúyàn (鳧雁):

"Fú" is pronounced with the *fēng* and *fū* initials as its phonetic. It refers to a water bird, the duck (*ānka*). It has markings on its back, is blue-green in color, has short legs, and a short beak;
it is what is known as the wild duck (*fú*) or domestic duck (*ānka*).
Yuan (黿):

The character for yuan is pronounced with the *yuán* rhyme (as in the word for fish), sounding like "yuan. The *Sāncāng* commentary states that it resembles a soft-shelled turtle (*biē*) but is much larger.

Some say that the female is the soft-shelled turtle, and when the yuan calls, the turtle responds. The *Bencao* states that it is the largest among turtles, and its shape resembles that of a *shǒugōng* (gecko).
It is one or two *zhang* in length, with scales and shells covering both its back and tail. It is skilled at attacking river bends and shores, and it bellows and roars at night;
mariners greatly fear it. Its elders can also act as malevolent spirits (*mèi*).

Its eggs are as large as those of chickens or ducks, and a single brood consists of one or two hundred. The *Yierya yi* states: "The *yuán* (or *yù*) is the largest of the turtles; its breadth may reach one or two *zhang*."
At the beginning of heaven and earth, the Jie-tan gave birth to the Xian-long; the Xian-long gave birth to the Xuan-yuan;

the Xuan-yuan gave birth to the Ling-gui; the Ling-gui gave birth to the Shu-gui. All creatures with shells are born from the Shu-gui. Thus, the [Yuan] is the progenitor of the shelled insects (*jichong*).
Although there is this theory, it is not necessarily so.

*Jiānrèn* (堅靭). It is synonymous with *rèn* (韌). Pronounced *rèn*. In ancient times it was written as *rèn* (肕). That which is both firm and supple is called *rèn*; it refers to that which is firm yet flexible and difficult to sever.
As the *Guǎnzǐ* says: "The sinews are *rèn* and the bones are strong. This is what that means.

In Sanskrit, *araṇya* is called *paṇḍavana*; here it is translated as "forest" (*conglin*). *Cong* (叢): pronounced with the initial *cu* and the final *hong* (徂紅切), with the tone of the level (*ping*) class.
It refers to the appearance of grasses and trees growing in clusters. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "a gathering. To write it differently as *cong* (藂) is incorrect.
Sini-sini is the general name for the Nirgrantha (Jaina) heretics; it is not the name of a single individual. Some call him Śāṇakavāsin;
this means "having an army. As for Pāṭaliputra, *pāṭali* is the name of his mother. *Persian*... [text truncated]
Pāṭaga is also called Pārśvaśiras, or Śūli; these are his names.
This man, having falsely contended with the Tathāgata regarding supernatural powers, was utterly devoid of any skill.
Filled with shame and humiliation, he tied a large stone to his neck and threw himself into a deep abyss. The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: Śāriputra addressed [the Buddha], saying...

The Buddha said: "How is it that the Tathāgata, who always says one must not kill any living being, even down to an ant, yet on the eighth day of the twelfth month at the Long Water River in Śrāvastī, competed in magical arts with the heretic Śūli?

First, he constrained him by means of his supernatural power, causing him to fall into defeat. That man was filled with shame and threw himself into the water to end his life; his eyes were seen sinking."
"He has passed away. Did he not rescue you, nor did he kill you? Then, addressing the assembly again, he said: "Śūli held fast to this evil dharma and deluded sentient beings.
Since his past roots of goodness have now matured, he has extinguished this evil body and been reborn in the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarśana).
Is this not truly a joy? My disciples, on this very day, you should prepare a pure bath to wash away the impurities of the body and maintain mindfulness."
To eliminate inverted views: if the body is pure, the mind is also pure. You resemble a hired servant who possesses neither compassion nor mercy.
The Buddha said: "O one of great wisdom, you have been able to ask about this essential truth for the sake of those who have not yet attained realization.
The Tīrthika Śūlika has accumulated the habit of false views throughout immeasurable ages, vowing to obstruct the True Dharma. In the past, under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara..."
At that time, while I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I passed through a village where many people suffered from leprosy and the dead lay scattered everywhere.
I gathered various medicines and provided relief according to their needs, so that all were healed. Among them was one man named Adharaka.
This was the study of that brahmin. Arrogant in his own many abilities, he refused to believe or submit. Only as death approached did he finally seek me out.
I said to him: "You should have sought treatment earlier; you would not take the medicine I gave you. Now that your life-force is about to end, you come seeking help again.
At this moment, even medicine cannot save you. He replied: "I am now unable to judge further."
"Superiority and inferiority—let us settle our victory or defeat together in a future age. If I should lose, I shall take my own life to seek rebirth as your disciple;
if you should be the inferior one, you shall become my servant. At that time, I replied, "Excellent, excellent!
Therefore, we have now been born in this land to meet one another. Our karma has ripened at the end of our lives, and we have reached this agreement through our shared resolve."

He spoke these words and lost his composure. Ashamed of his kinsmen, he threw himself into the water to take his own life. Although his body died, because his mind had given rise to goodness, he was born within my Dharma;
since there was a superior progress [toward liberation], I did not save him. The rest is explained in detail in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
(*Lì* [pronounced *lì*] refers to pestilence—the illness caused by the disharmony of the four seasons.)

The eighth day is the eighth day of the first lunar month. The *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Parables) states: "On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, the Buddha subdued the six heretical teachers through his supernatural powers.
The six teachers were defeated; they threw themselves into water and died. Thereupon, he extensively preached the Dharma and delivered all the non-Buddhists."
The non-Buddhists were subdued and converted. They addressed the Buddha, saying: "The Buddha has washed the impurities of our hearts with the water of the Dharma.
We now request that the Sangha bathe so as to remove the filth from our bodies; let this be our regular practice.

This is the origin of the current custom on the eighth day of the twelfth month to prepare pure fragrant water to bathe the monks (from the first day to the fifteenth day, it is called the Month of the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Great Supernatural Powers).
The summit of Mount Sumeru is the abode of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; it is the second heaven within the realm of desire, as previously explained.
As for the Brahmā heavens—

"Brahmā" means purity. The four dhyānas of the form realm are collectively termed the Pure Heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*). Now, the Buddha manifests his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), and his body reaches the Brahmā Heaven;
this refers to the Brahmā Heaven of the first dhyāna (as explained in detail previously).
Regarding the phrase "six times, eighteenfold shaking":
the six times refers to one movement, two risings, three surges, four quakings, five roars, and six strikes. The three types—movement, rising, and surging—are forms;
the three types—quaking, roaring, and striking—are sounds. Within these forms and sounds, one type from each category is cited here.

Therefore, it is said that there are "movements and tremors. Within these six types of reversal, each further possesses three characteristics, thus forming eighteen characteristics of movement and trembling.
"Movement" refers to the state of being unsteady and swaying. There are three characteristics of movement: when one direction alone moves, it is called "movement";
when all four directions move together, it is called "universal movement"; and when all eight directions move simultaneously, it is called "all-pervasive universal movement. As for "arising":

"Rising" refers to gradually ascending from below. There are three characteristics of rising: when it rises in one direction alone, it is called "rising"; when it rises simultaneously in all four directions, it is called "universal rising";
when it rises evenly in all eight directions, it is called "all-pervasive rising. "Surging" refers to suddenly leaping upward. There are three characteristics of surging:

when it surges in one direction alone, it is called "surging"; when it surges simultaneously in all four directions, it is called "universal surging"; [when it surges in all eight directions, it is called "all-pervasive surging"].* *(Note: The source text for the final phrase regarding the eight directions is incomplete, but based on the established pattern, this is the logical conclusion.)*
"Simultaneously surging" (*pāñcika-utsarpaṇa*) refers to surging everywhere. "Quaking" (*pra-kampita*) means the emergence of a deep, rumbling sound.

There are three aspects of quaking: quaking in one direction alone is called "quaking"; quaking in all four directions together is called "universal quaking"; and quaking simultaneously in all eight directions is called "all-pervasive quaking.
"Roaring" (*pra-rava*) refers to a fierce and violent sound. There are three aspects of roaring: roaring in one direction alone is called... [text fragment]...
"Roaring. Roaring in all four directions is called "Universal Roaring. Roaring simultaneously in all eight directions is called "All-Pervasive Universal Roaring.

"Striking" refers to the production of a crashing resonance. There are three aspects to striking: striking in one direction alone is called "Striking"; striking in all four directions together is called "Universal Striking";
striking simultaneously in all eight directions is called "All-Pervasive Universal Striking. These constitute the six reversals and eighteen tremors.
Also. *Lún* (wheel) and *gǔ* (hub):
the character *gǔ* is pronounced like *gǔ*. It refers to the hub of a chariot where the spokes converge; that is, thirty spokes all meet at a single hub. *Gǔ*.
This refers to that which dwells at the very center of the wheel and is the point where the spokes converge. *Huángyào* (晃曜):

"huáng" is pronounced with the third tone (*guǎng*) and "yào" is pronounced with the fourth tone (*huì*). It means radiance, brilliance, and expansive luminosity. It refers to what is called the illumination of light.
It is a luminous body.
As for the "three thousand great thousandfold world systems," these collectively constitute a single Sahā world. By means of one sun and moon...
Circling through the four continents, wherever its light shines constitutes one world (that is, one land). Within such a thousandfold world system,
there are a thousand suns and moons, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, four thousand sets of four continents, four thousand great oceans,
four thousand evil realms, a thousand Yama Kings, a thousand Four Heavenly Kings, and a thousand Trāyastriṃśa Heavens, up to a thousand...
Brahmā, this constitutes a small thousand-world system (meaning one thousand lands, like a string of one thousand coins).
One thousand such small thousand-world systems constitute a medium thousand-world system (meaning one thousand small thousand-world systems, like a string of one thousand strings of coins).

One thousand such medium thousand-world systems constitute a great thousand-world system (meaning one thousand medium thousand-world systems, like a string of one thousand strings of one thousand coins). It is so called because it is expressed by way of three successive thousands.
It is called a trichiliocosm. Within it, there are ten billion Sumeru mountains, four continents, suns, and moons, up to the Brahma heavens;
these together are collectively termed a single trichiliocosm, universally designated as the Sahā world.
This is entirely the realm where a single Tathāgata manifests his transformative influence (as detailed in the commentary on the phrase "four continents" within the thirty matters).

"Benefiting sentient beings" (Lìyì zhòngshēng) was the name of an ancient king; he is none other than the present King Śuddhodana. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*) states that his name was Śuddhodana.
The name Huishi (Wisdom-Matter) was that of the Queen of an ancient king; she is the present-day Lady Māyā. A sutra states:
"Her name is Sūryaparā."

The Lamp of Wisdom was the crown prince of an ancient king. Later, he succeeded to the throne and extensively practiced *dāna* (generosity), exhorting others to cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).
This was the World-Honored One practicing the bodhisattva path in a former life as a great king. The Sūtra says "Nāpa... [and so forth].

Luo-man (羅滿) means "wisdom-light" (*prajñā-āloka*). "Lamp" carries the meaning of "light. [This phrase should originally follow the entry for Kūṣmāṇḍī; it is placed here at the beginning for the sake of clarity.]
As for Hārītī, she was Hārītī in a past life. As for the present Hārītī, formerly,
on a mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, there dwelt a yakṣa deity named Sata, who protected the king, his ministers, and the people.
The assembly was never subject to famine. Within his own clan, not long after he had taken a wife, a daughter was born who was of exquisite beauty and a sight that all who saw her loved.
All the yakṣas rejoiced, and thus they gave her the name "Joy" (Nandā).
As she gradually grew up, there was at that time in the northern kingdom of Gandhāra a yakṣa named Pañcāla.
She was named Khaṇḍikā. She took Prahlāda as her husband.

Due to the force of the habitual tendencies from the evil and perverse vows she had made in a previous life, she said to her husband, "I desire to take and eat all the children—both boys and girls—born among the people currently residing in the city of Rājagṛha.
Her husband forbade it and would not permit it, but her mind did not accept this, and she harbored resentment.
Be silent for now. Later, he gave birth to five hundred sons in succession. The youngest was named Priyaputra (Beloved Son).
Relying on his sons' power and strength, he sought to commit unlawful acts. Although his husband repeatedly exhorted and instructed him, he ultimately refused to accept his words.
He then began to take the children born within the city of Rājagṛha—both boys and girls—in succession and eat them. The people were filled with anguish and distress, not knowing what was happening.
When calamities and misfortunes occurred, the king heard of them and was struck with wonder; he consulted diviners and learned that they were the work of yakṣas.

He immediately prepared food and drink and performed sacrifices in every place, yet the disasters were not averted. At that time, the guardian deity of the city spoke to the people in a dream, saying:
"You men and women have all been devoured by the yakṣa Prahlāda;

you should go to the place of the World-Honored One, for the Buddha shall subdue whatever calamities and sufferings you face. The people replied to the deity, "Since he has taken our sons and daughters as his food, he is a wicked and murderous yakṣa;
how can he be named 'Joy' (Prahlāda)? Because of this, everyone thereafter called him [the Yakṣa]...
When the people of Rājagṛha heard this matter concerning the yakṣiṇī Hārītī (the Sūtra calls her Hāritī;
she is the one now known as Guizimu), they all went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and said to him: "World-Honored One, this yakṣiṇī has for a long night wrought harm;
she steals our newborn sons and daughters to eat them. We pray only that the World-Honored One [will intervene]."
"Have compassion for us and act as our subduer. At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the request and covered his beloved son with his alms bowl.
The yakṣī, not seeing her beloved son, beat her breast and wept in grief, searching for him everywhere.

He traveled through cities, towns, mountains, rivers, and lakes, as well as the four continents, the hells, the palace of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, and the summit of Mount Sumeru, yet he could not find him anywhere.
He then appealed piteously to the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, who replied, "You should go quickly to the presence of the World-Honored One and take refuge in him;
this will enable you to see him. Hearing this, he rejoiced and went to where the World-Honored One was.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said, “World-Honored One, I have been separated from my young son for a long time.
I pray only that, out of compassion, you will allow me to see him. The Buddha asked, “How many sons do you have? He replied, “I have five hundred sons.
The Buddha said, “If one of those five hundred sons were missing, what suffering would there be? He replied, “World-Honored One, if I were to—”
"Today I do not see my beloved son; he will surely vomit hot blood and meet his end.

The Buddha said, "If one does not see even a single child among five hundred sons, one undergoes such suffering; how much more so for the loss of another's only son? You stole and ate him—how great will be that suffering?
He replied, "That suffering would be many times greater than mine. The Buddha said, "Since you clearly understand the suffering of being separated from those you love..."
“Suffering! How can one consume the children of others? He replied, “I only pray that the World-Honored One will instruct me.
The Buddha said, “You may receive my precepts; grant safety to all the people currently within the city of Rājagṛha.
If you can do this, you shall see your beloved son. He replied, “World-Honored One, from this day forward, I shall abide by the Buddha’s instructions.”
He bestowed fearlessness upon them all. At that time, the Buddha caused her to see her beloved child.
Then Hārītī took refuge in the Tathāgata and requested to receive the precepts. The multitude of people in the city all attained peace and happiness, being freed from all anxieties and distresses.

Having received the precepts, she had nothing to eat; therefore, the Buddha instructed the assembly of bhikṣus that at every mealtime, they should set aside a portion from the end of their rows for her.
He ate a single plate of food and called out their names; he caused both [the father] and his sons to eat their fill. He further entrusted them with this charge:

"Within Jambudvīpa, at the dwellings of monks and nuns, until the Dharma and Vinaya have ceased to exist, you must always, day and night, protect them with a diligent mind so that they do not decline, but may abide in peace and happiness. At that time, the bhikṣus requested the World-Honored One:
[The Buddha] said: "Hārītī, what karma did she previously perform to give birth to five hundred sons, to suck the vital energy of people, and to devour the children born of the people of Rājagṛha?
The Buddha replied: "In the distant past, when there was no Buddha in the world, a single Pratyekabuddha appeared among men.
At that time, a great festival was being held in the city of Rājagṛha, and there were five hundred people [there]."
Each of them adorned themselves, took various foods and drinks, and accompanied by music, they proceeded together toward a fragrant garden.
On the way, they encountered a pregnant cowherd woman carrying a jar of curd-milk. The people said to her, "Come dance with us;
let us enjoy ourselves together. She then joined them in dancing. Due to this exhaustion, she immediately suffered a miscarriage. The people continued on toward the garden, while the woman...
While dwelling there in sorrow, she purchased five hundred mangoes with curd-milk. At that time, the Pratyekabuddha approached;
seeing him, the woman prostrated at his feet, offered the fruit as a gift, threw herself upon the ground, and with palms joined, made this aspiration:
"By the merit of this offering made to this true field of merit, may I, in the future, be born into a royal [family]."
In the city of Śrāvastī, I used to seize and eat every boy and girl born within its walls.
That cowherd girl of that time is now the yakṣiṇī Hārītī;
because she made a wicked vow after offering five hundred *āmra* fruits to a pratyekabuddha in the past, she has now been born in Rājagṛha as a yakṣiṇī and has given birth to five hundred sons.

They inhale the vital essence of people and devour all the men and women within the city (as recorded in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*; the details are found in that text and are not fully recorded here).

*Zōngliàn* (綜練). *Zōng* is pronounced with the *qièyùn* "zuò" (作) and "nòng" (弄); *zōng* is in the departing tone (*qùshēng*). It means to practice. *Liàn* is also written as *liàn* (鍊). To refine is called *liàn*.
This refers to being skilled in practicing various arts so that one's mastery of ritual procedures is precise and mature; hence it is called *zōngliàn*.
Explanations of Terms and Meanings in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume 34. Phonetic Transcriptions:
*Xuānxiáo* (諠囂):
The upper character is pronounced *xuān* (as in *xuānwēn*), meaning clamor. The lower character is pronounced *xiáo* (as in *yáoxiáo*), meaning noisy bustle.
*Kù* (pronounced like *gǔ*) refers to the hub; it is that toward which the spokes converge.
*Fú* (pronounced like *fǒu* with a departing tone) refers to the spokes; they converge upon the hub. The spokes gather together at the hub.
*Wǎng* (pronounced like *wǎng*) refers to the rim; the outer circumference of the wheel is called the rim.
*Chuī-lǚ*: The upper character is pronounced *cuī*; it refers to rafters and cross-beams. The lower character is pronounced *lǚ*; it refers to the continuous wooden joints at the ends of the rafters.
*Huì*: The pronunciation is *wèi*; it means "category" or "kind.
*Dié*: The pronunciation is *dié*.
*Pǐ* (upper tone): the sound of *pǐ*; it means to destroy or ruin. *Chè* (lower tone): the sound of *cè*;
it means to split or crack. *È* (tone of *è*): the sound of *è*; it means to grasp or hold, or to seize.
*Dàn*: identical to *dàn* and *dàn*; it means to eat or consume.
In "suǒxiè" (瑣屑), the first character is pronounced as suǒ; the second is pronounced as xiān in the entering tone.
In "mán" (鞔), the pronunciation is màn.
In "yī" (欹), the pronunciation is yī.
*Yi* (圿) is pronounced with the initial *gu* and the final *xie* (cut), sounding like *jie* (戞). It refers to dirt or grime.
*Wei* (萎) is pronounced like *hui* (穢); it means not fresh.
"Spreading in four directions" refers to extending the hands and feet while prostrating upon the ground.
The character 渧 (dì) has the upper phonetic *lì* and the lower phonetic *dì*. The character 惋 (wàn) has the phonetic *wàn*;
it signifies a cry of astonishment or lamentation.
*Huì*: The sound of a bird pecking. *Yàn*:
The same as *yàn* (wild goose). *Qí*:
The same as *qí* (pronounced *qí*); it refers to the edge of a curved bank.

*Pēng-kě*: the upper character is pronounced *pēng*. It refers to the sound of stones crashing together; it also refers to the sound *pēng-bàng*. The lower character is pronounced *kě*, and also *kǎi*.
It denotes the sound of things striking against one another.
