*Vinaya Piṭaka*, Fascicle Fifty-two.
The five paths are also called the five destinies (*gati*): namely, devas, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings. If one speaks of six paths, the asura destiny is added;
it is not mentioned here because the single path of the asuras is subsumed within the realm of the devas.

Regarding the realms of humans, animals, and ghosts, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Long after the Buddha’s passing, as the sūtras and Dharma were transmitted, after five hundred years there arose many differences;
some spoke of five destinies (*gati*), while others spoke of six destinies. Upon examining the meaning of various sūtras, [one finds this to be the case].
There ought to be six realms of existence. Because wholesome karma has superior, middling, and inferior degrees, there are three good destinies;

because unwholesome karma has superior, middling, and inferior degrees, there are three evil destinies. If it were otherwise, there would be three types of retribution for the evil while there would be only two for the wholesome, which would be contradictory.
If there are six realms, there is no contradiction in principle. Therefore, these asuras [belong here].

At the time of the causal stage, harboring a mind of suspicion and jealousy, although one practices the five constant virtues, because of the desire to surpass others, one performs the ten wholesome actions of the lower grade,
which brings about rebirth in this realm of the body of the Way.
Śiṃśapā is also written as Śiśapā, or sometimes as Śiśivā. This wood is hard and solid, with a very lustrous texture;
as it does not exist in this region, it is not translated [into Chinese]. It is also similar to yellow boxwood (huángyáng). King Bimbisāra once fashioned an almsbowl from this wood.
[Someone] offered an alms-bowl to a bhikṣu. The Buddha said: "You should not keep it; this is the practice of non-Buddhists. The *Mahā-śāstra* states:

"A wooden bowl retains grease and filth because it is impure; therefore, its possession is not permitted. A clay or iron bowl that has not been fired [with lacquer] is also not permitted to be kept, because such a bowl does not retain grease due to the lack of firing.
As for the Buddha’s own use of a stone bowl and his prohibition against bhikṣus keeping one, it was because of its heaviness.
Therefore, the Buddha’s strength from suckling as an infant surpassed that of eighty thousand white fragrant elephants; thus, [the bowl] was not considered heavy.
Furthermore, it was the almsbowl of a heavenly king and was difficult to obtain. Moreover, he wished to distinguish the Buddha from his disciples.
The country of Vāgati is also rendered as Vākṣatī and Vāgadha, as explained above.
The Vatsiputriyas...
They are also called *vatsa*, as explained in the first chapter.
*Licchavi* is also called *likṣā*, as explained in the first chapter.
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is also called Nigaṇṭha Nāthaputta,
as explained in the *Śīlaskandhaka* (Chapter on Receiving Precepts).
He is also known as Satyaka Nigaṇṭhaputra.
In the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, [the name] is translated as "Fire-seed" (*Agnivaiśyāyana*). Master Yuan states: *Satya* means "existence.
As for *Nirgrantha*, the full form is *Nirgranthajñātiputra*. *Nir* means "not"; *grantha* means "bondage.
This refers to a class of non-Buddhist practitioners who go naked and starve themselves, considering this to be having few desires because they are not bound by food or clothing.

Now, according to our examination, "Nirgrantha" is the general designation for the heterodox sect of the *Vītarāga* (those who have severed ties), while "Saccaka" should be understood as a specific name or perhaps his clan name (*gotra*).
The rest is as explained in the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*.
*Fēngnáng* (韛囊):
*fēng* is pronounced with the *bó* and *mài* rhymes, sounding like *bài*. It refers to a leather bellows (*wéináng*). It is also called a *nángdài* (sack-bag) or a *gǔnáng* (drum-bellows);
all are made from tanned hide. This is the kind used by smiths to blow fire, similar to a wind chest. Thus it is.
Xuànqì (鏇器):
Pronounced jiàn (如賤). It refers to a lathe or revolving axis. This means using a cord to rotate an axis in order to carve objects into round vessels. Xūn bō (熏鉢):
[To fumigate a bowl].
The Buddha said: "I permit you to make a brazier—whether of brick, tile, or jar—and coat it with various kinds of clay.

Mix apricot seeds and hemp seeds into the clay, level the ground with ashes, and prepare a site for fumigating the bowl. Set up a support and place the bowl upon it; then cover the bowl with the brazier."

One should fill the four sides with ash and press it down with the hand to make it firm. Alternatively, if one fills the four sides with firewood or cow dung and burns them, one should perform the fumigation in this manner.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "The Buddha permitted the making of a bowl-fumigation furnace; [it may be made] of sesame seeds..."
If one takes sesame seeds, crushes them, and uses the paste to coat the surface of a bowl-oven, placing the bowl inside to fumigate it;
once this oven has finished fumigating the bowl, it should be carefully handled so that it does not encounter rain. The *Nidāna* states:

At one time, there was a bhikṣu who possessed an iron bowl that had become stained, damaged, and full of cracks and holes. He reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "In general, regarding the keeping [of bowls]..."
"An iron alms-bowl should be thoroughly fired. At that time, the bhikṣus piled up a great deal of firewood to burn the bowl, and it was immediately damaged and broken.
The Buddha said, "It should not be done in this way. When firing the bowl with fire, it should be placed inside a cage to be burned.
They did not know how to make such a cage. The Buddha said, "There are two kinds of cages: one is made by a craftsman..."
[They] made [them]. There are two ways: by having a craftsman make them, or by making them oneself. Regarding "having a craftsman make them," this refers to a potter.
Regarding "making them oneself," sometimes one uses a blockage (a stopper) or a jar; having broken it, one places it on the ground and strikes it until it shatters. The Buddha said:
"Fill it with ashes, have someone hold it, and then, using a nail, gradually bore holes through it. Thus it was fashioned.
There were two sections [of the bowl]. At that time, he did not apply clay to the exterior. The Buddha said: "One should use straw and bran to make a paste and coat it all over.
He did not use any material to smear or polish the interior. The Buddha said: "One should use hemp dregs to make a paste, smear and polish the interior, and wait for it to dry.
However, the fired bowl still had not yet acquired its proper color. The Buddha said: "Place rice bran inside and cover it with a basket."
[The bowl] was smeared with mud around its rim. He then placed the bowl on the ground to fumigate it. The Buddha said, "One should use a support to hold it up and place [the fire] above it.
When the matter was the same as this, [he found that] the support was thin and small, so the bowl would stick to it.
The Buddha said, "It should be supported high so that they do not touch each other. It still did not take color. The Buddha said, "It should be washed frequently, and then..."
It burned even more intensely, and smoke issued from within the basket. The Buddha said, "One should block the opening with ash.
He then piled up cow dung into a large heap; when it burned, it damaged the bowl. The Buddha said, "One should stack the cow dung and set fire to it from the top.
Not knowing whom he should send to watch the fire, the Buddha said, "A bhikṣu should personally keep watch. If there is another obligation, he may entrust it to another bhikṣu."
The bhikṣus looked [at the ground] and then departed. Because they were burning their bowls on the ground, many insects were harmed. The Buddha said, "One should sprinkle and sweep [the area] clean.
Therefore, I now permit the bhikṣus to keep a bowl-smoking rack and whatever items are required for this rack;
using them in this way constitutes no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that one should use the kernels of the āmalaka fruit or the kernels of the khadira tree.
*Gumo*. Bamboo-root incense (*gumo* refers to cow dung). A bhikṣu named Wanzi drew a thousand-armed Vaiśravaṇa (the *wanzi*) on his almsbowl.
The Buddha said, "You should not do so. He had drawn his own name upon the bowl.
The Buddha said, "It should not be done. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "In general, one should not write one's own name upon an almsbowl.
If one makes such a private mark, there is no offense" (the circumstances for this are found in the third fascicle of the *Nidāna*).

Regarding the character "wan" (萬), it refers to the Indian character for ten thousand, and not to the Chinese characters for ten thousand (萬) or the auspicious *svastika* (卍). However, the Vinaya does not specify the actual form of that character; according to...
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one or two examples are briefly cited; both are signs of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s auspicious myriad virtues.

Master Yuan’s commentary states: throughout the upper and lower sections of the sūtra, according to the Chinese edition, there are seventeen characters in total that are all pronounced as "wan" (myriad).
For instance, the Sanskrit letter *u* represents the auspicious mark on the Buddha’s chest; the letter *ṛ* represents... [text fragment ends].
The mark of auspicious and supreme virtue arises from the hair curling to the right; it resembles the shape of the letter *ṃ*. If one writes it as *ṛ*, it is likewise a mark of virtuous sound.
It was originally not a Brahmi script, but rather a creation of this land, much like the *svastika* (卍), which is fundamentally not a letter.
It was this very symbol that the Sovereign provisionally established during the second year of the Changshou era of the Great Zhou dynasty.
It is inscribed upon the celestial body. "Wan" (萬) refers to ten thousand; it signifies the gathering place of the ten thousand auspicious virtues. (The character 虒 is a scribal error for 虒).
*Niú shǐ* (ox-dung). *Tóng shǐ*, *shǐ*, *shǐ*. Pronounced *shǐ*; it means excrement. The *Biography of Yaśas* states:

"According to the local customs of the Western Regions, because oxen can till the soil and produce all things, ox dung is considered pure. [Thus,] Brahmā, Śakra, and the ox [are all associated with purity]."

They established temples side by side to enshrine them. Because the Buddha accords with sentient beings, they were treated equally as objects of purity (those who require yellow oxen; water buffaloes are unfit for use).
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make a bowl-bag. It should be made with a strap to carry over the shoulder. The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "One should make a square cubit-sized cloth bag;

lift its two corners and place the bowl inside. Short loops should be attached to the corners so that when one goes out to beg for food, it can be carried. This prevents [the bowl] from being obstructed.
Dust and soil. Furthermore, it is easy to lift and carry. The commentary states: "In China recently, there has been no such bag for the bowl.
By leaving a pointed corner at the bottom, the bowl remains steady and does not shake, unlike a flat cloth which, when moved, causes [the contents] to spill over.

When making it, one should take cloth measuring two small cubits (chi) square; the sides should be trimmed away, and horizontal straps should be attached. When used, it is extremely practical and secure."
It is stable. The *Neifa zhuan* (Biographies of the Inner Dharma) states: One may take a cloth approximately two chi long and one chi wide;
fold both ends toward the center and sew them together at the meeting point. Attach a single strap to both ends, just one *zhai* (span) in length.
Place the bowl inside it, covering the mouth of the bowl so that dust and dirt do not enter. Because its base is pointed, the bowl does not shift or turn. This...
This is the style for the alms-bowl bag. The bag used for storing the bowl when not on an alms-round—during ordinary times—is different from this;
it may be made as a bowl-cavity or a bowl-cage to store it, following the design prescribed in the Vinaya. This shall not be described in detail here.
*Zhǐtā* (指沓): Pronounced *tà*.
It refers to the thumb-guard used when sewing clothes. It is also called *wéitā* (韋沓) or *wéitāo* (韋韜).

This refers to making it from leather; in common parlance it is called a "leather finger-guard. In ancient script it was written as [韋*沓]. It resembles the leather finger-guard used for archery today.
It is an archer's finger-guard.
*Zhě* (赭) is pronounced *zhǐ yě qiè*, with the phonetic value of *zhě*. According to the *Sāncāng*: "Zhě" refers to red earth; it is also called white plaster (*báisàn*).
[The character for] "shang" is pronounced with the initial *qie* (cut) and the final *shàn*. It refers to white earth; it is also called white chalk (*báihuò*).
It is a yellowish-white color like gold, and resembles mica (*yúnmo*) in its crystalline structure. Its surface is striated and can be split into a thousand layers; it is highly prized by painters.
It is said that it is produced in the Yin Mountains. There is gold in the Yin Mountains; because the essence of the gold is infused [with sulfur], realgar is produced.
There is also a variety that is black, with a color like iron.
*Śābarā* grass:
*śā* is pronounced with the *shi* and *che* initials combined, sounding like *she*. *Śābarā* means "illusion" (*māyā*) in this language.
*Kiṃśuka* grass.
The four characters *an*, *qi*, *ji*, and *jia* are all phonetically close to the Sanskrit original (the character *jia* is pronounced with a half-vowel).
The tradition states that the Buddha’s broom was made of *kāśa* grass; the broom was over three feet long and about seven inches in circumference.
However, its specific plant form is unknown, and as it does not exist here in this land, it cannot be translated.
*Maṇika* (in Sanskrit: *parisrāvaṇa*), which is translated here as "water-strainer. The Buddha said:
"I permit the making of a water-strainer bag shaped like a ladle, or triangular, or made as a *maṇika*, or as a straining jar. The term *maṇika* is not clearly defined [in this context].
Explaining it according to the characters: *Hong* (宏) means vast and great. *Kuo* (墎) is the same as *guo* (郭), meaning the outer wall surrounding an inner city.
If one uses *kuo* (廓), it refers to stretching what is small to make it large; this is called *kuo*. As for the current term *hong-kuan* (宏墎), its form is not yet understood;

I suspect it may be a foreign word (*hu-yu*). Alternatively, one might fashion a frame from materials to take on the shape of a city wall; or one might fashion a frame from bamboo or wood and place a bag within it.
In the middle [section], there is that which resembles a tube; its meaning is defined by being square or round. As the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"It is also permitted to keep a water-strainer tube (*parisrāvaṇa*). It may be made of copper, iron, bamboo, wood, ceramic, or stone. Its mouth should be covered with fine cloth.

The use of discarded rags (referring to a cloth with one end tied and the other end used for pouring water) is not permitted. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* says: At one time, there was a bhikṣu who was straining water for the great assembly. Subsequently...
They became weary from the exertion. The Buddha said, "If the assembly is large and the water supply is insufficient due to the delay, one should construct a water-strainer."
Not knowing how to make it, the Buddha said: "Whether made of copper, iron, or clay, it should be fashioned in the shape of a bowl with a hole at the bottom."
It should be about the size of a cup, shaped like a lotus pedestal, and approximately four finger-widths high. At the bottom, it should have many holes as large as coarse chopsticks;
the top is wrapped with felt or silk cloth and bound with fine cord. Water is filtered through it.
When finished using, wash it, cover it, and dry it in the sun so that it does not quickly deteriorate (the rest is as explained in the section on the ninety matters).

If one reads "lāo" (with the initial *l* and final *-ao*), the pronunciation is "láo," meaning "to take. To submerge and take up [an object] is called "lāo. Master Ying says that it is a borrowed sound for "lìdǎo" (力導);
in Guanzhong it is called "mò" (磨), while in Shandong it is called "lāo. It is made by weaving thorny branches to flatten clods of earth.
The bhikṣu Yebatu was a bhikṣu who performed services for various non-Buddhist (tīrthika) teachings. The Buddha said: "One should not serve other various non-Buddhist teachings.
What are called 'non-Buddhist teachings' refer to the ninety-six types of doctrines in the Western Heaven (India), as well as those in this land (China).
The teachings of the hundred schools stop at the cultivation of the person; they are termed "external. The teachings of the three vehicles aim to still the delusions of the mind;

they are termed "internal. The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* states: "Those whose learning deviates from the principle of the Truths, who follow their own deluded sentiments, and who do not turn back toward internal awakening, are called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Master Kumārajīva said: "Those of heterodox studies who are able to engage in great debate are termed..."

They are also non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Among the non-Buddhists of the Western Regions, there are eighteen kinds of great scriptures, namely the Bhikṣu-lakṣaṇa, Sāṃkhya, Veda, and so forth.
Furthermore, all the seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijña*) likewise possess their own scriptures."
Magical arts and skills: namely, the four Vedas; the six Aṅga spells; knowledge of the sun, moon, and five planets;
the original treatise on dreams; earthquakes; the speech of ghosts; the speech of birds; the language of hand gestures; and the speech of four-footed beasts and those possessed by spirits.

The treatises on statecraft, physiognomy, divination of fortune and misfortune, the conjunctions of the sun, moon, and five planets, medicine, divination by charts and calculation, numerology, divination by lot, song and dance, and music—these and other such treatises on arts and crafts.
(As for the various other dharmas practiced by non-Buddhists, they are as described in the *Madhyama Āgama*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa, immeasurable..."
At the age of one hundred, there were certain śramaṇas who associated with kings, ministers, and elders;

they practiced divination and astrology, diligently pursued the art of medicine, kept male and female slaves, and possessed gold, silver, lapis lazuli, *musāragalva*, agate, crystal, pearls, coral, amber, jade, and conch shells; they studied various arts and crafts, such as that of the painter.
Masonry; the making of books and teaching them; various types of root-cultivation; sorcery, incantations, and illusions; the compounding of medicines; performing as singers and musicians;
adorning the body with perfumes and flowers; playing at dice and go; and learning various crafts and skills—if there is a bhikṣu who [engages in these].
"One who is able to distance themselves from such evil matters should be called my true disciple. Furthermore, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Those who have left the household life should cultivate the study of wisdom and investigate the sūtras;
they must not peruse the texts of external paths, such as those of the Lokāyata. They should always dwell in mountains, marshes, or secluded, quiet rooms, practicing meditation and paying homage."
[He] recited: "To sever the heterodox and manifest the orthodox is the doctrine you uphold. Furthermore, you said:

'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be śrāvaka disciples who are ignorant and violate the precepts, delighting in inciting strife and contention. They will abandon the twelve divisions of the sūtras and instead read and recite various non-Buddhist texts, prose and verse compositions, and manuscripts.
They will accept and store all manner of impure things, claiming that these are permitted by the Buddha.'"
Such a person trades fine sandalwood for tiles and wood; exchanges gold for brass; exchanges silver for tin;
exchanges silk for coarse woolen cloth; and exchanges nectar for virulent poison. As the *Mahā-śāstra* says:
"Studying non-Buddhist texts is like using a knife to cut mud; the mud is not formed, yet the knife is only damaged. It is also like looking at...
The sunlight causes the eyes to become dim. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Just as when a person gazes at the sun, their vision becomes unclear;
so too, when one contemplates the scriptures and treatises of non-Buddhists, it causes the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) to become impure.

Conversely, when one contemplates the sūtras and śāstras of the Buddha-dharma, it causes the eye of wisdom to become clear and pure. This is because contemplating the mundane teachings of outsiders..."
It is like grasping a monkey: it only produces filth. If one seeks the Buddha-dharma through reflection, it is like refining pure gold:

the more it is refined, the purer it becomes. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If a bodhisattva abandons what has been taught by the Buddha and fails to study it, instead practicing the heterodox treatises of external paths or worldly scriptures, this is called an offense. It is a grave offense; it is an offense that is defiled."

[The precept] begins: If one is a person of superior intelligence who is able to receive and study [the teachings] quickly and attain immovable wisdom (*akopyajñāna*), and within the course of a day and night constantly devotes two parts to studying the Buddha-dharma and one part to external treatises, this is called non-offense.

If, however, one takes pleasure in worldly classics, heterodox paths, or false teachings and does not abandon them, nor forms the intention to discard them, this is called an offense. This constitutes a grave offense.

This constitutes a transgression arising from defilement. The *Fayuan* states: "If a student of the Buddha-dharma abandons internal [practice] even for a moment to seek the external, they immediately incur guilt.

Even if one understands the principles and practices, such [external study] may only be practiced temporarily; it is permitted only to subdue non-Buddhists, after which one must still cultivate weary detachment."
One should advance in the cultivation of internal practice, striving to ensure its increase and excellence. If one becomes biasedly attached, it will destroy the True Dharma.

For now, let us briefly discuss those of middling and inferior capacity who, possessing meager learning and shallow understanding, claim their wisdom surpasses others. They give rise to great arrogance, displaying an unrestrained and haughty demeanor;
they treat all with contempt, as if encompassing heaven and earth, and they sit with insolent ease before their teachers and elders, shouting commands at their superiors.

The Way is fundamentally one of harmony and integration; to be a monk, one must be reverent and compliant. Since your mind and form have already become contrary and opposed, how can you constitute the Jewel of the Sangha?
Some are devoted solely to reading secular classics, singing songs, playing the lute or chess, and chanting the *Shi* and *Shu*; they thus waste their days in vain.

The Dharma and medicinal teachings of our inner school take the salvation of sentient beings as their primary urgency; its texts are profound and its principles deep, with language that is ornate, esoteric, and vast. One who is able to understand this...
A single phrase can expound immeasurable meanings; yet among the thousands of fascicles of new and old sutras and treatises, I have never once examined them.
I have diligently studied non-Buddhist texts day and night as if fearing that laypeople would mock me for being ignorant and failing to study secular classics.
How much worse it is, then, when worldly people question me on the meaning of the scriptures and I am unable to answer?

To be unacquainted with external affairs while dwelling within is not yet sufficient cause for shame; but to lack understanding of internal matters while remaining within is a disgrace all the more profound.
This is truly because we are in the age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*), when human life has become increasingly brief, impermanence brushes shoulders with us, and one cannot plan for tomorrow.
I fear that once one enters the dark paths, it will be difficult to emerge for many kalpas; should one encounter the Buddha-dharma again, there would likely be no way to see it.

Although the Sūtras and Vinaya permit a small portion of study in external teachings for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhists, this is taught for those of superior intelligence who have first mastered the internal [teachings] and are further made to know the external.
Their eloquence is sharp and incisive, their speech is grounded in the classics, and they have extensively investigated both the internal and external traditions.

To be worthy of serving as a teacher requires that one attains what is described in the sutras. To subdue those of external paths, I have now examined myself and found myself incapable in every undertaking.

My consciousness is perpetually closed, while my ignorance and stupidity are ever-present. If I cannot even save myself, how can I benefit others? With neither form nor fragrance penetrating me, how can I distinguish beans from wheat?
I pray that you will allow me to withdraw into private life, so that I may examine myself and pursue true learning.

*Zuò zhù* (作櫡) is synonymous with *zhù* (箸). Pronounced *zhù* (with the second tone, *chí jù qiè*). It refers to eating utensils, namely spoons and chopsticks. It is incorrect to write it separately as *jìn* (筯). [Also:
*dēng shù* (燈樹), "lamp-tree"].
The *Mūlakalpa* states: "Single-layered lamp-stands, double-layered lamp-stands, and multi-layered lamp-stands may all be kept.
The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: "When bhikṣus light lamps during the summer months, they harm insects. The Buddha said: 'One should make a lamp-shade.
One should make the shade from bamboo strips and cover it with thin cloth. If such materials are difficult to obtain, one should use paper, silk, or thin [cloth]. "
[One] covers it with an object. The *Nidāna* states: The Buddha said, "One should not leave a lamp burning through the night.

Once you have finished putting away [the items], you may extinguish it" (meaning that when one has finished any task, one should extinguish the lamp). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one wishes to extinguish a lamp, one is not permitted to blow it out with the mouth.
The commentary says: This is because there are fire-eating insects; it is feared that the breath from the mouth might harm the insects. Therefore...
One must not blow upon [the food] with the mouth.

"Jiànròu" (雜糅) means mixed. "Jì" (粈) refers to two forms. "Tóngrěn" (同忍) is pronounced with the second tone; "róu" (柔) is in the third tone. "Ròu" (糅) means mixed. This refers to various colored substances being combined.

The *Jí* (Collection) says: "To intermingle. This refers to the account in the *Biographies of the Former Han*, which states: "The heterodox and the orthodox were intermingled; the loyal and the sycophants advanced together. This is precisely that point.

The Buddha did not permit the intermingling of non-Buddhist doctrines with the Buddhist scriptures. He permitted the recitation and study of the Buddhist scriptures according to the linguistic conventions and dialects understood within each country.
The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (*Záshì*) states: "A bhikṣu should not chant or draw out the tones when reciting the Dharma. If...
If a bhikṣu utters the *chanda* sound while reciting the scriptures, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*vayadharmika-apatti*).

However, if the local dialect of a region requires the drawing out of sounds, there is no offense when doing so. (The term *chanda* refers to the method of recitation used by Brahmins: they draw out the sounds for a long duration, marking the pauses by pointing at the air with their hands;
the teacher first chants, and the others follow in recitation.)
"Gambling with objects" means betting.
The group of six bhikṣus gambled with others. The Buddha said, "One should not do so. When they obtained objects, they took them.
The Buddha said, "One should not do so. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in such matters as these.
Upon arriving, they immediately used their robes, alms bowls, waist-bands, and other belongings as stakes for gambling.
When their secular companions saw this, they were all filled with derision and shame, saying: "O worthy ones, can you truly act like worldly folk?
To come here on some business and then gamble away your robes and bowls is not reasonable. They replied: "What is unreasonable about this? Are we eating leeks and garlic, or drinking wine?"
He remained silent. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "It is indeed appropriate that the layperson reproaches you with shame.
A bhikṣu must not gamble with objects; whoever does so incurs a *vinayātikrama* offense."

*Gaidǒu* (蓋枓): The pronunciation is *dǒu*. It refers to the "pitcher" (*dǒu*) atop a pillar. Regarding the *gǒngdǒu* (拱枓), it is here used by extension; it is also written as *dǒu*. The *Abhidharma* states:
"The *gaidǒu* receives and contains the *gàizi* (蓋子); it serves as the support for the *gàizi*, because the *gaidǒu* is able to sustain all the *gàizi*."
It means "not to scatter or destroy. What the common people call a "parasol support" (*sǎntuō*) is precisely this.
"Gài" (canopy) refers to something vast; it should be read as "héng" (horizontal). "Héng" means a railing or enclosure.
Māluya, also called Māluta, or Mālukya (formerly transcribed as Māluka).
This is a type of creeper that grows by trailing and winding itself around trees until they die.

What is currently called a *gai* (umbrella) refers to the handle of an umbrella. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: "There are two kinds of umbrellas: first, those made of bamboo; second, those made of leaves.
The handle shall be two cubits long, or equal in length to the canopy itself. When entering a village, one must not hold it upright; rather, it should be carried tilted."

Remove [the "sun" radical from the character for *qù* (to remove). Its width is as explained in the section on "Wearing the Three Robes Neatly" among the "One Hundred Matters. The original form of the character *yú* (at) was derived from wood; by removing the branches and retaining the base, it takes the shape of a wooden trunk.
This is a semantic compound used interchangeably with *gān* (pole). *Gān* refers to a straight stalk of bamboo).
*Jiè* (作楬):
pronounced *jiè* (as in 傑), it refers to a wooden stake. It may also be written as *shuān* (栓) or *jué* (橛); pronounced *jué* (as in 掘), it refers to a piece of wood, and is likewise a stake.
*Zuòtàn* (錔託):
the second character is pronounced *tà*. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "To cover or conceal something with gold or silver.
The *Guangyun* states: "The knob or head of a vessel. This is what is meant here.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus carried staffs while walking through the air, which led to the derision and resentment of the laity. Consequently, the Buddha did not permit their use.
However, when the bhikṣus were traveling on the road and encountered venomous creatures such as snakes, scorpions, and centipedes, those who had not yet abandoned desire all became terrified.
The Buddha said: "I allow you to carry a *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) and shake it. If it is made of bamboo, one may place pebbles inside the tube and shake it to make a sound;

or if it is made of split bamboo, one may shake it to produce a sound. Regarding the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kaṭhina-vastu*: because a bhikṣu entered another person's house while begging for alms in silence...

Seeing the private affairs of others, the Buddha instructed them to make a sound [before entering]. They then made a "ha-ha" sound and entered amidst a clamor, which led the laity to mock and reproach them.
The Buddha then prohibited this. Consequently, they began to knock on the door with their fists to make a sound before entering; the family members asked them in astonishment why they were doing so.
"Why do you knock on my door? he asked, but they remained silent and gave no answer. The Buddha said, "One should not knock on the door; one should instead make a *khakkhara* (monk’s staff).
The bhikṣus did not understand. The Buddha said, 'A ring should be attached to the head of the staff, circular like the rim of a cup, with a small loop fixed upon it.'"
He shook [the staff] to make a sound as a warning, whereupon the dog came out and barked; he struck it with the *khakkhara*. The Buddha said, "One should not strike a dog with a staff;
one should raise it to frighten it. At that time, there was a vicious dog whose anger intensified when frightened.

The Buddha said, "One should take a handful of rice, throw it on the ground, and let it eat. When he went to the house of a person who lacked faith and shook the *khakkhara* for a long time, [the man] eventually became resentful.
[The monk] became weary, yet the family members did not come forward to inquire after him. The Buddha said: "One should not shake [the staff] for a long time;

it may be shaken two or three times. When no one comes to inquire, one must depart immediately. For these various reasons, this staff was prescribed. In the Sanskrit language, its name is *khakkhara*;
translated here, it is called a *xi-zhang* (staff of sound). This is because when it is shaken, it produces a ringing sound (*khakkhara*).

Because it produces the sound of metal, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* calls it the "Sound Staff" (*śabda-daṇḍa*), naming it after its sound; as for its substance, it may be made of copper or iron and is not restricted to tin.
According to the *Kṣīrapāṇi-ḍaṇḍa-sūtra*, it is called the "Wisdom Staff" (*jñāna-daṇḍa*) or the "Virtue Staff" (*guṇa-daṇḍa*) to manifest holy wisdom.
It is the root of practicing merit, the insignia of the sages, the clear record of the worthy, and the upright banner of the Dharma for entering the Way.
It establishes the resolve for the meaning of mindfulness; all Buddhas of the three periods of time uphold it.

Although that sutra provides layered explanations of its name and meaning through exquisite metaphors, these are merely provisional illustrations and not its original title. Furthermore, the text of that sutra is not the definitive version.
This text has no translator’s name. Master Sengyou appended it to the catalog of the Eastern Jin period. Its phrasing is largely fragmented and its terminology is not that of the Buddha’s word;
therefore, the masters of antiquity judged it to be spurious. Its meaning contradicts the Tripiṭaka, and its regulations exceed those of the established norms. The wise should examine this:
one should adopt the general path, eliminate errors and anomalies, and not accept long-standing misconceptions as correct. One ought to aspire to [the authentic].

The original intention was established by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing, who witnessed it with his own eyes in India. He recorded the fundamental regulations in his *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas).
Therein he states: "As for what is called a 'staff' (*zhàng*), the Sanskrit term is *khakkhara*, which carries the meaning of 'emitting sound.'"

When ancient translators rendered it as "xi" (cīvara), they intended to capture the sound produced by striking the staff. Thus, the term "carrying a *cīvara*-staff" (*zhíxī*) was used according to their preference.
From my own observation in the West, the *khakkhara* held there consists of a single iron ring at the top, approximately two or three inches in diameter, into which a tube is inserted;
this tube is about four or five finger-widths long. The shaft is made of wood, its thickness varying according to custom, and its height...

It should reach level with the eyebrows. At the bottom, install iron rings approximately two cun wide; these rings may be circular or flat, joined together at the center so as to accommodate the thumb.
There may be six or eight of them, which are passed through and secured upon the thighs. Whether made of copper or iron is left to one’s preference.
The original intent of this design was to protect against cattle and dogs while begging for food; why then undergo such hardship and exert oneself in carrying [the bowl] with such laborious effort?

Furthermore, some [staffs] are made entirely of iron; with four-pronged heads fixed atop them, they are heavy and cumbersome to carry, and extremely cold and slippery—this was certainly not the original intent of their design.

Moreover, when Western monastics go outside or when begging for alms, they place all their jars, bowls, and personal belongings on one shoulder, cover them entirely with their *kāṣāya*, and depart carrying an umbrella. This...

All of these are the rituals for renunciation within the Buddha’s teachings. Having leisure, one carries a *spraśaka* (touch-bottle) and a leather sandal bag in hand, with a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*) slung across the shoulder;
one’s every movement is composed and serene. The *Śakuntaka-sūtra* provides a fitting analogy for this state.

As for the City of Kings and the Bodhi Tree, Vulture Peak and the Deer Park, the site where the *sāla* trees turned white like cranes, and the desolate place of the magpie’s mound—[all these are sacred sites].
When the ritual regulations were established, people gathered from all four directions by the thousands every day, all following this same custom.
As for Nālandā Monastery, the virtuous and learned monks all traveled by carriage; none rode on saddled horses. This was also the case at the Great King’s Monastery.
All [the monks] were likewise the same. All their requisites were carried by men, or they were held up by young novices.

This is the ritual custom of the monastic community in the West (now, in the city of Hila in Northern India, there is a Buddha’s mendicant staff with rings made of iron and a shaft made of red sandalwood).
Máo (毛): preceded by the radical for "hair" [Xiào* Máo].
Pronounced xiāo. It refers to the appearance of hair. The *Tōngsùwén* states: "Dense hair is called máo-máo. It is also written as xiào.
"Jīvañjīvaka" refers to the tail-feathers of a bird (the character [召*毛] is pronounced *tiáo*; it denotes the appearance of feathers).
When the bhikṣus were making fans, they suffered from insects, grass, dust, and dew falling upon their bodies. The Buddha said: "I allow you to make fans using grass."
If made from tree bark or leaves using thread, or if made from scraps of cut silk, a bhikṣu who obtains a tail-whisk (*puccha-vālavyajana*) may keep it;
thus the Buddha said. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, however, the use of one made from white yak-tail hair or horsehair is not permitted.
Once the robes have been dyed to change their color, their use is permitted.
Regarding the *elirāya* robe, this refers to wearing a robe while carrying items, as if one were wearing a white robe.
The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "At that time, the group of six bhikṣus [acted as follows]... [The text continues with the description of how they tucked up their robes.]
When a monk carried a heavy load on his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment), he walked with his head bowed, causing his body to be exposed and drawing the resentment of laypeople.
The Buddha said: "From this day forward, I do not permit monks to carry heavy loads while folding up their robes. However, if there is a specific cause or necessity, it is permitted."
Regarding matters for the Three Jewels, those who must fold and tuck [their robes] should manage it well themselves so that their bodies do not become visible.
*Pātra-śī-dhāraṇa* (or *pātra-dhaṃsapa*). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: *pātroṇa-paṭa*. In the Han language, this means "silk. This...
It is also the name of a country. Since the robes originate from that country, they receive this name. (*Dhen* [pronounced *tan*];
*pātra* is the same as *bō*).
*Tottara* is explained as in the first fascicle.
*Duò* (馱):
pronounced like *tuó* (駝). It means to carry or bear. Generally, when any animal carries an object, it is called *duò*. — Upāli.
Upāli: The meaning is as explained above. This youth Upāli is not the same as Upāli, the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
Now, while the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, he had the youth shave his hair. The youth then entered the fourth dhyāna.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that there were three causes and conditions for which this youth dared to shave the Buddha’s hair.
First, he shaved his hair because of ignorance. Second, he shaved it through the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, desiring that they might attain the fourth dhyāna.
Third, he shaved it so that future generations of sentient beings would know that shaving the hair possesses great merit.
Gopāli is also called Gopāla, and again Kūbara; this is translated as "Cow-Protector" (Niu-hu).
He was the son of King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Ujjayinī. The details of his life story are explained extensively below.

Regarding the construction of a stūpa and its significance, this has been explained above in the section on the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma). At that time, the faithful lay devotees thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would permit us, and if we were to construct a stūpa while the World-Honored One is still present, we would then erect one. The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to build them. [The monks] did not know how to build them. The Buddha said: "They should be made square, or octagonal, or circular.
They should be constructed using bricks, stones, or wood. Once completed, they should be plastered with black mud, or straw mud, or cow-dung mud;
or one may use white mud, lime, or white plaster. It is permitted to construct a base for the stupa and to build a railing around its four sides."
The railings. The rest is as explained in the Vinaya texts. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: Regarding the method for constructing a stūpa: the lower foundation is square, surrounded by railings;
it rises in two circular tiers with four square projections at the corners; on top are placed a circular canopy, a long pillar, and the wheel symbol.
The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: The Buddha said that one should use bricks to construct a foundation two layers thick;

next, install the main body of the stūpa, and above that, place an inverted bowl (*pātra*) of any height desired. Set upon it a flat top (*samaśīrṣa*) one or two feet high and two or three feet square, proportioned according to the size [of the stūpa].
Erect a pole for the wheel (*cakra-yaṣṭi*) in the center, and then affix the wheel symbols (*cakrākāra*). As for the number of tiers of these wheels, they may be...
One, two, three, four; up to thirteen. Next, place the precious vase (*ratnaghaṭa*).
If one is constructing a stūpa for a Tathāgata, it should be made complete as previously described. If it is for a Pratyekabuddha, do not place a precious vase.
For an Arhat, there should be four tiers of wheels; for a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), three; for a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), two; and for a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), one.

Ordinary persons and virtuous people may have only a flat top (*piṇḍaka*), without the wheel and canopy. The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "If an ordinary monk who is purely virtuous has no wheel-shaft above, it is called a 'flat-topped caitya' (*piṇḍaka-caitya*).

The *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* states: "Ordinary monks have only the *kadalī-leaf* and the *maṇi-jewel*. Ordinary monks should pay homage according to their respective order. As the World-Honored One said, "It should be done thus.
When the bhikṣus did not know how to install [the image], the Buddha said: "In the manner that the World-Honored One dwells in the Dharma, so should it be placed."

Regarding food, one should follow the instructions of the donor. If there are many flowers, one may give them to a florist and say:

This would no longer manifest the intended purpose. The Elder addressed the Buddha, requesting that a high eaves be constructed. The Buddha said, "As you wish. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

Regarding the property of the Saṃgha: if a danger arises, one must not simply abandon the goods and depart. One should instead have a trustworthy person hide the property of the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
First, one should scout and observe the thieves so that they do not arrive suddenly and unexpectedly.

Regarding food: one should have a young bhikṣu observe from a concealed place so that the thieves may see the signs.

Wash, dye, and fumigate it with incense. As the *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "If one obtains a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe), soak it in water for a long time and wash it clean using pure ash.

The village of the Brahmins called Dūḍi (also transcribed as Dūyī or Dūkī); the *Faxian zhuan* states it is fifty *li* west of Śrāvastī.
They arrived at a town named Tukhāra. This was the birthplace of Kāśyapa Buddha, the place where father and son met, and the place of his parinirvāṇa;

The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: Over sixty li to the northwest of the great city of Śrāvastī (formerly called Shewei), there is an old city.
This was the birthplace of Kāśyapa Buddha during the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
To the south of this city is a stūpa at the place where he first beheld his father after attaining perfect enlightenment. To the north of the city...
There is a stūpa containing the entire bodily relics of Kāśyapa Buddha, which was built by King Aśoka (formerly called King Ayù;

O King, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the Buddha told King Prasenajit:

"In a past age, at the time of the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a king named Kṛkin who wished to construct a stūpa made of the seven precious substances. At that time, a minister addressed the king, saying:
'In a future age, there will appear those who do not act according to the Dharma; they shall destroy this stūpa and incur a grave offense. I only pray that Your Majesty [will take heed of this].'"
It was constructed of bricks and covered with gold and silver. If one were to remove the gold and silver, the stūpa would remain intact.
The king followed the minister’s words; he had it built of bricks and covered with thin gold leaf. It stood one yojana high and half a yojana wide on each side, with railings made of copper.
After seven years, seven months, and seven days, it was completed. Once finished, it was honored with incense and flowers.
For the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, niches were constructed on the four sides of the stūpa; above them were figures of lions and elephants, painted in various colors.
A railing was made in front, providing a place for flowers. Inside the niches, silk banners and canopies were suspended.
On all four sides, various gardens, flowering trees, and lotus ponds were created; within the ponds were various types of lotuses and miscellaneous blossoms. The Buddha...
On the four sides of the stūpa, erect jeweled caityas, adorned with carved patterns, engravings, and various colorful paintings;

offer worship with all manner of song, dance, and musical performances. (A stūpa containing relics is called a *stūpa*; one without relics is called a *caitya*). At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni—
He himself erected a stūpa for Kāśyapa Buddha. Its foundation was square, surrounded by a balustrade, and it rose in two circular tiers with four square projections extending outward.
Above, it was provided with a bowl-shaped canopy and a long flagpole topped with a *cakra*. The Buddha said, "The method for constructing a stūpa should be like this."
When the stupa was completed, the World-Honored One, out of reverence for the Buddhas of the past, personally paid homage to it and spoke this verse:
"Even if one were to give as alms a hundred thousand pieces of gold, It would not equal the merit of a single virtuous mind That reverently pays homage to a Buddha-stupa."
To take hundreds of thousands of carts of pure gold and use them to practice giving is not as good as a single virtuous mind making offerings of incense and flowers to a stūpa.
To give hundreds of thousands of Jambudvīpas filled with pure gold is not as good as a single gift of the Dharma.

Even if one were to offer pure gold filling hundreds of thousands of worlds as an act of giving, it would not equal the merit of a single gift of Dharma that accords with practice and leads to the vision of the True Reality.
The *Mukha* states: "In constructing a stūpa, one that is small may be made larger, but one that is large should not be reduced in size.
If there are laypeople capable of building it on a grand scale, that is well; if they are unable to provide for it, the bhikṣus should exhort and assist them in its construction.
If the parasol-crested pinnacle (*cakra*) of a stūpa has become old and dilapidated, the Buddha said: 'It should be repaired. At that time, there was previously..."

rather, once the creation of the new is finished, only then should the old wheel be removed. If the clay body of a Buddha image is damaged or worn away, the bhikṣus became doubtful and did not dare to polish or decorate it.
The Buddha said: "One may enlarge it, or make it similar [to the original]; do as you wish with the colors."
Regarding wall paintings that have become indistinct, they should be wiped away and repainted anew.
As for other paper scrolls upon which the Buddha’s scriptures have faded, one should wipe the old ones and transcribe them anew.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying, "As the World-Honored One has taught that drums and music should be sounded, we do not know who should perform this. The Buddha said, "Let the laypeople do it."
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "May monks play drums and music? The Buddha said, "It is not permitted, except when making offerings to the Buddha.
He then told the musicians: "Virtuous ones, you should now make offerings to the Great Teacher;
you must not beat drums or perform music without cause. Whoever does so shall incur an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*)."
At that time, the community of monks received great offerings at the bathhouse. The bhikṣus did not exercise moderation, and consequently they fell ill.
Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya informed the Buddha, saying, "If you permit the bhikṣus to construct a bathhouse, they may suffer less illness. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

It was found that bathing caused illness; therefore, it was permitted to construct a separate small bathhouse. The remaining details are as explained in the Vinaya. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

When one wishes to bathe, one should have the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) sweep and sprinkle [the area] to make it clean, prepare firewood and charcoal so that the temperature is appropriate, and then strike the *gandī*.
It should be known that those entering the bath must each tie their robes with a waistband to serve as a marker and place them on the clothing rack.
When entering, one must not enter with both arms dangling; rather, one should enter with one hand covering the front.
If one wishes to have the teacher rub [the body], one should first announce this intention; there is no fault in doing so. One must not raise both hands at once.

One should first have the teacher rub one arm and one hand, and after that side is finished, proceed to rub the other arm and hand, as well as the remaining internal and external parts, and then close [the door].
He sat with his back against the door and caused sweat to break out from his body. He was instructed to measure his use of water and not use it excessively.

If it is pond water, one may use it at will without fault. It is not permitted to bathe naked in the open air; however, if the water reaches the waist or the armpits, its use is permitted and there is no fault.
If one sits in the water up to the navel, that is also permitted. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: At that time, the bhikṣus [experienced] physical...
A person fell ill. A physician informed him, "I have studied the medical treatises of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin).
They state that bathing the body in a bathhouse can eliminate illness. However, I do not know what its form is like. The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "The method for a bathhouse is that it should be wide inside and narrow outside, shaped like a gourd jar. A window should be made in the middle."
If smoke escapes outside while birds and pigeons enter the room, one should install windows and shutters. If wind and rain enter from the sides, door panels should be fitted;
these should be opened and closed using a "ram's hoof" staff (a crossbar). The room should be equipped with doors, as well as horizontal bolts, rings, and knobs.
If water in a jar placed on the ground becomes cold, it should be kept inside the room; platforms should be installed on both sides, and the jar placed upon them at a height [appropriate for use].
One should kneel with the knees level and place bricks or stones upon the ground before lighting the fire. If the flames are fierce, one should not enter immediately;
rather, one should wait until the smoke and flames have subsided before entering as desired. If the scattered embers die out quickly, one should use a shovel to gather them back together.
When a bhikṣu faints from the heat of the fire, one should place a small amount of mustard seed oil mixed with roasted flour into the fire.
This will cause them to awaken. If there is a foul odor, one should burn incense. If tears flow from the eyes, use a ball of parched grain flour (*maṇḍaka*) to wipe them away.
If the tears still do not cease, one should take the powder of *āmalaka* fruit, knead it into small balls, and use them to suppress the tears.
When stepping upon the ground, one may be soiled by dust; in such a case, one should spread green grass. If green grass is difficult to obtain, one should moisten it with water and apply oil.
If the body itches, one should not scratch until it breaks the skin; instead, one should use a pumice stone to grind away its sharp edges before using it.
Once used, it should be tied with a cord and hung on an ivory peg. Because the pumice stone is oily and greasy, it should not [be left lying about].
It should be washed frequently and may be placed within a fire. If the room is cold, it should be closed when entering;
the same applies when leaving. One should have a bhikṣu guard the door. Furthermore, there are two protocols for the time of bathing: first, the recitation of Dharma discourse.
The two sages remained silent; one should not engage in idle conversation. At that time, a bhikṣu bathed inside his room and consequently became covered in mud.
The Buddha said: "One should not bathe with water inside this room. One should build a separate room for bathing.
If there is still mud there, it should be paved with bricks or sand, and drainage channels should be made."
Open the waterway so that the water flows out. When pouring the water, have the person bathing positioned below and the person pouring the water above.
In the bathhouse, provide tooth-sticks (*dantakāṣṭha*), cleansing powder (*śīrṇa-kaṣāya*), cow dung, and powdered earth in advance.

Once the bathing is finished and the body is weak and exhausted, one may eat a light meal. If the hands are greasy, they are difficult to wash clean immediately; if one waits longer to wash them, [the oil will set].

At that time, fearing that it would be too late, one should eat using a spoon. Or, if one obtains hot gruel, one may likewise use a spoon (in the Western Regions spoons and chopsticks are not normally used;
here, based on the abbreviated teaching, their use is permitted). The Buddha ordered that bathhouses be constructed. Not knowing whom to dispatch to do so, the Buddha said:
"Disciples and followers should work together on them. If there is a donor, one may also rely upon them for assistance. When bathing, one should..."
He led his disciples inside and ordered them to rub and massage his body. The commentary states: "This is the system for bathhouses in the Western Regions (India).

They are constructed by stacking double-layered bricks into a shape resembling a grain stack—pointed at the top and wide at the bottom, approximately one *zhang* high with a base width of seven or eight *chi*.
A door is opened on one side and must be fitted with a sliding panel. The interior and exterior are plastered with lime; it must not be thin or leaky. It may [be so].
At the rear, install a small niche and place within it either a stone image or a bronze image.
Having first bathed the image, carry it to another location. Others may enter afterwards; one should offer worship with a focused mind and make vows to do so constantly.
The expense is not great, yet the merit obtained is inexhaustible. Inside the room, install an earthen brazier about one chi deep. When it is time for the ritual bathing, at...
This charcoal may be burned, or perhaps firewood may be lit, to observe the temperature and adapt it to the season. Within the room, a bright lamp is lit and smoke exits through the windows.
When wishing to bathe, one puts on a bathing skirt; having entered the room, one sits in a corner in a squatting posture (*khuṭṭaka*).
After a short while, when the body is covered in sweat, one applies oil to the body and has an attendant rub and wipe it, whereby chronic ailments are eventually cured.

Cold-natured constitutions, wind-accumulations (vāta), and fatigue—all such ailments are eliminated without the need for other medicines; this is not merely like washing with hot water to remove surface grime.
Thereafter, one should move to another room and bathe the body with medicinal decoctions at an appropriate time.
This is the bathing method of Śakra Devendra. Whether the Buddhist instructions for bhikṣus differ from this remains unknown; fearing that readers might not understand, I have briefly [recorded it].
This has been excerpted from the commentary. If one is free from illness and seeks to practice economy, one may act according to the season and the specific circumstances.

However, in the hot lands of Central India, those who practice this are rare; whereas in the cold countries of the North, it is found everywhere. This is written to inform you. The *Jiwen-shi jing* (Sūtra on the Warm Bathhouse) states:
The Buddha told the elder Jīvaka (also known as Qiyu): "The method for bathing requires seven items to eliminate [impurities]."
There are seven ailments; one obtains seven meritorious rewards. What are these seven things? First, fire; second, pure water;
third, cleansing powder; fourth, ghee and ointment; fifth, concentrated lye; sixth, a willow branch;
seventh, an undergarment. These are the methods for bathing. What are the seven ailments removed? First, the four great elements become peaceful and secure. Second, ... [text continues]

First, it removes wind-related illnesses. Second, it removes phlegm-related illnesses. Third, it removes rheumatism. Fourth, it removes cold and chill. Fifth, it removes heat. Sixth, it removes impurities and filth.
Seventh, the body becomes light and agile, and the eyes become clear and bright. These are the seven ailments removed for the Sangha.
By making offerings in this manner, one obtains seven blessings: first, the four great elements will be free from disease; wherever one is born...
First, they are always at peace; they are brave, martial, and robust, held in high esteem and reverence by all. Second, their birth is pure;

their countenances are upright and handsome, such that dust and water do not adhere to them, and they are respected by others. Third, their bodies are constantly fragrant and their clothing is clean and pure.
1. All who see him rejoice; there are none who do not hold him in reverence. 2. His physical form is moist and lustrous; his majestic radiance and virtue are so great that all revere and praise him.
He walks alone without peer. 3. He is followed by many attendants; he brushes away dust and defilement, naturally receiving blessings.
He constantly remembers his past lives. 4. His teeth and mouth are fragrant and beautiful; they are square, white, and even. Whatever teachings he proclaims—

"Everyone who hears this will not fail to apply themselves with solemnity. Seventh, in whatever place one is born, one will naturally possess garments adorned with precious jewels, such that all who see them are struck with awe and reverence.
The Buddha told Jīvaka: "Performing this bath for the assembly of monks brings these seven blessings.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one may become a minister or a sovereign, or a sun or moon deity, or one of the four heavenly kings, or..."
Whether as Śakra, a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or a Brahmā deity, one receives immeasurable merit;
or as a Bodhisattva, one resolves the mind and cultivates the stages, until the task is accomplished and the vow fulfilled, ultimately attaining Buddhahood. The *Jieguizhuan* states:
"Regarding the method of bathing, the Western Regions differ from the Eastern Lands. It merely involves harmonizing with the seasons, which differs slightly from the rest."
In this land, flowers and fruits are always present throughout the twelve months; one knows neither snow nor ice, though there may be a slight, thin frost.
Although it is often hot, it is not an oppressive heat; when it is hot, the body breaks out in no rashes, and when it is cold, the feet do not crack.
Because of this, people bathe frequently, keeping their bodies pure and clean. Every day, they will not eat unless they have first washed.
Furthermore, in every place there was an abundance of pond water. At that time, the people all considered digging ponds to be a meritorious act.
If one traveled for a single *yì* (a distance of approximately seven kilometers), twenty or thirty such ponds would come into view.

They ranged from one *mǔ* to five *mǔ* in width, with *tāla* trees planted around their four sides, reaching heights of forty to fifty feet. These ponds were fed entirely by rainwater and remained as clear and still as a mirror.
Along the riverbanks, at each of the eight *caityas*, there are bathing pools where the World-Honored One once washed; their waters are clear and exquisite, differing from all others.
At Nālandā Monastery, there are more than ten large ponds. Every morning, when the monastery strikes the *ghanṭī* (wooden gong), it summons the monastic community to bathe.
Each person brings their own bathing robe, and groups of hundreds or thousands emerge together from the monastery.
Outside, they disperse toward the various ponds to bathe. Regarding the method for the bathing cloth (*snāna-śāṭī*): take a piece of cotton cloth five cubits long and one and a half cubits wide;
wrap it around the body so that it encircles it completely. Remove the old garment, turn both ends so that they face forward, and take the upper corner of the left side.
With the right hand, pull it down toward the waist, drawing it close to the body. Then, gather and press the right side together.
It is tucked inside the waist; this is called the method for wearing the bathing skirt (*udakasāṭikā*). When lying down, one wears the skirt in the same manner.

When wishing to exit the pool, one should shake it out slowly and emerge so as not to allow insects to adhere to it. If one bathes in a place other than the monastery pool, the wearing of the skirt is the same.
Water may be sent by others to pour over one; at any time and in any place, one may use it as a screen. This was the instruction given by the World-Honored One.
Regarding the bathhouse: one may construct a brick pool in an open space, or prepare medicinal decoctions for removing ailments, or have oil applied all over the body;
these bring profound benefit and are all based on the sacred teachings, which I cannot describe in detail here as they are found extensively in the Vinaya.
Furthermore, those who bathe must do so when hungry, eating only after the bath has been completed. This has two benefits: first, the body becomes clean and...
It is empty and free from all impurities; secondly, phlegm and mucus are dispersed, enabling one to consume food.
One should wash only after eating one's fill; this is what the medical experts prohibit. Thus, we know that the saying "washing when hungry and bathing when full" is not a comprehensive principle.
If one wears a three-foot bathing robe, it is narrow and reveals the body; or if one does not wear it at all and bathes naked, it is deeply [improper].
This deviates from the principles of the teachings. One should instead use a four-panel bathing skirt (*snānaśāṭī*) to cover the body, which is both pleasing and appropriate;

this not only ensures strict adherence to the holy teachings but also avoids bringing shame upon oneself before humans and deities. Other matters may be left as they are; the wise should understand this fully.

If one does not even change one’s appearance when bathing at night, how could one possibly lack concealment when facing others? (Regarding the "sheep-claw staff" [*meṣaśṛṅgī*]: it is a small iron fork made in the shape of a sheep's hoof.)

The Master [did so] because his calculations did not accord with the ways of the world.

*Shou* (溲) is pronounced with the *qie* of *sou* (蒐) in the rising tone; it refers to mixing flour with water.

*Sǒng* (pronounced *sǒng*): To be startled; to fear; to be terrified.

This is for many reasons; it is permitted to keep a carrying net (*vīta*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

The Buddha said, "Ordinary people all delight in long life. When you see someone sneeze, [you should wish them well]."
One should say, "Long life. If any bhikṣus see an elder sneeze, the juniors should rise and perform a prostration, saying aloud, "Vandāmi" (I pay homage).
If a junior sneezes, the seniors should say, "May you be free from illness. If one does not do so, both incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one sneezes while in a meditation hall, one must not [speak]."

For those near mountain retreats, acorn branches and kudzu vines are preferred; for those in level fields, paper mulberry, peach, locust, and willow may be used as one pleases.

The water flows out; rinse thoroughly with plenty of water—this is the method.

There are some who do not even know this, though such cases are not within the scope of this discussion. Nevertheless, among the monastics and laity of the Five Indias, chewing the tooth-stick has been a constant practice for three thousand years.
