The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that among the upāsikās who made offerings to the noble assembly, Lady Śyāmāvatī was foremost. *Bhadra* means "Virtuous" in this language.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are eight types of Brahmin lineages: first, the Kautsa; second, the Kaundinya; third, the Vāsiṣṭha; fourth, the Parāśara; fifth, the Bhāradvāja;

sixth, the Maudgalyāyana; seventh, the Gautama; and eighth, the Agniveśya. (Note: The provided Chinese text lists six names, which correspond to the following Sanskrit equivalents: 1. Gautama, 2. Kaundinya, 3. Vasiṣṭha, 4. Śaradvat, 5. Ātreya, 6. Viśvāmitra.)
Seventh, the Tāpasa; eighth, the Nirgranthaputra. Furthermore, the Abhidharma speaks of eight lineages (*gotra*):
first, the Vatsa; second, the Kaurava; third, the Śāṇḍilya; fourth, the Bhāradvāja (i.e., Bhāradvāja);
fifth, the Kāṇṭheviddhi; sixth, the Māṭhara; seventh, the Kauṇḍinya; eighth, the Pārāśarya.

(Alternatively, it is called *pārasavī*. Some say this is a hybrid species; that is to say, one born from a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇa is named *pārasavī*, just as one born from a donkey and a horse is called a mule.)

*Qíjú* (chessboard) and *qí* (chess pieces) are the same as *qí*. "Qí" is pronounced with the *qú* and *yí* initials, sounding like *qí*. It refers to go (weiqi). In antiquity, there were three hundred and sixty lines;
nowadays, it consists of only nineteen horizontal and vertical lines. Furthermore, when it was decorated with ivory, it was called "Elephant Chess" (*xiàngqí*). Nowadays, [it is made] with...
"Nine straight and ten cross" constitutes the pattern of the chessboard (*xiqí*). The *Zuozhuan* states: "In the game of *yì*, the player moves his pieces without certainty," which refers to this.
*Bóyǎn* is a gambling game; it means the gambling game of seizing others' wealth and goods. The character for *bó* (gambling) should follow the radical for bamboo (*zhú*). — *Shuowen Jiezi*.
It is said: *Bo* (簙) refers to board games. One version uses six counting sticks (*zhu*) and six pieces (*qi*), which is called *Liubo* (六博), also known as *Liubo*.

It involves twelve pieces. Regarding *yan* (掩), the *Zuǎnwén* states that *pòyǎn* (撲掩) is a game of leaping coins; colloquially it is called *shèyì* (射意). Another version says it is *shèshù* (射數). [Note:
*Liubo* was a "double-six" game played by the Prince of Chen-si during the Wei dynasty.]
The explanation of *chupū* (dice) is as given in the "Falling" chapter.
The eight paths and ten paths.
"Dao" (道) means "road. It refers to arranging [the board] with eight or ten paths running lengthwise and crosswise for moving the game pieces.
"Pai" (拍)—pronounced *pò* (as in *pò*)—means to strike or to tap. "Pai-shí" (拍石) refers to the game of *tánqí* (彈棊). *Tánqí* was a game played in the Han palaces.
"Human Beauty Casket" (*Ren Zhuanglian*) is a game. Some say it is "stone-throwing," which refers to *touhu* (pitch-pot).

In antiquity, stones were used for *touhu*, whereas nowadays arrows are used. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One must not engage in games such as *chupu* (backgammon), *weiqi* (go), *bolosai* (chess), *tanqi* (checkers), or *liubo* (six-sided dice);
nor shall one play ball, stone-throwing, *touhu*, *quandao*, *badao*, or *xingcheng*. All such games and jests [are forbidden]."
One must not perform [this].

"Sui" (彗) is pronounced *suì* (with the initial *xú* and final *zuì*). It refers to a portentous star. Its shape is like a broom; hence it is called a "sweeping star" (*huì*). This refers to its stellar light.
Gradually it grows longer, resembling a comet. People of the world sometimes call it the Diāo Star, or sometimes the Zhidòu Star;
it is an omen for the removal of the old and the establishment of the new. Wén Yǐng says: "The three stars—*huì* (comet), *bò* (meteoric blaze), and *cháng* (long)—differ in their prognostications.
The *bò* has short rays that radiate out in all directions, spreading thick and billowing. The *huì* has long rays that extend far and wide."
Like a broom or a comet, its radiance may point directly upward, extending across the entire sky or for ten, three, or two *zhang*.
The appearance of a *pò* or a comet generally portends the removal of the old and the establishment of the new, as well as fires and disasters. Long comets mostly signify warfare and conflict.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "When a comet appears, all the people throughout the world will suffer from famine, disease, and emaciation."
Suffering and distress (as detailed above). *Yue-shi* (月蝕):

the second character is pronounced with the *zhí* (職) radical and the phonetic *shí* (石). It refers to the waning of the sun or moon. The *Shiming* (釋名) states: "The waning of the sun or moon is called *shi* (eclipse). [It occurs] gradually...
To be eclipsed and diminished is like insects devouring the leaves of trees and grasses. The *Hanshu* states: "The sun and moon undergo *bo-shi* (eclipses).

The commentary notes: "When the sun and moon lose their radiance, it is called *bo*; when they are deficient or obscured, it is called *shi*. In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, saying:
"Good son, it is like the asura king Rāhu, who covers the moon with his hand; people of the world all say that there is an eclipse of the moon.
Yet the asura king cannot truly eclipse it. It is because the asura obstructs its light that the moon appears full and without any diminution;
it is merely because the hand obstructs it that it does not appear. If he withdraws [his hand]..."
At that time, the world all says that the moon has been born again; everyone says that this moon has undergone much suffering and affliction.
Even if there were hundreds of thousands of asura kings, they could not afflict it; yet the nature of this moon truly has no increase or decrease.

Those who witness its eclipse always see it as a full moon. Good son, it is like a person on earth who sees a lunar eclipse once every six months, whereas the gods above see a lunar eclipse in the space of a mere moment. Why is this? Because the days of those gods are long.
Because the days are short for humans, he lies on his right side with his legs stacked;
this is the reclining posture of the Lion King. The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "The lion, king of beasts, during the day seeks food..."
Having walked, he enters his cave. When he wishes to sleep, he places one foot upon the other, extends his tail behind him, and lies on his right side.
At dawn, after the night has passed, he turns and looks at his body; if his body is not straight, he is displeased upon seeing it.
If its body is well-proportioned and upright, upon seeing it, he is pleased. When it lies down or rises, it emerges from its cave.
Having emerged, it groans repeatedly. Having groaned, it examines its own body. Having examined its own body, it looks around in all four directions.
Having looked, it roars two or three times. Having roared, it goes forth to seek food. Such is the manner in which the lion, the king of beasts, lies down.

As for the rule regarding a bhikṣu’s lying down: suppose a bhikṣu residing in a village or town, having passed the night, puts on his robes and takes up his bowl at dawn to enter the village for alms, well-guarding his body, restraining his sense faculties, and established in right mindfulness; he then departs from that village or town.
Having finished the almsround, he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, and goes to a secluded place.
There, he either walks in meditation or sits in meditation to purify the obstructive states within his mind.

Having purified them, during the first watch of the night, he again either walks in meditation or sits in meditation to purify the obstructive states within his mind. Having purified them, at the time of the middle watch of the night, he enters...

When he wishes to lie down in his chamber, he folds his *uttarāsaṅga* into four layers and spreads it upon the bed; he uses his *saṃghāṭī* as a pillow and lies on his right side with one foot resting upon the other.
With his mind fixed on the perception of light, maintaining right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, he constantly maintains the thought of rising.
During the latter part of the night, he quickly rises from his rest to either walk in meditation (*caṅkrama*) or sit in dhyāna, purifying the mind within.
Regarding these obstructive dharmas: thus, O Bhikṣu, is the lion’s posture for lying down. The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya states: "The lying down of pretas is not permitted;
nor is the lying down of asuras; nor is the lying down of those possessed by desire. If one lies on one's back, it is the lying down of an asura;
if one covers oneself with the ground, it is the lying down of a preta; if one lies on the left side, it is the lying down of one possessed by desire. A bhikṣu should lie like a lion."

The King of Beasts lies down with his body aligned. When spreading [the bedding], one must not spread it on the left; it should be spread on the right, with the head toward the hem of the robe (kāsāya).
One must not point one's feet toward the two teachers. Elder bhikṣus must not lie down at the beginning of the first watch of the night by merely declaring "it is late" and falling asleep;
they should instead practice right mindfulness of their task. Reaching the middle watch of the night, they then lie down, placing their right side downward, as the Teacher did.

When the Prince lies down to sleep, he places his two feet together, closes his mouth, and presses his tongue against the upper palate. He rests on his right hand and extends his left hand along his body.
Without abandoning mindfulness and wisdom, he maintains the thought of awakening and does not sleep until sunrise.

He resolves that he shall rise during the latter part of the night, sit upright, and contemplate his own practice. If he should fall into a deep sleep at night and unconsciously turn over, or if he is old or ill—
If there is a sore on the right side, there is no offense. This is the proper method for a bhikṣu to lie down. If one does not do so, one transgresses the rules of decorum.
[The fifth covering.]
First, the hindrance of sensual desire; second, the hindrance of ill will; third, the hindrance of sloth and torpor; fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse;
fifth, the hindrance of doubt. The *Dharmadhātu-anukrama* states: "Hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*) takes the sense of covering or obscuring.

It is so called because it can cover and obscure the practitioner’s pure and wholesome mind, preventing it from unfolding; thus, it is named a "hindrance. Regarding "sensual desire": it refers to the insatiable drawing-in and grasping [of objects].
Greed (*rāga*) means to long for, desire, and yearn;

it refers to the craving for the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects of the world, as well as wealth and other such things, without ever reaching satiety. Anger (*pratigha*) is the state of mind characterized by resentment;
it is called anger because it arises toward objects that are disagreeable. Sleep (*middha*) is the dulling of the mental consciousness.
"Ripening" refers to sleep. When the five sensory faculties are dark and obscured, it is called "sleeping. If the mind relies upon the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then ignorance (*avidyā*) increases;
thus, the mental consciousness becomes dull and ripened, while the five sensory faculties are dark and obscured, lacking any conscious awareness—this is termed "sleep.

Regarding agitation and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*): the movement of thoughts with a deviant mind is called "agitation"; having become agitated, one reflects upon it, and the resulting distress within the mind constitutes "regret."
*Regret* (*kaukṛtya*): If one follows ignorance and erroneously grasps, then the mind becomes agitated by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Since what has been done is contrary to the truth, when one reflects upon it later, there arises sorrow and regret. *Doubt* (*vicikitsā*): When the deluded mind seeks the principle but wavers and cannot decide, this is called doubt.

If one practices the dharmas such as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), yet due to the dullness and darkness of ignorance, one cannot distinguish between the true and the false, because of this, uncertainty arises.
"Yü" (豫) means that when the mind lacks decisive judgment, it is all termed "doubt" (疑). Question: The unwholesome dharmas are immeasurable and boundless;

for what reason do you speak only of these five? Answer: Although these five dharmas seem narrow in name, their meaning encompasses the three poisons and also universally subsumes the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*).
As for the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), it is precisely...
The hindrance of sensual desire is the poison of greed; the hindrance of ill will is the poison of hatred; the hindrances of sloth-and-torpor and doubt are the poison of delusion;

and the single hindrance of restlessness-and-remorse is subsumed under the category of the "equally distributed" (sādhāraṇa). Combined, these constitute the fourfold afflictions within the first [category].
Thus, there are twenty-one thousand [afflictions] within each of the four [categories], totaling eighty-four thousand gates of worldly dust and toil (*kleśa*).
Therefore, if one can eliminate these five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), one will be able to simultaneously abandon all unwholesome dharmas.
The remainder is as extensively explained in the sūtras and śāstras.
○ Regarding the Dharma of the Five Hundred-fold Council:

The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, is the eternally abiding Dharma-body. By nature, he is free from arising and ceasing, and utterly transcends coming and going. It is only out of compassion that he manifests traces in this world;

thus, whether for a long or short duration, he acts in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. When the conditions for response arise, he sits at the site of enlightenment; when his karmic conditions are exhausted, he returns.
Manifesting his entry into nirvana, he was born in the Lumbinī Garden; his golden body measured sixteen feet, and he passed away in secret beneath the Śāla trees at the age of eighty.
Truly, his manifestations as an emanation are inconceivable, and his appearances and disappearances are difficult to fathom.

Yet, his arising was a rare encounter after vast eons, and his passing has left the great trichiliocosm bereft of its protector. Fortunately, he left behind these subtle words, which we rely upon through the aid of the various sages.

The Councils were convened; the teachings were entrusted to the *tāla* leaves of the palm-leaf manuscripts, numbering eighty thousand, while the Sanskrit texts were inscribed upon jade rollers, comprising three thousand precious treasuries.
Thus, it may be said that the Sun of the Buddha shines once more, the waves of the Dharma-sea surge forth, and the transmission of the sacred teachings shall not fall into decline.
The truth lies herein. This is also the exercise of skillful means (*upāya*) in governing all things: to open the perfect sound (*pariṣphuṭa-ghoṣa*) throughout long kalpas;

for the radiance of compassionate vows to flow forth, spreading stupas (*stūpa*) in this degenerate age; so that those who gaze upon them may transcend the cycle of suffering, and those who hear them may awaken to eternal tranquility.
This is because the Tathāgata established his merit over three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas and planted the fruits of his realization over a hundred kalpas; thus he has enabled these shrines to circulate.
The Eightfold Eloquence: His essence manifests myriad virtues; his wisdom pervades the Dharma-realm; his Way is wondrously unconditioned.

Lofty and peerless, he is the King among all dharmas. From the heavens above to the earth below, there are none who do not turn to him in reverence. Whether wise or foolish, all receive his saving grace.

I only regret that I was born too late to witness the Buddha’s own preaching. Furthermore, having heard nothing of the True Dharma or the Semblance Dharma, I was entrusted to these peripheral and degenerate times.

At the age of six, I had not yet heard the names of the Triple Gem; it was only when I reached the age of seven that I first knew how to take refuge. Although I long for liberation, [the conditions are lacking].
Ultimately lacking the moisture of guidance, I set out alone with staff and satchel to travel everywhere and consult the wise and enlightened.
Desiring to repay the Buddha’s kindness, I sought not to fail in my non-action. Thereupon, I perused the Tripiṭaka and personally investigated the five divisions of the Vinaya.
Observing that the virtuous elders of this land mostly venerated the Dharmaguptaka school, I accordingly followed its *pātimokkha* rules, including all the Chinese and Sanskrit texts.
Regarding the difficult points that are hard to penetrate, I have set them forth and explained them.

However, because my primary task has been the matters within my own person, and because I have applied my efforts with inconsistent diligence—pausing whenever it was not summer—it has taken four or five years to reach this point. Now, by good fortune, this volume is complete;

it serves merely as a key to the Vinaya for the convenience of future students, so that they need not trouble themselves with extraneous matters. I hope that those of virtuous character will behold the World-Honored One [through this work].
Reflecting upon these compassionate instructions and the earnest exhortations of Kāśyapa, one must firmly propagate the disciplinary models and revere the *mokṣa*.
Only then will the Jewel of the Saṃgha remain eternally radiant, and the World-Honored Śākyamuni abide forever.

The city of Kuśī is fully called Kuśinagara; this means "horn," referring to the fact that the city was triangular in shape. Alternatively, it is called the "Grass City" (Kuśa-pura), meaning that the city was covered with and grew from this *kuśa* grass.
Or it is called the "City of the Rishis" (Ṛṣi-pura), meaning that in ancient times the lifespan of the rishis was long.
He resided here; because he honored that person, the country was named after him. Master Fasheng says: it is also called Kauśāmbī (or Kuīnàjié).
"Nàjié" is the Sanskrit term *nagara*, which means "city. Translated, it is called "City of Superior Reed."

Because there is an abundance of fine *māḍa* grass. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "In the kingdom of Kuśinagara, the foundations of the old city are made of brick and are over ten *li* in circumference.
Three or four *li* to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River;
not far from the western bank, one reaches the Śāla grove. Four trees therein are exceptionally tall; this is the place where the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa. [End of] Original Text.
The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, within this city there are six great cities, namely:
Śrāvastī, Sāketa, Campā, Vārāṇasī, Vaiśālī, and Rājagṛha.
For what reason, World-Honored One, have you abandoned such auspicious and magnificent lands to come to this place?"
"In a wilderness, a desolate borderland, and a lowly place, he has entered parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do not speak such words. Why is this? This city of Kuśinagara was, in ages past, the capital of a noble king.
The city was named Kuśāvatī; it was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with a flourishing population, extending twelve yojanas in length."
It is seven yojanas in width. The city is surrounded by seven tiers of walls and courtyards, all of which are composed of the four precious substances:
namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The city gates are likewise constructed from these four precious substances.
At each gate there is a great flower-pillar, also made of precious materials, standing seven men high. The city...
The outer moat is three and a half men deep. Its banks are paved with precious bricks. Within the seven courtyards, there are rows of *tāla* trees, all composed of the four jewels:
the golden *tāla* trees have branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits made of silver;
the silver trees are adorned with gold; the lapis lazuli trees are adorned with crystal; and the crystal trees are adorned with lapis lazuli.
Adorned with crystal. When these various trees are stirred by the wind, they produce subtle and exquisite sounds that delight the hearts of all.
Within these groves of trees, there are bathing pools; their foundations, steps, and pathways are likewise composed of the four precious substances, and they are surrounded on all sides by railings.
It is likewise composed of the four precious substances. Within its ponds and along their banks, there are many lovely flowers that bloom in accordance with the seasons.

Furthermore, within this city, there are always various kinds of drums and music, stringed and wind instruments, songs, and dances, which produce wondrous sounds all exhorting and praising the cultivation of meritorious deeds, the observance of fasts and precepts, and so forth. In this city, there is a king named Mahāsāla.

He saw that [the king] was endowed with the seven treasures and possessed four wonders. The so-called seven treasures are: the wheel-treasure, the elephant, the horse, the jewel, the woman, the householder-treasure, and the military-treasure.
As for the four wonders, they are: the king’s long life;
his first stage as a prince, second as a crown prince, third ascending the throne, and finally practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*). In these four stages, each lasted for eight [thousand years].
For fourteen thousand years; this is called the first rarity. Furthermore, that king’s appearance was upright and handsome, peerless in the world;
this is the second rarity. Moreover, he had few illnesses and little affliction, and as for the food and drink he consumed—

He was peaceful and timely; this was the third rare wonder. Furthermore, the multitude of people served the king with loyalty and filial piety, regarding him as their father, while the king loved and cherished them as if they were his own infants.
When the king went out on a journey, he would leave his carriage behind and depart.
The King commanded his charioteer, saying, "You should now draw the carriage slowly so that the multitude may see me.
A king should always give rise to compassion for the common people; this is the fourth rare wonder... (and so forth). At that time, the King cultivated each of the four Brahma-abodes one by one.
He severed all desires, yet as his life was drawing to a close and he was pressed by death, a sense of distress arose within him.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"From the city of Kuśinagara to the banks of the Hiranyavatī River, the twin śāla grove, the birthplace of the Mallas, and the Makuṭabandhana Caitya—within this circuit of twelve yojanas, the Tathāgata, when he was formerly a Cakravartin King, gave up his life six times."
Now, having entered *parinirvāṇa* here once again, this is the seventh [instance].
Furthermore, for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, there shall be no eighth place in the worlds of the ten directions where he relinquishes his body and life. Why is this?
Because my births have been exhausted, all afflictions and karma have been severed, and I shall not undergo further existence elsewhere. (There were also various [events] in past lives...)
Regarding the causes and conditions (as explained in the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*):
"Malla" in Malla-garden means "power"; it refers to a strongman, or alternatively, a "mighty man. In the *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Past Deeds), he himself...
It is said: "We were born in this land; our lineage is known as the Mallas. Among men, we are Mallas whose strength rivals that of a thousand men.
There are thirty thousand such people living together, independent of any sovereign, maintaining themselves through the Dharma, and free from violence or disorder;
they are indeed true gentlemen. As for what is called a 'garden,' it refers to the Śāla grove.
*Sāla-vana* is translated here as "Forest of Firmness" (*jiangu lin*). Beiyuan states: "Because it does not change in winter or summer, it is called 'Firmness'. Master Yuan says:
"*Sāra*" is translated here as "High and Remote," because its trees stand tall and dense, rising above all other forests.
It is also [so]. The old translation as "solid" (堅固) is erroneous. This is because the sounds of *bala* and *sāla* are closely related.
If one says "solid," the tongue is rolled back; if one says "lofty" (高遠), it is pronounced directly. The *Xiyuji* states:
"Sāla trees resemble the oak (*hu*), with bark that is greenish-white and leaves that are extremely glossy. Four such trees stand out..."
Gao (High). It is also called Shuanglin (Double Forest) or Heli (Crane Forest). The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in its latter section, states:
"At that time, the World-Honored One entered various meditative absorptions three times. Having three times instructed the assembly, he lay upon a couch of seven treasures on his right side.
His head rested toward the north, his feet pointed toward the south, his face was turned toward the west, and his back was toward the east. Regarding those seven [treasures]...
A jeweled throne was adorned with exquisite necklaces. In the *śāla* grove, there were four pairs and eight individual trees:
one pair to the west stood before the Tathāgata; one pair to the east stood behind the Tathāgata; one pair to the north stood at the head of the Buddha;
and one pair to the south stood at the feet of the Buddha. At that time, the World-Honored One was in the *śāla* grove.
He descended and lay upon a jeweled couch. In the middle of the night, he entered the fourth dhyāna; all was silent and still.

At that very moment, he entered parinirvāṇa. After the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One had entered nirvāṇa, the two pairs of śāla trees to the east and west merged into a single tree, and the two pairs to the north and south merged into a single tree, drooping down to cover the jeweled couch.
Upon the Tathāgata, that tree immediately turned a somber white, like a white crane;
its branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, bark, and trunk all burst apart and fell away, gradually withering until it was completely shattered and destroyed. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
"After the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the twin trees produced flowers that hung down as an offering. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: [the same].
The pair in the east destroys impermanence and attains permanence; likewise, the pair in the north destroys impurity and attains purity.
To summarize them collectively: the pair in the east is a metaphor for permanence and impermanence.
The pair in the south symbolizes pleasure and non-pleasure. The pair in the west symbolizes self and non-self.
The pair in the north symbolizes purity and impurity. In each direction, one side is withered while the other flourishes. The *Nirvāṇa Commentary* states:

"The four withered and four flourishing [trees] have their lower roots connected and their upper branches joined; their joining resembles entwined trunks (*li-li*), and their flourishing and withering resemble an interlacing."
Its leaves are lush and verdant; its flowers are like chariot wheels; its fruits are as large as jars, as sweet as honey, and complete in color, fragrance, and flavor.

The region west of the River [Hexi] says: "The two trunks that have withered represent the extinction of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*; the two trunks that flourish represent the eternal presence of the *dharmakāya*.
Furthermore, the Bodhi tree does not grow in segments; when one segment withers, it marks the extinction of the Buddha-dharma."

Both trunks withered. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The World-Honored One lay down to enter parinirvāṇa rather than sitting because he wished to make it easy for the great assembly to clearly perceive all parts of the Buddha’s body.

Furthermore, by having the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa while lying down, the dimensions of his body can be perceived directly without the need for further analysis. Moreover, [he did so] to manifest that..."
[The Buddha] comes [to sit], because he is free from deceit and falsehood. If the Buddha were to sit in *nirvāṇa*, then those who lack faith would say:
"This is a deception; how can one who is dead remain sitting upright?
Furthermore, it is taught for the sake of preventing future slander against the noble ones (*ārya*). If he were to sit in *nirvāṇa*, then at this very time, the various Arhats...
The Han people say: "If [the Buddha], being physically weak and frail, entered nirvana while lying down, then the world would slander him, saying he was not an Arhat.
If he were such a one, why did he not enter parinirvāṇa sitting cross-legged like the Buddha? Furthermore, during the middle watch of the night, the World-Honored One..."
As for his attaining parinirvāṇa at this time, it is because this moment is one of tranquility;
the Tathāgata always delights in tranquility and praises tranquility, and therefore he attained parinirvāṇa during the middle watch of the night. Furthermore, at all times, the Buddha—

Because he delights in abiding in the Middle Way. (According to the *Jingnan ji*: In the first year of the Yongkang era, beneath a monk’s bed in the Xian'an Monastery at Baling, a tree suddenly sprouted.

Whenever it was cut down, it grew back again; this happened more than once. The growth of the tree became increasingly rapid, and everyone marveled at it. They left it there without pruning it. Within ten days, its trunk had reached the height of the ridgepole. Consequently, they moved their quarters to avoid it. From that time on, the tree’s growth slowed, but it bloomed very late;

it only produced flowers and leaves in midsummer, and fell in autumn no differently from other trees. Many years passed, yet no one recognized it. Later, a foreign monk saw it, climbed upon it, and wept, saying: "This is a śāla tree. The Buddha attained parinirvāṇa beneath it.")

"Ban, I am weeping because I recall past events. Previously, the flowers bloomed small and white; they were not worth observing or gathering. In the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era, suddenly a flower grew, its form and color like that of a lotus (*fúróng*).
The tree still exists today; this too is a miracle of this region."
*Parinirvāṇa*, fully expressed as *mahāparinirvāṇa*, means "Great Extinction. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"You should now go to the city of Kuśinagara and proclaim my words to the five hundred [monks]."
"O valiant ones! All of you should know that the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, will certainly this very day, at the hour of midnight, enter the wondrous realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: The Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, for what reason does the Tathāgata enter parinirvāṇa in the second month? The Buddha said, “Good son, the second month is called spring.

It is the month of spring’s warmth when all things grow and flourish; when roots and seedlings are planted, flowers and fruits bloom and prosper, rivers and streams overflow, and the hundred beasts conceive and give birth.
At this time, sentient beings mostly give rise to the notion of permanence. It is to shatter such views in sentient beings that [the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa] in this manner.”
The Tathāgata’s constant mind teaches that all phenomena are entirely impermanent, yet he alone declares that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Good son, among the six seasons, midwinter is withered and bleak, and the multitude finds no joy in it; whereas the spring sun is warm and moist, and people greedily cherish it.
It is for the sake of shattering the worldly pleasures of sentient beings that [the Buddha] expounds upon permanence, bliss, self, and purity; it is likewise so in this case.
In order to destroy the worldly notions of self and purity, the Tathāgata speaks of the true self and purity of the Tathāgata.

The mention of the second month is a metaphor for the two kinds of *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata. "Not delighting in winter" means that the wise do not delight in the Tathāgata’s impermanence and entry into *nirvāṇa*.
"Delighting in the second month" is a metaphor for the wise who love and delight in the permanence of the Tathāgata.

"Pleasant, self, and pure. "The planter" is a metaphor for all sentient beings who, upon hearing the Dharma, rejoice and resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, planting various roots of goodness.
"The river" is a metaphor for the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions who come to where I am.
"Receiving and studying the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra" refers to my disciples. "The various beasts giving birth to their young" is a metaphor for the production of all roots of goodness.

"Flowers" are a metaphor for the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). "Fruit" is a metaphor for the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]. For this reason, I enter great parinirvāṇa in the second month. Siṃhanāda said:
"Whether the Tathāgata was first born, left home, attained the Way, or turned the wondrous wheel of Dharma, it was in all cases..."
On the eighth day, [the question was asked]: "For what reason does the *nirvāṇa* occur specifically on the fifteenth day? The Buddha said:
"Good son, just as on the fifteenth day the moon has neither waning nor waxing, so too it is with all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Upon entering great *nirvāṇa*, there is no waning or waxing. For this reason, they enter *parinirvāṇa* on the fifteenth day. The latter section states: "The World-Honored One entered..."
Upon his parinirvāṇa, all the mountains upon the great earth simultaneously quaked and split apart, collapsing entirely and emitting a great sound that roared through the world, crying out:
"Alas! The great earth and the void have become silent and pitch-black;
the brilliant light of the sun and moon no longer shines. Suddenly, a black wind rises in fury and agitation, blowing and fanning up dust and sand."
The world became utterly dark; all the herbs, woods, medicinal plants, and various trees were completely broken and shattered, falling away until nothing remained.
Rivers, streams, brooks, and springs were all overturned and dried up. The *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou) states:
In the fifty-third year of King Mu of Zhou’s reign, on the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of Renshen, at dawn...
A violent wind suddenly arose, damaging houses and breaking trees; the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the palaces all shook violently.
After midday, the sky became overcast and the clouds turned black; from the west appeared twelve white rainbows that pierced straight through from south to north, not fading throughout the night.
King Mu asked the Grand Astrologer Hu Duo, "What omen is this? Hu Duo performed a divination and said, "The West..."
It is only when the Great Sage enters parinirvāṇa that the signs of decline appear; this is precisely the sign of the Tathāgata’s entry into nirvana.
Calculating by the secular calendar, the Buddha was born in a Jia-Yin year and passed away in a Ren-Shen year, which means he was seventy-nine years old at his birth.
Various sutras sometimes state that he was eighty, such as in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, where the Bodhisattva Xinxiang says:
While he was reflecting thus, the lifespan of Śākyamuni Tathāgata appeared short, being only eighty years.
At that time, his dwelling suddenly became vast, expansive, and pure. Four Tathāgatas appeared before him and addressed him, saying:
One may know the number of drops in all the waters; one may know the weight in *jin* of all the Sumeru mountains;
one may know the number of dust motes in the entire earth; one may know the boundaries of the reaches of space. Yet there is no one able to calculate the lifespan of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni.
You should not give rise to doubt. (Even seventy-nine or eighty characters are but a great number. As it says in the Verses on the Three Teachings:)
The fourth emperor, King Zhao of Zhou, in the year Jia-yin: Śākyamuni was born in Kapilavastu.
King Mu of Zhou, in the year Ren-shen, [53 years after the birth]: the Tathāgata, at eighty years of age, entered parinirvāṇa.
One thousand eight hundred years later: the teaching spread during the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of Han.
The Buddha passed away four hundred and twenty-two years before Laozi was born during the reign of King Ding;
the Buddha passed away four hundred and seventy-seven years before Confucius was born during the time of King Ling.
According to the stone pillar inscription at the Bodhi Temple in India, from the Nirvana of the Tathāgata until the third year of the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty...
It has already been twelve hundred years. Some say one thousand three hundred years; others say one thousand five hundred years.
However, the stone pillar before the Great Shrine (Mahācetiya) in the Śāla grove records only the manner of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, and does not record its year or month.
This was truly a manifestation of the Tathāgata’s skillful transformation. It appeared—
It transcends that which can be measured by quantity; indeed, it is something that ordinary minds cannot fathom.
*The Explanations of Names and Meanings in the Four-Part Vinaya*, Fascicle Thirty-Six:
Phonetic Glossary.
*Guan* (pronounced *juǎn*) means to entice.

*Quan* (upper tone, pronounced *quán*) refers to a fish trap; *di* (lower tone, pronounced *tí*) refers to a rabbit snare. This refers to what is called "having obtained the fish, one forgets the trap;
having obtained the rabbit, one forgets the snare."
Cǎn (慘) is pronounced with the third tone; it means pain or sorrow.
Gū (觚) is pronounced gū.
Hóng (虹) is pronounced hóng.
*Hé* (pronounced *què*): the exhaustion of water.

*The Explanatory Glossary of Terms and Meanings in the Four-Part Vinaya*,
Fascicle Thirty-Seven. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Guangzhou at Jiqiu,
and proofread by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongli of Luofeng, Xin’an.
*Śarīra* is sometimes called *śili*. According to the correct Sanskrit pronunciation, it should be *śarīra*, which translates as "body. It is now abbreviated and corruptedly written as *śarīra*.
The reason it is not translated [into Chinese] is for fear of confusing it with the physical bones of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, it is said:
*Dhātu*. This means "indestructible. There are two types of meaning: first, the whole body; second, the fragmented body.
Regarding the fragmented body, there are three kinds: first, bone *śarīra*, which is white in color; second, flesh *śarīra*, which is red in color.
Third are the hair-relics (*śarīra*), which are black in color. Bodhisattvas and Arhats all possess three kinds [of relics], whereas only the relics of a Buddha possess five colors.
Through supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā*), they cannot be destroyed by any object; even when struck with a hammer, they cannot be broken.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, it has always been fully present; this is the meaning of *dhātu*.
Originating from this *śarīra*, it is that which has been cultivated through the perfuming of morality, concentration, and wisdom, and where all virtues converge.
It is extremely difficult to obtain and is the supreme field of merit (the *śarīra* of the Buddha’s disciples crumbles upon being struck).
*Muguo* (木槨): the second character is pronounced *guò*. The outer coffin is called a *guò*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "In burials, there are wooden enclosures (*guò*).

In this region, the Yellow Emperor was the first to create coffins and outer enclosures; the Yu family used earthenware coffins, while the Yin and Zhou dynasties replaced these with wood. The *Lüben* (Fundamentals of the Law) says: [as cited above].

A wooden outer coffin was made, and an iron inner coffin was placed within it. According to other sūtras and vinayas, it is often said to be a "golden coffin" (*suvarṇa-kośa*) or a "golden inner coffin," or a "metal outer coffin.
These variations arise because the underlying principles expressed by each school differ, leading to such divergent interpretations.

Furthermore, these discrepancies may result from the translators conforming to local vernacular expressions, or from the fact that sentient beings possess either Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna perspectives. Thus, these differences have come about.
It is different. Even a Wheel-Turning King in his ordinary state uses a golden coffin, let alone the Tathāgata, the Most Holy One, whose body is the embodiment of ten thousand virtues.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Latter Part, states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "When I enter nirvāṇa, I shall remain for seven days like a Wheel-Turning King, and then enter the golden coffin.
I shall fill the coffin with exquisite fragrant oil and seal the lid of the coffin securely."
The four sides of the coffin should be adorned with an intermingling of the seven precious jewels. All manner of jeweled banners, incense, and flowers should be offered as worship.
After seven days have passed, the golden coffin should be opened.

Once the body has been removed from the coffin, the Tathāgata’s body should be washed and bathed with all kinds of exquisite perfumed waters. Having completed the washing, [it should be wrapped] with the finest *tūla* cotton.
Cotton was wrapped all over the body. Next, one thousand sheets of exquisite, priceless white woolen cloth were wrapped around the Tathāgata’s body upon the cotton.
Then he was placed into the golden coffin. Furthermore, exquisite fragrant oil was poured into the coffin until it was full.
The coffin was closed and made airtight. Thereupon, [the area was perfumed] entirely with exquisite gośīrṣa sandalwood, agallochum, and all kinds of fragrant woods.
A chariot made of the seven treasures was fashioned, adorned with every kind of precious jewel. Upon it was placed the jeweled coffin, and it proceeded to the site of the cremation.

Countless jeweled banners, countless jeweled canopies, countless jeweled robes, countless celestial music, and countless fragrant flowers filled the entirety of space as a sorrowful offering. All the devas and humans, along with the countless great assemblies, [should...]
Each used sandalwood, aloeswood, and exquisite fragrant oils to cremate the Tathāgata, wailing and yearning with grief.
When the cremation was completed, the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly collected the relics and placed them in a vessel made of the seven precious gems within that city.
At the crossroads, erect a stupa made of the seven treasures to enshrine and honor the śarīra;
this can cause sentient beings to attain great merit, leave behind the suffering of the three realms of existence, and reach the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Pāpā, also known as Pōpō, means "evil" in this language. It was also a settlement of the Kṣatriya (Warrior) caste,
located adjacent to the city of Kuśinagara.
*Mandārava* flowers—
here translated as "flowers that please the mind"— were scattered by devas and humans to the height of the knees at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. These were celestial flowers,
not the mundane *mandārava* flowers [referred to in the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, which states that the heretic Ahva obtained a single *mandārava* flower from the presence of the Tathāgata].
*Mahallaka*, or as it is sometimes called *Makhalaka*, means "old" in this language, or "ignorant. It refers generally to one who is old and ignorant.
According to other sūtras and vinayas, these are all referred to as *mahallaka bhikṣus*; however, in the present vinaya, they refer to the Śākya son Upananda.

To address the Buddha as "Mahallaka" (the Elder) is an error. Furthermore, upon examining the texts of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, we find that Vāṇada had already passed away before the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*.
After his death, his personal belongings were valued at three hundred million gold coins.
Based on this evidence, it is certainly an error. In India, when addressing any foolish or aged person...
Those who know him all call him Mahallaka. Now this bhikṣu has another name;
however, because he is aged, senile, and foolish, and does not distinguish between good and evil, he utters such unlawful words, and for that reason he is called Mahallaka.

The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: Among the five hundred followers brought along by Mahākāśyapa, there was an elderly bhikṣu (*mahallaka*) who was by nature dull-witted and unable to distinguish between good and evil. He then uttered these coarse words: "How wonderful! How joyful!
From this day forward, we shall be free from being constrained by the various precepts and rules that dictate, 'This should be done' and 'This should not be done.'"
"All these matters have ceased. From this day forward, whether you can uphold them or not will depend entirely upon me. Practice what is appropriate;

discard what is unnecessary. When that old man spoke these words, the devas in the sky, hearing his unrighteous speech, immediately used their supernormal powers to muffle the sound so that no one else could hear it, except for Kāśyapa, who led [the assembly].
Having understood these words, the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Entry into Nirvāṇa* states:

There was an elderly bhikṣu named Pāthikaputta who said, "When the Buddha was alive, he constantly restrained us and did not allow us freedom. Now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, we have attained autonomy.
At that moment, a deva heard Pāthikaputta’s words and raised his hand to strike him; Kāśyapa then stepped forward to intercept him.
He held on to it. The deva stopped him, saying, "Upavāna, the Buddha is now entering parinirvāṇa; everyone has lost their reliance.
You alone are foolish to instead feel joy and satisfaction. When Upavāna heard these words, he immediately attained the fruit of arhatship.
The river Hiraṇyavatī is also transcribed as *Hilanyuo*, *Xilianchan*, or *Xilianchanni*; it means "the river of non-attachment.
Crossing this river is the place where the Tathāgata cremated his body. To the west of the Bahudā River is where the Tathāgata... [resided].
Regarding the place of *nirvāṇa*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The river Āciravatī," or alternatively, "the river Aśi-tuo-fa-di.
The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "The river Aśi-tuo-fa-di," which in the language of Tang means "Unconquerable" (*Ajita*).
This is the common designation used in this world. The older transcription "Āli-lo-ba-ti" is erroneous. The older [tradition] further says it is called "Śrīraṇa."
The Vardī River. Translated as "The Golden River" or "The River of Gold Dust," so called because gold dust is produced within its waters.
Dharma Master Zong of the Liang Dynasty said: "The Buddha had a specific intention for coming to the banks of this river to enter parinirvāṇa; the river's current flows with great force."
If the flow of birth and death is swift, yet the golden sand remains unmoved, this serves as a metaphor for the permanence of the Buddha-nature.

Furthermore, it was here on the ground of his causal stage that the Buddha sacrificed his body; therefore, he now enters parinirvāṇa there. However, the Hiraṇyavatī and the Vārakā rivers are separated from one another;
the Vārakā is large, being said to be either twenty *zhang* or forty *zhang* wide, located three or four [li] to the northwest of the city.
A *li* away from the west bank of the river, one reaches the Śāla grove, the place where the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
The small [river] Hiraṇyavatī—some say it is forty feet wide, others say eighty feet—is located to the north of the city.
According to the Vinaya-mūla, after Mahākāśyapa and five hundred great bhikṣus had gone to the city of Kuśinagara, they left the city, crossed the Hiraṇyavatī River, and proceeded toward Heaven...
Guansi (Crown Temple) is located to the northwest of the city, while the site of his self-immolation is to the north of the city.
Guansi is also called Xiguanta (Tomb of the Tied Crown) or Baoguanzhití (Jeweled Crown Stūpa). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that the Buddha said: "By power..."
This is the place where the Śākyamuni was born. This is where, in the past, I was a Cakravartin King; here I removed my precious celestial crown and placed it upon a Pratyekabuddha stūpa.
This is the most supreme and wondrous site where I performed the cremation of my own body. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the Buddha’s body was cremated near the Crown Stūpa.
The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that one crosses the river more than three hundred li north of the city.
Proceeding further, there is a stūpa at the site where the Tathāgata performed the cremation of his body. The ground is now yellowish-black, the soil being mixed with ash and charcoal.

If one makes a sincere supplication, one may obtain śarīra relics. The latter section of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "This ground is the place where all Buddhas of the three periods perform the *caitya-vibha* (cremation).
The World-Honored One of Great Enlightenment, by virtue of his great power of vows, performed the *caitya-vibha* at this very spot."
"Vī. This place contains the various ancient Buddhas and immeasurable jeweled stupas, a site of indestructible diamond-like solidity.
As for the term 'si' (temple): it refers to a saṃghārāma established near a Tiānguān (Heaven-Crown) stupa.

However, 'si' was originally the name for a government office in this region; the *Fēngsùtōng* states that 'si' means 'to oversee. It is extended [to religious sites] because they possess laws and regulations."

It is so called because it was where feudal lords stayed; all such residences were termed *si* (monasteries/temples). The *Guangya* states: "The *si* is governance. The *Sancang* states: "The *si* is an official residence.
The *Shiming* states: "The *si* means succession (*si*). Those who manage affairs succeed one another within it."
Formerly, when Western monks first arrived, they were temporarily stationed at the Honglu Si (Court of State Ceremonial) within the government offices;
later, they were moved to a separate residence. Yet, not forgetting their origin, they retained the name of the temple. The *Sengshi lüe* (Brief History of the Sangha) states:

"The Honglu Si was originally the guesthouse for the envoys from the four barbarian regions and distant lands. Subsequently, a separate location was selected outside the Yong Gate to the west of Luoyang to establish [the monastery]. It was one...
As for the vihāra, because the scriptures were brought on the back of a white horse, it was named after the white horse and called the Baima Si (White Horse Monastery).
It is also called a sengfang (monk’s quarters); a "fang" refers to a separate building. It is also called a jingshe (vihāra) or a daochang (place of practice).
These are all merely names used in this region. In the Western lands [India], they are called *saṃghārāma*, or sometimes *caitya* (zhāotí), or *vihāra*.
*Vihāra* means "place of wandering" (*yóuxíngchù*), referring to the place where the *saṃgha* wanders and treads upon (it is also written as *bìhélà*).

Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty issued an edict that all monasteries throughout the empire should be named *bodhimanda* (*dàochǎng*), meaning the place where the disciples of the Buddha cultivate [the Way].

The Way is the site [of practice]. (Regarding *zhāotí*: the correct Sanskrit term is *cātuspatha*, which means "four directions. It refers to a location that serves as the dwelling place for the Saṃgha from all four directions. There are those in the world who interpret this based on the characters alone.)
"Zhao" (招) means to summon or attract; "ti" (提) means to lift up or lead away—these are merely colloquial expressions.
"Ziranran" (自然然) means to burn. The sutras refer to it as *chāpī* (荼毗), which means "to cremate"; alternatively, it is called *yàxún* (耶旬) or *shājī* (闍).
All of these are foreign languages. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that after the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, it was called *niryāpaṇa*;

the old term "cremation" (*shàowéi*) is an error. Thus, the *Tonghuì yīnyì* (Explanations of Pronunciation and Meaning by Tonghui) records that he personally questioned Indian monks and had never heard the name "cremation.
The *Vinaya-mūla* states: At that time, Mahākāśyapa, sighing with grief, recited verses and circumambulated the coffin seven times.
The fire does not burn spontaneously. The latter part of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"At that time, by the power of great compassion, the Tathāgata caused fire to leap from within his chest out onto the outside of the coffin. It gradually cremated [the body] until, after seven days had passed, it consumed the Pavilion of Wondrous Incense."

Thereupon, as the verses state in the sutra, they were finally finished. As for the "Fragrant Tower" (Gandhakūṭāgāra): at that time, the assembly of humans, devas, and others took exquisite fragrant wood and piled it up high to form a great fragrant tower, upon which the precious coffin was placed.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and the various Dragon Kings filled precious vases with scented water and poured it over the fire to extinguish it, desiring to take up the relics;
however, the intensity of the flames increased further and would not be extinguished at all.
Then Śakra, holding a vase of the seven treasures and various articles of worship, arrived at the site of the cremation, and the fire was instantly and spontaneously extinguished. Śakra...
Śakra then opened the precious coffin of the Tathāgata. From within the Buddha’s mouth, at the upper right jaw, he took one tooth-relic and returned to the heavens to erect a stūpa and offer worship.
At that time, there were two swift rākṣasas who followed behind Śakra with their bodies concealed, invisible to all;
they stole a pair of the Buddha’s tooth-relics. Then, the people within the city...
The assembly immediately opened the Buddha’s coffin. The white *karpāsa* cloth and the *tūla* cotton were perfectly intact, unburned at all.
Then Āniruddha, for the sake of the devas, humans, and the entire great assembly, slowly lifted the white cloth and the *tūla* cotton from the coffin.
The thousand pieces of white woolen cloth belonging to Kāśyapa and the others were not burned at all by the fire.

As for the thousand pieces of white woolen cloth belonging to the people within the city, with the exception of one pair, the rest were reduced to ashes (the Sarvāstivādins say that only one pair on the outside and one pair on the inside remained intact).
The *tūla* cotton was exactly as it had been before. Rāhula took the white woolen cloth and the *tūla* cotton, tore them into fine pieces, and gave them to the various great [monks].
He commanded the assembly to erect stūpas to make offerings to them. Furthermore, he took the ash from the cloth and distributed it, instructing them to erect stūpas;
as for the remaining embers and ashes, each member of the assembly took their portion to erect stūpas and make offerings (and so forth).

At that time, by the power of his great compassion, the World-Honored One shattered his adamantine body into powdered śarīra, leaving behind only four teeth which could not be destroyed. This is the fundamental [account].
The Vinaya states: At that time, the seven kingdoms arrayed their fourfold armies and proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara to contend for the division of the śarīra.
Then the brahmin Drona (alternatively said to be of the Droṇa clan) took a vessel to measure the śarīra and divided it into eight portions.
The first portion was given to the city of Kuśinagara; the second portion was given to the town of Pāpā; the third portion was given to Chāla... [and so forth].
The city of Pāṭaliputra was the fourth share; the village of Ārāmavatī was the fifth share;
the city of Vairaṇyā was the sixth share; the city of Kapilavastu was the seventh share; and the kingdom of Magadha was the eighth share.
Once these people had each received their portions, they returned to their respective places and erected stūpas.

With reverence and respect, they offered abundant worship with music, incense, and flowers (the *Xiyu ji* states: at that time, the devas and nāgas contended over [the relics] and divided them into three portions:

first for the devas, second for the host of nāgas, and third for the human world; these eight kingdoms then further divided them). At that time, Drona took the vessel that had measured the śarīras and erected a stūpa in his native village to offer worship.
There was also a young brahmin (*maṇava*) present in the assembly who immediately begged for the remaining ashes.
He returned to the site of the Pippala tree and erected a stūpa there for veneration.
At that time, there were eight stūpas containing the relics of the World-Honored One in Jambudvīpa; the ninth was the vase stūpa, and the tenth was the ash stūpa.
The Tathāgata’s relics totaled eight *shè* and six *dǒu*, which were divided into eight portions. Seven portions remained in Jambudvīpa, while the fourth portion was [received by] Arāma.
As for the location where it was obtained: it was enshrined and venerated in the Dragon Palace. Furthermore, the Buddha has four tooth-relics (*śarīra*):
one is in the abode of Śakra; one is in the kingdom of Gandhāra; one is in the kingdom of Kaliṅga; and one is in the town of Ālambhika.
Each of these locations erected stupas to enshrine and venerate them. Later, in the town of Pāṭaliputra, King Aśoka...
(Formerly called Aśoka), he opened the seven stupas and took their relics. Throughout Jambudvīpa, he extensively erected eighty-four thousand miraculous stupas, making offerings to them everywhere.
By the majestic power of these stupas, the world was adorned, and devas, nāgas, and yakṣas [were inspired].
All the various spirits and deities alike revere, honor, and make offerings to them, enabling the True Dharma to shine brightly and not perish.
Whatever they may seek or desire shall be fulfilled according to their wishes (some say: King Aśoka opened the kingdom of Magadha;

regarding the stūpas containing śarīra-relics obtained by King Ajātaśatru, he caused spirits and deities to erect eighty-four thousand stūpas in a single day; in China there were nineteen such sites; subsequently, the stūpas of the kingdom of Magadha were restored).
*Yi*: pronounced like *ya* (from the characters *yi* and *jia*). It means to lean against. The modern expressions "to rest" (*yixi*) and "to lean back" (*queyi*) are both correct.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "From the first watch of the night until after the middle watch, Ānanda contemplated his body but had not yet attained anything. Ānanda... [text continues].
He reflected: "The World-Honored One spoke these words in the past: 'If you have already cultivated merit and enter into meditative concentration, you will swiftly attain arhatship.
The Buddha’s word is not false; it should accord with my own mind. Yet, my diligent application has been excessive.
Now I must deliberate and adopt the Middle Way. Thereupon, he descended from the place of walking meditation to the place for washing his feet, and having washed his feet, [he sat down].
He entered his room and sat back upon his bed, wishing to rest for a short while.
As he leaned his body down to lie, his feet had already left the ground but his head had not yet touched the pillow; in that very interval, he attained arhatship.

If anyone were to ask, "Who among those in the Buddha-dharma has attained the Way apart from walking, standing, sitting, or lying down? it is Ānanda. This is according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*.
The Vinaya states: "The Venerable One realized the fruit [of Arhatship] at Vaiśālī. Other schools mostly say: "He attained the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) at Rājagṛha.
As the Mūlasarvāstivāda school says: "The Venerable One, together with a great assembly, went to Rājagṛha.
Having been rebuked and expelled by the Venerable Kāśyapa, he went to the village of Uruvilvā and entered the summer retreat there. There he heard this verse being recited:"
The essential meaning is as follows: before his head even touched the pillow, Ānanda exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*). Furthermore, the *Xiyu ji* states:

To the northwest of the First Council at Rājagṛha, there is a stūpa where Ānanda, having been censured by the Saṃgha and excluded from the council, sat in meditative seclusion and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Only after realizing this fruit did he finally join the assembly.
"Going to Rājagṛha" refers to the five hundred noble ones going to Rājagṛha to compile the Dharma-piṭaka. The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya states:
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying, "We should go to Rājagṛha to compile the Dharma-piṭaka. Why is this?"
The World-Honored One prophesied that among the śrāvaka upāsakas, King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, is foremost in his rootless faith.
He then went together with a thousand bhikṣus to the Kṣatriya Cave in Rājagṛha, where he prepared mats and bedding (and so forth). The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states: At that time, the Venerable Ka...
Upāli said to the assembly: "The World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Magadha; beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: King Ajātaśatru addressed the Sangha, saying: "I now..."
"O Great Virtues, you shall turn the Wheel of Royal Authority; you shall expound the Unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.
Thereupon, by the side of Mount Tiṣyaṃgaparvata, at the entrance of the meditation hall, they first established a lecture hall.

Through the sovereign power of the King, it was completed in a mere moment, like the second heaven of the Trāyastriṃśa, with its rafters and beams fashioned by the celestial artisans, the Viśvakarman-devas.
The rafters, pillars, screens, and stairways were all exquisitely carved with various wondrous designs.

The interior of the hall and its floor were adorned with rare treasures and ornaments, with hanging flowers arranged in rows like those in the palaces of the Brahma Heaven. Five hundred seats were prepared, all facing north.
Furthermore, a high throne decorated with various jewels was set up facing east, intended for the Dharma-preacher to sit upon. (Recorded from the Western Regions)

The record states: In Rājagṛha, at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, five or six *li* to the southwest, on the northern side of the Southern Mountains, within a great bamboo grove, there is a large stone chamber.
This is where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with various great Arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka. In front [of the chamber] is an old foundation; it was for King Ajātaśatru...
The great Arhats assembled the Dharma-piṭaka and constructed this hall (and so forth).
Ānanda, who was renowned for his power of hearing and retaining [the teachings], as praised by the Tathāgata, compiled the Sūtra-piṭaka (formerly called the Sūtra-piṭaka).

To the northwest of the site of the council, there is a stūpa; this is the place where Ānanda realized the fruit of arhatship.

They said to one another, "While the Tathāgata was in the world, we were fellow students under the same teacher. Now that the Dharma King has entered parinirvāṇa, he has excluded us from his favor.
To repay the Buddha’s kindness, we must collect the treasury of the Dharma. Thereupon, ordinary beings and sages gathered together, and the wise and the ignorant assembled in full.

*Saṃgīti*. They further compiled the *Sūtra-piṭaka*, the *Vinaya-piṭaka*, the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*, and the *Mantra-piṭaka*, thus establishing five distinct collections (*piṭakas*).
This council was attended by both ordinary and noble beings; therefore, it is called the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly School).

Regarding the *Dīrgha-āgama*:
the *Vinaya* states that all long sūtras were collected to form the *Dīrgha-āgama*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says it is that which collects those with long prose and verses.

It constitutes the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Master Zao stated: "This *Dīrgha Āgama* consists of four divisions (*caturvarga*) and four recitations (*catuḥparivarta*), comprising thirty sūtras in total as a single collection.
*Āgama* is translated in the Qin language as 'Dharma-gati' (The Return to the Dharma).

This 'Return to the Dharma' is, in essence, the deep reservoir of all virtues and the grove of *dhāraṇī*. As a scripture, it is profound, vast, extensive, and rich; its contents are dense yet ever more expansive, illuminating [the truth]."
It proclaims fortune and calamity, and traces the conduct of the wise and the foolish; it discerns the true from the false and reveals the source of divergent deliverances.

It chronicles the rise and fall of events throughout antiquity and the present, encompassing the two realms of heaven and earth and the categories of all things. There is no path that the Way does not traverse, and no phenomenon where the Dharma is not present.
It is like the vast ocean, into which all rivers flow; therefore, it is named "The Return to the Dharma," opening and analyzing the long journey of cultivation.
Because that which is recorded therein spans vast distances of time, it is titled with the word "Long" (Chang). Those who study this scripture find their long-standing delusions suddenly dispelled.

Where the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox was difficult to discern, it becomes as clear as day and night; where retribution and response were obscure, they are illuminated as clearly as shadows and echoes.

Though kalpas may be remote, they appear as close as morning and evening; though the six directions may be vast, they manifest as if before one's eyes. This may truly be called the brightening of the Great Light within the darkness.
Master Hui bestowed his five eyes upon the multitude of the blind; without looking through doors or windows, his wisdom was all-encompassing.
In the fifteenth year of the Hongshi era, the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra, the Śramaṇa Buddhayaśas, together with the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou, translated it, producing twenty-two fascicles.

This scripture consists of four divisions (*varga*) and five recitations (*bhāṣya*), comprising eighteen chapters (*varga*) in total, amounting to two hundred [discourses].
The twenty-second scripture was translated from the Sanskrit (Fan) into Chinese (Jin) by the Śramaṇa Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin in North India,

The number ends at ten; by adding one more, it is called the *Ekottarika* (Incremental). Furthermore, as each numerical category increases, "increase" (*vṛddhi*) constitutes its primary meaning.
As for its content, it records many prohibitions and precepts with strict and rigorous standards; it serves as a means of worldly discipline and comprehensive regulation.
Within it, there are frequent citations of Vinaya terminology that are not shared with the foreign *śrāmaṇeras* or laypeople.
This scripture consists of four divisions, eight recitations, and a total of fifty-two chapters, comprising five hundred and fifty-five sūtras.

*Gupta*. The old translation "Mixed" (*zā*) captures its essential meaning. The Vinaya states:

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Those whose phrases and sentences are miscellaneous were compiled as the *Saṃyuktāgama*.

The second is called "Middle" (*Majjhima*). The third is called "Long" (*Dīgha*). The fourth is called "Miscellaneous" (*Saṃyutta*). Taking "one" as the basis, they proceed up to eleven;

because the subject matter is moderate and appropriate, it is called "Middle. As for "Long": it explains events of remote antiquity, spanning across kalpas.
"Jue" (Ultimate) refers to the fundamental origins and the sequence of events spanning seven Buddhas and the seven treasures of the Sage Kings; hence it is called "Long" (Chang).

"Za" (Miscellaneous) refers to the various sutras on severing the fetters; they are difficult to recite and difficult to memorize, as their contents are so varied and fragmentary that they easily cause one to forget them;
hence it is called "Miscellaneous. The *Tiantai Wenzhu* states: "The *Ekottarika Āgama* clarifies the causes and effects of humans and devas, while the *Dīrgha Āgama* refutes..."
*Mithyādṛṣṭi*. The *Madhyamāgama* elucidates profound meanings; the *Saṃyuktāgama* elucidates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). [The term] *Āgama* is synonymous with *Āgama* (the scriptures).

Regarding the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*, it is as explained in the Vinaya texts. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "Other miscellaneous discourses were collected into one section, named 'Miscellaneous' (*Kṣudraka*)."
The *Piṭaka* (Basket): from the *Dīrgha Āgama* up to the *Kṣudraka Āgama*, these are collectively termed the *Sūtra Piṭaka*.

Regarding the *Abhidharma Piṭaka*, it is said that the *Mātṛkā Sūtra* compiles the difficult points, the non-difficult points, the bound [topics], the corresponding [topics], and the bases of composition into the *Abhidharma Piṭaka*.

It is said: There are five types—namely, *praśnavyākaraṇa* (analytical exposition), *apraśnavyākaraṇa* (non-analytical exposition), *saṃgraha* (inclusion), *saṃprayoga* (association), and *sthānaja* (arising from location)—which are called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
(The detailed explanation is as found in the *Vibhaṅga*, and a brief summary follows below).

The Tripiṭaka consists of: first, the Vinaya Piṭaka; second, the Sūtra Piṭaka; and third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka. To state it briefly, these are collectively called the three piṭakas of Vinaya, Sūtra, and Śāstra.
According to other schools, it is commonly said that the Sūtra Piṭaka was compiled first; this present text...
Both the Vinaya and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* state that the Vinaya-piṭaka was compiled first. As the *Samantapāsādikā* says:
"The Venerable Kāśyapa asked the elders: 'Which was taught first, the Dharma-piṭaka or the Vinaya-piṭaka? The bhikṣus replied:"
"Venerable Sir, the Vinaya Piṭaka is the life-span of the Buddha-dharma. When the Vinaya Piṭaka abides, the Buddha-dharma also abides.
Therefore, we first brought forth the Vinaya Piṭaka. Based on this, the collection of the Vinaya Piṭaka was established first;

however, for the sake of textual convenience, the translator has placed its exposition later. Furthermore, when speaking in terms of the three trainings, the Vinaya also comes first. (The Four Teachings)

The *Yi* (義) states: "When teaching, it is not the time for practice; when the teaching arises, the *Āgama* comes first. When beginning the practice of cultivation, the *Prātimokṣa* is foremost. Therefore, the *Chuyao jing* (出曜經) explains the sequence of the teachings as: first the Sūtras, next the Vinaya, and finally the Śāstras."
The Sarvāstivādins say: At that time, Kāśyapa had this thought: "People of future generations will have little wisdom and dull faculties;

they will understand according to the literal text and fail to penetrate the profound meaning. It would be appropriate for me now to personally compose the *mātṛkā*, so that the meaning of the Sūtras and Vinaya shall not be lost.
Having formed this thought, he then performed the formal motion and the second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
Having ground [the stone], he informed the assembly so that they would know. Once the assembly had granted permission, he ascended the high seat and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Mātṛkā, I shall now speak of my own accord, making clear all that has been understood. That is to say:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, the four dharma-phrases, the knowledge of non-contention and the knowledge resulting from aspiration,
as well as the meditative absorption of the limit, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the various meditative absorptions practiced in alternation,
the correct entry into clear realization, and conventional knowledge; śamatha, vipaśyanā, the collection of dharmas, and the aggregates of dharmas— these are collectively termed *mātṛkā*.
Kāśyapa. This is the Abhidharma Piṭaka. The original Vinaya does not state that it was compiled by Kāśyapa;

rather, as some say, he further requested Ānanda to compile the Abhidharma Piṭaka. Since the Abhidharma Piṭaka was also personally taught by the Buddha, it did not require Kāśyapa to produce it separately.
As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states: "He immediately requested Ānanda to ascend the lion throne and inquire of the Buddha..."
In what place was the Abhidharma first taught? Ānanda, receiving the mission of the Saṃgha, spoke thus: "Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the city of Śrāvastī. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

'If the five fears, the five offenses, and the five enmities are not extinguished, for this reason and condition, one will experience immeasurable suffering of body and mind within this very life. Furthermore...

In future lives, one will fall into the evil realms. Because all beings possess these five fears, five offenses, and five enmities as their causes and conditions, they experience various forms of physical and mental happiness in this life, and in future lives, they are born in the bliss of the heavens.
What are the five fears that should be avoided? First, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech.
Fifth is drinking alcohol. Such [categories] as these are called the Abhidharma-piṭaka; therefore, the Vinaya does not state that it was spoken by Kāśyapa.
Alternatively, it is said that Kātyāyanīputra compiled the essential wisdom of various sūtras and presented them to the Buddha for his approval, naming them the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
The *Pinfen gongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit) states: "The Sūtras are the teachings spoken by the Buddha, or [those spoken] for the sake of various..."
For celestial kings, or for those of external paths and heterodox studies, [the teachings] provide understanding according to their respective circumstances.
As for *sūtra*, it means that like a thread, it connects the principles of meaning so as to form the dharmas of practice; hence it is called *sūtra*.
*Vinaya* refers to prohibitions and discipline. It is taught for the two assemblies of monks to restrain evil and curb what is improper; it consists of either two hundred and fifty [precepts], or...
The five hundred matters cite the Dharma to prevent misconduct; they are like the secret treasury of a king, which is not for the private use of external officials.
Therefore, it is called the "Inner Treasury. This Vinaya Piṭaka is likewise: it is not something that śrāmaṇeras or lay followers (upāsakas and upāsikās) may hear or see.
Therefore, it is called the "Vinaya Piṭaka. As for Abhidharma, it is the Great Dharma. This is why it is called "Great."
This refers to the Great Wisdom of the Four Noble Truths, the vanguard banner of all dharmas, which severs all false views and the vast delusion of ignorance;
therefore, it is called the "Great Dharma. It is also named the "Peerless Dharma" (Anupama-dharma).

Because the eight knowledges and ten wisdoms, as well as untainted right view, transcend the obstructions of the three realms and have no equal, it is called the "Peerless Dharma. Kātyāyanīputra compiled these various sūtras.
The essential wisdom was excerpted and presented for the Buddha’s approval; thus it is named the Great Dharma Treasury (*Mahādharmakośa*). Ānanda reflected:
"The meaning of these three baskets corresponds to the three liberations. Why? The sublime wisdom of the *Sūtras* accords with the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

the *Vinaya* restrains evil, its profound nature being identical to signlessness (*animitta*); the Right View of the Great Dharma follows the trace of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Therefore, they are called the Three Baskets."
The three liberations (vimokṣa) are a profound convergence of dark traces. (In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the four piṭakas are designated, which includes the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* by implication.

Pūraṇa (also transcribed as Púlánà or Bùlànnà); this means "Full" or "Complete. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
