● Vinaya Piṭaka, Volume 59:
Five Unlawful Matters.
The Teacher has five unlawful acts; the disciple should confess them and depart, and should speak thus to the Teacher.
He says: "The preceptor does not know whether I am acting in accordance with the Dharma (1). He does not know whether I am not acting in accordance with the Dharma (2).
If I commit an offense, he neither corrects nor rebukes me (3). If I commit one, he does not even know it (4). If I confess my offense, he still does not know it (5).
When a preceptor possesses these five qualities, the disciple should confess and depart. — *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü)
The Vinaya states: "If the upādhyāya or ācārya commits a transgression, the disciple should offer counsel. One must not use harsh language;
rather, one should speak with gentle words according to the method of instruction: 'Master, you should not do such a thing. If he follows this advice, it is well.
If, however, he instead responds with reproach, then if it is the upādhyāya, the disciple should abandon him and go far away; if it is the ācārya, the disciple should take his robes and depart."
The alms bowl. Having stayed overnight outside the boundary, one should return to rely upon another person as a preceptor. If that person has influence, one should go far away;
otherwise, one should rely upon a virtuous and eminent person. Furthermore, there are four kinds of ācāryas:
first, one who has neither food nor the Dharma—one should leave without asking; second, one who has food but no Dharma—one should ask before leaving; third, one who has... [text truncated]
Regarding the rules for food: even if it is bitter, one should not leave as long as one's life lasts. Fourth, regarding those who have both food and the Dharma:
even if they are driven away, one should not leave as long as one's life lasts. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"If a disciple sees a fault in their teacher—whether real or unreal—their own mind will be ruined, and they will no longer be able to obtain the benefits of the Dharma. If you see a fault in your teacher, do not give rise to resentment; rather, you should [reflect as follows]:"
He reflects: "Because my merit was not sufficient in previous lives, I did not encounter a Buddha.
Now that I have encountered this teacher of miscellaneous practices, I must not dwell upon his faults, lest I obstruct and lose the Prajñāpāramitā myself. As for the teacher's faults—"
Do not be attached to the self. I have merely received the Dharma of Prajñā from my teacher. It is like a dog-skin bag containing precious jewels;
one should not discard the jewels because of the bag. It is like a criminal holding a candle to light the path;
one should not refuse its light because of the person's crime, thereby falling into a ditch oneself. Furthermore, it is like traveling on a road and sending a small...
When a person guides one on the Path, one should not disregard their words simply because that person is of small stature. For such reasons as these, one should not distance oneself from the teacher.

Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra: "Again, there may be a teacher of the Dharma who maintains pure precepts, is free from the five desires, is highly learned and widely known, possesses a good reputation, and is honored for his majestic virtue; the disciple receives the Dharma from him."
Yet they do not take notice of you. In this matter, you must not harbor resentment. You should think to yourself:
"It is because of the sins of my past lives that I am now a person of small merit. It is not that the teacher holds me in low regard; it is simply that I lack the fortune to draw near to him.
Furthermore, I must abandon pride in the presence of the teacher in order to seek the benefit of the Dharma. There are many such teachers as these.
Because a bodhisattva seeks prajñā, they should with single-minded reverence disregard the teacher’s faults.

If one can practice such patience and maintain a single-minded mind toward the teacher without conceiving thoughts of increase or decrease, you will fully obtain the sublime Dharma from the teacher, just as a vessel that is sound and sturdy does not leak what it receives.
(The method for revering the teacher is explained in detail in the *Sūtra on Proper Reverence*.)

Regarding the five types of transgressions, there are those that may be committed. For some, one performs repentance through self-reflection (as when a transgression is not intentional; having committed a *tṛṣkṛta* offense of mental remorse, one repents within one's own mind and does not commit it again).

For others, there is the commission of a minor offense for which one seeks repentance from another (as when one commits an intentional *tṛṣkṛta* offense, or speaks harsh words to a single person, whereby it may be eliminated). Or there is...

Regarding the commission of a medium offense, one must likewise confess before another person (as in the case of a *pāyattika* offense). For an offense that is inherently minor or a preparatory *sthūlātyaya*, confession before a single person is sufficient to bring about its purification.
There may be those who have committed grave offenses. For example, regarding offenses such as *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, they are extinguished through the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) of twenty persons;

likewise, for heavy *sthūlātyaya* bordering on *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or *pārājika*, they are extinguished by the community performing the ritual together with four or more members (in the case of heavy *sthūlātyaya* bordering on *pārājika*, the entire Saṃgha performs the ritual together). There may also be other offenses.

It cannot be expiated (this refers to the *pārājika* offense). The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one commits any of the offenses of the five categories, each incurs three types of transgressions.

For example, in committing a *pārājika*: by violating the essence of the precept, it is a *pārājika*; by contravening the Buddha’s teaching, it is a *pāyattika*; and by violating the rules of decorum, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This applies even to the numerous rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*); committing them constitutes three transgressions, including the violation of the precept itself."

The transgression of the *śīla* essence is a *duṣkṛta*; violating the Buddha’s words is a *pāyattika*; and violating the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*) is a *duṣkṛta*. Each of these constitutes three offenses.
When performing repentance, one need only repent for the *śīla* essence, and the other two offenses are extinguished along with it, because the *śīla* essence is the root.

(This is the intent of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*. If one follows the *Mūlasarvāstivāda*, when repenting for the primary offense, all preparatory acts, violations of the teachings, and concealments must each be named in succession as they are repented; however, they need not be mentioned separately.)

The ancient masters of the Mahīśāsaka school first repent of secondary offenses, such as those arising from birth or concealment, and subsequently repent of the fundamental offense; this is because they follow the principle of addressing the lighter first and the heavier later (the intention of the Mahīśāsaka school is likewise the same).

The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* states: "There are cases where one commits a grave offense but the retribution is light; there are cases where one commits a light offense but the retribution is heavy; there are cases where one commits a grave offense and the retribution is also grave;
and there are cases where one commits a light offense and the retribution is also light. Regarding those who commit a grave offense but receive light retribution, there was a bhikṣu who...
If one acts as a matchmaker for men and women, if they are brought together, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if they are not brought together, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu privately constructs a dwelling without informing the Saṃgha and requesting formal authorization (*karmavācanā*), and it remains unfinished, he commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once completed, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; this is called a grave transgression with a light retribution.
Regarding a light transgression with a heavy retribution: if a bhikṣu, with a mind of anger, strikes an arhat; or again, with a mind of desire, touches an arhat, giving rise to defiled attachment;
or even striking the Buddha, giving rise to a mind of lustful desire toward the Buddha; or using harsh speech to revile an arhat.
In the Vinaya of the Han [tradition], as well as in the Buddha's teachings, it is stated that to revile those who are physically deformed or lack sensory faculties constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;

this is called "a light offense with a heavy retribution. Regarding "a grave offense with a grave retribution," this refers to the *pārājika* offenses, as well as the two cases of groundless slander against noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
One incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense in four cases: first, defiling the families of others; second, employing means to subvert the Wheel of Dharma and the Saṃgha;
third, following those who subvert the Wheel of Dharma and their followers; fourth, being of evil character and refusing to accept admonition from others. These constitute grave offenses.
The retribution is also heavy. Regarding those offenses that are light and whose retribution is also light:

if a bhikṣu enters a village without maintaining mindfulness, failing to restrain the four deportments of the body and the four faults of speech, and commits an offense through forgetfulness or error, he should confess before one person; this is a *pāyattika*.

*Ti*. *Duṣkṛta*. If a bhikṣu commits an offense but forgets to confess it, and only remembers it at the time of the *poṣadha*, if he wishes to confess it but fears disturbing the Sangha’s hearing of the precepts, he should mentally recite it in silence; once the recitation of the precepts is finished, he should then perform the confession.
In cases such as these, the offense committed is light and the retribution is likewise light. As for *pārājika*, although the name of the offense is the same, the karmic fruit is different.

They are different. Why is this? Just as the objects of sexual misconduct are not uniform—whether involving animals or humans—and among humans there are those who have left the household life and those who have not;
and among those who have not left the household life, there are two kinds: those who observe the precepts and those who do not;

and among those who have left the household life, there are five kinds, including both those who observe the precepts and those who do not, up to and including the noble ones (*ārya*). Such are the distinctions.
They are distinct. Although the names of the offenses are the same, their retributive fruits differ. Regarding the second *pārājika*:

if one cuts off the life-faculty of such persons as devas, humans, or even noble ones (*ārya*), one incurs a *pārājika*. Although the term "cutting off" is the same, [the gravity of the offense varies].
The retributive results are also different. Regarding the third *pārājika*: the locations from which theft occurs are not uniform;

there are distinctions between stealing from those who have left the household life and those who remain in it, as well as among laypeople themselves. Among those who have left the household life, there are also distinctions in theft.
Furthermore, there are distinctions regarding theft from the Triple Gem. Therefore, although the name *pārājika* is the same, [the offenses differ].
There are differences in the retribution [received]. Regarding the fourth *pārājika*, there is also a distinction:

if one speaks of having attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) to a layperson, the offense is grave; if one speaks of it to a renunciant, the offense of having attained superhuman states is light.
Therefore, although the name of the offense is the same, the retribution differs. Furthermore, some offenses require a formal ritual (*kamma*), while others do not.
Regarding those requiring *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action): these include the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses up to harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). Regarding those not requiring *karmavācanā*:
these are the three *pārājika* offenses. Once a *pārājika* offense has been committed, it can be removed through *karmavācanā*, as in the case of the bhikṣu Nandika, who had no concealment;
his mind was continuous from moment to moment without a single thought of hiding [the offense], nor did he take pleasure in abandoning the dharma-robes.
The Sangha performs the *karmavācanā* for him to obtain the precepts. As for why he obtains the precepts: first, this person has seen the Buddha;
second, his mind in revealing [his transgressions] is grave. For these reasons, he obtains the precepts. This is called "having necessity" and "not having necessity," as explained above.
There are seven types of violations of the precepts, namely: from *pārājika* down to *duṣkṛta*. Regarding *pārājika*, it does not arise...
Roots of goodness can never be restored through repentance, nor can the offense be removed by means of *karmavācanā*.
There are *sthūlātyaya* offenses that cannot have their guilt removed by *karmavācanā*. Why? For example, Devadatta’s shedding of the Buddha’s blood is such a case.
This *sthūlātyaya* prevents the arising of untainted roots of goodness forever, and there is no *karmavācanā* by which its guilt may be removed. There are also *pāyattika*...
[If one] does not give rise to roots of goodness, there is also no *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) by which the offense can be removed. Why?

For example, if a bhikṣu, out of a mind of hatred, desires to take the life of a Buddha or strikes the Buddha, he incurs a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation), which cannot be atoned for through confession.

There is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) that does not give rise to roots of goodness, and likewise there is no *karmavācanā* for removing the offense. Why? [Because this applies even to] śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās...
Kṣāmaṇī. Among the four *pārājika* offenses, if one commits even a single one, this transgression cannot be expiated.

Therefore, for those who have committed [an offense], there is that which requires a formal act (*karmavācanā*) and that which does not. That which requires a formal act followed by further formal acts refers to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
That which, once the formal act has been performed, requires no further formal act refers to the thirty matters, the ninety matters, and so forth. This is it.

Regarding offenses committed through forgetfulness or error: they are extinguished by mental reflection and self-reproach. As for "extinguished by mental reflection and self-reproach," this refers to those among the *śaikṣa-dharmas* (rules of training) that are not intentionally committed.
Regarding intentional offenses: those of the lower grade are called "light" when one confesses them before a single person.
Those of the middle grade—namely, the *svabhāva-sthūlātyaya*, the *pāyattika*, and the *pratideśanīya*—are [extinguished] therein.

Regarding offenses: one may repent before a single person. As for the grave offenses—namely, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the *sthūlātyaya* bordering on *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the *sthūlātyaya* bordering on *pārājika*—these are the gravest among those that can be repented of. There are four types of offenses that cannot be repented of:
the four *pārājika*, the *duṣkṛta*, the *pāyattika*, and the *sthūlātyaya*; these sins cannot be repented of.
There are five faults in breaking the precepts:
first, self-harm; second, being rebuked by the wise; third, the spread of an evil reputation; fourth, giving rise to regret at the time of death;
and fifth, falling into the evil realms after death. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "A person who upholds the precepts contemplates the person who breaks them."
This is a transgression. You should exert yourself and maintain the precepts with a single mind. What is called the transgression of a person who breaks the precepts?
A person who breaks the precepts is not respected by others; their home is like a cemetery, a place where people do not go. A person who breaks the precepts loses all merits;
they are like a withered tree that no one loves or delights in. A person who breaks the precepts is like a lotus flower covered in frost.
People do not delight in seeing one who has broken the precepts; such a person with an evil mind is as fearsome as a rākṣasa.
People do not turn toward one who has broken the precepts, just as a thirsty person does not approach a dried-up well.

One who has broken the precepts is constantly filled with doubt and regret, like a person who has committed a crime and is perpetually afraid that punishment will arrive. One who has broken the precepts is like a field that has been...
Hailstones are not to be relied upon; likewise, one who has broken the precepts is like a bitter gourd—though its shape resembles that of a sweet seed, it is unfit for consumption.
One who has broken the precepts is like a village of bandits; they are not to be relied upon for refuge. One who has broken the precepts...
For example, just as people do not wish to approach a sick person, one who has broken the precepts cannot escape suffering.
For example, just as it is difficult to traverse a perilous road, one should not dwell together with one who has broken the precepts.

For example, just as it is difficult to draw near a wicked thief, one who has broken the precepts is like a pit of fire; practitioners avoid them, for one who has broken the precepts is difficult [to associate with].
One may dwell together with them; however, a person who has broken the precepts is like a venomous snake and must not be approached or touched.
A person who has broken the precepts is like a great fire. A person who has broken the precepts is like a shattered boat and cannot be used for crossing over.

A person who has broken the precepts is like vomited food and must not be eaten again. When a person who has broken the precepts is among a virtuous assembly, they are like a vicious horse among good ones.
Among horses, one who has broken the precepts is different from a good horse, like a donkey in a herd of oxen.
Among those who are diligent, one who has broken the precepts is like a weakling among the strong.
Although one who has broken the precepts resembles a bhikṣu, they are like a corpse among sleeping people. One who has broken the precepts is like a counterfeit pearl among genuine ones.
Among pearls, a person who has broken the precepts is like an *eranda* tree growing amidst a grove of sandalwood.
Although such a person may outwardly resemble a virtuous one, within they possess no wholesome dharmas; though they shave their heads, don dyed robes, and take up the counting sticks in succession.
Though called a bhikṣu, he is not truly a bhikṣu; he is a person who has broken the precepts.
If such a person wears the Dharma robes, they are like sheets of hot copper and red-hot iron wrapped around his body. If he holds an alms bowl, it is like a vessel for molten copper.
Whatever food he eats is like swallowing glowing iron balls or drinking hot molten copper. If he receives offerings from others...
To give [such things] is to be in hell. If the hell-wardens and their keepers enter a vihāra, it is as if they have entered a great hell;
if they sit upon the beds and couches of the Saṃgha, it is as if they are sitting upon beds of glowing iron. Furthermore, this applies to those who have broken the precepts.
He is constantly filled with dread and anxiety, like a gravely ill person who always fears the arrival of death;

or like one who has committed the five heinous crimes, whose mind perpetually reflects, "I am a thief of the Buddha," hiding and seeking cover like a robber fearing men as the months, years, and days pass by.
They are never at peace. Although a person who has broken the precepts may receive offerings, profit, and comfort, such pleasure is impure.
It is like a fool offering worship and adorning a corpse; when a wise person hears of it, they loathe it and do not wish to see it.
Thus, there are various and immeasurable transgressions of breaking the precepts that cannot be fully described. A practitioner should maintain them with a single-minded resolve.
Regarding the precepts:
among the five kinds of salt mentioned here, two of these five kinds are as explained in the Bhaiṣajyavastu (The Chapter on Medicines).

"Cat skin" should be called "wild cat skin. A wild cat is the same as a wild *li* (weasel); a domestic *li* is simply a cat. The character for "cat" (*māo*) is pronounced with the second tone on *biāo*, sounding like "miao";
it is the beast that catches mice. At dawn and dusk its eyes are both round; at noon they contract until they are like a thread.
The tip of the nose is always cold; it is warm for only one day at the summer solstice. This is because it belongs to the category of yin.
Thus, its resonance with yin energy is as such.
(Yi Shi Pi)
As detailed in the *Carma-vastu*,
the Vinaya states that there are five rules for a junior bhikṣu to perform repentance before a senior bhikṣu: he shall bared his right shoulder.
Having removed his leather sandals, he should pay homage at the elder’s feet, place his right knee on the ground, and join his palms.

He should state the name and category of the offense, speaking as follows: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense; I confess it before the Venerable Elder. The Elder should reply:
"Reproach yourself and give rise to a sense of weary detachment. The other replies: "So be it. The Elder remains seated while the other stands below him.
One should confess before a seated bhikṣu. There are four procedures: bare the right shoulder; remove the leather sandals; kneel with the right knee on the ground and join the palms;
and state the name of the offense committed, saying: "I have committed such-and-such an offense; I now confess it before the Elder. The other should say:
"You should reform and repent, and give rise to a mind of weary detachment. He should reply: "So be it. The *Mātṛkā Sūtra* states that the senior monk [should act] toward the junior monk.
If one has committed an offense, one should stand before [the preceptor] and confess by means of four dharmas:

first, baring the right shoulder; second, removing the leather sandals; third, joining the palms; fourth, declaring the offense committed. When a junior monk confesses an offense to a senior monk, five dharmas should be established before him;
the third [dharma] is added: kneeling on the right knee, which thus constitutes five dharmas. Other schools [state this].
All follow this same format. As for the statement that "the *upādhyāya* kneels on his haunches" (*hukui*), this is likely an error in the original text.
Regarding "kneeling on the haunches": one places both feet flat on the ground with both knees upright; one gathers and tucks up the robes so they do not trail on the floor.
This is the standard procedure for confessing offenses (*pāpadeśanā*) before others, for the ritual of purifying robes (*cīvara-śuddhi*), or when addressing the assembly.
And thus they show respect; or, having been rebuked, they request forbearance; or, upon receiving full ordination, they prostrate to the Sangha—all such cases are identical to this.
(In Sanskrit, this is called *utkuṭuka*, which here means "squatting," that is, kneeling with one knee on the ground.)

The names of the categories of offenses refer to the distinctions among the six groups (*ṣaḍ-varga*). "Species" (*jāti*) refers to differences such as keeping extra robes or being separated from one's robes; there are thirty such matters.

"Nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the difference between being singular or manifold. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "A single name with many species; self-nature and non-self-nature; abiding in distinct differences. (10)
The recitation says: The Buddha spoke to Upāli: "There is one kind of offense whose natures are each distinct;
the nature of a *pārājika* is each distinct; the nature of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is each distinct; the nature of a *pāyattika* is each distinct."
The nature of the *pāṭidesanīya* offenses is distinct for each; the nature of the *duṣkṛta* offenses is distinct for each.
The remainder is as explained in the *Śikṣāpada-vastu*.
The Vinaya states regarding visiting bhikṣus: A young visiting bhikṣu should pay homage to an elder, resident bhikṣu by means of five things.
He should bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, grasp the elder’s feet, and say: "Venerable sir, I..."
Saying "Namo. If a junior monk bows to a visiting senior (*upādhyāya*) monk, it is also done in this manner. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"The person receiving the bow must not remain like a mute sheep without speaking; they should exchange greetings. They ought to ask whether [the visitor] has few ailments."
"Are you free from affliction? Are you at ease? Have you not been fatigued by the journey? Thus should the visiting bhikṣu ask.
He should inquire, "Who is the senior monk of the Saṃgha? Who is the second and third senior monk? and he should pay homage at their feet.

The resident bhikṣus should ask, "Venerable sir, how many years have you been ordained? If the visiting bhikṣu is junior, they should offer him a seat and have him sit; if there is [a meal], it should be before or after the meal.

Regarding food, oil for anointing the feet, and non-timely beverages, a visiting or resident bhikṣu should act in this manner. If one does not, it is a transgression of the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*).
The *Nèfǎchuán* (Inner Dharma Transmission) states: "In the past, while the Great Master was alive, he personally served as the Teacher. When visiting bhikṣus arrived..."

One should personally announce, "Welcome. Furthermore, it is the established rule for the monastic community in the Western Regions that whenever anyone new arrives—whether a guest, a resident, a disciple, or a follower—the senior members must immediately step forward and chant "Svāgata" (translated as "Welcome").
The guest, upon hearing this, should then respond with "Susvāgata" (translated as "Most Welcome"). If one does not speak thus, [there is a fault].
This violates the monastic regulations. Second, according to the Vinaya, there is an offense; regardless of whether one is senior or junior, all cases are treated in this manner.

He shall immediately take up the [disciple’s] water jar and bowl and hang them on a wall hook, then sit down in a suitable place to allow him to rest. The junior monk should move to a screened-off area.
When the person of higher status is in front, the one of lower status shows reverence by grasping their calf muscles, moving from the back to the entire body;
when the person of higher status is below, they repeatedly press upon their back, but not as far as the waist or feet. Among those of equal age, there is no distinction in these matters.
Once his fatigue had been relieved, he then washed his hands and feet. Next, he approached the Venerable One to extend his salutations;
he performed a single prostration and knelt to touch the Venerable’s feet. The Venerable then extended his right hand and stroked the disciple’s shoulders and back.
If they had not been separated for a long time, he would not have performed this stroking. The Teacher then asked after his well-being, and the disciple answered according to the circumstances.
Thereafter, they withdrew to one side and sat respectfully. In truth, there is no fixed rule for this;

however, according to Western (Indian) custom, people mostly sit on small stools and keep their feet bare. Since these practices do not exist in the Eastern Land (China), the ritual of clasping the feet is not observed here.
When the sutras describe humans and devas coming to the Buddha’s presence, prostrating at his two feet and withdrawing to sit on one side, it refers precisely to this.

This is the proper procedure. Thereafter, one should release [the restrictions] regarding the timing and provide hot drinks, such as *sarpis* (clarified butter), honey, and granulated sugar, to be consumed according to one’s inclination.

At times, there are eight types of syrups (*aṣṭau pānakāni*), all of which must be strained through a cloth filter; only when they are clear may they be drunk. If they are mixed with turbid dregs, this is strictly not permitted.

As for preparations such as apricot soup, their substance is inherently thick and turbid; according to the principles of the Vinaya, these are entirely outside the scope of permissible drinks. *Vinaya*.
It is said: Generally, when beverages are filtered and purified, their color is like that of yellow reeds; this refers to the Western Regions (India).
Regarding the etiquette for welcoming between masters and disciples, or between new and old guests meeting one another:

how could there be such haste as to set aside one's robes and bundles, perform a hurried *vaṃdana*, and act with such agitation—whether arriving suddenly in the cold, coming newly in the heat, with sweat pouring from every limb, or with hands and feet frozen stiff?
This deeply deviates from established norms; yet you, Master, have established it. To occasionally inquire about other matters is indeed too hasty.
This is intended for the propagation and flourishing [of the Dharma] (if one were to perform prostrations at another time, as detailed below).
*Vaṃ-nam* (or *bā-nam*) is what is said. Master Ying states that the correct term is *pántán*, which translates as "I pay homage.
If one says *namo siddhārtha*, this is translated as "prostration" (*lǐbài*). (*Namaḥ* means "taking refuge" or "dedicating one's life"; to say "prostration" is also not the precise translation).
Regarding the distinction between *namas* (bowing) and *vandanā* (prostration), their respective applications are roughly as follows.

Among the lay followers of the Western lands who possess faith and reverence, when they see Brahmins or non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), they utter the word "kneeling prostration" (*kuei-pai*). However, if they see a *bhikṣu*, they say "reverential salutation" (*jing-li*).
This is the specific differentiation within the ritual laws of the Western lands. The new translations of the scriptures correctly render this as *praṇāma* (畔睇).—Master Tripiṭaka Yi Jing.
It is said: as for the term "wǎnnán" (和南), in Sanskrit it is called *vandana* or *vandamāna*, translated as "reverential salutation" (*jìnglǐ*).
However, because the colloquial pronunciation was not accurate, it came to be called "wǎnnán. To capture the correct phonetics, one should say *vandana*.
For instance, when the monastics of the Western lands wish to go outside to pay homage to sacred images, if someone asks them, "Where are you going? [they reply accordingly].
The disciple replied, "I was just now paying homage at a certain caitya; that is precisely what it refers to.
Furthermore, the intent behind all acts of prostration is to show reverence to those above and to observe the etiquette of self-humility.

When wishing to pay respect or when making a formal request, one first adjusts the dharma robe, draping it over the left shoulder and tucking the left arm through the armpit so that it stays in place against the body, and then uses the left hand—
Bend downward. Cover the left side of the robe with the right hand, following the hem of the skirt as it reaches the lower edge;
roll the cloth up toward the knees so that both knees are covered and the body is not revealed. Ensure the edge of the robe behind is drawn close to the body;
tuck in the garments so they do not hang down to the ground. Keep both heels firmly planted and the spine straight. Ten.
He prostrated himself with his fingers touching the ground; only then did he strike his head in homage. Yet, beneath his knees, there was absolutely no clothing.
He returned to join his palms, then struck the ground again, paying his respects with such earnest devotion that he repeated this three times.

Had it been an ordinary occasion, he would have ceased after a single prostration, with no further purpose for rising in between. When those in the Western Regions saw him perform these three prostrations, everyone marveled at it, fearing [it might be excessive].
If there is dust upon the forehead, one must first rub the hands to cleanse it, and only then wipe it away.

Next, one should brush off the dust from both knees, adjust one’s robes, and sit to one side; alternatively, one may stand for a short while. If the Venerable One deems it appropriate to grant a seat, one should sit;
however, if there is to be a reprimand, there is no harm in remaining standing. This was the practice when the Buddha was in the world. Up to...
In these latter ages, the transmission from master to disciple has continued without interruption to this day. As it is stated in the Sūtras and Vinaya:
"One approaches the Buddha’s presence, prostrates at the Buddha’s feet, and sits to one side"—it does not say that one spreads out a sitting mat.
One prostrates three times and stands to one side; such is the teaching. However, in places where elders reside, many seats must be provided. Should anyone arrive, one should act accordingly.
One sits according to the prescribed ritual. All who sit do so with their feet planted firmly on the ground; there has never been a method of resting the knees [on the seat].
If one follows the manner of squatting, it should be done as described above; alternatively, one may place both knees on the ground, keep the body upright, and join the palms.
This is indeed the manner of gazing upon and praising the Fragrant Terrace (Gandhakuṭī). However, performing prostrations upon a bed is a practice unknown in any other country;
nor have I ever seen the spreading of mats or carpets for such a purpose. To desire to show reverence while instead acting with negligence—how could this possibly constitute a valid principle?

As for matters such as beds and mats, one does not even offer formal respect when sitting upon them in a state of equanimity; how much less so when performing the rites of worship toward a venerable teacher or a Great Master? This matter...
How could it be appropriate [to use large beds]? Within the lecture halls and dining halls of the Western Regions (India), large beds have traditionally never been placed;
instead, many wooden stools and small benches are provided. When attending lectures or eating, one uses these to sit in a squatting posture (*jūza*).

This is the original method. In the Divine Land (China), however, one sits on large beds in a cross-legged position. Although this practice has long existed, even if one may adapt the ritual to the times, [it is not the original tradition].
One must recognize the source of both the root and the branches. Furthermore, regarding the method of ritual respect, one must accord with the proper etiquette.

If one does not follow the teachings, one will stumble even on level ground; thus the Buddha said: "There are two kinds of defiled contact for which one should neither accept prostrations nor prostrate to others.
If one violates these teachings, every single bow incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). The first is [when one has been engaged in] eating or drinking."

Defilement. Second is impure defilement (the two types of defiled touch are as set forth in the *Vihāra-khandhaka* under the section on "salutation"). Furthermore, when a great assembly has gathered...
During the sequence of a *poṣadha* assembly, joining the palms is itself an act of reverence; therefore, one need not perform the full prostration.
To perform the full prostration would contravene the teachings. Whether in a crowded or narrow place, on impure ground, or while on a road, performing the prostration constitutes the same offense.
If it is at another time, one should indeed perform the full prostration, as the Buddha told Upāli: "Whenever one says with the mouth, 'I now pay homage...'"
Ritual courtesy (*li*) consists merely of verbal acts of respect. If one bows the body while saying "vaṃde" (I prostrate), although this is a form of courtesy, it is not complete.
There are, however, two types of respectful salutation: first, touching the five wheels [of the body] to the ground; second, grasping the calves with both hands.
In both cases, one should say, "I now pay my respects," and the other should reply, "May you be free from illness. If it is otherwise, [it is incomplete].
Both incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: The Buddha told Upāli:
"To utter 'Vandana' (homage) is verbal; if one bends the body, this is called mental purity.

When a bhikṣu performs prostration, he should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, and join both hands to the feet of the senior monk (*sthavira*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* [states]: ...

It is said: There are three kinds of *vaṃdana* (homage): of body, speech, and mind. Regarding the body: whether the person before one is sitting or standing, one prostrates with the head at their feet;
this is called homage of the body. Regarding the speech: if the person is far away, one joins the palms, bows the head, and speaks these words.
*Vandana*. This is called verbal [reverence]. As for the mind: if one is turning away, one should join the palms in a gesture of respect;
this is called reverence of body, speech, and mind. If one sees a senior monk (*upādhyāya*) approaching and does not rise to greet him with *vandana* and reverence, it constitutes a *vinaya*-offense.
The above has clarified the ritual protocols for the monastic community to extend reverence; hereafter, the praise of the Sage shall be described.

Regarding the ritual for venerating virtue, Master Yijing stated: "In the land of China, it has been handed down from antiquity that people merely know how to prostrate before the Buddha and record their names;
for the most part, they do not extol or praise his virtues. Why is this? When one hears a name, one merely listens to it and fails to recognize the relative heights of their wisdom.
Praise, however, fully sets forth those virtues; thus, the name embodies the vastness and profundity of the virtues themselves. It is just as follows:"
One should pay homage at the stūpas of the West and perform the customary rites of veneration.
Every afternoon or at twilight, the assembly exits the hall and circumambulates the stūpa three times. Having prepared incense and flowers, everyone sits in a squatting posture (utkuṭaka).
Those capable of it should chant with a plaintive yet elegant voice, clear and resonant, praising the virtues of the Great Master—either ten verses or twenty.
Verse: They returned to the monastery in succession and arrived at the regular assembly hall. Once they were seated, they had a scripture master ascend the lion throne to recite a short sutra.
The lion throne was positioned at the head of the senior monk (upādhyāya), placed appropriately according to the space;
it was neither too high nor too large. As for the sutra to be recited, they mostly chanted the "Threefold Prostration" (Tri-khandaka), which was composed by the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa.
This is where they gather. At the beginning, one may recite approximately ten verses to praise the Triple Gem according to the intent of the sutras.

Next, one recites the main scripture, which was spoken directly by the Buddha. Once the chanting of praises is finished, one further presents about ten additional verses for dedication and the making of vows.
Because these three sections are opened up, it is called "Threefold Opening" (Sanki). When the sutra is concluded, the entire assembly says: "Subha."
*Śāstṛ* means "Teacher. *Sū* is "wonderful" (*sūkṣma*). *Vāstava* means "speech. This is intended as praise for the sutra, meaning it is "sublime speech.

Alternatively, it is called *svādu*, which means "excellent. When the Sutra Master is about to descend from the seat, the Elder rises first, pays homage to the Lion Throne, and completes his acts of reverence.
Next, he pays homage to the seat of the Noble Sangha and returns to his own place. The second Elder follows the same procedure.
Having first paid homage at the two locations, one next pays homage to the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) before taking one’s own seat.
The third *upādhyāya* and those following in succession do likewise, continuing until the end of the assembly.

If the assembly is large, exceeding three or five persons, the remainder all simultaneously rise to pay homage toward the assembly and then depart as they please. This method is that of the Eastern Holy Land, Dharmarājikā.
As for the monastic regulations and practices of the country of Ti (Tibet), they are similar to those at Nālandā Monastery. There, the population is vast and the monks number over five thousand;
it is difficult for them to assemble and disperse even in moments of leisure. The monastery consists of eight courtyards and three hundred rooms;

consequently, the monks must perform their liturgical recitations according to the season, each at their own location. However, according to the custom of this monastery, one capable leader is appointed to lead the chanting on every occasion.

At the hour of *pradoṣa* (the late afternoon), they performed circumambulation, prostrations, and hymns of praise. Attendants and novices, carrying various incenses and flowers, led the way as they passed through every courtyard and paid homage before every hall.
At each instance of prostration, they chanted praises aloud—three or five verses at a time—their resonance pervading everywhere.
Only when evening fell did they finally conclude; this chanting master was constantly receiving [these offerings].
In the monastic quarters, one may offer separate provisions for sustenance; or, facing the incense altar alone, one may sit singly and praise with the mind;

or, when visiting a Buddhist temple, one may kneel with the assembly and proclaim [the teachings] from on high. Thereafter, one spreads the ten fingers upon the ground and performs three prostrations with the head bowed.
This is the ritual of reverent homage inherited from the Western Regions, which those who are aged or infirm are permitted to practice.
Regarding the small seat: those who praise the Buddha have done so since ancient times; however, the practice has slightly diverged and is not identical to that of India.

For instance, when performing the ritual of paying homage to the Buddha, those who extol the Buddha’s physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa* and *vyañjana*) should raise their voices directly and offer a long chant of praise.
Or ten verses, or twenty verses—this is the method. Furthermore, the *Tathāgata-gāthās* and other such hymns were originally intended as praises of the Buddha;
however, because their prosody is somewhat lengthy, their meaning is difficult to manifest clearly.

Therefore, on occasions such as a vegetarian feast or a quiet night when the great assembly is moved with solemnity, one who is skilled should recite the *One Hundred and Fifty Praises*, the *Four Hundred Praises*, and other miscellaneous verses.

Praise! This is indeed excellent. (However, there are only two matters for which one may employ the style of chanting: first, praising the virtues of the Great Master; second, reciting the *Triśaraṇa-gāthā* [Three Refuges Sutra]. As for all other recitations of various sutras and dharmas, none of them should be performed in this manner.
Nevertheless, in the Western Regions, the practice of veneration is prevalent, and the custom of offering praise is widely transmitted.
Among those possessed of talent, there is none who does not extol the venerable ones they revere. For example, the Venerable Mātṛceṭa.
This person was one of great talent and profound virtue from the Western Regions, whose brilliance surpassed all the eminent men of his time (Mātṛ means "mother" and Citta means "son").
The Buddha had previously prophesied: "After my parinirvāṇa, Matriceta shall extensively praise and extol my true virtues.
That man had initially left the household life as a non-Buddhist ascetic, serving Maheśvara. Since that deity was his object of veneration, he had devotedly recited hymns in his honor.
Later, upon seeing the name recorded in the prophecy, he changed his mind and took refuge in the Buddha; he donned the dyed robes and renounced the world.

He extensively composed hymns of praise, first creating four hundred verses and subsequently one hundred and fifty verses, collectively expounding upon the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) to clarify all the sublime virtues of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
These may be described as having a literary style so elegant and beautiful that they share their fragrance with celestial flowers;
their principles so pure and lofty that they vie in height with the earth’s mountains. Among those who compose hymns in the West, [he stands preeminent].
There are none who do not unanimously follow this ancestral tradition. Both the Bodhisattvas Asaṅga and Vasubandhu looked up to its principles;

thus, in the land of the Five Indias, even those who have first left the household life must, once they have mastered the recitation of the five precepts and the ten precepts, be taught first to recite these two hymns.
Whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, all alike observe this. There are six reasons for this: first, it is able to...
First, one comes to know the profound depth of the Buddha’s virtues; second, one understands the structure and sequence of the texts;

third, the faculty of the tongue is purified; fourth, the chest and inner organs are opened and unobstructed; fifth, one is not intimidated when among the assembly; and sixth, one attains longevity and freedom from illness.
Only after one has mastered this [text] should one study other sūtras. Furthermore, the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa also composed lyrics and the *Śrīkārikā-śāstra*, as well as the *Buddhacarita-kāvya*.
If translated into Chinese, the original version consists of more than ten fascicles.

Its purport recounts the Tathāgata’s life from his departure from the royal palace until his passing between the twin śāla trees; the entirety of the Buddha’s teachings throughout his lifetime is compiled here into verse. In the Five Indias...
Throughout the South Seas, there are none who do not recite [this work]. Its meaning is clear while its characters are few, yet it encompasses a vast range of significance.
Furthermore, it causes the reciter’s mind to rejoice and forget weariness; moreover, it preserves the holy teachings and is able to generate merit and benefit (and so forth).

The one hundred and fifty verses of praise, along with other hymns and recitations, are fully contained within the Tripitaka and have been carved for circulation; they are not set forth here at length.

Those who take pleasure in this should investigate and practice it themselves. For now, I have briefly recorded from various sūtras and śāstras a number of verses and hymns of praise to facilitate beginners in extending their reverent salutations and understanding the ritual for extolling virtues. First are the incense praises; next, one may chant according to one’s inclination.
As a verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says (one should maintain a dignified and orderly demeanor, holding an incense burner in hand, and recite):
The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, and the fragrance of liberation— Cloud-palaces of radiant light pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
Making offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, All who see or hear are universally perfumed and realize quiescence.
(Furthermore, the verse for scattering flowers says:)
Scattering flowers to adorn the pure radiance, Adorning with exquisite blossoms as a canopy,
Scattering various flowers throughout the ten directions, I offer them to all the Tathāgatas.
(Alternatively, it is also excellent to recite a standard hymn of praise for incense and flowers.)
Hymn in Praise of the Triple Gem (compiled from one hundred verses of gāthās by the Sages and Saints):
I prostrate to all those who have transcended the world, The most honored in the three realms, oceans of merit.
The Wise One can burn away the defilements of affliction; I now take refuge in and pay homage to the Perfectly Awakened One.

I bow my head in reverence to the one who can pull us from the perils of birth and death, Who dries up the ocean of sorrow, distress, greed, and delusion, And shatters the mountain of worldly toil and sinful karma.
I now take refuge in and pay homage to the Jewel of the Sublime Dharma.
I prostrate to all Buddhas who are praised; To those adorned by the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path,
Whose unconditioned meditative concentration gradually becomes perfectly clear— I now take refuge and pay homage to this jewel-like Sangha,
Praising them all with universal reverence.
(The author of the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra* praises the Buddha in verse:
I pay homage to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, Boundless as space, with immovable wisdom,
the World-Saviors, Great Compassionate Honored Ones.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Ratnagotravibhāga* says:
I now take refuge in all the Unsurpassed Honored Ones, Who, for the sake of opening the treasury of the Dharma King and extensively benefiting all sentient beings,
Reveal that the Buddha-nature has no prior limit And no intermediate limit.
Furthermore, there is no subsequent limit; it is known through self-awakening in its tranquility.

Having awakened to this oneself, one awakens others and causes them to awaken. Therefore, for their sake, [the Buddha] teaches the fearless, eternal path through the power of Buddha-wisdom and compassion.
Capable of grasping the vajra pillar, he shatters the mountains of all views.

Therefore, I now pay homage to the inconceivable Dharma— Beyond the realm of wisdom derived from hearing, transcending the path of speech, The inner wisdom that is cool and serene. That truly wondrous Dharma-sun is pure and free from dust;
With the radiance of great wisdom, it shines universally upon all worlds.
Because you can shatter all obscurations— Discursive thought, greed, hatred, delusion, And all afflictions—I now pay homage to you.
Because you know that very nature, The intrinsically pure mind, and see that afflictions lack reality, You are free from all afflictions; Unobstructed and pure is your wisdom.
Seeing the self-nature of the pure mind of sentient beings as it truly is,
with the eye of unimpeded pure wisdom regarding the realm of the Buddha’s Dharma-body, you see the nature of all sentient beings pervading immeasurable realms;
therefore, I now pay homage to you.
(Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* contains a verse in praise of the Buddha, which says:
I pay homage to all Buddhas, The peerless Tamer of Men; I also pay homage to the true Dharma-body of sixteen feet, And to the Buddha’s stūpas:
The place of birth, the place of attaining the Way, The place of turning the Wheel of Dharma, and the place of Nirvāṇa.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one bows to all [the Buddhas] in every place.
The inconceivable, wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise so; both the ability to believe in it and its karmic fruit are likewise inconceivable.
One who uses these gāthās to praise the Tathāgata, for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas—
Not falling into the various evil destinies (*geya*; this is a verse).
Praising the Honored One Śākyamuni (*Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: Kāśyapa, the bodhisattva praised the Buddha with a verse, saying):

To the Great King of Physicians who has compassion for the world, Whose body and wisdom are both tranquil and selfless, yet within the dharma of no-self there is a true self— I pay homage to this Unsurpassed Honored One.
The initial resolve and the ultimate fulfillment are not two; Of these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
"Before having crossed over oneself, one first delivers others; therefore, I pay homage to those who have first resolved their minds.
(From the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Puṣpakūṭa praises the Buddha and the Dharma in verse.)
The World-Honored One’s physical body is like a mountain of gold;
Like the light of the sun, it illuminates the world, Able to uproot all manner of suffering and affliction. I now prostrate to the Great Dharma King.
The Lord of the World, the Dharma King, is most rare; Such a wondrous Dharma surpasses even this.
Difficult to see, difficult to hear, and difficult to encounter—those who behold it shall attain perfect enlightenment.
(From the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, where Śrīmālā praises and pays homage with these verses:)
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body is peerless in the world;
Incomparable and inconceivable, I now pay homage to him. The body of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so;
All phenomena are eternally abiding—therefore I take refuge in him, Having subdued the faults and evils of the mind.
And with the four kinds of bodies, you have reached the stage that is difficult to subdue;
therefore, I pay homage to the Dharma King who knows all *jñeyas*. You possess mastery over the body of wisdom and uphold all dharmas;
therefore, I now pay respectful homage. Homage to you who transcend all measure; homage to you who are beyond all analogy.
Homage to the boundless Dharma! Homage to the inconceivable!
May you take pity on me and protect me, so that the seeds of the Dharma may increase in this life and in future births. May the Buddha always hold me in his compassionate care.

(The verse "In heaven and on earth there is none like the Buddha," the verses beginning with "The Buddha’s face is like the pure full moon," and other praises may be recited as desired; they are well known and need not be set forth here in detail.)
Hymn in Praise of the Three Bodies (The Hymn in Praise of the Buddha’s Three Bodies; the verse praising the Dharmakāya reads):
I now prostrate to the Buddha of the Dharmakāya, Whose universal wisdom is beyond analogy and inconceivable.
Pervading the dharma-realm without obstruction, Profoundly tranquil and peerless,
A reality that is neither existent nor non-existent, Neither many nor few, transcending all measure,
Equal and signless like space— The benefit to self and others is likewise so.
(The Verse on the Reward Body states:
I now prostrate to the Buddha of the Reward Body, The Great Muni who dwells in profound serenity;
Out of compassion, he transforms and delivers the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Sitting within the gathering like the sun that shines everywhere.
Having accumulated all merits over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, He is finally able to perfect the path of tranquility;
With a great voice he proclaims the sublime Dharma, Universally causing all to attain the fruit of equality.
(The verse of the *nirmāṇakāya* says:)
I now prostrate my head before the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha, Who attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree;
Whether manifesting transformations or abiding in stillness, Or proceeding to transform beings throughout the ten directions,
Or turning the wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park, Or appearing as a great radiance like a mass of fire.
The retributions of suffering in the three miserable realms can all be eliminated; The peerless Great Muni of the triple world (as the dedication verse says):
"Such a Buddha-body and its untainted wisdom— I shall always believe and understand, purifying my three karmas."
With immeasurable wisdom and great meritorious conduct, With a single mind, you show compassion for all living beings.
By means of this verse of praise to the Buddha of the Three Bodies, May the seeds of merit thus obtained, which are free from outflows,
Cause me to swiftly realize the Bodhi of the Buddhas, And lead all sentient beings to return to the Right Path.

If one were to pay homage to and praise the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and so forth, it would be explained extensively in the sūtras and śāstras; these details are not recorded here at length to avoid prolixity.
As for the term *jñeya*, this is translated as "the knowable," also as "that which should be known," and furthermore as "the objective sphere" (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the "Holy Land of the East," this refers to Eastern India. As for what is called the "Fragrant Terrace" (*gandhakūṭī*), it is also referred to as the "Fragrant Hall. (From the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu*).
The commentary states: In the Western Regions, the hall where the Buddha resides is called *gandhakūṭī*. *Gandha* means "fragrance" and *kūṭī* means "hall";
thus, it signifies the meaning of a fragrant chamber, a fragrant terrace, or a fragrant palace. One must not touch the venerable countenance directly.
Therefore, one simply calls it by the name of the hall where [the Buddha] resides, just as in this land one refers to the King as "His Majesty" (Chengxia).
To call it a "Buddha Hall" (Fotang) or a "Buddha Temple" (Fodian), however, does not accord with the meaning of the Western [tradition].
Explanations of Terms and Meanings in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume 39. Phonetic Transcription: Gǒuhè (溝壑).
The upper character (溝) is pronounced gōu; it refers to a water channel. The lower character (壑) is pronounced hào; it refers to a valley, a pit, or a great abyss.
It is "hai" (海).
The pronunciation of "bō" (雹) is *bak*.
This is a variant of the ancient text and a different character.
*Níng* (pronounced *néng*): weak; distressed.
*Jiàn* (pronounced *jiàn*): strong; possessing strength without weariness.
*Cù* (pronounced *jù*): fearful; ashamed.
*Ñok-nuò*: two pronunciations; to press down. *Chuǎn*:
pronunciation *shàn*; the calf of the leg.
*Pū*: pronunciation *bū*; the hour of *śun*.
*Qīyīn* (悽音): the sound *qī*; it means grief and sorrow.
*Wěiyīn* (蘤音): the sound *wěi*; it means the flourishing of plants.

In the Kalinga country, within the Śīra forest,
Pāmanaka and Kambila caused the True Dharma to perish rapidly;
knowing this, the Arhat Bhadraśreṇya [departed].
The six offenses arising from the *akṣara* (evil syllables), the six fundamental roots,
the weeds, the tares, the chaff, and the husks— everywhere one strikes,
one encounters resistance, stumbling, and falling.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Guangzhou at Jiqiu.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongli of Xin’an. Lóufēng (羅峰).
Kāliṅga is the name of a country within the region of South India; it is also written as Jīlíngjiā (羯飢-几+夌伽) or Kālíngjiā (迦陵伽).
Master Yuan states that translated according to its meaning, it is called the "Age of Conflict over Names and Characteristics" (*nāmalakṣaṇa-kalaha-yuga*).

This name was established based on the fact that the country was founded during a period of conflict. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "The kingdom of Kāñcī has a circumference of more than five thousand *li*.
Its capital city is more than twenty *li* in circuit. Crops are sown at the proper seasons, flowers and fruits flourish in abundance, and forests and marshes stretch out in continuous succession."
It extends for several hundred *li*. It produces wild blue elephants, which are prized by neighboring countries. The climate is hot, and the customs are impetuous and violent.
By nature, the people are mostly fierce and unruly, yet they place great store in good faith and honor. Their speech is light and quick, and their tones are pure and correct;
their style and principles differ considerably from those of Central India. In former times, the population and customs of this country were very prosperous.

Shoulders brushed against one another and chariots collided; when they raised their sleeves, they formed a curtain. There were seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) who dwelt upon the crags to cultivate their essential nature.

If anyone should offend or provoke them, they would lose their supernatural powers and, employing malevolent incantations and arts, bring ruin and slaughter upon the people of the land, leaving none spared among the young or old, and causing both the wise and the foolish to perish.
Human habitation was cut off for many years. Although people have gradually migrated back there, it is still not yet fully populated. Therefore—

At present, the population of this country is still small. Not far to the south of the city is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, beside which are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

On a ridge of the great mountain at the northern frontier of the kingdom’s borders stands a stone stūpa over one hundred feet high; it dates from the beginning of the kalpa, when the lifespan of humans was immeasurable.

In this year, a Pratyekabuddha attained parinirvāṇa here. From this point, traveling northwest through mountains and forests for more than one thousand eight hundred li, one arrives at Kauśala in Central India.
The Jīraka forest and the Jīraka [incident], as explained above in the ninety matters and in the Bhaiṣajyavastu (Section on Medicines). Pāmanā.
This elder is also among the ranks of the senior monks (sthavira), though the circumstances of his [attainment] have not yet been fully detailed.
"Kimbhīra" translates here as "Majestic Like a King. This elder was originally the king of the kingdom of Suvarṇabhūmi; by nature he was intelligent and great.
He was powerful and valiant, ruling over thirty-six thousand kingdoms and cities. His military forces were vast and formidable; none could oppose him.

His majestic influence resounded afar, and all were subdued by it. He dispatched an envoy bearing a letter to the kingdom of Śrāvastī, desiring that King Prasenajit should suddenly submit and present tribute.
The Buddha immediately transformed himself into a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin) and received the letter. He then instructed the envoy to return home.
They arrived at the appointed time to present their tribute. When the envoy returned and reported this in detail to his king, the king heard it and reproached himself deeply.

He led the various minor kings and proceeded to pay court to the Transformation King (Nirmāṇarāja). At that time, the Transformation King manifested various rare and miraculous spiritual transformations and preached the Dharma.

Furthermore, if one does not form the thought, "I shall wait for a pure person of like mind and then act according to the Dharma," yet remains silent, one incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense. Alternatively, there may be circumstances where no offense is incurred (meaning that by not acting, one does not commit a transgression).

Or, there may be circumstances where an offense is heavy but becomes light (meaning that when a bhikṣu who has committed a *pāyattika* offense approaches one with evil and heterodox views, or when one who has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya*) repents).

Or, there may be circumstances where an offense is light but becomes heavy (meaning that when a bhikṣu who has committed a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense approaches one who slanders the Sūtras, or when one who has been subject to formal censure repents, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense).

There are also offenses with heavy conditions, even very heavy ones (referring to a bhikṣu who commits a pāyattika offense and then confesses toward one who has been formally charged for slandering the sūtras; he incurs a pāyattika. This is such a case).

There are offenses that are light by nature (referring to a bhikṣu who commits a *vinayātikrama* offense and confesses it before one who has not received full ordination; this is not considered a formal act [of confession], and he incurs another *vinayātikrama* offense).

There are offenses incurred at the time of receiving (referring to accepting raw meat, raw grain, gold or silver, elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, oxen, sheep, male or female slaves, women, fields, houses, or dwellings).

There are offenses incurred at the time of eating (referring to eating separately from the community, eating at various places, eating from the same vessel, or eating impure fruit). There are offenses incurred through the completion of an action (referring to the construction of a small hut...).

The "large dwelling" (mahā-śālā) refers to all cases where one has been formally admonished three times. In some instances, not accepting [the robe] constitutes an offense, whereas accepting it entails no offense (referring to the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe, by which one obtains the five privileges).

There are cases where there is no offense for giving, but there is an offense for not giving (this refers to when a bhikṣu obtains new cloth and does not apply one of the three types of discoloration; if he uses it after performing the *paryodāna* [purification] with only one type of color, it is a *pāyattika*).

There are cases where there is an offense in a village, but not in an *arañña* (this refers to entering a village without wearing the *saṃghāṭī*, entering a village without fastening the buttons, entering a village without wearing a waist-belt, entering a village without carrying an alms-bowl, leaving the community without informing others, or entering a village at an improper time). There are cases where there is an offense in an *arañña*, but not in a village.

"Fall" (meaning: when a bhikṣu travels on a road with bandits, or with women, or with bhikṣuṇīs; this is it). There are offenses that occur both in the forest (*āraṇya*) and in the village (*grāma*) (meaning: striking with the fist, or brandishing a hand or a blade; this is it).

There are offenses that occur neither in the forest nor in the village (meaning: entering the royal gate; this is it). There are offenses that occur at the proper time (*kāla*), not at the improper time (*akāla*) (meaning:

eating apart from the community, eating here and there, eating from the same vessel, or eating fruit that has not been purified; these are it). There are offenses that occur at... [the text ends]... the proper time.
"Improper time" (*akāla*). This is not the proper time (meaning: entering a village without prior announcement at an improper time; eating at an improper time; instructing bhikṣuṇīs after sunset).

There are offenses that are both at the proper time and at an improper time (meaning: striking with the fist; brandishing the palm as a blade). There are offenses that are neither at the proper time nor at an improper time (meaning: during the midday meal period).

There are offenses that exist at night but not during the day (namely: staying in the same room as a woman; staying more than three nights with one who has not received full ordination; and instructing bhikṣuṇīs after sunset).

There are offenses that occur during the day but not at night (namely, eating in a group apart from the community, up to and including eating impure fruit; these are such cases). There are also offenses that occur both during the day and at night.

Furthermore, there are offenses committed at night (such as striking with a fist or brandishing a blade with the palm); there are offenses committed neither by day nor by night (such as when the dawn light appears);

and there are offenses committed in a concealed place rather than an exposed one (such as sleeping in the same room as a woman, staying more than three nights with one who has not received full ordination, sitting on a prepared seat within [a dwelling], or sitting in a secluded spot).

There are offenses that occur in an open space, not in a covered place (this refers to cases where one spreads bedding for oneself or instructs another to spread it on the ground in a public area, and then departs without informing others;

if one leaves within twenty-five cubits, it is a *pāyattika* offense). There are offenses that occur both in a covered place and in an open space (this refers to striking with the fist or brandishing the palm as if wielding a blade).

There are offenses that occur neither in a covered place nor in an open space (this refers to being under the eaves of a roof). There are offenses that occur while walking, not while standing (this refers to a bhikṣu [with a woman]).

[There are offenses] involving traveling with a bandit companion; [there are offenses] involving a bhikṣuṇī, where she makes an appointment to travel together on a road. If the Saṃgha and the two teachers tell her not to go and she nevertheless goes, she incurs an offense.

(This refers to cases where there is an offense for going, but not for staying—namely, staying near a prostitute, near a liquor seller, near gamblers, or near prisoners; or standing at a doorway. If the Saṃgha and the two teachers tell her not to stay and she nevertheless stays, she incurs an offense.

This refers to cases where there is an offense for staying. [There are offenses] that involve both going and staying (namely, striking with the fist or brandishing a knife with the palm). [There are offenses] that involve neither going nor staying (namely, when sitting or when sleeping). [There are offenses] that involve [only] staying.

There are offenses incurred while standing, not while sitting (referring to standing near a prostitute, up to and including when the two teachers say "do not stand" and one nevertheless stands; in such cases, one incurs an offense).

There are offenses incurred while sitting, not while standing (referring to sitting on an oversized bed, on a mattress stuffed with *tūla* cotton, on a leather seat, or sitting near a prostitute, at a tavern, at a gambling table, or beside a prisoner; or when the Sangha or the two teachers say "do not sit" and one nevertheless sits; in such cases, one incurs an offense).

There are offenses incurred both while standing and while sitting (referring to striking with the fist or brandishing a palm-weapon). There are offenses incurred neither while standing nor while sitting.

(This refers to cases such as walking or sleeping). There are offenses that consist of sitting, but not sleeping (referring to sitting on an oversized bed, or even sitting when told by the Saṃgha or two teachers not to sit; one commits an offense in so doing).

There are offenses that consist of sleeping, but not walking (referring to staying in the same room as a woman, staying more than three nights with one who has not received full ordination, sitting on an oversized bed, using a mattress stuffed with *tūla* cotton, or using a seat made of leather).

There are offenses that consist of both sitting and sleeping (referring to striking with the fist or brandishing a hand or blade). There are offenses that are neither... [text ends]... sitting nor sleeping.

Sitting is not sleeping (referring to when one is walking or standing). There may be offenses that are sleeping but not walking (referring to staying overnight in the same room as a woman, up to sleeping on a leather mat).

There may be an offense that is due to action, not due to sleep (referring to a bhikṣu who, having been accompanied by women as thieves, even after his two teachers told him not to go, nevertheless goes; in such cases, he incurs an offense).

There may be an offense that is both due to sleep and due to action (referring to striking with the fist or brandishing a palm-sword). There may be an offense that is neither due to sleep nor due to action (referring to the time when one is sitting or standing).

There may be an offense that occurs in a secluded place, not in a public assembly (referring to when one does not desist after being admonished three times in a secluded place). There may be an offense that occurs in a public assembly, not in a secluded place...

"In private" (meaning among a large group of people; this applies when one does not relinquish [the offense] after three admonitions). There are also offenses that are both "in private" and "among a large group" (meaning striking with the fist or brandishing a hand or a blade).
There may be an offense that is not in private and not in a large group (meaning it occurs among the Saṃgha).

There may be an offense that is in a large group but not in the Saṃgha (meaning it occurs among a large number of people, such as when one does not relinquish [the offense] after three admonitions). There may be an offense that is in the Saṃgha but not in a large group (meaning when one does not relinquish [the offense] after three admonitions within the Saṃgha).

There may be an offense that is both in a large group and in the Saṃgha (meaning striking with the fist or brandishing a palm or blade). There may be an offense that is neither in a large group nor in the Saṃgha.

There are offenses that are not in the midst of the Saṃgha (meaning: those where one does not relinquish [the offense] after three admonitions in private). There may be offenses that are in the midst of the Saṃgha, but not in private (meaning:

those where one does not relinquish [the offense] after three admonitions in the midst of the Saṃgha). There may be offenses that are in private, but not in the midst of the Saṃgha (meaning: those where one does not relinquish [the offense] after three admonitions in private).

There may be offenses that are both in the midst of the Saṃgha and in private (meaning: such as striking with a fist or brandishing a hand or a blade). There may be offenses that are neither in the midst of the Saṃgha nor in private (meaning: such as [committing them] among a large group of people). Three...

If one does not desist after being admonished, this constitutes an offense. There are offenses that occur in winter but not in spring (referring to a bhikṣu who, having reached the fifteenth day of the eighth month, does not relinquish his *varṣāśāṭī* robe;

if he relinquishes it on the sixteenth day, he incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense). There are offenses that occur in spring but not in winter (referring to a bhikṣu who has received the *kaṭhina* robe and should relinquish it by the fifteenth day of the twelfth month;

if he does not relinquish it until the sixteenth day, he incurs a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense). There are offenses that occur both in winter and in spring (referring to striking with the fist or brandishing the palm as a weapon). There are offenses that do not occur in winter [but occur in spring].

It is not spring (referring to the period of the *varṣā* retreat). Or, there may be an offense that occurs in spring but not in summer (referring to a bhikṣu who has accepted the *kāṭhina* robe and does not relinquish it until the sixteenth day of the twelfth month).

An offense of *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline). Or there is an offense that pertains to the summer retreat (*varṣā*) but not to the spring: namely, when a bhikṣu reaches the sixteenth day of the fourth month and should enter the retreat (*anupravrāj*), yet fails to do so, he commits an offense of *vinayātikrama*.

If one arrives for the later retreat (*paścimā varṣopagamana*) but does not enter the retreat, one incurs two offenses of *vinayātikrama*. There are offenses that pertain to both spring and summer (namely, striking with the fist or threatening with the palm as a blade).

There are offenses that pertain neither to spring nor summer (namely, during the winter season). There are offenses that pertain to summer but not winter (namely, failing to enter the retreat during either of the two retreats, thereby incurring two offenses of *vinayātikrama*).
There are offenses that pertain to winter but not summer (namely, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, when one ought to relinquish the rain-bathing robe, yet...).
[If one] does not relinquish [the offense], by the sixteenth day, one incurs guilt). Some offenses occur in both summer and winter (referring to striking with a fist or brandishing a palm or blade);
some offenses occur neither in summer nor in winter (referring to the spring season).

pronounced *bǐ*. The *Shuowen* states: "Unformed grain. This refers to the passage in the *Shangshu*:

*Zà xián zà*.

first, those burned by fire; second, those chewed by oxen; third, those gnawed by rats; fourth, those [soiled] by a bride on her first wedding day; and fifth, [those soiled by] impurity.

first, the cemetery robe; second, the traveling robe; third, the ownerless robe; and fourth, the tattered rag robe. These four types should be kept.
